HaltSQL is a policy firewall for LLM-generated PostgreSQL. It checks whether an exact SQL string is allowed for a caller under a declarative policy, and returns a verdict with machine-readable reasons. It never rewrites SQL and never connects to the database. These docs describe version 0.0.1 (pre-1.0). The verdict format and reason codes are stable; other interfaces may still change. See Versioning and upgrades.

documents.s: ADR-0007: Deny-only external policy (OPA) and an opt-in admin API

documents.t: Enterprises want two things the 0.1 sidecar does not offer: Organisation-specific rules that live outside HaltSQL policies, often already written in Rego for Open Policy Agent (OPA): time windows, ticket requirements, per-team data classifications. Operational visibility: which policy bundle version a running server serves, whether its sources and audit sinks are healthy, and what a policy in shadow mode would have denied. Both affect stable contracts: the reason-code list (ADR-0004), the verdict JSON and the HTTP API. Both also add new ways for an allow to be produced or information to leak, so they must fail closed.

External policy (OPA). OPA is consulted only after HaltSQL has allowed a statement (and, in shadow mode, to report what it would have denied). It is never consulted instead of HaltSQL. OPA can only turn an allow into a deny, never a deny into an allow. There is no configuration that changes this. An OPA denial uses a new stable reason code, E_EXTERNAL_POLICY, with rule opa.decision. Under ADR-0004 the code is never renamed or reused. OPA-supplied reasons are capped (16 reasons, 200 bytes each) and stripped of control characters. A denied verdict carries no bind_params, the same as every other denial. Any OPA error (undefined decision, malformed result, non-200 status, TLS or connection failure, timeout, response over 1 MiB) goes through on_error. The default is deny; allow_haltsql_verdict exists only for advisory rules and must be set explicitly. Admin API. GET /v1/admin/status (served generation, bundle versions, source and sink health, pending audit restarts) and GET /v1/admin/report (the rolling shadow/enforce report and suggestions). Off by default. With server.admin disabled, both return 404. When enabled, callers must authenticate (401) and be listed in server.admin.callers as token:<name>, oidc:<provider> or mtls:<identity> (403 otherwise). Anonymous callers never match. Responses never contain secrets or tokens. Reports identify statements by SQL hash and fingerprint; raw SQL appears only when audit.log_raw_sql is explicitly enabled.

Let OPA decide on its own, or override HaltSQL denials. This would make tenancy and column rules bypassable by a misconfigured Rego policy. HaltSQL's parser-based checks are the security boundary, so OPA can only narrow them. Reuse an existing code (for example E_FUNCTION_DENIED or E_INTERNAL) for OPA denials. That would make an external denial impossible to tell apart from a HaltSQL denial in audit records and agent hints, and would change an existing code's meaning, which ADR-0004 forbids. Fail open on OPA errors by default. Rejected: an unreachable OPA would silently disable every external rule. Expose status and reports on the public /v1/verify listener without a caller list. Rejected: bundle versions, sink endpoints and denial patterns help an attacker. The API is opt-in and authorised per caller.

Clients that already treat unknown reason codes as denials (required by ADR-0004) handle E_EXTERNAL_POLICY with no change. Each allowed request costs one extra HTTP round trip to OPA when it is configured; timeout_ms bounds it, and a timeout denies by default. The admin API is a new authenticated surface to keep stable within /v1: fields may be added, never renamed or removed.

Tests against a real OPA container cover allow, deny, every on_error mode, OPA down and "OPA cannot allow a HaltSQL deny" (test/opa, test/e2e/test_opa.py). Admin API authorisation is covered in test/server, test/wiring and the E2E suite.
Status: Superseded by ADR-0006 Date: 2026-11-07 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Related: PLAN.md §4; LICENSE; NOTICE

HaltSQL is security infrastructure intended for use inside companies. Its adopters' legal teams look for a well-known, permissive license with clear patent terms. HaltSQL also builds on third-party work: libpg_query (BSD-3-Clause) and the Postgres sources it contains (PostgreSQL License), vendored in vendor/libpg_query; the policy design of the sql-guardrail project (MIT), whose design (not code) inspired HaltSQL, and whose test cases may be adapted for conformance tests; OCaml libraries under permissive licenses.

License HaltSQL under the Apache License 2.0. Keep a NOTICE file crediting libpg_query, PostgreSQL, and sql-guardrail. Ship third-party license texts with source and binary releases (vendor/libpg_query/LICENSE is included in release archives) and publish a CycloneDX SBOM per release. Any test cases adapted from sql-guardrail keep their MIT attribution in the files that contain them. Contributions are accepted under the Developer Certificate of Origin (git commit -s), not a CLA.

MIT. Simple and compatible, but no explicit patent grant. AGPL / BSL / other source-available licenses. Would discourage adoption as an embedded security control. An open-core model for future components (for example a proxy or policy UI) remains an open question and would need its own ADR; it does not change the license of what is released here. CLA instead of DCO. More friction for contributors; DCO is sufficient for an Apache-2.0 project of this size.

Users get a patent grant and a familiar license. All dependencies must be compatible with Apache-2.0 distribution; the security workflow's dependency review denies strong copyleft licenses. Release archives must include LICENSE, NOTICE, and the libpg_query license.
Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-08 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Supersedes: ADR-0005 Related: LICENSE; NOTICE
ADR-0005 chose Apache-2.0. The maintainer prefers the MIT License: it is short, widely understood, and the same license as sql-guardrail, whose design inspired HaltSQL.

License HaltSQL under the MIT License, copyright Arnav Dadarya. Every package carries the same license identifier (MIT): the opam packages, the Python, MCP, TypeScript, Go and Java clients, the container image label and the OpenAPI document. Keep NOTICE for third-party attributions (libpg_query, PostgreSQL, sql-guardrail).

MIT has no explicit patent grant, unlike Apache-2.0. Adopters who need one should know this. Vendored libpg_query (BSD-3-Clause) and PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL License) sources keep their own licenses. Both are compatible with MIT distribution, and their license texts still ship in every release. Test cases adapted from sql-guardrail are MIT, the same as the rest of the project, and are still attributed in the files that contain them.

documents.s: ADR-0001: Parse SQL with a vendored libpg_query and our own thin C binding

documents.t: HaltSQL decides whether a SQL string is safe to run on PostgreSQL. If HaltSQL parses a string differently from the server, an attacker can write SQL that looks harmless to HaltSQL and does something else in Postgres (a parser differential). The parser is therefore the foundation of every guarantee. Options for parsing Postgres SQL from OCaml: A hand-written or generated grammar in OCaml (Menhir). A general-purpose multi-dialect SQL parser. libpg_query, which extracts the actual Postgres parser (gram.y, scanner, and supporting code) into a C library, through the opam pg_query bindings. libpg_query, vendored, through our own thin C stubs. Facts we found while prototyping: The opam pg_query bindings bundle an old libpg_query (Postgres 13 grammar) that fails to compile on current macOS toolchains, and depend on ctypes and libffi. libpg_query 17-6.2.5 tracks the Postgres 17.7 grammar and builds cleanly with a C compiler and make. libpg_query keeps parser state in thread-local memory, so the OCaml runtime lock can be released during a parse.

Vendor libpg_query 17-6.2.5 (Postgres 17.7 grammar) in vendor/libpg_query, with its LICENSE (BSD-3-Clause for libpg_query; the PostgreSQL License for the extracted Postgres sources). Test data, examples, and temporary directories are removed. Bind it with our own C stubs in lib/pgquery (pgquery_stubs.c, pgquery_raw.mli), exposing only what HaltSQL needs: parse to JSON, fingerprint, and the Postgres version. The stubs release the OCaml runtime lock while parsing, so verification scales across OCaml 5 domains and server threads. The stubs reject input containing a NUL byte before calling C. A C string would stop at the NUL, so text after it would be invisible to the parser but might still reach the server through a driver that sends the full buffer. The JSON parse tree is converted into HaltSQL's typed AST (ADR-0002). No ctypes/libffi dependency. Upgrading libpg_query: replace vendor/libpg_query with a new release tarball, delete its test/, testdata/, tmp/, and examples/ directories, update NOTICE if needed, and run the full test suite and attack corpus. A new Postgres major requires a new ADR and a changelog entry.

Own grammar in OCaml. Postgres's grammar is large and changes every release. Any divergence is a potential bypass. Rejected. Multi-dialect SQL parser. Approximates Postgres rather than being Postgres; same differential risk. Rejected. opam pg_query bindings. Old grammar, build failures on current macOS, extra libffi/ctypes dependency, and no control over the runtime lock or NUL handling. Rejected for now; we can revisit if they track current libpg_query. libpg_query protobuf output instead of JSON. Typed and faster, but adds a protobuf decoder to the trusted computing base. JSON is simpler to audit. We may switch later if parsing cost matters; the AST conversion isolates the choice.

HaltSQL parses with the real Postgres 17 grammar. Running against older servers is checked in the lab rather than guaranteed (see the threat model). We own a few hundred lines of C, which must be fuzzed and reviewed with the same care as the analyzer. Building from source needs a C compiler and make, which are present on standard CI runners and in the Alpine builder. Static Linux binaries are straightforward (musl, no shared libffi). libpg_query upgrades are deliberate events with full corpus runs.
Fuzz the C stubs and the JSON-to-AST converter. Track libpg_query releases and security fixes.
Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-07 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Related: PLAN.md §6.3; docs/tenancy.md
documents.s: ADR-0003: Tenant isolation by per-occurrence, per-scope conjunct proof

documents.t: The most valuable asset in a multi-tenant application is other tenants' rows. An LLM agent under prompt injection will try to read them. Common bypass shapes are well known: OR 1=1, a filter only in an outer query, a UNION branch without a filter, a LEFT JOIN whose ON clause does not restrict the preserved side, and a wrong tenant literal. We need rules that are (a) sound, so that every allowed query is restricted to the tenant, (b) simple enough to audit and explain to an agent, and (c) checkable without a database.

Every occurrence of a tenant-scoped relation, in every scope (CTE bodies, subqueries, LATERAL, EXISTS/IN subqueries, scalar subqueries, each set-operation branch), must have a tenant predicate for each of its tenant columns. A tenant predicate is a top-level conjunct (part of the AND chain) of the scope's WHERE, or of a join ON clause that filters the occurrence: an inner join's ON covers both operands; an outer join's ON covers only its nullable side; FULL JOIN ON, USING, HAVING, and other scopes cover nothing. OR, NOT, and CASE break the proof. Accepted shapes are deliberately narrow: a.col = $n (bound mode), a.col = <literal> (literal mode), and for sets of tenant values a.col = ANY($n) (bound) or a.col IN (<literals>) (literal). Bound mode is the default and recommended. HaltSQL returns bind_params with the context value for each tenant parameter, and the caller must bind them. Every $n in the query must be a tenant parameter. The model never sees the tenant ID. Literal mode requires exact equality with the context value (no trimming or case folding), type-checked against the catalog when known. Composite keys: each tenant column maps to a named tenancy key; each needs its own predicate. Sets of tenant values (context value is a list) allow hierarchical tenancy without weakening the proof. Equality propagation within one scope only. An occurrence may be proven by a top-level a.tenant_col = b.tenant_col conjunct in one of its own locations when b is proven in the same SELECT and both columns carry the same tenancy key (added after 0.0.2; originally every occurrence needed a direct predicate). It does not cross subquery boundaries.

Accept a tenant predicate anywhere in the query. Unsound: an outer filter does not restrict what an inner aggregate reads. Rejected. Rewrite queries to inject tenant predicates. Changes the SQL the caller runs, hides problems from the agent, and requires a deparser in the trusted path. Out of scope for verify mode (it may appear in the proxy later). Rely on Postgres RLS only. RLS is strongly recommended as a second layer, but it gives the agent no actionable feedback and is easy to misconfigure. HaltSQL complements it. Full logical implication (SMT) over predicates. More permissive, much harder to audit and explain. Rejected for 0.x.

Some safe queries are denied (for example a tenant equality that reaches into a correlated subquery). Agents get a precise hint and can add the direct predicate. The rules are short enough to document completely and test exhaustively. The enterprise lab uses Postgres RLS as an independent oracle: any allowed query that returns a row RLS would hide is an escape and a release blocker. The semantics in docs/tenancy.md are normative; changes require a new ADR.

Attack-corpus cases for each rule and each bypass shape. Property tests applying evasion transforms to allowed queries. Equality propagation within one scope is done (decision 8); propagation into correlated subqueries and USING joins is still open.
Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-07 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Related: PLAN.md §4, §6.1; ADR-0001
documents.s: ADR-0002: Convert to a typed AST and fail closed on anything unmapped

documents.t: libpg_query produces a parse tree with roughly 250 node types. A rule engine that walks that raw tree generically (for example, "find all RangeVar nodes") is easy to write but easy to fool: a node type the author did not think about can carry a table reference, a function call, or a subquery that the rules never inspect. Every such gap is a potential bypass, and new Postgres releases add node types.

HaltSQL converts the parse tree into its own typed AST (lib/core/ast.ml) that covers exactly the subset of SQL it understands. Anything the converter does not map precisely becomes an explicit Unsupported, Unsupported_from, or Other constructor carrying the original node name. The converter never silently drops a node. The analyzer denies every unsupported node (E_UNSUPPORTED) and every statement kind outside the policy (E_STATEMENT_KIND). Rule code matches AST constructors exhaustively, without wildcard (_ ->) arms, so adding a constructor causes compile errors in every rule that must consider it. Haltsql.verify is total: every exception is caught and becomes an E_INTERNAL denial. Parse errors (E_PARSE), empty input (E_EMPTY), and limit breaches (E_LIMIT) are denials, never exceptions. Limits on input bytes, tree depth, and node count are enforced before or during conversion.

Walk the raw JSON tree with generic traversal. Fast to build, but unknown nodes are silently ignored. Rejected. Generate the full typed AST from libpg_query's srcdata definitions. Complete coverage and mechanical upgrades, but a much larger surface to analyze, most of it irrelevant for agent queries. A curated subset with explicit Unsupported is easier to reason about and audit. We may generate types later, keeping the fail-closed rule. Best-effort analysis with warnings for unknown nodes. Turns unknowns into allows. Rejected: the goal is deny by default.

Some valid, safe SQL is denied until the AST and rules support it. This is a false positive, which is visible and fixable; the alternative is a silent false negative. Supporting a new construct is an explicit change: AST constructor, converter, rules, tests, and docs. Postgres upgrades that add syntax produce E_UNSUPPORTED rather than bypasses. E_INTERNAL must be alerted on: it indicates a bug, even though it is safe.
Track E_UNSUPPORTED frequency on benign corpora to prioritize support. Fuzz the converter to ensure no input raises past verify.
Status: Proposed Date: 2026-11-10 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Related: ADR-0002; ADR-0003; ADR-0004; docs/policy-reference.md; docs/verdict.md; docs/authentication.md
documents.s: ADR-0008: Deny casts by default, pin the search path, and make shadow execution opt-in

documents.t: A review of 0.0.2 found four places where a verdict promised more than the system delivered. Each touches a stable contract (policy schema, verdict JSON, config, SDK behaviour), so they are decided together. Casts were a denylist in a system that is deny-by-default everywhere else. Only the reg* types were refused; 'x'::xml, CAST(x AS oid) and casts to user-defined types passed. A cast runs the target type's input or conversion function, so this was an unlisted function call. The verdict assumed a search path nobody enforced. Unqualified names are resolved against the policy's search_path; the session that ran the SQL could use another one (ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path), so a verified orders could be a different table. Shadow mode returned allowed: true and every guarded executor ran on allowed. One reloaded policy line turned enforcement off, with no signal on the client. Static tokens authenticated a caller but not a tenant. The request body supplied the whole context, so any holder of a service token could ask for a verdict, with its bind_params, for any tenant.

Casts. A new policy section casts (allow, extend) is an allowlist of cast target types. Its default is the built-in scalar types with pure input functions (text, the integer and float types, numeric, bool, the date and time types, uuid, json, jsonb, bytea). A bare name matches the type unqualified or pg_catalog.-qualified; a type in another schema must be listed as schema.type. deny_casts stays and wins over casts. The reason code is unchanged (E_CAST_DENIED); the rule name casts.allowlist is new. Search path. The verdict's policy object gains search_path. Executors that own the transaction set it: the Python guard (and so the MCP server and the Python integrations) with a transaction-local set_config, applied after caller settings; the proxy at upstream startup, verified with SHOW search_path before the first client statement. The single-statement guards of the TypeScript, Go and Java SDKs run one statement on the caller's connection and do not change session settings; they expose the field and document the requirement. Their transaction-owning forms, added afterwards (see Follow-up), pin it the way the Python guard does. Shadow mode. The verdict is unchanged: allowed: true with shadow_reasons. The guarded executors of all four SDKs and the MCP server treat a verdict with non-empty shadow_reasons as a denial unless the application opts in (HALTSQL_ALLOW_SHADOW=1 or guard.set_allow_shadow(True); allowShadow: true; AllowShadow(); .allowShadow()). A shadow rollout therefore needs a server-side switch and a client-side one. Token context. server.auth.tokens[] accepts context and request_context_fields, with the semantics mTLS identities already have: the configured context is fixed, the body may add only the listed fields, anything else is 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. A token with neither key keeps the old behaviour and the server logs a warning when its policy isolates tenants. Audit records carry context and context_source (authenticated or request).

Keep casts a denylist and extend it. Every new type or extension would need a new entry; the failure mode is an allow. Rejected. Make allowed: false in shadow mode and add a separate "would run" flag. Cleaner for clients, but it breaks every existing caller that implements shadow rollouts on allowed, and it changes the meaning of a field ADR-0004 froze. The client-side opt-in gets the safety without changing the verdict. Schema-qualify every name instead of pinning the search path. HaltSQL never rewrites SQL, and requiring qualified names would deny most generated queries. Pinning makes the assumption true instead of forbidding its use. Require a context on every token. Correct for multi-tenant agents, wrong for a trusted backend that takes the tenant from its own session. A warning and a documented default-safe pattern were chosen over a breaking requirement; this can be tightened before 1.0.

Breaking: queries that cast to a type outside the default list are now denied; shadow rollouts need the client opt-in; every policy's version hash changes because the canonical policy includes casts. The verdict JSON grows one field (policy.search_path). Clients ignore unknown fields, so older SDKs keep working, but they also do not pin. All four changes fail closed: an unlisted cast denies, a search path that cannot be set fails the transaction (the proxy ends the session), an un-opted shadow verdict does not run, a body field outside a bound token's allowance is refused. What stays outside the proof: views, function bodies, triggers and partitions. haltsql schema check reports the cases it can see (views, stale catalog entries, shadowing relations); row-level security remains the boundary.

Decide before 1.0 whether an unbound static token should be refused for a policy that isolates tenants. Done: the TypeScript, Go and Java guards have a transaction-owning mode that pins the search path (guardedTransaction / guardedTransactionOnClient; GuardedQueryTx / GuardedExecTx; JdbcGuard.queryInTransaction / updateInTransaction). It follows the Python guard: READ ONLY for a select verdict, caller settings, then a transaction-local set_config('search_path', ...), then the verified SQL. The single-statement functions keep their behaviour and are documented as not pinning. Still open: decide before 1.0 whether to deprecate them. Function allowlist entries are still by name; an entry allows every overload.
Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-07 Deciders: Arnav Dadarya Related: PLAN.md §6.1, §6.2; docs/verdict.md; docs/reason-codes.md
documents.s: ADR-0004: Versioned verdict schema and stable reason codes

documents.t: HaltSQL's output is consumed by programs: agent frameworks that feed denials back to a model, audit pipelines, dashboards, alerting, and CI tests. If the output changes shape or meaning between releases, integrations break silently, and in the worst case a client misreads a denial as an allow.

Every check returns a verdict (lib/core/verdict.ml) whose JSON form is a public API, versioned with apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 and the HTTP /v1 prefix. Verdict fields: allowed, reasons, shadow_reasons, policy {name, version}, statement_kind, tables, columns, bind_params, fingerprint, sql_sha256, elapsed_us. Within v1, fields are only added, never renamed, removed, or changed in meaning. Clients must ignore unknown fields. Each reason has a stable code (lib/core/reason.ml), plus message, rule, optional loc (byte offset), and optional hint for agents. Reason codes are never renamed or reused, even before 1.0. New codes may be added in minor releases; clients must treat unknown codes as denials. message, rule, and hint are human-oriented and may change at any time. Integrations must match on code only. In enforce mode, allowed is true exactly when reasons is empty. In shadow mode, allowed is always true and would-be denials go to shadow_reasons. bind_params is always empty when a query is denied. policy.version is a SHA-256 over the normalized policy, identical for YAML and JSON forms, so every decision can be traced to an exact policy. Determinism: for the same SQL, policy, and context, allowed, the reason codes, tables, columns, and bind_params are identical across runs and platforms. elapsed_us is the only intentionally nondeterministic field.

Boolean only. Gives agents nothing to act on and makes audits weak. Rejected. Free-text reasons. Unstable for programs and localization. Rejected. Numeric codes. Harder to read in logs and prompts; string codes are self-describing. HTTP errors for denials. Conflates "the query is not allowed" with "the request failed". Denials are 200 verdicts; HTTP errors mean the check did not happen, which clients treat as a denial.

Adding a rule means choosing an existing code or adding a new one with documentation in docs/reason-codes.md and an OpenAPI update. Golden tests pin the verdict JSON shape. A v2 verdict format, if ever needed, will be served side by side with v1.

HaltSQL ships small Python packages for five agent frameworks. Each one gives the agent a tool that runs read-only SQL after HaltSQL has verified it: Framework Package (directory) What you get OpenAI Agents SDK (openai-agents) haltsql-openai-agents (integrations/openai_agents) haltsql_query_tool() (a FunctionTool), haltsql_tool_input_guardrail() LangGraph haltsql-langgraph (integrations/langgraph) haltsql_query_tool() (works with ToolNode), build_sql_agent_graph() with a retry-on-deny loop Semantic Kernel (Python) haltsql-semantic-kernel (integrations/semantic_kernel) HaltSQLPlugin (one kernel_function) CrewAI haltsql-crewai (integrations/crewai) HaltSQLQueryTool (a BaseTool) Google Agent Development Kit (google-adk) haltsql-google-adk (integrations/google_adk) HaltSQLQueryTool (a BaseTool), haltsql_before_tool_callback(), HaltSQLGuardPlugin, build_sql_agent() The packages are thin layers over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard. For LangChain, LlamaIndex and Vanna, see integrations.md.

All five packages follow the same rules: One tool, one argument. The tool is named haltsql_query. Its only argument is query, the SQL text. In Semantic Kernel the tool is the query function of the haltsql plugin, so the model sees haltsql-query. The context comes from your application. The tenant and any other context come from state that your application sets and the model cannot write. Where that state lives depends on the framework: OpenAI Agents SDK: the run context. LangGraph: the runtime context. ADK: session state. Semantic Kernel and CrewAI: a mapping or callable you give the tool. The context is never a tool argument. If the model adds extra arguments such as tenant_id, they never reach HaltSQL: the OpenAI Agents SDK, ADK, CrewAI and Semantic Kernel tools refuse the call, and the LangGraph and LangChain tools drop the extra argument and use the trusted context. If no context is configured, the query is refused before it is verified. Verify, then execute. The packages call haltsql.guard.authorize and then guard.execute. The database receives the exact string HaltSQL verified, with the verdict's bind_params. It runs in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement_timeout (default 5000 ms) and a row cap (default 200). Only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select are run. Nothing runs when HaltSQL is unavailable. If the sidecar or CLI fails, times out, or returns a verdict for a different string, the query does not run. The database connection is opened only after HaltSQL allows the query. Refusals go back to the model. A refused query is returned as a structured result, so the model can fix the SQL and retry. It is not raised as an exception. The result has the same shape in every package. ADK returns it as a dict, LangGraph as the ToolMessage artifact, and the other packages as JSON text: {"status": "ok", "executed": true, "columns": ["id", "status"], "rows": [[1, "open"], [3, "paid"]], "row_count": 2, "truncated": false} {"status": "denied", "executed": false, "reasons": [{"code": "E_TENANT_MISMATCH", "message": "...", "hint": "Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message": "HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} {"status": "error", "executed": false, "message": "SQL verification is unavailable; the query was not executed."} A status of error with executed: true means HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example because of a statement timeout. The message gives the error class and its first line. See reason-codes.md for the codes.

Every package exports the same HaltSQLToolRunner. It holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits: import psycopg from haltsql import HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # a read-only role; called only after an allow max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=lambda ctx: {"app.tenant_id": ctx["tenant_id"]}, # optional, e.g. for RLS ) connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. The runner closes it after each query. Use a database role that can only read, and row-level security, as defense-in-depth.md describes.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field from agents import Agent, Runner from haltsql_openai_agents import HaltSQLToolRunner, haltsql_query_tool @dataclass class AppContext: # passed to Runner.run(context=...); never sent to the model user_id: str haltsql_context: dict = field(default_factory=dict) agent = Agent(name="analyst", instructions="Answer with SQL.", tools=[haltsql_query_tool(runner)]) result = await Runner.run(agent, "How many open orders?", context=AppContext(user.id, {"tenant_id": user.tenant_id})) By default the tool reads the haltsql_context attribute or key of the run context. Pass context_from=lambda app: {...} to map your own context object. haltsql_tool_input_guardrail(verifier, sql_arg="query") is a tool input guardrail for SQL tools you already have (@function_tool(tool_input_guardrails=[...])). It verifies the tool's SQL argument before the tool runs. If HaltSQL does not allow it, the guardrail calls reject_content: the tool does not run and the model gets the refusal JSON. The guardrail cannot pass $n values to the tool. So it refuses any SQL that HaltSQL allows only with bound parameters. Use it with a policy in literal tenancy mode (see tenancy.md), or use haltsql_query_tool. The guardrail checks only the SQL. The guarded tool must still apply read-only access, timeouts and row limits itself.

from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode from haltsql_langgraph import HaltSQLToolRunner, haltsql_query_tool, build_sql_agent_graph tool = haltsql_query_tool(runner) # ToolNode([tool]) works as usual graph = build_sql_agent_graph(llm.bind_tools([tool]), tool, max_denials=3) out = graph.invoke({"messages": [("user", "How many open orders?")]}, context={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}}) The tool takes LangGraph's ToolRuntime, which is hidden from the model, and reads haltsql_context from the runtime context (graph.invoke(..., context=...)). It uses response_format="content_and_artifact". The ToolMessage content is the JSON for the model, and artifact is the same result as a dict. is_denial(message) tells you whether a message is a refusal. build_sql_agent_graph is an example graph: After a refusal, the model gets the hints and tries again. After max_denials refusals, the graph stops with a short message instead of looping.

import contextvars from semantic_kernel import Kernel from haltsql_semantic_kernel import HaltSQLPlugin, HaltSQLToolRunner, PLUGIN_NAME current_ctx = contextvars.ContextVar("haltsql_ctx", default=None) # set per request kernel = Kernel() kernel.add_plugin(HaltSQLPlugin(runner, context=current_ctx.get), plugin_name=PLUGIN_NAME) context is a mapping, or a zero-argument callable that is evaluated on every call. The callable runs in a worker thread, and contextvars values are copied into that thread. A callable that returns None refuses the query. The plugin never reads the context from KernelArguments, because automatic function calling merges the model's arguments into them. If the model sends arguments the function does not declare, Semantic Kernel itself refuses the call.

from crewai import Agent from haltsql_crewai import HaltSQLQueryTool, HaltSQLToolRunner tool = HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=runner, context=lambda: {"tenant_id": session.tenant_id}) analyst = Agent(role="Analyst", goal="Answer questions about orders", backstory="Writes careful SQL.", tools=[tool]) Build the tool, or the crew, per request, with that request's context. Do not take the tenant from crew inputs or task text. The argument schema forbids extra fields, so a model-written tenant_id is a validation error.

from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner from haltsql_google_adk import HaltSQLToolRunner, build_sql_agent agent = build_sql_agent(runner, model="gemini-2.5-flash") # an LlmAgent with HaltSQLQueryTool adk = InMemoryRunner(agent=agent, app_name="analytics") session = await adk.session_service.create_session( app_name="analytics", user_id=user.id, state={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}}) HaltSQLQueryTool reads the context from session state, from the haltsql_context key by default (state_key= changes it). Set that key when you create the session. Do not let a tool or an agent's output_key write it. If the value is not a mapping, the query is refused. The tool returns the result dict as the function response. ADK has database tools for BigQuery, Spanner and Bigtable. It can also load the tools of MCP Toolbox for Databases through ToolboxToolset, which includes postgres-execute-sql. To guard tools like these that run PostgreSQL, use one of these: LlmAgent(before_tool_callback=haltsql_before_tool_callback(verifier)) guards one agent. Runner(..., plugins=[HaltSQLGuardPlugin(verifier)]) guards every agent the runner executes. Both use tools= to map tool names to their SQL argument. The default is {"execute_sql": "sql"}. Tools that are not listed are not checked. For a listed tool, the guard verifies the SQL with the tenant from session state. If HaltSQL does not allow it, the guard returns the refusal dict instead of running the tool. Like the Agents SDK guardrail, it refuses any verdict that needs bound parameters, because the other tool cannot pass them. Use literal tenancy for those tools. The guard checks only the SQL: run those tools with a read-only role and their own timeouts. Plugins run before an agent's own callbacks. If you use the callback form, list it first and do not let a later callback change the arguments. Do not use the guard with BigQuery or GoogleSQL Spanner tools: HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

Each package has tests that use the real framework objects, the real haltsql CLI (LocalVerifier), a real haltsql-server process, and the lab Postgres. Nothing in those tests fakes HaltSQL or the database: OpenAI Agents SDK: tool calls go through the SDK's function-tool executor. LangGraph: a real ToolNode and StateGraph. Semantic Kernel: Kernel.invoke and Kernel.invoke_function_call. CrewAI: BaseTool.run and the structured-tool path. ADK: an InMemoryRunner session and ADK's function-call handler. The tests never call an LLM. Where a graph needs a model turn, a short deterministic script writes the tool calls. make -C lab up # Postgres 17 on 127.0.0.1:5417 dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./bin/server/main.exe ONLY=agents clients/python/run-all-tests.sh # or FULL=1 for every Python suite The frameworks pin conflicting dependency versions, so the script gives each package its own virtualenv (integrations/<pkg>/.venv, Python 3.11 to 3.13). Each package's constraints.txt lists the exact versions the tests were run with. Integration tests skip with a message when the binaries or the lab Postgres are missing.

Every verify request produces one audit record per configured sink. Each record is one JSON line: {"ts":"2024-06-01T12:00:00Z","request_id":"...","caller":"support-bot","policy":"support", "policy_version":"v3","allowed":false,"shadow":false,"codes":["E_TABLE_DENIED"], "sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"...","elapsed_us":183, "prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} Records are hash-chained: hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ L), where L is the compact JSON of the record without its hash field. The first record of a chain has prev_hash = 64 zeros. Each sink keeps its own chain. A modified, deleted, inserted or reordered record breaks verification (see Verifying a chain). Sink Durability Use for stdout your log pipeline containers with log shipping file local disk, appended per record VMs, sidecars with a volume s3 S3 or S3-compatible, optionally WORM (Object Lock) compliance archives on AWS / MinIO gcs Google Cloud Storage compliance archives on GCP elasticsearch Elasticsearch or OpenSearch index / data stream search, dashboards and SIEM rules kafka a Kafka topic (acknowledged by the brokers) feeding a SIEM pipeline or data lake The cloud sinks are in library haltsql.cloud, modules S3_sink, Gcs_sink and Object_sink. The streaming sinks (elasticsearch, kafka) are in library haltsql-server.siem; see Streaming sinks.

write seals the record into the sink's chain and appends it to the current batch. The call is synchronous and never waits on the network. A batch closes when it holds batch.max_records records (default 500) or is batch.max_seconds old (default 10). The closed batch becomes one object: <prefix>YYYY/MM/DD/HH/<host>-<run>-<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl YYYY/MM/DD/HH: the UTC hour when the batch closed; <host>: the sanitized hostname; <run>: the run id of the process that sealed the batch: its UTC start time with microseconds, then its pid (e.g. 20240601T115900.042000Z.7). Two runs never share a sequence namespace, and run ids sort by start time; <seq>: a zero-padded per-sink sequence number; <sha256>: the SHA-256 of the object body. Example: haltsql/audit/2024/06/01/12/haltsql-7f9c-20240601T115900.042000Z.7-0000000042-9b1e....jsonl. Objects are uploaded strictly in order. If an upload fails, that object stays at the head of the queue and nothing behind it overtakes it. The chain spans objects. The first record of object n+1 carries the hash of the last record of object n. Concatenate a sink's objects in <seq> order and the result verifies as a single chain: Each host has its own chain. Within one host, sorting the full object names gives chain order: by hour, then by run (start time), then by <seq>. Batches close in <seq> order and keep the hour they closed in, even when uploaded later. Across restarts the chain is only continuous with a spool directory (see Restarts): aws s3 cp --recursive s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/2024/06/01/ ./audit/ find ./audit -name 'haltsql-7f9c-*.jsonl' | sort | xargs cat > day.jsonl python3 verify_chain.py day.jsonl # see "Verifying a chain" below A chain that starts mid-stream (e.g. one day of objects) begins with a non-zero prev_hash; verify it from that record onwards. Objects are create-only. S3 PUTs send If-None-Match: * and GCS uploads send ifGenerationMatch=0, so an existing object is never overwritten. The object name embeds the body's SHA-256, so a "precondition failed" reply on a retry means the object is already stored, and it counts as delivered.

Mode While uploads fail Recovery fail_closed (default) After an upload has failed every attempt (3 by default, with backoff), the sink reports unhealthy. Every audit write is refused and /v1/verify answers 503. No request is ever served without its audit record. The background loop retries the held objects every batch.max_seconds. The first success makes the sink healthy again. buffer Writes keep succeeding while failed objects wait, up to 100 000 waiting records (the ?max_buffer_records argument of the library's S3_sink.create / Gcs_sink.create; it is not a config-file key). At the bound, writes are refused (503). Records are never silently dropped. Same background retry; the buffer drains in order. Records accepted into a batch but not yet uploaded live in memory. To make them survive a crash, give the sink a spool directory (spool_dir in the sink's config, or S3_sink.create ~spool_dir). Use one directory per sink, on persistent storage: Every record is appended to <spool>/current.jsonl before write returns. Writes are refused if the spool cannot be written. Closed batches stay on disk as batch-<seq>.jsonl until they are uploaded, then they are deleted. Each batch's object name is kept beside it in batch-<seq>.key. Each time a batch closes, the chain head and the next sequence number are written to <spool>/head.json (temporary file, fsync, rename). On restart, the sink re-queues the spooled batches under their original object names, and continues the chain and the sequence from the last sealed record. This holds even when every batch had already been uploaded. A corrupt head.json or spool file stops the sink from starting; it is never silently reset.

With spool_dir Without spool_dir After a restart the chain continues: the new run's first record has the prev_hash of the previous run's last record, and <seq> keeps counting the new run starts a new chain at genesis (prev_hash = 64 zeros) and <seq> 0, under its own <run> Objects of an earlier run deleted detected: the later run's first record points to a hash that is gone not detected by the chain alone Crash after an upload, before the spool file is removed the batch is retried under the same object name, so the create-only PUT reports it as already stored (nothing is spooled) Without a spool directory, verify each run on its own: group a host's objects by <run>, and verify each group from genesis. To make an earlier run's objects impossible to delete, enable S3 Object Lock (object_lock), or a GCS retention policy.

Object_sink.metrics_text renders these metrics for /metrics: Metric Type Alert when haltsql_audit_sink_healthy{sink} gauge == 0: writes are being refused haltsql_audit_sink_buffered_records{sink} gauge growing steadily: uploads are failing (buffer mode) haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects{sink} gauge > 0 for longer than a few max_seconds haltsql_audit_sink_objects_uploaded_total{sink} counter flat while traffic flows haltsql_audit_sink_upload_failures_total{sink} counter rate > 0 haltsql_audit_sink_rejected_writes_total{sink} counter rate > 0: requests got 503 sink is s3://<bucket>/<prefix> or gs://<bucket>/<prefix>.

audit: sinks: - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 prefix: haltsql/audit/ object_lock: { mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 365 } batch: { max_records: 500, max_seconds: 10 } credentials: { source: web_identity } on_error: fail_closed Every PUT is signed with AWS Signature Version 4, verified against AWS's published test vectors. Each PUT sends: Content-MD5 and x-amz-checksum-sha256, so S3 rejects a body corrupted in transit; x-amz-content-sha256; If-None-Match: *; with object_lock: x-amz-object-lock-mode: GOVERNANCE|COMPLIANCE and x-amz-object-lock-retain-until-date (upload time + retain_days). The bucket must have Object Lock enabled; S3 refuses lock headers otherwise. URLs. Without endpoint, requests go to https://<bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com/<key> (virtual-hosted style). With endpoint (MinIO, Ceph, LocalStack), they go to <endpoint>/<bucket>/<key> (path style). Credentials (credentials.source): Source How env (default) AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, optional AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. static Keys from the config. Always use secret placeholders, e.g. secret_access_key: ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/s3#secret}. web_identity EKS IRSA / OIDC federation. Reads AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE and AWS_ROLE_ARN (optional AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME) and calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity as a form POST, so the token never appears in a URL. The endpoint is https://sts.<region>.amazonaws.com, or AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS. instance EC2 instance profile via IMDSv2: a session token from PUT /latest/api/token, then the role's credentials. AWS_EC2_METADATA_SERVICE_ENDPOINT overrides the endpoint; AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true disables it. Temporary credentials are cached and refreshed 5 minutes before they expire. If a refresh fails while the cached credentials are still valid, those are used. If S3 answers ExpiredToken, InvalidToken, RequestExpired or TokenRefreshRequired, the cache is dropped and the upload is retried. 429, SlowDown and 5xx are retried. Other 4xx errors, such as AccessDenied, are not retried within a flush, but the object is still kept. Minimal IAM policy: {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:PutObjectRetention"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/*"}

audit: sinks: - type: gcs bucket: corp-haltsql-audit prefix: haltsql/audit/ credentials: { source: metadata } # or: { source: service_account_file, file: /var/run/gcp/key.json } on_error: buffer Upload. Objects are uploaded with the JSON API simple upload (uploadType=media, ifGenerationMatch=0). The md5Hash that GCS returns must equal the MD5 of the body, otherwise the upload counts as failed. For WORM storage, use a bucket retention policy (Bucket Lock). Credentials. Choose one: Metadata server (GKE Workload Identity, GCE). The sink sends Metadata-Flavor: Google and requires that header on the response. GCE_METADATA_HOST overrides the host. Service-account key file. The sink builds an RS256 JWT and exchanges it at the key's token_uri, which must be https. Tokens are cached and refreshed 60 s before expiry. A 401 refreshes the token once. Emulators. STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST (for example localhost:4443) redirects uploads to an emulator. Grant the identity roles/storage.objectCreator on the bucket.

The elasticsearch and kafka sinks ship records as they are written, instead of uploading objects. The configuration keys are in the configuration reference. Both sinks work the same way: write adds two fields to the record and seals it into the sink's own hash chain: prev_hash and hash, exactly as in every other sink. This call is synchronous and never waits on the network. Sealed records wait in an in-memory queue, in chain order. A batch is sent when the queue holds batch.max_records records (default 500) or batch.max_bytes bytes (default 5 MiB), or when its oldest record is batch.flush_interval_ms old (default 1000). One request is in flight at a time, so batches are never reordered. The destination answers per record: Delivered records leave the queue. Records the destination rejects for good leave the queue too. Examples: an Elasticsearch mapping error, or a Kafka record larger than the broker allows. They are counted in haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total{reason} and logged with their hash and the error type, never their contents. They are never dropped silently. Records that hit a transient error are sent again, alone, on the next attempt. Each batch gets 3 attempts, with exponential backoff and jitter between them: 0.2 s × 2^n, capped at 30 s, times a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5. After the last attempt the batch stays at the head of the queue, so nothing overtakes it, and the sink is failing. A background loop retries it after a growing, jittered delay. Each process starts a new chain at genesis (prev_hash = 64 zeros). The streaming sinks have no spool: records still queued when the process dies are lost. Use a file, s3 or gcs sink with a spool directory next to a streaming sink when that matters.

Mode While the destination is unreachable At the bound (max_buffer_records) fail_closed (default) After a batch has failed all its attempts, the sink is unhealthy: every audit write is refused and /v1/verify answers 503 until a retry succeeds. Writes are refused. buffer Writes keep succeeding; records wait in the queue. Writes are refused (fail closed). drop New records are dropped before they are sealed, so the chain of shipped records stays intact. They are counted with reason="on_error_drop" and write succeeds. Records already queued are kept and retried. New records are dropped. drop is the only mode that serves requests without an audit trail in that sink. Use it only next to another sink that fails closed.

Haltsql_siem.Siem.metrics_text renders these metrics. Their names differ from the object sinks' metrics, so both can be on one /metrics page. Labels: sink (for example kafka://kafka-1:9093/haltsql.audit) and type (elasticsearch or kafka). Metric Type Alert when haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy gauge == 0: writes are being refused haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivering gauge == 0: deliveries are failing (also in buffer and drop modes) haltsql_audit_stream_sink_buffered_records gauge growing steadily haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_written_total counter haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_delivered_total counter flat while traffic flows haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total{reason} counter rate > 0. Reasons: mapping, too_large, on_error_drop haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivery_failures_total counter rate > 0 haltsql_audit_stream_sink_retries_total counter haltsql_audit_stream_sink_rejected_writes_total counter rate > 0: requests got 503 A dropped record (mapping or too_large) was already sealed, so the verifier reports a gap at that point in the chain. The log line names the missing record's hash.

audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch urls: [https://es-1.corp.example:9200, https://es-2.corp.example:9200] data_stream: logs-haltsql-prod # or index: haltsql-audit auth: { api_key: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/es#api_key}" } tls: { ca_file: ./certs/es-ca.pem } on_error: buffer The sink only uses the _bulk API, so it works with Elasticsearch and OpenSearch alike. The test suite runs against Elasticsearch 8.15 (security on, TLS, API key) and OpenSearch 2.17. Requests. Each batch is one POST <url>/_bulk (with ?pipeline= when pipeline is set). Each record is a create action whose _id is the record's hash: {"create":{"_index":"logs-haltsql-prod","_id":"9b1e…"}} {"@timestamp":"2024-06-01T12:00:00Z","ts":"2024-06-01T12:00:00Z",…,"prev_hash":"…","hash":"9b1e…","event":{"original":"{\"@timestamp\":…,\"hash\":\"9b1e…\"}"}} @timestamp is added to the record before it is sealed (a copy of ts), because data streams require it. A top-level event field would be renamed haltsql_event; audit records have none. The document holds the record's fields, so they are searchable, and event.original: the exact sealed line, the bytes the hash covers. Ingest pipelines and synthetic _source re-serialize documents. Synthetic _source is the default for logs-*-* data streams. So a verifier always starts from event.original, and checks that the searchable fields match it. The cost is about twice the storage per record. create never overwrites. When a response is lost and the batch is sent again, Elasticsearch answers 409 for records it already stored. Their _id is their hash, so a 409 means "this exact record is stored", and counts as delivered. (In a data stream, _id is unique per backing index: a retry that spans a rollover can store a record twice. The verifier skips duplicates.) Responses. Answer What the sink does item 2xx or 409 delivered item 429 or 5xx that record is retried alone item 400 with mapper_parsing_exception, document_parsing_exception, strict_dynamic_mapping_exception or mapper_exception that record is dropped: records_dropped_total{reason="mapping"}, logged with its hash and the error type any other item error (e.g. 403 cluster_block_exception, a pipeline failure) that record is retried; while it keeps failing, the sink is failing and on_error applies whole request: connection error, timeout, 5xx the attempt fails; the next attempt uses the next URL in urls whole request: 401, 403, 413, 429 the attempt fails The sink asks for filter_path=errors,items.*.status,items.*.error.type, so item error reasons are not even downloaded: they can quote field values. Only error types are logged. Authentication. auth.api_key is sent as Authorization: ApiKey <key>, using the encoded value that POST /_security/api_key returns. Basic auth (username/password) also works. Neither is ever logged. Minimal role for an API key: {"haltsql-audit": {"indices": [{"names": ["logs-haltsql-*"], "privileges": ["create_doc", "auto_configure"]}]}} TLS. https URLs are verified against the system roots, or against the CA bundle in tls.ca_file, including the host name. Plain http is accepted only for loopback addresses. Mapping. Strings in audit records are short. With an index, create an index template first, or rely on dynamic mapping. A field that changes type (for example after you add a field to the record from a custom integration) produces mapping drops. Watch that metric.

Export the documents and run the verifier. It is the script test/siem/verify_chain.py in the repository; the test suite runs it against real clusters. curl -s --cacert es-ca.pem -H "Authorization: ApiKey $KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ "https://es-1.corp.example:9200/logs-haltsql-prod/_search" \ -d '{"size":10000,"query":{"range":{"@timestamp":{"gte":"2024-06-01","lt":"2024-06-02"}}}}' \ > day.json python3 verify_chain.py es day.json # chain from genesis: 8123 records, head 4f0c… # OK: 8123 records in 1 chain(s) The documents carry no sequence number. The verifier links them by prev_hash, starting from genesis (64 zeros). For each document it: recomputes the hash of event.original; checks that _id is that hash; checks that the searchable fields equal event.original. It tolerates synthetic _source sorting and de-duplicating arrays. An ingest pipeline that adds or changes fields makes this check fail even though event.original itself verifies; enrich into a separate index, or relax the check in your copy of the script. Each process run is one chain from genesis, so an index written by several runs (restarts) or replicas holds several chains from genesis; the verifier follows each one. Two records claiming the same non-genesis prev_hash are a fork and fail. A chain that starts anywhere else follows a record that is missing from the export: a record dropped for a mapping error, a deleted document, or a time range that cuts the chain. That makes the verifier exit with status 1. For an export that is expected to begin mid-chain (a time range), pass --any-start: python3 verify_chain.py es --any-start day.json. For more than 10 000 documents, page with search_after and pass the hits as a JSON list. To make deletion impossible, give the HaltSQL key only create_doc, and put the index under an ILM policy without a delete phase. Or snapshot it to a WORM repository.

audit: sinks: - type: kafka brokers: [kafka-1.corp.example:9093, kafka-2.corp.example:9093] topic: haltsql.audit acks: all tls: { ca_file: /etc/haltsql/kafka/ca.pem } sasl: { mechanism: scram-sha-512, username: haltsql, password: "${env:KAFKA_PASSWORD}" } on_error: fail_closed The producer is written in OCaml and needs no librdkafka. It implements only what audit shipping needs: Bootstrap. The brokers are tried in turn. Each connection negotiates protocol versions (ApiVersions), authenticates, and fetches the topic's metadata. Topics are never created automatically: create the topic first. A missing topic is a delivery failure (UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION), and on_error applies. One partition per chain. Each record is one Kafka message. Its value is the sealed record, byte for byte. Its key is the chain id haltsql/<host>/<run>. Every record of a sink goes to one partition, so the chain is that partition's offset order. The partition is chosen once, the way the Java client's default partitioner does it: murmur2(key) mod partitions. It stays the same for the life of the process, even if partitions are added. Produce. One RecordBatch v2 per request: magic 2, CRC-32C, no compression, no headers. acks: all is sent as -1, acks: 1 as 1. The sink waits for the acknowledgement before sending the next batch. Leader changes. NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE, UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION, leader-epoch errors and connection failures close the connection and forget the leader. The next attempt asks the bootstrap brokers again and reconnects to the new leader. Too large. On MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE or RECORD_LIST_TOO_LARGE, the batch is split in halves. A single record that is still too large is dropped and counted with reason="too_large". TLS uses the same tls-lwt stack as the rest of HaltSQL. The broker certificate and host name are verified against the system roots or tls.ca_file. A broker name that is neither an IP address nor a valid DNS host name (for example kafka_1: _ is not allowed in host names) cannot be checked, so the sink refuses to connect to it; this applies to the configured brokers and to the leaders they advertise. An optional client certificate (cert_file + key_file) enables mTLS; the test suite runs it against a broker with ssl.client.auth=required. SASL: PLAIN, SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-512 (RFC 5802 / RFC 7677). With SCRAM, the broker's final signature is verified: a broker that does not prove it knows the password is refused. Passwords never appear in logs or errors. PLAIN without TLS is only allowed to loopback brokers (localhost, ::1, a literal 127.0.0.0/8 address), and the rule is applied to every connection: a leader that the bootstrap broker advertises at a non-loopback address is refused instead of receiving the password in clear text. Delivery is at least once. There is no idempotent producer. When a request times out after the broker stored the batch, the batch is sent again. The partition then holds the same records twice: the whole batch can follow itself (offsets 3-7 repeated at 8-12, for example), and nothing on the sink side shows it. verify_chain.py kafka skips an exact re-delivery of a record it has already seen (same hash, content verified) and keeps linking from the last new record. haltsql audit verify reports such copies as duplicate_record errors unless you pass --allow-redelivery, which makes them warnings; missing, reordered or modified records still fail either way. Limits. Protocol versions: Produce v3-v8, Metadata v1-v8, SaslHandshake v1, SaslAuthenticate v0-v1, all supported by Kafka 1.0 and later (4.x included). The test suite runs against Apache Kafka 3.9 (KRaft). One request in flight per sink. Throughput is about one batch per broker round trip, which is far more than one HaltSQL instance produces. Not supported: compression, transactions, the idempotent producer, OAUTHBEARER and GSSAPI (Kerberos), SASLprep of user names and passwords (Kafka's own client does not apply it either). Records queued in memory are lost if the process dies. Minimal ACL for the HaltSQL principal: kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server … --add --allow-principal User:haltsql \ --operation Write --operation Describe --topic haltsql.audit

Read the topic with the broker's own console consumer. Print the key, so each chain can be told apart, and run the verifier: kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 \ --consumer.config client.properties --topic haltsql.audit --from-beginning \ --timeout-ms 30000 --property print.key=true --property key.separator=$'\t' \ > audit.tsv python3 verify_chain.py kafka audit.tsv # chain haltsql/haltsql-7f9c/20240601T115900.042000Z.7: 5120 records from genesis, head 4f0c… # OK: 5120 records in 1 chain(s) Message values are the exact bytes HaltSQL hashed, so the verifier hashes them as they are (no re-serialization). With several partitions, read them all: each chain lives in one partition, in offset order. Records deleted by retention make a chain start mid-stream. The verifier then exits with status 1 (records before the chain are missing); --any-start verifies from there. Use cleanup.policy=delete with a long retention.ms, or tiered storage, for audit topics. Never use compaction: it keeps one record per key, and every record of a chain has the same key.

From OCaml, call Haltsql_cloud.Audit_chain.verify_lines. It accepts ?initial_prev:None for a chain that starts mid-stream. For Kafka and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch exports, use verify_chain.py (see Verifying from Kafka and Verifying from Elasticsearch or OpenSearch). Without OCaml, this script checks the same invariants. It never re-serializes JSON: it hashes the exact bytes written, minus the trailing "hash" member. import hashlib, json, sys prev = None # None: accept the first record's prev_hash count = 0 for n, line in enumerate(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"), 1): line = line.rstrip("\n") if not line: continue i = line.rindex(',"hash":"') body, claimed = line[:i] + "}", json.loads(line)["hash"] p = json.loads(body)["prev_hash"] if prev is not None and p != prev: sys.exit(f"line {n}: prev_hash does not match the previous record") if hashlib.sha256((p + body).encode()).hexdigest() != claimed: sys.exit(f"line {n}: hash mismatch (record was modified)") prev = claimed count += 1 print(f"OK: {count} records")

haltsql audit verify checks the hash chain of HaltSQL audit records: the file and stdout sinks of haltsql-server and haltsql-proxy, logs that mix audit records with other lines, and the objects written by the S3 and GCS sinks, either downloaded to a directory or read straight from S3 (or an S3-compatible store such as MinIO). haltsql audit verify /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl # /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl: OK, 18234 records, 1 chain # head /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl: 9f2c...

Every record is one JSON line ending in "prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>", where hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ L) and L is the compact JSON of the record without its hash member (see audit-sinks.md). For each input the command checks: Record hashes. Each record's content matches its hash. An edited field is reported at its line (bad_hash). Links. Each record's prev_hash is the previous record's hash. A deleted, inserted or rewritten record breaks the next link (broken_link). When a record links to an earlier record instead, the message says the records were reordered and points to that record. An exact copy of an earlier record is reported as duplicate_record. With --allow-redelivery (exports of at-least-once sinks such as Kafka, where a retried produce request can store a whole batch twice) such copies are warnings and skipped; a copy whose content does not match its hash is still bad_hash. Start. The first record must link to genesis (64 zeros), unless --any-start or --initial-prev HASH is given (mid_chain_start, start_mismatch). Restarts. A record whose prev_hash is genesis in the middle of a stream starts a new chain (a stdout sink after a restart, for example). This is a warning (chain_restart), and an error with --strict. Truncation. An incomplete last line (truncated). Whole lines missing at the end cannot be seen in the records themselves: compare against a head you recorded elsewhere with --expect-head HASH (head_mismatch), or, for object sinks, against the spool (--spool). Malformed lines. Lines that are not JSON, or JSON without valid prev_hash/hash (invalid_record). JSON objects without either field are log lines (not_audit_record); --mixed skips them, along with any non-JSON line and container log prefixes before the {. Messages never quote record contents (records may carry SQL).

Point the command at a directory of downloaded objects (searched recursively, symlinks are not followed), or at s3://BUCKET/PREFIX. Objects are named <prefix>YYYY/MM/DD/HH/<host>-<run>-<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl. Every .jsonl file under the directory must have such a name (unrecognized_name); other files are ignored. Check Problem The body's SHA-256 equals the one in the name body_mismatch (modified or truncated object) Every body ends with a newline and holds at least one record truncated, empty_object The same body is stored only once duplicate_object No two objects claim the same host, run and sequence number conflicting_objects Within a run, sequence numbers have no holes seq_gap Within a run, the objects form one chain in sequence order broken_link (with a reordering diagnosis when an object continues another one) A run starting at genesis starts at sequence 0 seq_gap A run that does not start at genesis continues another run of the same host (spool continuity across restarts), at the next sequence number broken_link, seq_gap A run continues a run that started earlier run_order No two runs continue the same run fork Each host has its own chains. A run that starts at genesis while the host has earlier runs is a new chain (a sink without a spool directory restarts its chain): a warning, or an error with --strict. The earliest run of a host must start at genesis unless --any-start or --initial-prev is given (for example when you verify one day of objects).

With --spool DIR (the sink's spool_dir, for the objects of one host; use --host when the directory holds several), the command also checks: the spooled batches that are not uploaded yet (batch-<seq>.jsonl) and current.jsonl continue the chain of the newest run, at the next sequence numbers (a spooled batch whose body was already uploaded is skipped); head.json names the last sealed record: its seq is the newest sealed sequence number plus one and its prev is that record's hash (spool_head_mismatch). This detects objects deleted from the end of the bucket, which the chain alone cannot.

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... \ haltsql audit verify s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/2026/11/07/ --any-start # MinIO or another S3-compatible store (path-style requests) haltsql audit verify --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9000 s3://audit/haltsql/audit/ The command lists the prefix with ListObjectsV2 (all pages) and downloads every .jsonl object with SigV4-signed GET requests, using the same client and credential providers as the S3 sink: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (optional AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), then web identity, then the EC2 instance profile. The signing region is --region, else AWS_REGION, else us-east-1. --endpoint must be https, or http on a loopback address. The identity needs s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the prefix. GCS is not read directly: download the objects (gcloud storage cp -r gs://bucket/prefix ./audit/) and verify the directory.

haltsql audit verify [OPTION]... INPUT... Input Meaning FILE JSON lines from a file or stdout sink (server or proxy), or a log with --mixed. DIR Downloaded S3/GCS objects. - Standard input. s3://BUCKET/PREFIX Objects read directly from S3. Inputs are verified independently; the command fails if any of them fails. Option Effect --concat Treat the file inputs (and -), in the order given, as one chain, e.g. a rotated audit.jsonl.1 followed by audit.jsonl. --any-start Accept a first record that does not link to genesis. --initial-prev HASH The first record must link to HASH (the head of the previous segment). --expect-head HASH The last record must be HASH (detects records missing at the end). --strict A new chain starting mid-stream is an error. --mixed Skip lines that are not audit records (logs, container log prefixes). --spool DIR Check the objects against the sink's spool (one host). --host HOST Only verify the objects written by HOST. --endpoint URL, --region R For s3:// inputs. --json Machine-readable output. Exit codes: 0 every chain verifies, 1 a chain is broken (any problem with severity error), 2 usage error or an input that cannot be read (missing file, empty object directory, S3 access denied or unreachable).

# the proxy's file sink haltsql audit verify /var/log/haltsql/proxy-audit.jsonl # stdout records in container logs (operational log lines are skipped) kubectl logs deploy/haltsql-proxy | haltsql audit verify --mixed - docker logs haltsql 2>&1 | haltsql audit verify --mixed - # rotated files, oldest first haltsql audit verify --concat audit.jsonl.2 audit.jsonl.1 audit.jsonl # objects downloaded from the bucket, checked against the live spool aws s3 cp --recursive s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/ ./audit/ haltsql audit verify --spool /var/lib/haltsql/spool --host haltsql-7f9c ./audit/ # anchor a daily check on yesterday's head haltsql audit verify --json --expect-head "$(cat last-head)" audit.jsonl | jq .ok Text output lists, per input, the record and chain counts, each chain's head hash, every problem with its location (file:line, or the object key) and finally the first broken link: broken.jsonl: BROKEN, 4 records, 1 chain head broken.jsonl: 4dc0... error broken_link at broken.jsonl:2: prev_hash does not match the previous record's hash; records before this one were deleted, inserted, reordered or rewritten error broken_link at broken.jsonl:3: prev_hash does not match the previous record's hash; it continues the record at broken.jsonl:1 instead: records were reordered error truncated at broken.jsonl:5: the last line is incomplete (truncated write) first broken link: broken.jsonl:2: prev_hash does not match the previous record's hash; ... --json prints one object: {"ok": false, "records": 4, "inputs": [{"source": "broken.jsonl", "kind": "file", "ok": false, "records": 4, "objects": 0, "chains": 1, "skipped_lines": 0, "heads": [{"chain": "broken.jsonl", "hash": "4dc0..."}], "problems": [{"severity": "error", "kind": "broken_link", "source": "broken.jsonl", "line": 2, "message": "..."}]}], "first_broken": {"severity": "error", "kind": "broken_link", "source": "broken.jsonl", "line": 2, "message": "..."}} kind values are stable: bad_hash, broken_link, duplicate_record, invalid_record, not_audit_record, truncated, mid_chain_start, start_mismatch, chain_restart, head_mismatch, body_mismatch, unrecognized_name, duplicate_object, conflicting_objects, empty_object, seq_gap, run_order, fork, spool_corrupt, spool_head_mismatch.

A hash chain shows that records were not changed, removed or reordered relative to each other. Someone who can rewrite the whole file can rebuild a valid chain. To make that detectable, keep an independent copy of the head hash (--expect-head), ship records to a second sink, or store objects in a WORM bucket (S3 Object Lock, GCS retention). Without a spool directory, a sink restarts its chain at every process start, so deleting all objects of an earlier run is not detected.
documents.s: What a chain does not prove

documents.t: dune test test/audit test/audit/test_audit.ml builds chains with the real sealing code (Audit_chain.seal, Object_sink uploading into a directory) and tampers with them: an edited field (with and without a recomputed hash), deleted, swapped and duplicated lines, a truncated last line, a cut tail against --expect-head, mid-chain starts, restarts, mixed logs; objects deleted, duplicated, modified, truncated, reordered and conflicting, runs in the wrong order, an earlier run deleted, and a spool whose head shows missing objects. It runs the command-line binary for exit codes, --json, stdin, --concat and usage errors. test/audit/test_audit_minio.ml starts a real MinIO server in Docker (host port 16000), writes objects with the S3 sink, verifies them through s3:// and then tampers through the S3 API (a deleted object, a forged object, wrong credentials, a missing bucket). It skips when Docker or a MinIO image is unavailable (HALTSQL_MINIO_IMAGE selects the image; nothing is pulled).

haltsql-server decides two things about every /v1/* request before it looks at the SQL: who is calling and which context the verdict uses. Both come from the caller's credentials, never from the prompt. This page covers built-in TLS, client certificates (mTLS), OIDC/JWT bearer tokens and static tokens. The configuration keys are listed in config-reference.md; the HTTP behaviour in http-api.md.

mTLS. When the connection presented a client certificate (already verified against server.tls.client_ca by the TLS layer) and its identity matches a server.auth.mtls entry, that entry authenticates the request. A bearer token on the same request is ignored. A valid certificate that matches no identity falls through to step 2. OIDC. A bearer token shaped like a JWT whose unverified iss equals a configured provider's issuer is verified by that provider only. A rejection is final (401, or 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE when the provider's keys cannot be fetched). Tokens from other issuers, and opaque tokens, go to step 3. Static tokens. The token's SHA-256 is compared in constant time with every server.auth.tokens entry. Every identity is pinned to exactly one policy. A request that names another policy gets 403 FORBIDDEN.

Caller Context used for the verdict mTLS identity the identity's static context + body fields listed in its request_context_fields OIDC token values of context_claims + body fields listed in the provider's request_context_fields static token with context or request_context_fields the token's static context + body fields listed in its request_context_fields static token without either key, anonymous the request body's context A body field outside request_context_fields is refused with 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED; it is never silently dropped or overridden. A body field that repeats an identity-provided field with exactly the same value is accepted, so clients that always send their context keep working. The config loader rejects request_context_fields that overlap context_claims or the static mTLS context.

server: listen: 0.0.0.0:8443 tls: cert: /etc/haltsql/tls/tls.crt # chain, leaf first key: /etc/haltsql/tls/tls.key client_ca: /etc/haltsql/tls/ca.crt # enables client certificates client_auth: optional # none | optional | required min_version: "1.2" # or "1.3" TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. TLS 1.2 is limited to ECDHE key exchange with AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); TLS 1.3 to AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Renegotiation is disabled. The handshake must finish within 10 seconds. The private key must match the certificate; startup (exit code 2) and reload fail otherwise. client_auth: optional asks for a certificate and verifies it when one is sent; required also refuses handshakes without one. Verification is RFC 5280 path validation against client_ca at the current time. Rotation. SIGHUP, or file watching (reload.watch), re-reads the certificate, key and client CA. New connections use the new material; existing connections are not interrupted. If the new files are broken or mismatched, the previous material stays active and the reload is counted in haltsql_tls_reload_total{result="error"}. This works with cert-manager and Kubernetes secret volumes (the kubelet updates the files in place). Turning TLS on or off requires a restart. Probes. With client_auth: required, kubelet probes cannot present a certificate. Start the server with --health-listen 0.0.0.0:8081 to serve only /healthz and /readyz over plain HTTP on a second port.

server: tls: cert: /etc/haltsql/tls/tls.crt key: /etc/haltsql/tls/tls.key client_ca: /etc/haltsql/tls/ca.crt client_auth: required auth: mtls: identities: - spiffe_id: spiffe://corp.example/ns/agents/sa/analytics policy: saas-analytics context: { tenant_id: acme } - subject_cn: support-bot policy: support-bot request_context_fields: [tenant_id] spiffe_id matches the certificate's URI SAN exactly. Following the X.509-SVID rules, a certificate with more than one URI SAN has no SPIFFE ID and never matches a spiffe_id entry. subject_cn matches the subject common name exactly (case-sensitive). The CN is decoded from UTF8String, PrintableString, BMPString or UniversalString; a TeletexString, malformed, empty or control-character CN never matches (fail closed). Server certificates that haltsql-server checks (OIDC issuers, bundle sources, OPA, audit sinks) are matched by host name against DNS SubjectAltName entries only: a certificate with the name only in its CN is rejected. The first matching identity in configuration order wins. Audit records carry caller_type: "mtls" and subject set to the SPIFFE ID, or the CN. With SPIRE, point client_ca at the trust bundle and have the agent workload use its X.509-SVID as the client certificate.

server: auth: oidc: - name: corp-okta issuer: https://corp.okta.com/oauth2/default audiences: [haltsql] # jwks_uri: discovered from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration algorithms: [RS256, ES256] leeway_seconds: 60 jwks_cache_seconds: 300 policy_claim: haltsql_policy allowed_policies: [saas-analytics, support-bot] context_claims: tenant_id: https://corp.example/tenant # a claim name containing dots org_id: org.id # or a dot path required_claims: scope: sql.verify request_context_fields: [user_id] What is checked, in order: Check Rule Failure shape three base64url segments, JSON objects without duplicate members at any depth, no crit header, no "b64": false, at most 16 KiB 401 malformed token algorithm header alg is in algorithms; none and every HMAC algorithm are always rejected 401 key the header's kid names a JWKS key of the matching type (RSA for RS*/PS256, P-256 for ES256, P-384 for ES384, Ed25519 for EdDSA), with use absent or sig, key_ops absent or containing verify, and alg absent or equal; RSA keys must be 2048 to 8192 bits with an odd public exponent of at least 3; Ed25519 keys of small order, keys with private members or duplicate members, and symmetric keys are never loaded; header members that carry a key (jwk, jku, x5u, x5c) are ignored 401 (missing or unknown kid) signature verified with that key 401 iss equals issuer exactly 401 aud a string, or an array of strings, containing one of audiences 401 exp required, a finite number; now < exp + leeway 401 token has expired nbf, iat if present, not later than now + leeway 401 required_claims a string must equal the claim, or be an element of an array claim, or a word of a space-separated claim such as scope; a list requires every value 401 policy policy, or the string value of policy_claim if it is in allowed_policies, or the first policy_from_groups rule the token's groups match (see Policies from IdP groups) 401 context each context_claims path must exist; strings and integral numbers become one value, non-empty arrays of those a set; anything else is rejected 401 The sub claim is recorded as the audit subject; the token itself is never logged or stored.

Discovery: when jwks_uri is not set, it is read from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration (a trailing / of the issuer is removed first). The document's issuer must equal the configured issuer exactly; its jwks_uri must be https (or http with allow_insecure_http, for tests) and carry no credentials. HTTPS uses the system CA store and checks the host name. Responses are limited to 1 MiB and 5 seconds; redirects are not followed. Keys are fetched at startup and cached for jwks_cache_seconds. A token with an unknown kid triggers one refresh, at most once every 30 seconds per provider (key rotation without a restart, without letting random kids hammer the IdP). If a refresh fails, the cached keys stay usable for at most min(jwks_cache_seconds, 3600) seconds past their expiry (stale-while-error). After that, every token from that provider gets 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE until the IdP is reachable again. Failed refreshes are retried at most every 5 seconds. A hot reload keeps the key cache of providers whose configuration did not change.

Pin a provider to one policy with policy: NAME when all its tokens belong to one agent. Use policy_claim + allowed_policies when one IdP issues tokens for several agents: the token cannot select a policy outside the allowlist. Use policy_from_groups when the IdP already sorts callers into groups or roles: no custom claim is needed.
