server: auth: oidc: - name: corp-keycloak issuer: https://sso.corp.example/realms/corp audiences: [haltsql] policy_from_groups: claim: groups # default; a dot path such as realm_access.roles works map: # ordered: the first entry the token matches wins - { group: data-platform-admins, policy: admin-readonly } - { group: support, policy: support-bot } - { group: analysts, policy: saas-analytics } default: null # no match: 401 How a verified token's policy is chosen: Overage check. If the token says its groups did not fit (Azure AD / Entra ID "groups overage", below), it is rejected: 401, reason groups_overage. Lookup. claim is looked up like context_claims: first as one claim name (so an Auth0 namespaced claim https://corp.example/groups works), then as a dot path through nested objects. A missing claim is 401 (missing_claim). Shape. A string is one group and is never split on spaces; an array must contain only strings. Anything else (a number, an object, an array with a non-string) is 401 (bad_claim). First match. The map entries are tried in the order written, and the first one whose group the token has wins, whatever the order of the groups inside the token. A caller in both support and analysts above gets support-bot, so list the most specific or most privileged groups first. Groups are compared exactly (case-sensitive). Default. If nothing matches, default is used. Without a default the token is rejected: 401, reason no_group_policy (the message does not echo the token's groups). The token is still pinned to the selected policy (a request naming another policy gets 403 FORBIDDEN), and context_claims, required_claims and request_context_fields work as for any OIDC provider. IdP Claim to use Notes Okta groups Add a groups claim to the authorization server's access token, with a filter (for example "starts with haltsql-") so it stays small. Keycloak groups, or realm_access.roles / resource_access.<client>.roles Add a Group Membership mapper to the client (or a client scope) with Full group path off, so groups are analysts and not /analysts; enable Add to access token. Realm and client roles are in the access token by default. Keycloak omits the claim for a user in no group, which is a 401 (missing_claim). Auth0 a namespaced claim, e.g. https://corp.example/groups Set it from a post-login Action (api.accessToken.setCustomClaim). Azure AD / Entra ID groups (object ids) or roles (app roles) See overage below. App roles (roles) are usually the better choice: they are scoped to the application and never overflow. Azure AD / Entra ID groups overage. When a user is in more groups than fit in a token (200 for JWTs), Entra ID leaves the groups claim out and adds _claim_names: {"groups": "src1"} and _claim_sources pointing at Microsoft Graph (or, for implicit-flow tokens, hasgroups: true). HaltSQL never calls Graph: a partial or missing group list could select the wrong policy, so such a token is rejected with groups_overage, even if a groups claim is also present. To avoid it, set groupMembershipClaims to ApplicationGroup and assign only the relevant groups to the enterprise application, or map app roles with claim: roles. Group mapping is only as good as the IdP's group administration: anyone who can add a user to data-platform-admins grants that user the admin-readonly policy.

Static tokens remain supported. Store only token_sha256; each token is pinned to one policy. Bind each token to its tenant. Give the token a context and the request body can no longer claim another tenant: server: auth: tokens: - name: acme-agent token_sha256: "..." policy: analytics-agent context: { tenant_id: acme } # fixed for this token request_context_fields: [user_id] # the body may still add these A body field outside request_context_fields gets 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. Use one token per tenant, or OIDC / mTLS when tenants are many. A token with neither context nor request_context_fields is unbound: it authenticates the calling service, and the request body supplies the whole context. Any holder of an unbound token can obtain a verdict for any tenant it names, so use unbound tokens only when the caller is your own trusted backend that takes the tenant from its authenticated session. Audit records carry the context and context_source (authenticated or request) either way.

haltsql_auth_total{method,result}: method is token, oidc, mtls, anonymous or none; result is ok, rejected or unavailable. haltsql_tls_reload_total{result}. OIDC rejections are logged at info with a stable reason code (expired, bad_signature, wrong_audience, groups_overage, no_group_policy, ...) and the peer address. JWKS refresh failures are logged at warn.

Algorithm confusion (alg: none, HS256 signed with the RSA public key) is impossible: HMAC and none are never accepted and the key type must match the algorithm. Tenant spoofing: an OIDC or mTLS caller cannot change its tenant via the request body (CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED). Issuer confusion: a token is only verified by providers whose issuer equals its iss, and then must pass that provider's checks. IdP outage: bounded stale keys, then fail closed. Fail closed: every verification error is a denial; clients must treat any non-200 response as a denial. Group claims: a token whose groups overflowed (Entra ID overage), whose groups claim is missing or malformed, or whose groups match no rule without a default, is rejected. Group membership is read only from the signed token, never from the request.

Signatures, hashes, HMAC, PBKDF2 and base64 come from maintained OCaml libraries (mirage-crypto, digestif, kdf, base64). The compact-JWS decoder, JWK parsing and the claim checks in lib/auth are HaltSQL's own code on top of those primitives.

Replacing lib/auth/jwt.ml and jwk.ml with the jose opam package was evaluated against jose 0.11.0 and not adopted. In that version: RS384, RS512 and PS256 are not verifiable (three of the seven algorithms HaltSQL accepts), and there is no RSA-PSS support. Jws.validate chooses the verification routine from the key type and does not compare it with the header alg, so the algorithm is not bound to the key. Jwk.of_pub_json and Jwks.of_json accept kty: oct keys from a JWKS, which then verify by HMAC-SHA256. HaltSQL never accepts symmetric keys. A non-JSON header, an unknown enc, a JWKS that is not an object and a short ECDSA signature raise exceptions instead of returning errors. Padded and non-canonical base64url, crit headers, sub-2048-bit RSA keys and JWKs carrying private members are accepted. Keeping the checks listed under Threat notes would have required HaltSQL's decoder, key checks and three algorithms to stay, with the library wrapping the same mirage-crypto calls for the other four. The oidc package depends on jose and was not adopted for the same reason. Because the code stays in-tree, it is tested the way a library would be: Known-answer vectors (test/auth/test_jose_vectors.ml). The RS256 and ES256 examples of RFC 7515 appendix A, the Ed25519 example of RFC 8037 appendix A and the RS256 example of RFC 7520 section 4 must verify; the HS256, ES512, PS384 and unsecured examples of the same documents must be rejected. The examples are extracted from the RFC texts by a script, not retyped. A second set holds one token for each of the seven accepted algorithms, signed by pyca/cryptography. Both sets were verified with pyca/cryptography before the tests relied on them (test/auth/vectors/interop_vectors.py check). Negative tables (test/auth/test_jose_negative.ml, about 700 rows in the style of Project Wycheproof). Each row is one malformed signature, key, header or claim with the error it must produce; an exception is a failure. ECDSA: r or s of 0 or at least the group order, DER instead of the fixed-width r || s, wrong lengths, a curve that does not match the algorithm. RSA: signatures shorter or longer than the modulus or not below it, PKCS #1 v1.5 presented as PSS and the reverse, the wrong hash, wrong PSS salt length or MGF hash, hand-built padding errors. EdDSA: S at or above the group order, public keys of small order. Keys: oct, private members, use, key_ops, a contradicting alg, duplicate kids, duplicate members, even or tiny RSA exponents, RSA moduli outside 2048 to 8192 bits. Headers: alg: none in any letter case, crit, "b64": false, and tokens that carry their own key (jwk, jku, x5u, x5c). Claims: exp, nbf and iat as strings, fractions, negative, non-finite and oversized numbers; aud as a string and as an array; the exact leeway boundaries. Fuzzing (test/fuzz/fuzz_jwt.ml, on every dune test). Valid tokens for all seven algorithms and their JWKS are mutated. The decoder, the JWKS parser and verification must never raise, and a token is accepted only if it is byte for byte one of the valid tokens. Three behaviours are deliberate and pinned by those tests: An ECDSA signature is accepted with either of its two s values. JWS has no low-s rule and identity providers emit both. haltsql-server never identifies a token by its signature bytes. When a JWKS has several keys with the same kid, the first one that fits the token's algorithm, in document order, is the only one tried. typ is not interpreted. A token is told apart from other JWTs of the same issuer by aud and required_claims.

An operator who wants no JWT handling inside haltsql-server can leave server.auth.oidc empty and validate tokens in front of it: Envoy's jwt_authn filter, oauth2-proxy, or a service mesh's request authentication. haltsql-server then authenticates the edge itself, not the end user: set client_auth: required and give the proxy's client certificate (or its SPIFFE ID) an entry under server.auth.mtls.identities, which pins the policy and the context as described under mTLS identities. haltsql-server does not read an identity, a policy or a tenant from request headers the edge adds (a forwarded JWT payload, X-Forwarded-User and similar); nothing of the validated token reaches the verdict. Every request through one edge identity therefore gets that identity's one policy and static context, plus the body fields named in its request_context_fields, which the edge must then be trusted to set correctly. When the policy or the tenant has to come from the token, either run one edge identity per tenant or use the built-in OIDC verification.
documents.s: Verifying tokens at the edge instead

documents.t: HaltSQL ships two executables: haltsql: verify SQL, debug denials, validate and convert documents, run policy tests. haltsql-server: the HTTP sidecar (see http-api.md). Every command accepts --help.

Code Meaning 0 Success. For verify/explain: the query is allowed. For validate/test: everything passed. 1 For verify/explain: the query is denied. For test: at least one case failed. For validate: at least one document is invalid. 2 Usage error, or a policy, config, context, or input file could not be loaded. A shadow-mode policy always yields allowed: true, so verify exits 0; would-be denials appear in shadow_reasons.

Check one SQL statement against a policy. haltsql verify --policy FILE [--context JSON | --context-file FILE] [--sql SQL | --file FILE] [--json] haltsql verify --policy FILE --batch [--jobs N] [--context JSON | --context-file FILE] Flag Meaning -p, --policy FILE Policy document (YAML or JSON). Required. -c, --context JSON Context as a JSON object, for example '{"tenant_id":"acme"}'. Values are strings, integers, or arrays of those. --context-file FILE Read the context from a YAML or JSON file. -s, --sql SQL The SQL string to check. -f, --file FILE Read the SQL string from a file. --json Print the verdict as JSON (see verdict.md). Without it, ALLOWED or DENIED is printed with the reasons, hints, and values to bind. --batch Read JSONL requests from stdin and write one JSON verdict per line. -j, --jobs N With --batch: verify on N OCaml domains in parallel. Output order is preserved. Default 1. If neither --sql nor --file is given, the SQL is read from stdin. If no context is given, the context is empty, and any policy with tenancy keys will deny with E_CONTEXT_MISSING. Examples: haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ --sql 'SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10' echo 'SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10' | \ haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context-file ctx.json --json In scripts, branch on the exit code: if haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context-file ctx.json --file q.sql; then echo "allowed" else case $? in 1) echo "denied" ;; *) echo "error" ;; esac fi

--batch checks many statements with one process. Each input line is a JSON object: {"id": "q1", "sql": "SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10", "context": {"tenant_id": "acme"}} {"id": "q2", "sql": "SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10", "context": {"tenant_id": "acme"}} Field Required Meaning id yes Any JSON string or number; echoed back so you can match results. sql yes The SQL string. context no Context for this line. If omitted, the --context / --context-file value is used. Each output line is the compact verdict JSON with "id" as the first field, in input order (also with --jobs). Blank lines are skipped: {"id":"q1","allowed":true,"reasons":[],"bind_params":[{"param":1,"value":"acme"}], ...} {"id":"q2","allowed":false,"reasons":[{"code":"E_TENANT_MISSING", ...}], ...} A line that cannot be read (invalid JSON, missing sql, invalid context) produces {"id": ..., "error": "message"} and does not stop the batch. In batch mode the exit code is 0 once all lines are processed, whatever the verdicts, and 2 if the policy or default context cannot be loaded; check each line's allowed field.

Same inputs as verify (except --batch and --json), but prints a human-readable report for debugging a denial: haltsql explain --policy FILE [--context JSON | --context-file FILE] [--sql SQL | --file FILE] The report shows: the verdict and the policy name and version; the statement kind; the tables and columns the statement touches; each reason with its code, message, position in the SQL (with a caret under the offending text when the position is known), and the hint; the values to bind, when allowed in bound mode. Exit codes are the same as verify. The output format is for people and may change between releases; use verify --json in scripts.

Check one or more documents of any kind. The kind is detected from the kind field: Policy, Config, TestSuite, Catalog, or Scenario. haltsql validate FILE... All errors are printed with file, line, column, and key path. Exit code 0 if all documents are valid, 1 if any is invalid, 2 if a file cannot be read.

Convert a document between YAML and JSON without changing its meaning. haltsql convert FILE --to json|yaml [-o OUT] The result is written to stdout, or to OUT with -o/--output. The input is validated first; an invalid document is not converted. A converted policy has the same policy_version as the original.

Write the JSON Schemas (draft 2020-12) for every document kind, for editor autocomplete and CI validation. haltsql schema export --out DIR Writes files such as policy.schema.json, config.schema.json, catalog.schema.json, and scenario.schema.json into DIR (created if needed).

Run policy test suites (kind: TestSuite). haltsql test SUITE_FILE... [--filter TAG] [-v] --filter TAG runs only cases tagged TAG; -v/--verbose also shows the reasons for passing cases. Each case is checked against the suite's policy. A case passes when the verdict matches expect, every code in codes appears in the reasons, and (when given) bind equals the returned bind_params. Failing cases are printed with the reason. Exit code 0 if all cases pass, 1 if any fail, 2 if a suite or its policy cannot be loaded. See testing.md for the format.

Report risky or suspicious settings in a policy: tables exposing all columns, unused tenancy keys, shadow mode, a missing require_limit, large function allowlists, and tables missing from the catalog. Exits 0 unless the policy fails to load (2). haltsql lint-policy FILE

Print the effective configuration after merging the config file, HALTSQL_* environment variables, and defaults. Secrets are replaced by "<redacted>". ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} and ${gcp-sm:...} placeholders are resolved from the config's secrets section first (see secrets.md); haltsql validate does the same for kind: Config documents. haltsql config show --config FILE (--effective is accepted for compatibility; the output is always the merged result.)

haltsql schema check -p POLICY (--dsn DSN | --snapshot FILE) [--strict] [--json] compares a policy with the live schema and exits 1 on drift (a stale catalog:, missing tables or columns, a shadowing relation); see schema-and-pii.md. Snapshot a live Postgres catalog into a Catalog document (schema pull, read-only, TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256), import PII labels from dbt, DataHub, Unity Catalog, Atlan or Collibra exports (schema import), or fetch them from a live data catalog API (schema fetch; the token comes from an environment variable or a file, never the command line). See schema-and-pii.md. haltsql schema pull --dsn postgres://... -o catalog.json haltsql schema import --from dbt|datahub|unity|atlan|collibra FILE -o pii.json haltsql schema fetch --from PROVIDER --url https://... [--token-env VAR | --token-file FILE] \ [--service S] [--database D] [--schema S]... -o pii.json [--snapshot-out fetched.json] --snapshot-out writes a non-authoritative snapshot (metadata.authoritative: false): policy draft accepts it and drafts without catalog: (so SELECT * stays denied), and a policy catalog: refuses it.
documents.s: haltsql schema pull / schema import / schema fetch

documents.t: Write a reviewable starter policy from a catalog snapshot and PII manifest: explicit column lists without PII columns, tenant columns, and require_limit. See schema-and-pii.md.

Generate idempotent PostgreSQL role, grant and row-level-security DDL from a policy (rls generate), and report drift between a live database and the policy (rls check; exit 1 on drift). See rls-generation.md.

Build, sign (Ed25519), verify and inspect signed policy bundles: bundle keygen, bundle build, bundle sign, bundle verify, bundle inspect; publish and fetch them as OCI artifacts with bundle push --oci REF and bundle pull --oci REF (exit code 3 when the registry is unreachable or refuses the request; see policy-bundles.md). The server loads bundles listed under policies and refuses any whose signature does not verify. See policy-bundles.md and, for CI, policy-ci.md.

Shadow-mode analytics over audit records written by haltsql-server or haltsql-proxy (files, directories, or -), and conservative policy suggestions (--suggest), optionally applied to a copy of a policy (--apply-to FILE -o OUT). Exit 1 if applying would turn a tenancy denial into an allow or the patched policy does not validate. See shadow-reports.md. haltsql report audit.jsonl --since 7d --suggest --policy-file policies/shop.yaml

Verify the hash chain of audit logs: files, rotated sets (--concat), mixed container logs (--mixed), downloaded object-sink directories (with --spool), and s3://bucket/prefix read directly. Exit 0 when every chain verifies, 1 when one is broken, 2 on usage or input errors. See audit-verify.md. haltsql audit verify /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl haltsql audit verify --json s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/
Print the HaltSQL version, the Postgres grammar version of the vendored libpg_query, and the OCaml version. --json prints them as JSON. haltsql version [--json]

Run the HTTP sidecar. haltsql-server --config FILE [flags] haltsql-server --policy FILE [--policy FILE ...] [flags] At least one of --config or --policy is required. Flag Meaning --config FILE Config document (see config-reference.md). -p, --policy FILE Load a policy file (repeatable). Added to the config's policies; a policy with the same name replaces the config's. --listen HOST:PORT Override server.listen (default 127.0.0.1:8080). --allow-unauthenticated Accept requests without a bearer token. Local development only. --default-policy NAME Policy used by unauthenticated requests. --log-level LEVEL debug, info, warn, or error. --log-format FORMAT json or text. Logs go to stderr. --audit SINK stdout, file:PATH, or none (repeatable; replaces the config's sinks). --log-raw-sql Include the raw SQL in audit records. --watch / --no-watch Reload when policy or config files change (polled every 2 seconds). --max-request-bytes N Maximum request body size (HTTP 413 above). A body whose declared Content-Length is over the limit is rejected before any of it is read, and before authentication. --max-connections N Maximum open client connections (default 1024). At the limit the server stops accepting and new clients wait in the listen backlog. The --health-listen port has its own budget of 64. --request-timeout SECONDS Time allowed to receive a request's head and body once its first byte arrives (default 30). Request heads are capped at 64 KiB. --idle-timeout SECONDS How long a keep-alive connection may stay silent, and how long a response write may stall (default 60). --shutdown-timeout SECONDS How long SIGTERM waits for in-flight requests to finish (default 15). --no-metrics Disable GET /metrics. --health-listen HOST:PORT Extra plain-HTTP listener serving only /healthz and /readyz (for probes when the main port requires client certificates). Flags override HALTSQL_* environment variables, which override the config file. The server reloads all policies atomically on SIGHUP (keeping the last good set on error), and shuts down gracefully on SIGTERM or SIGINT. Exit code 0 after a graceful shutdown, 2 if the configuration cannot be loaded or the listener cannot start. Quick local start: haltsql-server --policy policy.yaml --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 --allow-unauthenticated For anything beyond localhost, turn on built-in TLS with server.tls (see Authentication and TLS), or terminate TLS in a proxy or service mesh in front of the server.

The HaltSQL verifier never connects to the database: it parses SQL with the PostgreSQL 17 grammar and checks it against your policy. The question for a Postgres flavour is therefore whether what HaltSQL proves about a query (tenant filter, allowed columns, no side effects) still holds when that flavour executes it, and whether haltsql-proxy works in front of it. This page lists what has actually been run. A row says "not yet run" until someone runs it; nothing here is extrapolated.

Every engine runs the same haltlab scenario as pr-smoke (the saas_shared fixture, 8 tenants, seed 42, 200 benign and 400 adversarial generated queries; see testing.md and lab/README.md). A run has three parts, all against the same engine: Oracle self-test. The workload runs with an allow-everything stand-in verifier. The database oracles (RLS differential, honeytokens, column-privilege role, side-effect checks) must catch tenant escapes, column leaks and side effects on that engine. Without this, a clean HaltSQL result on an engine could just mean that the oracles do not work there. HaltSQL. haltsql verify --batch decides. Every allowed query is executed under the oracles inside a read-only, repeatable-read transaction that is always rolled back. The run passes only with zero escapes, zero side effects and zero column leaks. Proxy parity. The workload goes through a live haltsql-proxy whose upstream is the engine (extended protocol, psycopg/libpq). The client sends another tenant's id for every tenancy parameter. The proxy must make the same decision as the CLI for every query, and must return exactly the rows of direct execution, with no foreign honeytokens. Run it yourself: cd lab && make venv compat/run.sh up && compat/run.sh local all && compat/run.sh down See lab/compat/README.md for details.

Local engines in Docker (compose profile compat). Run on 2026-11-07 on an arm64 Mac with HaltSQL built from branch feat/enterprise-adoption. Engine Version Scenario Executed Escapes Side effects Proxy parity Notes PostgreSQL 18 (postgres:18.4-alpine) 18.4 compat-pg18 268 of 600 0 0 600/600 same decisions, 261 executed through the proxy, 0 escapes Oracle self-test caught 167 escapes, 37 column leaks and 34 side effects. Supabase Postgres (supabase/postgres:17.11.0.018) 17.11 compat-supabase 268 of 600 0 0 600/600, 261 executed, 0 escapes The lab connects as Supabase's postgres role, which is not a superuser (it has CREATEROLE, CREATEDB and BYPASSRLS), as on hosted Supabase. Self-test: 167 / 37 / 34. AlloyDB Omni (google/alloydbomni:17.10.0) 17.10 compat-alloydb-omni 268 of 600 0 0 600/600, 261 executed, 0 escapes Self-test: 167 / 37 / 34. Citus 14.2 (citusdata/citus:14.2.0-alpine) 18.4 compat-citus 268 of 600 0 0 600/600, 261 executed, 0 escapes Single node. Tenant tables are co-located single-shard distributed tables and currencies is a reference table. Self-test: 167 / 37 / 34. amd64 image, emulated. See Citus. TimescaleDB 2.31.0 (timescale/timescaledb:2.31.0-pg17) 17.11 compat-timescaledb 268 of 600 0 0 600/600, 261 executed, 0 escapes app.audit_events (27 chunks) and app.orgs (12 chunks) are hypertables. Self-test: 167 / 37 / 34. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL - compat-aurora-postgresql not yet run (workflow provided) Neon - compat-neon not yet run (workflow provided) Supabase (hosted) - compat-supabase-cloud not yet run (workflow provided) Google AlloyDB - compat-alloydb not yet run (workflow provided) Amazon Redshift - grammar suite only not applicable Not supported. See Amazon Redshift. How to read the table: Executed: queries HaltSQL allowed, all of which were run under the oracles. The other 332 were denied. The false-positive rate on benign queries was 0.030 on every engine. 7 execution errors on every engine: an allowed query failed in the database with SQLSTATE 42P18 ("could not determine data type of parameter $1"). These come from the query generator (an untyped parameter) and happen identically on the PostgreSQL 17 baseline: pr-smoke on 17.11 also executed 268 queries with the same 7 errors, 0 escapes and 0 side effects. They are not counted as executed through the proxy, which is why that count is 261. The proxy column counts all 600 queries: the proxy allowed exactly the 268 the CLI allowed and denied the other 332 with SQLSTATE 42501.

The fixture is installed exactly as on stock Postgres. Some engines then convert it to their native storage, after the data is loaded so the query generators see the same catalog everywhere (lab/compat/engines.py). Row-level security, ownership and column grants are kept, so the oracles judge the converted tables. PostgreSQL 18, Supabase, AlloyDB Omni: no changes. TimescaleDB: CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb. Each tenant table with a NOT NULL created_at timestamptz, a single-column primary key and no incoming foreign keys becomes a hypertable with 30-day chunks and its data migrated. Its primary key is widened to (id, created_at), as TimescaleDB requires. RLS on the hypertable applies to queries through it. Citus: see below.

The Citus run uses one node: the coordinator holds all shards. Tenant tables become co-located single-shard distributed tables (create_distributed_table(t, NULL), the building block of Citus schema-based sharding). Global tables become reference tables. Foreign keys are dropped for the conversion and then restored. Hash-distributed tables were not used, for two reasons: The fixture keeps NULL tenant ids on purpose, and Citus rejects NULL distribution keys. Multi-shard queries and repartition joins run over extra connections. Those connections do not carry the transaction's SET LOCAL ROLE and app.* settings, so the RLS and column oracles cannot judge those queries. What the Citus result shows: HaltSQL's verdicts hold for queries that the Citus router planner runs in the session's own backend. It does not cover multi-node clusters or multi-shard execution. Citus itself changes two settings inside the transaction: enable_self_join_elimination while planning any distributed query, and citus.enable_local_execution while running EXPLAIN. The side-effect oracle ignores those two settings on Citus only. Every other setting is still compared, and HaltSQL denies SET and set_config anyway.

Aurora PostgreSQL, Neon, hosted Supabase and AlloyDB could not be reached from the environment where this page was produced. .github/workflows/compat-cloud.yml (manual workflow_dispatch) runs the same three parts against each service. It reads the DSN from an optional repository secret and skips a service whose secret is unset: Service Secret Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL HALTLAB_DSN_AURORA_POSTGRESQL Neon HALTLAB_DSN_NEON Supabase (hosted) HALTLAB_DSN_SUPABASE_CLOUD Google AlloyDB HALTLAB_DSN_ALLOYDB To run one by hand: HALTLAB_DSN='postgresql://admin:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/postgres?sslmode=require' \ lab/compat/run.sh cloud neon Requirements and effects: Use a disposable server, never production. The DSN's role must be able to CREATE DATABASE and CREATE ROLE. Each run creates and drops haltlab_compat_<engine>_pg17 and haltlab_compat_<engine>_proxy_pg17. It creates the NOLOGIN roles haltlab_owner, haltlab_rls and haltlab_cols, and grants them to the DSN's role. A cloud scenario without HALTLAB_DSN refuses to run. It does not fall back to the local lab server. The proxy's upstream TLS follows sslmode: require stays require. verify-full needs sslrootcert=FILE. verify-ca is upgraded to verify-full. prefer and allow are refused. Reports never contain the DSN. Add results to the table above only from such a run.

Redshift is not supported. It speaks the Postgres wire protocol, but its SQL forked from PostgreSQL 8.0.2. It also differs in ways that matter here: Area Redshift What HaltSQL does Grammar TOP n, QUALIFY, MINUS, APPROXIMATE COUNT(DISTINCT ...), PIVOT/UNPIVOT, GROUP BY ALL Not in the PG17 grammar: denied with E_PARSE. DDL and data movement DISTKEY, SORTKEY, DISTSTYLE, ENCODE, IDENTITY(seed, step), WITH NO SCHEMA BINDING, UNLOAD, COPY ... IAM_ROLE E_PARSE. Grouping ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS (valid in both) E_UNSUPPORTED: the analyzer does not model them. Names three-part database.schema.table E_UNSUPPORTED. Functions and pseudo-columns GETDATE, SYSDATE, NVL, NVL2, DECODE, LEN, LISTAGG, MEDIAN, RATIO_TO_REPORT, DATEADD/DATEDIFF/DATE_PART with a bare date part, CONVERT_TIMEZONE, MONTHS_BETWEEN, REGEXP_SUBSTR, STRTOL, JSON_PARSE, IS_VALID_JSON, PG_LAST_QUERY_ID, CURRENT_USER_ID Unknown to the policy: E_FUNCTION_DENIED, E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED or E_COLUMN_DENIED (a bare date part such as day reads as a column). SUPER / PartiQL c.payload.key, FROM t, t.items i Read as PostgreSQL names, which do not resolve: E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED, E_TABLE_DENIED. System catalog STV_*, SVV_*, SVL_* E_TABLE_DENIED. Row-level security CREATE RLS POLICY ... WITH (...) USING (...), ATTACH RLS POLICY ... TO ROLE Not PostgreSQL RLS: E_PARSE. haltsql rls output does not apply. Transactions and roles no SET ROLE, serializable isolation only The lab oracles cannot run, so there is no lab scenario for Redshift. test/corpus/compat-redshift.suite.yaml pins this behavior. It has 71 cases: 45 Redshift-only statements, all denied (fail closed) with the codes above. 26 common analytics queries written in SQL that is valid on both PostgreSQL 17 and Redshift. They are allowed with the usual tenant proof and bind_params. lab/compat/run.sh redshift runs the suite, and so does the workflow's redshift job. What this does not show: That HaltSQL's semantics match Redshift's. The portable cases were checked against the PG17 grammar and the policy, not run on a Redshift cluster. That haltsql-proxy works in front of Redshift. Its authentication methods and protocol details were not tested. Do not rely on HaltSQL as a security control for Redshift.

A config controls how the CLI and haltsql-server run: where to listen, TLS, who may call (static tokens, OIDC, mTLS), which policies to load (files, inline, signed bundles, or signed bundles pulled from a registry, S3 or HTTPS), audit logging (stdout, files, S3, GCS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Kafka), an optional Open Policy Agent check, the admin API, metrics and OpenTelemetry, and where secrets come from. It is a YAML or JSON document with kind: Config, loaded with the same rules as a policy (see policy-reference.md): unknown and duplicate keys are errors, and errors are located by file, line, and key path. A config does not change what SQL is allowed. That is the policy's job.

apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Config server: listen: 127.0.0.1:8080 # pod-local; TLS is terminated in front (see below) auth: allow_unauthenticated: false tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${env:HALTSQL_ANALYTICS_TOKEN_HASH} policy: analytics-agent # each token is pinned to one policy - name: support-bot token_sha256: ${file:/run/secrets/support-bot.sha256} policy: support-bot policies: - path: ./policies/analytics-agent.yaml - path: ./policies/support-bot.json # formats can be mixed default_policy: null reload: watch: true audit: sinks: - type: file path: /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl log_raw_sql: false telemetry: metrics: prometheus: true logging: level: info format: json limits: max_request_bytes: 1048576 Top-level keys: apiVersion (haltsql.dev/v1), kind (Config), server, policies, default_policy, reload, audit, telemetry, logging, limits, secrets, opa. Any other key is an error. A larger example using the enterprise features: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Config server: listen: 0.0.0.0:8443 tls: cert: /etc/haltsql/tls/server.crt key: /etc/haltsql/tls/server.key client_ca: /etc/haltsql/tls/clients-ca.pem client_auth: optional # mTLS identities below, OIDC for everyone else min_version: "1.3" auth: oidc: - name: corp-okta issuer: https://corp.okta.com/oauth2/default audiences: [haltsql] policy_claim: haltsql_policy allowed_policies: [saas-analytics, support-bot] context_claims: tenant_id: https://corp.example/tenant user_id: sub required_claims: scope: sql.verify mtls: identities: - spiffe_id: spiffe://corp.example/ns/agents/sa/analytics policy: saas-analytics context: { tenant_id: acme } policies: - path: ./policies/support-bot.yaml - bundle: ./bundles/prod.haltsqlbundle public_keys: [./keys/release.pub] audit: sinks: - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 object_lock: { mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 365 } credentials: { source: web_identity } telemetry: otlp: endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318 headers: authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/otel#token}" secrets: vault: address: https://vault.corp.example:8200 auth: { method: kubernetes, role: haltsql }

Key Type Default Meaning server.listen string host:port 127.0.0.1:8080 Address the HTTP server binds to. server.tls mapping none Built-in TLS (see server.tls). Without it, terminate TLS in front of the server (Envoy, nginx, or a service mesh) and bind to 127.0.0.1 or a pod-local address. See authentication.md. server.auth.tokens list [] Bearer tokens (see below). server.auth.oidc list [] OpenID Connect providers whose JWTs are accepted (see server.auth.oidc). server.auth.mtls mapping none Client-certificate identities (see server.auth.mtls). server.auth.allow_unauthenticated boolean false Accept requests without a token. For local development only. server.admin mapping disabled Admin API (see server.admin). Each token entry: Key Type Meaning name string Label used in logs and audit events. Never the secret. Must be unique. token_sha256 hex string SHA-256 of the bearer token as 64 lower-case hex characters. The token itself is never stored. Must be unique. policy string Name (metadata.name) of the one policy this token may use. context mapping Optional. Context values bound to this token (for example tenant_id: acme). The request body cannot supply or override them. request_context_fields list Optional. Context fields the request body may still supply. Setting this or context binds the token: any other body field gets 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. Without either key the body supplies the whole context (see authentication.md). A token can only use its pinned policy, so a compromised agent cannot pick a looser one. Generate a token and its hash with, for example: token="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" printf '%s' "$token" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1 # goes in token_sha256

Key Type Default Meaning cert path or PEM none Server certificate chain. Required together with key. key path or PEM none Private key. Required together with cert. Always shown as <redacted> by config show. client_ca path or PEM none CA bundle used to verify client certificates (enables mTLS). client_auth none, optional, required none Whether client certificates are requested. optional and required need client_ca. min_version "1.2", "1.3" "1.2" Minimum TLS version. Relative paths are resolved against the config file's directory. A value that starts with -----BEGIN (for example from ${file:...} or a secret provider) is used as inline PEM. Setting client_ca, client_auth or min_version without cert and key is an error.

Each entry describes one OpenID Connect provider. A request whose bearer token is a JWT signed by the provider is authenticated by it. Key Type Default Meaning name string required Unique provider name, used in logs and audit events. issuer URL required Must equal the token's iss. https only (no credentials, query or fragment); http only with allow_insecure_http: true. audiences list required Non-empty; the token's aud must contain one of them. jwks_uri URL discovered Default: jwks_uri from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration. algorithms list [RS256, ES256] Subset of RS256 RS384 RS512 PS256 ES256 ES384 EdDSA. none and HS* are rejected. leeway_seconds integer 0-300 60 Clock skew allowed for exp, nbf, iat. jwks_cache_seconds integer 10-86400 300 How long fetched keys are cached. policy string none Pin every token from this provider to one policy. policy_claim claim path none Instead of policy: the claim whose value names the policy. Needs allowed_policies. allowed_policies list none The only policies policy_claim may select (non-empty). policy_from_groups mapping none Instead of policy / policy_claim: pick the policy from the token's groups (see policy_from_groups). context_claims map {} Context field -> claim path. The path is first tried as one claim name (so https://corp.example/tenant works), then as a dot path (org.id). required_claims map {} Claim -> string or list. A string must equal the claim, or be contained in it when the claim is an array or a space-separated string such as scope. A list requires every value. request_context_fields list [] Context fields the request body may still supply. They must not also appear in context_claims. allow_insecure_http boolean false Allow http issuer and JWKS URLs. For tests only. Exactly one of policy, policy_claim or policy_from_groups is required. Every referenced policy must be loaded (see policies for bundles). policy_from_groups​ Maps IdP groups (or roles) to policies, so one provider can serve several kinds of caller without a custom claim: server: auth: oidc: - name: corp-keycloak issuer: https://sso.corp.example/realms/corp audiences: [haltsql] policy_from_groups: claim: groups # default; dotted paths like realm_access.roles work map: # ordered: the first entry the token matches wins - { group: data-platform-admins, policy: admin-readonly } - { group: analysts, policy: saas-analytics } - { group: support, policy: support-bot } default: null # no match: the token is rejected (401) Key Type Default Meaning claim claim path groups Claim holding the groups. Looked up like context_claims paths: first as one claim name, then as a dot path (realm_access.roles). map list required Non-empty, ordered list of {group, policy}. Groups are compared exactly (case-sensitive) and must be unique. default string none Policy for a token that matches no entry. Without it such a token is rejected. The claim may be a string (one group; it is never split on spaces) or an array of strings. A missing claim, or a claim of any other shape (a number, an object, an array containing a non-string), rejects the token. The map is walked in order and the first entry whose group the token has wins, so put the most privileged or most specific groups first. policy_from_groups cannot be combined with policy, policy_claim or allowed_policies. Every policy in map and default must resolve, with the same rule as other references (bundles with name_prefix, see policies).

server: auth: mtls: identities: - spiffe_id: spiffe://corp.example/ns/agents/sa/analytics # exact URI SAN policy: saas-analytics context: { tenant_id: acme, region: [eu-1, eu-2] } request_context_fields: [user_id] - subject_cn: support-bot # exact subject CN policy: support-bot Each identity has exactly one of spiffe_id (a valid spiffe:// URI with a lower-case trust domain) or subject_cn, a policy, an optional static context (strings, integers or non-empty lists of those) and request_context_fields (default [], must not repeat a static context field). Identities must be unique. Non-empty identities require server.tls.client_ca and server.tls.client_auth set to optional or required.

A list of policies to load. Each entry is one of: Form Meaning { path: FILE } Load a policy file (YAML or JSON). Relative paths are resolved against the config file's directory. { inline: { ...policy document... } } Embed a whole policy document, so a small deployment can be one file. { bundle: FILE, public_keys: [...], name_prefix: STR } A signed .haltsqlbundle. public_keys (non-empty) lists trusted ed25519 keys, each a file path, inline PEM (-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----) or the base64 of the 32 raw key bytes. name_prefix (optional) is prepended to the names of the bundle's policies. { bundle_source: {...}, public_keys: [...], ... } A signed bundle fetched from an OCI registry, S3 (or an S3-compatible store) or HTTPS, and polled for updates. See bundle_source. Policy names (metadata.name) must be unique. Every token's policy must name a loaded policy. bundle_source​ policies: - bundle_source: oci: ghcr.io/corp/haltsql-policies:prod # or registry/repo@sha256:<digest> public_keys: [./keys/release.pub] # mandatory name_prefix: prod. poll_interval_s: 60 cache_dir: /var/cache/haltsql/bundles auth: { username: robot$haltsql, password: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/registry#password}" } - bundle_source: s3: bucket: corp-haltsql-bundles key: prod/policies.haltsqlbundle region: us-east-1 endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:9000 # S3-compatible store such as MinIO credentials: { source: static, access_key_id: "${env:BUNDLE_AK}", secret_access_key: "${env:BUNDLE_SK}" } public_keys: [./keys/release.pub] - bundle_source: https: https://bundles.corp.example/prod.haltsqlbundle public_keys: [./keys/release.pub] auth: { token: "${env:BUNDLE_TOKEN}" } Key Type Default Meaning bundle_source mapping required Exactly one of oci, s3 or https (below). public_keys list required Trusted ed25519 keys, as for bundle. Signature verification is mandatory: a source without keys is a config error. name_prefix string none Prepended to the names of the bundle's policies (1-64 of letters, digits, ., _, -, starting with a letter or digit). poll_interval_s integer 10-86400 60 Seconds between update checks. cache_dir path none Directory holding the last verified bundle (relative to the config file). auth mapping none oci and https only: {token} (bearer token) or {username, password}. Not allowed for s3, which uses s3.credentials. bundle_source forms: Form Meaning oci: REF An OCI artifact. REF is registry[:port]/repository:tag, registry[:port]/repository@sha256:<64 hex> (or sha512:<128 hex>), or both (:tag@digest). The registry host is mandatory (there is no implicit Docker Hub): it must contain a . or a : or be localhost. Repository components are lower-case letters, digits, ., _ and -. Pin a digest for immutable deployments. plain_http: true With oci only: talk plain HTTP to the registry. Allowed only for loopback registries (localhost, 127.x, [::1]), for local tests. Default false. s3: {bucket, key, region, endpoint, credentials} An S3 object. bucket, key and region are required; key must not start with /. endpoint is an S3-compatible URL (MinIO). credentials has the same shape as for S3 audit sinks (env by default). https: URL An https URL (plain http only for loopback addresses). No credentials, query or fragment in the URL; use auth. Two entries with the same source are an error. poll_interval_s, cache_dir and auth are only allowed with bundle_source; public_keys and name_prefix only with bundle or bundle_source. Bundles and bundle sources are parsed and checked when the config loads, but they are fetched, verified and loaded by the server afterwards. So when a config lists bundles (of either form), a policy name used by a token, OIDC provider (including policy_from_groups map entries and default), mTLS identity or default_policy that is not one of the plain policies is accepted at config load time. If every bundle and bundle source has a name_prefix, such a name must start with one of them. The server re-validates every reference after loading the bundles and refuses to start (or rejects the reload) if one is still missing. If any policy fails to load, the whole config fails to load (at startup) or the reload is rejected and the last good set stays active (at runtime).
Name of the policy used for unauthenticated requests when allow_unauthenticated is true, and for requests that name no policy. Must name a loaded policy. Default: none.

Key Type Default Meaning reload.watch boolean false Watch the config and policy files (polled every 2 seconds) and reload on change. The server also reloads on SIGHUP. A reload is atomic: either all policies are swapped in, or none are. What a reload (file change, SIGHUP, or a new bundle from a bundle source) applies, and what needs a restart: Applied on reload Restart only policies (paths, inline policies, local bundle files and their signatures) and default_policy server.listen, the health listener server.auth.tokens, allow_unauthenticated enabling or disabling server.tls (certificates and keys themselves reload) server.auth.oidc (including policy_from_groups; key caches of unchanged providers are kept) and server.auth.mtls audit (all sinks, log_raw_sql): two writers on one chain would fork it. A reload that changes audit.sinks keeps the running sinks, logs a warning and sets audit_restart_pending in GET /v1/admin/status server.tls certificate, key and client CA files the list of bundle_source entries: adding, removing or changing an entry needs a restart (the running pollers keep their settings; new bundles they fetch are applied as reloads) opa (url, decision path, timeout, on_error, headers) limits, logging, telemetry.metrics.prometheus server.admin (enabling, callers, report_window, max_tracked_queries; disabling it drops the report window) telemetry.otlp A reload that fails (any load, validation, reference or TLS error) changes nothing: the last good configuration stays active and the failure is logged and counted in haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}.

Key Type Default Meaning audit.sinks list [{type: stdout}] Where audit events go: stdout, file, s3, gcs, elasticsearch or kafka (below). audit.log_raw_sql boolean false Include the raw SQL in audit events. Off by default because SQL can contain sensitive literals; events always include sql_sha256 and the fingerprint. Every sink accepts on_error: fail_closed (default; if the sink cannot be written, requests are refused with HTTP 503) or buffer (records are kept in memory and retried). Sink Keys stdout type, on_error file type, path (relative to the config file), on_error s3 type, bucket, region (required); prefix (default haltsql/audit/), endpoint (S3-compatible URL, e.g. MinIO), object_lock: {mode: GOVERNANCE|COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 1-36500}, batch, credentials, spool_dir, on_error gcs type, bucket (required); prefix (default haltsql/audit/), batch, credentials, spool_dir, on_error batch: max_records (1-100000, default 500) and max_seconds (1-3600, default 10). spool_dir (s3/gcs, optional, relative to the config file; one directory per sink, on persistent storage): records are spooled there before upload, and the hash-chain head and object sequence number are persisted, so after a restart or crash the chain continues instead of starting again at genesis, and a batch uploaded just before a crash is not stored twice. Without it, each process starts a new chain (see Audit sinks). S3 credentials.source: env (default; the standard AWS_* variables), static (needs access_key_id and secret_access_key, optional session_token; use secret placeholders and never write keys in the file), web_identity (IRSA / OIDC federation) or instance (instance profile). The static keys are only allowed with source: static. GCS credentials.source: metadata (default) or service_account_file (needs file, relative to the config file). Bucket names are validated (3-63 characters; S3: lower-case letters, digits, . and -; GCS also _). A prefix must not start with / or contain ... Streaming sinks: elasticsearch and kafka​ The elasticsearch and kafka sinks stream records as they are written instead of uploading objects. They accept a third on_error value and their own batch shape: Key Type Default Meaning on_error fail_closed, buffer, drop fail_closed fail_closed refuses requests (HTTP 503) when records cannot be delivered. buffer keeps up to max_buffer_records in memory and retries; when the buffer is full the sink fails closed. drop discards records that cannot be delivered (they are counted and logged); requests keep being served without an audit trail in this sink, so use it only next to another fail-closed sink. max_buffer_records integer 1-1000000 10000 (or batch.max_records if larger) Only with on_error: buffer. Must be at least batch.max_records. batch.max_records integer 1-100000 500 Records per request at most. batch.max_bytes integer 1024-104857600 5242880 (5 MiB) Request body size at most. batch.flush_interval_ms integer 10-60000 1000 Milliseconds before a partial batch is sent. elasticsearch (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, bulk API): audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch urls: [https://es-1.corp.example:9200, https://es-2.corp.example:9200] data_stream: logs-haltsql-prod # or index: haltsql-audit auth: { api_key: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/es#api_key}" } pipeline: haltsql-enrich tls: { ca_file: ./certs/es-ca.pem } timeout_ms: 10000 batch: { max_records: 500, max_bytes: 5242880, flush_interval_ms: 1000 } on_error: buffer max_buffer_records: 20000 Key Type Default Meaning url / urls URL / list required Exactly one of them. Node URLs: https, or plain http only for loopback addresses. No credentials, query or fragment (a path prefix is allowed). urls must be non-empty and unique. index / data_stream string required Exactly one of them. Lower-case letters, digits, ., -, _, +; at most 255 characters; not starting with -, _ or +; not . or ... auth mapping none {api_key} (the encoded key, sent as Authorization: ApiKey <value>) or {username, password} (basic auth; the user name must not contain :). Use secret placeholders. pipeline string none Ingest pipeline run on every record (letters, digits, ., _, -). tls.ca_file path or PEM system roots CA bundle for the cluster certificate. Only allowed when a URL is https. timeout_ms integer 100-120000 10000 Request timeout. kafka (one message per audit record): audit: sinks: - type: kafka brokers: [kafka-1.corp.example:9093, kafka-2.corp.example:9093] topic: haltsql.audit client_id: haltsql-prod acks: all tls: { ca_file: /etc/haltsql/kafka/ca.pem } sasl: { mechanism: scram-sha-512, username: haltsql, password: "${env:KAFKA_PASSWORD}" } on_error: fail_closed Key Type Default Meaning brokers list required Non-empty, unique host:port bootstrap brokers (DNS name, IPv4, or [IPv6]). topic string required 1-249 of letters, digits, ., _, -; not . or ... client_id string haltsql Kafka client id (1-255 of letters, digits, ., _, -). acks all, 1 all Acknowledgements required per batch. 0 (fire and forget) is rejected: audit records must be acknowledged. tls mapping none (plain text) enabled (default true when tls is given), ca_file, and a client certificate as cert_file + key_file (both or neither). The other keys are only allowed when enabled is true. Values are paths (relative to the config file) or inline PEM. sasl mapping none mechanism (plain, scram-sha-256, scram-sha-512), username and password (all required). plain without tls is rejected unless every broker is a loopback address, because it sends the password in clear text. The streaming sinks sit in the same audit.sinks list as the others and can be mixed with them; listing only streaming sinks means no stdout sink.

An optional Open Policy Agent check that runs after HaltSQL has allowed a query: opa: url: https://opa.corp.example:8181 decision_path: haltsql/allow timeout_ms: 500 on_error: deny headers: Authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/opa#token}" tls: { ca_file: ./certs/opa-ca.pem } Key Type Default Meaning url URL required OPA base URL. https, or plain http only for loopback addresses (an OPA sidecar on 127.0.0.1). No credentials, query or fragment. decision_path string required The decision below /v1/data, as Rego identifiers separated by /, without a leading /: haltsql/allow queries POST <url>/v1/data/haltsql/allow. timeout_ms integer 10-5000 500 Decision request timeout. on_error deny, allow_haltsql_verdict deny What happens when OPA cannot be reached, times out, or answers with an error or an undefined/non-boolean decision. deny refuses the query; allow_haltsql_verdict keeps HaltSQL's verdict. headers map {} Extra HTTP headers (for example a bearer token). Values may use secret placeholders, must not contain CR/LF, and are redacted by config show. tls.ca_file path or PEM system roots CA bundle for the OPA certificate. Only allowed with an https url. Semantics: OPA can only further deny. A query HaltSQL denies is denied without asking OPA, and OPA's answer can never turn a HaltSQL denial into an allow. A query HaltSQL allows is allowed only if OPA's decision is true (or, with on_error: allow_haltsql_verdict, if OPA could not give a decision). An OPA denial is reported with its own reason code so it can be told apart from HaltSQL's own reasons.

The admin API serves GET /v1/admin/report (shadow-mode analytics: which queries would have been denied, by reason and policy, over the report window) and GET /v1/admin/status. It is off by default. server: admin: enabled: true callers: - token:ops-dashboard # a server.auth.tokens name - oidc:corp-okta # any token verified by this provider - mtls:spiffe://corp.example/ns/ops/sa/console # a configured mTLS spiffe_id - mtls:ops-console # a configured mTLS subject_cn report_window: 24h max_tracked_queries: 10000 Key Type Default Meaning enabled boolean false Serve the admin endpoints. callers list [] Who may call them. Required and non-empty when enabled is true. Each entry is token:<name>, oidc:<provider> or mtls:<spiffe-id or subject CN> and must name a configured token, OIDC provider or mTLS identity. Unauthenticated callers can never use the admin API. report_window duration 24h How far back the report looks: a whole number followed by s, m, h or d, between 1m and 30d. max_tracked_queries integer 1-1000000 10000 Distinct query fingerprints tracked for the report; the least recently seen are evicted first.

Key Type Default Meaning telemetry.metrics.prometheus boolean true Serve Prometheus metrics at GET /metrics. telemetry.otlp mapping none OpenTelemetry (OTLP/HTTP) export, below. telemetry.otlp_endpoint URL none Legacy shorthand for telemetry.otlp.endpoint with all other defaults. Cannot be combined with telemetry.otlp. Must be an http(s) URL. telemetry.otlp: Key Type Default Meaning endpoint URL required Collector base URL, e.g. http://collector:4318. headers map {} Extra HTTP headers. Values may use secret placeholders, must not contain CR/LF, and are redacted by config show. service_name string haltsql service.name resource attribute. traces boolean true Export traces. metrics boolean true Export metrics. export_interval_seconds integer 1-3600 15 Metric export interval. timeout_seconds integer 1-300 5 Export request timeout.
Key Type Default Meaning logging.level debug, info, warn, error info Minimum log level. logging.format json, text json Log line format. Logs go to stderr.
Key Type Default Meaning limits.max_request_bytes integer (1024 to 67108864) 1048576 Largest accepted HTTP request body. Larger requests get HTTP 413.

Configures the secret providers used by the ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} and ${gcp-sm:...} placeholders. Values in this section may only use ${env:...} and ${file:...} (a provider cannot configure itself). Key Meaning secrets.vault.address Vault URL. https, or http for loopback addresses only. secrets.vault.namespace Vault Enterprise namespace (optional). secrets.vault.auth.method token (needs token), kubernetes (needs role; jwt_path defaults to /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, mount to kubernetes) or approle (needs role_id and secret_id; mount defaults to approle). Fields of other methods are errors. secrets.vault.ca_file CA bundle for the Vault server certificate (optional). secrets.aws.region, secrets.aws.endpoint AWS Secrets Manager region (required) and optional endpoint (tests). secrets.gcp.project, secrets.gcp.endpoint Default project for short secret names, and optional endpoint (tests). Vault tokens, AppRole role and secret ids are redacted by config show. config show also redacts: Elasticsearch API keys and passwords, the Kafka SASL password and TLS client key, bundle source passwords and tokens, static S3 credentials (sinks and bundle sources), OPA and OTLP header values, the server TLS key and token hashes. Inline PEM values are shown as <inline PEM>.

Config values can load secrets without writing them into the file: Placeholder Replaced by ${env:NAME} The value of environment variable NAME. ${file:/path} The contents of the file (at most 1 MiB), with one trailing newline (\n or \r\n) removed. Relative paths are resolved against the config file's directory. ${vault:<path>#<field>} Field <field> of the Vault secret at <path> (e.g. secret/data/haltsql/otel#token). ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]} An AWS Secrets Manager secret, or one key of its JSON value. ${gcp-sm:<name>[#<json-key>]} A Google Secret Manager secret (projects/P/secrets/S/versions/V or a short name in secrets.gcp.project), or one key of its JSON value. $${ A literal ${. The provider placeholders are resolved by the program loading the config (the server and CLI build a resolver from the secrets section first, then load the rest). A provider placeholder in a program or context with no resolver is a load error ("secret provider not configured"). Each distinct reference is fetched once per load. Rules: A placeholder that cannot be resolved (unset variable, unreadable file, missing secret) is a load error. HaltSQL never substitutes an empty string. Placeholders are allowed only in Config documents. They are rejected in policies, which may only use ${ctx.*}. Resolved secrets are never printed. haltsql config show replaces them with "<redacted>".

Runtime settings come from four places. Higher rows win: Priority Source Example 1 (highest) Command-line flags haltsql-server --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 2 HALTSQL_* environment variables HALTSQL_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:9000 3 Config file server.listen: 0.0.0.0:8443 4 (lowest) Built-in defaults 127.0.0.1:8080 Environment variables recognized in 0.0.1: Variable Overrides HALTSQL_LISTEN server.listen HALTSQL_LOG_LEVEL logging.level HALTSQL_LOG_FORMAT logging.format HALTSQL_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED server.auth.allow_unauthenticated (true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off) HALTSQL_DEFAULT_POLICY default_policy An invalid value in one of these variables is a load error, not ignored. Use haltsql config show --config FILE to print the effective, merged config with secrets redacted. Run it after every change; it is the fastest way to see what the server will actually do.

For local experiments, the server accepts a policy directly: haltsql-server --policy policy.yaml --listen 127.0.0.1:8080 --allow-unauthenticated --policy is repeatable and adds to (or, by name, replaces) the config's policies. See cli.md for all server flags. Use a config file with tokens for anything shared or deployed.
documents.s: Quick start without a config file

documents.t: Base path /api/v1. JSON in and out (content-type: application/json). Timestamps are RFC 3339 UTC strings with milliseconds. Counts are integers. The machine-readable contract is openapi.yaml.

Errors always look like the verifiers' errors: { "error": { "code": "FORBIDDEN", "message": "role analyst lacks permission restart_verifiers" } } Status Code When 400 BAD_REQUEST Malformed JSON, missing or invalid field or parameter, or a path parameter that decodes to /, \, NUL, . or ... 401 UNAUTHENTICATED No or invalid credentials. Checked before routing, so unknown endpoints also answer 401 to unauthenticated callers. 403 FORBIDDEN Authenticated, but the role lacks the permission. 403 REASON_REQUIRED The permission is "with a reason" and none was given. 403 CSRF A state-changing request came from another site (see Requests below). 403 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED Dev mode only: the Host header is not a loopback name or address (see Requests below). 404 NOT_FOUND Unknown route or object (authenticated callers only). 405 METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED The route exists but not for this method. 409 CONFLICT State conflict (for example a case already resolved). 413 TOO_LARGE The request body is over 1 MiB. 415 UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE A request body that is not application/json. 429 RATE_LIMITED Too soon to repeat the action (for example POST /data/refresh). 500 INTERNAL Unexpected server error (details are only logged). 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED The action needs verifier support that does not exist yet. 502 UPSTREAM A verifier, catalog, GitHub or Kubernetes call failed. Message has no secrets. 503 NOT_CONFIGURED The feature needs configuration that is missing (for example no GitHub integration). 503 OVERLOADED More than 512 requests are in flight; retry later. 503 TIMEOUT The request took longer than 30 seconds and was abandoned. Requests. Every /api/ request is authenticated first, then routed. For methods other than GET, HEAD and OPTIONS: a non-empty body must be sent as content-type: application/json (parameters such as ; charset=utf-8 are fine), else 415; an Origin header, when present, must be allowed, and Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site is refused, else 403 CSRF. When public_url or allowed_origins is configured, the Origin (scheme, host and port) must be one of those and Host is not looked at, so a reverse proxy may rewrite Host. Otherwise the Origin must name the same host and port as the Host header (a missing port means the Origin scheme's default), and a reverse proxy in front of the console must preserve Host. In dev mode every /api/ request, GET included, must carry a Host header naming a loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 or [::1], any port), else 403 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED. This stops a web page from reaching a local dev console through DNS rebinding. Bodies are read as a stream and refused with 413 as soon as they pass 1 MiB (or immediately when Content-Length says so). Reasons. Permissions marked Reason need a non-empty reason, sent as the x-haltsql-reason header or a "reason" field in the body (the body wins). It is stored in the activity log with what the person saw or did. Pagination. List endpoints take limit (default 50, max 500) and an opaque cursor; responses have "next_cursor": "..." or null. Time ranges. range=1h|24h|7d (default 24h), or explicit since and until (RFC 3339). Explicit wins.

In order: OIDC bearer token: Authorization: Bearer <JWT> verified against a configured auth.oidc provider (JWKS, iss, aud, expiry). Name from name/email/sub, groups from the provider's groups_claim. Trusted auth proxy (auth.proxy, off by default): an identity-aware proxy in front of the console (oauth2-proxy, AWS ALB OIDC, Google IAP, Azure App Service auth) sets the user and groups headers named in config. The headers are only trusted from a peer inside auth.proxy.trusted_proxies and/or when auth.proxy.secret_header carries the shared secret (one of the two is required); otherwise the request gets 401. auth.proxy.group_prefix is prepended to proxy groups. Service token: Authorization: Bearer <token> matched (constant time) against auth.tokens[].sha256; the token carries a fixed role. Dev mode (auth.dev, never in production): every request is the configured dev user and role (default dev). Dev mode must be the only auth method and listen must be a loopback address; the console refuses to start otherwise. --dev ROLE clears the other methods and applies the same check. OIDC sign-ins older than auth.session_hours (from auth_time, else iat) are rejected with 401. Groups map to roles through auth.roles. A user gets every role their groups map to (see Several roles below). A user with no mapped group gets 401.

dev (agent developer), analyst (security analyst), owner (policy owner), audit (compliance), admin (platform admin). Permission id dev analyst owner audit admin Use the Playground use_playground yes yes yes no yes Search queries, hashes only search_queries yes yes yes yes yes See raw SQL see_raw_sql no reason reason reason no Pause a caller pause_caller no reason no no reason Accept suggestions, open PRs propose_changes yes yes yes no yes Approve a policy change approve_change no no yes no no Approve a PII exception approve_exception no no yes no no Build evidence packs build_evidence no yes yes yes no Restart verifiers restart_verifiers no no no no reason Manage roles and integrations manage_access no no no no yes Open and update cases write_cases no yes yes no yes See the activity log view_activity no yes yes yes yes yes is allowed, reason is allowed with a reason (x-haltsql-reason header or a reason body field; the reason is written to the activity log), no is 403 FORBIDDEN. The matrix is Rbac.grant in bin/console/lib/rbac.ml; test/console/test_rbac.ml checks it against this table. Several roles. A person whose groups map to several roles has every one of them, and each permission is the best grant any of those roles has (yes beats reason beats no). For example owner + admin can both approve a policy change and restart verifiers, and analyst + audit can pause a caller with a reason and write cases. Role precedence (admin, owner, audit, analyst, dev) only picks the primary role shown in the UI (role in /me); it never decides access. Every role can read Overview, Signals, Agents, Fleet, Data classification and Policies. The activity log needs view_activity. Cases are readable by everyone and writable with write_cases.

GET /healthz 200 {"status":"ok"} while the process runs. No auth. GET /readyz 200 {"status":"ready"} when state_dir was writable at the last probe (at startup, then every 30 s; the probe result is cached) and no background loop is in crash backoff; 503 with reasons and per-loop loops status otherwise. No auth.

{ "user": { "id": "dana.reyes@acme.com", "name": "Dana Reyes", "auth": "oidc:okta", "groups": ["haltsql-analysts"] }, "roles": ["analyst"], "role": "analyst", "role_label": "Security analyst", "permissions": { "use_playground": "yes", "see_raw_sql": "reason", "restart_verifiers": "no", "...": "..." }, "environment": { "org": "Acme Corp", "name": "Production", "region": "us-east-1" } } roles lists every role the user's groups map to; permissions is the union of their grants (see Roles). role and role_label are the primary role, for display only.

{ "range": { "since": "...", "until": "...", "bucket_seconds": 3600 }, "updated": "2026-11-07T14:21:00.000Z", "verifiers_reporting": 8, "totals": { "checked": 88904, "denied": 2868, "denied_by_opa": 46, "shadow_denied": 131, "p99_ms": 1.8 }, "series": [ { "start": "...", "allowed": 2900, "denied": 110, "shadow_denied": 4 } ], "posture": [ { "id": "bundle_in_sync", "state": "ok|warning|error|unknown", "title": "...", "detail": "..." } ], "signals": { "open": 5, "high": 1, "medium": 3, "low": 1 } } denied counts every enforce denial (HaltSQL or OPA); denied_by_opa is the subset whose codes include E_EXTERNAL_POLICY. p99_ms comes from the records' elapsed_us (null when no record carries it). series never has more than 2000 buckets: for a wide explicit range bucket_seconds grows to a multiple of the usual bucket. Posture checks: bundle_in_sync (every verifier serves the same signed bundle version), audit_chains (last chain verification result), pii_exposure (no tagged column allowed without an approved exception), in_process_agents (agents configured as in-process are not centrally audited), restart_pending (any verifier with audit_restart_pending).

GET /api/v1/signals?status=open|all&limit=&cursor= returns { "signals": [Signal], "next_cursor": "..." | null }, most severe and newest first (signals known only from their stored snapshot are included). { "id": "sig_cross_tenant_support-bot_20261107T1356", "kind": "cross_tenant | deny_spike | opa_errors | sink_buffering | shadow_ready | new_caller | bundle_drift | restart_pending | chain_broken", "severity": "high | medium | low", "status": "open | investigating | contained | resolved | acknowledged", "title": "support-bot is filtering on other tenants", "body": "37 queries in 6 minutes compared tenant_id to 9 values other than acme. All were denied ...", "first_seen": "...", "last_seen": "...", "caller": "mtls:spiffe://prod/ns/support/sa/bot", "policy": "support-copilot", "policy_version": "sha256:...", "verifier": "haltsql-5", "assignee": null, "case_id": null, "link": { "kind": "investigation | fleet | rollout | agent", "target": "..." }, "facts": { "records": 37, "distinct_values": 9, "codes": { "E_TENANT_MISMATCH": 21 } } } GET /api/v1/signals/{id} returns the signal plus its investigation: { "signal": { "...": "..." }, "timeline": { "bucket_seconds": 60, "series": [ { "start": "...", "allowed": 4, "denied": 3 } ] }, "shapes": [ { "fingerprint": "6c1e0b7f3a2d9e41", "example_shape": "SELECT id, subject, status FROM tickets WHERE tenant_id = ?", "count": 21, "stopped_at": "tenancy", "codes": ["E_TENANT_MISMATCH"], "request_ids": ["..."] } ], "caller": { "id": "...", "agent": "support-bot", "policy": "support-copilot", "usual_per_minute": 4.0, "usual_deny_rate": 0.002 }, "request_ids": ["..."] } timeline.series items also carry shadow_denied; the investigation covers at most the 24 hours before the signal's last_seen (plus 15 minutes either side) and its timeline at most 2000 buckets. shapes group the signal's records by fingerprint; example_shape is the raw SQL with every literal (any quoting, including $$...$$, E'...' and U&'...', and numbers) replaced by ? and comments dropped, when the producer logged SQL and the shape can be derived safely (the statement parses and the shape keeps its libpg_query fingerprint); otherwise it is the fingerprint. Viewing a signal's investigation is written to the activity log (signal.view). A signal no longer in memory (after a restart, or a week after it cleared) is served from the snapshot stored with its workflow, in the same shape. POST /api/v1/signals/{id} with { "status": "investigating", "assignee": "dana.reyes@acme.com" } (either field; assignee: null clears it) updates workflow state. Needs write_cases (checked before the body is read, so a caller without it gets 403 even for a malformed body). acknowledged is for low signals (400 otherwise). Returns the signal. A signal's id is its kind, subject and the start of the window bucket the episode began in; re-detections update the same signal. A signal whose condition has cleared for 30 minutes (signals.resolve_after_minutes) becomes resolved unless someone set its status. If the condition comes back after that, it is a new signal (a new id, suffixed _2, _3, ... when the bucket is the same) and is notified again, even if the old one had an assignee or a case; a signal whose status a person set (other than resolved) keeps absorbing recurrences. The cross_tenant signal needs the tenant values a query compared against. Records only carry codes, so the detector counts E_TENANT_MISMATCH records per caller in a sliding 10-minute window (threshold signals.cross_tenant.min_records, default 10); when raw SQL is logged it also extracts the distinct values by re-verifying.

GET /api/v1/queries?q=&caller=&policy=&outcome=allowed|denied|shadow_denied&code=&table=&fingerprint=&verifier=&since=&until=&limit=&cursor= q matches a request id prefix, caller substring, fingerprint prefix, or table name. Records never include sql. Without since, until or range the whole retention window is searched (so an old request id can still be found); range applies only when given. table matches schema.table or the bare table name. Permission search_queries. { "records": [ { "request_id": "01930c4e-7a2f-7c41-9d2e-5b8f0a63e1d4", "ts": "...", "verifier": "haltsql-2", "source": "server | proxy", "caller": "...", "caller_type": "mtls", "policy": "support-copilot", "policy_version": "sha256:...", "outcome": "denied", "codes": ["E_TENANT_MISMATCH"], "tables": ["app.tickets"], "fingerprint": "6c1e0b7f3a2d9e41", "sql_sha256": "...", "elapsed_us": 240, "has_raw_sql": true } ], "next_cursor": null, "total": 37 } Newest first (equal timestamps: most recently ingested first). The cursor names the last record returned (its timestamp and request id), and the next page is what sorts after it, so records that arrive between pages never shift a later page. total is counted on the first page only and is null on later pages. GET /api/v1/records/{request_id}: { "record": { "...": "as above" }, "trail": [ { "stage": "parse | tables | tenancy | limit | functions | opa | verdict", "state": "passed | denied | not_run | skipped", "detail": "..." } ], "trail_source": "reverified | codes", "reasons_detail": "codes | redacted | full", "reasons": [ { "code": "E_TENANT_MISMATCH", "rule": "tenancy.mismatch", "message": "...", "hint": "..." } ], "policy": { "name": "support-copilot", "version": "sha256:...", "bundle": "prod 1.4.0", "loaded_version": "sha256:..." }, "custody": { "verifier": "haltsql-2", "seq": 8412096, "hash": "...", "prev_hash": "...", "neighbours": [ { "seq": 8412095, "request_id": "...", "hash": "...", "prev_hash": "...", "outcome": "allowed" } ], "location": "s3://acme-audit/haltsql/2026/11/07/13/haltsql-2-20261107T130000.000001Z.42-0000000412-<sha256>.jsonl#L412", "chain_state": "intact | gap | broken | unknown", "first_break": { "seq": 8412001, "request_id": "...", "location": "...", "message": "hash mismatch (record was modified)" }, "last_verified": "...", "verify_command": "haltsql audit verify s3://acme-audit/haltsql/ --host haltsql-2 --region us-east-1" } } GET /records/{id} needs search_queries and never includes SQL. reasons has one entry per recorded code; rule and hint are null when only the code is known. Re-verification (trail_source: reverified) names the rule behind each code, but its messages and hints can quote SQL literals (the other tenant's value in E_TENANT_MISMATCH), so by default they are replaced by the generic description of the code (reasons_detail: redacted). GET /records/{id}?details=full returns them (reasons_detail: full); it needs see_raw_sql and its reason, and is written to the activity log as record.view_details. policy.bundle comes from the last fleet snapshot of the record's verifier and policy.loaded_version is the version of the policy the console loaded (both null when unknown); a re-derived trail uses the loaded policy, so compare the two versions. Custody. seq is the record's position in its verifier's stream as ingested (files in name order, objects in key order); neighbours are the records up to two positions before and after. The chain is checked locally over the records in the index, in seq order, following hash links: a record continues the segment whose last hash is its prev_hash, so independent chains under one verifier name (several hosts under one prefix) are checked separately. A record that links to no segment starts a new one when its prev_hash is the genesis hash (a new chain, as after a restart without a spool), when it is the first record read from its file or object-sink host (its predecessor may have left the retention window), or right after an ingestion gap (rotation or truncation that may have skipped records, or an object skipped after repeated read failures); otherwise the link is broken. Every hash must verify. chain_state is that of the record's segment: broken (with first_break) when any record in it fails, gap when the segment starts after an ingestion gap, unknown when the record has no hash. The check is incremental (only records added since the last check are hashed); POST /records/{id}/verify-chain re-walks the verifier's whole stream, yielding to other requests as it goes, shares one walk between concurrent calls, and serves the incremental result within 30 seconds of the last walk. The published chain status (chains[]) carries state (intact, gap, broken, unknown), records, segments, gaps, first_break and checked_at. verify_command re-verifies the original records with the CLI: haltsql audit verify <file> for files, haltsql audit verify s3://bucket/prefix/ --host <host> (plus --region/--endpoint when configured) for S3, and, because the CLI does not read gs:// directly, a gcloud storage cp -r of the prefix followed by haltsql audit verify <dir> --host <host> for GCS. <host> is the host in the object name. The trail is re-derived by re-verifying the SQL against the named policy when raw SQL and the policy are available (trail_source: "reverified", with the record's context if it has one, else a placeholder context); otherwise from the codes alone (trail_source: "codes"). Either way the record's own codes decide each stage's state; re-verification only adds the detailed messages, rules, hints and tables. Codes map to stages as follows: parse from E_PARSE, E_EMPTY, E_LIMIT, E_MULTI_STATEMENT, E_STATEMENT_KIND, E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE, E_LOCKING_CLAUSE, E_SELECT_INTO, E_UNSUPPORTED, E_INTERNAL; tables from E_TABLE_*/E_COLUMN_* and E_WRITE_DENIED; tenancy from E_TENANT_*, E_CONTEXT_MISSING, E_PARAM_UNBOUND; limit from E_LIMIT_REQUIRED, E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH, E_JOIN_BUDGET; functions from E_FUNCTION_DENIED, E_OPERATOR_DENIED, E_CAST_DENIED; opa from E_EXTERNAL_POLICY; unknown codes are named in the verdict stage. After a hard parse failure (E_PARSE, E_EMPTY, E_LIMIT, E_MULTI_STATEMENT, E_UNSUPPORTED, E_INTERNAL) the other analyzer stages are not_run. OPA is not_run when HaltSQL denied, because OPA is only asked after an allow. tenancy is skipped when the loaded policy has no tenancy keys. In shadow mode a stage that would deny is denied (detail says "Shadow mode") and the verdict is passed. GET /api/v1/records/{id}/sql see_raw_sql with reason. { "sql": "...", "logged": true }, 404 when the producer didn't log it. Logged as record.view_sql (the SQL itself is never logged). POST /api/v1/records/{id}/verify-chain search_queries. Re-verifies the record's verifier chain now; returns custody and updates the chain status Overview reads. Logged as record.verify_chain. The console also re-verifies every verifier's chain every 5 minutes; the result ({ "checked_at", "chains": [ { "verifier", "state": "intact | broken | unknown", "records", "segments", "first_break", "checked_at" } ] }) feeds the audit_chains posture check and the chain_broken signal.
