GET /api/v1/cases?status=open|all&assignee=me&limit=&cursor= { "cases": [Case], "next_cursor" }, newest first POST /api/v1/cases { "title", "signal_id"?, "request_ids"?: [], "assignee"? } → 201 Case GET /api/v1/cases/{id} Case PATCH /api/v1/cases/{id} { "title"?, "status"?, "assignee"?, "note"? } POST /api/v1/cases/{id}/records { "request_ids": [] } adds records POST /api/v1/cases/{id}/steps/{n} { "done": true } checks off a next step { "id": "CASE-1042", "title": "...", "status": "open | contained | resolved", "assignee": "...", "created": "...", "updated": "...", "created_by": "...", "signal_id": "...", "request_ids": ["..."], "notes": [ { "at": "...", "by": "...", "text": "..." } ], "steps": [ { "text": "Confirm nothing leaked", "done": false } ] } Case ids are CASE-<n> from a counter in the store, starting at 1000. status=open (the default) lists every case that is not resolved. A case created with signal_id links both ways (the signal gets case_id), adds the signal's request ids, and for cross_tenant signals starts with default steps; an unknown signal is 400, a signal already linked to a case 409. {n} in /steps/{n} is the step's 0-based index. A resolved case only accepts PATCH { "status": "open" } (reopen); other changes are 409 CONFLICT. Limits (400 when exceeded): 1000 request ids per request, 10000 per case, 200 bytes per request id, 500 bytes per title, 320 per assignee, 10000 per note and 500 notes per case. Mutations check write_cases before reading the body. When integrations.jira is set the case also has "jira": { "key", "url" } (or null if the issue could not be created).

{ "minutes": 60, "reason": "..." }, pause_caller with reason. Verifiers do not yet consume a signed deny list, so this returns 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED after logging the attempt. Until then, revoke the caller's token or identity at the identity provider.

GET /api/v1/agents?via=sidecar|proxy|mcp|in_process&sort=denied|queries|newest&range=7d { "counts": { "all": 14, "sidecar": 7, "proxy": 3, "mcp": 2, "in_process": 2 }, "agents": [ { "name": "analytics-agent", "team": "Data platform", "via": "sidecar | proxy | mcp | in_process", "stack": "LangGraph, Python", "identity": "oidc:okta svc-analytics", "callers": ["oidc:okta"], "policy": "analytics", "policy_version": "v12", "mode": "enforce", "shadow": ["analytics-v13"], "queries": 41220, "denied": 1566, "deny_rate": 0.038, "first_seen": "...", "last_seen": "...", "audit": "central | in_app" } ] } Agents come from agents: in the config (name, team, via, stack, which callers belong to the agent) merged with every caller seen in the index; only the configured callers belong to a configured agent (a caller whose id equals a configured agent's name is still its own agent). A caller seen in records but not configured becomes its own agent with via guessed from the record (proxy source → proxy, verifier kind mcp → mcp, else sidecar). In-process agents have queries: null. Agents also carry caller_types and configured (listed in agents:), and the response has the range it covers. sort defaults to denied. GET /api/v1/agents/{name} adds top_codes: [{code, count, top_object}] and policies: { enforced: {name, version, mode, origin, loaded}, shadow: [...] }. top_object is the most frequent object denied with that code (column, function, table, LIMIT n), named from detailed reasons re-derived from raw SQL when it was logged, else the most frequent table of those records.

use_playground. Nothing touches a database. { "sql": "SELECT ...", "context": { "tenant_id": "acme" }, "caller": "analytics-agent", "targets": [ { "policy": "analytics" }, { "policy": "analytics", "draft": "<policy YAML>" } ], "opa": true } When targets is omitted, caller (an agent name) picks the targets: its enforced and shadow policies (at most 10). It does not pick a context: the context is the request's context, or {}. caller is also sent to OPA as the input's caller.name (default console:<user id>). At most 10 targets per check (400 above that), and a draft is at most 256 KiB. Response: { "results": [ { "label": "analytics (live)", "policy": "analytics", "version": "sha256:...", "where": "live | shadow | draft", "allowed": false, "stages": [ { "stage": "parse", "state": "passed", "detail": "One SELECT." } ], "verdict": { "...": "verdict JSON exactly as haltsql-server returns it" }, "opa": { "asked": false, "allowed": null, "ms": null, "error": null, "outcome": "skipped", "reasons": [] } } ], "columns": [ { "column": "app.orders.region", "tags": [], "sources": ["dbt"], "allowed_by": ["analytics"] } ], "test_case": "- name: ...
 # policy: analytics
 context: {"tenant_id":"acme"}
 sql: ...
 expect: allow
", "sql_sha256": "..." } Stages are parse, tables, tenancy, functions, limit, opa, each passed | denied | not_run | skipped with a detail (not_run after a parse failure, and for OPA when HaltSQL denied). allowed is true when the final verdict has neither reasons nor shadow reasons (a shadow policy that would deny reports false). An invalid draft returns 400 with error.errors: ["<load error>", ...]; an unknown live policy 404. OPA is consulted only when the HaltSQL verdict allows, opa is configured in the console (same opa: block as the server) and the request does not set "opa": false. The input document is the server's (caller.type is playground); timeout_ms and on_error apply as on the server. The targets of one check are sent to OPA one after another; once those calls have taken 10 seconds, the remaining targets are not sent (opa.asked: false, opa.error: "time budget spent", stage opa not_run). test_case is one case in the haltsql test suite format, from the first result (expect and, for a denial, codes); suite cases have no per-case policy, so the policy is a comment. The activity log entry (playground.check) stores the SQL's SHA-256, never the SQL.

GET /api/v1/policies `{ "policies": [ { "name", "version", "mode": "enforce GET /api/v1/policies/{name} Policy detail: the list fields plus description, format, yaml (the source; normalized YAML for inline and bundle policies), statements, require_limit, tenancy, tables ([{table, columns, tenant_columns, writes}]), functions. GET /api/v1/policies/{name}/report?since=&compare=<shadow policy> Shadow comparison and suggestions. POST /api/v1/policies/{name}/pull-request propose_changes. { "suggestions": ["<id>"], "tests": ["<yaml>"], "title"?, "create_file"? } opens or updates a PR in integrations.github.repo. 503 NOT_CONFIGURED without GitHub. Report response: { "policy": "analytics", "compare": "analytics-v13", "days_in_shadow": 6, "comparison": { "records": 248310, "denied_now_allowed": 1412, "allowed_now_denied": 0, "tenancy_relaxed": 0 }, "suggestions": [ { "id": "analytics/column/app.orders.region", "kind": "column | function | table | limit", "title": "...", "evidence": { "records": 1412, "distinct_queries": 37, "callers": 3 }, "yaml": "...", "review": null } ], "never": [ { "category": "sensitive_column | tenancy | external_policy | query_fix", "codes": ["E_COLUMN_DENIED"], "records": 88, "advice": "..." } ], "pull_request": { "number": 212, "url": "...", "state": "open", "checks": [ { "name", "state", "detail" } ], "approvals": [ { "by", "at" } ], "required_approvals": 2 } } Suggestions come from Report.Suggest.compute, so tenancy, writes, OPA denials and PII columns are never suggested. Details of the report: Records are the index records of the policy since since (RFC 3339, a date or a duration such as 7d; default the whole retention window), at most the 50,000 most recent (truncated: true when older records were left out). Records with raw SQL are re-verified to name the denied objects, like haltsql report (each distinct SQL once per policy version). The response also has version, since, records, truncated and missing_detail. The analysis yields to other requests while it runs and is cached for 30 seconds per (policy, since, compare) while the loaded policies and the record index are unchanged; concurrent identical reports share one computation. A pull request reuses the analysis of the default report. compare defaults to the first shadow sibling (<name>-*, <name>_*, <name>.* in shadow mode); null (and comparison: null) when there is none. days_in_shadow counts from the oldest record logged under the compare policy. comparison re-verifies the raw SQL of the policy's records under the compare policy (compared of records had SQL). Records do not carry context values, so the re-verification uses placeholder tenancy values: in literal tenancy mode, tenant literals then never match. tenancy_relaxed counts records denied with an E_TENANT_* code that the compare policy allows. Suggestions also carry code, applicable, notes and evidence.denied/shadow_denied; review is {pull_request, url} when the stored PR includes the suggestion, else null. never has one row per code that is never suggested, plus one per sensitive column (target) and unsafe function. E_TENANT_* and E_CONTEXT_MISSING are tenancy, E_EXTERNAL_POLICY is external_policy, everything else (query fixes, writes, statement kinds) query_fix. pull_request is null until a PR was opened from the console. Its live state (open | closed | merged | missing | unknown), check runs and approvals (each reviewer's latest decisive review) are read from GitHub and cached for 30 seconds; concurrent cache misses share one refresh. A failed read gives state: "unknown" and error. POST /api/v1/policies/{name}/pull-request applies the chosen suggestions to the policy file in the repository with Report.Patch (validated before committing; 409 when the patched policy does not validate or nothing applies), appends tests (each one case or a list of cases in the haltsql test format; 400 when invalid) to <tests_path>/<name>.yaml, commits both in one commit on <branch_prefix><name> and opens a PR, or updates the open PR for this policy: the one it stored, else an open PR GitHub has for that branch (also adopted when opening a PR fails with 422 because one exists). Proposals for one policy run one at a time. A branch with no open PR is reset to base only when its head is a commit the console made (each console commit carries a HaltSQL-Console-Policy: <name> trailer); otherwise 409, so commits someone else pushed are never discarded. The policy file is found as described under integrations.github.path and policy_paths in the config reference; when no file matches, suggestions are 409 unless create_file: true. Response 201 (opened) or 200 (updated): { "number": 212, "url": "...", "branch": "haltsql-console/analytics", "head_sha": "...", "state": "open", "created": true, "applied": ["analytics/column/app.orders.region"], "skipped": [ { "id", "reason" } ], "files": ["policies/analytics.yaml", "tests/analytics.yaml"] } The PR is stored (number, url, branch, head_sha, suggestions) and the action logged as policy.pull_request.

GET /api/v1/fleet: { "updated": "...", "config_generation": 14, "verifiers": [ { "name": "haltsql-1", "kind": "server | proxy | mcp", "location": "shared service, zone a", "url": "...", "state": "ready | buffering | restart_pending | not_ready | unreachable", "version": "0.0.1", "uptime_seconds": 345600, "policies": [ { "name", "version", "mode", "origin" } ], "bundle": { "source", "bundle", "version", "signed_by", "revision", "checks", "last_success", "last_error" }, "bundles": [ { same fields as bundle, one per bundle source } ], "sinks": [ { "name", "type", "healthy" } ], "unhealthy_sinks": [], "opa": { "configured": true, "timeouts": 12 }, "restart_pending": false, "connections": null, "verifies_per_second": 310.2, "note": "...", "error": null } ], "bundles": [ { "source", "version", "signed_by", "revision", "verifiers": 8, "in_sync": true } ], "sinks": [ { "type": "kafka", "target": "...", "state": "healthy | buffering | failing", "verifiers": 7 } ], "opa": { "decision_path", "endpoint", "timeout_ms", "on_error", "in_sync": true, "configs": [ { "decision_path", "endpoint", "timeout_ms", "on_error", "verifiers": [names] } ], "decisions": { "allowed", "denied", "error_denied", "skipped" } } } verifies_per_second and OPA decisions come from /metrics when the verifier exposes it (deltas between polls); null otherwise. Before the first poll the document is empty: updated and config_generation are null and the lists are empty. Details: state: unreachable (no HTTP answer, or for a proxy no TCP connection; error says why), buffering (an audit sink is unhealthy or has buffered records), not_ready (/readyz is 503 for another reason: no policy, draining), restart_pending (audit_restart_pending), else ready. note is a human sentence about the state. error reports a failed probe even when the state is known (e.g. a 403 on the admin status). config_generation (top level) is the highest generation reported; each verifier also carries its own config_generation. Extra fields: verifier sinks[].buffered_records, buffered_records (total), opa.external_policy_denials; bundle versions: [ { version, revision, signed_by, verifiers: [names] } ] (majority first; the top-level version is the majority's); sink buffered_records, peak_buffered_records, unhealthy_verifiers; opa.configured, opa.decisions.error_allowed and opa.window_seconds. opa.timeouts (per verifier) counts OPA errors (error_allowed + error_denied: timeouts and failures), and opa.decisions the decisions of every verifier, both over the in-memory history (the last 120 polls, window_seconds). Fields are null when the verifier has no /metrics. bundle is the verifier's first bundle source (kept for compatibility); bundles lists every source. Source ids and last_error have the query, fragment and userinfo of any URL replaced (?<redacted>), since every role can read this document. opa: the top-level settings are the majority's; configs groups the verifiers by OPA settings (majority first) and in_sync is false when they differ. error on an unreachable verifier that is backing off says when it is probed next (fleet.max_concurrent_probes in config.md). kind: mcp/proxy verifiers without admin status get their state from /readyz and /metrics (404s are not errors); a proxy with a non-HTTP url from a TCP connect. POST /api/v1/fleet/{name}/restart: restart_verifiers, which every role that has it holds only "with a reason", so a restart always needs one. Restarts the verifier's Kubernetes workload (fleet.kubernetes, a rollout restart patch on its Deployment or StatefulSet) and returns { "verifier", "workload": "deployment/haltsql-1", "restarted_at", "result": "ok | no_rollout" }. no_rollout (with a warning) means the patch was accepted but will not restart pods: a paused Deployment or a StatefulSet with updateStrategy: OnDelete. The intent is logged as fleet.restart_requested before the Kubernetes call (the restart is refused if that write fails), and the outcome as fleet.restart. 404 for an unknown verifier, 503 NOT_CONFIGURED without fleet.kubernetes or the verifier's workload, or when the console's own setup fails at restart time (token file unreadable, bad CA), 502 UPSTREAM when the Kubernetes API fails (the message carries the HTTP status and Status reason, never the token).

GET /api/v1/data/columns?show=allowed|all&q=: { "updated": "...", "loaded": "...", "shadow_denials_counted": "...", "sources": [ { "kind": "dbt", "label": "dbt", "detail": "manifest.json from acme/analytics", "as_of": "...", "authoritative": true, "error": null } ], "totals": { "tagged": 312, "tables": 41, "blocked": 309, "exception": 2, "needs_review": 1 }, "columns": [ { "column": "billing.invoices.tax_id", "tags": ["PII", "government id"], "sources": ["datahub"], "authoritative": true, "allowed_by": ["finance-agent"], "status": "needs_review | exception | blocked", "exception": { "column", "policy", "owner", "ticket", "expires", "expired": false }, "shadow_denials": 0 } ] } show defaults to allowed (every status but blocked); totals always count every tagged column. q matches a substring of the column or of a tag. exception is null unless an exception matches; for needs_review it is the expired (or partial) exception, with expired. Column sources are catalog labels (default: the kind); authoritative is false when only live fetches tag the column. See config.md for how the status is derived. A column allowed by a policy is exception when listed in data.exceptions (owner, ticket, expiry), otherwise needs_review. shadow_denials comes from a background scan of the record index every minute (shadow_denials_counted is when it last finished, null before the first); GET never scans the index. POST /api/v1/data/refresh re-reads every catalog and recounts shadow denials (any role; rate-limited to once a minute, 429 RATE_LIMITED otherwise; logged as data.refresh) and returns { "updated", "sources", "totals" }. A live fetch (DataHub, OpenMetadata) only flags columns; it is never loaded as a policy catalog.

GET /api/v1/evidence/controls?framework=soc2|iso27001|gdpr|hipaa Any role. Control mapping (default soc2): { framework, framework_name, disclaimer, controls: [ { id, name, what, evidence: [string] } ] } POST /api/v1/evidence/packs build_evidence. { "framework", "since", "until"?, "include_sql"? } (until defaults to now) → 202 { id: "pack_<n>", state: "building" }. include_sql: true also needs see_raw_sql and its reason (403 REASON_REQUIRED without one). One build at a time per console: 409 BUILD_IN_PROGRESS while another is building. A period holding more than 1,000,000 records is refused (400). Logged as evidence.build (detail include_sql; the reason when SQL is included). GET /api/v1/evidence/packs build_evidence. { "packs": [ { id, framework, since, until, built_by, created, state: "building|ready|failed", records, chains: {verified, total}, manifest_sha256, bytes, include_sql, sql_redacted, gaps: [ { kind, name, detail } ], error } ] }, newest first. GET /api/v1/evidence/packs/{id}/download build_evidence. application/gzip, streamed from disk (with content-length): a .tar.gz with manifest.json, audit records, chain reports, policy versions, activity log extract and README.md. 409 CONFLICT while building or after a failure. Logged as evidence.download. DELETE /api/v1/evidence/packs/{id} build_evidence. Deletes the pack's file and listing entry → { id, deleted: true }. 409 while building, 404 when unknown. Logged as evidence.delete. Control ids: soc2 CC6.1, CC6.3, CC7.2, CC8.1, A1.2; iso27001 A.5.15, A.8.2, A.8.15, A.8.16, A.8.32; gdpr Art. 5(1)(f), Art. 25, Art. 30, Art. 32; hipaa 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D), 164.312(a)(1), 164.312(b), 164.312(c)(1). Wording follows security/compliance.md. The archive has one top-level directory pack_<n>/ with README.md (scope, disclaimer, gaps, file list), manifest.json (SHA-256 and size of every other file, record counts per verifier, chain results, builder, period, generator), records/<verifier>.jsonl (the audit lines in the period, as ingested except that SQL text, sql and statement, is removed unless the pack was built with include_sql; sql_sha256 stays. A verifier name that is not a safe file name gets a sanitised name plus a short hash, and each records file's verifier is in the manifest), chains.json (per verifier, with the same rules as the chain-of-custody page: state intact | broken | unknown, verified (chained records checked), segments (a genesis prev_hash starts a new segment, e.g. after a restart without a spool), unchained (records without a hash), and first_break { line, problem, request_id, location }, line being the line of the records file; the first record of each segment may link to a record outside the period and is accepted as is. Verification runs on the records as ingested, so a line whose SQL was removed does not verify on its own from the pack; verify it against the audit store with haltsql audit verify), policies.json (seen_in_records versions and the loaded policies), activity.jsonl, exceptions.json and controls.json. manifest_sha256 in the listing is the SHA-256 of manifest.json; raw_sql in the manifest is { included, reason, redacted_records }. The gzip stream uses uncompressed (stored) DEFLATE blocks; it is a standard gzip file. Gap kinds: in_process_agent (agents with via: in_process), source_error (audit sources whose ingestion reports an error) and retention (the period starts before the index's retention window, audit.retention_hours, or records of the period were evicted by audit.max_records; the detail names the first covered time). Packs are built in a worker thread and written to a temporary file (fsynced, then renamed), so the console keeps serving requests during a build. The 20 most recent finished packs are kept: after each successful build, older ones and their files are deleted. The pack states plainly that HaltSQL holds no certification and lists gaps (in-process agents, sources that could not be read, periods outside retention).

Needs view_activity (see Roles). Newest first. { "entries": [ { "seq": 48213, "at": "...", "actor": "dana.reyes@acme.com", "role": "analyst", "action": "record.view_sql", "target": "01930c4e-...", "reason": "CASE-1042 triage", "detail": {} } ], "next_cursor": null, "total": 1, "window_oldest_seq": 1 } actor matches exactly, action is a prefix, since is RFC 3339. Every entry has a seq: a persisted integer that only grows (it resumes after a restart). Paging is keyset on seq: the cursor is the last seq returned, so entries logged between two requests never shift or repeat a page; they appear on a fresh first page. Queries cover the in-memory window: the most recent 50,000 entries, loaded from the tail of the log at startup. window_oldest_seq is the oldest seq in it (null when the log is empty); older entries are only in the files. Evidence packs read every file, not the window. Storage: each entry is one JSON line appended (and fsynced) to activity.jsonl in state_dir. When that file reaches 64 MiB it is renamed to activity-<first seq>.jsonl and a new file is started. Rotated files are never deleted by the console: the log is an audit trail, so retention and archival (for example moving old files to object storage) are an operator concern.

GET /api/v1/access/roles Any role. { "roles": [ { "id", "label" } ], "permissions": [ { "id", "name", "grants": { "dev": "yes", ... } } ], "mapping": { "admin": ["okta:haltsql-admins"] }, "safeguards": [ { "id", "title", "detail", "verified" } ], "dev_mode" } GET /api/v1/integrations `{ "groups": [ { "name": "Caller identity", "items": [ { "id", "name", "detail", "state": "configured mapping (the group-to-role mapping from auth.roles) is included only when the caller has manage_access; for everyone else the field is omitted. Roles, the matrix and the safeguards are visible to every role. Each safeguard says whether the console itself checks it (verified): id detail verified two_person_rule Policy changes need two owners, never the requester. Expected to be enforced by branch protection on the policy repository; the console cannot see that setting. false sessions OIDC sign-ins older than auth.session_hours are rejected (from the token's auth_time, else iat). true Integration state values: state meaning configured Present in the console configuration; no live check has run (or none exists for it). not_set_up Not in the configuration. connected A live check succeeded. degraded A live check succeeded partially; error says what is wrong. error A live check failed; error says why. Live checks: OIDC providers (JWKS reachable, checked at most every 5 minutes: degraded when the JWKS has no usable key, error when unreachable), bundle sources (from the fleet snapshot; degraded when verifiers serve different versions), catalogs (connected after a load, error when the last load failed, configured before the first load), audit sources (connected once ingestion has read them, error when it reports one, configured before it reports), audit sinks (from the fleet snapshot; degraded unless healthy). OPA, Slack, PagerDuty, Jira and GitHub are configured or not_set_up. Credentials are never returned; URLs are shown without user info or query.

The console is a control plane for a HaltSQL deployment. It never sits in the query path: agents keep talking to haltsql-server, haltsql-proxy or haltsql-mcp, and the console only reads what those verifiers already publish (audit records, /v1/admin/status, /v1/admin/report, /readyz) plus the policy and catalog files the verifiers load. If the console is down, nothing about enforcement changes. agents (SDKs, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vanna, CrewAI, ADK, MCP clients, psql) │ verify / wire protocol / MCP ▼ ┌───────────────────────────┐ audit JSONL (file, S3, GCS) ┌──────────────────────┐ │ haltsql-server / proxy / │ ───────────────────────────────▶│ │ │ haltsql-mcp (verifiers) │ GET /v1/admin/status, report, │ haltsql-console │──▶ browser (frontend, later PR) │ │◀─────── /readyz, /metrics ──────│ /api/v1/* │──▶ GitHub, Slack, PagerDuty └───────────────────────────┘ │ │ ▲ policies / bundles / catalogs (same files) └──────────┬───────────┘ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ state_dir (cases, activity, signal state, evidence packs)

haltsql-console is an OCaml binary in the haltsql-server opam package (bin/console, private library haltsql_console in bin/console/lib). It reuses the libraries the verifiers use, so the console and the verifiers can't disagree about what a record means or what a policy allows: Concern Library reused Parse audit records from server and proxy haltsql.report (Record) Shadow report and suggestions haltsql.report (Summary, Suggest) Re-verify a record, Playground haltsql (Haltsql.verify, Policy_load) Audit hash chain haltsql.cloud (Audit_chain) S3/GCS listing and secrets haltsql.cloud Data catalogs (dbt, DataHub, Unity, OpenMetadata) haltsql.catalog_fetch, haltsql.catalog_tools OIDC token verification haltsql-server.auth (Oidc_client) HTTP cohttp-lwt-unix, same as haltsql-server

Module Role Console_config YAML config: listen, environment, auth, verifiers, audit sources, policies, catalogs, integrations. Rbac The five roles and the permission matrix, an exhaustive grant : role -> permission -> grant (see api.md). A principal's access is grant_union over all of its roles; precedence only picks the display role. Console_auth Authenticates a request: OIDC bearer, trusted auth-proxy headers, static service tokens, or dev mode. Store Durable JSON documents in state_dir (one JSONL file per collection, rewritten atomically). Activity Append-only activity log ("who saw or did what, and why"). Index In-memory index of audit records for the retention window, with search and aggregation. Ctx The shared runtime context passed to every handler: config, store, index, a typed per-feature state registry, and require for permission checks. Api JSON responses, errors, query parameters, body parsing. Router Method and path-pattern routing; collects every feature's routes. feature modules Overview, Signals, Records, Cases, Agents, Playground, Policies, Fleet, Data, Evidence, Access. Each exports routes and, when it needs one, a background start loop. Console_server Listener, background loops, graceful shutdown, static frontend.

Audit ingestion (Ingest): every audit.sources entry (file glob, directory, s3://, gs://) is polled; new lines are parsed with Report.Record.of_line and added to the Index with their request id, hash, previous hash, verifier name and location (file and line or object key). Records older than audit.retention_hours are dropped. Fleet polling (Fleet): every fleet.poll_seconds (with jitter) each configured verifier's /v1/admin/status (with its admin token), /readyz (no token) and /metrics (the token only when metrics_url has the verifier's own origin) are read, at most fleet.max_concurrent_probes verifiers at a time; unreachable verifiers back off. A kind: proxy verifier with a non-HTTP url gets a TCP connect check instead. The token goes only over https (verified with verifiers[].ca_file or the system store) or loopback http, unless allow_insecure_http is set. The last snapshot and its history feed Fleet, Posture and Signals. Signals (Signals): detectors run over the index and the fleet snapshot every 30 seconds and open, update or close signals. Their workflow state (assignee, status, acknowledgement) is kept in Store. Policies (Policies): the console loads the same policy files or server config as the verifiers, to run the Playground, re-derive decision trails and compute exposure of tagged columns. Shadow reports come from the index (and, when configured, each verifier's /v1/admin/report).

Ctx.t carries only what every feature shares (config, store, index, start time). It has no per-feature fields. Runtime state a feature derives (the fleet snapshot, loaded policies, catalog tags, ingestion and audit-chain status) lives in a typed, heterogeneous registry on the context: module Key : sig type 'a t val create : string -> 'a t end val get : Ctx.t -> 'a Key.t -> 'a option val set : Ctx.t -> 'a Key.t -> 'a -> unit Each feature declares its key privately and exports read accessors only: (* fleet.ml *) let state : Fleet_state.t Ctx.Key.t = Ctx.Key.create "fleet" let snapshot ctx = Ctx.get ctx state (* exported *) (* the poll loop calls Ctx.set ctx state s *) Because the key isn't exported, only the owning module can write its state; other features read it through the owner's accessors, with the owner's types. Adding a feature never edits Ctx. Keys are built on Type.Id, so two keys never collide even with the same name, and get before the first set is None.

Everything the console derives (index, fleet snapshots, signals) is rebuilt from the verifiers on restart. Only human input is durable, in state_dir: cases, signal workflow state, activity log, evidence packs. One replica per environment; state_dir on a persistent volume. The store is a deliberate seam: a Postgres-backed Store is a later change and needs no API change.

The console holds verifier admin tokens (read-only endpoints) and, optionally, a GitHub token and webhook URLs. All are read from the secrets manager through the same ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...} and ${env:...} placeholders as the server config. Raw SQL is never returned by search endpoints. GET /records/{id}/sql requires the see_raw_sql permission and a reason, and the view is written to the activity log. Every mutating endpoint is permission-checked and logged. The console never writes to verifiers. Actions that change enforcement (policy changes) go through a pull request; restarts go through the Kubernetes API with a namespaced service account.

The console's HTTP server bounds its own resources: a request is abandoned after 30 seconds (503 TIMEOUT) and at most 512 requests are handled at once (503 OVERLOADED; /healthz and /readyz are exempt); at most 1024 client connections are open at once; a connection over the cap is closed as soon as it is accepted; a connection with no request in progress is closed 15 seconds after it was opened or after its last response was produced. This bounds how long a client may take to send request headers and how long a keep-alive connection may sit idle. The idle timer is per connection, not per header byte, and the server has no limit on concurrent TLS handshakes because it doesn't terminate TLS. Run the console behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (an ingress controller, an ALB, Cloud Load Balancing, Application Gateway, nginx, Envoy) that terminates TLS and enforces its own header-read and idle timeouts and connection limits. Set public_url to the URL users open, so the CSRF check compares origins with it instead of relying on the proxy to preserve Host (see config.md). See api.md for the HTTP contract and deploy.md for running it locally and on AWS, GCP and Azure.

haltsql-console --config console.yaml (or HALTSQL_CONSOLE_CONFIG). YAML or JSON. A complete example is deploy/console/console.example.yaml. Unknown keys are errors. Secrets. Any string can contain ${env:NAME}, ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} or ${gcp-sm:...}. Provider placeholders need a secrets: section with the same shape as the server's (secrets.md). $${ writes a literal ${. Resolved values are never logged or returned by the API. When placeholders are resolved depends on the section: At load: the sections the console reads at startup (listen, environment, state_dir, frontend_dir, auth, verifiers, fleet, audit, policies, data, agents). A placeholder that cannot be resolved is a startup error. On demand: opa, integrations, signals and catalogs (catalogs are resolved on every catalog load, so a rotated catalog token is used by the next load; signals takes only numbers, so it has no placeholders in practice). At load each placeholder is only checked: valid syntax, a known scheme, the provider configured in secrets:, and for ${env:...} the variable set. Errors stop startup. The value is fetched only when a feature needs it (for example when it posts to Slack). Provider values are cached for at most 5 minutes, so a rotated secret is picked up without a restart, and the console does not keep these secrets in memory between uses. The configuration document the console keeps for feature-specific keys is the file as written, with its placeholders unresolved.

Key Default Meaning listen 127.0.0.1:8090 host:port to serve on. --listen, then HALTSQL_CONSOLE_LISTEN, override it (the container image sets HALTSQL_CONSOLE_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8090). public_url none The URL browsers use to reach the console, for example https://console.example.com: http or https, a host, an optional port, no path. Its origin is added to allowed_origins. allowed_origins [] More browser origins (scheme://host[:port]) allowed to send state-changing requests, for example a frontend dev server. See Origins. environment.org, .name, .region HaltSQL, Default, none Shown in the environment switcher. state_dir ./console-state Durable state (cases, activity log, signal workflow, evidence packs). Must be writable; /readyz is 503 otherwise. Put it on a persistent volume. frontend_dir none Directory with the built web frontend, served at /.

At least one of oidc, proxy, tokens, dev. dev cannot be combined with the others. Key Meaning oidc[] name, issuer, audience (or audiences), optional jwks_uri, groups_claim (default groups), group_prefix (default <name>:), leeway_seconds, allow_insecure_http (tests only). Tokens are verified like the server verifies callers (JWKS, iss, aud, expiry; RS256, ES256, PS256, EdDSA), and the sign-in must be recent enough for session_hours. proxy Trusts identity headers set by an identity-aware proxy. See auth.proxy. tokens[] name, sha256 (hex SHA-256 of the token), role. For automation. dev true, or { user, role }. The role defaults to dev. Every request without credentials is that user. Development only: see Dev mode. --dev ROLE does the same. roles { admin: [groups], owner: [...], analyst: [...], audit: [...], dev: [...] }. A user gets every role one of their groups maps to, and their permissions are the union of those roles. The most privileged role (admin, then owner, audit, analyst, dev) is shown as their primary role. A user whose groups map to no role is refused. session_hours 1 to 720, default 8. An OIDC token is refused with session expired; sign in again when its auth_time claim (or iat when there is no auth_time) is more than session_hours old. A token with neither claim is accepted until it expires, unless require_auth_time is set. Not applied to proxy headers or service tokens: set the session length on the proxy. require_auth_time Default false. When true, an OIDC token without an auth_time claim is refused (session expired; sign in again), so session_hours is measured from the actual sign-in. Check that your provider sets auth_time (some only do when the client asks for it, for example with max_age). The Access page shows the Sessions safeguard as verified only when OIDC is the only auth method and this is true.

Key Meaning user_header Required. Header with the user's id (for example X-Auth-Request-Email). name_header Optional display-name header. groups_header Optional header with comma-separated groups. group_prefix Prepended to each proxy group before role mapping. Default "". Set it (for example proxy:) when OIDC is also configured, so a proxy group can't collide with an OIDC group. label Shown as the auth method, proxy:<label>. Default proxy. trusted_proxies IPs or CIDRs (IPv4 or IPv6) of the proxy, for example [10.0.0.0/8, "fd00::/8"]. The TCP peer of the request must be in one of them. secret_header, secret_sha256 A header the proxy adds with a shared secret, and the hex SHA-256 of that secret. The header must hash to secret_sha256. The comparison is constant-time. You must set trusted_proxies, the shared secret, or both. When both are set, both checks must pass. A request that carries user_header but fails a check gets 401 (proxy identity headers from an untrusted source). It is not treated as anonymous. Still make sure the console can only be reached through the proxy, and that the proxy strips these headers from client requests.

auth.dev is refused at startup unless: it is the only auth method: no oidc, proxy or tokens, and listen is a loopback address: 127.0.0.0/8, ::1 ([::1]:port) or localhost. An empty host or * means 0.0.0.0, which is not loopback. These rules also apply after --listen and --dev overrides (either one alone or both), and the server checks them again before it binds. When dev mode is not configured, a request without credentials is always 401. In dev mode, every /api/ request must also be addressed to a loopback host: its Host header must be localhost, an address in 127.0.0.0/8 or [::1] (any port), else 403 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED. This blocks DNS rebinding, where a web page on another site resolves its own name to 127.0.0.1 and calls the console from the browser.

State-changing /api/ requests (anything but GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) are checked against cross-site request forgery. A request without an Origin header (curl, scripts) passes. A request with one passes when: public_url or allowed_origins is set: the Origin's scheme, host and port are one of the configured origins (a missing port is the scheme's default). The Host header is not used, so this works behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that rewrites Host. neither is set: the Origin names the same host and port as the Host header. A proxy in front must then pass Host through unchanged. Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site is refused in both cases.

Key Meaning name Unique; matches the verifier of audit sources. url Base URL of the verifier's HTTP API (for kind: proxy, its PostgreSQL address; see fleet). kind server (default), proxy, mcp. location Free text shown in Fleet. token Admin bearer token; the verifier must list it in server.admin.callers. A secret placeholder (${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...}, ...) is resolved at load and again on every poll (provider values are cached for at most five minutes), so a rotated token is picked up without a restart; a resolve failure is shown as the verifier's error. ca_file PEM CA bundle that verifies an https:// url (and a same-origin metrics_url), e.g. a private CA. Default: the system trust store. allow_insecure_http Default false. With a token, url must be https:// or http:// on a loopback host (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost); any other http:// URL is refused at load, because the admin token would cross the network in cleartext. Set true only when the network path is trusted (for example plain HTTP inside one cluster); prefer https:// with ca_file. metrics_url Default <url>/metrics. workload Kubernetes workload to restart, deployment/<name> or statefulset/<name> (deploy/, sts/ also accepted). Checked at load.

fleet: poll_seconds: 30 # probe_timeout_seconds: 5 # history_size: 120 # max_concurrent_probes: 16 kubernetes: # optional: enables POST /api/v1/fleet/{name}/restart namespace: haltsql # api: https://kubernetes.default.svc # token_file: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token # ca_file: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt Key Default Meaning poll_seconds 30 How often every verifier is polled (with +-10% jitter). Each poll reads <url>/v1/admin/status (with token), <url>/readyz (no token) and metrics_url (with token only on the same origin), concurrently per verifier, each with probe_timeout_seconds. probe_timeout_seconds 5 Timeout of each probe request (1 to 60). history_size 120 Metric samples kept per verifier (2 to 10000). The window in time is history_size x poll_seconds. max_concurrent_probes 16 Verifiers probed at the same time (1 to 1024); each uses up to three requests. A verifier that stays unreachable is probed less often: after n failed polls in a row it is skipped for min(2^(n-1) - 1, 8) polls (its error says so), and probed every poll again once it answers. kubernetes.namespace required Namespace of the verifier workloads. Must be a valid namespace name (checked at load). kubernetes.api https://kubernetes.default.svc API server URL. https:// is verified against ca_file; http:// is accepted only for a loopback host (tests, kubectl proxy), since the service-account token would otherwise be sent in cleartext. Checked at load. kubernetes.token_file in-cluster service-account token Re-read on every restart, so projected tokens rotate. A missing file is logged as a warning at startup and makes restarts return 503 NOT_CONFIGURED; it does not stop the config from loading (so a config can be validated outside the pod). kubernetes.ca_file in-cluster CA Cluster CA bundle (PEM), used when api is https://. Missing: warned at startup, restarts fail, as for token_file. What each verifier kind exposes: server: everything. /v1/admin/status needs server.admin enabled with the console's token in server.admin.callers; without it (404) the state comes from /readyz and /metrics only. A 401/403 is shown as the verifier's error. mcp: polled the same way; a 404 on any endpoint is not an error. proxy: haltsql-proxy has no HTTP endpoints. Give its PostgreSQL address as url (postgres://host:6432 or tcp://host:6432) and the console checks that it accepts TCP connections. An http(s):// url is polled like a server. The admin token is sent to metrics_url only when it has the same scheme, host and port as url. Rates (verifies_per_second), OPA decision counts, OPA errors (timeouts) and buffered-record peaks are computed from the last history_size polls kept in memory, so they restart from zero when the console restarts. Each sample is timestamped when that verifier's /metrics answer arrives, so a slow verifier does not skew the rates of the others. Bundle source ids and last_error texts from the verifiers' admin status are shown to every role, so the console strips the query, fragment and userinfo from any URL in them (https://bucket/b.tar.gz?<redacted>) before they enter the fleet document.

A restart is the patch kubectl rollout restart sends (a new kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt pod-template annotation) on the verifier's workload (deployment/<name> or statefulset/<name>). The console's service account needs only patch on those workloads in that namespace: apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: { name: haltsql-console-restart, namespace: haltsql } rules: - apiGroups: ["apps"] resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets"] # optionally pin resourceNames: ["haltsql-1", "haltsql-2"] verbs: ["patch"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: { name: haltsql-console-restart, namespace: haltsql } roleRef: { apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: Role, name: haltsql-console-restart } subjects: - { kind: ServiceAccount, name: haltsql-console, namespace: haltsql } Restarts need the restart_verifiers permission (admin) and a reason. The intent is written to the activity log as fleet.restart_requested (result: pending) before the Kubernetes call, and the restart is refused if that write fails; the outcome is then written as fleet.restart (ok, no_rollout or error, also when the Kubernetes call fails).

Where the console reads audit records. The console only reads; the verifiers keep writing their sinks as configured. audit: sources: # one of these per location; a file is read by the first source that names it - { verifier: haltsql-1, file: /var/log/haltsql-1/audit.jsonl } - { verifier: auto, file: /var/log/haltsql/ } # every *.jsonl / *.log inside - { verifier: auto, file: "/var/log/haltsql-proxy/audit-*.jsonl" } - { verifier: auto, s3: "s3://acme-audit/haltsql/", region: us-east-1 } - { verifier: auto, gcs: "gs://acme-audit/haltsql/" } retention_hours: 168 max_records: 2000000 poll_seconds: 5 Key Default Meaning sources[] none Exactly one of file (alias path), s3 or gcs, plus verifier. The same file, directory, glob or URI listed twice is a configuration error. A file matched by two sources (a file and the directory holding it) is read only by the first, and the later source reports it under overlaps in the ingest status. sources[].verifier auto Verifier name the records belong to (matches verifiers[].name). With auto, the name comes from the object name (object sinks write <host>-<run>-<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl, so the host), else the file's basename without extension. sources[].file A file, a directory (every *.jsonl and *.log directly inside, in name order) or a glob with */? in the last path segment. Files are tracked by inode and tailed by byte offset through a descriptor kept open between polls; only complete lines are read. After a rename rotation the old file's unread tail is read first (record locations keep the path the file was first seen at), and a glob that also matches rotated names does not read a file twice. A file that shrinks, or whose first line changed (copytruncate), is read again from the start and the chain check reports a gap there instead of a break. A record identical to one already read for the same verifier is skipped. sources[].s3 s3://bucket/prefix. Every .jsonl object under the prefix is read once, in key order. Only keys from the YYYY/MM/DD/HH/ partition of the retention start on are listed (the object-sink layout; with a prefix that does not end in / the whole prefix is listed), and keys before it are forgotten. An object that cannot be read holds back the later objects of the same host and is retried on the next polls; after object_attempts failures it is skipped, listed under skipped_objects in the ingest status, and the chain check reports a gap. Credentials: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (optional AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), web identity (IRSA), ECS/EKS Pod Identity or the instance profile. Needs s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject only. sources[].region AWS_REGION, else us-east-1 S3 signing region. sources[].endpoint AWS S3-compatible endpoint (path-style; https, or http on loopback). sources[].gcs gs://bucket/prefix, read like S3 through the JSON API. Credentials: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS (service-account key file), else the metadata server (Workload Identity). Needs storage.objects.list and storage.objects.get. STORAGE_EMULATOR_HOST overrides the API base: it must be https, or http on a loopback host, and no credentials are sent to it. Credentials are not cached after a failure, and a changed key file is re-read. retention_hours 168 Records older than this are dropped from the in-memory index. max_records 2000000 Index size cap; the oldest records are evicted first. poll_seconds 5 How often every source is polled. A source that fails is retried after poll_seconds, doubled per consecutive failure up to 5 minutes. max_object_mb 256 Largest S3/GCS object read; a larger one fails (and is skipped after object_attempts). max_line_mb 64 A file line longer than this is skipped (it still counts for line numbers). request_timeout_seconds 60 Timeout of each S3/GCS request. relist_minutes 10 How often objects are listed from the retention start; in between, listings start at the partition of an hour ago. Objects uploaded late under an older partition (a spool replay) are picked up by the next full listing. object_attempts 5 Failed reads before an object is skipped. chain_check_seconds 300 How often the published audit-chain status is refreshed (incrementally). Each verifier's records are numbered (seq) in the order they are read; the chain of custody check walks that order. Per-source state (records read, last successful read, last error, skipped_objects, overlaps, and next_poll while backing off) is kept as the console's ingest status for the other views. File I/O runs off the event loop, and object sources are polled concurrently (at most four at a time), so a slow mount or bucket does not hold up the others. Prefer a prefix that holds only HaltSQL audit objects.

The console loads the same policies as the verifiers, for the Playground, policy detail, shadow reports and suggestions. Loading runs at startup and every 60 seconds; a load that fails anywhere keeps the last good set (like the server's hot reload), and the errors are shown in GET /api/v1/policies (errors, file basenames only). A policy file is read and parsed once per change: a reload reuses the parsed policy while the file's modification time and size are unchanged. Key Meaning policies.server_config A haltsql-server config file. Only its policies section is decoded, with the server's loader: the console never resolves the server's other secrets (database, admin tokens, OPA headers), so its identity needs no access to them. A secret provider placeholder inside policies (for example a bundle key) is resolved through the file's own secrets: section, with one resolver kept for an hour across reloads. Supported: policies[].path, policies[].inline, and local signed bundles (policies[].bundle with public_keys and name_prefix; the signature is verified). Not fetched: remote bundle_source entries; their policies appear only through fleet status (loaded: false). policies.files Policy files, or directories whose *.yaml/*.yml/*.json documents with kind: Policy are loaded (other documents, such as test suites, are skipped). They replace server-config policies of the same name, like the server's --policy flags. Relative paths are resolved against the console config file's directory. A policy's version is the same sha256: the verifiers log as policy_version. A shadow sibling of policy P is a loaded shadow-mode policy named P-*, P_* or P.*; it is the default compare of GET /api/v1/policies/P/report and an agent's default shadow policy. opa has exactly the shape of the server's opa block (url, decision_path, timeout_ms, on_error, headers, tls.ca_file). When set, the Playground asks OPA after a HaltSQL allow, with the same input document as the server (caller.type is playground), honouring timeout_ms and on_error. policies: server_config: /etc/haltsql/server.yaml files: [/etc/haltsql/policies/drafts] opa: url: https://opa.internal:8181 decision_path: haltsql/allow timeout_ms: 500 on_error: deny

Detectors run every 30 seconds (interval_seconds) over the record index, the fleet snapshot and the last audit-chain verification. Every key is optional; numbers may be integers or decimals unless the table says integer. Unknown keys, non-numbers and values outside the range are configuration errors at startup. signals: cross_tenant: { window_minutes: 10, min_records: 10 } deny_spike: { window_minutes: 15, factor: 3.0, min_records: 50, min_baseline_rate: 0.01 } opa_errors: { window_minutes: 15, min_records: 10 } shadow_ready: { min_records: 1 } new_caller: { hours: 24 } interval_seconds: 30 resolve_after_minutes: 30 forget_after_days: 7 max_reverify: 500 notify_timeout_seconds: 5 Key Default Range Meaning cross_tenant.window_minutes 10 1-1440 Sliding window for E_TENANT_MISMATCH records per caller. cross_tenant.min_records 10 integer 1-1000000 Records in the window that open a high cross_tenant signal. deny_spike.window_minutes 15 1-1440 Window whose deny rate is compared with the caller's previous 24 hours. deny_spike.factor 3.0 1-1000 The window's deny rate must be at least this many times the baseline. deny_spike.min_records 50 integer 1-1000000 Minimum records from the caller in the window. deny_spike.min_baseline_rate 0.01 0-1 Baseline deny rate used when the real one is lower, so one denial after a quiet day is not a spike. opa_errors.window_minutes 15 1-1440 Window for E_EXTERNAL_POLICY denials and for the fleet's OPA error counter delta. opa_errors.min_records 10 integer 1-1000000 E_EXTERNAL_POLICY denials in the window that open a signal (any increase of the fleet's OPA error counter also does). shadow_ready.min_records 1 integer 1-1000000 Shadow-denied records in 24 hours that open a shadow_ready signal for a policy. new_caller.hours 24 1-720 A caller first seen this recently and not listed under agents opens a low signal. Only checked once the index holds older records, so a fresh console does not flag every caller. interval_seconds 30 5-3600 Time between detector passes. resolve_after_minutes 30 1-10080 A signal whose condition has cleared this long is resolved automatically (unless someone set its status). forget_after_days 7 1-365 A resolved signal leaves memory this long after it cleared; its workflow and snapshot stay in state_dir. max_reverify 500 integer 0-10000 cross_tenant: statements per signal re-verified to extract tenant values (results are cached per record). notify_timeout_seconds 5 1-60 Timeout of each Slack or PagerDuty request. sink_buffering, restart_pending and bundle_drift come from the fleet snapshot and chain_broken from the last chain verification; they have no settings. Detector output is kept in memory and rebuilt after a restart. When someone sets a status, an assignee or a case, that workflow state and a snapshot of the signal are stored in state_dir (signals.json); after a restart a re-detected condition re-attaches to its workflow while the workflow is still open, and GET /api/v1/signals/{id} serves the snapshot until then. Each pass yields to the HTTP server between detectors, groups records by caller once, and scans the whole index for first-seen callers only on the first pass, hourly, or when older records appear.

Agents shown in GET /api/v1/agents. Every caller seen in audit records that no agent claims becomes its own agent (via guessed: proxy records → proxy, a verifier of kind mcp → mcp, else sidecar). Key Meaning name Required, unique. team, stack, identity Free text shown on the agent. via sidecar (default), proxy, mcp or in_process. In-process agents verify inside the app, so the console has no records for them (queries: null, audit: in_app). callers Audit caller values that belong to this agent (exact match). policy Its enforced policy; default the most frequent policy of its records. agents: - name: analytics-agent team: Data platform stack: LangGraph, Python callers: ["oidc:okta:svc-analytics"] policy: analytics

Catalogs are read at startup, every 15 minutes, and on POST /api/v1/data/refresh. Export files are parsed in a worker thread, so a large manifest.json never stalls the console, and the 15-minute reload re-parses a file only when its modification time or size changed; POST /api/v1/data/refresh always re-reads every file. A catalog that cannot be read is reported (in GET /api/v1/data/columns sources[].error and as error under Integrations); the others still load. catalogs: - { kind: dbt, manifest: /etc/haltsql/catalogs/manifest.json } - { kind: unity, file: /etc/haltsql/catalogs/unity-column-tags.json } - { kind: datahub, file: /etc/haltsql/catalogs/datahub-export.json } # live fetch: see the note below; no live provider is built in yet # - { kind: openmetadata, url: https://om.acme.internal/api, token: "${vault:secret/om#token}", service: prod_pg, database: app } - { kind: file, file: /etc/haltsql/policies/pii.json, label: reviewed } data: exceptions: - { column: app.customers.email, policy: support-copilot, owner: Lee Park, ticket: SEC-88, expires: "2027-02-01" } catalogs[] key Meaning kind dbt, datahub, openmetadata, unity or file. label Name shown in column sources and Integrations. Default: the kind. manifest dbt: the manifest.json (column tags, meta, config.tags, config.meta, policy_tags, nested meta.pii). catalog dbt, optional: catalog.json (column comments). file datahub: a file-sink export or GraphQL response. unity: information_schema.column_tags rows or table JSON. file: a HaltSQL PII manifest (the haltsql schema import format). url datahub, openmetadata, unity: read the catalog's API live through Haltsql_catalog_fetch (same providers as haltsql schema fetch). https://, or http:// on loopback. Pending: no live provider is built into this release yet (the DataHub and OpenMetadata providers land separately), so a catalog with url reports the error no live <kind> provider is built into this console. Use an export file (dbt, datahub, unity) until then; openmetadata has no file mode. token Bearer token for url. Use a secret placeholder; never returned or logged. service, database, schemas Live fetch scope, as haltsql schema fetch --service/--database/--schema. ca_file, timeout_seconds Live fetch: trust only this CA bundle; per-request timeout (default 30). tags, terms Labels that mark a column as sensitive (default: pii, sensitive, confidential, restricted, gdpr, phi, pci, personal, email, phone, ssn, secret), as --pii-tag/--pii-term. detail Free text shown as the source's detail. The importers are the ones haltsql schema import and haltsql report --pii use (see schema-and-pii.md). Columns are merged per schema.table.column (lower-cased): tags and sources are the union. Live fetches are non-authoritative. A catalog's view of table structure can lag behind the database, so a live-fetched source is reported with authoritative: false and only flags columns. The console never loads it as a policy catalog. Status of a tagged column. allowed_by lists the loaded policies whose allowlist lets a SELECT read the column (the table is listed and the column is listed, or the table allows "*"). With no such policy the column is blocked. Otherwise it is exception when every allowing policy is covered by an unexpired data.exceptions entry for the column (an entry without policy covers every policy), and needs_review otherwise, including when the matching exception has expired. shadow_denials counts shadow-denied records that read the column (from the record, or re-derived from raw SQL when it was logged). The counts come from a background scan of the record index that runs every minute (and on POST /api/v1/data/refresh), so a new record is counted within about a minute; shadow_denials_counted in the document is when the last scan finished. Columns re-derived from SQL are cached per verifier and request id, dropped when the record leaves the index, and re-derived after a policy reload. The classification follows a policy reload immediately. data.exceptions[] key Meaning column schema.table.column. policy Optional: only this policy is covered. owner Required. Who approved it. ticket Optional reference. expires Optional date (2027-02-01, valid through that day UTC) or RFC 3339 time. An unparsable value counts as expired.

Used by POST /api/v1/policies/{name}/pull-request (and the PR state in policy reports). Without it that endpoint returns 503 NOT_CONFIGURED. Key Default Meaning repo required owner/name of the policy repository. token required Token with contents: write and pull_requests: write (and checks: read). Use a secret placeholder, e.g. ${env:GITHUB_TOKEN}. Never returned or logged. base main Branch PRs target. path policies Directory of policy files in the repo. The file patched is <path>/<basename of the loaded file> (<name>.yaml for inline and bundle policies); when that is missing, the only file under <path> (any depth) with that basename, else the only one (of the first 25 policy documents) whose metadata.name is the policy's name. Several matches are 409; no match is 409 unless the request sets create_file: true (the loaded source is then added at the default path). policy_paths none Mapping of policy name to its file in the repo (for example analytics: teams/data/analytics.yaml), used instead of the lookup above. tests_path tests Directory of test suites; tests are appended to <tests_path>/<policy>.yaml (created, pointing at the policy file, when absent). branch_prefix haltsql-console/ PR branch is <branch_prefix><policy>; an open PR for the policy (the one the console stored, else any open PR GitHub has for that branch) is updated instead of opening another. A leftover branch with no open PR is reset to base only when its head is a commit the console made; otherwise the request is 409. required_approvals 1 Shown next to the approvals in the PR state. api https://api.github.com API base URL (GitHub Enterprise: https://ghe.example.com/api/v3). https, or http for loopback only. Reads (GETs) are retried up to three times on a network error, a 5xx, a 429 or a rate-limit 403, honouring Retry-After and x-ratelimit-reset (a wait over 5 seconds is not taken: the call fails instead). Writes are never retried. Reviews and check runs are read 100 per page, following Link: rel="next" for up to 10 pages. integrations: github: repo: acme/haltsql-policies token: ${env:GITHUB_TOKEN} path: policies required_approvals: 2

integrations: slack: { webhook: "${vault:secret/slack#webhook}" } pagerduty: { routing_key: "${vault:secret/pagerduty#key}" } Key Meaning slack.webhook Slack incoming-webhook URL. pagerduty.routing_key PagerDuty Events API v2 integration (routing) key. pagerduty.events_url Default https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue; override for a proxy or EU endpoint. Each new high signal is posted to every configured channel (PagerDuty: event_action: trigger, dedup_key = the signal id, severity critical). When a high signal resolves (automatically, or a person sets resolved), the PagerDuty incident is resolved with event_action: resolve and the same dedup_key. Delivery is best effort: a request that gets HTTP 429, a 5xx or a transport error is retried twice (0.5 s, then 1 s later); other failures are logged with the HTTP status only, never the URL or key. Placeholders in these keys are resolved on each use; one that cannot be resolved is logged and the channel is skipped. Slack text escapes &, < and > in every field, so a caller name cannot mention @channel or disguise a link. URLs must be https (plain http only on a loopback host).

integrations: jira: { url: https://acme.atlassian.net, project: SEC, email: haltsql-bot@acme.com, token: "${vault:secret/jira#token}" } Key Meaning url Jira base URL. project Project key for new issues. token API token. With email, sent as Basic auth (Jira Cloud); without, as a Bearer token (Jira Data Center personal access token). email Optional; the account the API token belongs to. issue_type Default Task. Creating a case also creates a Jira issue and stores its key on the case (jira: { key, url }). If Jira is unreachable the case is still created, with jira: null.

haltsql-console is the control plane for a HaltSQL deployment. It reads what the verifiers (haltsql-server, haltsql-proxy, haltsql-mcp) already publish (audit records, GET /v1/admin/status and /v1/admin/report, /readyz, /metrics) and the policy files they load. It is never in the query path: if the console is down, enforcement does not change. See architecture.md for the design, config.md for every configuration key and api.md for the HTTP API. This guide covers running it locally (Docker Compose or the bare binary), on Kubernetes with the Helm chart, and on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, both on their Kubernetes services and on their serverless container platforms. Path What it is Dockerfile (target console) The ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console image: static binary on distroless/static:nonroot. deploy/console/ Example config, the local Compose stack, demo-traffic.sh. deploy/helm/haltsql-console/ Helm chart. Values reference in its README. deploy/cloud/{aws,gcp,azure}/console/ Values overlays, IAM, ECS / Cloud Run / Container Apps definitions. deploy/terraform/examples/console-kubernetes/ Terraform root module: the chart through helm_release.

Whatever the platform, the console needs the same five things: One replica and a persistent state_dir. Cases, the activity log, signal workflow state and evidence packs are the only durable state, kept as files in state_dir (/var/lib/haltsql-console in the image). Run exactly one replica per environment on a single-writer volume, and stop the old instance before the new one starts (Kubernetes Recreate, ECS minimumHealthyPercent: 0, Cloud Run and Container Apps maxScale: 1). Everything else (the record index, fleet snapshots, signals) is rebuilt from the verifiers at startup. /readyz answers 503 while state_dir is not writable. An admin token on every verifier. The console polls each verifier's admin API with a bearer token. On the verifier, that token is an ordinary server.auth.tokens entry (every token is pinned to a policy) whose name is listed in server.admin.callers: # verifier config (haltsql-server) server: auth: tokens: - name: console token_sha256: ${env:HALTSQL_CONSOLE_TOKEN_SHA256} policy: analytics-agent # any loaded policy; used only for admin calls admin: enabled: true callers: [token:console] # or oidc:<provider>, mtls:<identity> # console config verifiers: - name: haltsql url: http://haltsql.haltsql.svc:8080 token: ${env:HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN} # the raw token, from a secret workload: deployment/haltsql # optional: restarts from Fleet The admin endpoints are read-only. With the haltsql Helm chart, add server.admin through extraConfig and the token through tokens. The audit trail. audit.sources points at what the verifiers write: files (a shared volume), s3://bucket/prefix/ or gs://bucket/prefix/. Raw SQL is only in the records if the verifiers set audit.log_raw_sql. The verifiers' policies. policies.server_config (or policies.files) points at the same config and policy files the verifiers load, mounted read-only, so the Playground, decision trails and exposure use exactly the verifiers' policies. Authentication in front. One of: OIDC (auth.oidc), an identity-aware proxy that is the only way to reach the console (auth.proxy, for example the chart's oauth2-proxy sidecar), or automation tokens (auth.tokens). Roles come from groups (auth.roles), so the identity source must provide group membership. Never expose the console publicly; keep it on an internal load balancer or behind a private ingress. Secrets (admin tokens, GitHub token, webhook URLs) go in ${env:NAME}, ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} or ${gcp-sm:...} placeholders, never in the file. Resolved values are never logged or returned by the API.

docker build --target console -t haltsql-console-local:dev . # or: make console-image scripts/console-docker-smoke.sh # or: make console-smoke Release images are ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console:<version>, multi-arch (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), built by the release workflow from the same builder stage as the haltsql image, with SPDX SBOM and SLSA provenance attestations, signed keylessly with cosign. Pin by digest in production; the identity regexp accepts only the release workflow on a version tag, not any workflow or branch of the repository: cosign verify ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console@sha256:<digest> \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console@sha256:<digest> --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL Property Value Base gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot (no shell, no libc, no package manager) User 65532:65532 Root filesystem Read-only (docker run --read-only, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true) Entrypoint / command haltsql-console / --config /etc/haltsql-console/console.yaml Port 8090 (HALTSQL_CONSOLE_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8090) Writable volume /var/lib/haltsql-console (state_dir, VOLUME, owned by 65532) Frontend /usr/share/haltsql-console/web is reserved for frontend_dir Health HEALTHCHECK runs haltsql-console --healthcheck (GET /healthz on the listen port). Orchestrators should use HTTP probes: liveness /healthz, readiness /readyz. Signals SIGTERM/SIGINT stop the listener and exit 0; configuration errors exit 2. --listen > HALTSQL_CONSOLE_LISTEN > listen: in the config, so listen: has no effect inside the image. Change the address with --listen or the environment variable (--healthcheck probes that same address, using loopback when it listens on all interfaces).

deploy/console/docker-compose.yaml runs a complete stack from this checkout: Service What it does postgres PostgreSQL 17 with a small app schema (local/seed.sql). haltsql haltsql-server with local/haltsql.yaml: two policies (saas-analytics enforced, support-bot in shadow mode), server.admin enabled for the console's token, a file audit sink on the shared audit volume, log_raw_sql: true. Port 127.0.0.1:18080. console haltsql-console with console.local.yaml (demo tokens: demo-admin-token is an admin, demo-automation-token an auditor): reads the audit file read-only, polls the server's admin API, loads the server's config. Port 127.0.0.1:8090. make console-up # docker compose -f deploy/console/docker-compose.yaml up -d --build make console-demo # deploy/console/demo-traffic.sh curl -s -H 'authorization: Bearer demo-admin-token' localhost:8090/api/v1/me curl -s -H 'authorization: Bearer demo-admin-token' 'localhost:8090/api/v1/overview?range=24h' make console-down # stops the stack and deletes its volumes demo-traffic.sh sends a mix of queries through POST /v1/verify: allowed tenant-scoped reads, denials (PII column, DELETE, missing LIMIT, system catalog), cross-tenant attempts (another tenant's literal, OR across tenants, no tenant predicate) and shadow-mode would-be denials. ROUNDS=20 produces enough cross-tenant records to trip the cross-tenant signal; EXECUTE=1 also runs each allowed query on the stack's Postgres as a read-only role, the way an agent uses HaltSQL (verify, then execute). The stack is a demo: the tokens in local/haltsql.yaml and console.local.yaml are well-known strings, and both ports are bound to 127.0.0.1. It does not use dev mode: dev mode only runs on a loopback listen address, and inside the container the console listens on 0.0.0.0. All containers run read-only with every capability dropped.

opam exec -- dune build ./bin/console # or: make console cp deploy/console/console.example.yaml console.yaml # edit verifiers, audit, auth mkdir -p console-state _build/default/bin/console/main.exe --config console.yaml --listen 127.0.0.1:8090 --dev admin --dev ROLE authenticates every request as a local user with that role. It replaces every other auth method in the config, and the console refuses to start with it unless listen is a loopback address (see Dev mode). Release builds are static (HALTSQL_STATIC=1 dune build --profile release ./bin/console, on musl). For a VM, run it under systemd with the same hardening as deploy/systemd/haltsql-server.service and StateDirectory=haltsql-console.

kubectl -n haltsql create secret generic haltsql-console-env \ --from-literal=HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN="$CONSOLE_ADMIN_TOKEN" helm upgrade --install haltsql-console deploy/helm/haltsql-console -n haltsql \ -f my-console-values.yaml The chart (values reference) renders: a Deployment with one replica and the Recreate strategy, the same hardening as the haltsql chart (uid/gid 65532, read-only root filesystem, no capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no service-link env vars, no service account token at pod level; with restarts enabled the token is projected into the console container only, never the oauth2-proxy sidecar or extraContainers), and startup, liveness and readiness probes. The chart has no dev mode: it refuses console.devRole and --dev in extraArgs, since dev mode needs a loopback listen address and signs every request in; a PersistentVolumeClaim for state_dir (ReadWriteOnce, 10 Gi; persistence.existingClaim to bring your own); a ConfigMap with the console config (console.config; the chart sets listen and state_dir), or your own (console.existingConfigMap). The default audit.max_records is 200,000: an index entry takes about 2.4 KB of memory, so keep max_records x 2.4 KB under half of resources.limits.memory (1 Gi by default) and raise both together. The console's own default of 2,000,000 records needs about 5 GB; secrets from existingSecret (every key becomes an environment variable for ${env:...} placeholders), so tokens live in External Secrets, the Secrets Store CSI driver or Sealed Secrets, never in values; the verifiers' config and policies mounted read-only at /etc/haltsql/config and /etc/haltsql/policies (verifierConfig; with the haltsql chart these are the <release>-config and <release>-policies ConfigMaps); a Service (ClusterIP) and an optional Ingress; a ServiceAccount and, with rbac.create, a namespaced Role and RoleBinding that allow only patch on the listed Deployments and StatefulSets (verifier restarts); the chart then sets fleet.kubernetes.namespace and projects the token into the console container. RBAC cannot limit a patch to the restartedAt annotation the console sets, so the Role allows any patch of those workloads (image, command, env); see Keeping it private for an admission policy that narrows it; a NetworkPolicy: ingress only on the HTTP port from ingressFrom (empty = every pod in the release namespace); egress only to DNS, the verifiers (pods of the haltsql chart on 8080 by default), TCP 443 (IdP, GitHub, Slack, PagerDuty, catalogs, S3/GCS, secret managers, the Kubernetes API) and extraRules; an optional oauth2-proxy sidecar (oauth2Proxy.enabled): the console then listens on 127.0.0.1 only, the Service points at the sidecar, and the chart sets auth.proxy to trust X-Forwarded-Email, X-Forwarded-Groups and X-Forwarded-Preferred-Username, which oauth2-proxy sets from the session and overwrites on every request, with trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1/32, "::1/128"] (the console refuses an auth.proxy without trusted_proxies or a shared secret). Set oauth2Proxy.allowedGroups (or a provider group flag in extraArgs) so only the console's groups can sign in; the release notes warn otherwise. An auth.proxy of your own, without the sidecar, must set trusted_proxies or secret_header + secret_sha256, and without the secret the chart also requires a non-empty networkPolicy.ingressFrom; a PodDisruptionBudget (off by default) and a ServiceMonitor (off; the console has no Prometheus endpoint yet). The verifiers' NetworkPolicy must admit the console, even in the same namespace: a policy whose ingressFrom lists only the agents' namespace drops the console's admin API calls. The shipped verifier policies (values-gke.yaml, the EKS and AKS networkpolicy-shared.yaml) admit pods labelled app.kubernetes.io/name: haltsql-console in their namespace; add the same podSelector to your own: networkPolicy: # the haltsql chart's values ingressFrom: - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: agents } } - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: haltsql-console } } If the console runs in a different namespace, put a namespaceSelector for it in the same entry as that podSelector, and set rbac.namespace to the verifiers' namespace. Plain manifests: helm template haltsql-console deploy/helm/haltsql-console -n haltsql -f my-values.yaml > console.yaml produces reviewable YAML for GitOps tools that do not run Helm.

deploy/terraform/examples/console-kubernetes installs the chart with helm_release next to a haltsql release (for example one created by the haltsql-kubernetes module), wiring the verifier URL, the restart Role, the verifiers' ConfigMaps and the state volume. Cloud specifics come from the overlays below through values_files: cd deploy/terraform/examples/console-kubernetes terraform init terraform apply -var kube_context=my-eks \ -var 'values_files=["../../../cloud/aws/console/eks.values.yaml"]' The admin-token Secret is referenced by name (admin_token_secret) and is never written to Terraform state. automation_tokens are applied after values_files, because Helm replaces lists: a values file that sets console.config.auth.tokens would otherwise drop them silently. The cloud overlays leave auth.tokens unset for the same reason.

deploy/cloud/aws/console/eks.values.yaml installs the console next to the shared service from deploy-aws.md (namespace haltsql): kubectl -n haltsql create secret generic haltsql-console-env \ --from-literal=HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN="$CONSOLE_ADMIN_TOKEN" kubectl -n haltsql create secret generic haltsql-console-oauth2 \ --from-literal=OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID=... --from-literal=OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET=... \ --from-literal=OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET="$(openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -- '+/' '-_')" helm upgrade --install haltsql-console deploy/helm/haltsql-console -n haltsql \ -f deploy/cloud/aws/console/eks.values.yaml IRSA. The ServiceAccount haltsql-console is annotated with the role haltsql-console, whose trust policy (irsa-trust-policy.json) admits only system:serviceaccount:haltsql:haltsql-console. Its permission policy (iam-policy.json) is read-only and scoped to the audit prefix and the secrets the console itself resolves (${aws-sm:...}); list each one by name, never the whole haltsql-console/ prefix: { "Action": "s3:ListBucket", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::corp-haltsql-audit", "Condition": { "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["haltsql/audit/", "haltsql/audit/*"] } } }, { "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/*" }, { "Action": "kms:Decrypt", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": "s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" } } }, { "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": ["arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:haltsql-console/admin-token-??????"] } No s3:PutObject or DeleteObject: the console never writes the audit trail. AWS credentials come from the standard chain (web identity under IRSA), as for the server (secrets.md). Audit source. { verifier: auto, s3: "s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/", region: eu-west-1 }, the bucket and prefix of the verifiers' S3 Object Lock sink. Secrets. The admin token comes from the haltsql-console-env Secret (synced from Secrets Manager by External Secrets Operator, for example), or directly from Secrets Manager with token: ${aws-sm:haltsql-console/admin-token} and console.config.secrets.aws.region. Sign-in. An internal ALB (alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internal, TLS 1.3 policy, ACM certificate) forwards to the oauth2-proxy sidecar, which signs users in with your IdP (Okta, Entra ID, Cognito) and passes X-Forwarded-Email/-Groups to the console. The ALB's own auth-type: oidc action is not used: it forwards identity in x-amzn-oidc-* headers without a plain groups header, so the console could not map users to roles. State. An EBS gp3 volume (EBS CSI driver), with helm.sh/resource-policy: keep so helm uninstall does not delete it. Restarts. rbac.create: true with deployments: [haltsql]. If the EKS API endpoint is private and not on 443 from the pod network, add its CIDR under networkPolicy.egress.kubernetesAPI. Network. The NetworkPolicy admits only the VPC CIDR (the ALB targets pod IPs) and allows egress to the verifiers, DNS and 443. Keep the console in private subnets; reach it over VPN or Direct Connect.

console-task-definition.json runs the console and an oauth2-proxy container in one Fargate task, with state_dir on an EFS access point (POSIX user 65532, transitEncryption and IAM authorization enabled): Build the config image with Dockerfile.ecs, which bakes console.ecs.yaml and the verifiers' config and policies into a derived image, the same pattern as the verifier on ECS (deploy-aws.md).
