The console listens on 127.0.0.1:8090; only oauth2-proxy (port 4180) is registered with an internal ALB target group (health check /readyz). Secrets (HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN, the oauth2-proxy client and cookie secrets) are injected by ECS from Secrets Manager; the execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on them. The oauth2-proxy secrets live under their own name (haltsql-console-oauth2), outside the haltsql-console/ prefix, so the task role (which the console's code runs with) cannot read the cookie secret and forge oauth2-proxy sessions. console.ecs.yaml sets auth.proxy.trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1/32, "::1/128"]: the containers of a task share the loopback interface, and the console accepts identity headers only from that connection. oauth2-proxy admits only the console's groups (--allowed-group). The task role gets the S3 read and Secrets Manager statements of iam-policy.json plus elasticfilesystem:ClientMount and ClientWrite on the access point. Create the service with desiredCount: 1, minimumHealthyPercent: 0 and maximumPercent: 100 so ECS stops the old task before starting the new one (two tasks must never share state_dir). Verifier restarts are Kubernetes-only; on ECS use aws ecs update-service --force-new-deployment from your runbooks.

deploy/cloud/gcp/console/gke.values.yaml installs the console next to the GKE shared service from deploy-gcp.md: kubectl apply -n haltsql -f deploy/cloud/gcp/console/iap-backendconfig.yaml helm upgrade --install haltsql-console deploy/helm/haltsql-console -n haltsql \ -f deploy/cloud/gcp/console/gke.values.yaml Workload Identity. Bind the Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a Google service account that can only read the audit prefix and the console's secrets: gcloud iam service-accounts create haltsql-console --project "$PROJECT_ID" gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \ haltsql-console@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \ --member "serviceAccount:$PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog[haltsql/haltsql-console]" # Read-only on the audit objects (condition: only the haltsql/ prefix). gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://$PROJECT_ID-haltsql-audit" \ --member "serviceAccount:haltsql-console@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role roles/storage.objectViewer \ --condition='title=haltsql-audit-prefix,expression=resource.name.startsWith("projects/_/buckets/'"$PROJECT_ID"'-haltsql-audit/objects/haltsql/")' gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding haltsql-console-admin-token \ --member "serviceAccount:haltsql-console@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor Listing objects under a condition on resource.name needs the bucket-level storage.objects.list; if your organization does not allow conditional objectViewer, grant it on a dedicated audit bucket instead. Audit source. { verifier: auto, gcs: "gs://PROJECT-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/shared/" }, the verifiers' GCS sink. Secrets. token: ${gcp-sm:haltsql-console-admin-token} with secrets.gcp.project; credentials come from the metadata server (Workload Identity). Sign-in with IAP. The internal Application Load Balancer (className: gce-internal) has Identity-Aware Proxy enabled through the BackendConfig, so only principals with roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor reach the console at all. IAP sets x-goog-authenticated-user-email (accounts.google.com:user@example.com) and a signed x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion, but no group membership, and the console derives roles from groups. The overlay therefore runs the oauth2-proxy sidecar behind IAP with the Google provider, which looks up Workspace groups through the Admin SDK (--google-group, a service account with domain-wide delegation and the read-only group scope) and passes them in X-Forwarded-Groups. If you need IAP's header alone, the console cannot map roles from it yet. State. A premium-rwo Persistent Disk; schedule snapshots with a VolumeSnapshotClass or a GKE Backup plan. Network. The NetworkPolicy admits Google's health-check ranges and the internal ALB's proxy-only subnet; egress is DNS, the verifiers, 443 and the GKE metadata server (169.254.169.252:988, and 169.254.169.254:80 on Dataplane V2), without which Workload Identity tokens, and with them the ${gcp-sm:...} admin token and GCS audit reads, fail. The verifiers' values-gke.yaml admits the console's pods on the API port.

cloudrun-service.yaml runs the console as a Cloud Run service with: one instance only: minScale: 1 and maxScale: 1, and cpu-throttling: "false" so the background loops (audit ingestion, fleet polling, signals) keep running between requests; ingress: internal and Direct VPC egress, so it is reachable only from the VPC and reaches the verifiers over private ranges; oauth2-proxy as the ingress container (port 4180), the console on 127.0.0.1:8090; state_dir on a Filestore NFS share (gen2 execution environment). A Cloud Storage FUSE volume also mounts, but the console replaces its state files with an atomic rename, which Cloud Storage FUSE does not guarantee; use it only for disposable demos. The share must be writable by uid 65532; the console config mounted from Secret Manager, and the verifiers' config (the haltsql-internal-config secret of service-internal.yaml) at the verifier's own path, /etc/haltsql/config/config.yaml, with the signed bundle it loads on the same read-only Cloud Storage volume at /etc/haltsql/bundles. Without the bundle the console loads no policies and the Playground, decision trails and exposure stay empty. Grant haltsql-console@ roles/storage.objectViewer on the policy bucket. The console config (secret haltsql-console-config) points at those paths and trusts oauth2-proxy over loopback only: auth: proxy: user_header: X-Forwarded-Email name_header: X-Forwarded-Preferred-Username groups_header: X-Forwarded-Groups label: oauth2-proxy trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1/32, "::1/128"] # required; oauth2-proxy is on loopback roles: { admin: [haltsql-admins@acme.example], audit: [compliance@acme.example] } policies: server_config: /etc/haltsql/config/config.yaml audit: max_records: 400000 # about 2.4 KB each; fits the 2 GiB limit Verifier restarts are not available on Cloud Run; redeploy the verifier service from your runbooks.

deploy/cloud/azure/console/aks.values.yaml installs the console next to the AKS shared service from deploy-azure.md: kubectl apply -n haltsql -f deploy/cloud/azure/console/secretproviderclass.yaml kubectl apply -n haltsql -f deploy/cloud/azure/console/audit-share.yaml helm upgrade --install haltsql-console deploy/helm/haltsql-console -n haltsql \ -f deploy/cloud/azure/console/aks.values.yaml Workload Identity. A user-assigned managed identity federated with system:serviceaccount:haltsql:haltsql-console; the pod carries azure.workload.identity/use: "true": az identity create -g "$RG" -n id-haltsql-console az identity federated-credential create -g "$RG" --identity-name id-haltsql-console \ --name haltsql-console --issuer "$AKS_OIDC_ISSUER" \ --subject system:serviceaccount:haltsql:haltsql-console --audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange # Read only the console's secrets. az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --assignee "$CLIENT_ID" \ --scope "$KV_ID/secrets/haltsql-console-admin-token" Secrets. Key Vault is not a console secrets provider yet. The Secrets Store CSI driver (secretproviderclass.yaml) fetches the admin token with the workload identity and syncs it into the haltsql-console-env Secret, which the chart exposes as HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN for ${env:HALTSQL_ADMIN_TOKEN}. The CSI volume is mounted (extraVolumes) because the driver syncs only for mounted pods. Audit source. Azure Blob is not a console audit source yet. The verifiers write one file sink per pod (/var/log/haltsql-shared/${env:POD_NAME}.jsonl) to an Azure Files share (audit-share.yaml, ReadWriteMany, files owned by 65532), alongside the stdout or Blob sinks they already have; the console mounts the same claim read-only (auditVolume) and reads /var/log/haltsql/*.jsonl. Sign-in. An Application Gateway (AGIC, private frontend IP) routes to the oauth2-proxy sidecar, which signs users in with Entra ID (provider: oidc, issuer https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0). Turn on groupMembershipClaims: SecurityGroup on the app registration; group claims are object IDs, so auth.roles lists object IDs. State. An Azure Disk (managed-csi-premium, or -zrs for zone redundancy); Azure Files also works if you need to move the volume across zones. Network. The NetworkPolicy admits only the Application Gateway subnet; egress is DNS, the verifiers and 443 (Entra ID, Key Vault through the CSI driver, the AKS API).

containerapp.yaml runs the console with minReplicas: 1, maxReplicas: 1 and activeRevisionsMode: Single, internal-only ingress to an oauth2-proxy container (Entra ID), and the console on 127.0.0.1:8090: state_dir is an Azure Files share registered as environment storage, mounted with uid=65532,gid=65532; secrets are Container Apps secrets that reference Key Vault through the app's managed identity (keyVaultUrl + identity); Container Apps resolves them and the console sees plain environment variables; the console config is mounted from a secret volume; its auth.proxy sets trusted_proxies: [127.0.0.1/32, "::1/128"] (as in the Cloud Run example above), since oauth2-proxy reaches the console over the replica's loopback; oauth2-proxy admits only the console's Entra groups (--allowed-group with the groups' object IDs); the verifiers' file audit sinks are read from a shared Azure Files share. Verifier restarts are not available on Container Apps; restart the verifier revision from your runbooks (az containerapp revision restart).

Only state_dir needs backups; everything else is rebuilt from the verifiers. Its files are rewritten atomically, so a crash-consistent volume snapshot is a valid backup: Platform Backup Kubernetes VolumeSnapshot on a schedule (EBS, PD and Azure Disk CSI drivers support it), or Velero. AWS ECS AWS Backup plan on the EFS file system. Cloud Run Filestore backups. Container Apps Azure Files share snapshots or Azure Backup for file shares. VM / compose Stop the console (or snapshot the filesystem) and copy the directory. To restore, stop the console, restore the volume, start it again. Evidence packs can also be downloaded (GET /api/v1/evidence/packs/{id}/download) and archived elsewhere.

Read the release notes; the console and the verifiers share a version and are released together. Upgrade the verifiers first, then the console (the console reads what the verifiers publish). Pin the new image digest and verify its signature (above). helm upgrade (or a new ECS task definition, Cloud Run revision or Container Apps revision). The single replica is replaced in place (Recreate), so expect a short console outage; enforcement is unaffected. Changes to console.config roll the pod through the checksum/config annotation. Changes to console.existingConfigMap, existingSecret or secretEnv do not (the chart cannot see the first two, and does not put a hash of secret values in a pod annotation): run kubectl rollout restart deployment/haltsql-console or use a reloader. After the upgrade, /readyz must answer 200 and Fleet must show every verifier; the record index rebuilds from the audit sources in the background. Roll back with helm rollback (or the previous revision). Take a snapshot of state_dir before upgrades that the release notes say change its format.

Expose the console only through an internal load balancer or a private ingress with authentication in front; keep service.type: ClusterIP. Enable auth.proxy only when the proxy is the sole path to the console (the chart guarantees this for its sidecar by binding the console to loopback). Keep the NetworkPolicy on and narrow allowHTTPS to known CIDRs where your IdP and APIs have stable addresses. Verifier admin tokens are read-only, but rotate them like any secret: add the new token to the verifiers, update the console's secret, restart the console, then remove the old token. The console never writes to verifiers. Restarts go through a namespaced Role that allows only patch on the named workloads. RBAC cannot narrow that patch to the kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation, so a compromised console container could change those workloads' image, command or env. To close that, admit only restart patches from the console's service account, for example with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (Kubernetes 1.30+): apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy metadata: { name: haltsql-console-restart-only } spec: failurePolicy: Fail matchConstraints: resourceRules: - apiGroups: [apps] apiVersions: [v1] operations: [UPDATE] resources: [deployments, statefulsets] matchConditions: - name: console expression: request.userInfo.username == "system:serviceaccount:haltsql:haltsql-console" validations: - expression: >- object.spec.template.spec == oldObject.spec.template.spec && object.spec.replicas == oldObject.spec.replicas message: haltsql-console may only restart workloads Bind it with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding scoped to the verifiers' namespace.

HaltSQL should be one of three layers, never the only one: Database role: a dedicated, read-only role with SELECT granted on exactly the policy's tables and columns, and a statement_timeout. Postgres row-level security (RLS): tenant policies keyed on a session setting that your application sets, not the model. HaltSQL: blocks bad queries before they reach the database, gives the agent a specific reason it can act on, and leaves an audit trail. Each layer covers the others' failure modes. If HaltSQL has a bug, the role and RLS still hold. If someone misconfigures RLS, HaltSQL still denies the query and says why. If the application forgets to call HaltSQL, the database still enforces the basics. The examples below match this policy: search_path: [app] tenancy: { mode: bound, keys: { tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" } } tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id app.currencies: columns: "*"

Create a role used only for agent queries. It cannot log in directly with an owner's privileges, cannot write, and can read only what the policy allows. -- Run as an administrator. CREATE ROLE agent_readonly LOGIN PASSWORD 'use-a-secret-manager' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOINHERIT NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 20; -- Start from nothing. REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM agent_readonly; REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app FROM agent_readonly; REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC; -- default on PG 15+, explicit for older versions GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA app TO agent_readonly; -- Column-level grants: exactly the columns in the policy. GRANT SELECT (id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at) ON app.orders TO agent_readonly; GRANT SELECT (id, tenant_id, name, created_at) ON app.customers TO agent_readonly; -- email and phone are not granted GRANT SELECT ON app.currencies TO agent_readonly; -- Session defaults for this role. ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET search_path = app; -- same as the policy's search_path ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET default_transaction_read_only = on; ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET statement_timeout = '5s'; ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET lock_timeout = '1s'; ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s'; ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET work_mem = '16MB'; ALTER ROLE agent_readonly SET temp_file_limit = '256MB'; -- requires superuser to set Also review function privileges. By default, PUBLIC can execute most functions. Revoke the dangerous ones from PUBLIC (or at least from this role's reach) if your security baseline allows it: REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_catalog.pg_sleep(double precision) FROM PUBLIC; -- pg_read_file, lo_import, lo_export, dblink, etc. are already restricted to -- superusers or specific roles in current Postgres versions; verify on yours: SELECT p.oid::regprocedure, p.proacl FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'pg_catalog' AND p.proname IN ('pg_sleep', 'set_config', 'pg_read_file', 'lo_import'); Keep the role's search_path identical to the policy's search_path. If they differ, an unqualified name could resolve to a different table in Postgres than the one HaltSQL checked.

RLS makes the database itself filter rows to the current tenant. The tenant comes from a setting your application sets on the connection, from its authenticated session. The model never sets it, and HaltSQL denies set_config() and SET statements so the model cannot change it either. ALTER TABLE app.orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE app.customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; -- Apply RLS to the table owner too, so a misconfigured role does not bypass it. ALTER TABLE app.orders FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE app.customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON app.orders FOR SELECT TO agent_readonly USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)); CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON app.customers FOR SELECT TO agent_readonly USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)); current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) returns NULL when the setting is missing, so a connection that forgot to set it sees no rows (tenant_id = NULL is never true). If tenant_id is not text, cast the setting: tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::bigint. For sets of tenants (a parent organization seeing its children), store the list in the setting and compare with ANY: CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON app.orders FOR SELECT TO agent_readonly USING (tenant_id = ANY (string_to_array(current_setting('app.tenant_ids', true), ',')));
documents.s: Layer 2: row-level security keyed on a session setting

documents.t: Set the tenant inside a transaction with SET LOCAL (or set_config(..., true)), so it cannot leak to the next request on a pooled connection: BEGIN READ ONLY; SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true); -- $1 = tenant from the session, bound by your app -- the verified agent query, exactly as checked, with bind_params bound: SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50; COMMIT; This works with PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode because the setting is scoped to the transaction. In bound mode, the same tenant value is bound twice: once by your application for the RLS setting, and once for the $n in bind_params. Both come from your session, never from the model.

HaltSQL runs before the query reaches the database: It denies queries the other layers would also stop, but with a precise, machine-readable reason (E_COLUMN_DENIED, E_TENANT_MISSING) that the agent can use to correct itself, instead of a generic permission error or a silent empty result. It denies things the other layers do not cover well: multiple statements, data-modifying CTEs, costly functions, missing LIMIT, unbounded joins. It records every decision with the policy version, query fingerprint, and SQL hash.

verdict = haltsql.verify(sql=agent_sql, context={"tenant_id": session.tenant_id}) if not verdict["allowed"]: return feedback_to_agent(verdict["reasons"]) with pool.connection() as conn, conn.transaction(): conn.execute("SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY") conn.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", [session.tenant_id]) params = [p["value"] for p in sorted(verdict["bind_params"], key=lambda p: p["param"])] rows = conn.execute(agent_sql, params).fetchall() # the exact verified string See integrations.md for complete client examples. The enterprise lab uses exactly these database-side controls as oracles: if HaltSQL allows a query that RLS or the column grants would block, the lab reports it as an escape (see testing.md).

Dedicated role for agent queries, NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS. Column-level GRANT SELECT matching the policy's columns. search_path on the role equals the policy's search_path. default_transaction_read_only = on and queries run in READ ONLY transactions. statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout set. RLS enabled and forced on every tenant-scoped table. Tenant setting applied with SET LOCAL / set_config(..., true) per transaction. HaltSQL policy in enforce mode, bound tenancy, tokens pinned to policies. Audit logs shipped somewhere durable; alerts on E_INTERNAL.

This guide covers four ways to run HaltSQL on AWS: haltsql-server as a sidecar on Amazon EKS; haltsql-server as a shared service on EKS or on Amazon ECS (Fargate); haltsql-proxy in front of Amazon RDS or Aurora PostgreSQL. It covers IAM, networking, TLS, the S3 Object Lock audit trail, observability, scaling and cost. The manifests, task definitions, IAM policies and a small Terraform module are in deploy/cloud/aws/. The general deployment guide is deployment.md, and the trade-offs between the modes are explained in how-it-works/deployment-modes.md. haltsql-server never connects to the database. On AWS it makes at most these outbound calls: Call When Config STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity IRSA credentials, refreshed 5 minutes before they expire credentials: { source: web_identity }; the ${aws-sm:..} chain EC2 IMDSv2 instance-profile credentials credentials: { source: instance }; the ${aws-sm:..} chain Secrets Manager GetSecretValue at startup and on every reload ${aws-sm:<id>[#key]} + secrets.aws.region S3 PutObject one object per audit batch audit.sinks[].type: s3 OIDC discovery / JWKS OIDC callers, cached server.auth.oidc OTLP/HTTP traces and metrics export telemetry.otlp Terraform. To provision these patterns as code, use the modules in deploy/terraform (terraform.md): haltsql-aws runs haltsql-server on ECS on Fargate, and haltsql-kubernetes installs the Helm chart on any cluster. This guide explains the architecture and the settings those modules expose; the manifests in deploy/cloud/aws/ are the equivalent by hand.

Pattern Pick it when Enforcement Audit on AWS A. EKS sidecar Agents run on EKS. This is the default recommendation. The agent (or the SDK's guarded execute) acts on the verdict. S3 Object Lock, using IRSA. B. EKS shared service (Helm) Many agents on EKS, with central policy rollout. Same as A, with one network hop. S3 Object Lock, using IRSA. C. ECS Fargate shared service Agents on ECS, Lambda or EC2 call one internal endpoint. Same as A. CloudWatch Logs (stdout). See Audit on ECS. D. haltsql-proxy in front of RDS You cannot change the client (BI tools, vendor agents), or you do not trust the app to honor verdicts. The proxy. The database is reachable only through it. CloudWatch Logs (stdout). Whichever pattern you choose, keep the database-side controls: a least-privilege role, default_transaction_read_only for read-only agents, and row-level security (defense-in-depth.md).

Only the features below exist in the code (lib/cloud/). Each limitation noted here shapes the patterns that follow. Area Supported Not supported (today) Credentials env (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY/AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), static (from the config, through secret placeholders), web_identity (IRSA: AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE + AWS_ROLE_ARN), instance (EC2 IMDSv2) The ECS task role (container credentials, AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI), EKS Pod Identity (AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI), shared config/profile files, SSO Secrets ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#json-key]} placeholders, resolved at startup and on each reload, with the chain env → web_identity → instance Rotation without a reload (send SIGHUP, or let reload.watch see a file change) Audit s3 sink: SigV4, create-only PUTs, Content-MD5 + SHA-256 checksums, Object Lock headers, spool directory, fail_closed or buffer SSE-KMS headers per object (use bucket default encryption instead), Firehose or CloudWatch sinks Telemetry OTLP/HTTP (JSON) to any collector; Prometheus /metrics SigV4-signed OTLP straight to X-Ray or CloudWatch (send it through an ADOT collector) Proxy Upstream password and SCRAM verifiers from ${env:}/${file:}; upstream tls.mode: verify-full against the RDS CA bundle ${aws-sm:}, S3 audit, metrics, RDS IAM database authentication, TLS key/cert as inline PEM (they must be files) Note that the S3 sink's credentials.source defaults to env, not to the chain. On EKS, set credentials: { source: web_identity } explicitly.

A VPC with private subnets in at least two Availability Zones. For private subnets without a NAT gateway, these VPC endpoints: com.amazonaws.<region>.sts (interface, needed for IRSA); secretsmanager (interface); s3 (gateway); logs (interface); for ECS: ecr.api, ecr.dkr; for ADOT: xray, aps-workspaces. The image ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version>, mirrored to ECR if your nodes cannot reach GHCR. Verify its cosign signature and pin it by digest (deployment.md). An audit bucket with Object Lock. deploy/cloud/aws/terraform/ creates it, together with its KMS key, the least-privilege policy and an optional IRSA role: cd deploy/cloud/aws/terraform terraform init terraform apply \ -var audit_bucket_name=corp-haltsql-audit \ -var 'secret_arns=["arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/haltsql/tokens-??????"]' \ -var 'irsa={oidc_provider_arn="arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLE",oidc_issuer_host="oidc.eks.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/id/EXAMPLE",namespace="agents",service_account="analytics-agent"}' Policies validated and tested in CI (haltsql validate, haltsql test, see policy-ci.md).

Each agent pod gets a haltsql container. The agent calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/verify, so verification never leaves the pod. Only the agent talks to Aurora. The sidecar uses IRSA for these calls: STS, to obtain credentials; Secrets Manager, to read the token hashes; S3, to write audit batches. It also sends OTLP to an ADOT collector.

IAM role. Attach deploy/cloud/aws/iam/haltsql-policy.json (or the Terraform policy_arn) to a role. Its trust policy (iam/irsa-trust-policy.json) must allow exactly system:serviceaccount:agents:analytics-agent with audience sts.amazonaws.com. Secrets. Store the token hashes as one JSON secret. The agent keeps the raw token; the sidecar sees only the hash. TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" aws secretsmanager create-secret --name prod/haltsql/tokens \ --kms-key-id alias/haltsql-secrets \ --secret-string "{\"analytics-agent\":\"$(printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)\"}" kubectl -n agents create secret generic analytics-agent-haltsql --from-literal=token="$TOKEN" Config. deploy/cloud/aws/eks/sidecar.yaml contains the full config. The AWS-specific parts are: server: auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${aws-sm:prod/haltsql/tokens#analytics-agent} policy: analytics-agent audit: sinks: - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 prefix: haltsql/audit/analytics-agent/ object_lock: { mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 365 } credentials: { source: web_identity } spool_dir: /var/lib/haltsql/spool on_error: fail_closed telemetry: otlp: endpoint: http://adot-collector.observability:4318 service_name: haltsql-analytics-agent secrets: aws: region: eu-west-1 ServiceAccount and pod. Annotate the ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn. Annotate the pod with eks.amazonaws.com/skip-containers: agent, so that only the haltsql container receives the web-identity token and the AWS_* variables. The agent then cannot write audit objects or read the hashes. Mount the ConfigMaps as directories, not with subPath, so that reload.watch sees policy updates. Apply and check. kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/aws/eks/sidecar.yaml kubectl -n agents logs deploy/analytics-agent -c haltsql | head # "policies loaded", no credential errors aws s3 ls s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/analytics-agent/ --recursive | tail A startup error such as aws-sm: no AWS credentials found (...) or STS returned HTTP 403 AccessDenied stops the pod with exit code 2. Check the role's trust policy (namespace, ServiceAccount name and audience) and the STS endpoint.

Use the chart in deploy/helm/haltsql with the overlay deploy/cloud/aws/eks/values-eks.yaml: helm upgrade --install haltsql deploy/helm/haltsql -n haltsql --create-namespace \ -f deploy/cloud/aws/eks/values-eks.yaml \ --set-file 'policies.analytics-agent\.yaml=policies/analytics-agent.yaml' kubectl apply -n haltsql -f deploy/cloud/aws/eks/networkpolicy-shared.yaml The overlay does the following: annotates the chart's ServiceAccount with the IRSA role; renders an s3 sink with credentials: { source: web_identity } and a spool in the chart's /var/log/haltsql emptyDir; turns on built-in TLS from a cert-manager Secret (for example issued by AWS Private CA through aws-privateca-issuer); runs three or more replicas spread across zones, with a PDB and an HPA. Limitations of the chart on AWS: NetworkPolicy. The chart's NetworkPolicy denies all egress. With an S3 sink that blocks STS and S3, and with fail_closed every request then gets 503. The overlay sets networkPolicy.enabled: false and ships networkpolicy-shared.yaml instead, which allows DNS, HTTPS to the VPC endpoints, and OTLP. The policy is only enforced if the VPC CNI's network-policy agent (or Calico or Cilium) is enabled. No secrets or telemetry.otlp values. The chart cannot render secrets.aws or telemetry.otlp, so ${aws-sm:..} placeholders and OTLP export are not available through it. Feed the token hashes in with existingTokenSecret, a Secret synced from Secrets Manager (for example by External Secrets Operator). Get metrics by scraping /metrics with ADOT or an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus scraper. If you need OTLP traces, use the sidecar manifest style (a hand-written ConfigMap). Agents reach the service at https://haltsql.haltsql.svc:8080, and need the cluster CA that signed haltsql-tls.
An internal Application Load Balancer spreads requests over haltsql-server tasks in two or more AZs. Each task runs the server and an ADOT collector sidecar.

Bake config and policies into an image. ECS has no ConfigMaps. The distroless image has no shell, so the config cannot be written at start-up. deploy/cloud/aws/ecs/Dockerfile adds config.yaml and policies/ to the official image. Each policy change becomes a new image digest, which leaves a clean audit trail. Signed policy bundles (policies: [{bundle: ..., public_keys: [...]}]) work the same way. docker build -f deploy/cloud/aws/ecs/Dockerfile -t "$ECR/haltsql-config:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" deploy/cloud/aws/ecs docker push "$ECR/haltsql-config:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" Secrets. The ECS task role cannot be used by HaltSQL today (see What HaltSQL supports), so do not use ${aws-sm:..} on Fargate. Instead, let ECS inject secrets as environment variables and reference them with ${env:..}. ECS fetches them with the execution role (iam/ecs-task-execution-policy.json). "secrets": [ { "name": "HALTSQL_TOKEN_ANALYTICS_AGENT_SHA256", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/haltsql/tokens-AbCdEf:analytics-agent::" }, { "name": "HALTSQL_TLS_KEY", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/haltsql/tls-GhIjKl:key::" } ] server.tls.cert and server.tls.key accept inline PEM, so cert: ${env:HALTSQL_TLS_CERT} works. Rotated secrets are picked up when ECS starts new tasks (force a new deployment). Task definition. See deploy/cloud/aws/ecs/task-definition.json. In it: HALTSQL_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8443. The image sets HALTSQL_LISTEN, and environment variables override the config file. The task runs as user: 65532:65532 with readonlyRootFilesystem. Logs use awslogs in blocking mode, so that audit lines on stdout are never dropped. stopTimeout: 30. It runs on ARM64 (Graviton). The ADOT container runs the built-in /etc/ecs/ecs-amp-xray.yaml config (OTLP in; X-Ray and AMP remote-write out). It uses the task role (iam/adot-task-role-policy.json), because the collector supports container credentials. Load balancer. Create an internal ALB with an HTTPS :443 listener and an ACM certificate (from AWS Private CA or a public certificate for a private hosted zone name). Add a target group with: protocol HTTPS, port 8443, target type ip; health check GET /readyz, matcher 200, interval 10 s; deregistration delay 30 s. The ALB does not validate target certificates, so a private-CA certificate on the tasks is enough to encrypt ALB → task traffic. Service. Set the desired count to at least 2 per AZ that you use, with: minimumHealthyPercent: 100, maximumPercent: 200; the deployment circuit breaker with rollback; Service Auto Scaling on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization (about 60%) or ALBRequestCountPerTarget.

On Fargate there is no IMDS, and HaltSQL cannot use the task role, so the S3 sink has no good credential source. The choices, best first: stdout → CloudWatch Logs (the reference setup). Records are still hash-chained per task, so tampering is detectable when you export a stream and verify it (audit-sinks.md). Encrypt the log group with KMS. Set its retention to your compliance period. Restrict logs:DeleteLogStream and logs:PutRetentionPolicy with an SCP. If you need WORM storage, export or subscribe the log group to an Object Lock bucket. Run haltsql on EKS (pattern B) or on EC2. Use the S3 sink with web_identity or instance credentials. credentials: { source: static }, with keys of a dedicated IAM user that holds only the s3:PutObject/s3:PutObjectRetention statement, injected from Secrets Manager. This works, but it means long-lived keys to rotate. Use it only as a stopgap.

Clients connect to an internal Network Load Balancer on TCP 6432. The NLB forwards to haltsql-proxy tasks. The proxy authenticates the client (SCRAM or client certificate), verifies every Query and Parse, and rewrites tenancy parameters in every Bind. It then forwards the SQL over TLS (verify-full) to RDS. The database security group admits port 5432 only from the proxy's security group, so clients have no path that bypasses the proxy. TLS must pass through the NLB. Use a TCP listener, not a TLS listener. PostgreSQL negotiates TLS in-band after an SSLRequest, so the NLB cannot terminate it. The proxy's tls.cert and tls.key must be files. In ecs/proxy-task-definition.json, a short-lived init container writes them from injected secrets to a task-scoped volume. On EKS, mount them with the Secrets Store CSI driver (AWS provider) instead. Upstream. Use upstream.tls: { mode: verify-full, ca: ./rds-global-bundle.pem }. Bake the public RDS CA bundle into the derived image (ecs/Dockerfile.proxy). Set rds.force_ssl = 1 in the DB parameter group, and use a dedicated least-privilege upstream.user. RDS IAM database authentication is not supported; the password comes from ${env:UPSTREAM_PASSWORD}. Health checks. Use a TCP health check on 6432. The proxy has no HTTP health or metrics endpoint. Audit. One JSON line per statement on stdout, going to CloudWatch Logs. Clients use prepared statements for tenant-scoped queries (proxy.md).
documents.s: D. haltsql-proxy in front of RDS

documents.t: deploy/cloud/aws/iam/haltsql-policy.json is the whole policy for haltsql-server (patterns A and B): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "WriteAuditObjectsUnderPrefix", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:PutObjectRetention"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/*" }, { "Sid": "ReadHaltsqlSecrets", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/haltsql/tokens-??????", "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:111122223333:secret:prod/haltsql/otel-??????" ] }, { "Sid": "UseCustomerManagedKeyViaS3AndSecretsManager", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:GenerateDataKey"], "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": [ "s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com", "secretsmanager.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" ] } } } ] } Notes on the policy: No read, list or delete on the bucket. HaltSQL only PUTs, with If-None-Match: *, so it cannot overwrite an object either. s3:PutObjectRetention is needed because each PUT carries Object Lock headers. kms:GenerateDataKey is required to write objects into an SSE-KMS bucket. Turn on S3 Bucket Keys to cut KMS request costs. Secret ARNs end in -??????. That matches the random suffix that Secrets Manager adds to the name, and only that suffix. Use one role per agent in pattern A, each with its own audit prefix, so that one compromised pod cannot write into another agent's prefix. Trust policy. Pin both :sub (namespace and ServiceAccount) and :aud (sts.amazonaws.com). For ECS, the execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (plus kms:Decrypt with kms:ViaService for Secrets Manager) on the injected secrets, together with AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy for ECR and logs.

Security group Inbound Outbound agents as your app needs 443 to alb-haltsql (C); 5432 to db (A–C); 6432 to nlb-proxy (D) alb-haltsql (C) 443 from agents 8443 to haltsql haltsql (C) 8443 from alb-haltsql 443 to the VPC endpoints (Secrets Manager, ECR, logs, X-Ray, AMP) haltsql-proxy (D) 6432 from the NLB (or from agents when the NLB preserves client IPs) 5432 to db; 443 to VPC endpoints db 5432 from agents (A–C), only from haltsql-proxy (D) none vpce 443 from haltsql, haltsql-proxy, EKS nodes none More rules: EKS nodes. Set the IMDSv2 hop limit to 1 in the node launch template, so that pods cannot reach the node role through IMDS. Pods that need AWS use IRSA. Without this, the agent container in pattern A could borrow the node's credentials. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Keep a no-ingress policy on agent pods (pattern A). For pattern B, use networkpolicy-shared.yaml. When you rely on an S3 gateway endpoint, egress rules also need the S3 prefix-list CIDRs. Load balancers stay internal. HaltSQL is never exposed to the internet.

Hop Option Agent → sidecar (A) Plain HTTP on loopback inside the pod. Tokens are still required. Agent → service (B) Built-in TLS (tls.enabled, cert-manager + AWS Private CA). Probes move to the plain-HTTP health port. Agent → ALB → task (C) An ACM certificate on the ALB, then HTTPS to the task's built-in TLS. Callers authenticate with static tokens or OIDC bearer tokens, which pass through the ALB. mTLS identities Need the client certificate at haltsql-server itself. ALB terminates TLS, and its mTLS mode passes the certificate in an HTTP header that HaltSQL does not read. So use an NLB with a TCP listener (TLS passthrough) to the tasks, with server.tls.client_ca and client_auth: required, plus --health-listen for health checks. Client → proxy (D) Proxy TLS through an NLB TCP listener; tls.required: true. Proxy → RDS (D) upstream.tls.mode: verify-full with the RDS CA bundle. For OIDC on AWS, use an IdP whose access tokens carry an aud claim that matches audiences (for example Okta, Entra ID or Auth0). Amazon Cognito access tokens carry client_id instead of aud, so check your token's claims before you rely on Cognito. The server must reach the issuer's JWKS URL over HTTPS (NAT or proxy egress).

The Terraform module creates the bucket with: Object Lock, enabled at creation (it cannot be added later), with a default retention that backs up the per-object retention HaltSQL sends; versioning; SSE-KMS with a Bucket Key; Block Public Access and BucketOwnerEnforced ownership; a bucket policy that denies non-TLS requests; a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 days. Pick the lock mode: COMPLIANCE cannot be shortened or removed by anyone, the root user included, until the retention date. Use it for regulatory retention. Test with a short retain_days first. GOVERNANCE can be bypassed by principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention. Use it while you are still tuning. Keep the sink's object_lock.retain_days equal to the bucket default. For chain continuity across restarts, give every S3 sink a spool_dir. In Kubernetes an emptyDir survives container restarts but not pod rescheduling. A new pod starts a new chain under its own <run> id, which is expected and verifiable. Object Lock makes the earlier runs undeletable, which covers the gap that a missing spool would otherwise leave (audit-sinks.md). To verify a day's audit trail for one host: aws s3 cp --recursive s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/analytics-agent/2026/11/08/ ./audit/ find ./audit -name 'analytics-agent-7f9c-*.jsonl' | sort | xargs cat > day.jsonl python3 verify_chain.py day.jsonl # script in docs/audit-sinks.md

Signal Pattern A/B Pattern C Pattern D Traces OTLP → ADOT collector (EKS add-on) → X-Ray OTLP → ADOT sidecar → X-Ray none Metrics /metrics scraped by ADOT or an AMP managed scraper; or OTLP → ADOT → AMP OTLP → ADOT → AMP none (audit stream only) Logs stderr → Fluent Bit / CloudWatch Observability add-on → CloudWatch Logs awslogs → CloudWatch Logs awslogs → CloudWatch Logs Audit S3 Object Lock CloudWatch Logs (stdout) CloudWatch Logs (stdout) HaltSQL's OTLP exporter does not sign requests with SigV4, so it cannot post directly to the X-Ray or CloudWatch OTLP endpoints. Always send it through an ADOT (or other OpenTelemetry) collector. The SQL text is never exported in spans; join spans to audit records on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256. Alarms, as AMP alerting rules or CloudWatch alarms (observability.md): haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0, or rate(haltsql_audit_sink_rejected_writes_total[5m]) > 0: S3 writes are failing, and with fail_closed requests are answered with 503. rate(haltsql_audit_sink_upload_failures_total[5m]) > 0: an early warning (for example AccessDenied after an IAM change). rate(haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}[5m]) > 0. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.05. ALB: HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, UnHealthyHostCount. ECS: running task count below desired.

Statelessness. haltsql-server is stateless and CPU-bound. A verification typically takes well under a millisecond, so a sidecar needs 50m CPU and 64Mi of memory as a request. Scale shared services on CPU. Spread across AZs. Use topologySpreadConstraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone (B), or two or more subnets in different AZs (C, D). Keep a PDB (minAvailable: 2) or ECS minimumHealthyPercent: 100. Readiness (/readyz) means that at least one policy is loaded. A failed hot reload keeps the last good policies and does not make the task unready. fail_closed versus buffer. With fail_closed (the default), an S3 or STS outage turns into 503s once uploads have failed every attempt. Clients must treat those as denials. If availability matters more, choose on_error: buffer: records are held in memory, up to max_buffer_records, and never dropped, and writes are refused only when the buffer is full. With a spool directory, held records also survive a crash. Graceful shutdown. SIGTERM stops accepting connections, finishes in-flight requests, and flushes the last audit batch. Keep terminationGracePeriodSeconds/stopTimeout at 20–30 s, and at least as long as the ALB deregistration delay. Secret rotation. Rotated Secrets Manager values are read on the next reload (SIGHUP or a config-file change) or on the next pod or task start.

Sidecar overhead is one small container per agent pod. A shared service is cheaper with many small agents, at the price of a network hop. Fargate on ARM64 (Graviton) costs less than x86 for the same vCPU and memory. The image is multi-arch. Interface VPC endpoints are billed per endpoint, per AZ, per hour, plus data processed. Share them across workloads in the VPC. The S3 gateway endpoint is free. S3 PUT requests. Each sink in each replica uploads at most one object per batch.max_seconds (default 10 s) while traffic flows, or one per 500 records. That is at most about 8,640 PUTs per replica per day. Raise max_seconds to cut requests; records are spooled in the meantime. CloudWatch Logs ingestion is usually the largest cost when audit goes to stdout (patterns C and D). Keep log_raw_sql: false, which also keeps sensitive literals out of logs. KMS. S3 Bucket Keys reduce GenerateDataKey calls to a few per bucket, rather than one per object. Long-term audit storage. Move it to Glacier Instant Retrieval with the lifecycle rule. Object Lock itself has no additional charge.

Image pinned by digest; its cosign signature is verified in CI before it is promoted to ECR. allow_unauthenticated: false. Every token, OIDC provider or mTLS identity is pinned to one policy. Token hashes live in Secrets Manager (KMS CMK). Raw tokens exist only in the callers' secrets. IRSA role trust is pinned to one ServiceAccount (:sub and :aud). skip-containers keeps the agent away from it. The IMDSv2 hop limit on nodes is 1. IAM policy: PutObject and PutObjectRetention on the prefix only; GetSecretValue on named ARNs; KMS limited by kms:ViaService. Audit bucket: Object Lock (COMPLIANCE once tested), versioning, SSE-KMS with a Bucket Key, TLS-only bucket policy, Block Public Access, lifecycle rule. The S3 sink sets credentials.source explicitly, has a spool_dir, and its on_error choice is documented. Private subnets in two or more AZs. VPC endpoints for STS, Secrets Manager, S3, logs (and ECR, X-Ray, AMP as needed). Load balancers are internal. Security groups: the database admits only the agents (A–C) or only the proxy (D). NetworkPolicy: no ingress to agent pods. The shared service allows egress to the endpoints (not the chart's deny-all). TLS on every hop that leaves a pod. Proxy → RDS uses verify-full; rds.force_ssl = 1. The database role is least-privilege and row-level security is on (defense-in-depth.md). Alarms are set for audit sink health, upload failures, reload errors, p99 latency, and 5xx and unhealthy targets. Policies go through shadow mode first; rollouts are a new image or ConfigMap, never an edit in place (deployment.md). Chain verification is scheduled (for example a daily job that downloads yesterday's objects and runs the verifier).

To run haltsql-console (the control plane) next to these deployments: on EKS with the haltsql-console chart, IRSA for S3 audit reads and Secrets Manager, an internal ALB and an EBS volume for its state; or on ECS Fargate with EFS for its state. See console/deploy.md and deploy/cloud/aws/console/. Each verifier needs server.admin enabled with the console's token in server.admin.callers.

The architecture images on this page are drawn as code with mingrammer/diagrams, one script per diagram: deploy/diagrams/aws_*.py. Every other diagram on this page is Mermaid, inline in the Markdown. You need Graphviz (dot). From the repository root: make diagrams # every cloud, in a managed virtualenv deploy/diagrams/.venv/bin/python deploy/diagrams/aws_<name>.py # one diagram Each script writes the matching docs/assets/cloud/aws-<name>.png. Commit the PNG together with the script change. See deploy/diagrams/README.md for the shared style.

This guide covers three ways to run HaltSQL on Azure: AKS sidecar (recommended): haltsql-server runs in the agent's pod. Azure Container Apps: as a sidecar container in the agent's app, or as a shared internal service. haltsql-proxy in front of Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, for agents you cannot change. Ready-to-edit manifests are in deploy/cloud/azure/. The general deployment guidance in deployment.md and how-it-works/deployment-modes.md also applies here. Read this first: HaltSQL has no Azure-native integrations yet. HaltSQL reads secrets from environment variables, files, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and Google Secret Manager. Its object-store audit sinks are S3 and GCS. It cannot call Azure Key Vault, write to Azure Blob Storage, or use a managed identity. This guide gets the same results with standard Azure tooling: the Key Vault CSI driver or Container Apps secret references (exposed to HaltSQL as files), a log shipper for Blob, and an OpenTelemetry Collector for Azure Monitor. The full list of gaps is in Current limitations on Azure. What does work without changes on Azure: Microsoft Entra ID as the OIDC issuer. HaltSQL's JWT authentication is generic OIDC, so it accepts Entra ID access tokens, including tokens that agents get through AKS Workload Identity or a Container Apps managed identity. Built-in TLS and mTLS, signed policy bundles, Prometheus metrics and OTLP/HTTP export. haltsql-server never connects to the database, and it needs no Azure permissions of its own. In both server patterns, the only Azure identities belong to the agent, the CSI driver or Container Apps platform (to read Key Vault), and the log shipper (to write Blob). Keep the haltsql container out of every identity binding. Terraform. To provision these patterns as code, use the modules in deploy/terraform (terraform.md): haltsql-azure runs haltsql-server on Container Apps, and haltsql-kubernetes installs the Helm chart on any cluster. This guide explains the architecture and the settings those modules expose; the manifests in deploy/cloud/azure/ are the equivalent by hand.

Pattern Latency Isolation Auth Ops effort Best for AKS sidecar loopback, sub-millisecond per pod; policy ships with the agent static token from Key Vault (or Entra ID) low most production agents AKS shared service one in-cluster hop central; one policy rollout for all agents Entra ID JWT, TLS medium platform teams serving many agents Container Apps sidecar loopback per replica static token from Key Vault low serverless agents Container Apps shared service ingress hop (Envoy) central Entra ID JWT, TLS at ingress low many small agent apps haltsql-proxy one Postgres hop enforced: the agent cannot skip it SCRAM or client certificates medium agents and BI tools you cannot change

Azure CLI 2.60 or later, with the containerapp extension for Container Apps (az extension add -n containerapp --upgrade), plus kubectl and Helm 3 for AKS. Permission to create resource groups, managed identities, role assignments (Owner or User Access Administrator on the resource group) and an Entra ID app registration (Application Developer or higher), if you use Entra ID authentication. A VNet with separate subnets: AKS nodes (or the Container Apps environment, delegated to Microsoft.App/environments), private endpoints, and Flexible Server (delegated to Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL/flexibleServers). Policies that pass haltsql validate and haltsql test in CI (see policy-ci.md). The image ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version>. Import it into your Azure Container Registry so nodes do not pull from the internet, and pin it by digest: az acr import -n "$ACR" --source ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 --image haltsql:0.0.1 To verify the signature first, see deployment.md. The commands below use these shell variables: RG=rg-haltsql LOC=westeurope AKS=aks-agents KV=kv-haltsql-prod # globally unique ST=sthaltsqlaudit # globally unique, 3-24 lowercase letters/digits ACR=acragents # globally unique TENANT_ID=$(az account show --query tenantId -o tsv)

The agent calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/verify inside its own pod. The call never leaves the pod. The agent runs the exact SQL it verified against Flexible Server, using its own Entra ID identity. HaltSQL never sees database credentials. Container Azure identity Reads Writes agent user-assigned managed identity (Workload Identity) raw HaltSQL token (CSI volume) SQL to Flexible Server haltsql none (excluded with azure.workload.identity/skip-containers) token hash (CSI volume), ConfigMap audit file, stdout, OTLP vector same managed identity, Blob write only audit file (read-only mount) Blob (immutable container) The CSI driver reads Key Vault with the pod's identity before any container starts.

az group create -n "$RG" -l "$LOC" az aks create -g "$RG" -n "$AKS" \ --zones 1 2 3 \ --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity \ --enable-addons azure-keyvault-secrets-provider,monitoring \ --enable-secret-rotation \ --enable-azure-monitor-metrics \ --network-plugin azure --network-plugin-mode overlay \ --network-dataplane cilium --network-policy cilium \ --enable-private-cluster \ --vnet-subnet-id "$AKS_SUBNET_ID" \ --attach-acr "$ACR" \ --generate-ssh-keys ISSUER=$(az aks show -g "$RG" -n "$AKS" --query oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl -o tsv) monitoring turns on Container Insights (logs to Log Analytics), and --enable-azure-monitor-metrics turns on Managed Prometheus. A network policy engine is required for the NetworkPolicy in the manifest.
documents.s: 1. Cluster with Workload Identity, the Key Vault CSI driver and monitoring

documents.t: az identity create -g "$RG" -n id-analytics-agent MI_CLIENT_ID=$(az identity show -g "$RG" -n id-analytics-agent --query clientId -o tsv) MI_PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az identity show -g "$RG" -n id-analytics-agent --query principalId -o tsv) az identity federated-credential create -g "$RG" \ --identity-name id-analytics-agent --name fc-analytics-agent \ --issuer "$ISSUER" \ --subject system:serviceaccount:agents:analytics-agent \ --audience api://AzureADTokenExchange
documents.s: 2. Managed identity, federated with the agent's ServiceAccount

documents.t: Generate the agent's bearer token and its hash. Store both in Key Vault. The agent container mounts only the token; the haltsql container mounts only the hash. az keyvault create -g "$RG" -n "$KV" -l "$LOC" \ --enable-rbac-authorization true --enable-purge-protection true \ --public-network-access Disabled KV_ID=$(az keyvault show -n "$KV" --query id -o tsv) # Run from a host with private access to the vault (or open access briefly). TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" az keyvault secret set --vault-name "$KV" -n haltsql-agent-token --value "$TOKEN" -o none az keyvault secret set --vault-name "$KV" -n haltsql-token-sha256 \ --value "$(printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)" -o none unset TOKEN # Least privilege: only these two secrets, read-only. for s in haltsql-agent-token haltsql-token-sha256; do az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID" \ --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \ --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope "$KV_ID/secrets/$s" done Create a private endpoint for the vault (az network private-endpoint create ... --group-id vault) in the private endpoint subnet, with the privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net private DNS zone linked to the VNet.
documents.s: 3. Key Vault and the token secrets

documents.t: az storage account create -g "$RG" -n "$ST" -l "$LOC" \ --sku Standard_ZRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 \ --allow-blob-public-access false --allow-shared-key-access false \ --public-network-access Disabled ST_ID=$(az storage account show -g "$RG" -n "$ST" --query id -o tsv) az storage container-rm create -g "$RG" --storage-account "$ST" -n haltsql-audit # Time-based retention (WORM): blobs cannot be modified or deleted for 365 days. az storage container immutability-policy create -g "$RG" --account-name "$ST" \ -c haltsql-audit --period 365 Test the pipeline end to end, then lock the policy. A locked policy cannot be shortened or removed (this is what auditors ask for, for example for SEC 17a-4(f)): ETAG=$(az storage container immutability-policy show -g "$RG" --account-name "$ST" \ -c haltsql-audit --query etag -o tsv) az storage container immutability-policy lock -g "$RG" --account-name "$ST" \ -c haltsql-audit --if-match "$ETAG" Give the shipper write access to that container only: az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID" \ --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \ --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \ --scope "$ST_ID/blobServices/default/containers/haltsql-audit" Storage Blob Data Contributor includes delete, which the immutability policy blocks anyway. For a strictly create-only identity, define a custom role with only the data actions Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/write and .../blobs/add/action, and set healthcheck.enabled: false on the Vector sink, because its health check needs read access. Add a private endpoint with --group-id blob and the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone.
documents.s: 4. Immutable Blob container for audit records

documents.t: Edit the REPLACE_* values in aks/secretproviderclass.yaml, aks/agent-sidecar.yaml and aks/otel-collector.yaml, then: az aks get-credentials -g "$RG" -n "$AKS" kubectl create namespace agents kubectl create namespace observability kubectl -n observability create secret generic appinsights \ --from-literal=connection-string="$APPINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING" kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/azure/aks/otel-collector.yaml kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/azure/aks/secretproviderclass.yaml kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/azure/aks/agent-sidecar.yaml kubectl -n agents rollout status deploy/analytics-agent The haltsql configuration in agent-sidecar.yaml, abridged: server: auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${file:/mnt/secrets/haltsql/haltsql-token-sha256} # CSI-mounted from Key Vault policy: analytics-agent reload: { watch: true } audit: sinks: - type: file # shipped to immutable Blob by Vector path: /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl on_error: fail_closed - type: stdout # Container Insights, for search and alerts telemetry: otlp: endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4318 Every key is a standard HaltSQL config key (see config-reference.md). There is nothing Azure-specific in the config itself.

For a central service, install the chart with aks/values-aks.yaml. It sets up Entra ID authentication, built-in TLS 1.3, three replicas spread across zones, a PodDisruptionBudget and an HPA. kubectl create namespace haltsql kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/azure/aks/networkpolicy-shared.yaml helm upgrade --install haltsql deploy/helm/haltsql -n haltsql \ -f deploy/cloud/azure/aks/values-aks.yaml The overlay has to work around three chart limitations: The chart's NetworkPolicy denies all egress. OIDC must fetch the JWKS from login.microsoftonline.com, so the overlay turns off the chart's NetworkPolicy, and networkpolicy-shared.yaml replaces it (DNS, HTTPS, OTLP). The chart's ServiceMonitor uses the monitoring.coreos.com group, but Managed Prometheus only reads azmonitoring.coreos.com. The overlay turns it off, and networkpolicy-shared.yaml adds a PodMonitor instead. The chart has no extraVolumes. You cannot mount a CSI volume into it. The TLS Secret haltsql-tls must come from cert-manager, or from Key Vault through External Secrets Operator (aks/externalsecret-tls.yaml). With Entra ID authentication, the service needs no other secrets.

Container Apps runs all containers of an app in one replica, so they share localhost. There are no ConfigMaps, so build a small image that adds your config and policies on top of the HaltSQL image (containerapps/Dockerfile). The image is immutable and versioned, and it is the unit you roll back. Secrets stay out of the image: they are Key Vault references that the platform reads with the app's managed identity and mounts as files.

az containerapp env create -g "$RG" -n cae-agents -l "$LOC" \ --infrastructure-subnet-resource-id "$CAE_SUBNET_ID" \ --internal-only true \ --enable-workload-profiles \ --zone-redundant \ --logs-destination log-analytics \ --logs-workspace-id "$LAW_CUSTOMER_ID" --logs-workspace-key "$LAW_KEY" az identity create -g "$RG" -n id-analytics-agent # Grant it "Key Vault Secrets User" on the secrets (as in Pattern 1) # and "AcrPull" on the registry. az acr build -r "$ACR" -t haltsql-analytics:1.0.0 \ --build-arg CONFIG=sidecar.yaml deploy/cloud/azure/containerapps

az containerapp create -g "$RG" -n analytics-agent \ --yaml deploy/cloud/azure/containerapps/app.yaml haltsql serves the verify API on 127.0.0.1:8080 only. Platform probes use --health-listen 0.0.0.0:8081, which serves only /healthz and /readyz. Ingress targets the agent's port, never HaltSQL. The token hash is mounted at /mnt/secrets/haltsql-token-sha256 from a Key Vault reference (storageType: Secret volume). The raw token reaches only the agent, as an environment variable. otel-collector is a third container. It receives OTLP/HTTP on 127.0.0.1:4318 and exports to Application Insights. You need it because the Container Apps managed OpenTelemetry agent accepts only gRPC, and HaltSQL exports OTLP over HTTP with JSON encoding. Size the containers together: 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.25 vCPU and 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 GiB adds up to an allowed Consumption combination (1 vCPU, 2 GiB).

az acr build -r "$ACR" -t haltsql-shared:1.0.0 \ --build-arg CONFIG=shared.yaml deploy/cloud/azure/containerapps az containerapp create -g "$RG" -n haltsql \ --yaml deploy/cloud/azure/containerapps/shared-service.yaml Agents call https://haltsql.internal.<environment default domain>/v1/verify with an Entra ID access token (see Identity). Ingress terminates TLS. To encrypt traffic between replicas inside the environment too, turn on peer-to-peer encryption: az containerapp env update -g "$RG" -n cae-agents --enable-peer-to-peer-encryption minReplicas: 2 keeps the firewall from scaling to zero. Do not let it scale to zero: the agent would block on a cold start, or fail open if it was written carelessly. activeRevisionsMode: Multiple lets you canary a new policy image with traffic weights.

Use the proxy when the agent (or a BI tool) speaks plain Postgres and cannot call /v1/verify. The proxy authenticates clients (SCRAM or client certificates), maps each one to a policy and context, verifies every statement, and forwards only allowed statements to Flexible Server over verify-full TLS. See proxy.md. aks/proxy.yaml runs two replicas spread across zones, with secrets from Key Vault via CSI. The database side: az postgres flexible-server create -g "$RG" -n "$PG" -l "$LOC" \ --tier GeneralPurpose --sku-name Standard_D2ds_v5 --version 16 \ --high-availability ZoneRedundant --zone 1 --standby-zone 2 \ --vnet "$VNET" --subnet snet-postgres --private-dns-zone "$PG_DNS_ZONE" # Turn on Microsoft Entra authentication for human and agent access # (check `az postgres flexible-server create --help` for the flag names in # your CLI version). The proxy's own upstream role uses a password; see below. az postgres flexible-server parameter set -g "$RG" -s "$PG" \ -n require_secure_transport --value on Create a dedicated read-only role for the proxy (haltsql_service) with SELECT on the policy's tables only, and keep row-level security on (see defense-in-depth.md). Store its password in Key Vault as pg-haltsql-service-password. Download the CA certificates that Flexible Server currently chains to (DigiCert Global Root G2 and Microsoft RSA Root Certificate Authority 2017 at the time of writing; check Microsoft's "TLS/SSL with Azure Database for PostgreSQL" page). Store them as the azure-pg-ca ConfigMap. On the NSG of the Flexible Server subnet, allow 5432 only from the subnet the proxy runs in. On AKS, also give agent pods a NetworkPolicy that blocks egress to 5432. Otherwise an agent can bypass the proxy.
documents.s: Pattern 3: haltsql-proxy in front of Flexible Server

documents.t: Principal Role Scope Agent's managed identity Key Vault Secrets User the agent's token secret only Agent's managed identity app role SQL.Verify on the haltsql app (shared-service patterns) the app registration Agent's managed identity Entra database role on Flexible Server the agent's database and schema Shipper identity (may be the same MI) Storage Blob Data Contributor, or a custom create-only role the haltsql-audit container Container Apps app identity Key Vault Secrets User, AcrPull its secrets; the registry Proxy's identity (CSI only) Key Vault Secrets User proxy secrets haltsql-server nothing -

The shared-service patterns authenticate agents with Entra ID access tokens. Each agent's managed identity gets a token for the haltsql app registration. HaltSQL checks the issuer, audience, signature, expiry, azp and roles claims, then pins the caller's policy. Create the app registration once: APP_ID=$(az ad app create --display-name haltsql --query appId -o tsv) az ad app update --id "$APP_ID" --identifier-uris "api://$APP_ID" # v2.0 tokens: iss = https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0, aud = APP_ID az ad app update --id "$APP_ID" --set api.requestedAccessTokenVersion=2 cat > roles.json <<EOF [{"allowedMemberTypes": ["Application"], "description": "Call HaltSQL /v1/verify", "displayName": "SQL.Verify", "isEnabled": true, "value": "SQL.Verify", "id": "$(uuidgen)"}] EOF az ad app update --id "$APP_ID" --app-roles @roles.json az ad sp create --id "$APP_ID" # Only identities with an assigned app role can get a token for this app. az ad sp update --id "$APP_ID" --set appRoleAssignmentRequired=true # Assign the role to an agent's managed identity. HALTSQL_SP=$(az ad sp show --id "$APP_ID" --query id -o tsv) ROLE_ID=$(az ad app show --id "$APP_ID" --query "appRoles[?value=='SQL.Verify'].id | [0]" -o tsv) az rest --method POST \ --uri "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals/$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID/appRoleAssignments" \ --body "{\"principalId\":\"$MI_PRINCIPAL_ID\",\"resourceId\":\"$HALTSQL_SP\",\"appRoleId\":\"$ROLE_ID\"}" The matching HaltSQL config (also in values-aks.yaml and containerapps/haltsql/shared.yaml): server: auth: oidc: - name: entra-analytics-agent issuer: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/v2.0 audiences: [<HALTSQL_APP_CLIENT_ID>] algorithms: [RS256] policy: analytics-agent # pinned required_claims: azp: <AGENT_MI_CLIENT_ID> # which identity roles: SQL.Verify # element of the roles array request_context_fields: [tenant_id] Notes that are easy to get wrong: Token version. Without requestedAccessTokenVersion = 2, Entra ID issues v1.0 tokens whose iss is https://sts.windows.net/<tenant>/, and HaltSQL rejects them because iss must equal issuer exactly. (You could instead configure the v1 issuer, with jwks_uri set to https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/discovery/keys and the App ID URI as the audience. Do not mix the two.) Selecting a policy. policy_claim needs a string claim, and Entra's roles claim is an array. Add one provider entry per agent identity instead: the same issuer, a different required_claims.azp, and a pinned policy. HaltSQL tries every provider whose issuer matches, in order, and uses the first that verifies. Tenant context. App-only tokens carry no end-user tenant. Either list tenant_id in request_context_fields (the agent sends it, as above), or use a separate identity per tenant with a static context. mTLS identities can carry a static context. Egress. JWKS is fetched from login.microsoftonline.com:443. Allow it in Azure Firewall, a Cilium FQDN policy or the NSG. If the keys cannot be refreshed for longer than min(jwks_cache_seconds, 3600) past expiry, requests get 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE. In the agent (Python, azure-identity): from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential # Workload Identity or managed identity token = DefaultAzureCredential().get_token(f"api://{HALTSQL_APP_ID}/.default").token requests.post(f"{HALTSQL_URL}/v1/verify", json=body, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=2)
documents.s: Entra ID as the OIDC issuer

documents.t: No public endpoints. Use a private AKS cluster, an internal Container Apps environment, Flexible Server with VNet integration (or a private endpoint), and private endpoints for Key Vault, Blob and ACR, each with its privatelink.* DNS zone linked to the VNet. Disable public network access on the vault and the storage account. NSGs. On the Flexible Server subnet, allow inbound 5432 only from the agent subnet (or only from the proxy subnet in Pattern 3). On the private endpoint subnet, allow 443 only from the workload subnets. On the AKS or Container Apps subnet, send egress through Azure Firewall (a UDR to the firewall) with FQDN rules: login.microsoftonline.com (Entra ID OIDC and token exchange), your Application Insights ingestion endpoint, and mcr.microsoft.com plus your ACR for images. Inside the cluster. The sidecar manifest lets only kube-system (Managed Prometheus) reach port 8080 from outside the pod. The shared-service policy admits only the agents namespace. HaltSQL's own traffic. The sidecar with static tokens makes no outbound calls except OTLP to the collector. Entra ID authentication adds HTTPS to login.microsoftonline.com. The proxy needs only Flexible Server.

Hop How agent to sidecar loopback inside the pod or replica; no TLS needed agent to AKS shared service built-in TLS (tls.enabled, minVersion: "1.3"); certificate from cert-manager or Key Vault (ESO); hot-reloaded on rotation agent to Container Apps shared service Container Apps ingress (managed certificate for the internal domain); turn on peer-to-peer encryption for traffic inside the environment agent to haltsql-proxy proxy tls with required: true; clients use sslmode=verify-full proxy or agent to Flexible Server require_secure_transport=on; verify-full against the Azure CA bundle TLS files referenced by path (server.tls.cert, key, client_ca) are watched and reloaded. Secrets read through ${file:...} placeholders are read only at startup and on reload. See Current limitations.

HaltSQL audit records are hash-chained JSON lines (see audit-sinks.md). There is no native Blob sink, so use one of these routes: Route Byte-exact chain Retention Use for file sink + Vector to Blob (AKS) yes: Vector's text codec writes each line unchanged; concatenating a pod's blobs in name order reproduces the file locked time-based immutability on the container the compliance record stdout to Log Analytics (AKS and Container Apps) no: Container Insights parses JSON lines into columns, so the original bytes (and the hash input) are not guaranteed to survive workspace and table retention, up to 12 years with long-term retention search, dashboards, alerts Log Analytics data export to Storage no (as above) immutability policy on the export container low-effort archive when a verifiable chain is not required Operational notes for the file and Vector route: Each haltsql process has its own chain, and each pod writes under haltsql/audit/<namespace>/<pod>/ in Blob. When a pod restarts in place, the chain continues: file resumes from the last line, and the emptyDir outlives container restarts. A new pod starts a new chain at genesis. HaltSQL does not rotate the audit file. Size the emptyDir for the pod's lifetime (the manifest uses 2 GiB; a record is about 400 bytes) and alert on haltsql_audit_errors_total. With on_error: fail_closed, a full disk turns into 503s rather than unaudited verifies. Verify a day's chain by downloading one pod's blobs (az storage blob download-batch --auth-mode login ...), concatenating them in name order, and running the script in audit-sinks.md. On Container Apps, only the stdout route is available. A shipper container can share an EmptyDir volume, but replicas are replaced freely, so files are lost more often than on AKS.

Signal AKS Container Apps Metrics Managed Prometheus scrapes /metrics through a PodMonitor (azmonitoring.coreos.com/v1); Managed Grafana for dashboards. OTLP metrics also go to App Insights through the collector. OTLP metrics through the collector sidecar to App Insights. There is no Prometheus scraping. Traces OTLP/HTTP to the in-cluster OpenTelemetry Collector, then the azuremonitor exporter, then Application Insights the same, with the collector as a sidecar on localhost:4318 Logs stderr JSON logs to Container Insights (ContainerLogV2) ContainerAppConsoleLogs Audit see Audit retention stdout to Log Analytics Spans never contain SQL text. Join a span to its audit record on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256. Recommended alerts (Managed Prometheus alert rules, or Log Analytics alerts on the OTLP metrics): Condition Action rate(haltsql_audit_errors_total[5m]) > 0 Page: the audit sink is failing, and with fail_closed requests get 503. rate(haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}[5m]) > 0 Warn: a bad policy was rejected, and the last good one is still active. haltsql_policies_loaded == 0 Page: the pod is not ready. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.05 Investigate latency. rate(haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 The collector is unreachable. Verification is unaffected. Vector component_errors_total{component_id="audit_blob"} Blob shipping is failing.

Zones. Use AKS node pools across zones 1, 2 and 3 with topologySpreadConstraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone (in both manifests), a zone-redundant Container Apps environment, ZRS storage, and zone-redundant HA on Flexible Server. Sidecar. It scales with the agent automatically. HaltSQL is stateless and CPU-bound. 50m CPU and 32 MiB of memory are enough for most agents. Shared service. At least 3 replicas on AKS (2 on Container Apps), with a PDB minAvailable: 2, an HPA on CPU (or the Container Apps HTTP concurrency rule), and maxUnavailable: 0 rolling updates (the chart's default). Policy rollout. On AKS, ConfigMap updates are hot-reloaded (reload.watch). The swap is atomic, and a bad policy is rejected. On Container Apps, ship a new image revision and shift traffic with weights. Signed policy bundles (policy-bundles.md) work the same on both. Failure mode. If HaltSQL is unavailable, agents must fail closed: run no SQL. The SDKs do this by default.

Prices change and vary by region, so these are relative. HaltSQL itself costs little: about 50m CPU and 32 MiB per sidecar, or 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GiB per Container Apps replica. A shared service of three small replicas is usually the cheapest option for dozens of agents. On Container Apps, keeping minReplicas: 2 means you pay for idle time. Log Analytics ingestion is usually the largest line item. An audit record is about 400 bytes, so 10 million verifies a day is about 4 GB a day of audit data, before application logs. Consider the Basic table plan for ContainerLogV2, and keep the full-fidelity copy in Blob. Blob with the Cool access tier is inexpensive for append-once audit data. Immutability policies cost nothing extra, but locked data cannot be deleted early, so set the retention period deliberately. Private endpoints are billed per hour and per GB. Azure Firewall has a significant fixed hourly cost. Share both through a hub VNet. Application Insights bills by ingestion. Sample traces in the collector (probabilistic_sampler) for high-volume agents. HaltSQL honors the caller's sampled flag. Managed Prometheus bills by samples ingested. One scrape every 30 seconds per pod is negligible.

Image imported into ACR, pinned by digest, signature verified. Policies validated and tested in CI; mode: enforce (or a planned shadow period first). allow_unauthenticated: false; every identity pinned to one policy. Sidecar: the token in Key Vault, the agent mounts the token, haltsql mounts only the hash; Workload Identity skipped for the haltsql container. Shared service: Entra app with requestedAccessTokenVersion = 2, appRoleAssignmentRequired = true, one provider per agent (azp + roles); TLS 1.3 on; egress to login.microsoftonline.com allowed. Key Vault: RBAC mode, purge protection, private endpoint, per-secret role assignments. Storage: private endpoint, shared key access disabled, immutability policy locked after testing, shipper scoped to one container. audit.log_raw_sql: false unless approved; on_error: fail_closed. Flexible Server: private access only, require_secure_transport=on, zone-redundant HA, agent roles with least privilege, RLS on. Agents cannot reach 5432 directly when the proxy is the enforcement point. NetworkPolicies (AKS) and NSGs in place; network policy engine enabled. Alerts on audit errors, reload errors and readiness; Blob shipping errors alerted. Tested: a denied query never runs; HaltSQL down means the agent runs nothing; secret rotation procedure rehearsed (see below). A chain verified end to end from Blob with the verification script.

These are gaps in HaltSQL itself, not configuration choices. Each has a workaround above. Gap Status Workaround Azure Key Vault secret provider (a ${azure-kv:...} placeholder) Not supported natively yet. Supported schemes are env, file, vault, aws-sm and gcp-sm. Key Vault CSI driver (AKS) or Container Apps Key Vault references, read via ${file:...}. Or HashiCorp Vault with Azure auth. Azure Blob Storage audit sink Not supported natively yet. Object sinks are s3 and gcs only. Azure Blob has no S3-compatible API, so the s3 sink's endpoint cannot target it. file sink plus a Vector azure_blob shipper (Vector 0.55.0 or later for Workload Identity), or stdout plus Log Analytics export. Managed identity / Workload Identity credentials Not supported natively yet. HaltSQL has credential chains only for AWS (env, IRSA, IMDSv2) and GCP (metadata, key file). HaltSQL needs no Azure credential in the patterns above. Identity belongs to the CSI driver, the platform and the shipper. Azure Monitor exporter Not supported natively yet. Telemetry is Prometheus plus OTLP over HTTP with JSON encoding only. OpenTelemetry Collector (otlp receiver, azuremonitor exporter) in the cluster or as a sidecar. Container Apps managed OpenTelemetry agent Incompatible: it accepts gRPC only, and HaltSQL exports OTLP/HTTP. Collector sidecar on localhost:4318. Secret rotation for ${file:...} values Files referenced by placeholders are read at startup and on reload (SIGHUP, or a change to a watched config, policy or TLS file), not watched. The distroless image has no shell to send SIGHUP from a sidecar. Add the new token hash as a second token entry, roll the pods (kubectl rollout restart, or a new Container Apps revision), then remove the old entry. TLS files referenced by path are watched. Audit file rotation The file sink appends forever. Size the volume for the pod's lifetime; rely on pod replacement; alert on audit errors. Entra roles as the policy selector policy_claim requires a string claim, and roles is an array. One OIDC provider entry per identity, keyed by azp, with a pinned policy. Helm chart on AKS No extraVolumes, extraEnv or extraContainers (so no CSI volume and no shipper sidecar); no telemetry.otlp value; the NetworkPolicy blocks the egress that OIDC needs; the ServiceMonitor uses monitoring.coreos.com, not azmonitoring.coreos.com. Use the raw sidecar manifest; for the chart, use values-aks.yaml plus networkpolicy-shared.yaml (Managed Prometheus scraping instead of OTLP), and ESO or cert-manager for TLS. haltsql-proxy upstream Entra ID auth Not supported. The upstream password is read once at startup, and Entra tokens expire after about an hour. A password-authenticated, read-only service role, with the password in Key Vault via CSI. haltsql-proxy operations No metrics endpoint and no HTTP health endpoint. Audit goes only to stdout or file. TCP probes; the audit stream in Log Analytics. Byte-exact chain via Log Analytics Container Insights parses JSON log lines, so the exact bytes are not guaranteed to be preserved. Use the file and Blob route for the verifiable record.

To run haltsql-console (the control plane) next to these deployments: on AKS with the haltsql-console chart, Workload Identity, the Key Vault CSI driver for its secrets (Key Vault is not a console secrets provider yet), an Azure Files share for the verifiers' audit files, Entra ID sign-in through an oauth2-proxy sidecar behind Application Gateway, and an Azure Disk for its state; or on Azure Container Apps as a single replica with Azure Files. See console/deploy.md and deploy/cloud/azure/console/. Each verifier needs server.admin enabled with the console's token in server.admin.callers.

The architecture images on this page are drawn as code with mingrammer/diagrams, one script per diagram: deploy/diagrams/azure_*.py. Every other diagram on this page is Mermaid, inline in the Markdown. You need Graphviz (dot).
