From the repository root: make diagrams # every cloud, in a managed virtualenv deploy/diagrams/.venv/bin/python deploy/diagrams/azure_<name>.py # one diagram Each script writes the matching docs/assets/cloud/azure-<name>.png. Commit the PNG together with the script change. See deploy/diagrams/README.md for the shared style.

This guide shows how to run HaltSQL on Google Cloud with keyless authentication (Workload Identity and the metadata server), secrets in Secret Manager, a write-once audit trail in Cloud Storage, and traces and metrics in Cloud Trace and Cloud Monitoring. The manifests it refers to are in deploy/cloud/gcp/. Read deployment.md first for the general model. In short: haltsql-server only answers "is this SQL allowed?" and never connects to the database; the agent runs the exact SQL it verified. haltsql-proxy sits in front of PostgreSQL and enforces the answer itself. Pattern Runs on Use it when GKE sidecar GKE (Standard or Autopilot) Your agents run on GKE. One haltsql-server per agent pod, on 127.0.0.1. The default recommendation. GKE shared service GKE, Helm chart Many agents, central policy management, Google ID tokens instead of shared secrets. Cloud Run Cloud Run Your agents run on Cloud Run: either a sidecar container in the agent's service, or one internal haltsql service shared by several agents. Proxy in front of Cloud SQL GKE You cannot change the client (BI tools, vendor agents), or you do not trust the application to honor verdicts. Whatever you pick, keep the database-side controls of defense-in-depth.md: a least-privilege database role and row-level security on Cloud SQL. Terraform. To provision these patterns as code, use the modules in deploy/terraform (terraform.md): haltsql-gcp runs haltsql-server on Cloud Run, and haltsql-kubernetes installs the Helm chart on any cluster. This guide explains the architecture and the settings those modules expose; the manifests in deploy/cloud/gcp/ are the equivalent by hand.

HaltSQL calls two Google APIs: Secret Manager (to resolve ${gcp-sm:...} placeholders when the config loads) and Cloud Storage (the gcs audit sink). Both use an OAuth2 access token with the cloud-platform scope, cached and refreshed 60 seconds before it expires. The token comes from: Caller Source, in order ${gcp-sm:...} resolver GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS if set (a service-account key JSON file), otherwise the metadata server. gcs audit sink credentials.source in the sink config: metadata (default) or service_account_file with file. It does not read GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS. The metadata server is http://metadata.google.internal (override with GCE_METADATA_HOST). HaltSQL sends Metadata-Flavor: Google and rejects a response that does not carry the same header. On GKE with Workload Identity the GKE metadata server answers with the token of the Google service account (GSA) bound to the pod's Kubernetes service account (KSA). On Cloud Run it answers with the token of the revision's service account. Use the metadata server everywhere on Google Cloud. Do not create service-account keys. The key-file option exists for running outside Google Cloud; HaltSQL does not support Workload Identity Federation credential configuration files ("type": "external_account"), so outside Google Cloud a key is currently the only way (see Limitations). haltsql-proxy makes no Google API calls. Its secrets reach it as files (${file:...}).

A project with billing, and gcloud authenticated as someone who can create service accounts, secrets and buckets and grant IAM roles on them. For GKE: a cluster with Workload Identity Federation for GKE enabled (Autopilot enables it by default; on Standard, gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog and node pools with --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA). Native sidecars (used by the manifests) need GKE 1.29 or later. A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with private IP only in the same VPC (Private Services Access), and IAM database authentication enabled (cloudsql.iam_authentication=on) if the agent logs in as its service account. The tools: gcloud, kubectl, helm (shared service), openssl. Enable the APIs and create the audit bucket once per project: export PROJECT_ID=my-project REGION=europe-west1 deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh apis deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh audit-bucket # bucket with an (unlocked) retention policy setup.sh has one subcommand per pattern. Each creates the service account, secrets and IAM bindings that pattern needs and nothing else. Read a subcommand before running it in production.

The agent pod has three containers: agent: your code. It calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/verify and runs only allowed SQL. haltsql (native sidecar, starts first): haltsql-server with the policy from a ConfigMap. The token hash comes from Secret Manager; audit batches go to GCS; spans go to an OpenTelemetry Collector; Managed Service for Prometheus scrapes /metrics. cloud-sql-proxy (native sidecar): the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on 127.0.0.1:5432, connecting to the instance's private IP with IAM database authentication. haltsql-server never uses it. The KSA analytics-agent is annotated with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: haltsql-agent@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com, and that GSA holds exactly the roles in the IAM reference.

Create the GSA, secrets and bindings. This generates a random token, stores it in secret haltsql-analytics-agent-token (for the agent) and its SHA-256 in haltsql-analytics-agent-token-sha256 (for haltsql). The token is never printed. deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh gke-sidecar deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh collector The Workload Identity binding it creates is: gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \ haltsql-agent@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \ --member "serviceAccount:$PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog[agents/analytics-agent]" Fill in the manifests and apply them: grep -n REPLACE_ME deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/sidecar.yaml deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/otel-collector.yaml kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/otel-collector.yaml kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/sidecar.yaml Check that haltsql loaded its policy and can write audit objects: kubectl -n agents logs deploy/analytics-agent -c haltsql | head kubectl -n agents port-forward deploy/analytics-agent 8080:8080 & curl -s localhost:8080/readyz curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep haltsql_audit_sink_healthy The haltsql part of the config (in the ConfigMap): server: auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${gcp-sm:haltsql-analytics-agent-token-sha256} policy: analytics-agent audit: sinks: - type: gcs bucket: ${env:HALTSQL_AUDIT_BUCKET} prefix: haltsql/audit/analytics-agent/ credentials: { source: metadata } spool_dir: /var/spool/haltsql on_error: fail_closed telemetry: metrics: { prometheus: true } otlp: endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4318 service_name: haltsql-analytics-agent metrics: false secrets: gcp: project: ${env:GCP_PROJECT} The pod identity is shared by all three containers, so the agent can also create objects in the audit bucket. It cannot read, overwrite or delete any (the role is roles/storage.objectCreator and objects are create-only), and objects that do not continue the chain stand out when you verify it. If that is not acceptable, use the shared service, which has its own identity.

The Helm chart in deploy/helm/haltsql runs a haltsql-server Deployment behind a Service. On GKE the cleanest authentication is Google-signed ID tokens: each agent asks its own metadata server for an ID token with audience haltsql, and haltsql verifies it as an OIDC token from https://accounts.google.com. No secret is shared or rotated. values-gke.yaml sets, among other things: serviceAccount: name: haltsql annotations: iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: haltsql-server@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com automountServiceAccountToken: false oidc: - name: google-analytics-agent issuer: https://accounts.google.com audiences: [haltsql] algorithms: [RS256] policy: analytics-agent required_claims: sub: "112233445566778899000" # unique ID of the agent's GSA request_context_fields: [tenant_id] Add one oidc entry per calling GSA. Entries with the same issuer are tried in order, and the first that accepts the token decides the policy. Pin on sub, the GSA's numeric unique ID (gcloud iam service-accounts describe EMAIL --format='value(uniqueId)'). email is only in the token when the caller requests format=full. Agents on GKE should use the GSA annotation on their KSA: ID tokens from the metadata server are issued for the impersonated GSA. Check that your setup issues them before relying on direct principal bindings without a GSA. Google ID tokens carry no tenant, so request_context_fields: [tenant_id] lets the calling service supply it from its own session, exactly as with a static token. If the tenant must come from the identity, use one GSA per tenant, or mTLS identities with a static context. In the agent, fetch and cache the token (it is valid for one hour): import google.auth.transport.requests import google.oauth2.id_token token = google.oauth2.id_token.fetch_id_token( google.auth.transport.requests.Request(), "haltsql") Steps: deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh gke-shared kubectl create namespace haltsql # TLS: a kubernetes.io/tls Secret named haltsql-tls (cert-manager, Google CAS, ...) helm upgrade --install haltsql deploy/helm/haltsql -n haltsql \ -f deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/values-gke.yaml \ --set-file 'policies.analytics-agent\.yaml=policies/analytics-agent.yaml' kubectl apply -n haltsql -f deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/shared-extras.yaml The chart's NetworkPolicy denies all egress by default. values-gke.yaml opens DNS, TCP 443 (GCS and Google's JWKS), the GKE metadata server and the collector. Keep server.port: 8080: the image sets HALTSQL_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080, which outranks the listen address the chart writes into the config, so change the Service port instead.

Cloud Run can pull images only from Artifact Registry, Container Registry and Docker Hub. Mirror the image through an Artifact Registry remote repository first: deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh image # image: $REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/ghcr/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 Settings that matter on Cloud Run, for both variants: run.googleapis.com/cpu-throttling: "false" (instance-based billing). The GCS sink closes batches and retries uploads in the background, and the OTLP exporter sends spans in the background. With request-based billing, CPU is throttled between requests and both stall until the next request. Spool directory. Cloud Run has no persistent disk; the manifests use an in-memory emptyDir. It protects records across a container restart within an instance, but each new instance starts a new chain. Verify each run's objects on its own (see Audit). On SIGTERM, haltsql flushes the open batch before exiting, within Cloud Run's 10-second shutdown window. Configuration is mounted from Secret Manager (config.yaml, policies) or a read-only Cloud Storage volume (signed bundles). Set reload.watch: false and roll out changes as new revisions: each revision then pins one config version, which is what you want for audits.

cloudrun/service-sidecar.yaml has three containers: agent (the ingress container, port 8080), haltsql (listening on 0.0.0.0:8081; only the ingress container's port is reachable from outside the instance) and otel-collector. run.googleapis.com/container-dependencies starts haltsql, and waits for its startup probe on /readyz, before the agent. export POLICY_FILE=policies/analytics-agent.yaml deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh cloud-run-sidecar # SA, token, config/policy secrets, IAM gcloud run services replace deploy/cloud/gcp/cloudrun/service-sidecar.yaml --region $REGION The agent receives its raw token from Secret Manager as HALTSQL_TOKEN (secretKeyRef), and haltsql receives the hash as HALTSQL_TOKEN_SHA256, used by token_sha256: ${env:HALTSQL_TOKEN_SHA256}. Both are resolved by Cloud Run when the instance starts. The collector config (otel-collector-config.yaml) receives spans on localhost:4318 and scrapes localhost:8081/metrics, so the haltsql_audit_sink_* gauges (which OTLP does not carry) reach Managed Service for Prometheus too.

cloudrun/service-internal.yaml runs haltsql-server as its own service with ingress: internal and no allUsers invoker. Requests pass two checks: X-Serverless-Authorization is checked by Cloud Run (IAM invoker), which leaves Authorization for haltsql. Cloud Run removes the signature from the X-Serverless-Authorization token before forwarding it, so haltsql never relies on that header. haltsql's providers are in haltsql-internal-config.yaml, one per calling service account, as in pattern 1b. Policies come from a signed bundle on a read-only Cloud Storage volume (gcsfuse.run.googleapis.com, which needs the second-generation execution environment). The trusted public key is in the config, which lives in Secret Manager, so write access to the policy bucket is not enough to change policies. See policy-bundles.md. Internal ingress and callers. A request counts as internal when it comes from a VPC network of the project (for example GKE pods, with Private Google Access on the subnet) or from a Cloud Run service whose egress goes through the VPC with --vpc-egress=all-traffic. A Cloud Run caller with private-ranges-only egress reaches the run.app URL over the internet and is refused. With all-traffic, the caller needs Cloud NAT for any other internet destination (the LLM API, for example). deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh cloud-run-internal gcloud storage cp dist/prod.haltsqlbundle dist/prod.haltsqlbundle.sig gs://$PROJECT_ID-haltsql-policies/ gcloud run services replace deploy/cloud/gcp/cloudrun/service-internal.yaml --region $REGION gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding haltsql --region $REGION \ --member serviceAccount:analytics-agent@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/run.invoker Cloud Run terminates TLS in front of the container, so server.tls is not used here. The hop from the Google front end to the container is inside Google's network.

haltsql-proxy speaks the Postgres wire protocol, so it needs a TCP load balancer: run it on GKE (or Compute Engine). Cloud Run accepts only HTTP(S), gRPC and WebSockets. Clients connect to the haltsql-proxy Service (internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, port 6432, TLS required) with a proxy user and password (SCRAM-SHA-256) or a client certificate. Each user is bound to one policy and one tenant context in the proxy config. Every Query and Parse is verified; tenancy parameters in every Bind are overwritten with the session's context. Only verified SQL is forwarded. The upstream hop goes to the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on 127.0.0.1:5432 (in the same pod), which connects to the instance's private IP over mTLS, authorized by IAM (roles/cloudsql.client). Give the instance no public IP and no authorized networks, so only this path exists. Secrets (upstream password, TLS key and certificate, SCRAM verifiers) come from Secret Manager through the GKE Secret Manager add-on and are read with ${file:...} or as file paths. haltsql-proxy does not resolve ${gcp-sm:...} itself. Note that tls.key and tls.cert must be file paths, not ${file:...} placeholders. gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER --location $REGION --enable-secret-manager printf '%s' "$UPSTREAM_PASSWORD" | gcloud secrets create haltsql-proxy-upstream-password --data-file=- haltsql-proxy scram-verifier | gcloud secrets create haltsql-proxy-scram-analytics-agent --data-file=- gcloud secrets create haltsql-proxy-tls-crt --data-file=tls.crt gcloud secrets create haltsql-proxy-tls-key --data-file=tls.key deploy/cloud/gcp/iam/setup.sh proxy kubectl apply -f deploy/cloud/gcp/proxy/haltsql-proxy.yaml psql "host=PROXY_ILB_IP port=6432 dbname=app user=analytics-agent sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=ca.crt" The proxy writes one JSON audit line per statement to stdout (Cloud Logging). It has no metrics or HTTP health endpoint, so the manifest probes the TCP port. See proxy.md for the full reference.
documents.s: Pattern 3: haltsql-proxy in front of Cloud SQL

documents.t: Grant roles on the narrowest resource that supports them. Nothing in HaltSQL needs a project-wide Storage or Secret Manager role. Identity Role On Why haltsql (any pattern with a gcs sink) roles/storage.objectCreator the audit bucket Create audit objects. No read, list, overwrite or delete. HaltSQL uploads with ifGenerationMatch=0 and treats 412 as "already stored", so it never needs storage.objects.get. haltsql (with ${gcp-sm:...}) roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor each referenced secret Read secret payloads at load and reload. haltsql, Cloud Run 2B roles/storage.objectViewer the policy bucket Read signed bundles through the Cloud Storage volume. haltsql, Cloud Run roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor the config / policy / token-hash secrets Cloud Run mounts them with the revision's service account. OTel Collector roles/cloudtrace.agent project Write spans. OTel Collector (Cloud Run 2A) roles/monitoring.metricWriter project Write scraped metrics to Managed Prometheus. Cloud SQL Auth Proxy roles/cloudsql.client project (add an IAM condition on the instance name to narrow it) Connect to the instance. Agent logging in with IAM DB auth roles/cloudsql.instanceUser project (conditionable) IAM database login. KSA (GKE) roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser the GSA Lets PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA] impersonate the GSA. Each caller of the internal service roles/run.invoker the haltsql Cloud Run service Pass Cloud Run's IAM check. Example of a single-secret grant: gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding haltsql-analytics-agent-token-sha256 \ --member serviceAccount:haltsql-agent@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://$PROJECT_ID-haltsql-audit \ --member serviceAccount:haltsql-agent@$PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role roles/storage.objectCreator Nobody who operates haltsql day to day should hold storage.objects.delete or storage.buckets.update on the audit bucket. Keep readers (auditors) in a separate group with roles/storage.objectViewer.

Verification traffic. In the sidecar patterns it stays on loopback inside the pod or Cloud Run instance. In the shared patterns it stays inside the VPC: a ClusterIP Service, an internal passthrough load balancer (networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"), or Cloud Run with ingress: internal. Outbound calls from haltsql-server. Only what you configure: Secret Manager and Cloud Storage (*.googleapis.com:443), the metadata server, the OIDC issuer's discovery and JWKS URLs, and the OTLP collector. With private nodes, enable Private Google Access on the subnet; with VPC Service Controls, put Secret Manager, Cloud Storage and Cloud Trace in the perimeter and route *.googleapis.com to restricted.googleapis.com. NetworkPolicy on GKE. Workload Identity needs egress to the GKE metadata server: 169.254.169.252/32 port 988, or 169.254.169.254/32 port 80 on GKE Dataplane V2 clusters. The manifests allow both. Without it, token requests time out and the server refuses to start (${gcp-sm:...}) or the audit sink turns unhealthy. Database. Cloud SQL with private IP only. Only the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (agent pod, or proxy pod) reaches it on port 3307.

Hop How it is protected Agent to sidecar Loopback; no TLS needed. A token is still required. Agent to shared haltsql on GKE Built-in TLS (tls.enabled, TLS 1.3), or a service mesh (Cloud Service Mesh) with mTLS. Certificates from cert-manager with a Google CAS issuer rotate without restarts (reload.watch). Agent to internal Cloud Run service HTTPS terminated by Cloud Run. Client to haltsql-proxy tls.required: true; client certificates with auth.method: cert if you want them. haltsql-proxy / agent to Cloud SQL Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (mTLS, ephemeral certificates). The loopback hop to it does not leave the pod. haltsql to Google APIs HTTPS with the system trust store.

The gcs sink writes hash-chained batches (one object per batch.max_records records or batch.max_seconds seconds) with ifGenerationMatch=0, so an object is never overwritten, and checks the md5Hash Cloud Storage returns. See audit-sinks.md for the object layout and the chain. Make the bucket write-once: Create it with a retention policy (setup.sh audit-bucket uses 400 days; set AUDIT_RETENTION for your requirement). Objects cannot be deleted or replaced until they are that old. Once the period is right, lock it. Locking is irreversible: the policy can never be shortened or removed. gcloud storage buckets update gs://$PROJECT_ID-haltsql-audit --lock-retention-period Optionally add a lifecycle rule that deletes objects after the retention period, and a default Cloud KMS key on the bucket if you need CMEK (the sink needs nothing extra for either). HaltSQL sets no per-object retention or holds itself; WORM comes from the bucket policy. Keep spool_dir on storage that survives restarts where you can (on GKE an emptyDir survives container restarts but not pod deletion), so the chain continues across restarts; otherwise each run starts at genesis. To verify a day of one pod's objects: gcloud storage cp -r "gs://$PROJECT_ID-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/analytics-agent/2026/11/08/" ./audit/ find ./audit -name 'analytics-agent-7f9c-*.jsonl' | sort | xargs cat > day.jsonl python3 verify_chain.py day.jsonl # script in audit-sinks.md Without a persistent spool, group the objects by the <run> part of the name and verify each group from genesis.

Signal Path on Google Cloud Prometheus metrics (/metrics) Managed Service for Prometheus: PodMonitoring on GKE; the collector's prometheus receiver on Cloud Run. Includes haltsql_audit_sink_*. Traces (haltsql.verify spans) OTLP/HTTP (JSON) to an OpenTelemetry Collector, googlecloud exporter to Cloud Trace. haltsql cannot authenticate to Google's telemetry endpoints itself, so the collector is required. An incoming W3C traceparent is honoured, so spans join the agent's trace. Logs JSON lines on stderr, collected by Cloud Logging. haltsql writes level and msg (not severity and message), so filter on jsonPayload.level. Audit GCS (compliance copy); optionally also stdout for search in Cloud Logging. Set telemetry.otlp.metrics: false when Prometheus scraping is on, so the same counters are not ingested twice. Alerts worth creating (PromQL in Cloud Monitoring): Query Meaning min(haltsql_audit_sink_healthy) == 0 An audit sink refuses writes; with fail_closed, verify returns 503. rate(haltsql_audit_sink_upload_failures_total[5m]) > 0 Uploads to GCS are failing (IAM, network, quota). max(haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects) > 0 for 5 minutes Batches are stuck. increase(haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}[10m]) > 0 A policy or secret change was rejected; the old set is still active. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.05 Verification is slow. rate(haltsql_auth_total{result="unavailable"}[5m]) > 0 Google's JWKS cannot be fetched (shared patterns). The SQL text is never exported in spans. Join a span to its audit record on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256.

haltsql-server is stateless and CPU-bound; a verification usually takes well under a millisecond. As a sidecar it scales with the agent. 50m CPU and 32-64 MiB is a reasonable request for one agent. GKE shared service: at least 3 replicas spread across zones (topologySpreadConstraints), a PodDisruptionBudget, and an HPA on CPU. Use a regional cluster. Cloud Run: minScale of 1 or more avoids cold starts on the verify path (startup includes resolving secrets and, for OIDC, fetching JWKS). haltsql handles high concurrency; containerConcurrency of 80-250 is fine. Cloud Run is regional; deploy one service per region if agents are multi-region, each with its own audit prefix. Dependencies at runtime: Secret Manager is needed only at startup and reload; a failed reload keeps the last good config. GCS is on the write path: with on_error: fail_closed an outage makes verify return 503 after the retries are exhausted; with buffer, records are held in memory (up to 100 000) and uploaded later. Choose per your compliance requirements. haltsql-proxy: two or more replicas behind the internal load balancer. Size the Cloud SQL connection limit for replicas x max_connections.

Sidecars add a small, fixed CPU and memory request per agent pod or Cloud Run instance. A shared service is cheaper with many small agents. Cloud Run instance-based billing (cpu-throttling: false) charges for the whole instance lifetime. It is needed for timely audit flushes; keep minScale low and containerConcurrency high. Cloud Storage: one object per batch per instance (at least one per max_seconds while traffic flows). Raising batch.max_seconds and max_records lowers Class A operation counts. Retention means you pay for storage for at least the retention period; a lifecycle rule to a colder storage class reduces it (objects keep their retention). Cloud Logging: a stdout audit sink duplicates every record into Logging ingestion. Drop it when GCS is enough, or exclude it with a sink filter. Cloud Trace and Managed Prometheus bill per span and per sample. haltsql exports a span when the incoming traceparent has the sampled flag set, and always when there is no traceparent, so propagate your agent's sampling decision. Scrape every 30-60 seconds.

The image is pinned by digest, verified with cosign, and mirrored to Artifact Registry. No service-account keys anywhere; GKE uses Workload Identity, Cloud Run the revision's service account. Each GSA holds only the roles in the IAM reference, bound to single secrets and buckets. Audit bucket: uniform bucket-level access, public access prevention, retention policy locked, no delete permission for operators. on_error chosen deliberately (fail_closed for compliance), and haltsql_audit_sink_healthy alerts configured. audit.log_raw_sql stays false unless you have a reason and a data classification for it. Every token, OIDC provider and mTLS identity is pinned to one policy; allow_unauthenticated is false. Shared services: TLS on (or Cloud Run HTTPS), ingress limited to the agents' namespaces or ingress: internal, run.invoker only for the callers. NetworkPolicies allow the metadata server, Google APIs and the collector, and nothing else. Cloud SQL: private IP only, no authorized networks, a least-privilege role for the agent (or haltsql_service for the proxy), row-level security on. Policies ship as signed bundles (or through reviewed ConfigMap changes), and config changes roll out as new revisions on Cloud Run. haltsql config show (or haltsql-proxy validate) runs in CI against the exact config you deploy. The chain verification job runs regularly against the audit bucket.

Google credentials come only from the metadata server or a service-account key file. Workload Identity Federation credential files (external_account) are not supported, so running outside Google Cloud needs a key. The gcs sink does not read GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS; set credentials.source: service_account_file explicitly. The gcs sink sets no per-object retention or holds; rely on a bucket retention policy. OTLP export cannot authenticate to Google endpoints; use a collector. Secret Manager values are read at load and reload only. A rotated secret takes effect after SIGHUP, a file change with reload.watch, or a new Cloud Run revision. Log lines use level/msg, not Cloud Logging's severity/message. haltsql-proxy has no ${gcp-sm:...}, no GCS audit sink, no metrics and no HTTP health endpoint.

To run haltsql-console (the control plane) next to these deployments: on GKE with the haltsql-console chart, Workload Identity for GCS audit reads and Secret Manager, Identity-Aware Proxy in front and a Persistent Disk for its state; or on Cloud Run as a single always-on instance with a Filestore volume. See console/deploy.md and deploy/cloud/gcp/console/. Each verifier needs server.admin enabled with the console's token in server.admin.callers.

The architecture images on this page are drawn as code with mingrammer/diagrams, one script per diagram: deploy/diagrams/gcp_*.py. Every other diagram on this page is Mermaid, inline in the Markdown. You need Graphviz (dot). From the repository root: make diagrams # every cloud, in a managed virtualenv deploy/diagrams/.venv/bin/python deploy/diagrams/gcp_<name>.py # one diagram Each script writes the matching docs/assets/cloud/gcp-<name>.png. Commit the PNG together with the script change. See deploy/diagrams/README.md for the shared style.

HaltSQL runs in one of three shapes: Shape When to use Library (haltsql OCaml package) Your agent is written in OCaml. Lowest latency; no network hop. Sidecar (haltsql-server next to the agent, on 127.0.0.1) Recommended for everything else. One instance per agent pod. Shared service (haltsql-server behind a load balancer) Many agents, central policy management. Needs TLS in front and tokens pinned to policies. haltsql-server never connects to the database: the agent runs the exact string it verified. To verify every statement without changing the agent, put haltsql-proxy in front of PostgreSQL instead. In every shape, the database-side controls in defense-in-depth.md still apply.

Reference architectures, IAM policies and ready-to-edit manifests for each cloud live in their own guides. Their architecture diagrams are generated from code with mingrammer/diagrams (make diagrams, sources in deploy/diagrams/). Cloud Guide Patterns covered Manifests AWS deploy-aws.md EKS sidecar with IRSA, ECS Fargate shared service, proxy in front of RDS deploy/cloud/aws/ Google Cloud deploy-gcp.md GKE sidecar with Workload Identity, Cloud Run, proxy in front of Cloud SQL deploy/cloud/gcp/ Azure deploy-azure.md AKS sidecar with Workload Identity, Container Apps, proxy in front of Flexible Server deploy/cloud/azure/

haltsql-console is the control plane for a HaltSQL deployment: signals, records, agents, policies, fleet, data classification and evidence. It reads the verifiers' audit records and admin API and is never in the query path. It ships as its own image, ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console (target console in the same Dockerfile), with a Helm chart in deploy/helm/haltsql-console/ and a local Docker Compose stack in deploy/console/. Each verifier it watches needs server.admin enabled with the console's token in server.admin.callers. See console/deploy.md for local, Kubernetes, AWS, Google Cloud and Azure. TLS: haltsql-server has built-in TLS 1.2/1.3 and optional mTLS (server.tls, see authentication.md). As a sidecar bound to 127.0.0.1 it can also run without TLS, or behind a proxy or service mesh that terminates TLS.

Images are published for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64: ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version> # e.g. 0.0.1 ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<major.minor> # e.g. 0.1 The image runs haltsql-server by default; the haltsql CLI is included. docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \ -v "$PWD/policies:/etc/haltsql/policies:ro" \ -v "$PWD/config.yaml:/etc/haltsql/config.yaml:ro" \ -e HALTSQL_ANALYTICS_TOKEN_HASH \ ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 \ --config /etc/haltsql/config.yaml --listen 0.0.0.0:8080 Inside a container, the server must listen on 0.0.0.0 to be reachable through the published port; publish the port on 127.0.0.1 on the host as above, or only to the agent's network. Run the CLI from the same image: docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w --entrypoint haltsql \ ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 validate policy.yaml Pin images by digest in production (ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql@sha256:...) and verify the signature (see below).

Path Content /usr/local/bin/haltsql-server Entrypoint. Default command --config /etc/haltsql/config.yaml. /usr/local/bin/haltsql The CLI. /usr/local/bin/haltsql-proxy The PostgreSQL wire-protocol firewall (proxy.md). /var/log/haltsql Empty, writable by the image user, for file audit sinks. /etc/ssl/certs CA bundle (OIDC discovery, Vault, AWS, GCP). /usr/share/doc/haltsql LICENSE, NOTICE, LICENSE.libpg_query. The base image is gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot. It has no shell, no package manager and no libc, because the binaries are fully static. It runs as uid/gid 65532 (nonroot). HALTSQL_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080 is set. Port 8080 is the server and 6432 the proxy. There is no HEALTHCHECK, because the image has no shell or curl. Use orchestrator probes on GET /healthz (liveness) and GET /readyz (readiness). Run the proxy from the same image: docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:6432:6432 \ -v "$PWD/proxy:/etc/haltsql:ro" -e UPSTREAM_PASSWORD \ --entrypoint /usr/local/bin/haltsql-proxy \ ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 run --config /etc/haltsql/proxy.yaml Mounted files must be readable by uid 65532.

docker build -t haltsql-local:dev . # runtime image docker build --target scratch -t haltsql-local:scratch . # same binaries on scratch docker buildx build --target dist --output type=local,dest=dist . # just the binaries The Dockerfile has four stages: Stage What it does builder ocaml/opam:alpine-3.22-ocaml-5.3. Solves the dependencies against a pinned opam-repository commit (OPAM_REPOSITORY_COMMIT). Builds the three binaries with HALTSQL_STATIC=1 dune build --profile release, strips them, and fails unless file reports each one as statically linked, ldd finds no dynamic dependencies, and each binary runs. dist scratch holding only the binaries and licences. The release workflow exports it with --output. scratch The binaries on an empty filesystem. Its build runs haltsql version in exec form, so the build fails if anything is dynamically linked. runtime (default) The distroless image described above. Both the base image tag and the opam-repository commit are pinned, so a rebuild solves the same dependency set. Change them on purpose, as their own change. scripts/docker-smoke.sh tests a built image end to end: make -C lab up # Postgres 17 on localhost:5417 (for the proxy step) SCRATCH_IMAGE=haltsql-local:scratch scripts/docker-smoke.sh It checks the following: The image runs as non-root and has no shell. haltsql version, validate and verify work, with exit 0 for an allowed query and exit 1 for a denied one. haltsql-server answers GET /healthz and POST /v1/verify for both an allowed and a denied query, writes an audit record, and keeps raw SQL out of its output. haltsql-proxy runs against a real PostgreSQL, reached from the container as host.docker.internal:5417. Through psql from a postgres:17-alpine client container, an allowed query returns rows, while a cross-tenant query and a stacked DROP TABLE both get ERROR 42501 ... denied by policy, and the table is still intact afterwards. With SCRATCH_IMAGE set, all three binaries also run on the scratch image. The script creates its own containers, network and database, all named after its process id, and always removes them. Without a Docker daemon it prints SKIPPED and exits 0. If PostgreSQL is unreachable, it skips the proxy step with a message. Set REQUIRE_PROXY=1 to make that a failure instead (CI does this), or SKIP_PROXY=1 to skip the proxy step on purpose. Set PGHOST_FROM_DOCKER, PGPORT and HALTSQL_PGPASSWORD to point it at another server. The .github/workflows/build-images.yml workflow runs it on amd64 and arm64 for every pull request that touches the build.

The release tarballs (haltsql-<tag>-linux-{amd64,arm64}.tar.gz) hold the output of the dist stage, built on a native runner for each architecture by .github/workflows/release.yml. They are fully static musl executables with no runtime dependencies. They run on any Linux distribution, glibc or musl, and on scratch. $ file haltsql-server haltsql-server: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, ARM aarch64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped $ ldd haltsql-server not a dynamic executable Static linking is opt-in in the build (HALTSQL_STATIC=1, read by bin/link_flags.ml, which adds -ccopt -static). The default dune build stays dynamic. A static build needs musl, because glibc's static NSS is not usable. It also needs the static archives of the C libraries the binaries link: libgmp.a from Alpine's gmp-static package for zarith, and the vendored libpg_query.a, which dune builds. The mirage-crypto, digestif and Unix stubs are compiled from source.

deploy/helm/haltsql deploys haltsql-server as its own Deployment and Service, with the Config and policies in ConfigMaps, token hashes in a Secret, and an optional PodDisruptionBudget, HorizontalPodAutoscaler, NetworkPolicy and ServiceMonitor. values.yaml documents every value. For settings the chart has no dedicated value for: extraPolicies: Config policies[] entries appended to the rendered ones, for example a signed bundle_source (see policy-bundles.md). A bundle_source entry without cache_dir gets <cache.mountPath>/bundles, so a restarted pod can start from its last verified bundle while the source is down. extraConfig: Config keys deep-merged into the rendered Config (nested maps merge, extraConfig wins, lists and scalars replace), for example opa, secrets, telemetry.otlp or audit.sinks. extraConfig.policies is refused, because it would replace the chart's list; use extraPolicies. cache: the writable volume for bundle caches (mountPath, default /var/cache/haltsql, and volume, default an emptyDir). The root filesystem is read-only. Use a persistentVolumeClaim to keep the cache across rescheduling. Secrets (registry passwords, API keys) belong in ${env:...} or secret provider placeholders, never inline in these values. For CRD-driven deployments see the Kubernetes operator; for Terraform see terraform.md.

Run haltsql-server as a second container in the agent's pod. The agent calls http://127.0.0.1:8080. The server listens on 0.0.0.0:8080 so the kubelet can probe it, and a NetworkPolicy blocks that port from other pods. Policies and config come from a ConfigMap; token hashes from a Secret. apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: haltsql-config data: config.yaml: | apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Config server: listen: 0.0.0.0:8080 auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${file:/etc/haltsql/secrets/analytics-agent.sha256} policy: analytics-agent policies: - path: ./policies/analytics-agent.yaml reload: { watch: true } audit: sinks: [{ type: stdout }] logging: { level: info, format: json } policies-analytics-agent.yaml: | apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: { name: analytics-agent } search_path: [app] statements: { allow: [select] } require_limit: { max: 1000 } tenancy: { mode: bound, keys: { tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" } } tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id functions: { presets: [aggregates] } --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: haltsql-tokens type: Opaque stringData: analytics-agent.sha256: "<64 lower-case hex characters>" # sha256 of the agent's token --- apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: analytics-agent spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: { app: analytics-agent } template: metadata: labels: { app: analytics-agent } spec: securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } containers: - name: agent image: registry.example.com/analytics-agent:1.4.2 env: - name: HALTSQL_URL value: http://127.0.0.1:8080 - name: HALTSQL_TOKEN valueFrom: secretKeyRef: { name: analytics-agent-token, key: token } - name: haltsql image: ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 args: ["--config", "/etc/haltsql/config.yaml"] ports: - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 } readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 } periodSeconds: 10 resources: requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 32Mi } limits: { cpu: "1", memory: 128Mi } securityContext: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } volumeMounts: - name: config mountPath: /etc/haltsql/config.yaml subPath: config.yaml - name: config mountPath: /etc/haltsql/policies/analytics-agent.yaml subPath: policies-analytics-agent.yaml - name: tokens mountPath: /etc/haltsql/secrets readOnly: true volumes: - name: config configMap: { name: haltsql-config } - name: tokens secret: { secretName: haltsql-tokens } --- # Deny ingress to the agent pods from other pods. Kubelet probes are not # subject to NetworkPolicy in common CNI plugins; check yours. apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: analytics-agent-no-ingress spec: podSelector: matchLabels: { app: analytics-agent } policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: [] Notes: Tokens are required even inside the pod, so a compromised neighbor that reaches the port still cannot verify against a policy it holds no token for. If the agent pod must accept ingress (for example a web UI), narrow the NetworkPolicy to the agent's own ports instead of denying everything. ConfigMap updates mounted with subPath are not propagated to running pods. Mount the whole ConfigMap as a directory if you rely on reload.watch, or roll the deployment on policy changes (often the better audit trail). Scrape /metrics with your Prometheus setup, and alert on haltsql_reasons_total{code="E_INTERNAL"} and haltsql_audit_errors_total.

For VMs or bare metal, install the static binary and run it as an unprivileged service: sudo install -m 0755 haltsql haltsql-server /usr/local/bin/ sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin haltsql sudo install -d -m 0750 -o root -g haltsql /etc/haltsql /etc/haltsql/policies sudo install -d -m 0750 -o haltsql -g haltsql /var/log/haltsql /etc/systemd/system/haltsql.service: [Unit] Description=HaltSQL policy firewall sidecar After=network.target [Service] Type=simple User=haltsql Group=haltsql ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/haltsql-server --config /etc/haltsql/config.yaml ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID Restart=on-failure RestartSec=2s EnvironmentFile=-/etc/haltsql/haltsql.env # Hardening NoNewPrivileges=yes ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=yes PrivateTmp=yes PrivateDevices=yes ProtectKernelTunables=yes ProtectKernelModules=yes ProtectControlGroups=yes RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX RestrictNamespaces=yes LockPersonality=yes MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes SystemCallArchitectures=native CapabilityBoundingSet= ReadOnlyPaths=/etc/haltsql ReadWritePaths=/var/log/haltsql [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now haltsql sudo systemctl reload haltsql # reload policies (SIGHUP) journalctl -u haltsql -f Put secrets referenced with ${env:...} in /etc/haltsql/haltsql.env (mode 0640, group haltsql), or reference files with ${file:...}.

Change the policy in version control and run haltsql validate and haltsql test in CI. For a stricter policy, deploy it first with mode: shadow and watch shadow_reasons in the audit log and haltsql_verify_total{result="shadow_denied"}. Switch to mode: enforce. Reload (SIGHUP, file watch, or a rollout). Check /readyz, the policy.version in new verdicts, and the reload metrics. A failed reload keeps the previous policies active.

Each GitHub release has: SHA256SUMS: checksums of all archives, the Helm chart archive, the SBOM and haltsql-<tag>.oci.txt (the digests of the images and the chart in GHCR); *.sigstore.json: a keyless cosign signature bundle for each of those files; a GitHub build-provenance attestation for each archive and the chart; haltsql-<tag>.cdx.json: a CycloneDX SBOM. scripts/verify-release.sh <tag> runs all of the checks below, plus the image SBOM, provenance and Helm chart checks in supply-chain.md. By hand: # Checksums sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # Signature (keyless, issued to this repository's release workflow) cosign verify-blob \ --bundle haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \ haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz # Provenance (GitHub CLI) gh attestation verify haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL # Container image signature cosign verify ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com The Linux binaries are statically linked against musl and run on any Linux distribution. The macOS binary links only system libraries.
Short answers to the questions people ask when they evaluate or adopt HaltSQL. Each answer links to the page with the details. Terms are defined in the glossary.

It answers one question for each SQL statement an LLM writes: is this exact string allowed for this caller, under this policy? You give it the SQL, a policy in YAML or JSON, and a context from the caller's authenticated session, such as the tenant ID. It returns a verdict: allowed, plus reason codes and hints the agent can use to fix its query. It parses with libpg_query, the real PostgreSQL parser. See the quickstart.

No. HaltSQL never rewrites, reformats or appends to SQL. If the verdict allows a query, you run the exact string you checked. In bound tenancy mode the verdict also tells you which values to bind to $1, $2, and so on, so the tenant is added as a parameter, not by editing the text. The official SDKs check that the verdict's sql_sha256 matches the string they sent. See Verdict format and Guarded execution.

Verification does not. The library, the CLI's verify and haltsql-server never connect to the database. Only these parts do: haltsql schema pull and haltsql rls check, which read the system catalogs in a read-only transaction. haltsql-proxy, which forwards allowed statements to Postgres with its own service credentials. Your application, or tools such as haltsql-mcp and the agent framework tools, which run allowed queries on a connection you provide.

No to both. HaltSQL is deterministic: the same SQL, policy and context always get the same decision. It judges the SQL, not the prompt that produced it, so it does not depend on detecting the injection. See the threat model.
documents.s: Does HaltSQL use an LLM, or detect prompt injection?

documents.t: Four ways, all with the same verifier: as an OCaml library in your process; as the haltsql-server HTTP sidecar next to your agent; as haltsql-proxy in front of Postgres, for drivers you can't change; or from the CLI. Python can also verify in-process with the bundled engine. See Deployment and Deployment modes.

Not in bound mode, the recommended one. The model writes tenant_id = $1, and HaltSQL returns the value to bind from the context your application supplies. A tenant literal written by the model is denied with E_TENANT_MISMATCH. The context comes from your session, a bearer token, an OIDC claim or an mTLS identity, and is never a tool argument. See Tenancy and Authentication.
documents.s: Can the model choose the tenant?

documents.t: Row-level security (RLS) filters rows inside the database. HaltSQL decides before the query runs, and covers things RLS doesn't: which columns and functions may be used, a single statement per call, a required LIMIT, join and size budgets, and a reason the agent can act on instead of a silently empty result. They are meant to be used together. haltsql rls generate writes the RLS policies and column grants that mirror a HaltSQL policy. See Defense in depth and RLS generation.
documents.s: How is HaltSQL different from row-level security?

documents.t: Yes. HaltSQL is one of three layers. If HaltSQL had a bug, a policy were misconfigured, or a code path skipped the check, the role and RLS would still hold. See Defense in depth.
documents.s: Do I still need a restricted database role and RLS?

documents.t: Nothing runs. Every official client fails closed: a timeout, a connection error, an error response or a malformed verdict raises an error or returns a refusal. It is never treated as allowed. haltsql-server also refuses requests with 503 when it cannot write an audit record. Run one sidecar per agent pod and probe /readyz. See Python SDK and HTTP API.
documents.s: What happens if HaltSQL is down?

documents.t: Only what the policy allows. Statement kinds, tables, columns, functions, operators and casts are all allowlists. Syntax HaltSQL does not analyze is denied (E_UNSUPPORTED), and so is anything that hits an internal error (E_INTERNAL). Several statements in one string, data-modifying CTEs, SELECT ... INTO, FOR UPDATE and EXPLAIN ANALYZE are always denied. See Policy reference and Reason codes.

With a catalog, yes. When the policy has a catalog: snapshot, HaltSQL expands * to the table's real columns and denies the query (E_COLUMN_DENIED) if any of them is not allowed. Without a catalog, * is allowed only on tables declared with columns: "*", and denied everywhere else. See catalog.

In a limited way, and only when you enable them per table. INSERT ... VALUES with an explicit column list, UPDATE of listed columns and DELETE can be allowed. Tenant rules apply to every write, and a tenant column can never be updated. INSERT ... SELECT and ON CONFLICT are not supported. The MCP server and the agent framework tools run only SELECT. See writes and examples/policies/writes.yaml.
documents.s: Does it support writes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)?

documents.t: @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres was archived on 2025-05-28. It passes the model's string straight to the database, and its read-only guard can be escaped with COMMIT; .... haltsql-mcp keeps the same query(sql) tool and connection string. It also checks each query against your policy first, then runs it read-only with a statement timeout and a row cap, with the tenant fixed by configuration. See the safe drop-in replacement.
documents.s: How is haltsql-mcp different from the archived server-postgres?

documents.t: Every decision produces an audit record with the caller, policy version, decision, reason codes, a SHA-256 of the SQL and its fingerprint. The SQL text itself is not logged unless you set audit.log_raw_sql: true. Records are hash-chained, so haltsql audit verify detects edited, deleted or reordered records. See Audit sinks and Verifying audit chains.
documents.s: Are queries logged, and can logs be trusted?

documents.t: HaltSQL parses with the PostgreSQL 17 grammar (haltsql version prints it). The lab has run its full differential scenario, with zero escapes, on PostgreSQL 17 and 18, Supabase Postgres, AlloyDB Omni, Citus and TimescaleDB. The DDL from haltsql rls generate targets PostgreSQL 13 to 17. Older servers are expected to work for the SQL HaltSQL allows, but that is checked in the lab, not guaranteed. Managed services such as Aurora and Neon have not been run yet. See Database compatibility.
No. HaltSQL is PostgreSQL only, and other dialects are out of scope before 1.0. Amazon Redshift speaks the Postgres wire protocol but is not supported. See Amazon Redshift.
documents.s: Does it work with MySQL, SQL Server or Redshift?

documents.t: On the benchmark machine, a full verdict takes about 50 to 250 µs for realistic agent queries: 48 µs (p50) for a point lookup in the library, and 278 µs for a request to haltsql-server. The proxy adds about 246 µs to a point select. That is well below a database round trip, and far below an LLM call. See Performance, and run the harness on your own hardware before you plan capacity.

There are SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Go and Java, and an HTTP API for anything else. There are tools for the OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, Google ADK, Semantic Kernel and CrewAI (Agent frameworks), integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex and Vanna (Integrations), and an MCP server.
documents.s: Which languages and agent frameworks are supported?

documents.t: Yes, with haltsql-proxy. Clients connect to the proxy as if it were Postgres, and every statement is verified under the policy bound to the client's identity before it is forwarded. The client cannot skip the check or choose its tenant.
documents.s: Can I use it without changing my application?

documents.t: The CLI, haltsql-server and haltsql-proxy come as release binaries, as a container image, or from source with opam. See Quickstart: Install and Deployment. The Python and TypeScript packages are not on PyPI or npm yet. Install them from a clone of the repository, as the tutorials do.

No. haltsql schema pull snapshots your schema, haltsql schema import reads PII labels from dbt, DataHub, Unity Catalog, Atlan or Collibra, and haltsql policy draft writes a starter policy with sensitive-looking columns left out. Review the draft before you use it. See Catalog snapshots, PII metadata and starter policies.
documents.s: Do I have to write policies by hand?

documents.t: Write kind: TestSuite files with SQL that must be allowed or denied, and run haltsql test. The GitHub Action, GitLab templates and pre-commit hooks run the same checks in CI. See Testing, Policy CI and the tutorial Roll out a policy safely.
documents.s: How do I test a policy?

documents.t: Deploy it with mode: shadow. Queries are still allowed, and would-be denials are recorded in the audit log. haltsql report --suggest summarizes them and proposes conservative changes. It never relaxes tenant isolation. Switch to mode: enforce when the results look right. See Shadow reports.
documents.s: How do I roll out a new policy without breaking my agent?

documents.t: haltsql-server reloads policies on file change or SIGHUP, atomically, and keeps the last good set if a reload fails. For production, build a signed bundle in CI. Servers verify its Ed25519 signature before they load it, and can poll an OCI registry, S3 or HTTPS for new versions. See Signed policy bundles.
documents.s: How do policy changes reach production?

documents.t: Yes. A table can have several tenant columns (for example org_id and workspace_id), and a context value can be a set of tenants, such as a parent organization and its children. See Composite keys and Sets of tenant values.
documents.s: Can it handle composite or hierarchical tenants?

documents.t: Yes. haltsql-server can ask Open Policy Agent for a second decision after HaltSQL allows a query. OPA can only deny further, never allow what HaltSQL denied. See Open Policy Agent.
documents.s: Can I add organization-wide rules on top?

documents.t: HaltSQL is 0.0.1, a pre-1.0 preview. The verdict format within haltsql.dev/v1 and the reason codes are stable: reason codes are never renamed or reused. Other interfaces, including the policy schema and the HTTP API, may still change before 1.0. Before 1.0, a minor release may contain breaking changes, and the changelog calls them out. Pin versions, and review the threat model and testing to judge it for your use. See also Stability guarantees.
documents.s: Is HaltSQL production ready? What does pre-1.0 mean?

documents.t: MIT. See LICENSE and ADR-0006. The vendored libpg_query parser has its own license, listed in NOTICE.
Privately, through GitHub Security Advisories. Do not open a public issue. See SECURITY.md.
documents.s: How do I report a vulnerability or a policy bypass?

documents.t: HaltSQL terms in alphabetical order. Each entry links to the page that describes it in full. For questions rather than definitions, see the FAQ. Admin API. Optional haltsql-server endpoints, GET /v1/admin/report and GET /v1/admin/status, for the live shadow report and the server's status. Off by default, and only callers listed in server.admin.callers may use them. See server.admin. Allowlist. Every rule in a policy names what is allowed: statement kinds, tables, columns, functions, operators and casts. Anything not listed is denied. This is also called deny by default. See Policy reference. Audit chain. The hash chain that links audit records. Each record's hash is computed over its content and the previous record's hash (prev_hash), starting from 64 zeros. Editing, deleting, inserting or reordering a record breaks the chain, which haltsql audit verify detects. Each sink keeps its own chain. See Verifying audit chains. Audit record. One JSON line per verification, written by haltsql-server or haltsql-proxy. It holds the caller, policy name and version, decision, reason codes, sql_sha256, fingerprint and timing. It includes the SQL text only with log_raw_sql: true. See Audit sinks. Audit sink. Where audit records go: stdout, a file, S3, GCS, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, or Kafka. With the default on_error: fail_closed, a sink that cannot be written makes the server refuse requests. See Audit sinks. Bind parameters (bind_params). In bound tenancy mode, the list of {param, value} pairs in an allowed verdict: the values your code must bind to $1, $2, ... when it runs the query. Always empty when the query is denied. See Verdict format. Bound tenancy (bound mode). The recommended tenancy mode. The model writes a placeholder (tenant_id = $1), and HaltSQL returns the tenant value to bind from the context. The model never sees or chooses the tenant, and a tenant literal is denied. See Bound mode. Bundle. See Policy bundle. Bundle source. A config entry that makes haltsql-server fetch a signed policy bundle from an OCI registry, S3 or an HTTPS URL, and poll for newer versions. The signature is checked before anything is parsed, and older versions are refused (rollback protection). See Bundle sources. Caller. The authenticated identity that sends a verify request to haltsql-server: a static token's name, an OIDC provider and subject, or an mTLS identity. Every caller is pinned to one policy. See Authentication. Catalog (catalog snapshot). A kind: Catalog document with the complete, typed column list of each table, usually made by haltsql schema pull. A policy that references one can expand SELECT *, resolve columns precisely and type-check tenant literals. See catalog and Catalog snapshots. Composite tenant key. A table scoped by more than one tenancy key, for example org_id and workspace_id. Each tenant column needs its own predicate. See Composite keys. Config. A kind: Config document that controls how haltsql-server and the CLI run: listener, TLS, authentication, which policies to load, audit, telemetry and secrets. It never changes what SQL is allowed. See Config reference. Context. The facts about the caller that a policy may use, such as tenant_id or user_id, sent with each verification. It must come from the caller's authenticated session, a token or an identity, never from the model. See Tenancy and HTTP API. Defense in depth. Using HaltSQL together with a restricted database role and row-level security, so that each layer covers the others' failures. See Defense in depth. Enforce mode. The default policy mode. A query that breaks a rule gets allowed: false, with the reasons in reasons. Compare Shadow mode. See mode. External policy. An optional second decision from Open Policy Agent, asked by haltsql-server after HaltSQL allows a query. It can only deny further (E_EXTERNAL_POLICY). See Open Policy Agent. Fail closed. Any failure ends in "not allowed", never "allowed". Unsupported syntax and internal errors are denials. A client that cannot get a valid verdict does not run the query. A server that cannot write its audit record refuses the request. See Python SDK and Reason codes. Fingerprint. The libpg_query fingerprint of a statement. It is the same for queries that differ only in literal values, which makes it useful for grouping in logs, reports and dashboards. See Verdict format. Global table. A table in a policy with no tenant_column or tenant_columns, such as a reference table of currencies. It needs no tenant predicate. See Tenancy. Guarded execution. Running a model's query only through a helper that verifies it, checks that the verdict is for exactly that string, and then runs it unchanged with the bound parameters, in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement_timeout, transaction-local settings and a row cap. Provided by haltsql.guard in the Python SDK and used by haltsql-mcp and the agent framework tools. See Guarded execution. haltlab. The project's enterprise lab. It builds a realistic database, runs generated and adversarial queries through HaltSQL, and executes every allowed query under database oracles to check that nothing escaped. See Testing. haltsql-mcp. An MCP server, and a drop-in replacement for the archived @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres. It verifies each query with HaltSQL before running it read-only. See haltsql-mcp. Hint. A sentence in a reason that tells the agent how to fix its query, for example which columns it may read. Its text may change between releases; the reason code does not. See Verdict format. Lint (haltsql lint-policy). Checks a policy that loads for risky or suspicious settings, such as columns: "*" (W_BROAD_COLUMNS). Policy CI can fail on lint warnings. See CLI reference. Literal tenancy (literal mode). A tenancy mode where the model writes the tenant value as a literal, which must equal the context value exactly. It means the model must know the tenant ID, so prefer bound mode. See Literal mode. Local mode. Verifying without a sidecar: haltsql-mcp --local-policy and the Python SDK's LocalVerifier run the haltsql CLI with a policy file. See Local mode. Occurrence. Each place a table appears in a FROM clause or join tree. Every occurrence of a tenant-scoped table needs its own tenant predicate. See Tenancy. PII manifest. The output of haltsql schema import: columns labeled as personal or sensitive by a data catalog such as dbt, DataHub, Unity Catalog, Atlan or Collibra. haltsql policy draft leaves those columns out, and haltsql report never suggests adding them. See Catalog snapshots, PII metadata and starter policies. Policy. A kind: Policy document in YAML or JSON that declares what SQL one caller may run: statement kinds, tables and columns, tenancy, functions, limits and mode. Unknown or duplicate keys are errors, so a typo cannot loosen a policy. See Policy reference. Policy bundle. A single canonical JSON file (.haltsqlbundle) holding validated policies and, optionally, catalogs, with an Ed25519 signature in a .sig file. Servers verify the signature before they load it. See Signed policy bundles. Policy draft. A starter policy written by haltsql policy draft from a catalog snapshot and, optionally, a PII manifest. It uses bound tenancy, allows select only, requires a LIMIT and leaves out sensitive-looking columns. Review it before use. See haltsql policy draft. Policy version. The sha256: hash of a normalized policy, reported in every verdict and audit record as policy.version or policy_version. The YAML and JSON forms of a policy have the same version. See Verdict format. Proxy (haltsql-proxy). A PostgreSQL wire-protocol firewall. Clients connect to it as if it were Postgres, and it verifies every statement under the policy and context bound to the client's identity before it forwards the statement. Clients cannot skip the check. See haltsql-proxy. Reason. One entry in a verdict's reasons or shadow_reasons, with a code, a message, the rule, a hint and usually a loc (byte offset in the SQL). See Verdict format. Reason code. The stable, machine-readable identifier of why a query was denied, such as E_TENANT_MISSING or E_COLUMN_DENIED. Codes are never renamed or reused. See Reason codes. RLS generation. haltsql rls generate turns a policy into PostgreSQL DDL: a role, column-level grants and row-level security policies keyed on transaction-local settings. haltsql rls check reports drift. See RLS generation. Rollback protection. A server polling a bundle source accepts a new bundle only if its metadata.version is strictly greater than the current one. To roll back, publish the old policies under a higher version. See What the poller does. Row cap. The maximum number of rows guarded execution returns (max_rows, or --row-cap in haltsql-mcp). It limits what is returned, not what the database computes, so keep require_limit in the policy. See Guarded execution. Scope. One query level: a SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE .... Every CTE body, subquery and UNION branch is its own scope, and a tenant predicate only covers occurrences in its own scope. See Tenancy. search_path. The schemas a policy uses to resolve unqualified table names. Give the database role the same search_path, so that Postgres resolves names the same way HaltSQL checked them. See search_path. Session preamble. What the application runs in the same transaction as an allowed query when RLS is in use: set_config('haltsql.tenant_id', $1, true) with the same context value it sent to HaltSQL. See The session preamble. Shadow mode. A policy mode where every query is allowed, and what would have been denied is reported in shadow_reasons and the audit log. Use it to roll out a new or stricter policy. A shadow policy enforces nothing. See mode. Shadow report. The output of haltsql report (or GET /v1/admin/report): a summary of would-be denials from the audit log, and with --suggest, conservative policy changes that never relax tenant isolation. See Shadow reports. Sidecar (haltsql-server). The HTTP server that exposes verification as POST /v1/verify, usually run next to the agent on 127.0.0.1. It authenticates callers, pins each to a policy, writes audit records and hot-reloads policies. It never connects to the database. See HTTP API and Deployment. Signing key. The Ed25519 private key that signs policy bundles, made with haltsql bundle keygen. Only the public key is distributed to servers, in public_keys. Its key id is the sha256: of the raw public key. See Key management and rotation. SQL hash (sql_sha256). The SHA-256 of the exact SQL string, in every verdict and audit record. Clients check it to make sure a verdict is for the string they will run, and audit logs use it to refer to a query without storing it. See Verdict format. Statement kind. What a statement is: select, insert, update or delete. A policy's statements.allow lists the allowed kinds; anything else is E_STATEMENT_KIND. See statements. Tenancy key. A named dimension of tenancy in tenancy.keys, mapped to a context field, for example tenant: ${ctx.tenant_id}. See Tenancy. Tenant predicate. A condition that filters a tenant-scoped table to the caller's tenant, such as o.tenant_id = $1 in bound mode. It counts only as a top-level AND term of the WHERE or ON clause in the same scope. Under OR, NOT or in HAVING it proves nothing. See The rule. Tenant value. The context value for a tenancy key: one value ("acme") or a set of values (["acme", "acme-eu"]) for hierarchical tenants. See Sets of tenant values. Tenant-scoped table. A table with tenant_column or tenant_columns in the policy. Every occurrence needs a tenant predicate, or the query is denied with E_TENANT_MISSING. See Tenancy. Test suite (kind: TestSuite). A file of SQL cases that a policy must allow or deny, with the expected reason codes or bind parameters, run with haltsql test. See Policy test suites. Token pinning. Every caller of haltsql-server is pinned to exactly one policy, so a compromised agent cannot pick a looser one. A static token or an mTLS identity names its policy. An OIDC token gets it from its provider, or from a claim limited to the provider's allowed_policies. See HTTP API. Verdict. The JSON result of one verification: allowed, reasons, shadow_reasons, the policy name and version, statement kind, tables and columns touched, bind_params, fingerprint and sql_sha256. A denial is a normal verdict, not an error. See Verdict format. Verifier. Anything that turns SQL and a context into a verdict: the library, the CLI, haltsql-server (through an SDK client), LocalVerifier or the Python SDK's in-process NativeVerifier. They all run the same analyzer. See Python SDK.

The analyzer (lib/analyzer) takes one parsed statement, a compiled policy, and a request context, and produces the list of everything that is wrong with the statement. It is deny by default: a statement is allowed only when the analyzer finds no reason to deny it. val analyze : Policy.t -> Context.t -> Ast.stmt -> analysis (* analysis = { reasons; statement_kind; tables; columns; bind_params } *) It runs after parsing (see Parser) inside every verify call (see Verification pipeline).

File Responsibility analyzer.ml Entry point. Dispatches on the statement kind, then runs the end-of-walk checks (join budget, parameter rules) and builds the result. walk.ml The statement walker. Builds scopes level by level, resolves every relation and column, applies the per-node rules, and calls the tenancy prover for each SELECT or DML level. scope.ml Scopes and column-name resolution: what each FROM item is known to contain, and how an unqualified name is matched. rules.ml Context-free rules: statement kinds, functions, SQL value functions, operators, casts, and LIMIT. tenancy.ml Tenant isolation proofs for reads and tenant checks for INSERT values. See Tenancy proof. env.ml The per-call accumulator: reasons, tables, columns, parameters, tenant bindings, and the join count. ast_util.ml, util.ml Small pure helpers (locations, target names, de-duplication, integer normalization).

Env.create makes a fresh accumulator for each analyze call. Rules never return early; they emit reasons into it and the walk continues. The accumulator is never shared between calls or domains, and there is no global mutable state anywhere in the analyzer, so analyze behaves as a pure function from the outside and is safe to run in parallel. analyze wraps everything in an exception handler. If anything raises, the result is a single E_INTERNAL reason with the hint "This is a HaltSQL bug; the statement is denied (fail closed)."

A few properties of the walk: The statement kind check does not stop the walk. A DELETE under a select-only policy gets E_STATEMENT_KIND, and the rest of the statement is still analyzed, so the agent sees every problem in one round. EXPLAIN is unwrapped. If the policy has allow_explain, plain EXPLAIN of an allowed statement is analyzed as that statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and is always E_STATEMENT_KIND. Without allow_explain, EXPLAIN itself is E_STATEMENT_KIND. In both denied cases the inner statement is still analyzed, so its own problems are reported too. Every subquery is walked. CTE bodies, FROM subqueries, EXISTS, IN (SELECT ...), scalar subqueries, ARRAY(SELECT ...), and each arm of a set operation are all walked with the same rules. Every match is exhaustive. Each match over an AST type lists its constructors explicitly, with no wildcard arm. A new AST constructor breaks the build here instead of being silently accepted.

Name resolution is where many SQL firewalls go wrong, so HaltSQL models it explicitly (lib/analyzer/scope.ml). A scope is a stack of levels, innermost first. Each SELECT level, and the target level of an UPDATE, DELETE, or INSERT ... RETURNING, pushes one level holding its FROM items. Each item records: a unique id (one per occurrence, so the same table used twice is two items); the name usable as a qualifier (the alias, or the relation name); what is known about its columns; its source: a policy table (Base), a subquery, CTE, VALUES, or function (Derived), or a relation already reported as denied (Denied).

Knowledge Meaning Example Exact l The item has exactly the columns l. A table with columns: "*" and a catalog snapshot; a derived table whose output HaltSQL computed. At_least l The item has the columns l and maybe others. A policy table without a catalog snapshot; a set-returning function. Tables with an explicit column list are always treated as At_least, even with a catalog, so a stale catalog can never cause a read of a denied column to be attributed to another item.
documents.s: What HaltSQL knows about an item's columns

documents.t: Construct What the walker does FROM a, b Walks the items left to right and pushes one level with all of them. Each comma adds one to the join count. JOIN ... ON Walks left, then right, then the ON condition in a scope that contains both sides. Adds one to the join count. JOIN ... USING (c) records c as a merged column that reads both sides. LATERAL (subquery) The subquery sees the items to its left (the walker pushes the siblings processed so far). Function in FROM Implicitly LATERAL, as in Postgres. Its output is At_least its alias, column aliases, and function name. Subquery in FROM Walked in the enclosing scope (without siblings unless LATERAL). Becomes a Derived item whose columns are the subquery's output. WITH Each CTE is walked in order; later CTEs and the main query see earlier ones. A CTE name shadows a table of the same name, as in Postgres. Subquery in an expression Walked with the current scope stack, so a correlated reference to an outer column resolves to the enclosing level. Set operations Each arm is walked independently. The output columns come from the left arm. ORDER BY on the result sees only output columns.

This query (run against examples/policies/saas.yaml) uses a CTE, a join, and a correlated EXISTS: WITH recent AS ( SELECT o.id, o.customer_id FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND o.created_at > now() - interval '7 days' ) SELECT c.name, r.id FROM recent r JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invoices i WHERE i.order_id = r.id) LIMIT 50 The actual verdict denies it with two reasons, one per unproven occurrence: [ { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "rule": "tenancy.predicate", "loc": 229, "message": "app.invoices (as i) has no provable tenant predicate on i.tenant_id in the same SELECT" }, { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "rule": "tenancy.predicate", "loc": 165, "message": "app.customers (as c) has no provable tenant predicate on c.tenant_id in the same SELECT" } ] The tenant filter on orders inside the CTE does not cover customers or invoices: every occurrence of a tenant-scoped table needs its own proof in its own level. Adding AND c.tenant_id = $1 to the ON clause and AND i.tenant_id = $1 to the EXISTS makes the query allowed, with bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": "acme"}]. The full proof rules are in Tenancy proof and tenancy.md.

Postgres guarantees that an unqualified name that runs successfully matches exactly one item at the innermost level that has it. HaltSQL mirrors that, but never guesses: Qualified names (t.c, s.t.c) look up the item by name at the innermost level that has it. A bare name that matches no column but does match an item name is a whole-row reference, which reads every column of that item.
analyzer.ml labels the rule families A to M. Each one lives in a specific module.

SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must be listed in statements.allow (Rules.check_stmt_kind). Every other statement node (DDL, DO, CALL, COPY, SET, ...) is E_STATEMENT_KIND. EXPLAIN needs allow_explain, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE is never allowed.

FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, and the other locking clauses: E_LOCKING_CLAUSE. SELECT ... INTO: E_SELECT_INTO (it creates a table). WITH RECURSIVE: E_UNSUPPORTED. Recursion cannot be bounded by LIMIT, and an outer LIMIT does not bound the work of an aggregate, ORDER BY, or DISTINCT over it. The body is still analyzed so other problems are reported. Any Unsupported node from the parser: E_UNSUPPORTED. The walker also denies some mapped constructs it does not analyze: NATURAL JOIN (its column set depends on the schema), an alias on a JOIN, a column alias list on a base table, and sublink kinds other than EXISTS, ANY, ALL, scalar, and ARRAY.

When the policy sets require_limit.max, the outermost SELECT must have a constant integer LIMIT between 0 and the maximum (Rules.check_limit). Situation Code No LIMIT, LIMIT ALL, or LIMIT NULL E_LIMIT_REQUIRED LIMIT larger than the maximum, negative, or not an integer constant E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH Casts around the constant are looked through (LIMIT 10::int is fine). Subqueries do not need their own LIMIT.

Tables (E_TABLE_DENIED). A schema-qualified name must match a policy table exactly. An unqualified name walks the policy's search_path, with pg_catalog searched first unless the policy places it explicitly: a name starting with pg_ that is not a policy table resolves to the system catalog and is denied; a policy table in a later schema wins only if every earlier schema is known (from a trusted catalog snapshot) not to contain a relation with that name. Otherwise Postgres might resolve the name to something unlisted, so HaltSQL denies and asks for a schema-qualified name. A denied relation still becomes a Denied item in the scope, so column references to it do not produce a pile of confusing follow-up errors. Columns (E_COLUMN_DENIED). Every column read is checked against the table's columns list, wherever it appears: select list, WHERE, JOIN ... ON, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, window definitions, and RETURNING. * and whole-row references. SELECT *, t.*, and a bare t read every column of the item. HaltSQL needs to know every column to allow that: Table columns Catalog snapshot * result "*" (all) yes allowed; each column recorded "*" (all) no allowed; recorded as schema.table.* explicit list yes allowed only if every catalog column is in the list explicit list no E_COLUMN_DENIED A catalog entry counts only if it is trusted: at least one column carries a type, as snapshots from haltsql schema pull always do. When a policy has no snapshot, the loader derives untyped entries from the policy's own column lists, and those prove nothing about the real table, so they are ignored. This is what stops SELECT * from leaking a column the policy left out. Unresolvable references (E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED). Ambiguous names, unknown names, too many qualifiers (cross-database references), and names that could be either a column or a whole-row reference to a sensitive table are all denied.
documents.s: D and E: tables and columns

documents.t: Rule Check Code F Function names must be in the policy's expanded function list. Unqualified and pg_catalog. names match by bare name; any other schema must be listed as schema.fn. E_FUNCTION_DENIED F SQL value functions: only CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIME, and LOCALTIMESTAMP. Identity and session values (CURRENT_USER, SESSION_USER, CURRENT_SCHEMA, ...) are denied. E_FUNCTION_DENIED G Operators (including ANY/ALL, IN, LIKE, ILIKE, SIMILAR TO) must be in the operator list. An operator qualified with a schema other than pg_catalog is always denied. Built-in syntax such as BETWEEN, IS DISTINCT FROM, and NULLIF is not an operator lookup. E_OPERATOR_DENIED H A cast whose target type is not in casts (deny by default), or is in deny_casts, such as regclass. E_CAST_DENIED
documents.s: F, G, H: functions, operators, casts

documents.t: The walker counts joins across the whole statement, including subqueries and CTEs: each JOIN counts one, a FROM list of n items counts n - 1, and UPDATE ... FROM and DELETE ... USING count one per item. After the walk, a count above limits.max_joins (default 8) is E_JOIN_BUDGET.

HaltSQL only allows a $n placeholder when it can supply the value itself in bind_params, so the caller never binds something the model chose. The walker records every $n it sees, with its location. The tenancy prover records a binding each time a $n is the value side of a successful tenant proof. After the walk, finalize applies four checks: Conflicting bindings. If the same $n would have to be bound to two different tenant values, E_TENANT_MISMATCH (tenancy.param_conflict). Unbound parameters. A $n with no binding is E_PARAM_UNBOUND (params.unbound). In literal tenancy mode, every placeholder is unbound. Tenant placeholder used elsewhere. A tenant placeholder may appear only as the value of its tenant predicate.
