If $1 is bound by o.tenant_id = $1 but also appears anywhere else, for example $1::float8 IS NOT NULL, that is E_PARAM_UNBOUND (params.tenant_reuse), reported once per parameter. Any other use would let the query influence the type PostgreSQL infers for the parameter, and with it how the bound tenant value is compared. The surviving bindings become bind_params, sorted by parameter number. The check in step 3 compares locations: a $n occurrence is fine only if its exact location is one that a tenant proof used. A real verdict: { "code": "E_PARAM_UNBOUND", "message": "tenant placeholder $1 is used outside a tenant predicate; it may only appear as the value of the tenant comparison", "rule": "params.tenant_reuse", "loc": 53, "hint": "Use each tenant placeholder only in its tenant predicate (e.g. o.tenant_id = $1); do not cast it or compare it to anything else." } for SELECT o.id FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND $1::float8 IS NOT NULL LIMIT 10.

For every occurrence of a tenant-scoped table, in its own level, each tenant column must be proven by a top-level AND conjunct of the level's WHERE or of an eligible JOIN ... ON. The context must supply the tenant value (E_CONTEXT_MISSING otherwise, reported once per tenancy key). A literal that differs from the context is E_TENANT_MISMATCH; no proof at all is E_TENANT_MISSING. This is the most important rule and has its own page: Tenancy proof.
A CTE containing INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE whose kind is not in statements.allow is E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE. If the kind is allowed, the CTE is analyzed with the write rules below.

Only reachable when the policy allows the statement kind. Check Code The target table lacks the matching writes permission (insert, update, delete) E_WRITE_DENIED (writes.table) INSERT without an explicit column list E_WRITE_DENIED (writes.columns) INSERT names a column not in the table's columns list E_WRITE_DENIED UPDATE assigns a column not in writes.update E_WRITE_DENIED INSERT into a tenant table does not set every tenant column to the tenant value in every VALUES row, or uses DEFAULT VALUES E_TENANT_WRITE (tenancy.write) UPDATE assigns a tenant column E_TENANT_WRITE INSERT ... SELECT, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT E_UNSUPPORTED (only INSERT ... VALUES is analyzed) UPDATE and DELETE also go through the normal tenancy proof (Rule K), with their target table and any FROM or USING items in the same level.

The rule field of each reason names the check that produced it. Codes are stable (see reason-codes.md); rule ids are for debugging and may change. Family rule Code Emitted in (parse) parse E_PARSE, E_LIMIT, E_INTERNAL lib/parse/pg_parse.ml (count) statement.count E_EMPTY, E_MULTI_STATEMENT lib/haltsql/haltsql.ml A statement.kind E_STATEMENT_KIND rules.ml, analyzer.ml A statement.explain E_STATEMENT_KIND analyzer.ml B select.locking E_LOCKING_CLAUSE walk.ml B select.into E_SELECT_INTO walk.ml B syntax.unsupported E_UNSUPPORTED walk.ml, analyzer.ml B syntax.recursive_cte E_UNSUPPORTED walk.ml C limit.required E_LIMIT_REQUIRED rules.ml C limit.max E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH rules.ml D tables.allowlist E_TABLE_DENIED walk.ml D columns.resolve E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED walk.ml E columns.denied E_COLUMN_DENIED walk.ml E columns.star E_COLUMN_DENIED walk.ml F functions.allowlist E_FUNCTION_DENIED rules.ml F functions.sql_value E_FUNCTION_DENIED rules.ml G operators.allowlist E_OPERATOR_DENIED rules.ml H casts.allowlist, casts.deny E_CAST_DENIED rules.ml I joins.budget E_JOIN_BUDGET analyzer.ml J params.unbound E_PARAM_UNBOUND analyzer.ml J params.tenant_reuse E_PARAM_UNBOUND analyzer.ml J tenancy.param_conflict E_TENANT_MISMATCH analyzer.ml K tenancy.predicate E_TENANT_MISSING tenancy.ml K tenancy.mismatch E_TENANT_MISMATCH tenancy.ml K tenancy.context E_CONTEXT_MISSING tenancy.ml L statement.data_modifying_cte E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE walk.ml M writes.table E_WRITE_DENIED walk.ml M writes.columns E_WRITE_DENIED walk.ml M tenancy.write E_TENANT_WRITE walk.ml, tenancy.ml (guard) internal E_INTERNAL analyzer.ml, haltsql.ml

All violations are reported. Rules emit and keep going. One verdict can carry many reasons, so an agent can fix everything in a single retry. Order is emission order. Reasons come out in the order the walk found them, then the end-of-walk checks (join budget, parameters). The walk is deterministic, so the order is too. Identical reasons are de-duplicated. Two reasons are dropped as duplicates only when every field matches (code, message, rule, location, and hint), keeping the first. Distinct problems with the same code, such as two different tables missing a tenant predicate, are kept separately. Some reasons are reported once by design. E_CONTEXT_MISSING is reported once per tenancy key, and params.tenant_reuse once per parameter, so a single root cause does not flood the verdict. tables and columns are recorded as they are resolved, then sorted and de-duplicated. They may be partial for a denied query. A real example with several reasons at once (policy examples/policies/saas.yaml): SELECT email, pg_sleep(1) FROM customers FOR UPDATE Order Code Why 1 E_LOCKING_CLAUSE FOR UPDATE (checked as soon as the SELECT is entered, after its WITH clause) 2 E_LIMIT_REQUIRED outermost SELECT has no LIMIT 3 E_COLUMN_DENIED email is not in the readable columns of app.customers 4 E_FUNCTION_DENIED pg_sleep is not in the function allowlist 5 E_TENANT_MISSING customers has no tenant predicate What the analyzer returns then goes back to verify, which applies the policy mode and builds the verdict. See Verification pipeline.

HaltSQL answers one question: may this caller run this exact SQL string? It takes three inputs (a SQL string, a compiled policy, and a request context) and returns a verdict. Everything else in the repository is a way to load those inputs, deliver that answer, or act on it. This page is the map. The other pages in this section zoom in: Page What it covers Verification pipeline One verify call, end to end Parser libpg_query, the worker pool, and the typed AST Analyzer Scopes, rule families, and how reasons are collected Tenancy proof What HaltSQL must prove before it touches a tenant table Policies and config How documents become a compiled policy Deployment modes Library, CLI, sidecar, and proxy side by side Proxy internals The PostgreSQL wire-protocol firewall Server internals The HTTP sidecar Policy lifecycle Drafting, testing, signing, and rolling out policies Assurance How the guarantees are tested

Haltsql.verify is a pure function of its three inputs. It does not open a socket, read a file, or look at the clock except to report elapsed_us. That is what makes it cheap to embed, easy to test, and safe to run in parallel.
The repository is an OCaml (dune) monorepo. Libraries live in lib/, executables in bin/, and client code in clients/ and integrations/.

These libraries are all you need to verify SQL. None of them does network I/O. Component Library name Role lib/core haltsql.core Shared types: Ast (the typed SQL AST), Policy (compiled policy), Context, Catalog, Reason (stable reason codes), Verdict (result and its JSON form). Depends only on yojson. lib/pgquery haltsql.pgquery Thin C binding to the vendored libpg_query (Postgres 17 grammar). Parse to JSON and fingerprint, on a pool of big-stack worker threads. See Parser. lib/parse haltsql.parse Pg_parse: size and depth limits, then converts libpg_query's JSON into the typed Ast, failing closed on anything it does not map. lib/analyzer haltsql.analyzer Applies the policy to one Ast.stmt: scopes and name resolution, the rule families, and tenancy proofs. Depends only on haltsql.core. See Analyzer. lib/load haltsql.load Reads YAML or JSON documents (Policy, Config, Catalog, TestSuite), validates them, and compiles a Policy.t with its sha256: version. See Policies and config. lib/haltsql haltsql The public facade. Re-exports the modules above and defines verify (in lib/haltsql/haltsql.ml) plus Suite_runner for policy test suites. Notice what the analyzer does not depend on: the parser. It only ever sees the typed AST. That keeps the rule code independent of libpg_query's JSON shape.

Component Binary Role bin/haltsql haltsql The CLI: verify, explain, validate, convert, schema, test, config show, version, lint-policy, policy draft, rls, bundle. See cli.md. bin/server (+ bin/server/lib) haltsql-server HTTP sidecar: POST /v1/verify, GET /v1/policies, health, readiness, and /metrics. Adds authentication, audit, and telemetry around Haltsql.verify. See Server internals and http-api.md. bin/proxy + lib/pgwire haltsql-proxy PostgreSQL wire-protocol (v3) firewall. Clients connect to it as if it were Postgres; every simple Query and every Parse goes through Haltsql.verify, and the proxy binds tenancy parameters itself. See Proxy internals and proxy.md.

Component Library name Used by Role lib/auth haltsql-server.auth server Caller authentication: JWT/JWK, OIDC discovery and JWKS caching, mTLS identities, and merging the authenticated context with the request body context. lib/telemetry haltsql-server.telemetry server OpenTelemetry (OTLP/HTTP JSON) exporter for traces and metrics, with a bounded non-blocking queue. lib/cloud haltsql.cloud CLI, server Audit hash chain, S3 and GCS audit sinks, and secret resolvers for Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and GCP Secret Manager. lib/bundle haltsql.bundle CLI, server Signed policy bundles: canonical JSON, Ed25519 signatures, digest checks. See policy-bundles.md. lib/rlsgen haltsql.rlsgen CLI Generates role, grant, and row-level-security DDL that mirrors a policy, and checks a live database for drift. See rls-generation.md. lib/catalog_tools haltsql.catalog_tools CLI Catalog snapshots from a live Postgres (schema pull), PII metadata importers, and the starter policy drafter. See schema-and-pii.md.

Directory What it is clients/python Python SDK: sync and async clients, guarded execution for psycopg 3, asyncpg and SQLAlchemy, and a local CLI verifier. clients/typescript @haltsql/client for Node.js, with guardedTransaction and guardedQuery for node-postgres. clients/go Go client with GuardedQueryTx and GuardedQuery for database/sql. clients/java com.haltsql:haltsql-client with JdbcGuard for PgJDBC. clients/mcp haltsql-mcp, a Model Context Protocol server that gives an agent verified, read-only SQL access. clients/testvectors Shared request and verdict vectors that every client is tested against. integrations/langchain, integrations/llamaindex, integrations/vanna Agent framework wrappers built on the Python SDK. The clients talk to haltsql-server over HTTP. They all follow the same rules: fail closed, check that the verdict's sql_sha256 matches the SQL they sent, and execute exactly the verified string with bind_params. See integrations.md.

The arrows point from a component to what it depends on (taken from the dune files). Two things this graph guarantees: The core has no network code. haltsql.core, haltsql.parse, haltsql.analyzer, and haltsql.load pull in no HTTP or TLS libraries. Network code lives in the supporting libraries, which the core never imports. Every surface uses the same verifier. The CLI, the sidecar, and the proxy all call the same Haltsql.verify. A policy that passes haltsql test in CI behaves the same way in the sidecar and the proxy.
HaltSQL sits between the code that produces SQL (an LLM agent) and the code that runs it. There are two ways to place it.
documents.s: Where HaltSQL sits in your stack

documents.t: Your application asks HaltSQL, then acts on the answer. This is the most common setup. The context (for example tenant_id) comes from your authenticated session, never from the model. The SDKs implement this loop for you.

When you cannot change the code that runs the SQL (a BI tool, an unmodified driver), put haltsql-proxy in front of the database. The proxy authenticates each client, maps it to a policy and context, verifies every statement, and only forwards what is allowed. In both setups, run the SQL as a restricted database role with row-level security as a second layer. haltsql rls generate can produce that DDL from the same policy. See defense-in-depth.md and Deployment modes.

HaltSQL returns allow or deny. It never adds a WHERE clause, injects a LIMIT, or rewrites a table name. A rewriter would have to be correct for every query it touches, and a subtle bug would silently change what runs. A verifier only has to be correct about what it allows, and its mistakes show up as visible denials. The caller runs the exact string that was verified, and sql_sha256 in the verdict lets anyone check that. (The proxy fills in tenancy parameter values at Bind time, using the values from the verdict. It does not change the SQL text.)

Verification uses only the policy, the optional catalog snapshot inside it, and the context. There is no round trip to Postgres. That keeps latency in microseconds, keeps the verifier free of database credentials, and makes a verdict reproducible offline. Schema knowledge comes from a snapshot taken ahead of time by haltsql schema pull and committed next to the policy. The tools that do talk to a database (schema pull, rls check, and the proxy's upstream connection) are separate from the verification path.
documents.s: It never connects to the database to verify

documents.t: Anything HaltSQL does not fully understand is denied: SQL the converter does not map becomes an explicit Unsupported node, which the analyzer denies with E_UNSUPPORTED. See Parser. A statement kind outside the policy is E_STATEMENT_KIND. A column it cannot resolve unambiguously is E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED. It never guesses. Any exception inside verify becomes a single E_INTERNAL denial. verify is total: it always returns a verdict. Rule code matches AST constructors without wildcard arms, so adding a construct to the AST is a compile error until every rule handles it. See ADR-0002.

Every denial carries one or more reasons with a machine-readable code such as E_TENANT_MISSING. Codes are part of the public API: never renamed, never reused. Messages and hints can improve between releases; codes cannot. Agents and dashboards match on code. See reason-codes.md and ADR-0004.

For the same SQL, policy, and context, allowed, the reason codes, tables, columns, and bind_params are always the same. The analyzer keeps all its state in a per-call accumulator (lib/analyzer/env.ml) and has no global mutable state, so parallel calls cannot interfere. Only elapsed_us varies. The policy's version is a content hash, so a logged verdict names exactly the policy that produced it.

HaltSQL parses with libpg_query, which is the actual PostgreSQL grammar extracted into a C library. A hand-written grammar would drift from the server, and any difference between how HaltSQL and Postgres read a string is a potential bypass. See ADR-0001.
documents.s: It uses the real Postgres parser

documents.t: A firewall is only useful if you can trust what it allows. HaltSQL is tested in layers, and each layer answers a different question. The most important one, the haltlab enterprise lab, does not trust HaltSQL at all: it runs every query HaltSQL allows against a real database and lets the database decide whether the query was safe. For writing tests for your own policies, see testing.md and policy-lifecycle.md.

The arrows show the direction of increasing realism. Unit tests are fast and precise. The lab is slow but answers the question that matters: did anything actually leak? As of this writing there are about 3,300 OCaml test cases across 19 Alcotest suites (one per test/*/test_*.ml executable plus the corpus runner), together with the fuzzer smoke run. Exact counts change with every change.

Each OCaml library has its own suite under test/: Directory Covers test/pgquery, test/parse The libpg_query bridge and the conversion to the typed AST test/analyzer Every rule family, with positive and negative cases, against the fixture policies in test/fixtures/policies/ test/load YAML/JSON reading, typing, positions, policy and config decoding test/auth, test/cloud, test/telemetry JWT/OIDC/mTLS, secret providers and object sinks (with fake HTTP), OTLP export test/bundle Bundle build, signing and every verification step, including tampered bytes, wrong keys and non-canonical encodings test/catalog_tools, test/rlsgen Schema pull, PII import, policy draft, RLS generation (unit, golden and live)

The attack corpus (test/corpus/) is a set of TestSuite files, one per threat class: statement smuggling, data-modifying CTEs, side-effect functions, system catalogs, identifier confusion, comments and quoting, casts, resource limits, writes, and one file per tenancy shape (tenancy_joins, tenancy_scoping, tenancy_setops, tenancy_subqueries, tenancy_sets, and more). It has roughly 40 suite files and more than 1,200 cases. Every fixed bypass gets a case so it cannot come back. test/conformance/ ports the test cases of the MIT-licensed sql-guardrail project: 487 cases (180 allow, 307 deny), each tagged with its source test. Intentional differences are tagged (differs, differs-code) rather than hidden. See test/conformance/README.md. Both directories are run by one runner, test/runner/corpus.ml. It discovers every *.suite.yaml and *.suite.json, runs each case through Haltsql.verify, prints a summary per threat class, and reports one Alcotest case per corpus case. Because suites are ordinary TestSuite documents, a corpus case looks exactly like a test a user would write.

test/property/test_property.ml uses QCheck over the saas fixture policy: Safe generator. Random queries with a correct tenant predicate on every occurrence, allowed columns and functions, and a constant LIMIT. They must be allowed with bind_params = [(1, tenant)]. Evasion transforms. Meaning-preserving transforms (CTE or derived-table wrapping, case, quoting, U&"" escapes, comments, schema qualification, filtered UNION branches) must keep the query allowed. Isolation-breaking transforms must deny it with the expected code. Determinism. Verifying twice gives identical verdict JSON (apart from elapsed_us), and the YAML policy and its JSON twin give identical verdicts, including policy_version. Totality. Random bytes and SQL token soup never raise, and any denial uses only known reason codes, never E_INTERNAL. The seed is fixed (default 20261107) and printed, so a failure can be replayed. HALTSQL_QCHECK_SEED and HALTSQL_QCHECK_COUNT override it.

test/golden/test_golden.ml checks the full verdict JSON (minus elapsed_us) for a set of representative queries against snapshots in test/golden/expected/. Any change to a message, hint, location or field shows up as a diff in review. HALTSQL_GOLDEN_UPDATE=1 rewrites the snapshots deliberately.

test/fuzz/fuzz.ml is a mutation fuzzer. Its seeds are every SQL string in the corpus and conformance suites, plus the text of every policy, suite and catalog document. Each iteration applies 1 to 8 random mutations (bit flips, insertions, splicing, SQL-token insertion, truncation, deep nesting) and checks: Haltsql.verify never raises; a denial has at least one reason, every code is a known code, and never E_INTERNAL; an allowed verdict has no reasons; each verify takes under 2 seconds; the YAML and JSON readers and the policy loader never raise. dune test runs a short pass (3,000 iterations by default). Long runs use HALTSQL_FUZZ_ITERS. A failing input is minimized and written to test/fuzz/crashes/.

Suite What it drives test/cli/test_cli.ml The built haltsql binary: commands, exit codes, JSON output test/server/ haltsql-server in process and as a subprocess: HTTP API, auth end to end, signals, reload, integrations test/proxy/test_pgwire_unit.ml Wire-protocol parsing and proxy state, without a database test/proxy/test_proxy_integration.ml The haltsql-proxy binary against Postgres 17, with a real driver (psycopg) and a raw protocol client test/rlsgen/t_integration.ml Applies generated RLS to a live database twice (idempotence), checks isolation as the generated role, and checks that rls check finds exactly the injected drift Tests that need Postgres skip cleanly when it is not reachable, so dune test works on a laptop. CI runs them with a Postgres service.
lab/ is a Python harness (see lab/README.md in the repository). It is kept outside the OCaml build on purpose: the verifier under test and the judge share no code.
documents.s: haltlab: the database is the judge

documents.t: The fixtures are synthetic but shaped like real systems: saas_shared (shared tables keyed by tenant_id, PII columns, a global table), composite (org_id, workspace_id), hierarchical (a parent sees a list of child tenants), and erp_large (400+ generated tables across 12 schemas, quoted and reserved-word names, partitions, views). The data includes look-alike tenants such as ACME, acme with a trailing space, a Cyrillic а, and zero-width spaces, plus NULL and empty tenant rows. The adversarial workload applies evasion transforms from lab/generators/evasion.py (wrap in a CTE, add an OR true, add an unfiltered UNION branch, and many more). Every escaping query is written out as a ready-to-use TestSuite case, so lab findings flow straight into the attack corpus.

Each allowed query runs inside one REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction that is always rolled back (check_item in lab/harness/oracles.py). The tenancy settings that the fixture's RLS policies read (app.<context field>) are set with set_config(..., true), and the query is run under three roles: Role Property Used to detect haltlab_owner Owns the tables, not subject to RLS. What production would return. Reference result, honeytokens, side effects haltlab_rls NOBYPASSRLS, filtered by RLS to the caller's tenancy Rows the owner saw that RLS hides haltlab_cols SELECT only on the policy's allowed columns Allowed queries that read a denied column Why each oracle exists: RLS differential. Repeatable read gives all runs the same snapshot, so a legitimate query returns the same multiset of rows as owner and as the RLS role. Any extra row the owner sees is another tenant's row. The comparison is a multiset difference, so duplicates count. Honeytokens. Every tenant's rows carry unique markers (HT-<tenant>-<table>-<n>), and so does every column the policy denies (HTCOL-<table>-<column>-<n>). Finding one in the output is proof of a leak, even through aggregates or string functions that RLS comparison might not explain. Column privileges. If Postgres raises "permission denied" for a role that can only read the allowed columns, HaltSQL allowed a column it should not have. Side effects. A read-only transaction turns writes into SQLSTATE 25006. Settings are compared before and after. A query that ends the harness transaction, or leaves a session-level advisory lock (which survives ROLLBACK), is flagged. Timeouts. A query that exceeds statement_timeout (2 seconds by default) is resource abuse. Only RLS, honeytoken and column findings count as escapes. Errors that are none of the above, such as a query the generator built wrongly, are counted as execution errors.
documents.s: The oracles for one allowed query

documents.t: An oracle that never fires looks exactly like a firewall that never leaks. So the lab tests its own oracles. lab/harness/fake_verifier.py is a stand-in for haltsql verify --batch that allows everything and binds $n to the tenancy context values. Run against the adversarial workload, it must leak. lab/tests/test_integration.py asserts that, with the allow-everything verifier, the run reports more than 50 escapes, at least one column leak and at least one side effect. It also checks per transform: leaky ones (union_unfiltered_branch, or_true, left_join_preserved_side, star_over_pii) must produce escapes, and meaning-preserving ones (wrap_cte, wrap_subquery, quoted_identifiers, explain_plain) must not, so the oracles are not just flagging everything. Finally, a corpus file must be written. A second test uses a deny-everything verifier and asserts that nothing is executed. A third runs the real haltsql binary through the smoke scenario and asserts that it passes. make selftest runs scenarios/oracle-selftest.yaml --fake-verifier allow by hand.
documents.s: Testing the judge: the oracle self-test

documents.t: lab/proxy/ runs the same scenarios through a live haltsql-proxy. It sends every query with another tenant's ID in each tenancy parameter, and checks that the proxy's decision equals the CLI verdict, that allowed queries return the same rows as the SQL run directly with the CLI's bind_params, and that no foreign honeytoken appears. See proxy-internals.md.

Workflow When What .github/workflows/ci.yml Pushes to main, every PR, and on demand Formatting first. One test run of the whole suite with coverage, Postgres 17 and Helm (OCaml 5.2); one OCaml 5.4 build of the tree whose binaries the Python, TypeScript and action jobs reuse; the OS and OCaml grid on main (on a PR, macOS only, and only for changes to C stubs, the vendored parser, the native library or build files); Go and Java SDK jobs. On a PR each job runs only when the files it covers changed (.github/scripts/changes.sh); the CI ok check sums up the run .github/workflows/integration.yml Pushes to main, every PR, nightly, and on demand Docker-based OCaml suites and the end-to-end suite (on a PR: only when the server, the proxy, a library that talks to an outside service, or the suite itself changed), the operator and Terraform checks; the kind and Postgres-flavour jobs nightly. The nightly skips itself when main has not changed since the last one; the Integration ok check sums up the run .github/workflows/lab.yml Nightly (skipped when main has not changed), on PRs touching the engine, the proxy, lab/ or the workflow, and on demand Lab unit tests, the oracle self-test, scenarios (pr-smoke on PRs, the nightly set and the version matrix on schedule), proxy parity and proxy integration tests; reports uploaded as artifacts .github/workflows/build-images.yml, native-packages.yml PRs that change how images, wheels or npm packages are built; every push to main (packages); on demand Multi-architecture image builds with smoke tests and the benchmark gate; wheels and npm packages for every platform .github/workflows/security.yml Every PR, weekly (Mondays), and on demand Dependency review, Trivy image and configuration scans .github/workflows/pages.yml Pushes to main and PRs touching docs/ or website/, and on demand Builds this docs site; from main, publishes the build to the public HaltSQL/haltsql.github.io repository, which GitHub Pages serves .github/workflows/release.yml v* tags, and on demand for an existing tag Release build and artifacts

Binaries are built once per state of the OCaml sources. .github/actions/haltsql-binaries caches haltsql, haltsql-server, haltsql-proxy and libhaltsql.so under a hash of lib/, bin/, native/, vendor/ and the build files. Every job that only uses the binaries (SDKs, the action self-test, the end-to-end suite, the operator tests) restores them and installs no OCaml toolchain. A pull request that touches only an SDK builds no OCaml at all. One test run per pull request. The coverage job is the test run: the whole suite, with Postgres and Helm so nothing skips. The OS and compiler grid runs on main. Expensive jobs follow the files. macOS, the Docker-based suites, the end-to-end suite, image builds and native packaging each run on a pull request only when the change can affect them (changes.sh lists the areas). Everything runs on main and in the nightly, so a wrong guess is caught within a day, not shipped. Nothing runs twice for nothing. Superseded runs are cancelled, and the nightlies skip themselves when main has not moved. When you add a job that needs a binary, use the action instead of setting up OCaml; when you add an expensive job, give it an area in changes.sh.
tenancy-proof.md explains the rules most of these tests exercise. threat-model.md lists the threats the corpus classes map to.

HaltSQL has one verification core, Haltsql.verify policy context sql, and four ways to reach it. They differ in where the check runs, who binds the tenant values, where the context comes from, and whether the application can skip the check. Mode Binary or package Who enforces the verdict Embedded library / CLI haltsql OCaml library, haltsql CLI (bin/haltsql) Your code HTTP sidecar haltsql-server (bin/server) Your code (the server only answers) Wire proxy haltsql-proxy (bin/proxy, lib/pgwire) The proxy itself SDKs and MCP clients/*, integrations/* (on top of the sidecar or the CLI) The SDK's guarded-execute helper The first two modes answer the question "is this SQL allowed?". The caller must act on the answer. The proxy enforces the answer: the SQL never reaches the database unless it was verified. The SDKs sit in between: they enforce the answer for you, as long as your code goes through them.

The context (tenant id, user id, and so on) decides which rows a query may touch. It must come from something the model cannot influence: the authenticated session, a verified token, a client certificate, or a config file. It must never come from the prompt, from a tool argument the model fills in, or from the generated SQL. If the model could set the context, a bound tenancy policy would prove the query is scoped to whatever tenant the model chose. See tenancy-proof.md for what the proof covers. Each mode has its own trusted source of context: Mode Context comes from Library / CLI The Context.t your code builds, or --context / --context-file Sidecar, static token The request body's context (the calling service is trusted to fill it from its session) Sidecar, OIDC context_claims of the verified JWT, plus only the body fields in request_context_fields Sidecar, mTLS The identity's static context, plus only the body fields in request_context_fields Proxy The context of the SCRAM user or certificate identity in the proxy config MCP server HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT / --context-file (stdio) or the tokens file (HTTP); never a tool argument
documents.s: The rule that applies to every mode

documents.t: The OCaml library runs the whole pipeline in your process: parse with the vendored libpg_query, convert to the typed AST, analyze against the policy, return a verdict. There is no network hop and no extra process. The haltsql CLI wraps the same call. haltsql verify exits 0 when the query is allowed, 1 when it is denied, and 2 when the policy, context or input cannot be loaded (see ../cli.md). With --batch it reads JSON lines on stdin and writes one verdict per line, which is how the Python LocalVerifier (clients/python/src/haltsql/local.py) uses it. Your code owns every step after the verdict: refusing a denied query, running exactly the verified string, and binding bind_params as positional $n parameters. Nothing stops buggy code from running the SQL anyway, so wrap the call in one helper and use only that helper.

haltsql-server exposes POST /v1/verify (see ../http-api.md). The agent sends the SQL, and the server returns the same verdict JSON the library produces. The server never connects to a database. Trust boundaries in this mode: The server trusts its config: policies, token hashes, OIDC providers, mTLS identities. Each caller is pinned to exactly one policy, so it cannot ask for a looser one (403 FORBIDDEN). The agent is trusted to run only allowed SQL and to bind the values from bind_params. A compromised agent can still skip the check. That is why the database-side controls in ../defense-in-depth.md (a restricted role, row-level security) still matter. A denial is a normal 200 response with allowed: false. Any non-200 status, timeout or connection error must be treated as a denial. How the server works inside is described in server-internals.md.

The recommended shape is one haltsql-server container per agent pod. The agent calls http://127.0.0.1:8080, so verification traffic never leaves the pod. deploy/k8s/sidecar-example.yaml and ../deployment.md show the full manifests. Points worth knowing: Tokens are required even inside the pod, so a neighbor that reaches the port still cannot verify against a policy it holds no token for. ConfigMaps mounted with subPath are not updated in running pods. Mount the ConfigMap as a directory if you rely on reload.watch, or roll the deployment on policy changes. The Helm chart in deploy/helm/haltsql deploys the other shape: a shared haltsql-server Deployment behind a Service, with a PodDisruptionBudget, HPA, NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.ingressFrom) and ServiceMonitor. Use it when many agents share central policy management. Then turn on built-in TLS (tls.enabled) or terminate TLS in front of it, and pin every token or identity to its policy.

haltsql-proxy speaks the PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol. Clients connect to it as if it were Postgres. It authenticates them (SCRAM-SHA-256 or a TLS client certificate), connects upstream with its own service credentials, verifies every Query and Parse, and overwrites tenancy parameters in every Bind. What changes compared to the sidecar: No application changes beyond the connection string. Drivers that cannot be modified still get enforcement. The client never sees the database credentials and cannot pick its policy or its tenant. The context is bound to the proxy user in the config. The proxy binds tenant values. Whatever the client sends for a tenancy parameter is replaced with the session's context value. Queries that need bound tenancy parameters must use the extended protocol (prepared statements). Over the simple protocol they are denied with E_PARAM_UNBOUND, because there is no Bind message to rewrite. A denial arrives as an ordinary PostgreSQL ERROR (SQLSTATE 42501 by default), and the connection stays usable. proxy-internals.md walks through the protocol handling, and ../proxy.md is the configuration reference.

The official clients (clients/python, clients/typescript, clients/go, clients/java) and the framework integrations (integrations/langchain, integrations/llamaindex, integrations/vanna) call the sidecar, or the CLI in local mode. They add a guarded-execution helper so application code does not have to get the post-verdict steps right by hand. See ../integrations.md and the per-language guides (../sdk-python.md, ../sdk-typescript.md, ../sdk-go.md, ../sdk-java.md). The Python helper (clients/python/src/haltsql/guard.py: execute, execute_async, execute_on_engine) shows the flow every client follows: Why each step exists: The hash check (Verdict.matches_sql) proves the verdict is for this exact string, not a verdict for a different query that got mixed up. Running the same string matters because any rewrite (quoting, placeholder conversion, formatting values into the SQL) would run SQL that was never verified. psycopg's RawCursor and asyncpg send the text unchanged with native $n placeholders. bind_args() supplies the tenant values the server computed from the context, in parameter order. The model never supplies them. The read-only transaction is a second layer: even if a policy allowed more than intended, a SELECT path cannot write. haltsql-mcp (clients/mcp, see ../mcp.md) applies the same flow behind Model Context Protocol tools (query, explain_denial, list_tables, describe_policy). Its tenant context is never a tool argument: extra arguments such as tenant_id are ignored. Over stdio there is one context per process; over streamable HTTP each bearer token maps to its own context in a tokens file.
documents.s: Mode 4: SDKs and the MCP server

documents.t: Library / CLI HTTP sidecar Wire proxy SDKs / MCP Extra latency None for the library (in process); one process spawn per CLI call or batch One loopback HTTP round trip Verification per Query/Parse, plus one extra network hop for every message Same as the backend they use (sidecar or CLI) Code changes Call Haltsql.verify (OCaml only) or run the CLI Call /v1/verify, act on the verdict Change the connection string; use prepared statements for tenant-scoped queries Replace your execute call with the guarded helper Who binds tenant values Your code, from bind_params Your code, from bind_params The proxy, overwriting client values in Bind The SDK, from verdict.bind_args() Where the context comes from Your code Body (static token) or the verified identity (OIDC, mTLS) Proxy config, per SCRAM user or cert identity Your app's session (SDK); launch config or token map (MCP) Can the app skip the check? Yes Yes No Only by not using the helper Failure mode Fail closed is your job: deny on any error; CLI exit codes 1 and 2 both mean "do not run" Any non-200, timeout or connection error is a denial; the server answers 503 when it cannot audit or authenticate Denial is a SQL ERROR; upstream or auth problems are FATAL; nothing unverified is forwarded QueryDenied or HaltSQLUnavailable; nothing runs Audit Yours Hash-chained records per sink JSON lines per statement Through the sidecar's audit

Your agent is written in OCaml: embed the library. Lowest latency, no moving parts. Build one helper that verifies and executes, and use only it. Your agent is in Python, TypeScript, Go or Java: run the sidecar and use the official SDK's guarded execute. This is the default recommendation. The agent framework speaks MCP: run haltsql-mcp against the sidecar. The model gets SQL tools, and the tenant stays out of its reach. You cannot change the client (a BI tool, a vendor agent, a JDBC app), or you do not trust the application code to honor verdicts: use the proxy. It is the only mode where a compromised client still cannot run unverified SQL or pick another tenant. CI, notebooks and batch jobs: the CLI, or the Python LocalVerifier, with no server to run. Whatever you choose, keep the database-side controls: a role with the least privilege that works, and row-level security as a second layer (../defense-in-depth.md). HaltSQL proves things about the SQL text. The database still enforces who may read what. Related pages: architecture.md, verification-pipeline.md, policies-and-config.md.

Parsing happens in two layers: Layer Directory Job Haltsql_pgquery lib/pgquery A thin C binding to the vendored libpg_query. Turns a SQL string into libpg_query's JSON parse tree, or computes a fingerprint. Haltsql_parse.Pg_parse lib/parse Enforces size and depth limits, then converts the JSON tree into HaltSQL's typed AST (lib/core/ast.ml), turning anything it does not understand into an explicit "unsupported" node. The analyzer never sees JSON. It only sees the typed AST. For where parsing fits in a full verify call, see Verification pipeline.

HaltSQL decides whether a string is safe to run on PostgreSQL. If HaltSQL read a string differently from the server, an attacker could write SQL that looks harmless to HaltSQL and does something else in Postgres. This is called a parser differential, and it is the main reason HaltSQL does not have its own grammar. libpg_query extracts the actual Postgres parser (gram.y, the scanner, and the code around them) into a C library. HaltSQL vendors libpg_query 17-6.2.5, which tracks the PostgreSQL 17.7 grammar, in vendor/libpg_query. haltsql version prints the grammar version it was built with. Why vendored, with our own stubs, instead of the opam pg_query bindings? The reasons are recorded in ADR-0001: the opam bindings bundle an old libpg_query (Postgres 13 grammar) that failed to build on current macOS toolchains and depend on ctypes and libffi; owning the stubs gives HaltSQL control over the OCaml runtime lock, thread stacks, and NUL-byte handling; the stubs expose only what HaltSQL needs: parse to JSON, fingerprint, and the Postgres version. HaltSQL uses libpg_query's JSON output, not its protobuf output. JSON is simpler to audit and keeps a protobuf decoder out of the trusted code. The AST conversion isolates that choice, so it can change later. Upgrading libpg_query is a deliberate event: replace the vendored tree, run the full test suite and attack corpus, and write a new ADR for a new Postgres major.

The OCaml interface (lib/pgquery/pgquery_raw.mli) is small: val parse_json : string -> (string, string * int) result (* Ok json, or Error (message, cursorpos) where cursorpos is 1-based (0 if unknown) *) val fingerprint : string -> (string, string) result val pg_version : string (* e.g. "17.7" *) val pg_version_num : int (* e.g. 170007 *)

libpg_query keeps parser state in thread-local memory, so it is thread-safe. But two properties make calling it directly from OCaml unsafe. Both are described at the top of lib/pgquery/pgquery_stubs.c: Unbounded recursion. libpg_query's JSON writer and fingerprinter recurse over the parse tree with no stack-depth check. OCaml 5 domains run on secondary threads, which get small stacks (512 KB on macOS). A small but deeply nested input such as SELECT 1+1+1+...+1 could crash the process. A limited number of thread keys. libpg_query creates one pthread key per thread it sees, and the number of keys is limited (512 on macOS). Calling it from many short-lived threads would run out. So every libpg_query call runs on a fixed pool of long-lived worker threads with 256 MB stacks. The stack is virtual memory; only pages that are actually touched get committed, so the cost is low. Setting Value Stack per worker 256 MB (PGQ_STACK_BYTES) Pool size number of online CPUs by default Override HALTSQL_PARSER_THREADS, clamped to 1 to 64 Start lazily, on the first parse or fingerprint (pthread_once) Queue one FIFO job queue protected by a mutex and condition variable

The details matter for safety: The input is copied before the runtime lock is released. While the lock is released, the OCaml garbage collector may move or free the original string. The runtime lock is released while waiting. Other OCaml domains and threads keep running, so parsing scales across cores. For example, the CLI's verify --batch --jobs N verifies on N OCaml domains that parse in parallel. NUL bytes are rejected first. A C string ends at the first NUL, so text after it would be invisible to the parser but might still reach the server through a driver that sends the whole buffer. The stub returns query contains a NUL byte, which becomes E_PARSE. No workers means deny. If no worker thread could be started, the stub returns an error (parser worker threads unavailable) and the query is denied. It never falls back to parsing on the caller's small stack.
Each job has its own condition variable, so a caller wakes only when its own job is done.

fingerprint runs libpg_query's fingerprinter on the same pool. Two queries get the same fingerprint when they differ only in literal values, which makes it useful for grouping queries in logs and dashboards. It is a full second parse, so verify only computes it for input that already parsed into exactly one statement. Pg_parse.fingerprint also refuses very long input and input that fails the bracket prescan, and any error gives null rather than a failure. The fingerprint is informational: no rule depends on it.

Pg_parse.parse ~limits sql (lib/parse/pg_parse.ml) applies the policy's limits around the C call. The order is chosen so that expensive or recursive work only runs on input that is already known to be bounded: Bytes. Longer than limits.max_bytes (default 16,384): E_LIMIT. Bracket prescan. More than 10,000 levels of ( or [ nesting: E_LIMIT. Brackets are counted everywhere, including inside literals and comments, so this can only over-count. It is a cheap backstop that keeps absurd input away from the C parser and the JSON reader. Parse on the worker pool. A syntax error is E_PARSE, with loc set to the parser's cursor position (converted to a 0-based byte offset). Read the JSON. Unreadable parser output is E_INTERNAL. Measure the tree iteratively. Depth over limits.max_depth (default 64) or node count over limits.max_nodes (default 20,000): E_LIMIT. This walk uses an explicit stack, not recursion, and stops as soon as a limit is crossed. Convert to the typed AST. parse also catches Stack_overflow and Out_of_memory (both become E_LIMIT) and any other exception (E_INTERNAL), so it never raises.

libpg_query knows roughly 250 node types. A rule engine that walked that raw tree generically ("find all RangeVar nodes") would be easy to fool: a node type the author never thought about could carry a table reference, a function call, or a subquery that the rules never inspect. New Postgres releases add node types, so that gap would grow over time. Instead, HaltSQL converts the tree into its own typed AST that covers exactly the subset of SQL it understands (ADR-0002). The key rule: Note: nothing that could carry meaning is ever silently dropped. Anything the converter does not map precisely becomes an explicit "unsupported" node, and the analyzer denies every such node.
documents.s: From JSON to the typed AST

documents.t: Every converter function first checks the node's keys against the exact set of keys it understands (check_keys). An unknown key, an unknown enum value, an unknown node type, or a malformed shape raises an internal Unsup exception carrying a description and a location. That exception is caught at the nearest enclosing place in the AST that has a slot for "unsupported": Where the unknown is found What it becomes How the analyzer reports it Inside an expression Ast.Unsupported { node; loc } E_UNSUPPORTED ("expression node ...") Inside a FROM item Ast.Unsupported_from { node; loc } E_UNSUPPORTED ("FROM item ...") Anywhere else in a statement Ast.Other { kind = "Unsupported:<what>"; loc } E_UNSUPPORTED A statement node that is not SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or EXPLAIN Ast.Other { kind = "<NodeName>"; loc } E_STATEMENT_KIND A sublink kind HaltSQL does not handle (ROWCOMPARE, MULTIEXPR, CTE) Ast.Other_sublink name E_UNSUPPORTED Catching at the nearest slot keeps the damage local: one odd expression turns into one E_UNSUPPORTED reason, and the rest of the query is still analyzed so the agent sees every other problem too.

At the top, stmt_of_node maps exactly five statement nodes: libpg_query node AST SelectStmt Ast.Select InsertStmt Ast.Insert UpdateStmt Ast.Update DeleteStmt Ast.Delete ExplainStmt Ast.Explain anything else (CreateStmt, DoStmt, CopyStmt, VariableSetStmt, ...) Ast.Other { kind = node name } The libpg_query wrapper around each statement (RawStmt) is checked too: an unknown key there becomes Unsupported:RawStmt.<key>.

From haltsql verify --json with examples/policies/saas.yaml: SQL fragment Caught as Reason ... TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (10) FROM item RangeTableSample E_UNSUPPORTED: FROM item RangeTableSample is not supported ... GROUP BY ROLLUP(o.status) expression node GroupingSet E_UNSUPPORTED: expression node GroupingSet is not supported ... SELECT xmlelement(name foo) expression node XmlExpr E_UNSUPPORTED: expression node XmlExpr is not supported ... ORDER BY o.id FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES statement level, unknown enum value E_UNSUPPORTED: SelectStmt.limitOption=LIMIT_OPTION_WITH_TIES is not supported ... CREATE TABLE x (a int) statement node CreateStmt E_STATEMENT_KIND: CreateStmt statements are not allowed

A few properties of the typed AST are worth knowing when reading rule code: Identifiers are exactly as Postgres's scanner produced them. Unquoted identifiers are already folded to lower case, quoted identifiers keep their case, and U&"..." escapes are already decoded. HaltSQL never re-implements case folding. Integer constants are kept as text (Int of string) to avoid overflow. The analyzer normalizes them when it needs to compare values. Locations are byte offsets into the original SQL, or -1 when unknown. They become the loc field of a reason. Catalog-qualified names (db.schema.table) are not mapped; they become Unsupported_from. No wildcard matches downstream. The analyzer matches every AST type exhaustively, without _ -> arms. Adding a constructor to lib/core/ast.ml is a compile error in every rule that must consider it, so a new construct cannot be accepted by accident.

Putting the two layers together: What goes wrong Result Input too long or too deeply bracketed E_LIMIT before any C code runs NUL byte in the input E_PARSE Not valid PostgreSQL 17 syntax E_PARSE with loc Parse tree too deep or too large E_LIMIT before conversion Parser output unreadable, or an unexpected exception E_INTERNAL Worker threads unavailable denied (no fallback to the caller's stack) Syntax HaltSQL does not map an unsupported node, then E_UNSUPPORTED A statement kind outside the five mapped ones E_STATEMENT_KIND The cost of this design is that some valid, safe SQL is denied until support is added. That is deliberate: a false positive is visible and fixable, while a silently ignored node could be a bypass. Adding support for a construct is an explicit change to the AST, the converter, the rules, the tests, and the docs. Next: Analyzer explains what happens to the typed AST.

Every HaltSQL behaviour starts from a document: a policy that says what an agent may do, a config that says how the server runs, a test suite, a schema snapshot. This page explains how those documents get from a file on disk to a typed, validated value in memory, and why the loader is so strict. The loaders live in lib/load/. The reference pages for each document are policy-reference.md, config-reference.md and secrets.md.
documents.s: How policies and config are loaded

documents.t: A policy is a security control. A loader that guesses would turn typos into silent holes. A misspelled tenant_colum that is quietly ignored makes a tenant table global. A YAML 1.1 reader that turns no into false, or 012 into 10, changes values behind your back. So HaltSQL's loader follows one principle: anything it does not fully understand is an error, reported with its exact location.

All document kinds share the same front half. Docload (backed by lib/load/docpos.ml) turns bytes into a Yojson.Safe.t tree plus a table of source positions. Then a kind-specific decoder validates and compiles it. The decoders collect errors instead of stopping at the first one, so one run of haltsql validate shows everything that is wrong: policy.yaml:14:5: tables."app.orders".tenant_column: unknown column

Only plain (unquoted) YAML scalars are typed. Quoted, literal and folded scalars are always strings. The rules come from the YAML 1.2 core schema, with a few deliberate choices (see the header of lib/load/docpos.ml): Input Becomes Why true, False, TRUE boolean core schema yes, no, on, off, y, n string no "Norway problem" ~, null, empty null core schema 42, 0o17, 0x1F integer core schema 012, -007 string almost always an identifier (zip code, account number), and YAML 1.1 tools would read it as octal, so neither number is safe 1.5, -2e3 float core schema .inf, .nan error cannot be represented in JSON !!str x, !custom x error every explicit tag is rejected Aliases are expanded, but at most 10,000 nodes may be produced by alias expansion in total, which stops "billion laughs" documents. A stream must hold exactly one document. JSON input is read strictly, with duplicate-key detection and the same depth limit. The YAML printer used by haltsql convert quotes any string a YAML 1.1 tool might retype, so converted files mean the same thing everywhere.

Every document has apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 and a kind. These kinds exist in the code today: Kind Loaded by Purpose Policy lib/load/policy_load.ml What one agent may do. See policy-reference.md. Config lib/load/config.ml How haltsql-server and the CLI run: listen address, auth, policies, audit, telemetry, secrets. See config-reference.md. TestSuite lib/load/test_suite.ml Allow/deny cases for one policy, run by haltsql test. Catalog lib/load/catalog_load.ml A schema snapshot: the complete, typed column list of each table. kind is optional here; haltsql validate treats a document with only tables as a catalog. Scenario lab/harness/scenario.py (full), bin/haltsql/cmds.ml (top-level keys only) A haltlab test scenario. PolicyBundle lib/bundle/haltsql_bundle.ml Signed, canonical package of normalized policies and catalogs. See policy-bundles.md. ProxyConfig lib/pgwire/proxy_config.ml Configuration of haltsql-proxy. See proxy.md. haltsql validate understands Policy, Config, TestSuite, Catalog and Scenario. Bundles are checked with haltsql bundle verify, and a proxy config is checked when haltsql-proxy starts. How they refer to each other:

HaltSQL has two kinds of placeholders, and they are kept strictly apart. Placeholder Allowed in Resolved Purpose ${ctx.NAME} Policies, only in tenancy.keys At verify time, from the request context Says which context field holds each tenancy key ${env:NAME}, ${file:/path} Config and ProxyConfig At load time Keep values out of the file ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...} Config only, outside the secrets section At load time, by a resolver Pull secrets from a secret manager $${ Where placeholders are allowed At load time A literal ${ Why can a policy not use ${env:...}? Because then the same policy file could mean different things on different machines, and its version hash would no longer describe its behaviour. Policy_load scans every string and rejects ${env: and ${file: with "only allowed in Config documents", and rejects any other ${ outside tenancy.keys. Config placeholders are never resolved inside an inline policy: an inline policy follows the policy rules, even though it sits in a config file.

Provider placeholders raise a chicken-and-egg problem: the Vault address and login method are themselves in the config file. HaltSQL solves it with two passes (see the module doc in lib/load/config.mli and lib/cloud/secrets.mli). Pass one decodes only the secrets section (Config.secrets_of_file). That section may use ${env:} and ${file:}, but not provider placeholders, since a provider cannot configure itself. A Secrets.t is built from those settings. It scans the raw file text for every provider placeholder and fetches them concurrently, each distinct (scheme, reference) once. Pass two decodes the whole document (Config.of_file ~resolve). The resolver only serves values from the cache filled in step 2. Why this shape? lib/load stays pure. The config module never talks to the network. Only lib/cloud does, through the ?resolve hook. It is safe inside the server's event loop. Config.of_file is synchronous. Serving it from a prefetched cache means a reload never needs a nested Lwt_main.run (see reload_lwt in bin/server/lib/state.ml). Rotation works. Each load builds a fresh cache, so a reload picks up rotated secrets. Errors are located and never leak. A failed fetch becomes a normal load error at the placeholder's line and column. Error messages name the reference, never the value. A provider placeholder with no resolver configured is the located error "secret provider not configured". An unresolvable placeholder is always an error; HaltSQL never substitutes an empty string. After loading, settings are layered: command-line flags beat HALTSQL_* environment variables, which beat the file, which beats built-in defaults. haltsql config show prints the merged result with secrets replaced by "<redacted>".

After the generic checks, Policy_load turns a policy document into a Policy.t: Unknown keys are errors at every level, as are wrong types and duplicates. Identifiers follow Postgres rules. Unquoted names fold to lower case, and unqualified table names get the first search_path entry. Function presets are expanded. functions.presets: [aggregates, math] becomes the explicit list from Policy_load.function_presets. An unknown preset name is a load error. Presets never include functions with side effects. The catalog is loaded from a path (relative to the policy file) or an inline snapshot, and every table, allowed column and tenant column the policy names is checked against it ("table ... is not in the catalog snapshot", "column ... does not exist in ... according to the catalog").

The catalog snapshot must list the complete columns of each real table, with types. HaltSQL never builds one from the columns lists in tables. The allowlist is what the agent may read, and the real table usually has more columns than that. If the loader treated the allowlist as the full table, SELECT * would expand to "only allowed columns" and pass, while Postgres would actually return the hidden ones too. So without a snapshot, the analyzer is conservative: SELECT * and whole-row references are allowed only on tables with columns: "*". With a snapshot, * is expanded against the real column list and denied if it would read a column the policy leaves out. Snapshots come from haltsql schema pull, which reads pg_catalog rather than information_schema so that a restricted role cannot produce an incomplete snapshot (see schema-and-pii.md).
documents.s: The catalog is never derived from the allowlist

documents.t: Every compiled policy has a version of the form sha256:<hex>. It is computed in lib/load/policy_impl.ml: Policy_load.to_json renders the compiled policy in a normalized form: defaults filled in, presets expanded, the catalog inline, identifiers rendered canonically. Object keys are sorted recursively. The compact JSON string is hashed with SHA-256. Because the hash is taken over meaning, not bytes, the YAML policy and its JSON twin get the same version, and so does a reformatted file. A change that alters behaviour, such as adding a column, a preset function or a catalog column, changes the version. Every verdict carries the version, every audit record can be traced back to an exact policy, and a signed bundle stores exactly this normalized document.
policy-lifecycle.md follows a policy from a schema snapshot through tests, CI and signing to a running server. server-internals.md covers how the server holds and reloads these loaded values.

A HaltSQL policy is code. It is drafted from the real schema, reviewed in a pull request, tested by CI, packaged into a signed bundle, and loaded by servers that refuse anything they cannot verify. This page walks through each stage and explains what each one protects against.

Writing a policy by hand from memory is how columns get missed. HaltSQL starts from the database instead. The three commands are documented in schema-and-pii.md and implemented in lib/catalog_tools/. Step Command Output Why it matters Snapshot haltsql schema pull --dsn ... --schema app -o catalog.json kind: Catalog, the complete typed column list of every relation The analyzer expands SELECT * against this list, so it must be complete. It reads pg_catalog, not information_schema, so a restricted role cannot produce a short list. Classify haltsql schema import --from dbt manifest.json -o pii.json A PII manifest Reuses the sensitivity tags your data catalog already has. Draft haltsql policy draft --catalog catalog.json --pii pii.json --tenant-column tenant_id -o agent.yaml A kind: Policy file Every table gets an explicit column list with flagged columns removed and a comment saying why. The draft is safe by construction: bound tenancy, select only, require_limit: {max: 1000}, a few function presets, mode: enforce, and a catalog: reference. Tables with the tenant column get tenant_column, and the others are marked # GLOBAL. The draft is loaded with the normal policy loader before it is written, so a draft that would not load is never written. A draft is a starting point. Someone still has to remove tables the agent does not need and check every GLOBAL table by hand.

A TestSuite document pins down what the policy must allow and deny. Each case has an exact SQL string, a context, and an expectation. Deny cases can list the reason codes that must appear. Allow cases can list the exact bind_params that must come back. The format is in testing.md. apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: TestSuite metadata: name: tenancy-basic policy: ../policies/analytics-agent.yaml defaults: context: { tenant_id: acme } cases: - name: filtered select is allowed sql: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 expect: allow bind: [{ param: 1, value: acme }] - name: missing tenant filter sql: SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10 expect: deny codes: [E_TENANT_MISSING] haltsql test runs suites through the same Haltsql.verify the server uses (lib/haltsql/suite_runner.ml). For a policy in shadow mode, cases are checked against shadow_reasons, so the same suite keeps working when the policy later switches to enforce. Good suites cover, for each tenant table, one allowed query and the common bypass shapes (missing filter, OR, outer-only filter, UNION branch, LEFT JOIN preserved side), plus a denied-column case for each sensitive column. See tenancy-proof.md for why each shape is denied.

CI makes every policy change go through the same checks you run locally. All integrations call the same CLI commands, so CI and your laptop always agree. Details are in policy-ci.md. Integration Where What it runs GitHub Action action.yml at the repository root, scripts in .github/actions/policy-ci/ install (checksum-verified), validate, lint-policy, test, job summary, optional bundle GitLab CI ci/gitlab/haltsql.gitlab-ci.yml (hidden jobs .haltsql-check, .haltsql-bundle) the same, plus a JUnit report pre-commit .pre-commit-hooks.yaml validate, lint-policy, test The order matters. Validation catches documents that do not load. lint-policy catches documents that load but are risky. Tests catch policies that behave differently than intended. A bundle is built only after all three pass. The project dogfoods the action in its own CI (policy-ci-action job in .github/workflows/ci.yml): it runs the action against the YAML policies in examples/policies and the suites in examples/suites, then builds and signs a bundle with a throwaway key.

A server should not have to trust the file system, the copy step, or the artifact store between CI and production. A signed bundle removes that trust. The format is in policy-bundles.md, and the code is lib/bundle/. haltsql bundle keygen -o policy-signing.key creates an Ed25519 key pair. The private key goes into a CI secret. The .pub file is safe to commit. haltsql bundle build loads and validates every policy and catalog, then writes canonical JSON: sorted keys, no extra whitespace, one trailing newline, a sha256: digest over everything else. The same inputs always give byte-identical output, with no timestamps, so you can rebuild from a commit and compare. haltsql bundle sign refuses to sign a bundle that does not load, then writes BUNDLE.sig. The signature covers the domain separator haltsql.dev/v1 PolicyBundle signature plus a newline, followed by the exact bundle bytes. haltsql bundle verify and haltsql bundle inspect run the server's checks from the command line. The server verifies in a fixed order and stops at the first failure. Nothing in the bundle is parsed until a signature has verified. Key rotation works by listing both public keys on the servers, optionally dual-signing with --append, switching CI to the new key, and then removing the old public key. Removing a compromised key and reloading makes every bundle signed only by that key stop loading at once.

haltsql-server loads policies from its config: plain files, inline documents, and bundles. The reload logic is in bin/server/lib/state.ml. A reload is triggered by SIGHUP, or by the file watcher when reload.watch: true. The watcher polls the config file, every policy file, each bundle and its .sig, and the TLS files every 2 seconds (it compares mtime, size and inode). A reload rebuilds everything from scratch: Load the config, with a fresh secrets cache (so rotated secrets are picked up). Load and verify every bundle. A bundle policy may not duplicate a policy from the config file or from another bundle, so one signer cannot silently replace another's policy. Load the --policy files given on the command line. Check that every policy referenced by tokens, OIDC providers, mTLS identities and default_policy is loaded. Reload TLS material and reconfigure telemetry. Only if every step succeeds is the new snapshot swapped in, in one assignment. Otherwise the server logs "reload failed; keeping the last good configuration" and keeps serving the old set. Two details make this robust. No retry storm. After a failed reload, the server records the new file signatures anyway, so it does not retry the same broken file on every poll. It tries again when the files change once more. Some changes need a restart. Turning TLS on or off during a reload is rejected, because the listener was set up at startup. Certificates themselves can be rotated by reload. Reloads are visible: haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="success"} and {result="error"} in metrics, and a log line listing every loaded policy as name@version. At startup, any load error makes the server refuse to start. More about the server is in server-internals.md.

A stricter policy can break a working agent. Shadow mode lets you measure that before it happens. With mode: shadow in the policy: allowed is always true; every denial the policy would make is listed in shadow_reasons; the server counts them as haltsql_verify_total{result="shadow_denied"} and marks audit records with "shadow": true. { "allowed": true, "reasons": [], "shadow_reasons": [ { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "rule": "tenancy.predicate", "loc": 15, "message": "app.orders (as orders) has no provable tenant predicate on orders.tenant_id in the same SELECT" } ] } (Real output for SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 5 with test/fixtures/policies/shadow.yaml, trimmed.) The rollout is: deploy with mode: shadow, review the shadow denials, fix the policy or the agent, then switch to mode: enforce and reload. Changing the mode changes the policy version, so verdicts and audit records show exactly when enforcement began. A shadow policy enforces nothing, so never use it as the only control. See deployment.md.

HaltSQL checks queries before they run. If the application forgets to call HaltSQL, or HaltSQL has a bug, the database should still hold the line. haltsql rls generate (code in lib/rlsgen/, docs in rls-generation.md) turns the same policy into PostgreSQL DDL: a NOLOGIN NOBYPASSRLS agent role, with column-level GRANT SELECT that matches the policy's column lists; write grants only where the policy allows the statement and the table; row-level security on every tenant-scoped table, with policies comparing each tenant column to a transaction-local setting such as haltsql.tenant_id. A missing setting matches no rows. The application sets that setting from the same context it passed to HaltSQL, in the same transaction, then runs the allowed SQL under the agent role: BEGIN; SELECT pg_catalog.set_config('haltsql.tenant_id', $1, true); -- $1 = ctx.tenant_id SET LOCAL ROLE haltsql_agent; -- the exact SQL HaltSQL allowed, binding verdict.bind_params COMMIT; The output is deterministic and idempotent, so it can be committed and reviewed next to the policy. haltsql rls check connects to a live database and reports drift from the policy. See also defense-in-depth.md.
policies-and-config.md explains how each of these documents is loaded and why the policy version is stable. assurance.md explains how HaltSQL itself is tested.

haltsql-proxy is a PostgreSQL wire-protocol (v3) firewall. This page explains how it works inside. For configuration and operations, see ../proxy.md. For when to use it, see deployment-modes.md. The code lives in lib/pgwire and bin/proxy: File Role bin/proxy/main.ml CLI: run, validate, scram-verifier; signal handling lib/pgwire/proxy_config.ml Loads and validates kind: ProxyConfig; builds each user's or identity's binding (policy + context) lib/pgwire/server.ml Listener, connection limits (total and per-address before authentication), TLS server config, hot reload and which sessions it ends, graceful shutdown lib/pgwire/session.ml One client connection: startup, authentication, upstream search_path check, the enforcing relay, ending at a transaction boundary lib/pgwire/enforce.ml Decisions: verify, transaction-control allowlist, Bind rewriting, denial fields lib/pgwire/stmt_state.ml Prepared-statement bookkeeping across pipelined Sync segments lib/pgwire/wire.ml Message codecs lib/pgwire/scram.ml Server side of SCRAM-SHA-256 lib/pgwire/upstream.ml Connects to the real server (TLS, authentication, pinned search_path); forwards cancel requests lib/pgwire/paudit.ml The audit log: hash-chained records, sinks, failure policies lib/pgwire/offload.ml Bounded thread pool for verification and audit file writes lib/pgwire/plog.ml Operational JSON logs on stderr

The proxy sits on the only network path from untrusted clients to the database. The client holds a proxy credential. Only the proxy holds the database credential. Four properties follow from this layout: The client cannot skip verification. Every Query and Parse goes through Haltsql.verify before anything is forwarded. The client cannot choose its policy or tenant. Both are bound to the authenticated identity in the config, not to anything in the startup packet or the SQL. The forwarded SQL is the verified SQL. The SQL bytes sent upstream are always byte for byte the bytes that were verified. Only Bind parameter values for tenancy parameters are rewritten. The server reads names the way the verifier did. The upstream session's search_path is set from the bound policy and confirmed before the first statement, and a session keeps one policy for its whole life.

Session.run handles everything up to the first ReadyForQuery. Startup and authentication together must finish within limits.auth_timeout_seconds (default 30), otherwise the client gets FATAL 08006. Details that matter for security: Slots before authentication. A connection counts against limits.max_connections from accept. Until it has authenticated it also counts against limits.max_unauthenticated_per_ip (default 20) for its source address; the connection over that cap is refused at accept with FATAL 53300. Server keeps the per-address counter and decrements it when Session reports a successful authentication or the connection ends. TLS. An SSLRequest is answered with S and a TLS handshake when tls is configured, otherwise N. Plaintext bytes pipelined after the SSLRequest are a protocol violation (CVE-2021-23214). GSSENCRequest is always refused with N. With tls.required: true (the default), a client that did not upgrade gets FATAL 28000. Startup parameters. user is required. database must equal upstream.database (otherwise 3D000). Any replication parameter is refused. Only a printable application_name (63 bytes or less) is forwarded. options and every other parameter are ignored, so a client cannot set GUCs such as search_path. A newer protocol minor version or _pq_.* options get NegotiateProtocolVersion for 3.0. SCRAM (auth.method: scram). The proxy implements the server side of SCRAM-SHA-256 (no channel binding) and stores only verifiers in PostgreSQL's format (haltsql-proxy scram-verifier makes one). An unknown user goes through a full fake exchange using a per-process mock secret, so user names cannot be probed. Every failure is the same FATAL 28P01 password authentication failed for user "...". Client certificates (auth.method: cert). The TLS layer verifies the chain against tls.client_ca. The proxy then matches the leaf's subject CN or a URI SAN (spiffe_id) against auth.identities. The startup user name is not used for authorization. The binding. Authentication returns a binding: the policy name, the loaded Policy.t, and the Context.t from the config. Validation already checked that the context supplies every value the policy's tenancy needs. Everything after this point uses only the binding. Upstream sanity. The proxy always sends client_encoding=UTF8. If the server ever reports a different client_encoding, or standard_conforming_strings other than on, the session is terminated. The verified bytes must mean the same thing to Postgres as they did to the parser. Pinned search_path. The verifier resolves an unqualified name through the policy's search_path (pg_catalog first unless the policy places it). PostgreSQL resolves it through the session's search_path, which by default comes from ALTER ROLE / ALTER DATABASE or postgresql.conf and has nothing to do with the policy. So Upstream.connect puts search_path in the upstream startup packet (which overrides role and database settings): the policy's schemas, each double-quoted, then pg_temp. pg_temp is explicit and last because PostgreSQL otherwise searches temporary tables before everything else. When the upstream reports ReadyForQuery, Session.confirm_search_path sends SHOW search_path, parses the answer the way PostgreSQL parses the setting (Upstream.parse_search_path) and compares the schema lists. The client's ReadyForQuery is held back until the comparison passed, so no client statement can be forwarded before it; a mismatch ends the session with FATAL 08006. PostgreSQL 18 and later also report the setting as a ParameterStatus, at startup and on every change, and a reported value that differs ends the session. The path belongs to the session's binding, which never changes (see Lifecycle). Upstream transport. upstream.tls.mode is disable (the default), require (encrypted, any certificate accepted) or verify-full (chain and host verified); only the last authenticates the database. The proxy never sends a cleartext password without TLS, and refuses MD5 authentication without TLS unless upstream.allow_insecure_auth is set. Proxy_config.transport_notes produces the warning logged at start when TLS is off towards a host that is not a loopback address.

After startup, four promises run side by side (Lwt.pick; the first to finish ends the session): client_loop reads one frontend message at a time and passes it to handle_client_message, which verifies, rewrites, replaces or drops it. upstream_loop reads backend messages, updates statement bookkeeping, swaps injected errors for denial errors, and relays everything else. lifetime_timer asks the session to end after limits.max_session_lifetime_seconds. terminator waits for such a request (from the timer or from a reload) and ends the session at the next transaction boundary (see Lifecycle).

The proxy is one Lwt event loop: code that blocks blocks every session. Two things would, so they run on a bounded pool of system threads (Offload, limits.worker_threads, default the number of CPUs clamped to 2..8): Verification. Haltsql.verify waits for the parser's own worker pool and then analyses the statement. handle_client_message hands Enforce.simple / Enforce.parse to the pool and waits for the verdict. Audit writes to stdout and file sinks, which are blocking write calls (see Audit and logs). Ordering does not change. client_loop handles one message at a time and does not read the next one until the current one is verified, audited and forwarded (or replaced), so pipelined Parse / Bind / Execute reach the upstream in the client's order; only other sessions run while one waits. upstream_loop keeps relaying responses to earlier segments meanwhile, which is the same interleaving Stmt_state already handled for a Bind waiting on an earlier Parse. A pool job cannot be cancelled: if the session ended while its job ran, the result is discarded and nothing is forwarded.

A Query message is verified as a whole (Enforce.simple). It is denied if the verdict denies, or if the verdict has bind_params: the simple protocol has no Bind message, so the proxy has no way to supply tenant values. The denial carries E_PARAM_UNBOUND and a hint to use a prepared statement. When allow_transaction_control is on (the default), plain BEGIN, START TRANSACTION [modes], COMMIT, END, ROLLBACK and ABORT pass without a policy check, so drivers work outside autocommit. The match is exact token by token (Enforce.transaction_control): comments, quotes, savepoints, AND CHAIN and PREPARE TRANSACTION do not match and go to the policy.

This is where tenancy is enforced. The policy proves that each tenancy predicate compares the tenant column with a parameter such as $1, and the verdict's bind_params names those parameter positions. The proxy then fills those positions itself. Parse. Enforce.parse verifies the SQL and the verdict is audited. Denied: the message is replaced by a denial (see below). Allowed, but the named statement already exists: refused with 42P05 PROXY_STATEMENT_EXISTS. The proxy never lets a second Parse silently change what an existing name means. Allowed: the verdict is recorded as pending for that statement name, and the Parse is forwarded. Declared parameter types. A Parse may declare a type for each parameter, and PostgreSQL decodes the Bind value with that type. A declared type such as float8, name or "char" could change how the injected tenant value is read (rounding, truncation). So Enforce.reset_tenancy_param_types sets the declared type of every tenancy parameter to 0 (unspecified), and the server infers it from the tenant predicate. Other parameters keep their declared types. If nothing changed, the original bytes are forwarded. Bind. The proxy looks up the statement's verdict. An unknown statement is refused with 26000 PROXY_STATEMENT_UNKNOWN. If the verdict has no bind_params, the Bind is forwarded unchanged. Otherwise Enforce.bind: checks that the Bind supplies every tenancy parameter position; refuses binary format for a tenancy parameter (only text format is allowed, so the value cannot be reinterpreted); refuses conflicting tenancy values for one position; replaces each tenancy parameter's value with the session's context value, whatever the client sent. A single value is sent as is. A set of values is sent as a PostgreSQL array literal ({"a","b"}). A problem in steps 1 to 3 is a denial with E_PARAM_UNBOUND. The client cannot make the proxy skip the rewrite: any shape it cannot rewrite safely is refused. Execute. A verdict is recorded at Parse, but a prepared statement can run any number of times. Each Execute therefore writes an execute audit record before it is forwarded: the portal, the statement the portal was bound from, that statement's sql_sha256 and fingerprint, and the row limit, never parameter values. The session keeps a small portal table for this (filled at Bind, emptied on Close, when the statement is closed, and when the transaction that owned the portal has ended), so a portal the proxy did not bind is recorded with a null statement instead of a guessed one. If the record cannot be written under fail_closed, the Execute is replaced by a denial like any other refused message. Other messages. Describe, Close, Flush and Sync are validated and relayed. Close of a statement removes its verdict right away (removing early is safe, because a missing entry can only cause a denial).

Clients pipeline. A driver may send Parse, Bind, Execute for three statements and one Sync before reading anything. If the proxy wrote an error to the client directly, it could overtake the responses to earlier messages that the server has not answered yet. The driver would then pair responses with the wrong requests. Instead, the proxy lets PostgreSQL produce the error at the right position: It generates a random token haltsql_deny_<16 random bytes in hex> and stores it, with the denial's error fields, on the current segment. It forwards a message that cannot parse in place of the denied one: simple protocol: a Query whose text is the token; extended protocol: a Parse whose statement name and query are the token. The session then enters discarding mode and drops every client message up to the next Sync, as PostgreSQL itself does after an error. PostgreSQL answers with a syntax error at exactly that point in the stream, and skips to Sync on its own. upstream_loop sees an ErrorResponse whose message contains the token, and sends the stored denial fields to the client instead.
