The client sees a normal PostgreSQL error, in the right position, and the connection stays usable. Inside a transaction the denial aborts the transaction, exactly like a real permission error. The random token is new for every denial and never reaches the client. The error the client sees: Field Value S, V ERROR C deny_sqlstate (default 42501) M haltsql: query denied by policy "<name>": <first reason> D HaltSQL reasons: <codes> H the first reason's hint, when there is one

The proxy must know, for every Bind, which verdict applies to the statement it names. That is harder than it sounds: a Parse only takes effect when the server answers ParseComplete, and after an error the server ignores messages until Sync. Stmt_state models this exactly. Messages are grouped into segments: everything up to a Sync (or one simple Query) is one segment. Parse and Close are queued as pending operations of the current segment. ParseComplete commits the head operation's verdict to the committed table. CloseComplete removes one. ErrorResponse drops the remaining pending operations of the head segment (the server will ignore them). ReadyForQuery closes the head segment. A Bind looks in the current segment first, then the committed table. If the name has a pending operation in an earlier segment, the Bind waits until the server has answered it. A missing entry always denies. Bookkeeping can only err towards denial, and a client cannot get one statement's tenancy positions applied to another statement. A simple Query destroys the unnamed statement, as PostgreSQL does. An unnamed Parse replaces it. More than 10,000 pending segments or operations ends the session with 54000 too many pipelined statements. ConnectingUpstream includes the SHOW search_path round trip: the client sees its first ReadyForQuery only after it. In Ending the relay works as before (statements are still verified, under the session's own policy) until the upstream reports ReadyForQuery with status idle and nothing is in flight.

PostgreSQL cancels a running query through a separate connection that sends the backend's (pid, key). The proxy must not hand out the upstream's real pid and key, and must not let one client cancel another's queries. During startup, the upstream's BackendKeyData is replaced with a proxy-issued pair: a random non-zero 30-bit pid and a random 32-bit key. The process-wide cancel table maps it to the upstream pair. A CancelRequest is looked up by pid, and its key is compared in constant time. On a match, Upstream.send_cancel forwards the upstream pair over a fresh upstream connection (with TLS if configured). Wrong keys and unknown pids are logged and ignored. The entry is removed when the session ends.

Message Handling Why FunctionCall (fastpath) Denied in-band with PROXY_FUNCTION_CALL, through the same token trick (a simple Query with the token) It calls a function by OID without SQL, so there is nothing to verify CopyData, CopyDone, CopyFail from the client FATAL 08P01, connection closed COPY statements are already denied by the policy (E_STATEMENT_KIND) Upstream enters COPY mode anyway FATAL 08P01, connection closed Defense in depth Unexpected R, K, v from upstream after startup FATAL 08P01 The proxy has lost protocol sync Unknown types, malformed or oversized messages FATAL 08P01 (oversize is checked against limits.max_message_bytes) Never guess at bytes it cannot parse Terminate Forwarded, session ends Idle sessions are closed after limits.idle_timeout_seconds (off by default) with FATAL 57P05, but only when no request is in flight.

Paudit writes the audit log. Every verified statement produces one record, including statements let through by the transaction-control allowlist, and every forwarded Execute produces one more: {"ts":"...","event":"statement","session":"49fd05aacd53","user":"agent", "policy":"proxy-test","policy_version":"sha256:...","protocol":"extended", "allowed":false,"reasons":["E_COLUMN_DENIED"],"shadow_reasons":[], "sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"...","tables":["app.users"], "bind_params":[1],"statement":"","prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} {"ts":"...","event":"execute","session":"49fd05aacd53","user":"agent", "policy":"proxy-test","policy_version":"sha256:...","protocol":"extended", "portal":"","statement":"s1","sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"...", "max_rows":0,"prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} bind_params lists parameter positions only, never values. execute records carry no parameter values either. Proxy-level refusals have their own events (bind, parse, function_call) with reasons and message. The SQL text appears only with audit.log_raw_sql: true. Operational logs (Plog) go to stderr as JSON lines. Neither stream contains passwords, verifiers, SCRAM messages, keys or bind values. Hash chain. Records are sealed with the same Audit_chain code as the haltsql-server audit log: hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ L), L being the compact JSON of the record without hash, and the first record of a chain has 64 zeros as prev_hash. Each sink (stdout, file, s3, gcs) keeps its own chain; a file sink continues the chain of the existing file across restarts, and refuses to start on a file whose last line is not a sealed record. haltsql audit verify checks any of them. A record that cannot be written blocks the statement. With the default on_error: fail_closed, Paudit.record_async returns an error and the session replaces the statement (or the Execute) with a refusal: ERROR, SQLSTATE 58030, PROXY_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, delivered in-band through the same token mechanism as a policy denial. Nothing reaches the database without its audit record, and a denial that cannot be recorded is refused the same way. buffer queues records in memory up to max_buffer_records and refuses beyond that; drop discards, counts and logs. See ../proxy.md. Order and threads. record_async takes a process-wide FIFO lock, stamps the record, and writes stdout/file sinks on an Offload thread; object sinks append to their in-memory batch (and spool) on the event loop, where their uploader lives. One writer at a time, served in arrival order, means that in every sink the chain order, the timestamp order and the order in which statements were accepted are the same. The session waits for the outcome before it forwards, which is what keeps fail_closed true with the write off the loop. The retry loop that drains a buffer and the final flush at shutdown take the same lock.

haltsql-proxy run -c FILE loads and validates the config. SIGHUP, or a change to the config or a file it pulls in with reload.watch: true, reloads it (Server.reload). A configuration that does not load or validate is rejected and the current one stays in force. The listen address and the audit sinks only change with a restart. A session has one binding for life. It keeps the configuration snapshot it was accepted under; a reload never swaps the policy of an open session, because its upstream search_path was pinned for that policy and its prepared statements were verified under it. A reload ends the sessions it changes. Each authenticated session is registered with the listener (Session.live: principal, credential, binding, snapshot). After a reload, Session.stale compares it with the new configuration: user or certificate identity removed, SCRAM verifier or client CA bundle changed, bound to another policy, policy content (version) or context changed, upstream changed, or allow_transaction_control changed. Such a session is asked to end; all others continue untouched. reload.terminate_changed_sessions: false turns this off. Every session ends after limits.max_session_lifetime_seconds (default one hour, 0 for no limit), which bounds how long anything a reload does not see can stay in effect. Ending happens at a transaction boundary. The session goes on until the upstream reports ReadyForQuery with transaction status idle and no segment is in flight (immediately, if it is already there). Then the client gets FATAL 57P01 (admin_shutdown, what pg_terminate_backend produces, so drivers and pools reconnect) and both connections close. A client message that arrives at that point is neither verified nor forwarded. A session that does not get there within limits.termination_grace_seconds (default 30) is closed anyway, so holding a transaction open does not keep an old policy alive; the upstream rolls the transaction back. New connections above limits.max_connections, or above limits.max_unauthenticated_per_ip for their address, get FATAL 53300. On SIGTERM or SIGINT the proxy stops accepting, lets sessions finish for shutdown_grace_seconds, closes the rest, flushes the audit sinks and exits 0. Related pages: deployment-modes.md, tenancy-proof.md, verification-pipeline.md, ../defense-in-depth.md.

haltsql-server is the HTTP sidecar. It answers one question, POST /v1/verify, for callers in any language. It never connects to a database. This page explains what happens inside it. The HTTP contract is in ../http-api.md, and the auth configuration is in ../authentication.md. The code lives in bin/server/lib, with shared libraries in lib/auth and lib/cloud: File Role bin/server/lib/server.ml Listener, accept loop (plain or TLS), signals, file watcher, shutdown bin/server/lib/http.ml Routing, caller resolution, /v1/verify, /readyz, /metrics bin/server/lib/state.ml Startup settings, the hot-reloadable snapshot, reload logic bin/server/lib/auth.ml Static bearer tokens (SHA-256, constant-time comparison) bin/server/lib/audit.ml Audit records, hash chaining, stdout and file sinks, on_error bin/server/lib/metrics.ml Prometheus counters and histograms (mirrored to OTLP) bin/server/lib/telemetry.ml The process-wide OTLP exporter; swapped on reload bin/server/lib/integrations.ml Wires in secrets providers, S3/GCS sinks and signed bundles lib/auth/* JWT/JWK verification, OIDC discovery and JWKS cache, mTLS identity matching, context merging lib/cloud/* Secrets resolvers (Vault, AWS SM, GCP SM), object-store audit sinks, chain verification

Http.handle_verify wraps the request in an OTLP span, then handle_verify_inner runs the steps in a fixed order. The caller is resolved before the body is read, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer a large body. A denial is a normal 200 response. Errors that stop the request earlier: Step Failure Response Caller resolution missing or unknown token, JWT rejected 401 UNAUTHORIZED Caller resolution the IdP's keys cannot be fetched and no usable cache remains 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE with Retry-After: 5 Body larger than server.max_request_bytes 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE Body not JSON, unknown fields, wrong types 400 BAD_REQUEST Policy requested policy differs from the pinned one 403 FORBIDDEN Policy no policies loaded 503 NOT_READY Policy pinned policy not loaded 503 POLICY_UNAVAILABLE Context body sets a field the identity does not allow 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED Audit a sink refused the record 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE Clients treat every non-200 answer as a denial, so each of these fails closed.
documents.s: One verify request, end to end

documents.t: Http.resolve_caller tries three methods in order and stops at the first one that applies. Each produces a caller record: a name for the audit log, a type (token, oidc, mtls, anonymous), an optional subject, the pinned policy, and an optional authenticated context with the body fields it still allows. mTLS. The TLS layer verifies the chain against server.tls.client_ca during the handshake. Haltsql_auth.Mtls.find_identity then matches the leaf: a spiffe_id must equal the certificate's single URI SAN (a certificate with more than one URI SAN has no SPIFFE ID), and a subject_cn must equal the common name exactly. The first match in config order wins. A valid certificate that matches no identity falls through to bearer authentication. OIDC. Oidc_client.authenticate reads the token's unverified iss. Only a provider whose issuer equals it may verify the token. A token from any other issuer, or an opaque token, is "not applicable" and goes to the static check. Once a provider claims a token, its rejection is final. The provider checks the algorithm against its allowlist (none and HMAC are never accepted), finds the key by kid in its JWKS, verifies the signature, and checks iss, aud, exp/nbf/iat with leeway, and required_claims. The JWKS cache in lib/auth/oidc_client.ml keeps the IdP off the hot path: keys are fetched at startup (in the background) and cached for jwks_cache_seconds; an unknown kid forces one refresh, at most once every 30 seconds per provider, so key rotation works without letting random kids hammer the IdP; if a refresh fails, cached keys stay usable for at most min(jwks_cache_seconds, 3600) seconds past expiry, then the provider answers 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE until the IdP is back; fetches are limited to 1 MiB and 5 seconds, and redirects are not followed. Static tokens. Auth.authenticate hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and compares it, in constant time, with every configured token_sha256. It always scans the full list, so timing does not reveal which token matched. The server stores only hashes. Anonymous. Only a request with no Authorization header becomes anonymous, and only when server.auth.allow_unauthenticated is true. A request with a wrong token is still 401.

Every authenticated caller is pinned to exactly one policy: Caller Pinned policy Static token the token's policy OIDC the provider's policy, or the string value of policy_claim if it is in allowed_policies mTLS the identity's policy Anonymous none: the request's policy, else default_policy, else the only loaded policy If the body names a different policy, the answer is 403 FORBIDDEN. A caller can never select a looser policy than the one it was given. At load time, State.check_policy_refs refuses any config where a token, OIDC provider, mTLS identity or default_policy refers to a policy that is not loaded.

Haltsql_auth.Request_context.merge combines the authenticated context with the body: a body field that repeats an authenticated field with the same value is accepted (clients that always send their context keep working); a body field that changes an authenticated field, or that is not listed in request_context_fields, is refused with 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. It is never silently dropped or overridden; allowed extra fields are appended. For static tokens and anonymous callers there is no authenticated context: the body supplies all of it. That trusts the calling service to fill the context from its own authenticated session. Prefer OIDC or mTLS when the tenant must come from an identity the server can verify itself.

State.t separates what is fixed at startup from what can change: Fixed at startup (State.cfg) Reloadable (State.snap) listen address, health listener policies (files, inline, signed bundles) audit sinks, log_raw_sql static tokens max_request_bytes default_policy logging, whether /metrics is served OIDC providers (key caches of unchanged providers are kept) whether TLS is on mTLS identities allow_unauthenticated TLS certificate, key and client CA (when TLS is on) the OTLP exporter (replaced only when telemetry.otlp changed) Handlers read reloadable settings only from snap. A reload builds a complete new snapshot and swaps it in one assignment, so a request sees either the old configuration or the new one, never a mix. allow_unauthenticated is part of the snapshot, so turning anonymous access off takes effect on the next reload, without a restart.
documents.s: State: settings and the reloadable snapshot

documents.t: A reload starts on SIGHUP, or when the file watcher (reload.watch or --watch) sees a watched file change. The watcher polls every 2 seconds and compares each file's mtime, size and inode. Watched files are the config file, every policy file, each signed bundle and its .sig, and the TLS files. What makes this safe: All or nothing. If any policy, bundle signature, secret, policy reference or TLS file fails, nothing changes. The errors are logged as "reload failed; keeping the last good configuration" and haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"} goes up. No retry storm. After a failed reload, the server records the current file signatures, so the watcher does not retry the same broken files every 2 seconds. The next edit triggers a new attempt. Readiness is not affected. A failed reload does not make /readyz fail, because the last good policies are still serving. TLS on/off needs a restart. Adding or removing server.tls in a reload is rejected. Rotating the certificate, key or client CA is allowed; new connections use the new material and existing ones are not interrupted. Secrets are re-fetched. Reloads run inside the event loop, so the server first prefetches every provider placeholder concurrently with a fresh cache (Integrations.prefetching_secret_resolver), then loads with a resolver that serves only those values. Rotated secrets are picked up on the next reload.

Any string in a Config document, outside inline policies, may be a placeholder: ${env:NAME}, ${file:/path}, ${vault:<path>#<field>}, ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]}, ${gcp-sm:<name>[#<json-key>]} ($${ is a literal ${). The secrets section, which configures the providers, may itself use only env and file. Loading is two passes: decode the secrets section, build a resolver, then decode the whole document with it. A failure is a located load error, and the server refuses to start (exit code 2) or to reload. Error messages and logs never contain secret values. See ../secrets.md.

Every verify request that reaches a verdict produces one audit record per configured sink. Audit.record_fields builds it: {"ts":"...","request_id":"...","caller":"oidc:corp-okta","caller_type":"oidc", "subject":"user-123","policy":"support","policy_version":"sha256:...", "allowed":false,"shadow":false,"codes":["E_TABLE_DENIED"], "sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"...","elapsed_us":183, "prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} The SQL text is added only with audit.log_raw_sql: true. Raw tokens are never logged. Sealing. Audit.seal appends prev_hash, serializes the record as compact JSON (call it L), and computes hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ L). The first record of a chain has prev_hash equal to 64 zeros. Each sink keeps its own chain. Changing, deleting, inserting or reordering any record breaks verification from that point on. Audit.verify_lines and Haltsql_cloud.Audit_chain.verify_lines check a chain, and ../audit-sinks.md has a standalone Python verifier.
documents.s: Audit records and the hash chain

documents.t: Sink Chain start Where the chain lives stdout genesis, for each process your log pipeline file continues from the hash of the file's last line; refuses to start if that line is not a valid record the file (created 0640, append only) s3, gcs genesis, or the spooled head with spool_dir across objects, in sequence order Object-store sinks (lib/cloud/object_sink.ml, s3_sink.ml, gcs_sink.ml) seal each record into their own chain and append it to the current batch. Writing never waits on the network. A batch closes at batch.max_records (default 500) or batch.max_seconds (default 10), and becomes one object named <prefix>YYYY/MM/DD/HH/<host>-<run>-<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl. Objects upload strictly in order. Uploads are create-only (If-None-Match: * on S3, ifGenerationMatch=0 on GCS), and the name embeds the body's SHA-256, so a retried upload that finds the object already stored counts as delivered. The first record of object n+1 carries the hash of the last record of object n, so concatenating a host's objects in name order verifies as one chain.

The rule is simple: no request is answered with a verdict unless its audit record was accepted. Http.audit_record delivers the record to every sink. If any sink returns Failed, the request gets 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE instead of the verdict, and haltsql_audit_errors_total goes up. Sink type fail_closed (default) buffer stdout, file a failed write fails the request the record is queued (sealed later, so the chain stays intact) and the request succeeds; buffered records are written first on the next delivery; at 10,000 queued records writes fail s3, gcs after an upload has failed every attempt (3 by default), the sink turns unhealthy and refuses writes until a background retry succeeds writes keep succeeding up to max_buffer_records (default 100,000), then are refused; records are never dropped silently /readyz checks Audit.healthy for every sink. While any sink refuses writes, it answers 503 with the sink names in unhealthy_audit_sinks, so load balancers and the kubelet stop sending traffic to a replica that would refuse every verify anyway.

Object names include a run id: the process's UTC start time with microseconds, then its pid (for example 20240601T115900.042000Z.7). Two runs never share a sequence namespace, and run ids sort by start time. Batches that are accepted but not yet uploaded live in memory. With a spool_dir: every record is appended to <spool>/current.jsonl before the write returns (writes are refused if the spool cannot be written); closed batches stay on disk until uploaded; each time a batch closes, the chain head and next sequence number are written to <spool>/head.json (temporary file, fsync, rename); after a restart, spooled batches are re-queued under their original names, and the chain and sequence continue from the last sealed record. Without spool_dir, a restart starts a new chain at genesis under a new run id, and deleting an earlier run's objects is not detectable from the chain alone. Use S3 Object Lock or a GCS retention policy if that matters.

Prometheus. GET /metrics (when telemetry.metrics.prometheus is on) renders Metrics.render plus the object sinks' haltsql_audit_sink_* gauges and counters. The main series are haltsql_verify_total{policy,result}, haltsql_reasons_total{code}, haltsql_verify_duration_seconds, haltsql_policy_reload_total{result}, haltsql_audit_errors_total, haltsql_http_requests_total{route,status}, haltsql_auth_total{method,result} and haltsql_tls_reload_total{result}. The full list is in ../http-api.md and ../observability.md. OTLP. With telemetry.otlp, every Prometheus observation is mirrored to the OTLP exporter (Telemetry.exporter ()), and each verify request produces one SERVER span named haltsql.verify: attributes: haltsql.policy, haltsql.policy_version, haltsql.allowed, haltsql.shadow, haltsql.reason_codes, db.system, db.statement.sha256, haltsql.elapsed_us; the span carries the SQL hash, never the SQL, even with log_raw_sql. Join spans to audit records on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256; a denial is a correct answer, so the span status is OK; it is ERROR only when the request failed (any non-200 status); an incoming W3C traceparent is honored, and the span is exported only if the caller's sampled flag is set. Telemetry never slows verification: finished spans go into a bounded queue (2048 by default) and are exported in the background. When the queue is full, spans are dropped and counted in haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total.

Server.main installs the integrations (secret providers, S3/GCS sinks, signed bundles), loads the configuration, and exits 2 if anything fails. It configures telemetry, opens audit sinks, binds the listener (and the optional --health-listen port, which serves only /healthz and /readyz), and warms the OIDC key caches in the background. The accept loop gives each new connection the TLS configuration current at accept time, with a 10 second handshake limit. On SIGTERM or SIGINT it stops accepting, waits briefly for in-flight responses, does a final flush of batching audit sinks and the OTLP exporter, and exits 0. Related pages: deployment-modes.md, policy-lifecycle.md, policies-and-config.md, assurance.md.

The tenancy proof is the part of the analyzer that answers one question: can this exact SQL string ever touch a row that belongs to another tenant? If HaltSQL cannot prove the answer is "no", the query is denied. This page explains how the proof works and why it is built the way it is. The normative rules are in tenancy.md, and the design decision is ADR-0003. The code is lib/analyzer/tenancy.ml. The walker that feeds it is in lib/analyzer/walk.ml, and the parameter checks are in lib/analyzer/analyzer.ml. Note: Every example on this page is real output from haltsql verify --policy test/fixtures/policies/saas.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' --json, unless another fixture is named. That policy uses bound mode with one key, tenant: ${ctx.tenant_id}, and every app.* table except currencies and exchange_rates has tenant_column: tenant_id.

HaltSQL does not try to understand what a query means. It looks for a specific, easy-to-audit piece of evidence: for every place a tenant-scoped table is read, there must be an AND-ed equality between that table's tenant column and the caller's tenant value, in the same query level. If the evidence is there, the database itself will filter the rows. If it is missing, misplaced, or wrapped in something that might weaken it, the query is denied with a hint saying exactly what to add.

The proof works on two units. Occurrence: every place a table appears in a FROM clause or join tree. FROM orders a JOIN orders b has two occurrences of orders. Each one is checked separately, because each one reads rows separately. Scope: one query level. Every CTE body, derived table, LATERAL subquery, scalar subquery, EXISTS or IN subquery, and each branch of a UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT is its own scope. For each scope, the walker collects the occurrences in its FROM clause and, for each one, the candidate locations where a tenant predicate is allowed to live. Then Tenancy.check_level looks through those locations for a proof. The occurrence only counts if every tenant column of its table is proven.

This is the decision HaltSQL makes for each (occurrence, tenant column) pair. A few details in that chart are deliberate. Only = counts. The operator must be = (or pg_catalog.=), = ANY, or IN. <>, LIKE, IS DISTINCT FROM and anything else prove nothing. The column side must be bare. tenant_id::varchar(3) = $1 is not a proof. A cast on the column can change equality semantics (for example by truncating), so a different tenant's rows could compare equal. The value side may only use value-preserving casts. $1::text, int4, int8, bigint, uuid and a few others are stripped (see safe_cast_types in tenancy.ml). $1::varchar(3) is not, because the type modifier is invisible in the AST and could truncate the tenant ID. Literals compare exactly. In literal mode, 'acme ' and 'ACME' do not match acme. Integer literals compare after normalization, so 42 matches a context value of "42". -- Allowed, bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": "acme"}] SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1::text LIMIT 10 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING (cast with a length modifier on the value side) SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1::varchar(3) LIMIT 10 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISMATCH ("compared to a literal, but this policy uses bound mode") SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'acme' LIMIT 10

Tenancy.conjuncts flattens only AND. Every other node, including OR, NOT, CASE, function calls and COALESCE, is treated as one opaque conjunct, and an opaque conjunct cannot be a proof. The reason is simple logic. An AND conjunct must be true for a row to come back, so it really filters. A term under OR might not be true for a returned row, so it filters nothing. -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING, and E_PARAM_UNBOUND for $1 SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR status = 'open' LIMIT 10 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING (NOT and <> are both outside the accepted shapes) SELECT id FROM orders WHERE NOT (tenant_id <> $1) LIMIT 10 HAVING is never a candidate location either. It filters after grouping, by which point an aggregate may already have mixed several tenants' rows.

The most common way to get this wrong is to put the tenant filter in the outer query and assume it protects everything below it. It does not. The inner query reads the table first, and it can aggregate, join or reshape rows from every tenant before the outer filter runs. -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING on orders (loc 70, inside the subquery) SELECT * FROM ( SELECT count(*) AS n, max(tenant_id) AS tenant_id FROM orders ) x WHERE x.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 1 Here x.tenant_id is just the largest tenant ID in the whole table, and n counts every tenant's orders. The outer filter passes whenever the caller's ID happens to be the largest. The fix is to filter in the scope that reads orders. The same rule applies to correlated subqueries. A correlation such as o2.customer_id = o.customer_id does not carry the outer tenant filter inward: -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING on o2 SELECT o.id FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.status = 'refunded') LIMIT 10 -- Allowed: the same $1 is reused, bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": "acme"}] SELECT o.id FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.tenant_id = $1) LIMIT 10 Each set-operation branch is a scope too, so a UNION ALL branch without a filter is denied even when the first branch is fine. CTE bodies prove their own occurrences; a reference to the CTE by name is not a base table and needs no predicate: -- Allowed WITH r AS (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1) SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN r ON r.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10
documents.s: Why an outer WHERE does not protect a subquery

documents.t: A join's ON clause can be a candidate location, but only for the side whose rows it actually removes. The walker (walk_from in walk.ml) attaches each join's ON quals to these occurrences: Join kind ON quals are attached to INNER (or CROSS with quals) occurrences on both sides LEFT occurrences on the right (nullable) side only RIGHT occurrences on the left (nullable) side only FULL nothing USING, NATURAL nothing (NATURAL is denied as unsupported) The scope's WHERE is always a candidate location for every occurrence in the scope. Why can the ON of a LEFT JOIN not prove the left table? Because an outer join returns every row of the preserved side whether or not ON matched. The condition only decides whether the row gets a partner or NULLs. -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING on c, and params.tenant_reuse for the $1 in c.tenant_id = $1 SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND c.tenant_id = $1 AND o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 -- Allowed SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.tenant_id = $1 WHERE c.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Notice the second reason on the denied query. c.tenant_id = $1 sits in a location that cannot prove c, so that use of $1 is not part of any proof. That triggers the placeholder rule described below. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: its ON can prove the left side. For FULL JOIN, neither side can be proven by ON, so both need WHERE predicates.

An occurrence is also proven by a plain equality between its tenant column and the tenant column of another occurrence in the same SELECT that is itself proven, when both columns carry the same tenancy key: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id AND c.tenant_id = o.tenant_id WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 o has a direct predicate; c is proven through c.tenant_id = o.tenant_id. The same limits apply as for a direct predicate, and a few more: The equality must be a top-level AND condition in one of the occurrence's own locations (the WHERE, or a join ON that filters it). In customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.tenant_id = o.tenant_id, the ON does not filter c, so c still needs its own proof. Both sides must be bare column references: no cast, no COLLATE, no expression, and only the = operator. At least one occurrence in the chain needs a direct predicate. Two occurrences that are only equal to each other prove nothing. It does not cross a subquery boundary (EXISTS, IN (SELECT ...), LATERAL, CTEs), and USING (tenant_id) / NATURAL JOIN are not proofs. Write a direct predicate there. Why it is sound: the equality sits in a location that filters the occurrence, so every surviving row of c has c.tenant_id equal to the o.tenant_id of a real (not null-extended) row of o, and every such row of o carries the tenant's value. The prover starts from direct proofs and adds occurrences until nothing changes (Tenancy.transitive_proofs), so a cycle of unproven occurrences is never accepted.

In bound mode, the agent never sees the tenant ID. It writes a placeholder, and HaltSQL tells the caller what to bind. The verdict for that query: { "allowed": true, "reasons": [], "statement_kind": "select", "tables": [ "app.orders" ], "bind_params": [ { "param": 1, "value": "acme" } ] } (Other verdict fields are omitted here; see verdict.md.) How the binding is built: Each successful proof records a binding: the placeholder number, the context value, and the exact source location of that $n node (Env.add_binding). In Analyzer.finalize, bindings are grouped by placeholder. If one $n would need two different values, the query is denied with E_TENANT_MISMATCH (rule tenancy.param_conflict). Every $n that appears in the query must have a binding, otherwise E_PARAM_UNBOUND (rule params.unbound). HaltSQL must supply every bound value itself, so the agent cannot smuggle in a parameter for the caller to fill. A denied verdict carries an empty bind_params. Reusing $1 for several occurrences of the same key is fine; it is bound once. Reusing it across different keys only works when both keys resolve to the same value. With test/fixtures/policies/composite.yaml (keys org and workspace): -- context {"org_id":"o1","workspace_id":"w9"} -- Allowed, bind_params: [{"param":1,"value":"o1"},{"param":2,"value":"w9"}] SELECT id, name FROM projects WHERE org_id = $1 AND workspace_id = $2 LIMIT 20 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISMATCH (tenancy.param_conflict) SELECT id, name FROM projects WHERE org_id = $1 AND workspace_id = $1 LIMIT 20 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING (no workspace predicate) SELECT id, name FROM projects WHERE org_id = $1 LIMIT 20 That last query shows how composite keys work. A table with tenant_columns: { org_id: org, workspace_id: workspace } needs a separate proof for each column, in the same scope. A row comparison such as (org_id, workspace_id) = ($1, $2) is not recognized.

The context value for a key can be a list, for example a parent organization that may see its children. With a list: tenant_id = ANY($1) is a proof, and HaltSQL binds the whole list. The caller binds it as a Postgres array. tenant_id = $1 is not a proof, because a single placeholder cannot stand for a set. The message says so. An empty list allows nothing (E_CONTEXT_MISSING). -- context {"tenant_id":["acme","acme-eu"]} -- Allowed, bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": ["acme", "acme-eu"]}] SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = ANY($1) LIMIT 10 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING -- "... (the context holds several tenant values: use = ANY($n))" SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 In literal mode, tenant_id IN ('acme', 'acme-eu') is accepted when every literal is in the set; any literal outside it is E_TENANT_MISMATCH.

Finding a proof is not enough. Analyzer.finalize also checks that every use of a tenant placeholder is one of the proofs. It compares the location of every $n in the query with the locations recorded by the proofs. Any extra use is denied with E_PARAM_UNBOUND, rule params.tenant_reuse. -- Denied: E_PARAM_UNBOUND, rule params.tenant_reuse -- "tenant placeholder $1 is used outside a tenant predicate" SELECT id FROM orders WHERE $1::float8 IS NOT NULL AND tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 The predicate tenant_id = $1 is a perfectly good proof on its own. The problem is the other use. PostgreSQL infers one type for each parameter from how it is used. If the query also writes $1::float8, Postgres may infer $1 as float8, and the tenant comparison then happens in floating point. float8 rounds large bigint values, so a neighbouring tenant's ID could compare equal and its rows would match. The rule removes that whole class of trick: the agent cannot influence the type of the tenant parameter except through the tenant comparison itself. The same applies to status = $1, SELECT $1, or $1 = 'acme' under an OR.
documents.s: A tenant placeholder may only be a tenant value

documents.t: Writes use the same machinery, plus a few write-specific checks. The examples use test/fixtures/policies/writes.yaml, where app.tickets allows insert, update of some columns, and delete. Statement What must hold Code if not INSERT ... VALUES The column list names every tenant column, and every row sets it to the tenant value ($n in bound mode, the exact literal in literal mode) E_TENANT_WRITE INSERT ... DEFAULT VALUES on a tenant table Never allowed: it cannot set the tenant column E_TENANT_WRITE INSERT ... SELECT Not analyzed in the current version; denied E_UNSUPPORTED UPDATE Never assigns a tenant column, and its WHERE proves the target (tables in UPDATE ... FROM need their own proofs) E_TENANT_WRITE, E_TENANT_MISSING DELETE Its WHERE proves the target (tables in DELETE ... USING need their own proofs) E_TENANT_MISSING For UPDATE and DELETE, the target and the FROM/USING items form one scope whose WHERE is the candidate location, exactly like a SELECT (Tenancy.check_level is called the same way). -- Allowed, bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": "acme"}] INSERT INTO tickets (id, tenant_id, title, status) VALUES (101, $1, 'Printer down', 'open') -- Denied: E_TENANT_WRITE (bound mode: use a $n placeholder) INSERT INTO tickets (id, tenant_id, title, status) VALUES (101, 'acme', 'Printer down', 'open') -- Allowed UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE id = 7 AND tenant_id = $1 -- Denied: E_WRITE_DENIED, E_TENANT_WRITE and params.tenant_reuse UPDATE tickets SET tenant_id = $1 WHERE id = 7 AND tenant_id = $1 -- Denied: E_TENANT_MISSING DELETE FROM tickets WHERE id = 7 Note: INSERT ... SELECT is not supported: the analyzer (walk_insert in lib/analyzer/walk.ml) denies it as E_UNSUPPORTED.

analyzer.md explains the rest of the rule families the tenancy proof runs alongside. assurance.md shows how the proof is tested, including the lab that checks allowed queries against real Postgres row-level security. reason-codes.md lists every code mentioned here.

Every surface (the CLI, the HTTP sidecar, the proxy, the test runner) ends up calling the same function: val verify : Policy.t -> Context.t -> string -> Verdict.t It lives in lib/haltsql/haltsql.ml and is about fifty lines long. This page walks through it stage by stage. For the big picture see Architecture; for the inner workings of the two heavy stages see Parser and Analyzer.
verify never raises. Every stage either produces data for the next one or a reason that ends up in the verdict.

Before the SQL reaches any C code, Pg_parse.parse_unsafe (lib/parse/pg_parse.ml) applies two cheap checks: Check Limit Reason Length in bytes limits.max_bytes (default 16,384) E_LIMIT Bracket nesting ( [ hard bound of 10,000 E_LIMIT The bracket prescan is a backstop. It counts brackets everywhere, including inside string literals and comments, so it can only over-count, never miss. It exists so that absurd nesting is rejected before the C parser and the JSON reader ever see it.

The C stub (lib/pgquery/pgquery_stubs.c) rejects any input that contains a NUL byte, with E_PARSE and the message query contains a NUL byte. C strings stop at the first NUL, so libpg_query would only see the text before it, while a driver might still send the whole buffer to the server. Rejecting the input removes that gap.

libpg_query parses the string with the PostgreSQL 17 grammar and returns its parse tree as JSON. The call runs on a pool of long-lived worker threads with large stacks, and the OCaml runtime lock is released while it waits, so other domains keep working. A syntax error becomes E_PARSE, with loc set from the parser's cursor position when it is known. See Parser.

The JSON tree is measured iteratively (no recursion) before any recursive code walks it: Check Limit Reason Tree depth limits.max_depth (default 64) E_LIMIT Node count limits.max_nodes (default 20,000) E_LIMIT Measuring first means the recursive conversion only ever runs on trees of bounded size. As a last resort, a Stack_overflow or Out_of_memory while parsing is also turned into E_LIMIT, and any other exception into E_INTERNAL.

The JSON is converted into Haltsql_core.Ast. Anything the converter does not map precisely becomes an explicit Unsupported node instead of being dropped. The analyzer later denies those nodes with E_UNSUPPORTED. See Parser.

verify then looks at how many statements came back: Statements Result 0 (empty, whitespace, or only comments) E_EMPTY 1 analyze it 2 or more E_MULTI_STATEMENT, without analyzing any of them Requiring exactly one statement closes the classic SELECT ...; DROP TABLE ... attack. HaltSQL does not try to analyze each statement separately.

Analyzer.analyze walks the statement against the policy and the context. It resolves every table and column, applies every rule family, runs the tenancy proofs, and collects all violations (not just the first). It returns: reasons: every violation found, de-duplicated, in the order found; statement_kind: select, insert, update, or delete, when known; tables and columns: what the statement reads or writes, sorted and unique; bind_params: the value for each tenant placeholder $n. The analyzer has its own exception guard: any exception becomes a single E_INTERNAL reason. See Analyzer.

policy.mode allowed reasons shadow_reasons enforce (default) true exactly when there are no reasons the reasons [] shadow always true [] the reasons Shadow mode lets you roll out a new policy and watch what it would deny. It enforces nothing, so never rely on it as your only control. bind_params is filled only when the analysis found no reasons at all. In shadow mode this means a query with would-be violations comes back allowed: true with empty bind_params.

fingerprint: libpg_query's fingerprint, equal for queries that differ only in literal values. Use it to group queries in logs. It is a second full parse, so it is computed only when the input parsed into exactly one statement; oversized and malformed input stays cheap to reject. It is null otherwise, or if fingerprinting fails. sql_sha256: lower-case hex SHA-256 of the exact input string. Audit logs can refer to the query without storing it, and clients use it to check that the verdict is about the string they sent. elapsed_us: wall-clock microseconds spent in verify. Informational only; it is the one field that is not deterministic. The policy's name and version (a sha256: hash of the normalized policy) are copied into the verdict so every decision names the policy that made it.

E_INTERNAL can also come from the parse stage (unreadable parser output, or an unexpected exception) and from the outer guard in verify itself. All of these are denials. The complete list of codes is in reason-codes.md. Note that the stages before the analyzer stop at the first problem and produce a single reason, while the analyzer reports every problem it finds. A query that fails to parse tells you only that; a query that parses tells you everything that is wrong with it at once, which lets an agent fix it in one retry.
documents.s: Where each reason family can come from

documents.t: These come from the CLI (haltsql verify --json) with examples/policies/saas.yaml and the context {"tenant_id": "acme"}. Hash and timing fields are trimmed. An allowed query in bound tenancy mode: SELECT o.id, o.status FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 { "allowed": true, "reasons": [], "shadow_reasons": [], "statement_kind": "select", "tables": [ "app.orders" ], "columns": [ "app.orders.id", "app.orders.status", "app.orders.tenant_id" ], "bind_params": [ { "param": 1, "value": "acme" } ], "fingerprint": "d09f905ca477c373" } Two statements: rejected before analysis, so no fingerprint: SELECT 1; SELECT 2 { "allowed": false, "reasons": [ { "code": "E_MULTI_STATEMENT", "message": "expected exactly one statement, found 2", "rule": "statement.count", "hint": "Send a single SQL statement with no semicolon-separated extras." } ], "fingerprint": null } A syntax error, with loc pointing at the problem: { "code": "E_PARSE", "message": "syntax error at or near \"SELEC\"", "rule": "parse", "loc": 0, "hint": "Fix the SQL syntax; HaltSQL accepts PostgreSQL only." }

A verdict is only a guarantee about the exact string that was verified, with the exact parameters HaltSQL returned. The caller's side of the contract: If allowed is false, do not run the query. Return the reasons to the agent. The hint on each reason is written so a model can act on it. If allowed is true, run exactly the verified string. Do not reformat it, append to it, or template values into it. Any change means you are running SQL that was never checked. The sql_sha256 field lets you (and the SDKs) confirm the verdict matches the string. Bind bind_params in order of param. Each entry says which $n gets which value. In bound tenancy mode, the model writes o.tenant_id = $1 and never sees the tenant id; HaltSQL supplies the value from your context. value is a string, or an array of strings when the context holds a set of tenants (used with = ANY($n)). There are no other parameters to bind. A placeholder that is not a tenant predicate value is denied with E_PARAM_UNBOUND, so the model can never make you bind a value it chose. A tenant placeholder used anywhere other than its tenant predicate is denied too. Treat any failure as a denial. If the sidecar is unreachable, times out, or returns something you cannot parse, do not run the query. Log the decision. Record policy.version, fingerprint, sql_sha256, allowed, and the reason codes. The official SDKs do all of this for you; see integrations.md. The proxy does it itself: it overwrites tenancy parameters at Bind time, and on the simple query protocol (which cannot carry parameters) it denies a query that needs bind_params. See Proxy internals. Note: HaltSQL checks the SQL, not the database. Run the verified query as a restricted database role with row-level security as well. See defense-in-depth.md.
documents.s: How the caller must use the verdict

documents.t: haltsql-server exposes HaltSQL over HTTP so agents in any language can verify SQL. The machine-readable contract is openapi.yaml (OpenAPI 3.1). Everything under /v1 is covered by HaltSQL's compatibility guarantees: fields are only added, never renamed or removed. Start it with a config file, or with a single policy for local development: haltsql-server --config /etc/haltsql/config.yaml haltsql-server --policy policy.yaml --listen 127.0.0.1:8080

Requests to /v1/* are authenticated in this order (details, examples and the threat model in authentication.md): mTLS identity. With built-in TLS (server.tls) and client certificates enabled, a certificate issued by server.tls.client_ca whose SPIFFE ID (URI SAN) or subject CN matches a server.auth.mtls identity authenticates the request. The identity pins the policy and supplies a static context. A valid certificate that matches no identity falls through to bearer authentication. OIDC bearer token. A bearer token that is a JWT whose (unverified) iss equals a configured server.auth.oidc issuer is verified by that provider: signature against the provider's JWKS (RS256/RS384/RS512/PS256/ ES256/ES384/EdDSA; never none or HMAC), iss, aud, exp/nbf/iat with leeway, and required_claims. The policy is pinned by the provider or selected by a claim from allowed_policies; context_claims become the context. Static bearer token. Anything else is compared (constant time) with the SHA-256 hashes in server.auth.tokens. Authorization: Bearer <token> Every caller is pinned to exactly one policy, so it cannot pick a looser policy than the one it was given. Context from the identity is authoritative. For OIDC and mTLS callers the request body's context may only set the fields listed in the identity's request_context_fields. Any other field is refused with 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED, never silently overridden (repeating an identity-provided field with exactly the same value is accepted). Static tokens and unauthenticated requests supply the whole context in the body. Health, readiness, and metrics endpoints do not require a token; restrict them at the network level if needed, or serve the probes on a separate plain-HTTP port with --health-listen (only /healthz and /readyz are served there). If server.auth.allow_unauthenticated is true (development only), requests without a token use the policy named in the request, or default_policy.

Verify one SQL string. Request: { "sql": "SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50", "context": { "tenant_id": "acme" }, "policy": "analytics-agent" } Field Type Required Meaning sql string yes The exact SQL string to verify. context object no Context values from the caller's authenticated session: strings, integers, or arrays of those. Default {}. policy string no Policy name. For an authenticated caller it may be omitted; if given, it must equal the caller's pinned policy. Response 200 OK with the verdict JSON, for both allowed and denied queries. A denial is a normal result, not an HTTP error: { "allowed": true, "reasons": [], "shadow_reasons": [], "policy": { "name": "analytics-agent", "version": "sha256:4f1c9a..." }, "statement_kind": "select", "tables": ["app.orders"], "columns": ["app.orders.id", "app.orders.status", "app.orders.tenant_id"], "bind_params": [ { "param": 1, "value": "acme" } ], "fingerprint": "0a9d55c2e1f04b7c", "sql_sha256": "5e8f...", "elapsed_us": 94 } Errors use HTTP status codes and a JSON body: { "error": { "code": "UNAUTHORIZED", "message": "missing bearer token" } } Status error.code When 400 BAD_REQUEST Body is not JSON, sql is missing or not a string, or context is invalid. 401 UNAUTHORIZED Missing or invalid bearer token, or a JWT rejected by its OIDC provider (expired, wrong audience, bad signature, ...; the message says why). Sent with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header. 403 FORBIDDEN The requested policy is not the caller's pinned policy. 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED The body's context sets a field the caller's OIDC or mTLS identity does not allow (see Authentication). 404 POLICY_NOT_FOUND The request names an unknown policy, or names none and no default policy is configured. 404 NOT_FOUND Unknown path. 405 METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED Wrong HTTP method (with an Allow header). 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE Body exceeds limits.max_request_bytes. Checked before authentication, so an oversized request gets 413 even without a token. The connection is then closed. 500 INTERNAL Unexpected server error. 503 NOT_READY No policy is loaded. 503 POLICY_UNAVAILABLE The token's pinned policy is not currently loaded. 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE The audit record could not be written, so the request is refused (fail closed). 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE The OIDC provider's signing keys could not be fetched and no usable cached keys remain (fail closed; sent with Retry-After). The response carries a generic message; the underlying fetch error is logged server-side with the request ID. Every response carries an X-Request-Id header. Send your own X-Request-Id to correlate logs; otherwise the server generates one. Clients must treat any non-200 response, timeout, or connection error as a denial (fail closed). Example: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HALTSQL_TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql":"SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10","context":{"tenant_id":"acme"}}'

List the policies the caller may use: with a token, only its pinned policy; in unauthenticated development mode, every loaded policy. { "policies": [ { "name": "analytics-agent", "version": "sha256:4f1c9a...", "mode": "enforce" } ] }

Only when server.admin is enabled (otherwise 404 NOT_FOUND). The caller must authenticate (401) and be listed in server.admin.callers (403 FORBIDDEN otherwise): a token:<name> entry matches that static token, oidc:<provider> any token verified by that provider, and mtls:<spiffe-id or CN> the configured mTLS identity the client certificate matched. Anonymous callers never match. { "version": "0.0.1", "started": "2026-11-07T09:12:03.120Z", "uptime_seconds": 5400, "config_generation": 3, "default_policy": null, "policies": [ { "name": "remote-saas", "version": "sha256:4f1c9a...", "mode": "enforce", "origin": "bundle_source" } ], "bundle_sources": [ { "source": "oci:ghcr.io/corp/haltsql-policies:prod", "current": { "bundle": "prod", "version": "1.4.0", "signed_by": "sha256:a1b2c3d4...", "revision": "sha256:9c0e...", "origin": "source", "policies": ["remote-saas"] }, "checks": 87, "last_success": "2026-11-07T10:42:01.004Z", "last_error": null } ], "audit_sinks": [ { "name": "kafka://kafka-1:9093/haltsql.audit", "type": "kafka", "healthy": true } ], "audit_restart_pending": false, "opa": { "host": "127.0.0.1", "decision_path": "haltsql/decision", "timeout_ms": 500, "on_error": "deny" }, "report": { "tracked_queries": 412, "evicted_queries": 0, "sampled_out": 1290 } } origin is config (a policy in the config file), bundle_source, or bundle_or_file (a local bundle or a --policy file). audit_restart_pending is true when the last reload changed audit.sinks: audit sinks are opened once at startup, so records keep going to the listed running sinks until a restart (the reload also logs a warning). last_error carries the stable bundle-source code and message (policy-bundles.md). Header values and credentials are never included.

Shadow-mode analytics over the server's recent verdicts, with policy suggestions. Same authorization as /v1/admin/status. The query parameters (since, policy, suggest, top) and the response are described in shadow-reports.md. Every verdict whose audit record was written is fed into the report window.
Liveness. Returns 200 {"status":"ok"} while the process is running. Also accepts HEAD.

Readiness. Returns 200 {"status":"ready","policies":N} when at least one policy is loaded, otherwise 503 {"status":"not_ready","policies":0}. Also accepts HEAD. A failed hot reload does not make the server unready: the last good policies stay active. It is also 503 while an audit sink refuses writes: an S3/GCS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or Kafka sink in fail_closed mode after a failed delivery, or one whose buffer is full. The body then lists those sinks: {"status":"not_ready","policies":N,"unhealthy_audit_sinks":["s3://bucket/prefix/"]}. See audit-sinks.md.

Prometheus text format, when telemetry.metrics.prometheus is enabled. Metric names (stable within /v1): Metric Type Labels Meaning haltsql_build_info gauge version, pg Always 1; HaltSQL and Postgres grammar versions. haltsql_policies_loaded gauge none Number of loaded policies. haltsql_verify_total counter policy, result (allowed, denied, shadow_denied) Verify requests by outcome. haltsql_reasons_total counter code Denial and shadow-denial reasons, by reason code. haltsql_verify_duration_seconds histogram none Time spent verifying one SQL string. haltsql_policy_reload_total counter result Policy reload attempts. haltsql_audit_errors_total counter none Audit sink write failures. haltsql_http_requests_total counter route, status HTTP requests. haltsql_auth_total counter method (token, oidc, mtls, anonymous, none), result (ok, rejected, unavailable) Caller authentication attempts. haltsql_tls_reload_total counter result TLS certificate reload attempts. haltsql_opa_decisions_total counter outcome (skipped, allowed, denied, error_allowed, error_denied) OPA checks, when opa is configured (opa.md). haltsql_opa_duration_seconds summary none Time spent waiting for OPA (requests actually sent). haltsql_admin_requests_total counter endpoint (status, report), result (ok, unauthenticated, forbidden, disabled) Admin API requests. haltsql_bundle_source_healthy gauge source 1 when the last poll of the bundle source succeeded. haltsql_bundle_source_checks_total counter source Completed polls of the bundle source. S3/GCS sinks add the haltsql_audit_sink_* metrics and Elasticsearch/Kafka sinks the haltsql_audit_stream_sink_* metrics described in audit-sinks.md. Alert on any increase of haltsql_reasons_total{code="E_INTERNAL"}, haltsql_audit_errors_total, haltsql_opa_decisions_total{outcome="error_denied"}, haltsql_bundle_source_healthy == 0, and failed policy reloads.

Request size: keep requests under limits.max_request_bytes (default 1 MiB). The policy's limits.max_bytes (default 16 KiB) applies to the SQL itself and gives E_LIMIT. Hot reload: SIGHUP, or file watching (--watch / reload.watch, polled every 2 seconds), reloads policies, tokens, OIDC and mTLS settings, opa, server.admin and TLS material atomically (OIDC key caches of unchanged providers are kept). Enabling or disabling TLS, the audit sinks and the list of bundle sources need a restart (config-reference.md). Invalid policies are rejected and the last good set stays active. Audit: each request produces an audit event with the caller (token name, oidc:<provider> or mtls:<subject>), caller_type (token, oidc, mtls, anonymous), subject (OIDC sub, SPIFFE ID or certificate CN; null for static tokens), the context the statement was verified under and its context_source (authenticated when the caller's identity supplied it, request when the body did), policy version, fingerprint, SQL hash, verdict, and reason codes. Raw tokens are never logged. Raw SQL is logged only if audit.log_raw_sql is enabled. Audit is fail-closed: if an audit sink cannot be written, /v1/verify returns 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE instead of a verdict. TLS: server.tls enables built-in TLS 1.2/1.3 (ECDHE + AEAD ciphers only; min_version: "1.3" for TLS 1.3 only) with optional or required client certificates. SIGHUP or file watching reloads the certificate, key and client CA without dropping the listener; a broken or mismatched key keeps the previous material. Without server.tls, keep the listener on 127.0.0.1 inside the agent's pod, or terminate TLS in a proxy or service mesh in front of it.
The sidecar's HTTP API is small: one POST /v1/verify call per query.

Use these rather than the sketches below. Every one fails closed, checks that the verdict's sql_sha256 matches the SQL it sent, and has a guarded-execute helper that runs exactly the verified string with bind_params: Language / tool Location Guide Python (sync + async; psycopg 3, asyncpg, SQLAlchemy; local CLI verifier) clients/python sdk-python.md TypeScript / Node.js (node-postgres) clients/typescript sdk-typescript.md Go (database/sql, pgx, lib/pq) clients/go sdk-go.md Java (PgJDBC) clients/java sdk-java.md MCP server (haltsql-mcp) clients/mcp mcp.md LangChain integrations/langchain README LlamaIndex integrations/llamaindex README Vanna integrations/vanna README OpenAI Agents SDK integrations/openai_agents README LangGraph integrations/langgraph README Semantic Kernel integrations/semantic_kernel README CrewAI integrations/crewai README Google ADK (Agent Development Kit) integrations/google_adk README The four language SDKs share the same transport defaults: Python TypeScript Go Java Timeout per attempt 2 s 5 s 5 s 5 s Retries (after the first attempt) 2 (max_attempts=3) 2 2 2 Retried on connection errors, timeouts, 502/503/504 network errors, timeouts, 503 connection errors, timeouts, 503 connection errors, timeouts, 503 Private CA / mutual TLS verify=, cert= undici dispatcher WithTLSConfig sslContext() User-Agent haltsql-python/<v> haltsql-client-js/<v> haltsql-client-go/<v> haltsql-client-java/<v> In all of them TLS certificate verification is on by default, redirects are never followed, responses over 8 MiB are rejected, backoff is exponential with jitter and capped (also capping Retry-After), and the bearer token never appears in error messages or string representations. One client instance is safe to share across threads or concurrent requests and reuses connections. Clients can check their behaviour against the shared request/verdict vectors in clients/testvectors. Drivers that cannot be changed at all can connect through haltsql-proxy instead.

The snippets below show the raw protocol for languages and frameworks without an official client. They are sketches to adapt. Every integration follows the same rules: Take the context from your authenticated session, never from the model. If the verdict is not allowed, or the call fails in any way, do not run the query (fail closed). Return the reasons to the agent. If allowed, run exactly the verified SQL string, binding bind_params in order of param. Run it as a restricted database role with RLS (see defense-in-depth.md).

import os import requests import psycopg HALTSQL_URL = os.environ.get("HALTSQL_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8080") HALTSQL_TOKEN = os.environ["HALTSQL_TOKEN"] class QueryDenied(Exception): def __init__(self, reasons): super().__init__("; ".join(f'{r["code"]}: {r.get("hint") or r["message"]}' for r in reasons)) self.reasons = reasons def verify(sql: str, context: dict) -> dict: try: resp = requests.post( f"{HALTSQL_URL}/v1/verify", json={"sql": sql, "context": context}, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {HALTSQL_TOKEN}"}, timeout=2, ) except requests.RequestException as e: raise QueryDenied([{"code": "E_INTERNAL", "message": f"haltsql unavailable: {e}"}]) if resp.status_code != 200: raise QueryDenied([{"code": "E_INTERNAL", "message": f"haltsql HTTP {resp.status_code}"}]) verdict = resp.json() if verdict.get("allowed") is not True: raise QueryDenied(verdict.get("reasons", [])) return verdict def run_agent_sql(conn: psycopg.Connection, sql: str, tenant_id: str): verdict = verify(sql, {"tenant_id": tenant_id}) params = [p["value"] for p in sorted(verdict["bind_params"], key=lambda p: p["param"])] with conn.transaction(): conn.execute("SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY") conn.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', %s, true)", [tenant_id]) # RawCursor (psycopg >= 3.2) sends the SQL text unchanged with native $n # placeholders, so Postgres receives exactly the verified string. with psycopg.RawCursor(conn) as cur: cur.execute(sql, params) return cur.fetchall() Note on placeholders: HaltSQL verifies Postgres $n syntax. Use a driver path that sends the SQL text unchanged with positional parameters (psycopg's RawCursor, asyncpg's fetch(sql, *params), node-postgres, pgx). Never string-format values into the SQL.

import { Pool } from "pg"; const HALTSQL_URL = process.env.HALTSQL_URL ?? "http://127.0.0.1:8080"; const HALTSQL_TOKEN = process.env.HALTSQL_TOKEN!; type Reason = { code: string; message: string; hint?: string; loc?: number }; type Verdict = { allowed: boolean; reasons: Reason[]; bind_params: { param: number; value: string | string[] }[]; }; export class QueryDenied extends Error { constructor(public reasons: Reason[]) { super(reasons.map((r) => `${r.code}: ${r.hint ?? r.message}`).join("; ")); } } export async function verify(sql: string, context: Record<string, unknown>): Promise<Verdict> { let res: Response; try { res = await fetch(`${HALTSQL_URL}/v1/verify`, { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: `Bearer ${HALTSQL_TOKEN}` }, body: JSON.stringify({ sql, context }), signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000), }); } catch (e) { throw new QueryDenied([{ code: "E_INTERNAL", message: `haltsql unavailable: ${e}` }]); } if (res.status !== 200) { throw new QueryDenied([{ code: "E_INTERNAL", message: `haltsql HTTP ${res.status}` }]); } const verdict = (await res.json()) as Verdict; if (verdict.allowed !== true) throw new QueryDenied(verdict.reasons ?? []); return verdict; } export async function runAgentSql(pool: Pool, sql: string, tenantId: string) { const verdict = await verify(sql, { tenant_id: tenantId }); const params = [...verdict.bind_params].sort((a, b) => a.param - b.param).map((p) => p.value); const client = await pool.connect(); try { await client.query("BEGIN READ ONLY"); await client.query("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)", [tenantId]); const result = await client.query(sql, params); // node-postgres sends $n SQL unchanged await client.query("COMMIT"); return result.rows; } catch (e) { await client.query("ROLLBACK"); throw e; } finally { client.release(); } }

package haltsqlclient import ( "bytes" "context" "encoding/json" "fmt" "net/http" "sort" "time" ) type Reason struct { Code string `json:"code"` Message string `json:"message"` Hint string `json:"hint,omitempty"` } type BindParam struct { Param int `json:"param"` Value json.RawMessage `json:"value"` // string, or array of strings } type Verdict struct { Allowed bool `json:"allowed"` Reasons []Reason `json:"reasons"` BindParams []BindParam `json:"bind_params"` } type Client struct { URL string Token string HTTP *http.Client } func New(url, token string) *Client { return &Client{URL: url, Token: token, HTTP: &http.Client{Timeout: 2 * time.Second}} } // Verify returns the verdict, or an error if the query must not run. // Any transport or HTTP error is treated as a denial. func (c *Client) Verify(ctx context.Context, sql string, sessionCtx map[string]any) (*Verdict, error) { body, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"sql": sql, "context": sessionCtx}) req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, c.URL+"/v1/verify", bytes.NewReader(body)) if err != nil { return nil, err } req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json") req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.Token) resp, err := c.HTTP.Do(req) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("haltsql unavailable: %w", err) } defer resp.Body.Close() if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK { return nil, fmt.Errorf("haltsql HTTP %d", resp.StatusCode) } var v Verdict if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&v); err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("haltsql bad response: %w", err) } if !v.Allowed { return &v, fmt.Errorf("query denied: %v", v.Reasons) } sort.Slice(v.BindParams, func(i, j int) bool { return v.BindParams[i].Param < v.BindParams[j].Param }) return &v, nil } With pgx, run the verified string with tx.Query(ctx, sql, args...), decoding each BindParam.Value into a string or []string.

Expose a single "run SQL" tool whose implementation always verifies first and returns the reasons on denial, so the model can correct itself: from langchain_core.tools import tool def make_sql_tool(conn, session): @tool def run_sql(sql: str) -> str: """Run one read-only PostgreSQL SELECT. Use $1 wherever the tenant ID is needed (for example `WHERE o.tenant_id = $1`), qualify every column with a table alias, and always include LIMIT.""" try: rows = run_agent_sql(conn, sql, tenant_id=session.tenant_id) except QueryDenied as e: return "Query rejected. Fix it and try again:\n" + "\n".join( f'- {r["code"]}: {r.get("hint") or r["message"]}' for r in e.reasons ) return format_rows(rows, max_rows=50) return run_sql Notes: The tenant ID comes from session, captured when the tool is created. The model cannot pass it. The tool description teaches the model the policy's conventions (bound tenancy, aliases, LIMIT), which reduces denials. Cap retries (for example three attempts) so a model stuck in a loop does not burn tokens.

An MCP server can expose a query tool guarded by HaltSQL. The MCP server holds the database connection and the caller's identity; the model only supplies SQL. from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP mcp = FastMCP("haltsql-guarded-postgres") @mcp.tool() def query(sql: str) -> str: """Run one read-only SQL SELECT against the analytics database. Use $1 for the tenant ID, alias every table, and include LIMIT <= 1000.""" tenant_id = current_identity().tenant_id # from the MCP session's auth, not from the model try: rows = run_agent_sql(get_conn(), sql, tenant_id) except QueryDenied as e: return "Rejected by policy:\n" + "\n".join( f'- {r["code"]}: {r.get("hint") or r["message"]}' for r in e.reasons ) return to_markdown_table(rows) if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run() Expose a second read-only tool, such as describe_schema, that returns only the tables and columns in the policy, so the model does not guess names.

haltsql-server produces two kinds of output: a hash-chained audit log (one record per verify request, the compliance record) and telemetry (Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, logs). This page gives a recipe per destination, and shows how to reach a SIEM through the destinations HaltSQL supports. The references are audit-sinks.md, audit-verify.md and observability.md. Destinations covered: Audit: Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Apache Kafka, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch Telemetry: OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus SIEMs (Splunk, Datadog, Microsoft Sentinel, ...)

Destination Native Byte-exact, verifiable copy Survives a crash Use for stdout, file yes yes file: yes (appended per record) log pipelines; the source for most SIEM agents Amazon S3 (and S3-compatible stores) yes, type: s3 yes, with optional Object Lock with spool_dir the compliance archive on AWS or MinIO Google Cloud Storage yes, type: gcs yes, with a bucket retention policy with spool_dir the compliance archive on GCP Apache Kafka yes, type: kafka yes (message values are the exact records) no (in-memory queue) feeding SIEM and data-lake pipelines Elasticsearch, OpenSearch yes, type: elasticsearch yes, through event.original no (in-memory queue) search, dashboards, detection rules Splunk, Datadog, Sentinel, other SIEMs no depends on the forwarder depends on the forwarder detection, through one of the destinations above OpenTelemetry Collector yes, telemetry.otlp (telemetry, not audit) traces and metrics to any OTLP backend Prometheus yes, GET /metrics (telemetry, not audit) metrics and alerts Every audit sink keeps its own hash chain, and sinks can be combined: list them all under audit.sinks. A common production setup is one verifiable archive (S3 or GCS with a spool directory, in fail_closed mode) plus one detection feed (Kafka or Elasticsearch, in buffer mode). Audit sinks are fixed at startup; changing audit.sinks needs a restart. Each record looks like this (sql only appears with audit.log_raw_sql: true): {"ts":"2026-11-07T12:00:00Z","request_id":"...","caller":"oidc:corp-okta","caller_type":"oidc", "subject":"00u1abcd","policy":"support-bot","policy_version":"sha256:4f1c...","allowed":false, "shadow":false,"codes":["E_TENANT_MISSING"],"sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"0a9d55c2e1f04b7c", "elapsed_us":183,"prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} Note: haltsql-proxy supports the stdout, file, s3 and gcs sinks with the same keys, but not elasticsearch or kafka (proxy.md).

Config. audit: sinks: - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 prefix: haltsql/audit/ object_lock: { mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 365 } credentials: { source: web_identity } # env | static | web_identity | instance spool_dir: /var/lib/haltsql/spool/s3 # persistent volume, one per sink batch: { max_records: 500, max_seconds: 10 } on_error: fail_closed Records are batched into objects named <prefix>YYYY/MM/DD/HH/<host>-<run>-<seq>-<sha256>.jsonl, uploaded strictly in order with create-only PUTs. For S3-compatible stores (MinIO, Ceph), set endpoint; requests then use path-style URLs. Bucket and IAM. Create the bucket with Object Lock enabled if you use object_lock (S3 refuses the lock headers otherwise). The identity needs: {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:PutObjectRetention"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/*"} Credentials come from credentials.source: env (default), static (use secret placeholders), web_identity (EKS IRSA) or instance (EC2 IMDSv2). ECS task roles and EKS Pod Identity are not supported by the S3 sink; see Audit on ECS for the alternatives. Verify. Read the objects straight from the bucket (the identity needs s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject): haltsql audit verify --region eu-west-1 s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/ # one day only: the chain starts mid-stream haltsql audit verify --region eu-west-1 --any-start s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/2026/11/07/ Alerts. haltsql_audit_sink_healthy{sink="s3://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/"} == 0, rate(haltsql_audit_sink_upload_failures_total[5m]) > 0 and haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects > 0 for longer than a few max_seconds. Details: S3.

Config. audit: sinks: - type: gcs bucket: corp-haltsql-audit prefix: haltsql/audit/ credentials: { source: metadata } # or { source: service_account_file, file: /var/run/gcp/key.json } spool_dir: /var/lib/haltsql/spool/gcs on_error: fail_closed Objects have the same names and ordering as for S3, and are uploaded with ifGenerationMatch=0 so an existing object is never overwritten. Bucket and IAM. Grant the identity roles/storage.objectCreator on the bucket. For WORM storage, set a bucket retention policy and lock it (Bucket Lock). On GKE, use Workload Identity with source: metadata. Verify. GCS is not read directly by haltsql audit verify; download the objects and verify the directory: gcloud storage cp -r gs://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/ ./audit/ haltsql audit verify ./audit/ Alerts. The same haltsql_audit_sink_* metrics as S3, with sink="gs://corp-haltsql-audit/haltsql/audit/". Details: GCS.

Config. audit: sinks: - type: kafka brokers: [kafka-1.corp.example:9093, kafka-2.corp.example:9093] topic: haltsql.audit client_id: haltsql-prod acks: all tls: { ca_file: /etc/haltsql/kafka/ca.pem } sasl: { mechanism: scram-sha-512, username: haltsql, password: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/kafka#password}" } on_error: buffer max_buffer_records: 20000 Each record is one message whose value is the exact sealed record and whose key is the chain id haltsql/<host>/<run>, so a process's records stay in one partition, in order. Broker side. Create the topic first; HaltSQL never creates topics. Use cleanup.policy=delete with a long retention. Never use compaction: all records of a chain share one key. Grant the principal Write and Describe on the topic: kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server … --add --allow-principal User:haltsql \ --operation Write --operation Describe --topic haltsql.audit Supported: TLS (with optional client certificates), SASL PLAIN, SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-512, acks: all or 1, Kafka 1.0 and later (tested against Apache Kafka 3.9). Not supported: compression, transactions, the idempotent producer, OAUTHBEARER (and the IAM mechanisms of managed services built on it) and GSSAPI/Kerberos. A managed Kafka service works if it offers one of the supported SASL mechanisms; such services are not tested. Delivery is at least once. A retried batch can appear twice in the partition. Verify with --allow-redelivery or the repository's verifier script, which skip exact re-deliveries. Verify. kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 \ --consumer.config client.properties --topic haltsql.audit --from-beginning \ --timeout-ms 30000 --property print.key=true --property key.separator=$'\t' > audit.tsv python3 verify_chain.py kafka audit.tsv verify_chain.py is test/siem/verify_chain.py. Alerts. haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy == 0, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivering == 0, rate(haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 (labels sink="kafka://kafka-1.corp.example:9093/haltsql.audit", type="kafka"). Details: Kafka.

Config. audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch urls: [https://es-1.corp.example:9200, https://es-2.corp.example:9200] data_stream: logs-haltsql-prod # or index: haltsql-audit auth: { api_key: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/es#api_key}" } tls: { ca_file: /etc/haltsql/es-ca.pem } on_error: buffer The sink only uses the _bulk API with create actions whose _id is the record's hash. Each document holds the record's fields (searchable) and event.original, the exact sealed line. Cluster side. Create an API key whose role can only create documents: {"haltsql-audit": {"indices": [{"names": ["logs-haltsql-*"], "privileges": ["create_doc", "auto_configure"]}]}} Put the index under an ILM policy without a delete phase, or snapshot it to a WORM repository, if it must not be deleted. With an index instead of a data stream, create an index template first or rely on dynamic mapping. Verify. Export the documents and check them against event.original: curl -s --cacert es-ca.pem -H "Authorization: ApiKey $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ "https://es-1.corp.example:9200/logs-haltsql-prod/_search" \ -d '{"size":10000,"query":{"range":{"@timestamp":{"gte":"2026-11-07","lt":"2026-11-08"}}}}' > day.json python3 verify_chain.py es --any-start day.json An ingest pipeline that adds or changes fields makes the field check fail even though event.original verifies; enrich into a separate index instead. Alerts. The haltsql_audit_stream_sink_* metrics with type="elasticsearch". Watch haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total{reason="mapping"}: a field that changes type is dropped, which leaves a gap in the chain. Details: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch.

OpenSearch uses the same type: elasticsearch sink: it only needs the _bulk API. audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch url: https://opensearch.corp.example:9200 index: haltsql-audit # or data_stream:, with a matching index template auth: { username: haltsql, password: "${aws-sm:prod/haltsql/opensearch#password}" } tls: { ca_file: /etc/haltsql/opensearch-ca.pem } on_error: buffer Authentication is basic auth (username/password) for OpenSearch's security plugin. Give the user a role that can write (create) documents in the index; see the OpenSearch security documentation. Not supported: AWS SigV4 request signing, so Amazon OpenSearch Service domains that only accept IAM-signed requests cannot be used. A domain with fine-grained access control and an internal user (basic auth) can. Tested against OpenSearch 2.17 (index and data stream) without the security plugin; TLS and authentication are tested against Elasticsearch. Verification and metrics are as for Elasticsearch.

HaltSQL pushes traces and metrics over OTLP/HTTP with JSON encoding to <endpoint>/v1/traces and <endpoint>/v1/metrics. gRPC is not supported. HaltSQL config. telemetry: otlp: endpoint: http://otel-collector.observability:4318 headers: authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/otel#token}" service_name: haltsql-support-bot traces: true metrics: true export_interval_seconds: 15 timeout_seconds: 5 telemetry.otlp is applied on reload. Header values are treated as secrets and never logged. Collector config. The otlp receiver with the http protocol accepts it; route the data to any exporter your backend supports: receivers: otlp: protocols: http: endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318 processors: batch: {} exporters: debug: {} # replace with your backend's exporter service: pipelines: traces: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [debug] } metrics: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [debug] } Complete collector deployments are in deploy/cloud/gcp/gke/otel-collector.yaml (Google Cloud exporter) and deploy/cloud/azure/aks/otel-collector.yaml (Azure Monitor). What you get. One SERVER span named haltsql.verify per verify request, with haltsql.policy, haltsql.allowed, haltsql.reason_codes and db.statement.sha256 (never the SQL text), joined to the caller's trace through traceparent. Metrics have the same names as on /metrics. Join a span to its audit record on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256. Spans are dropped, never queued without bound, when the collector is slow: alert on rate(haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 in your OTLP backend (this metric is exported over OTLP only, not on /metrics). Verification is never slowed down by telemetry. Details: OpenTelemetry export.
