GET /metrics serves the Prometheus text format on the main listener when telemetry.metrics.prometheus is true (the default; --no-metrics turns it off). It needs no bearer token, so restrict who can reach it with network policy. It is not served on the --health-listen port. Scrape config. scrape_configs: - job_name: haltsql metrics_path: /metrics scheme: https # http when HaltSQL has no server.tls tls_config: ca_file: /etc/prometheus/haltsql-ca.pem # With server.tls.client_auth: required, Prometheus must present a # certificate signed by server.tls.client_ca: cert_file: /etc/prometheus/haltsql-client.crt key_file: /etc/prometheus/haltsql-client.key static_configs: - targets: ['haltsql.internal:8443'] On Kubernetes with the Helm chart, set serviceMonitor.enabled: true (Prometheus Operator) or podMonitoring.enabled: true (Google Managed Prometheus; not with the chart's TLS), and allow the scraper in networkPolicy.metricsFrom. Metric names. Metric Type Labels haltsql_build_info gauge version, pg haltsql_policies_loaded gauge haltsql_verify_total counter policy, result (allowed, denied, shadow_denied) haltsql_reasons_total counter code haltsql_verify_duration_seconds histogram haltsql_policy_reload_total counter result (success, error) haltsql_audit_errors_total counter haltsql_http_requests_total counter route, status haltsql_auth_total counter method (token, oidc, mtls, anonymous, none), result (ok, rejected, unavailable) haltsql_tls_reload_total counter result haltsql_opa_decisions_total counter outcome (skipped, allowed, denied, error_allowed, error_denied) haltsql_opa_duration_seconds summary haltsql_admin_requests_total counter endpoint, result haltsql_bundle_source_healthy gauge source haltsql_bundle_source_checks_total counter source haltsql_audit_sink_healthy, haltsql_audit_sink_buffered_records, haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects gauge sink (S3/GCS sinks) haltsql_audit_sink_objects_uploaded_total, haltsql_audit_sink_upload_failures_total, haltsql_audit_sink_rejected_writes_total counter sink haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivering, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_buffered_records gauge sink, type (Kafka/Elasticsearch sinks) haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_written_total, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_delivered_total, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivery_failures_total, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_retries_total, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_rejected_writes_total counter sink, type haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total counter sink, type, reason (mapping, too_large, on_error_drop) haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total is exported over OTLP only. The sink metrics only appear when such a sink is configured. Suggested alerts. groups: - name: haltsql rules: - alert: HaltSQLAuditSinkUnhealthy # requests are getting 503 expr: haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0 or haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy == 0 for: 1m - alert: HaltSQLAuditErrors expr: rate(haltsql_audit_errors_total[5m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLAuditDeliveryFailing # also in buffer and drop modes expr: haltsql_audit_stream_sink_delivering == 0 for: 5m - alert: HaltSQLAuditRecordsDropped # gaps in a streaming sink's chain expr: rate(haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLAuditUploadsStuck expr: haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects > 0 for: 10m - alert: HaltSQLInternalError expr: increase(haltsql_reasons_total{code="E_INTERNAL"}[5m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLPolicyReloadFailed # the last good config is still active expr: increase(haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}[10m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLBundleSourceUnhealthy expr: haltsql_bundle_source_healthy == 0 for: 10m - alert: HaltSQLIdPKeysUnavailable # OIDC callers are getting 503 expr: rate(haltsql_auth_total{method="oidc",result="unavailable"}[5m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLOPAErrorsDenied expr: increase(haltsql_opa_decisions_total{outcome="error_denied"}[5m]) > 0 - alert: HaltSQLSlowVerification expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.05 for: 10m - alert: HaltSQLDown expr: up{job="haltsql"} == 0 for: 2m Add severities, labels and routing to suit your Alertmanager. For dashboards, haltsql_verify_total by result and haltsql_reasons_total by code show what agents attempt and why it is denied; result="shadow_denied" shows what a shadow-mode policy would deny before you enforce it.

HaltSQL has no native Splunk, Datadog or Microsoft Sentinel integration. It reaches them through the destinations above: the SIEM's own collector reads the records from a file, container stdout, a Kafka topic or a bucket. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch are native destinations, so their security tooling can query the index directly. SIEM Supported route (configure the SIEM side with its vendor's documentation) Splunk A kafka sink and Splunk's Kafka connector; or an s3 sink and Splunk's AWS add-on; or a file/stdout sink and a Splunk forwarder or collector. Datadog A file or stdout sink collected by the Datadog Agent's log collection; or an s3 sink with Datadog's S3 log forwarding. Microsoft Sentinel A stdout sink collected into Log Analytics (for example by Container Insights on AKS), or a file sink shipped by an agent. See Deploying on Azure. Elastic Security, OpenSearch Security Analytics The elasticsearch sink, natively. Anything that consumes Kafka, S3 or GCS The matching sink. Things to keep in mind: Keep a verifiable copy outside the SIEM. Forwarders and SIEMs parse and re-serialize JSON, so the stored record may no longer be the exact bytes the hash covers, and SIEM retention is usually shorter than audit retention. Treat the SIEM copy as the detection feed, and keep a separate s3/gcs (with a spool directory), file or kafka sink as the record you verify with haltsql audit verify or verify_chain.py. Do not let the SIEM path stop verification. Give the detection sink on_error: buffer (or, for kafka and elasticsearch sinks, drop, only next to a fail_closed sink), so a SIEM outage does not turn into 503s. Raw SQL stays out by default. Records carry sql_sha256 and the fingerprint, not the SQL, unless audit.log_raw_sql: true. Leave it off unless the SIEM is cleared to hold query literals. Useful detections, on the record fields: Detection Condition Tenant bypass attempts codes contains E_TENANT_MISSING or E_TENANT_MISMATCH Probing for sensitive data repeated E_COLUMN_DENIED or E_TABLE_DENIED for one caller or subject Write attempts by a read-only agent codes contains E_STATEMENT_KIND or E_WRITE_DENIED Unexpected callers caller_type is anonymous in production, or an unknown caller Engine faults codes contains E_INTERNAL Policy drift a policy_version you did not deploy Reason codes are listed in reason-codes.md.

Audit sinks: sink internals, failure modes, spool directories and metrics. Verifying audit chains: haltsql audit verify. Observability: OTLP export, traces and metric semantics. Config reference: audit and telemetry. HTTP API: GET /metrics. Secrets managers: credentials for sinks and collectors.

haltsql-crewai gives a CrewAI agent a haltsql_query tool that runs read-only SQL only after HaltSQL has verified it. The tenant comes from a mapping or callable you give the tool when you build the crew for a request. It never comes from crew inputs, task text or tool arguments.

Name Kind What it does HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=..., context=...) CrewAI BaseTool A tool named haltsql_query whose only argument is query. Verifies, then runs the exact SQL in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. Returns JSON text. HaltSQLToolRunner Class Holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits. Shared by all five agent-framework packages. See The runner. context_from_app(app_state, key="haltsql_context") Function Reads and validates a context stored under a key of an object or mapping. Useful inside your own context callable. ContextUnavailable Exception Raised inside the package when no context is available. You see it as a refusal. TOOL_NAME, DEFAULT_CONTEXT_KEY Constants "haltsql_query" and "haltsql_context". The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize and guard.execute.

The package needs Python 3.10 to 3.13 and crewai 1.15 or newer, below 2. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e integrations/crewai The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

import os import psycopg from crewai import Agent, Crew, Task from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_crewai import HaltSQLQueryTool, HaltSQLToolRunner DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) def answer(user, question: str) -> str: tool = HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=runner, context={"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}) analyst = Agent(role="Analyst", goal="Answer questions about the user's orders", backstory="Writes careful SQL.", tools=[tool]) task = Task(description=question, expected_output="A short answer", agent=analyst) return str(Crew(agents=[analyst], tasks=[task]).kickoff()) user is your authenticated user. The runner is shared. The tool, and the crew that uses it, are built per request with that request's context.

context is either a mapping or a zero-argument callable. A callable is evaluated on every call, for example one that reads the current session from a contextvars.ContextVar: tool = HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=runner, context=lambda: {"tenant_id": session.tenant_id}) Do not take the tenant from crew inputs (kickoff(inputs=...)) or task text: the model can read and influence both. context Result A mapping, or a callable that returns one The query is verified with that context. A callable that returns None Refused before verification: "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run". {}, or a callable that returns {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. Not a mapping or callable TypeError when you create the tool. The argument schema forbids extra fields. If the model sends tenant_id as well as query, the call fails validation and nothing runs.

The tool returns JSON text. On success: {"status":"ok","executed":true,"columns":["id","status"],"rows":[[1,"open"],[3,"paid"]],"row_count":2,"truncated":false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason with its code and hint: {"status":"denied","executed":false, "reasons":[{"code":"E_TENANT_MISMATCH","message":"...","hint":"Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message":"HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} Other failures have "status": "error". With "executed": false, nothing ran: HaltSQL was unavailable, no context was configured, the statement was not a SELECT, or the database could not be reached. With "executed": true, HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example on a statement timeout. See reason-codes.md for every code.

HaltSQLToolRunner(verifier, connect, *, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). connect required Zero-argument callable that returns a new psycopg 3 connection. Called only after HaltSQL allows the query. The runner closes the connection after each query. max_rows 200 Row cap, 1 to 100000. truncated tells the model more rows were available. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query, 1 to 3600000. settings None Transaction-local settings: a mapping, or a function of the verified context, for example lambda ctx: {"app.tenant_id": ctx["tenant_id"]} for row-level security. HaltSQLQueryTool fields (keyword arguments): Field Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLToolRunner. context required A mapping, or a zero-argument callable that returns a mapping or None. name "haltsql_query" Tool name the model sees. description built-in text Tool description the model sees. runner and context are excluded from the tool's serialized form, and context is left out of its repr. Other BaseTool fields work as usual. Every query runs in a READ ONLY transaction, and only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select are run. These cannot be turned off.

The tool implements both _run and _arun. The async path runs verification and execution in a worker thread (asyncio.to_thread), so the event loop is not blocked. Use a sync verifier and a sync psycopg connection either way. Rows are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and call the tool directly: import json from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_crewai import HaltSQLQueryTool, HaltSQLToolRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): tool = HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=HaltSQLToolRunner(FakeVerifier(deny), no_db), context={"tenant_id": "acme"}) out = json.loads(tool.run(query="SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10")) assert out["status"] == "denied" and out["reasons"][0]["code"] == "E_TENANT_MISSING" The package's own tests use BaseTool.run, the structured-tool path and a real Agent, with the real haltsql CLI, a real haltsql-server and the lab Postgres. They never call an LLM: make -C lab up dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./bin/server/main.exe ONLY=agents clients/python/run-all-tests.sh integrations/crewai/constraints.txt lists the exact versions the tests were run with. See Testing.

Symptom Cause Fix "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run" The context callable returned None, or raised a LookupError. Build the tool per request with that request's context. Every query on a tenant table is denied The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs (E_CONTEXT_MISSING), or the model wrote a tenant literal (E_TENANT_MISMATCH). Check the context. In bound mode the model must write $1. A validation error about extra inputs, or "pass exactly one argument, 'query'" The model sent an argument other than query. Nothing to fix in your code; the call was rejected and nothing ran. "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string. An unexpected exception in the context callable is also reported this way. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary. Test the callable on its own. "The database is unavailable" connect raised. Check the DSN and network. TypeError: context must be a mapping or a zero-argument callable context was a string or another type. Pass a mapping or a callable. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

Read-only SELECT only. Write policies are not supported by this tool. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. Python 3.14 is not supported (the package requires Python below 3.14). HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.
Agent frameworks: what all five packages share. Python SDK: verifiers, guard.execute and errors. reason-codes.md and tenancy.md. defense-in-depth.md. Source: integrations/crewai.

Your data catalog already knows which columns hold personal data. HaltSQL turns those labels into a starter policy that leaves the labelled columns out, so an agent cannot read them. This page gives one recipe per catalog; the commands themselves are documented in schema-and-pii.md. Catalogs covered: dbt DataHub Databricks Unity Catalog Atlan Collibra OpenMetadata Catalog schema import (export file) in 0.0.1 schema fetch (live API) dbt yes: manifest.json, catalog.json no (dbt Cloud is not covered) DataHub yes: file-sink exports, GraphQL responses with the catalog live-fetch work Unity Catalog yes: column_tags rows, table JSON no Atlan yes: asset search results no Collibra yes: asset exports no OpenMetadata no with the catalog live-fetch work (an importer arrives at the same time)

Every catalog follows the same five steps. Only step 2 differs. # 1. Structure: snapshot the real tables and columns from PostgreSQL. PGPASSWORD=... haltsql schema pull --dsn postgres://ro@db.internal:5432/app \ --schema app -o policies/catalog.json # 2. Labels: turn the catalog's PII labels into a PII manifest (one per catalog). haltsql schema import --from dbt target/manifest.json -o policies/pii.dbt.json haltsql schema import --from unity column_tags.json -o policies/pii.unity.json # 3. Draft: every table, with the labelled columns left out. haltsql policy draft --catalog policies/catalog.json \ --pii policies/pii.dbt.json --pii policies/pii.unity.json \ --tenant-column tenant_id --schema app -o policies/agent.yaml # 4. Lint. haltsql lint-policy policies/agent.yaml # 5. Test: prove the labelled columns are denied. haltsql test policies/agent.test.yaml Structure always comes from PostgreSQL, labels from the catalog. The analyzer trusts a typed snapshot as the complete column list of each table (that is how it expands SELECT *). A catalog that has not yet crawled a new column would turn that trust into a leak, so HaltSQL never takes structure from a catalog. See Security model. What the draft looks like. Run against the sample manifest.json and column_tags.json in examples/metadata/, the draft for app.customers is: # excluded email (dbt+unity: pii, pii=email; name matches "email") # excluded phone (dbt+unity: class.phone_number, governance.sensitivity=restricted; name matches "phone") app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name, country, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id Each comment names the catalogs and labels that flagged the column. Several manifests are merged; a column flagged by any of them is left out. Columns are also left out when their name matches a heuristic (email, phone, ssn, ...); --no-name-heuristics turns that off. Review the draft before use: see Review before use. A test suite for step 5. Add one denied-column case for each column the catalog flagged, and one allowed case, so a later redraft that loses a label fails CI: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: TestSuite metadata: name: agent-pii policy: agent.yaml defaults: context: { tenant_id: acme } cases: - name: tagged column is denied sql: SELECT email FROM app.customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 expect: deny codes: [E_COLUMN_DENIED] - name: SELECT * would read a tagged column sql: SELECT * FROM app.customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 expect: deny codes: [E_COLUMN_DENIED] - name: untagged columns are allowed sql: SELECT id, name FROM app.customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 expect: allow bind: [{ param: 1, value: acme }] The suite format is in testing.md.

The rules are the same for every catalog (details): Labels are split into lower-case words on non-alphanumeric characters and camelCase boundaries. A term matches when its words appear consecutively: pii matches contains_pii, urn:li:tag:PII and pii_email, but not piiset. A single-word term of three or more letters also matches the acronym of a multi-word label, so Personally Identifiable Information matches pii. Key/value metadata becomes key (true values) or key=value. false, null, no, 0 and empty values do not count, so meta: {pii: false} does not flag a column. The default terms are pii, sensitive, confidential, restricted, gdpr, phi, pci, personal, email, phone, ssn, secret. --pii-tag and --pii-term replace the defaults; to add a term, repeat the defaults you want to keep.

Names must line up. Manifests are keyed by schema.table; the database or catalog name is ignored. If the catalog's schema or table name differs from PostgreSQL's, the label is lost. policy draft warns PII column app.users.email is not in the catalog for each label it could not place: treat those warnings as failures until each is explained. Two databases, one schema name. Because the database name is ignored, an export that covers staging.app.users and prod.app.users merges both into app.users. Export one database at a time. Wrong --from. A file in which the importer finds no column metadata at all exits 1. With -o, --json prints scanned_columns and pii_columns; a scan count far below your column count means the export is incomplete. Untagged sensitive data is only caught by the column-name heuristics. A catalog is a good source of labels, not a complete one.

What HaltSQL reads. From target/manifest.json: models, seeds, snapshots and sources (tests are ignored). Per column: tags, meta, config.tags, config.meta and policy_tags, including nested meta such as {governance: {sensitivity: restricted}}. The table is the node's schema plus its alias, identifier or name. From target/catalog.json: column comments, matched word by word and recorded as comment:<term>. Obtaining the input. dbt writes manifest.json to target/ on every dbt parse, dbt compile, dbt run or dbt build. catalog.json comes from dbt docs generate and holds the comments the database returns, which are your dbt descriptions only when persist_docs is enabled. Command. dbt parse --target prod haltsql schema import --from dbt target/manifest.json -o policies/pii.dbt.json # optional: column comments from the database dbt docs generate --target prod haltsql schema import --from dbt target/catalog.json -o policies/pii.dbt-comments.json Labels that match. From the sample dbt_manifest.json: columns: - name: email tags: [pii] # -> pii meta: { pii: true } # -> pii - name: phone config: meta: { governance: { sensitivity: restricted } } # -> governance.sensitivity=restricted - name: ssn tags: [gdpr] # -> gdpr meta: { classification: confidential } # -> classification=confidential - name: full_name policy_tags: [pii_name] # -> pii_name - name: password_hash meta: { security: secret } # -> security=secret - name: name meta: { pii: false } # does not count The sample is shown as YAML, the way you write it in a dbt properties file; the manifest holds the same values as JSON. Pitfalls. Use the target you deploy. The table key uses the schema dbt resolved for the target you parsed with. A manifest parsed with a dev target names dbt_alice.customers, which matches nothing in production. Parse with the production target, or the target whose schemas you pulled. Descriptions in manifest.json are not read in 0.0.1. A description such as "Primary contact email" only counts through catalog.json, and only when persist_docs wrote it to the database as a comment. dbt Cloud (the Discovery API) is not supported. Download the manifest.json artifact of a production job run and import it as above.

What HaltSQL reads. Tags (urn:li:tag:*) and glossary terms (urn:li:glossaryTerm:*, plus their name or properties.name) on the fields of schemaMetadata (set by ingestion) and editableSchemaMetadata (set in the UI or through the API). The table is the last two dot-separated parts of the dataset URN's name: urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:postgres,saas.app.customers,PROD) becomes app.customers. v2 field paths such as [version=2.0].[type=struct].[type=string].phone are reduced to phone. Dataset-level tags do not count. Obtaining the input. Two shapes are accepted, in any number in one JSON document: Ingestion file sink. Run your PostgreSQL ingestion recipe with DataHub's file sink instead of the REST sink. The output holds MCE snapshots and MCPs, which the importer reads, including MCPs whose aspect.value is a JSON string. source: type: postgres config: { host_port: db.internal:5432, database: saas, ... } sink: type: file config: { filename: ./datahub_export.json } GraphQL. Query each dataset through DataHub's GraphQL API and save the responses (one response, or a JSON array of them): query { dataset(urn: "urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:postgres,saas.app.payments,PROD)") { urn schemaMetadata { fields { fieldPath tags { tags { tag { urn properties { name } } } } glossaryTerms { terms { term { urn properties { name } } } } } } editableSchemaMetadata { editableSchemaFieldInfo { fieldPath tags { tags { tag { urn properties { name } } } } glossaryTerms { terms { term { urn properties { name } } } } } } } } Command. haltsql schema import --from datahub datahub_export.json -o policies/pii.datahub.json Labels that match. From the samples datahub_mce.json and datahub_graphql.json: Label on the field Recorded as urn:li:tag:PII PII urn:li:glossaryTerm:PersonalInformation.PhoneNumber PersonalInformation.PhoneNumber urn:li:tag:pci with properties.name: PCI PCI, pci a glossary term with a UUID id and properties.name: Payment Card Data (Sensitive) Payment Card Data (Sensitive) Pitfalls. UI tags are not in an ingestion export. Tags and terms applied in the DataHub UI live in editableSchemaMetadata, which an ingestion run does not emit. If your stewards tag columns in the UI, use the GraphQL export. Glossary terms with UUID ids only match by name. Include properties { name } in the query, or the term is recorded as an opaque id that matches nothing. Platform instances and databases are ignored (only schema.table is kept). Export one PostgreSQL database at a time.

Availability: live fetch from OpenMetadata/DataHub is not in the 0.0.1 release; it lands with the catalog live-fetch work. With that work, haltsql schema fetch --from datahub reads the same labels straight from DataHub's GraphQL API, so nobody has to export a file: export DATAHUB_TOKEN=... # a Personal Access Token; never on the command line haltsql schema fetch --from datahub --url https://datahub.example.com \ --database saas --schema app -o policies/pii.datahub.json --url is the GMS root (http://datahub-gms:8080) or the frontend root (https://datahub.example.com); HaltSQL posts to /api/graphql. https is required except for loopback hosts. The token is read from DATAHUB_TOKEN, or the variable named by --token-env, or --token-file. There is no option that takes the token itself. DataHub only checks tokens when metadata service authentication is enabled (METADATA_SERVICE_AUTH_ENABLED=true); otherwise requests go through as anonymous. Only postgres-platform datasets are read. --service is the platform instance (the recipe's platform_instance), --database the database and --schema the schemas. Without --database, every PostgreSQL database on the instance goes into one manifest, with a warning when there is more than one: pass --database. It was validated against DataHub v1.8.0. The options (--ca-file, --timeout, --max-pages, --snapshot-out, ...) are described in haltsql schema fetch.

What HaltSQL reads. Column tags, as tag_name and tag_name=tag_value. Two input shapes are accepted: rows of information_schema.column_tags (catalog_name, schema_name, table_name, column_name, tag_name, tag_value): a JSON array of objects, {"column_tags": [...]}, or a Databricks SQL Statement Execution API result (manifest.schema.columns plus result.data_array); table JSON (one table, a list, or {"tables": [...]}) whose columns carry tags as a map or as a list of {key, value}. The catalog name is ignored; the table is schema_name.table_name. Obtaining the input. Query the tags of the catalog that holds the tables the agent reads, and save the result as JSON: SELECT catalog_name, schema_name, table_name, column_name, tag_name, tag_value FROM main.information_schema.column_tags WHERE schema_name = 'app'; Any client that writes the rows as a JSON array works. With the SQL Statement Execution API, request format: JSON_ARRAY with disposition: INLINE and save the response body as it is. Command. haltsql schema import --from unity column_tags.json -o policies/pii.unity.json Labels that match. From the sample unity_column_tags.json: tag_name tag_value Recorded as Matches pii email pii, pii=email yes class.phone_number (empty) class.phone_number yes (phone) data_classification Restricted data_classification=Restricted yes (restricted) secret null secret yes domain geo no sensitivity internal no Pitfalls. The PostgreSQL schema must match the Unity schema name. Unity Catalog usually describes a lakehouse copy of the data. The labels only help if the copy keeps the source's schema and table names; otherwise every label is reported as "not in the catalog". Chunked results. A Statement Execution API response with a next_chunk_index holds only the first chunk. Narrow the query (by schema or table), or save the rows as a JSON array from another client. Live sync is not available. There is no schema fetch provider for Unity Catalog; the open-source Unity Catalog server has no column-tag API to validate one against (details).

What HaltSQL reads. Column assets from asset search results ({"entities": [...]}, a list, or {"entity": ...}): classifications and atlanTags (typeName, displayName, tagName), classificationNames, glossary meanings (displayText) and meaningNames. The table is tableName, viewName or materialisedViewName with schemaName, else the end of qualifiedName. Obtaining the input. Search for the Column assets of the schema with Atlan's search API or SDK, asking for the attributes above, and save the JSON response. Make sure the tags come back with their display names. Command. haltsql schema import --from atlan atlan_columns.json -o policies/pii.atlan.json Labels that match. From the sample atlan_assets.json: { "typeName": "Column", "attributes": { "name": "email", "tableName": "customers", "schemaName": "app", "qualifiedName": "default/postgres/1729912345/saas/app/customers/email" }, "classifications": [ { "typeName": "tQoN8XtNIRWkGWHgyHxYQx", "displayName": "PII" } ], "meanings": [ { "displayText": "Email Address" } ] } This column is recorded with PII and Email Address. Pitfalls. Opaque tag names. Atlan's classification typeName is often a hash such as tQoN8XtNIRWkGWHgyHxYQx, which matches nothing. Export with displayName, or the label is lost. Only what is in the file counts. HaltSQL reads the tags and terms present on each Column asset in the export; check that your search request returns them for every column.

What HaltSQL reads. Column assets from an asset export (a list, {"results": [...]} or {"assets": [...]}), identified by fullName (db>schema>table>column, or dotted). Labels are: attributes whose type name mentions classification, sensitivity, privacy, confidentiality, personal/PII or security (a list of {type: {name}, value} or a map); tags; classificationMatches and dataClassifications that are not REJECTED; relations to Business Terms. Obtaining the input. Export the Column assets of the database with the fields above (through the Collibra REST API or an export job) and save them as JSON. Command. haltsql schema import --from collibra collibra_columns.json -o policies/pii.collibra.json Labels that match. From the sample collibra_assets.json: { "name": "phone", "fullName": "saas>app>customers>phone", "type": { "name": "Column" }, "attributes": { "Data Classification": ["Restricted"], "Description": "Customer phone number" }, "classificationMatches": [ { "classification": { "name": "Phone Number" }, "status": "ACCEPTED" } ] } This column is recorded with Restricted and Phone Number. The Description attribute is not a label: its type name is not classification-like. Pitfalls. fullName must end in schema>table>column (or schema.table.column). Assets with fewer parts cannot be placed in a table and are skipped. Only REJECTED classification matches are ignored. A match with any other status, or with no status, counts. Review Collibra's automatic classification suggestions, or unreviewed ones will remove columns from the draft.

There is no OpenMetadata importer in 0.0.1: schema import --from accepts dbt, datahub, unity, atlan and collibra only. If the PII tags in OpenMetadata come from dbt, import the dbt manifest.json directly in the meantime. Availability: live fetch from OpenMetadata/DataHub is not in the 0.0.1 release; it lands with the catalog live-fetch work. That work adds both an importer (schema import --from openmetadata) and a live provider (schema fetch --from openmetadata). They read the same labels. What HaltSQL reads. Table entities as returned by GET /api/v1/tables?fields=columns,tags: columns[].tags[].tagFQN. Labels with source: "Glossary" are glossary terms, the others classification tags. The full FQN is matched, so PII.Sensitive and PersonalData.Personal count and Tier.Tier1 does not. Tags on nested children (STRUCT fields) flag the top-level column. Column descriptions and table-level tags are ignored. The table is databaseSchema.name plus name. Command. export OPENMETADATA_TOKEN=... # a bot JWT; never on the command line haltsql schema fetch --from openmetadata --url https://om.example.com/api \ --service prod_pg --database app --schema app -o policies/pii.om.json # or, from a saved response of GET /api/v1/tables?fields=columns,tags haltsql schema import --from openmetadata om_tables.json -o policies/pii.om.json --url is the server root (https://om.example.com) or the API root (https://om.example.com/api). The token is a bot JWT (Settings > Bots); a bot whose user has only the DataConsumer role is enough. It is read from OPENMETADATA_TOKEN, the variable named by --token-env, or --token-file. --service is the database service name, --database the database inside it (requires --service), --schema the schema names. It was validated against OpenMetadata 2.0.7. Labels that match. A column tagged PersonalData.Personal (source Classification) is recorded as PersonalData.Personal and matches personal. A column tagged only Tier.Tier1 is not flagged. Pitfalls. Misspelt scope returns nothing. OpenMetadata answers an unknown service or database name with an empty list, so "no tables found" usually means a typo in --service or --database. Descriptions are not labels. Tag the column; a description that says "contains PII" is ignored.

haltsql-google-adk gives a Google ADK agent a haltsql_query tool that runs read-only SQL only after HaltSQL has verified it. It also has a callback and a plugin that verify the SQL argument of other PostgreSQL tools, such as MCP Toolbox's postgres-execute-sql. The tenant comes from ADK session state, which your application sets when it creates the session.

Name Kind What it does HaltSQLQueryTool(runner, ...) ADK BaseTool A tool named haltsql_query whose only argument is query. Verifies, then runs the exact SQL in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. Returns a dict. haltsql_before_tool_callback(verifier, ...) Function returning a callback For LlmAgent(before_tool_callback=...). Verifies the SQL argument of the listed tools of one agent before they run. HaltSQLGuardPlugin(verifier, ...) ADK BasePlugin The same check for every agent a Runner executes. build_sql_agent(runner, ...) Function returning an LlmAgent An example agent with HaltSQLQueryTool and instructions for writing tenant-scoped SQL. DEFAULT_GUARDED_TOOLS Constant {"execute_sql": "sql"}: the tools the callback and plugin check by default. HaltSQLToolRunner Class Holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits. Shared by all five agent-framework packages. See The runner. context_from_app(app_state, key="haltsql_context") Function Reads and validates the context from session state or another mapping. ContextUnavailable Exception Raised inside the package when no context can be read. You see it as a refusal. TOOL_NAME, DEFAULT_CONTEXT_KEY Constants "haltsql_query" and "haltsql_context". The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize.

The package needs Python 3.11 or newer and google-adk 2.9 or newer, below 3. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e integrations/google_adk The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

import os import psycopg from google.adk.runners import InMemoryRunner from google.genai import types from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_google_adk import HaltSQLToolRunner, build_sql_agent DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) agent = build_sql_agent(runner, model="gemini-2.5-flash") adk = InMemoryRunner(agent=agent, app_name="analytics") async def answer(user, question: str) -> str: session = await adk.session_service.create_session( app_name="analytics", user_id=user.id, state={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}}, # from your auth ) reply = "" async for event in adk.run_async( user_id=user.id, session_id=session.id, new_message=types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part(text=question)]), ): if event.is_final_response() and event.content and event.content.parts: reply = event.content.parts[0].text or "" return reply user is your authenticated user. To add the tool to an agent of your own, use LlmAgent(..., tools=[HaltSQLQueryTool(runner)]).

HaltSQLQueryTool reads the HaltSQL context from session state, from the haltsql_context key by default (state_key= changes it). Set the key when you create the session, from your authenticated user. The value may also be a zero-argument callable that returns the mapping. Warning: session state is writable by tools and by an agent's output_key. Do not let any tool, callback or output_key write the haltsql_context key, or the model could influence the tenant. Session state Result haltsql_context holds a mapping The query is verified with that context. No haltsql_context key Refused before verification: "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run". haltsql_context is {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. haltsql_context is not a mapping Refused: "The query was not executed: 'haltsql_context' must be a mapping". The tool declares only query. If a function call carries any other argument, such as tenant_id, the tool refuses it and nothing is verified or run.

The tool returns a dict, which ADK sends to the model as the function response. On success: {"status": "ok", "executed": true, "columns": ["id", "status"], "rows": [[1, "open"], [3, "paid"]], "row_count": 2, "truncated": false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason with its code and hint: {"status": "denied", "executed": false, "reasons": [{"code": "E_TENANT_MISMATCH", "message": "...", "hint": "Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message": "HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} Other failures have "status": "error". With "executed": false, nothing ran: HaltSQL was unavailable, no context was configured, the statement was not a SELECT, or the database could not be reached. With "executed": true, HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example on a statement timeout. The instructions of build_sql_agent tell the model to retry after denied at most three times, and to report that the data is unavailable after error. See reason-codes.md for every code.

ADK can load PostgreSQL tools from other sources, for example the postgres-execute-sql tool of MCP Toolbox for Databases through ToolboxToolset, or your own execute_sql function. To verify their SQL before they run, use one of these: from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent from google.adk.runners import Runner from haltsql import LocalVerifier from haltsql_google_adk import HaltSQLGuardPlugin, haltsql_before_tool_callback verifier = LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") # a policy in literal tenancy mode # execute_sql is your existing tool; sessions is your session service. # One agent: agent = LlmAgent(name="db_agent", model="gemini-2.5-flash", tools=[execute_sql], before_tool_callback=haltsql_before_tool_callback(verifier)) # Every agent a runner executes: runner = Runner(agent=agent, app_name="analytics", session_service=sessions, plugins=[HaltSQLGuardPlugin(verifier)]) tools= maps tool names to the name of their SQL argument. The default is {"execute_sql": "sql"}. Tools that are not listed are not checked. For a listed tool, the guard verifies the SQL with the context from session state. If HaltSQL allows it without bound parameters, the tool runs. Otherwise the guard returns the refusal dict, and ADK sends it to the model instead of running the tool. Warning: the guarded tool cannot receive HaltSQL's $n values, so the guard refuses any SQL that HaltSQL allows only with bound parameters. Use literal tenancy for those tools (see tenancy.md), or use HaltSQLQueryTool. The guard checks only the SQL: run those tools with a read-only role and their own timeouts. Plugins run before an agent's own callbacks. If you use the callback form and the agent has several before-tool callbacks, list HaltSQL's first and do not let a later one change the arguments. Do not use the guard with BigQuery or Spanner tools: HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

HaltSQLToolRunner(verifier, connect, *, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). connect required Zero-argument callable that returns a new psycopg 3 connection. Called only after HaltSQL allows the query. The runner closes the connection after each query. max_rows 200 Row cap, 1 to 100000. truncated tells the model more rows were available. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query, 1 to 3600000. settings None Transaction-local settings: a mapping, or a function of the verified context, for example lambda ctx: {"app.tenant_id": ctx["tenant_id"]} for row-level security. HaltSQLQueryTool(runner, *, state_key="haltsql_context", name="haltsql_query", description=DEFAULT_DESCRIPTION): Argument Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLToolRunner. Anything else raises TypeError. state_key "haltsql_context" Session-state key that holds the context. name "haltsql_query" Tool name the model sees. description built-in text Tool description the model sees. haltsql_before_tool_callback(verifier, *, tools=None, state_key="haltsql_context") and HaltSQLGuardPlugin(verifier, *, tools=None, state_key="haltsql_context", name="haltsql_guard"): Argument Default Meaning verifier required Any object with verify(sql, context). tools None ({"execute_sql": "sql"}) Tool name to SQL argument name. Must not be empty. state_key "haltsql_context" Session-state key that holds the context. name "haltsql_guard" Plugin name (plugin only). build_sql_agent(runner, *, model="gemini-2.5-flash", name="sql_analyst", instruction=SQL_AGENT_INSTRUCTION, state_key="haltsql_context", **agent_kwargs): Argument Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLToolRunner. model "gemini-2.5-flash" Passed to LlmAgent. name "sql_analyst" Agent name. instruction built-in text Agent instruction. state_key "haltsql_context" Passed to HaltSQLQueryTool. **agent_kwargs none Other LlmAgent arguments. Every query that HaltSQLQueryTool runs is in a READ ONLY transaction, and only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select are run. These cannot be turned off.

ADK calls tools and callbacks asynchronously. HaltSQLQueryTool reads session state on the event loop, then runs verification and execution in a worker thread (asyncio.to_thread). The callback and plugin also verify in a worker thread. Use a sync verifier and a sync psycopg connection. Rows are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and check that a denial never opens a connection: from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_google_adk import HaltSQLToolRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): out = HaltSQLToolRunner(FakeVerifier(deny), no_db).run("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10", {"tenant_id": "acme"}) assert out["status"] == "denied" and out["reasons"][0]["code"] == "E_TENANT_MISSING" The package's own tests use an InMemoryRunner session and ADK's function-call handler, with the real haltsql CLI, a real haltsql-server and the lab Postgres. They never call an LLM: make -C lab up dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./bin/server/main.exe ONLY=agents clients/python/run-all-tests.sh integrations/google_adk/constraints.txt lists the exact versions the tests were run with. See Testing.

Symptom Cause Fix "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run" The session state has no haltsql_context (or your state_key). Pass state={"haltsql_context": {...}} to create_session. Every query on a tenant table is denied The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs (E_CONTEXT_MISSING), or the model wrote a tenant literal (E_TENANT_MISMATCH). Check the context. In bound mode the model must write $1. "pass exactly one argument, 'query'" The function call had extra or missing arguments. Nothing to fix in your code: the model sees the message. The guard refuses allowed SQL with "HaltSQL allows it only with bound parameters" The policy uses bound tenancy. Use HaltSQLQueryTool, or literal tenancy for that tool. The guard does not check a tool The tool's name is not in tools=. Add {"<tool name>": "<sql argument>"}. "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary. "The database is unavailable" connect raised. Check the DSN and network. ValueError: tools must map tool names to SQL argument names tools= is empty or has non-string entries. Pass a non-empty mapping of strings. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

HaltSQLQueryTool runs read-only SELECT only. Write policies are not supported. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. The callback and plugin check SQL only, cannot be used with bound tenancy, and do not check tools that are not listed in tools=. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only, so it cannot guard ADK's BigQuery, Spanner (GoogleSQL) or Bigtable tools.
