haltsql-server accepts OIDC access tokens (JWTs) from any provider that publishes an OpenID Connect discovery document and a JWKS. The token decides which policy the caller gets and which tenant the verdict is bound to, so an agent cannot widen its own access by changing the request. This page gives a setup recipe per provider; the full rules are in authentication.md. Providers covered: Generic OIDC (the building blocks every recipe uses) Keycloak Microsoft Entra ID Okta Auth0 Testing with a real token What is tested. HaltSQL's OIDC support is generic: nothing in it is specific to one vendor. Provider How it is tested Keycloak 26.4.2 End to end against a real Keycloak: discovery, JWKS fetch, real tokens from the password and client-credentials grants, groups mapped to policies, the tenant from a token claim, and the allowed queries run in PostgreSQL (test/e2e/test_identity.py, test/auth/test_keycloak.ml). Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0 Their token shapes (groups claims, Entra ID overage markers, Auth0 namespaced claims, Entra object ids) are covered by unit tests (test/auth/test_groups.ml). They are not tested against the live services. Any other OIDC provider Generic OIDC. It works if the provider issues signed JWT access tokens with the checks below. Provider console steps on this page are kept high-level, because consoles change; follow the provider's own documentation for them. The HaltSQL configuration is exact.

Every recipe is a server.auth.oidc entry: server: auth: oidc: - name: corp-idp # appears in logs and audit records as oidc:corp-idp issuer: https://idp.corp.example/ # must equal the token's iss exactly audiences: [haltsql] # the token's aud must contain one of these algorithms: [RS256] # default [RS256, ES256] # jwks_uri: discovered from <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration policy_from_groups: # or: policy, or policy_claim + allowed_policies claim: groups map: - { group: haltsql-support, policy: support-bot } - { group: haltsql-analysts, policy: saas-analytics } context_claims: tenant_id: tenant # context field <- claim path What you need from the provider: Setting Where it comes from issuer The issuer value of the provider's discovery document, character for character (including any trailing /). HaltSQL fetches <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration and refuses a document whose issuer differs. audiences The audience your provider puts in aud for tokens meant for HaltSQL (an API identifier, a client id, or a custom audience). jwks_uri Normally discovered. Set it only when discovery is not available; it must be https and must not point to a loopback host unless the issuer does. algorithms The signing algorithm of the provider's keys. HMAC (HS*) and none are always rejected, so a provider must sign with an asymmetric key (RS256, RS384, RS512, PS256, ES256, ES384 or EdDSA). Choosing the policy. Exactly one of: policy: NAME: every token from this provider gets one policy. Use it when the provider entry serves one agent; pin the agent with required_claims (for example its client id). policy_claim + allowed_policies: a string claim names the policy, and only policies in the allowlist can be selected. policy_from_groups: the first map entry whose group the token has wins, in the order written, so put the most privileged groups first. Groups are compared exactly (case-sensitive). Without default, a token that matches no entry is rejected (no_group_policy), and so is a token without the claim (missing_claim). See Policies from IdP groups. Tenant from claims. context_claims maps a context field (the one your policy reads as ${ctx.tenant_id}) to a claim. The path is tried first as one claim name, so https://corp.example/tenant works, then as a dot path through nested objects (org.id). The claim must exist, and must be a string, an integral number, or a non-empty array of those; otherwise the token is rejected. A request body cannot override these fields: a body field not listed in request_context_fields is refused with 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. Restricting tokens further. required_claims checks claims by value: a string must equal the claim, or be an element of an array claim, or a word of a space-separated claim such as scope; a list requires every value. Key rotation and outages. Keys are cached for jwks_cache_seconds (default 300). A token with an unknown kid triggers at most one refresh every 30 seconds, so key rotation needs no restart. If the provider is unreachable, cached keys stay usable for at most min(jwks_cache_seconds, 3600) seconds past their expiry; after that, its tokens get 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE until it is reachable again. See Key fetching and caching. Network. The server needs outbound HTTPS to the issuer's discovery document and JWKS. Responses are limited to 1 MiB and 5 seconds, and redirects are not followed.

Tested end to end with Keycloak 26.4.2. In Keycloak (see the Keycloak Server Administration Guide for the exact screens): In the realm, create a client for the agent (for example haltsql-agent). For an agent that runs as itself, enable client authentication and service accounts (client-credentials grant). Add an Audience mapper to the client with the included custom audience haltsql, added to the access token. Without it, Keycloak's access tokens do not carry the audience HaltSQL expects. Add a Group Membership mapper with token claim name groups, Full group path off (so groups are support, not /support), added to the access token. For the tenant, add a User Attribute mapper from the user attribute tenant to the claim haltsql.tenant, type String, added to the access token. Keycloak turns the dot into a nested object: {"haltsql": {"tenant": "acme"}}. Put users (or the client's service-account user) into the groups. HaltSQL config. This is the configuration the end-to-end test runs, with https instead of the test's local http issuer: server: auth: oidc: - name: keycloak issuer: https://sso.corp.example/realms/corp audiences: [haltsql] algorithms: [RS256] policy_from_groups: claim: groups map: - { group: support, policy: support-bot } - { group: finance, policy: finance-analyst } context_claims: { tenant_id: haltsql.tenant } The issuer is https://<host>/realms/<realm> (older Keycloak versions add /auth before /realms; copy the value from the realm's discovery document). Roles instead of groups. Realm roles are in realm_access.roles and client roles in resource_access.<client>.roles, both in the access token by default. Use either as the claim: policy_from_groups: claim: realm_access.roles map: - { group: haltsql-support, policy: support-bot } Pitfalls. No groups, no claim. Keycloak leaves groups out for a user in no group. HaltSQL rejects that token with missing_claim (unless you set a default), which is the safe result, but it looks like a configuration error when you test with a fresh user. A user without the tenant attribute gets a token without haltsql.tenant; the token is rejected, so the user cannot query unscoped. allow_insecure_http: true is only for local tests against a Keycloak in dev mode. Do not use it in production.

Generic OIDC; token shapes are unit tested. A complete worked example, with the az commands for the app registration and app roles, is in Entra ID as the OIDC issuer. In Entra ID: Register an application for HaltSQL (the API agents call) and set its access token version to 2 (api.requestedAccessTokenVersion = 2 in the manifest). Define app roles for the kinds of caller (for example SQL.Verify, or one role per policy), and assign them to the agents' identities or to users and groups. Optionally, require assignment so that only identities with a role can get a token. HaltSQL config: one policy per app role. App roles arrive in the roles claim, are scoped to the application and never overflow: server: auth: oidc: - name: entra issuer: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/v2.0 audiences: [<HALTSQL_APP_CLIENT_ID>] algorithms: [RS256] policy_from_groups: claim: roles map: - { group: HaltSQL.Support, policy: support-bot } - { group: HaltSQL.Analyst, policy: saas-analytics } HaltSQL config: one pinned agent identity. For an agent that calls with its managed identity or service principal, pin the identity with azp: - name: entra-analytics-agent issuer: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<TENANT_ID>/v2.0 audiences: [<HALTSQL_APP_CLIENT_ID>] algorithms: [RS256] policy: analytics-agent required_claims: azp: <AGENT_CLIENT_ID> roles: SQL.Verify request_context_fields: [tenant_id] Several entries can share an issuer; HaltSQL tries them in order and uses the first one that verifies the token. Groups and overage. You can map security groups instead of app roles with claim: groups. The values are group object ids, not names: policy_from_groups: claim: groups map: - { group: 8b0e5a9c-1c1f-4c55-9d2a-5f1f3c0f2a11, policy: admin-readonly } When a user is in more groups than fit in the token (200 for JWTs), Entra ID leaves groups out and adds _claim_names/_claim_sources pointing at Microsoft Graph (or hasgroups: true for implicit-flow tokens). HaltSQL never calls Graph, because a partial group list could select the wrong policy: it rejects such a token with groups_overage, even if a groups claim is present too. To avoid overage, set groupMembershipClaims to ApplicationGroup and assign only the relevant groups to the enterprise application, or use app roles. Pitfalls. v1.0 tokens. Without access token version 2, Entra ID issues tokens whose iss is https://sts.windows.net/<tenant>/, and they are rejected because iss must equal issuer exactly. If you must accept v1.0 tokens, configure that issuer in a separate entry, with the App ID URI as the audience and jwks_uri: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/discovery/keys; do not mix the two. tid is not your tenant. The tid claim is the Entra directory, not the customer tenant your tables are keyed by. App-only tokens carry no customer tenant at all: list tenant_id in request_context_fields, or use one identity per tenant. policy_claim does not work with roles. policy_claim needs a string claim and roles is an array; use policy_from_groups with claim: roles.

Generic OIDC; token shapes are unit tested. In Okta: Use a custom authorization server (for example the one named default). Its issuer looks like https://corp.okta.com/oauth2/default; its Audience setting is the aud of its access tokens. Add a groups claim to the access token, with a filter (for example "starts with haltsql-") so the claim stays small. For the tenant, add a custom claim from a user profile attribute (for example tenant from user.tenant). HaltSQL config: server: auth: oidc: - name: corp-okta issuer: https://corp.okta.com/oauth2/default audiences: [api://haltsql] algorithms: [RS256] policy_from_groups: claim: groups map: - { group: haltsql-admins, policy: admin-readonly } - { group: haltsql-support, policy: support-bot } context_claims: { tenant_id: tenant } required_claims: { scp: sql.verify } required_claims: {scp: sql.verify} only accepts tokens that were granted that scope; scp is an array in Okta access tokens, and the value must be one of its elements. Machine-to-machine tokens. Client-credentials tokens describe the application, not a user, so they carry no user groups. Give each agent application its own provider entry with a pinned policy and required_claims on its client id (Okta access tokens carry it in cid), for example required_claims: {cid: <AGENT_CLIENT_ID>}. Pitfalls. Use the custom authorization server's issuer, exactly as its discovery document reports it. Tokens from a different authorization server have a different iss and are not verified by this entry. An unfiltered groups claim can be large; HaltSQL rejects tokens over 16 KiB as malformed.

Generic OIDC; token shapes are unit tested. In Auth0: Create an API for HaltSQL. Its Identifier is the audience. Use the RS256 signing algorithm: HS256 tokens are always rejected. Add custom claims from an Action. Auth0 requires namespaced names for custom claims, for example https://corp.example/groups and https://corp.example/tenant. In a post-login Action: exports.onExecutePostLogin = async (event, api) => { api.accessToken.setCustomClaim('https://corp.example/groups', event.authorization?.roles ?? []); api.accessToken.setCustomClaim('https://corp.example/tenant', event.user.app_metadata.tenant); }; HaltSQL config: server: auth: oidc: - name: auth0 issuer: https://corp.eu.auth0.com/ # Auth0 issuers end in "/" audiences: [https://haltsql.corp.example] algorithms: [RS256] policy_from_groups: claim: https://corp.example/groups map: - { group: admins, policy: admin-readonly } - { group: support, policy: support-bot } context_claims: { tenant_id: https://corp.example/tenant } Namespaced claim names contain dots and slashes. HaltSQL looks a path up as one claim name first, so https://corp.example/groups is read as written, not as a dot path. Pitfalls. The trailing slash. Auth0's iss ends in /. Configure issuer with the slash, or every token fails wrong_issuer. (HaltSQL removes the slash only to build the discovery URL.) Missing tenant metadata. If a user has no tenant, the Action sets an empty claim or none, and the token is rejected. That is the safe result; fix the user's metadata. Machine-to-machine tokens do not run post-login Actions. Use a pinned policy per application, or set the claims in a credentials-exchange Action.

Do this once per provider before agents depend on it. Get a token the way the agent will. For a Keycloak client with a service account: TOKEN=$(curl -s https://sso.corp.example/realms/corp/protocol/openid-connect/token \ -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=haltsql-agent \ -d client_secret="$CLIENT_SECRET" | jq -r .access_token) Other providers have an equivalent token endpoint; see their docs. Read its claims and compare them with your config (iss, aud, exp, the groups claim, the tenant claim): python3 -c 'import base64,json,sys; p=sys.argv[1].split(".")[1]; print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(p+"="*(-len(p)%4))),indent=2))' "$TOKEN" Ask HaltSQL which policy the token selects. GET /v1/policies returns only the caller's pinned policy: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://haltsql.internal:8443/v1/policies # {"policies":[{"name":"support-bot","version":"sha256:...","mode":"enforce"}]} Verify a query and check that bind_params carries the tenant from the token: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ https://haltsql.internal:8443/v1/verify \ -d '{"sql":"SELECT id, subject FROM app.tickets WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10"}' Check the negative cases. A body context with another tenant must get 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED; a token from a user in no mapped group must get 401. When a token is rejected, the response says why, and the server logs oidc token rejected at info with a stable reason field: expired, wrong_issuer, wrong_audience, bad_signature, unknown_kid, alg_not_allowed, missing_claim, claim_mismatch, bad_claim, groups_overage, no_group_policy and others. JWKS fetch failures are logged at warn as oidc signing keys unavailable. The metric haltsql_auth_total{method="oidc",result="ok|rejected|unavailable"} counts the outcomes. Audit records of OIDC callers have caller: "oidc:<name>", caller_type: "oidc" and the token's sub as subject; the token itself is never logged.

Authentication and TLS: the request pipeline, all checks, mTLS and static tokens. Config reference: server.auth.oidc and policy_from_groups. Tenancy: how ${ctx.*} values bind tenant predicates. HTTP API: /v1/verify, /v1/policies and error codes. Deploying on Azure.

haltsql-langchain guards LangChain SQL agents with HaltSQL. It offers a haltsql_query tool whose only argument is the SQL, and a wrapper that makes an existing SQLDatabase verify every statement before it runs, so SQLDatabaseToolkit and create_sql_agent keep working. The tenant comes from a mapping or callable you pass in from your authenticated session, never from the model.

Name Kind What it does HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=...) LangChain BaseTool A tool named haltsql_query whose only argument is query. Returns JSON rows, or the reason codes and hints when nothing ran. Needs langchain-core. HaltSQLQueryRunner(verifier, context, ...) Class The framework-free core: verifies and runs SQL. run(sql) returns text for the model; execute(sql) returns a GuardedResult and raises on denial. guard_sql_database(db, verifier, context, ...) Function Returns a copy of a langchain_community SQLDatabase whose run and run_no_throw verify every statement first, and that never reads table rows outside HaltSQL. The copy is still an SQLDatabase. This package does not use HaltSQLToolRunner from the agent frameworks packages; its runner and result format are described on this page. It is a thin layer over the Python SDK: every query goes through haltsql.integration.authorize_guarded, then guard.execute or guard.execute_on_engine.

The package needs Python 3.9 or newer. The langchain extra installs langchain-core 0.3 or newer, langchain-community 0.3 or newer and SQLAlchemy 2. The package is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/langchain[langchain]' The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

A tool whose only argument is the SQL: import contextvars import os import psycopg from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_langchain import HaltSQLQueryRunner, HaltSQLQueryTool DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role current_tenant = contextvars.ContextVar("tenant") # set by your request handler runner = HaltSQLQueryRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") context=lambda: {"tenant_id": current_tenant.get()}, connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) tool = HaltSQLQueryTool(runner=runner) # give it to your agent's tools # Per request, after authenticating the user: current_tenant.set(user.tenant_id) print(tool.invoke({"query": "SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10"})) Guarding an existing SQLDatabase for create_sql_agent: from langchain_community.agent_toolkits import SQLDatabaseToolkit, create_sql_agent from langchain_community.utilities import SQLDatabase from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_langchain import guard_sql_database db = SQLDatabase.from_uri( "postgresql+psycopg://agent_ro@db/app", include_tables=["orders"], ) guarded = guard_sql_database(db, HaltSQLClient.from_env(), lambda: {"tenant_id": current_tenant.get()}) toolkit = SQLDatabaseToolkit(db=guarded, llm=llm) agent = create_sql_agent(llm, toolkit=toolkit) The engine must use psycopg 3 (postgresql+psycopg://). The guarded copy never reads table rows outside HaltSQL. A plain SQLDatabase adds sample rows of each table to the table descriptions it gives the model (sample_rows_in_table_info, default 3), read straight from the engine; on the guarded copy that setting is forced to 0, so get_table_info, table_info and get_context show the schema only. The internal _execute, which runs SQL on the engine without run, refuses. The original db is unchanged, so give the agent only the guarded copy. Note: the table descriptions still list every column of the tables, read by schema reflection, including columns the policy denies. Limit the tables with include_tables.

context is a mapping or a zero-argument callable. A callable is evaluated on every query, so one runner or guarded database can serve many requests. Reading a contextvars.ContextVar that your request handler sets is the usual pattern. The model never supplies the context: the tool's only argument is query, and SQLDatabase.run takes only SQL. If a tool call carries an extra argument such as tenant_id, LangChain drops it before the tool runs. context Result A mapping, or a callable that returns one The query is verified with that context. A callable that returns None Refused: nothing is verified or run. execute and the guarded run raise haltsql.integration.ContextUnavailable; the tool returns No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this request; the query was not executed. {}, or a callable that returns it Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy, typically with E_CONTEXT_MISSING. A callable that raises Nothing is verified or run. execute raises haltsql.HaltSQLUnavailable; the tool returns SQL verification is unavailable; the query was not executed., without the exception's details. As in the agent-framework packages, a missing context is refused before verification.

HaltSQLQueryTool (and HaltSQLQueryRunner.run) returns text. On success it is JSON: {"columns": ["id", "status"], "rows": [[1, "open"], [3, "paid"]], "truncated": false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason code with its hint (or the message, if a reason has no hint): HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry: - E_TENANT_MISSING: <hint> Other failures: Text Meaning No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this request; the query was not executed. The context callable returned None. SQL verification is unavailable; the query was not executed. The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, rejected the request, or returned a verdict for a different string, or the context callable raised. The query was not executed: <reason> The guard refused, for example a statement other than SELECT with read_only=True, or an unsupported connection. Database error: <class>: <first line> HaltSQL allowed the query but the database server rejected it (the error has an SQLSTATE). Database error: <class> HaltSQL allowed the query but the connection failed or another error occurred. The message is withheld because it can name hosts, roles or a connection string. The guarded SQLDatabase behaves like a normal one: run(sql) returns the rows as a string such as [(1, 'open')], or "" when there are no rows. On a denial it raises haltsql.QueryDenied; on other failures it raises the underlying error. run_no_throw(sql) returns Error: followed by the same text as above. LangChain's QuerySQLDatabaseTool, which SQLDatabaseToolkit uses, calls run_no_throw, so the model sees the codes and hints. The default tool description tells the model to filter tenant tables with alias.tenant_id = $1, never to write tenant IDs, and to fix the SQL and retry after a denial. See reason-codes.md for every code.

HaltSQLQueryRunner(verifier, context, *, engine=None, connect=None, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None, read_only=True): Argument Default Meaning verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). context required A mapping, or a zero-argument callable that returns one. engine None A SQLAlchemy engine using psycopg 3 (postgresql+psycopg://). Give exactly one of engine and connect. connect None Zero-argument callable that returns a new psycopg.Connection. Called only after HaltSQL allows the query; closed after each query. max_rows 200 Row cap. None means no cap. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query. None means none is set. settings None A mapping of transaction-local settings, for example {"app.region": "eu"}. Fixed for the runner; it cannot depend on the context. read_only True Run only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select, in a READ ONLY transaction. With False, see Read-only and writes. HaltSQLQueryTool fields (keyword arguments): Field Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLQueryRunner. name "haltsql_query" Tool name the model sees. description built-in text Tool description the model sees. guard_sql_database(db, verifier, context, **runner_kwargs) accepts max_rows, statement_timeout_ms, settings and read_only, as above. It uses the database's own engine; do not pass engine or connect.

With the default read_only=True, a statement runs only when the verdict's statement_kind is select. Anything else is refused before a connection is taken, even when the policy allows it, with GuardError: only SELECT statements run in read-only mode (this is DELETE). With read_only=False, the policy alone decides: a statement runs when HaltSQL allows it, whatever its kind. Writes run in a read-write transaction, and SELECT statements still run READ ONLY. A verdict without a statement_kind never runs. Allow writes in the policy (statements.allow) only for the agents and tables that need them.

None of the classes have async methods. HaltSQLQueryTool defines only a sync implementation, so LangChain's ainvoke runs it in a thread pool executor. The guarded SQLDatabase is sync, like SQLDatabase itself. Use a sync verifier and a sync psycopg connection or engine. Rows are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and check that a denial never opens a connection: import pytest from haltsql import QueryDenied from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_langchain import HaltSQLQueryRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): fv = FakeVerifier(deny) runner = HaltSQLQueryRunner(fv, {"tenant_id": "acme"}, connect=no_db) assert runner.run("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10").startswith("HaltSQL denied the query") with pytest.raises(QueryDenied): runner.execute("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10") assert fv.calls[0][1] == {"tenant_id": "acme"} The package's own tests cover the runner, the guarded SQLDatabase and the tool. Tests that need LangChain skip when it is not installed, and tests that run SQL need the lab Postgres: make -C lab up pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/langchain[langchain,test]' pytest -q integrations/langchain FULL=1 clients/python/run-all-tests.sh runs them with the other Python suites.

Symptom Cause Fix Every query on a tenant table is denied with E_CONTEXT_MISSING The context callable returned {}, or misses a key the policy needs. Check the callable. It is evaluated on every query. "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured", or ContextUnavailable The context callable returned None. Return the context for the current request, for example from a ContextVar your handler sets. "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, rejected the token, or returned a verdict for a different string; or the context callable raised. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary, and test the callable on its own. With execute, the original exception is in __cause__. GuardError: only SELECT statements run in read-only mode The policy allowed a write, but read_only=True. Ask for a SELECT, or pass read_only=False if the agent should write. GuardError: unverified SQL is not run Code called the guarded copy's internal _execute. Use run or run_no_throw. ValueError: pass exactly one of engine= or connect= Both or neither were given. Pass one. With guard_sql_database, pass neither. GuardError: caller-supplied parameters are not allowed Code called the guarded run with parameters=. HaltSQL binds the parameters; pass the SQL alone. GuardError: fetch='cursor' is not supported Code called run(fetch="cursor"). Use fetch="all" or "one". GuardError: could not find the SQLAlchemy engine of this SQLDatabase The object passed to guard_sql_database has no _engine or engine. Pass a langchain_community SQLDatabase. ImportError: HaltSQLQueryTool needs langchain-core The langchain extra is not installed. pip install -e 'integrations/langchain[langchain]'. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. The guarded SQLDatabase returns a string, so the model is not told when rows were cut at max_rows. HaltSQLQueryTool reports it as truncated. fetch="one" still fetches up to max_rows rows and returns the first. execution_options is accepted and ignored. run and run_no_throw are verified; _execute refuses, and get_table_info reads no rows. Schema reflection (table and column names, indexes) still uses the engine. The engine or connection must use psycopg 3. psycopg2 cannot send $n SQL unchanged and is refused. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

LangGraph: a ToolNode tool with the tenant in the runtime context, and a retry-on-deny graph. Python SDK: verifiers, guard.execute and errors. reason-codes.md and tenancy.md. defense-in-depth.md: the database role and row-level security to use with HaltSQL. Source: integrations/langchain.

haltsql-langgraph gives a LangGraph agent a haltsql_query tool that runs read-only SQL only after HaltSQL has verified it. The tool works with ToolNode, and the package includes an example graph that lets the model retry after a refusal, up to a limit. The tenant comes from the graph's runtime context, which your application sets and the model never sees.

Name Kind What it does haltsql_query_tool(runner, ...) Function returning a LangChain StructuredTool A tool named haltsql_query whose only model-facing argument is query. Verifies, then runs the exact SQL in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. Uses response_format="content_and_artifact". build_sql_agent_graph(model, tool, ...) Function returning a compiled graph An example agent graph with a bounded retry-on-deny loop. is_denial(message) Function True if a message is a ToolMessage from the HaltSQL tool whose query did not run. HaltSQLToolRunner Class Holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits. Shared by all five agent-framework packages. See The runner. context_from_app(app_state, key="haltsql_context") Function Reads and validates the context from an object or mapping. Used by default to read the runtime context. ContextUnavailable Exception Raised inside the package when no context can be read. You see it as a refusal. TOOL_NAME, DEFAULT_CONTEXT_KEY Constants "haltsql_query" and "haltsql_context". haltsql_langgraph.graph.SQLAgentState TypedDict State of the example graph: messages and denials. The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize and guard.execute.

The package needs Python 3.10 or newer, langgraph 1.2 or newer (below 2), langgraph-prebuilt 1.1 or newer and langchain-core 1.6 or newer. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e integrations/langgraph The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. You also need a chat model integration, such as langchain-openai. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

import os import psycopg from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_langgraph import HaltSQLToolRunner, build_sql_agent_graph, haltsql_query_tool DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) tool = haltsql_query_tool(runner) llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini") graph = build_sql_agent_graph(llm.bind_tools([tool]), tool, max_denials=3) def answer(user, question: str) -> str: out = graph.invoke( {"messages": [("user", question)]}, context={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}}, ) return out["messages"][-1].content user is your authenticated user. Build the tool and graph once at startup. Pass the context on every invoke. To use the tool in your own graph instead, put it in a ToolNode as usual: from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode tools = ToolNode([tool])

The tool takes LangGraph's ToolRuntime, which LangGraph injects and hides from the model. It reads the HaltSQL context from runtime.context, the value you pass as graph.invoke(..., context=...). By default it reads the haltsql_context key of a mapping, or the haltsql_context attribute of an object such as a dataclass. The value may also be a zero-argument callable that returns the mapping. To read the context from your own context object, pass context_from: tool = haltsql_query_tool(runner, context_from=lambda ctx: {"tenant_id": ctx.tenant_id}) If you use a typed context, pass its type to the example graph with build_sql_agent_graph(..., context_schema=AppContext). Runtime context Result Has haltsql_context (or context_from returns a mapping) The query is verified with that context. No context=, no haltsql_context, or context_from returns None Refused before verification: "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run". haltsql_context is {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. The tool's argument schema has only query. If a tool call carries an extra argument such as tenant_id, LangChain drops it before the tool runs, and the context still comes from the runtime.

Each call returns a ToolMessage. Its content is JSON text for the model, and its artifact is the same result as a dict for your graph's routing. On success: {"status":"ok","executed":true,"columns":["id","status"],"rows":[[1,"open"],[3,"paid"]],"row_count":2,"truncated":false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason with its code and hint: {"status":"denied","executed":false, "reasons":[{"code":"E_TENANT_MISMATCH","message":"...","hint":"Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message":"HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} Other failures have "status": "error". With "executed": false, nothing ran: HaltSQL was unavailable, no context was configured, the statement was not a SELECT, or the database could not be reached. With "executed": true, HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example on a statement timeout. is_denial(message) is true for both denied and error results. See reason-codes.md for every code.

check counts the tool messages for which is_denial is true, across the whole run, in the denials state key. When the count reaches max_denials, the graph adds the message "Stopping: HaltSQL refused N queries in this run." and ends, instead of looping. Because is_denial also counts error results, database errors and an unavailable verifier count toward the limit too. model can be a runnable such as llm.bind_tools([tool]), or a callable that takes the message list and returns an AIMessage. The graph supports both invoke and ainvoke.

HaltSQLToolRunner(verifier, connect, *, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). connect required Zero-argument callable that returns a new psycopg 3 connection. Called only after HaltSQL allows the query. The runner closes the connection after each query. max_rows 200 Row cap, 1 to 100000. truncated tells the model more rows were available. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query, 1 to 3600000. settings None Transaction-local settings: a mapping, or a function of the verified context, for example lambda ctx: {"app.tenant_id": ctx["tenant_id"]} for row-level security. haltsql_query_tool(runner, *, context_from=None, name="haltsql_query", description=DEFAULT_DESCRIPTION): Argument Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLToolRunner. context_from None f(runtime_context) -> mapping. Default: the haltsql_context key or attribute of the runtime context. name "haltsql_query" Tool name the model sees. description built-in text Tool description the model sees. build_sql_agent_graph(model, tool, *, max_denials=3, context_schema=None, extra_tools=None): Argument Default Meaning model required A runnable or callable that returns an AIMessage. tool required The tool from haltsql_query_tool. max_denials 3 Stop after this many refused queries in one run, 1 to 20. context_schema None Type of the runtime context, passed to StateGraph. extra_tools None Other tools served by the same ToolNode. Every query runs in a READ ONLY transaction, and only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select are run. These cannot be turned off.

The tool has both a sync and an async implementation. graph.ainvoke and ToolNode in async mode use the async one, which runs verification and execution in a worker thread (asyncio.to_thread) so the event loop is not blocked. Use a sync verifier and a sync psycopg connection either way. Rows are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported. LangGraph's own streaming of graph steps works as usual.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and check that a denial never opens a connection: from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_langgraph import HaltSQLToolRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): fv = FakeVerifier(deny) out = HaltSQLToolRunner(fv, no_db).run("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10", {"tenant_id": "acme"}) assert out["status"] == "denied" and out["reasons"][0]["code"] == "E_TENANT_MISSING" To test the graph without an LLM, pass a plain function as model that returns an AIMessage with scripted tool_calls. The package's own tests do this with a real ToolNode and StateGraph, the real haltsql CLI, a real haltsql-server and the lab Postgres: make -C lab up dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./bin/server/main.exe ONLY=agents clients/python/run-all-tests.sh integrations/langgraph/constraints.txt lists the exact versions the tests were run with. See Testing.

Symptom Cause Fix "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run" invoke got no context=, the context has no haltsql_context, or context_from returned None or raised a LookupError. Pass context= on every invoke and ainvoke. Every query on a tenant table is denied The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs (E_CONTEXT_MISSING), or the model wrote a tenant literal (E_TENANT_MISMATCH). Check the context. In bound mode the model must write $1. The graph ends with "Stopping: HaltSQL refused N queries in this run." The model reached max_denials. Read the ToolMessage artifacts to see the reasons. Improve the system prompt or the policy; raise max_denials only if retries are making progress. "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string. An unexpected exception in context_from is also reported this way. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary. Test context_from on its own. "The database is unavailable" connect raised. Check the DSN and network. TypeError: the model must return an AIMessage model returned something else. Return an AIMessage, or pass a chat model runnable. ValueError: max_denials must be an integer in 1..20 max_denials out of range. Use 1 to 20. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

Read-only SELECT only. Write policies are not supported by this tool. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. build_sql_agent_graph is an example. For more control, use the tool in your own graph and route on is_denial. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

haltsql-llamaindex guards LlamaIndex text-to-SQL with HaltSQL. LlamaIndex's SQL retrievers and query engines run SQL through SQLDatabase.run_sql, and this package returns a copy of your SQLDatabase whose run_sql verifies each statement first and runs only the exact verified string. The tenant comes from a mapping or callable you pass in from your authenticated session, never from the model.

Name Kind What it does guard_sql_database(db, verifier, context, ...) Function Returns a copy of a LlamaIndex SQLDatabase whose run_sql verifies, then runs the exact SQL with the bound parameters, and whose insert_into_table refuses. The copy is still an SQLDatabase, so you can pass it anywhere the original went. guarded_sql_retriever(db, verifier, context, ...) Function A SQLRetriever over a guarded copy of db. guarded_nl_sql_query_engine(db, verifier, context, ...) Function An NLSQLTableQueryEngine over a guarded copy of db, with denials turned into SQL errors the LLM can read. HaltSQLSQLError Exception (a NotImplementedError) Raised instead of the HaltSQL exception when denials_as_sql_errors=True. Its message lists the reason codes and hints; __cause__ is the original error. The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize and guard.execute_on_engine. It does not use HaltSQLToolRunner from the agent frameworks packages.

The package needs Python 3.9 or newer. The llamaindex extra installs llama-index-core 0.10 or newer and SQLAlchemy 2. The package is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/llamaindex[llamaindex]' The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. You also need an LLM integration for the query engine, such as llama-index-llms-openai. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

import contextvars from sqlalchemy import create_engine from llama_index.core import SQLDatabase from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_llamaindex import guarded_nl_sql_query_engine current_tenant = contextvars.ContextVar("tenant") # set by your request handler engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://agent_ro@db/app") # psycopg 3, a read-only role db = SQLDatabase(engine, include_tables=["orders"]) query_engine = guarded_nl_sql_query_engine( db, HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") lambda: {"tenant_id": current_tenant.get()}, # evaluated on every query tables=["orders"], llm=OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini"), ) def answer(user, question: str) -> str: current_tenant.set(user.tenant_id) # from your auth return str(query_engine.query(question)) To guard other components, pass the guarded copy wherever you passed the original SQLDatabase: from haltsql_llamaindex import guard_sql_database, guarded_sql_retriever guarded = guard_sql_database(db, verifier, ctx) # for any component that takes an SQLDatabase retriever = guarded_sql_retriever(db, verifier, ctx) # SQLRetriever: runs SQL you give it The engine must use psycopg 3 (postgresql+psycopg://). The guarded copy never runs SQL on the engine outside HaltSQL: run_sql is verified, and insert_into_table (which SQLStructStoreIndex uses to load rows) raises haltsql.GuardError instead of inserting. Table descriptions (get_single_table_info) come from schema reflection and read no rows. The original db and the copy's engine property still give the raw engine, so give the agent only the guarded copy.

context is a mapping or a zero-argument callable. A callable is evaluated on every run_sql, so one guarded database or query engine can serve many requests. Reading a contextvars.ContextVar that your request handler sets is the usual pattern. The model only writes SQL; it never supplies the context. context Result A mapping, or a callable that returns one The query is verified with that context. A callable that returns None Refused: nothing is verified or run. run_sql raises haltsql.integration.ContextUnavailable, or, with denials_as_sql_errors=True, a HaltSQLSQLError reading "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this request; the query was not executed." {}, or a callable that returns it Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy, typically with E_CONTEXT_MISSING. A callable that raises Nothing is verified or run. run_sql raises haltsql.HaltSQLUnavailable (the original exception is its __cause__), or a HaltSQLSQLError reading "SQL verification is unavailable" with denials_as_sql_errors=True. As in the agent-framework packages, a missing context is refused before verification.

On success, the guarded run_sql returns what LlamaIndex expects: the rows as a string, such as [(1, 'open'), (3, 'paid')], and a metadata dict: {"result": [(1, "open"), (3, "paid")], "col_keys": ["id", "status"], "truncated": False} Long string values are shortened the same way as in LlamaIndex's own run_sql. A statement that returns no columns gives ("", {}). On a denial, nothing runs. What happens next depends on denials_as_sql_errors: False (default for guard_sql_database and guarded_sql_retriever). run_sql raises haltsql.QueryDenied. Its message is the reason codes with their hints, such as E_TENANT_MISSING: <hint>. Other failures raise the underlying error (HaltSQLUnavailable, a database error, ...). Your code handles them. True (default for guarded_nl_sql_query_engine). Every failure raises HaltSQLSQLError with text written for the model: HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry: - E_TENANT_MISSING: <hint> Verification failures read "SQL verification is unavailable; the query was not executed." LlamaIndex's NLSQLRetriever, which NLSQLTableQueryEngine uses, catches errors from run_sql when handle_sql_errors=True (its default) and passes Error: <message> on to response synthesis. The query engine does not retry on its own. If you use it as a tool of an agent, the agent sees the error text and can ask again. See reason-codes.md for every code.

guard_sql_database(db, verifier, context, *, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None, read_only=True, denials_as_sql_errors=False): Argument Default Meaning db required A LlamaIndex SQLDatabase. Its engine must use psycopg 3. verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). context required A mapping, or a zero-argument callable that returns one. max_rows 200 Row cap. None means no cap. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query. None means none is set. settings None A mapping of transaction-local settings. Fixed for the guarded copy; it cannot depend on the context. read_only True Run only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select, in a READ ONLY transaction. With False, see Read-only and writes. denials_as_sql_errors False Raise HaltSQLSQLError with model-readable text instead of the original exception. guarded_sql_retriever(db, verifier, context, **kwargs) passes kwargs to guard_sql_database. guarded_nl_sql_query_engine(db, verifier, context, *, guard_kwargs=None, **engine_kwargs): Argument Default Meaning guard_kwargs None A dict of guard_sql_database options (max_rows, statement_timeout_ms, settings, read_only, denials_as_sql_errors). denials_as_sql_errors defaults to True here. **engine_kwargs none Guard options given as keywords (for example max_rows=50) go to the guard; the rest go to NLSQLTableQueryEngine, for example tables= and llm=. Guard options work as keyword arguments (max_rows=50) or in guard_kwargs (guard_kwargs={"max_rows": 50}). Giving the same option both ways, or an unknown key in guard_kwargs, raises TypeError.

With the default read_only=True, a statement runs only when the verdict's statement_kind is select. Anything else is refused before a connection is taken, even when the policy allows it, with GuardError: only SELECT statements run in read-only mode (this is UPDATE) (a HaltSQLSQLError with denials_as_sql_errors=True). With read_only=False, the policy alone decides: a statement runs when HaltSQL allows it, whatever its kind. Writes run in a read-write transaction, and SELECT statements still run READ ONLY. A verdict without a statement_kind never runs. Allow writes in the policy (statements.allow) only for the agents and tables that need them. insert_into_table refuses either way.

The guard is synchronous. run_sql verifies and runs on the calling thread, including when LlamaIndex's async methods (aquery, aretrieve) call it: their SQL step calls the sync run_sql. Use a sync verifier. Rows are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and a guarded database; a denial raises before the engine is touched: import pytest from haltsql import QueryDenied from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_llamaindex import HaltSQLSQLError, guard_sql_database def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) class NoEngine: def raw_connection(self): raise AssertionError("engine used after a denial") class FakeDB: # stands in for SQLDatabase in this unit test _engine = NoEngine() def test_denial_never_touches_the_engine(): g = guard_sql_database(FakeDB(), FakeVerifier(deny), {"tenant_id": "acme"}) with pytest.raises(QueryDenied): g.run_sql("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10") g = guard_sql_database(FakeDB(), FakeVerifier(deny), {"tenant_id": "acme"}, denials_as_sql_errors=True) with pytest.raises(HaltSQLSQLError, match="E_TENANT_MISSING"): g.run_sql("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10") The package's own tests use a real LlamaIndex SQLDatabase and SQLRetriever when llama-index-core is installed, and the lab Postgres for execution: make -C lab up pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/llamaindex[llamaindex,test]' pytest -q integrations/llamaindex FULL=1 clients/python/run-all-tests.sh runs them with the other Python suites.

Symptom Cause Fix Every query on a tenant table is denied with E_CONTEXT_MISSING The context callable returned {}, or misses a key the policy needs. Check the callable. It is evaluated on every query. ContextUnavailable, or "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured" The context callable returned None. Return the context for the current request, for example from a ContextVar your handler sets. GuardError: only SELECT statements run in read-only mode The policy allowed a write, but read_only=True. Ask for a SELECT, or pass read_only=False if the agent should write. GuardError: insert_into_table is not available on a HaltSQL-guarded SQLDatabase SQLStructStoreIndex or your code tried to insert rows through the guarded copy. Load data with the original SQLDatabase outside the agent, or with verified INSERT statements and read_only=False. Allowed SQL fails in Postgres with "relation does not exist" Postgres resolves unqualified table names with the role's search_path, which differs from the policy's. With SQLDatabase(schema=...), the guard does not add the schema prefix, because that would change the verified SQL. Set the role's search_path to the policy's search_path, and drop schema=. GuardError: could not find the SQLAlchemy engine of this SQLDatabase The object passed in has no _engine or engine. Pass a LlamaIndex SQLDatabase. GuardError: psycopg2 cannot send $n placeholders unchanged; use psycopg 3 The engine uses psycopg2. Use a postgresql+psycopg:// URL. TypeError: guard option 'max_rows' given both as a keyword and in guard_kwargs The same option was passed twice. Pass it one way. HaltSQLUnavailable, or "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string; or the context callable raised. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary, and test the callable on its own. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. SQLDatabase(schema=...) is not supported: the guarded run_sql does not prefix the schema. Use search_path instead. run_sql is verified and insert_into_table refuses. Schema reflection (table and column names) and the engine property still use the raw engine. The table descriptions LlamaIndex gives the model come from the database schema, not the policy, so they can name columns the policy denies. Limit them with include_tables. The engine must use psycopg 3. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

Python SDK: verifiers, guard.execute_on_engine and errors. reason-codes.md and tenancy.md. defense-in-depth.md: the database role and row-level security to use with HaltSQL. Agent frameworks: tools for agent SDKs. Source: integrations/llamaindex.

haltsql-mcp is an MCP server that runs model-written SQL on PostgreSQL only after HaltSQL allows it. This page shows how to add it to Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and any other MCP client, with Docker or a local install, verifying locally or through haltsql-server. For what the server does and every setting it takes, see mcp.md.

The server exposes four tools. All are annotated read-only. Tool Arguments What it does query sql Verifies the SQL, then runs exactly that string read-only, with statement_timeout and a row cap. explain_denial sql Verifies only and returns every reason, the tables and columns touched, and the policy name and version. Never executes. list_tables none The tables and columns the policy allows and which are tenant-scoped. Needs a policy file. describe_policy none The policy's name, version and mode (from haltsql-server) and its rules (from the policy file). The tenant is never a tool argument. If the model sends extra arguments such as tenant_id, they are ignored. See Tools for the result shapes.

You need three things whichever client you use: A policy. Draft one from your database with haltsql schema pull and haltsql policy draft, then review it. See Draft a policy from your database. A restricted database role. Connect as a login role that can only read, never as a superuser or table owner. See Use a restricted role and defense-in-depth.md. The server, as a Docker image or a local install. Docker. The ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp image contains haltsql-mcp and the haltsql CLI, so it can verify queries with no other process: docker pull ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp Local install. haltsql-mcp needs Python 3.10 or newer. Install it from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install ./clients/python './clients/mcp[yaml]' The yaml extra installs PyYAML, which the server uses to read YAML config and policy files. To verify locally you also need the haltsql CLI on your PATH, or in HALTSQL_BIN (see the quickstart).

Mode How to select it When to use it Local policy --local-policy FILE, HALTSQL_MCP_LOCAL_POLICY, or policy: in the config file. In Docker, a policy.yaml in /config is picked up when nothing else is set. One developer, one machine. Each query runs haltsql verify with the policy file. Nothing else needs to run. haltsql-server HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or a server: block in the config file. Shared or production use: central policies, hot reload and audit. See http-api.md. If you set neither, the server calls a sidecar at the default HALTSQL_URL, http://127.0.0.1:8080. When nothing answers there, every query fails with "verification is unavailable" and nothing runs. With haltsql-server, also set HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE (or policy_file:) to a copy of the policy if you want list_tables and the rules part of describe_policy to work. In local mode the local policy is used for that automatically.

The context (for example {"tenant_id": "acme"}) comes from whoever starts or authenticates to the server, never from the model: stdio (the default). One context for the whole process, from HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT (a JSON object), --context-file FILE, or context: in the config file. The client sets it in the server's env block. Streamable HTTP. Each client sends a bearer token. The server looks up the token's SHA-256 in a tokens file, and each entry has its own context. See Tenant context for the file format. Warning: with stdio, anyone who can edit the client's config file can change the tenant. That is fine for one developer working on their own data. When the person using the client must not choose the tenant, run the server over HTTP with a tokens file, and give each user only their own token. If the policy has no tenant tables, leave the context out. If it has tenant tables and the context is empty, queries on them are denied, typically with E_CONTEXT_MISSING. To also enforce the tenant with row-level security, set HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG, for example {"app.tenant_id": "tenant_id"}. Each query's transaction then sets app.tenant_id to the context's tenant_id. See rls-generation.md.

documents.t: Claude Desktop starts stdio servers listed in claude_desktop_config.json. The file is at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json on macOS and %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json on Windows. You can also open it from the app's developer settings. Restart Claude Desktop after you change it. Docker. Put policy.yaml in a folder and mount the folder at /config: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "docker", "args": [ "run", "-i", "--rm", "--read-only", "-v", "/path/to/haltsql:/config:ro", "-e", "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT", "ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp", "postgresql://agent_ro@host.docker.internal:5432/mydb" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT with no value passes the variable from env into the container. Inside the container, a database on your machine is host.docker.internal, not localhost (see Reaching your database from the container). Local install: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "/absolute/path/to/haltsql-mcp", "args": [ "--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}", "HALTSQL_BIN": "/absolute/path/to/haltsql" } } } } Use absolute paths. Desktop apps often start servers with a shorter PATH than your shell. Find the paths with which haltsql-mcp and which haltsql. Calling haltsql-server: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "/absolute/path/to/haltsql-mcp", "args": ["postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal:5432/app"], "env": { "HALTSQL_URL": "https://haltsql.internal:8443", "HALTSQL_TOKEN": "<sidecar token>", "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}", "HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE": "/path/to/policy.yaml" } } } } For a private CA or mutual TLS, add HALTSQL_CA_FILE, HALTSQL_CLIENT_CERT and HALTSQL_CLIENT_KEY. To keep the token out of the client config, use a config file with server.token_file (see Use a config file).

Add the server with claude mcp add. Everything after -- is the command that starts the server. -e sets an environment variable for it. Local install: claude mcp add postgres -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' -- \ haltsql-mcp --local-policy /path/to/policy.yaml postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb Docker: claude mcp add postgres -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' -- \ docker run -i --rm --read-only -v /path/to/haltsql:/config:ro -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT \ ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp postgresql://agent_ro@host.docker.internal:5432/mydb Shared HTTP server (see Other MCP clients): claude mcp add --transport http postgres http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $HALTSQL_MCP_TOKEN" By default the server is added for you in the current project only. Pass --scope project to write it to .mcp.json in the repository, so your team gets it too, or --scope user for all your projects. Do not commit a .mcp.json that contains a database password or a token. Run claude mcp list, or /mcp inside Claude Code, to check that the server connected.

Cursor reads ~/.cursor/mcp.json (all projects) and .cursor/mcp.json (one project). The stdio entries have the same shape as in Claude Desktop: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "haltsql-mcp", "args": [ "--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } For Docker, use the docker entry from Claude Desktop unchanged. For a shared HTTP server, give a url and a header: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <token>" } } } }

VS Code reads MCP servers from .vscode/mcp.json in the workspace. It uses a servers key instead of mcpServers: { "servers": { "postgres": { "type": "stdio", "command": "haltsql-mcp", "args": ["--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb"], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } For Docker, set "command": "docker" and use the same args and env as in Claude Desktop. For a shared HTTP server, use "type": "http". An input variable keeps the token out of the file. VS Code prompts for it the first time: { "inputs": [ { "type": "promptString", "id": "haltsql-mcp-token", "description": "haltsql-mcp token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "postgres": { "type": "http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:haltsql-mcp-token}" } } } } For user-level configuration and other options, see the VS Code documentation.

Any client that can start a stdio server needs three things: the command (haltsql-mcp, or docker with the run -i arguments above), its arguments, and its environment. The connection string can be the last argument, as with @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres, or --database-url, or HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL. Give it only once: a positional URL and a different --database-url together are an error. HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ haltsql-mcp --local-policy policy.yaml postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb The server speaks MCP on stdin and stdout and logs warnings to stderr.

Run one server for many clients. Each client authenticates with its own bearer token, and the token decides the tenant: TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32) # give this to one client printf %s "$TOKEN" | shasum -a 256 # put the hash in tokens.json { "tokens": [ { "name": "agent-acme", "token_sha256": "<sha256 hex>", "context": { "tenant_id": "acme" } } ] } haltsql-mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765 \ --tokens-file /etc/haltsql-mcp/tokens.json \ --database-url postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal/app \ --local-policy /etc/haltsql/policy.yaml Clients connect to http://HOST:8765/mcp and send Authorization: Bearer <token>. A missing or unknown token gets HTTP 401. TLS is not built in: keep the listener on loopback or put a TLS proxy in front of it. For the Docker version, see Shared HTTP server.

One YAML or JSON file can replace the arguments and most environment variables. Pass it with --config FILE or HALTSQL_MCP_CONFIG. In Docker, a haltsql-mcp.yaml in /config is loaded automatically. Relative paths are resolved against the file's directory. # haltsql-mcp.yaml, calling a central haltsql-server server: url: https://haltsql.internal:8443 token_file: token # a file holding the sidecar token ca_file: ca.pem # optional database_url: postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal:5432/app policy_file: policy.yaml # optional: for list_tables and describe_policy context: { tenant_id: acme } row_cap: 200 statement_timeout_ms: 5000 The client entry then only needs haltsql-mcp --config /path/to/haltsql-mcp.yaml, or docker run -i --rm --read-only -v /path/to/haltsql:/config:ro ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp. Flags override environment variables, and environment variables override the file. Unknown keys are an error, and an inline server.token is rejected. See Config file for every key.

Check the policy and context without the client. This uses the same policy and context the server will: haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ --sql 'SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10' Exit code 0 means allowed. Add --json to see the verdict. Start the server by hand with the same command, arguments and environment as the client config. A configuration error prints haltsql-mcp: <message> on stderr and exits with status 2. A valid stdio configuration starts and waits for input; stop it with Ctrl-C. Call the tools from a test client. The MCP Inspector starts the server and lets you call each tool: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ haltsql-mcp --local-policy policy.yaml postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb Call describe_policy, then query with an allowed query, then query with SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10. The last one should return "allowed": false with E_TENANT_MISSING and no rows. Try it in the client. Restart the client, ask a question about your data, then ask for every tenant's rows or for a column the policy does not allow. You should see a denial with reason codes, and no rows.

Configuration errors stop the server before it starts. Most clients then show the server as failed or disconnected. Read the client's MCP log for the haltsql-mcp: line. Claude Desktop writes its logs to ~/Library/Logs/Claude on macOS; for other clients, see the client's documentation. Message or symptom Cause Fix The client cannot start the server, or "command not found" haltsql-mcp or docker is not on the PATH the client uses. Use the absolute path in command. "verification is unavailable; the query was not executed" Local mode: the haltsql CLI is missing or failed. Server mode: haltsql-server cannot be reached, timed out, or failed TLS. With neither configured, the default http://127.0.0.1:8080 is not running. Set HALTSQL_BIN to the CLI, pass --local-policy, or check HALTSQL_URL and the CA settings. "verification refused (UNAUTHORIZED); the query was not executed" haltsql-server rejected HALTSQL_TOKEN. Other codes: FORBIDDEN, POLICY_NOT_FOUND. Check the token and HALTSQL_POLICY. "no database is configured for this server" No connection string. Pass it as the last argument, --database-url or HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL. "database connection failed: OperationalError" Postgres is unreachable or rejected the login. In Docker, use host.docker.internal (Docker Desktop) or --network host (Linux). Check the role and password. "database error: ..." HaltSQL allowed the query but Postgres rejected it, for example 57014 (statement timeout) or 42501 (permission denied). Raise HALTSQL_MCP_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS, or grant the role what the policy allows. If table names do not resolve, give the role the policy's search_path. Every tenant query is denied with E_CONTEXT_MISSING The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs. Set HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT, and check that the JSON is quoted correctly for the client config. "server misconfigured: context has no 'tenant_id' for app.tenant_id" HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG names a context key that is not in the context. Add the key to the context, or fix HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG. "no policy file is configured, so the table list is unavailable" list_tables needs the policy document. Server mode does not have it. Set HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE. "HTTP transport needs a tokens file ..." --transport http without --tokens-file. Add a tokens file. --insecure-static-context is for local development on a loopback address only. "a tokens file only applies to the HTTP transport" A tokens file was set with stdio. Remove it, or use --transport http. "config file ... is YAML; install PyYAML ..." The yaml extra is not installed. pip install './clients/mcp[yaml]', or write the file as JSON. "file not found: ..." A policy, tokens, CA or certificate path does not exist. In Docker, the path is inside the container. Use paths under the mounted /config folder. "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT is not valid JSON" The JSON is malformed, often from shell or JSON-in-JSON quoting. In JSON config, escape the inner quotes: "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}".

Agent frameworks: HaltSQL tools for agent SDKs instead of MCP. reason-codes.md: every denial code. tenancy.md: how tenant predicates are proven. defense-in-depth.md: the database role and row-level security to run alongside HaltSQL.

haltsql-openai-agents gives an OpenAI Agents SDK agent a haltsql_query tool that runs read-only SQL only after HaltSQL has verified it. It also has a tool input guardrail that verifies the SQL argument of a tool you already have. The tenant comes from the run context your application passes to Runner.run, never from the model.

Name Kind What it does haltsql_query_tool(runner, ...) Function returning a FunctionTool A tool named haltsql_query whose only argument is query. Verifies, then runs the exact SQL in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. haltsql_tool_input_guardrail(verifier, ...) Function returning a ToolInputGuardrail Verifies the SQL argument of another tool before that tool runs, and rejects the call if HaltSQL does not allow it. HaltSQLToolRunner Class Holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits. Shared by all five agent-framework packages. See The runner. context_from_app(app_state, key="haltsql_context") Function Reads and validates the context from an object or mapping. Used by default to read the run context. ContextUnavailable Exception Raised inside the package when no context can be read. You see it as a refusal, not as an exception. TOOL_NAME, DEFAULT_CONTEXT_KEY Constants "haltsql_query" and "haltsql_context". The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize and guard.execute.

The package needs Python 3.10 or newer and openai-agents 0.22 or newer, below 1.0. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e integrations/openai_agents The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need one of these: a running haltsql-server (use HaltSQLClient, see http-api.md), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (use LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (use NativeVerifier, see In-process verification).

import asyncio import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field import psycopg from agents import Agent, Runner from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_openai_agents import HaltSQLToolRunner, haltsql_query_tool DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role @dataclass class AppContext: # passed to Runner.run; never sent to the model user_id: str haltsql_context: dict = field(default_factory=dict) runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) agent = Agent( name="analyst", instructions="Answer questions about the user's orders with the haltsql_query tool.", tools=[haltsql_query_tool(runner)], ) async def answer(user, question: str) -> str: ctx = AppContext(user_id=user.id, haltsql_context={"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}) result = await Runner.run(agent, question, context=ctx) return result.final_output user is your authenticated user. Create the runner and the agent once at startup. Build the run context per request.

The tool reads the HaltSQL context from the run context, the object you pass as Runner.run(..., context=...). The SDK never sends that object to the model. By default the tool reads its haltsql_context attribute, or its haltsql_context key if it is a mapping. The value may also be a zero-argument callable that returns the mapping. To read the context from your own object, pass context_from: tool = haltsql_query_tool( runner, context_from=lambda app: {"tenant_id": app.session.tenant_id}, ) What happens in each case: Run context Result Has haltsql_context (or context_from returns a mapping) The query is verified with that context. No run context, no haltsql_context, or context_from returns None Refused before verification: "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run". haltsql_context is {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. The value is not a valid context (for example a float value) Refused: "The query was not executed: ..." with the validation error. The tool's JSON schema has only query, with additionalProperties: false and strict mode on. If a tool call carries any other argument, such as tenant_id, the call is refused and nothing is verified or run.

The tool returns JSON text. On success: {"status":"ok","executed":true,"columns":["id","status"],"rows":[[1,"open"],[3,"paid"]],"row_count":2,"truncated":false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason with its code and hint: {"status":"denied","executed":false, "reasons":[{"code":"E_TENANT_MISMATCH","message":"...","hint":"Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message":"HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} Other failures have "status": "error". With "executed": false, nothing ran: HaltSQL was unavailable, no context was configured, the statement was not a SELECT, or the database could not be reached. With "executed": true, HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example on a statement timeout. The message gives the database error's class and its first line. Verification failures are reported without internal details. The default tool description tells the model to filter tenant tables with alias.tenant_id = $1, never to write tenant IDs, and to fix the SQL and retry after a denial. See reason-codes.md for every code.

haltsql_tool_input_guardrail checks the SQL argument of an existing tool before the SDK runs it: from agents import function_tool from haltsql import LocalVerifier from haltsql_openai_agents import haltsql_tool_input_guardrail guard = haltsql_tool_input_guardrail(LocalVerifier("policy.yaml"), sql_arg="sql") @function_tool(tool_input_guardrails=[guard]) def run_sql(sql: str) -> str: """Run SQL against the warehouse.""" ... If HaltSQL does not allow the SQL, the guardrail calls reject_content. The tool does not run and the model gets the refusal JSON. The guardrail also rejects the call when the argument is missing, no context is configured, HaltSQL is unavailable, or the statement is not a SELECT. Warning: the guarded tool cannot receive HaltSQL's $n values, so the guardrail refuses any SQL that HaltSQL allows only with bound parameters. Use it with a policy in literal tenancy mode (see tenancy.md), or use haltsql_query_tool instead. The guardrail checks only the SQL. The guarded tool must still use a read-only role, a timeout and a row limit.
