documents.t: HaltSQLToolRunner(verifier, connect, *, max_rows=200, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning verifier required HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). connect required Zero-argument callable that returns a new psycopg 3 connection. Called only after HaltSQL allows the query. The runner closes the connection after each query. max_rows 200 Row cap, 1 to 100000. truncated tells the model more rows were available. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query, 1 to 3600000. settings None Transaction-local settings: a mapping, or a function of the verified context, for example lambda ctx: {"app.tenant_id": ctx["tenant_id"]} for row-level security. haltsql_query_tool(runner, *, context_from=None, name="haltsql_query", description=DEFAULT_DESCRIPTION): Argument Default Meaning runner required A HaltSQLToolRunner. context_from None f(run_context) -> mapping. Default: the run context's haltsql_context attribute or key. name "haltsql_query" Tool name the model sees. description built-in text Tool description the model sees. haltsql_tool_input_guardrail(verifier, *, sql_arg="query", context_from=None, name="haltsql_sql_guardrail"): Argument Default Meaning verifier required Any object with verify(sql, context). sql_arg "query" Name of the guarded tool's SQL argument. context_from None As for haltsql_query_tool. name "haltsql_sql_guardrail" Guardrail name. Every query runs in a READ ONLY transaction, and only statements whose verdict statement_kind is select are run. These cannot be turned off.

The tool is async. Verification and execution run in a worker thread (asyncio.to_thread), so they do not block the event loop. The guardrail also runs its check in a worker thread. Use a sync verifier (HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier) and a sync psycopg connection: the runner calls them from that thread. Results are returned whole; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and check that a denial never opens a connection: from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_openai_agents import HaltSQLToolRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): fv = FakeVerifier(deny) out = HaltSQLToolRunner(fv, no_db).run("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10", {"tenant_id": "acme"}) assert out["status"] == "denied" and out["reasons"][0]["code"] == "E_TENANT_MISSING" assert fv.calls == [("SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10", {"tenant_id": "acme"})] The package's own tests run tool calls through the SDK's function-tool executor with the real haltsql CLI, a real haltsql-server and the lab Postgres. They never call an LLM: make -C lab up dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./bin/server/main.exe ONLY=agents clients/python/run-all-tests.sh integrations/openai_agents/constraints.txt lists the exact versions the tests were run with. See Testing.

Symptom Cause Fix "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run" Runner.run got no context=, the context has no haltsql_context, or context_from returned None or raised a LookupError. Pass the run context, or fix context_from. Every query on a tenant table is denied The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs (E_CONTEXT_MISSING), or the model wrote a tenant literal (E_TENANT_MISMATCH). Check the context. In bound mode the model must write $1. "pass exactly one argument, 'query'" The tool call had extra or missing arguments. Nothing to fix in your code: the model sees the message and retries. "SQL verification is unavailable" The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string. An unexpected exception in context_from (other than LookupError or ValueError) is also reported this way. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary. Test context_from on its own. "The database is unavailable" connect raised. Check the DSN and network. ValueError when building the runner verifier has no verify, connect is not callable, or a limit is out of range. Fix the argument named in the message. The guardrail rejects allowed SQL with "HaltSQL allows it only with bound parameters" The policy uses bound tenancy. Use haltsql_query_tool, or literal tenancy for that tool. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

Read-only SELECT only. Write policies are not supported by this tool. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. psycopg2 and asyncpg are not supported here. The guardrail checks SQL only, and cannot be used with bound tenancy. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

haltsql-server and the haltsql CLI can read secrets in their Config document straight from HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Google Secret Manager, so the file holds only references. This page gives one recipe per secrets manager: how HaltSQL authenticates, what it needs to be allowed, the placeholder syntax, and what happens on rotation and failure. The reference is secrets.md. Secrets managers covered: HashiCorp Vault (KV version 2) AWS Secrets Manager Google Secret Manager Azure Key Vault (not supported; workaround)

A placeholder can stand for any string in a kind: Config document, for example an audit sink password, an OTLP header or an S3 key: Placeholder Source ${env:NAME} environment variable ${file:/path} file contents, minus one trailing newline ${vault:<path>#<field>} HashiCorp Vault KV v2 ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]} AWS Secrets Manager ${gcp-sm:<name>[#<json-key>]} Google Secret Manager $${ a literal ${ The vault, aws-sm and gcp-sm providers are configured in the secrets section, which may itself only use ${env:...} and ${file:...}. Behaviour shared by all three providers: When secrets are read. At startup and on every reload (SIGHUP, or a watched config or policy file changing). Each load fetches every distinct reference once, concurrently, before the rest of the config is decoded. There is no background refresh between loads. Rotation. A rotated secret is picked up on the next reload. HaltSQL does not watch the secrets manager, so trigger a reload (or a restart) after rotating. Values used by audit sinks (for example a Kafka SASL password or an Elasticsearch API key) only change on a restart, because audit sinks are not replaced on reload (reload rules). Failure. A placeholder that cannot be resolved is a load error that names the file position, the reference and the provider's error, never the secret. HaltSQL never substitutes an empty string. At startup the server exits with code 2; on reload it keeps the last good configuration and counts the failure in haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}. The CLI (haltsql config show, haltsql validate) exits 2. Timeouts. Each HTTP request to a secrets manager times out after 10 seconds. Redaction. Resolved values are never logged. haltsql config show prints them as "<redacted>". Where they work. In kind: Config documents read by haltsql-server and the haltsql CLI. Policies never accept placeholders (only ${ctx.*}). haltsql-proxy configs accept only ${env:...} and ${file:...} (proxy.md). Check a config before deploying it: haltsql config show --config haltsql.yaml resolves every placeholder with the same credentials the server would use, and prints the result with secrets redacted.

Placeholder. ${vault:<mount>/<path>#<field>} reads GET /v1/<mount>/data/<path> and returns data.data.<field>. Only KV version 2 is supported. If the path already has data as its second segment (secret/data/haltsql/otel#token), it is used as written; write mounts with several segments in that explicit form (team/kv/data/app#token). Numbers and booleans come back in their JSON spelling; objects and arrays are errors. Auth methods. auth.method Keys Login token token The token is sent as X-Vault-Token. Supply it with ${env:VAULT_TOKEN} or ${file:...}. kubernetes role; jwt_path (default /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token); mount (default kubernetes) POST /v1/auth/<mount>/login with {role, jwt}. approle role_id, secret_id; mount (default approle) POST /v1/auth/<mount>/login with {role_id, secret_id}. Keys that belong to another method are errors. Other Vault auth methods (AWS, Azure, GCP, JWT/OIDC, ...) are not supported. Config (Kubernetes). secrets: vault: address: https://vault.corp.example:8200 namespace: platform # Vault Enterprise, optional ca_file: /etc/haltsql/vault-ca.pem # optional; replaces the system trust store auth: { method: kubernetes, role: haltsql } audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch url: https://es.corp.example:9200 data_stream: logs-haltsql-prod auth: { api_key: "${vault:secret/data/haltsql/es#api_key}" } Config (AppRole). The AppRole credentials themselves come from the environment or a file, never from Vault: secrets: vault: address: https://vault.corp.example:8200 auth: method: approle role_id: "${env:VAULT_ROLE_ID}" secret_id: "${file:/var/run/secrets/vault/secret-id}" Vault policy. HaltSQL only reads. For the example above: path "secret/data/haltsql/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } Bind it to the auth role (for Kubernetes, a role bound to HaltSQL's service account and namespace). See Vault's documentation for the Kubernetes and AppRole auth methods. Caching and refresh. Every load (startup or reload) logs in again, at most once. Within a load the login token is reused until 30 seconds before its lease ends, and a 403 on a read triggers one re-login. Pitfalls. address must be https, or http for loopback addresses only (a local Vault agent). KV v1 mounts are not supported: the reader always uses the KV v2 data/ path. Short-lived secret ids. An AppRole secret_id with a use limit or TTL can be exhausted by reloads. Size it for the number of reloads and restarts you expect, or use the Kubernetes method.

Placeholder. ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]} calls GetSecretValue with the secret's name or ARN. The value is SecretString, or the decoded SecretBinary. With #key, the value is parsed as a JSON object and that key's scalar is returned. secrets: aws: region: eu-west-1 audit: sinks: - type: kafka brokers: [b-1.kafka.corp.example:9096] topic: haltsql.audit tls: { enabled: true } # system CA roots sasl: mechanism: scram-sha-512 username: haltsql password: "${aws-sm:prod/haltsql/kafka#password}" secrets.aws.region is required. The endpoint is https://secretsmanager.<region>.amazonaws.com, or secrets.aws.endpoint (for tests). Credentials. HaltSQL uses the first source in this chain that yields credentials: environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, optional AWS_SESSION_TOKEN); web identity (EKS IRSA): AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE and AWS_ROLE_ARN, exchanged with STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; container credentials (ECS task roles, EKS Pod Identity): AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI or AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI; the EC2 instance profile, through IMDSv2. Temporary credentials are cached and refreshed 5 minutes before they expire. On an expired-credential error, the credentials are refreshed and the call is retried once. IAM policy. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue", "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:prod/haltsql/*"} ] } Add kms:Decrypt on the key when the secrets are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Pitfalls. Versions and staging labels cannot be selected: HaltSQL always reads the current version (AWSCURRENT). Rotate by updating the secret, then reload. #key needs a JSON object. A plain-string secret with #key is an error; use the placeholder without #key. Region. One secrets.aws.region serves all aws-sm placeholders in the file.

Placeholder. ${gcp-sm:<name>[#<json-key>]}, where <name> is one of: projects/P/secrets/S/versions/V; projects/P/secrets/S (the latest version); S or S/versions/V, in the project secrets.gcp.project. HaltSQL calls GET /v1/<name>:access on https://secretmanager.googleapis.com (or secrets.gcp.endpoint, for tests), base64-decodes the payload and checks its CRC-32C checksum when the response carries one. With #key, the value is parsed as JSON and that key's scalar is returned. secrets: gcp: project: corp-prod # only needed for short names telemetry: otlp: endpoint: https://otel.corp.example:4318 headers: authorization: "Bearer ${gcp-sm:haltsql-otel-token}" The secrets.gcp section is optional when every placeholder uses a full projects/... name. Credentials. The service-account key file named by GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS when that variable is set; otherwise the metadata server (GKE Workload Identity, Cloud Run, GCE). Tokens from a key file are requested with the cloud-platform scope. A 401 refreshes the token once. IAM. Grant HaltSQL's service account roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on each secret (or on the project): gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding haltsql-otel-token \ --member="serviceAccount:haltsql@corp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor" Pitfalls. Pin versions for reproducible reloads. projects/P/secrets/S and a short S read the latest version at each load, so a new version reaches HaltSQL at the next reload whether or not you meant it to. Name the version (S/versions/3) if you want rotation to be an explicit config change. Name segments may only contain letters, digits, _ and -.

HaltSQL cannot read Azure Key Vault directly: there is no ${azure-kv:...} placeholder, and HaltSQL has no Azure managed-identity credential support. Use the platform to put Key Vault secrets on disk and read them with ${file:...}: AKS: the Key Vault Secrets Store CSI driver mounts secrets as files. Azure Container Apps: Key Vault secret references, mounted as files. Or HashiCorp Vault with its Azure auth method in front of HaltSQL's Vault support. Remember that ${file:...} values are read at startup and on reload; a changed file alone does not trigger a reload. The full pattern, including token rotation, is in Deploying on Azure (see Current limitations on Azure).

Secrets: loading order, provider details and the library API. Config reference: secrets and placeholders. Config reference: reload: what a reload applies and what needs a restart. Deploying on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure.

haltsql-semantic-kernel gives a Semantic Kernel (Python) agent a plugin with one function, query, that runs read-only SQL only after HaltSQL has verified it. With the suggested plugin name, the model sees the function as haltsql-query. The tenant comes from a mapping or callable your application gives the plugin, never from KernelArguments.

Name Kind What it does HaltSQLPlugin(runner, context) Class A native plugin with one kernel_function, query, whose only argument is query. Verifies, then runs the exact SQL in a READ ONLY transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. Returns JSON text. PLUGIN_NAME Constant "haltsql", the suggested plugin name. With the function name query, the model sees haltsql-query. HaltSQLToolRunner Class Holds the verifier, the connection factory and the limits. Shared by all five agent-framework packages. See The runner. context_from_app(app_state, key="haltsql_context") Function Reads and validates a context stored under a key of an object or mapping. Useful inside your own context callable. ContextUnavailable Exception Raised inside the package when no context is available. You see it as a refusal. TOOL_NAME, DEFAULT_CONTEXT_KEY Constants "haltsql_query" and "haltsql_context". The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize and guard.execute.

The package needs Python 3.11 or newer and semantic-kernel 1.44 or newer, below 2. It is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e integrations/semantic_kernel The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (HaltSQLClient), the haltsql CLI and a policy file (LocalVerifier), or a platform wheel of the SDK with the bundled engine (NativeVerifier). See the Python SDK.

import contextvars import os import psycopg from semantic_kernel import Kernel from semantic_kernel.connectors.ai.function_choice_behavior import FunctionChoiceBehavior from semantic_kernel.connectors.ai.open_ai import OpenAIChatCompletion, OpenAIChatPromptExecutionSettings from semantic_kernel.contents import ChatHistory from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_semantic_kernel import PLUGIN_NAME, HaltSQLPlugin, HaltSQLToolRunner DSN = os.environ["AGENT_DATABASE_URL"] # a read-only role current_ctx = contextvars.ContextVar("haltsql_ctx", default=None) runner = HaltSQLToolRunner( HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or LocalVerifier("policy.yaml") connect=lambda: psycopg.connect(DSN), # called only after HaltSQL allows the query ) kernel = Kernel() kernel.add_service(OpenAIChatCompletion(ai_model_id="gpt-4o-mini")) kernel.add_plugin(HaltSQLPlugin(runner, context=current_ctx.get), plugin_name=PLUGIN_NAME) async def answer(user, question: str) -> str: current_ctx.set({"tenant_id": user.tenant_id}) # from your auth, per request chat = kernel.get_service(type=OpenAIChatCompletion) settings = OpenAIChatPromptExecutionSettings(function_choice_behavior=FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto()) history = ChatHistory() history.add_user_message(question) reply = await chat.get_chat_message_content(history, settings, kernel=kernel) return str(reply) user is your authenticated user. The chat service and execution settings are standard Semantic Kernel; use whichever connector you already have. The HaltSQL part is the HaltSQLPlugin line and setting current_ctx per request.

context is either a mapping or a zero-argument callable. A callable is evaluated on every call, so one plugin can serve many requests. Reading a contextvars.ContextVar that your request handler sets, as above, is the usual pattern. The plugin never reads the context from KernelArguments, because automatic function calling merges the model's arguments into them. context Result A mapping, or a callable that returns one The query is verified with that context. A callable that returns None (for example a ContextVar that was not set) Refused before verification: "No trusted HaltSQL context is configured for this run". A callable that returns {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. Not a mapping or callable TypeError when you create the plugin. The callable runs in a worker thread, and contextvars values are copied into that thread, so a ContextVar set in the request's task is visible. If the model sends arguments the function does not declare, such as tenant_id, Semantic Kernel itself refuses the call with an "unexpected argument" error and the function does not run.

The function returns JSON text. On success: {"status":"ok","executed":true,"columns":["id","status"],"rows":[[1,"open"],[3,"paid"]],"row_count":2,"truncated":false} When HaltSQL denies the query, nothing runs, and the model gets each reason with its code and hint: {"status":"denied","executed":false, "reasons":[{"code":"E_TENANT_MISMATCH","message":"...","hint":"Use a $n placeholder (e.g. orders.tenant_id = $1) instead of a tenant literal; HaltSQL returns the value to bind."}], "message":"HaltSQL denied the query; it was not executed. Fix the SQL and retry:\n- E_TENANT_MISMATCH: Use a $n placeholder ..."} Other failures have "status": "error". With "executed": false, nothing ran: HaltSQL was unavailable, no context was configured, the statement was not a SELECT, or the database could not be reached. With "executed": true, HaltSQL allowed the query but the database rejected it, for example on a statement timeout. See reason-codes.md for every code.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing and invoke the function through the kernel: import asyncio import json from semantic_kernel import Kernel from semantic_kernel.functions import KernelArguments from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_semantic_kernel import PLUGIN_NAME, HaltSQLPlugin, HaltSQLToolRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): kernel = Kernel() runner = HaltSQLToolRunner(FakeVerifier(deny), no_db) kernel.add_plugin(HaltSQLPlugin(runner, context={"tenant_id": "acme"}), plugin_name=PLUGIN_NAME) result = asyncio.run(kernel.invoke(plugin_name=PLUGIN_NAME, function_name="query", arguments=KernelArguments(query="SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10"))) out = json.loads(str(result.value)) assert out["status"] == "denied" and out["reasons"][0]["code"] == "E_TENANT_MISSING" The package's own tests use Kernel.invoke and Kernel.invoke_function_call with the real haltsql CLI, a real haltsql-server and the lab Postgres. TypeError when creating the plugin runner is not a HaltSQLToolRunner, or context is neither a mapping nor callable. Fix the argument. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

Read-only SELECT only. Write policies are not supported by this plugin. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination. connect must return a psycopg 3 connection. Python only. The package does not cover Semantic Kernel for .NET or Java. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

haltsql-vanna guards Vanna with HaltSQL. Every SQL string Vanna generates is verified first, and only the exact verified string runs, with the bound tenant parameters, in a read-only transaction. It supports Vanna 2.x through a SqlRunner and the legacy Vanna 0.x VannaBase through a replacement run_sql.

Name Kind What it does HaltSQLSqlRunner(verifier, ...) Vanna 2.x SqlRunner Give it to RunSqlTool(sql_runner=...). Takes the tenant from the authenticated ToolContext.user, verifies, runs the exact SQL, and returns a pandas DataFrame. Async. install_legacy_run_sql(vn, verifier, context, ...) Function Replaces vn.run_sql on a Vanna 0.x VannaBase object with a guarded version that returns a DataFrame. Sync. context_from_user_metadata(user) Function The default Vanna 2.x context resolver: returns user.metadata["haltsql_context"], or raises PermissionError. to_dataframe(result) Function Turns a haltsql.GuardedResult into a pandas DataFrame. The package is a thin layer over the Python SDK. Every query goes through haltsql.guard.authorize (or authorize_async), then guard.execute (or execute_async). It does not use HaltSQLToolRunner from the agent frameworks packages.

The package needs Python 3.9 or newer. The vanna extra installs vanna 0.7 or newer and pandas 1.5 or newer. The package is not on PyPI yet, so install it and the Python SDK from a checkout of the repository: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/vanna[vanna]' The SDK depends on psycopg 3, which needs libpq on the machine. If you do not have it, also run pip install 'psycopg[binary]'. To verify queries you need a running haltsql-server (AsyncHaltSQLClient or HaltSQLClient), or the haltsql CLI and a policy file (AsyncLocalVerifier or LocalVerifier). See the Python SDK.

Vanna 2.x: from haltsql import AsyncHaltSQLClient from haltsql_vanna import HaltSQLSqlRunner from vanna.core.user import RequestContext, User, UserResolver from vanna.tools import RunSqlTool runner = HaltSQLSqlRunner( AsyncHaltSQLClient.from_env(), # or AsyncLocalVerifier("policy.yaml") dsn="postgresql://agent_ro@db/app", # a read-only role ) run_sql = RunSqlTool(sql_runner=runner) # register it with your Vanna agent class MyUserResolver(UserResolver): async def resolve_user(self, request_context: RequestContext) -> User: session = await authenticate(request_context) # your auth return User(id=session.user_id, metadata={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": session.tenant_id}}) authenticate stands for your own authentication. Register run_sql and MyUserResolver with your Vanna agent as Vanna's documentation describes. Vanna 0.x (legacy VannaBase): from haltsql import HaltSQLClient from haltsql_vanna import install_legacy_run_sql install_legacy_run_sql( vn, # your VannaBase instance HaltSQLClient.from_env(), # a sync verifier lambda: {"tenant_id": current_tenant.get()}, # from your auth, per query dsn="postgresql://agent_ro@db/app", ) vn.ask("How many open orders do we have?") install_legacy_run_sql also sets vn.run_sql_is_set = True and vn.dialect = "PostgreSQL".

Vanna 2.x. HaltSQLSqlRunner calls context_from_user(context.user) on every query, where context is Vanna's ToolContext and user is the user your UserResolver authenticated. The default reads user.metadata["haltsql_context"]. The LLM writes only RunSqlToolArgs.sql; it never supplies the context. User Result metadata["haltsql_context"] is a mapping The query is verified with that context. No user, no metadata, or no haltsql_context mapping PermissionError("no HaltSQL context for this user"). Nothing is verified or run. haltsql_context is {} Verified with an empty context. Tenant tables are then denied by the policy. A custom context_from_user returns None haltsql.integration.ContextUnavailable. Nothing is verified or run. To derive the context differently, pass context_from_user: runner = HaltSQLSqlRunner(verifier, dsn=DSN, context_from_user=lambda user: {"tenant_id": lookup_tenant(user.id)}) Vanna 0.x. context is a mapping or a zero-argument callable, evaluated on every run_sql. A callable that returns None raises haltsql.integration.ContextUnavailable, and nothing is verified or run. An explicit {} is verified as an empty context, which the policy denies for tenant tables. A callable that raises stops the query before verification.

On success, both versions return a pandas DataFrame with the result's columns, up to max_rows rows. On a denial, nothing runs, and haltsql.QueryDenied is raised. Its message lists each reason code with its hint, separated by ; : E_TENANT_MISSING: <hint>; E_COLUMN_DENIED: <hint> What the LLM sees then depends on Vanna: Vanna 2.x. RunSqlTool catches exceptions from the runner. In Vanna 2.0 it gives the LLM Error executing query: followed by the exception message, so the model gets the codes and hints. The same applies to a PermissionError for a missing context, and to verification and database errors. Vanna 0.x. The exception propagates from vn.run_sql. How ask reports it depends on your Vanna version and its settings. Verification failures raise HaltSQLUnavailable or HaltSQLRequestError; database errors raise the driver's exception. See reason-codes.md for every code.

HaltSQLSqlRunner(verifier, *, dsn=None, connect=None, context_from_user=context_from_user_metadata, max_rows=1000, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning verifier required AsyncHaltSQLClient (recommended), AsyncLocalVerifier, or a sync verifier such as HaltSQLClient. A sync verifier blocks the event loop while it verifies. dsn None libpq connection string. A new psycopg 3 AsyncConnection (autocommit) is opened per query, after verification. Give exactly one of dsn and connect. connect None async () -> connection, returning a psycopg AsyncConnection or an asyncpg connection. Called after verification; closed after each query. context_from_user context_from_user_metadata (user) -> mapping. Raise to refuse. max_rows 1000 Row cap. None means no cap. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query. None means none is set. settings None A mapping of transaction-local settings. Fixed for the runner; it cannot depend on the context. install_legacy_run_sql(vn, verifier, context, *, dsn=None, connect=None, max_rows=1000, statement_timeout_ms=5000, settings=None): Argument Default Meaning vn required Your Vanna 0.x VannaBase instance. verifier required A sync verifier: HaltSQLClient, LocalVerifier, NativeVerifier, or any object with verify(sql, context). context required A mapping, or a zero-argument callable that returns one. dsn None libpq connection string; a psycopg 3 connection (autocommit) is opened per query. Give exactly one of dsn and connect. connect None Zero-argument callable that returns a psycopg.Connection. Closed after each query. max_rows 1000 Row cap. None means no cap. statement_timeout_ms 5000 statement_timeout for the query. None means none is set. settings None A mapping of transaction-local settings. Both always run in a READ ONLY transaction. This cannot be turned off.

HaltSQLSqlRunner.run_sql is async, as Vanna 2.x requires. With an async verifier and the default dsn (psycopg AsyncConnection) or an asyncpg connect, nothing blocks the event loop. The legacy run_sql is sync and needs a sync verifier: an async verifier raises GuardError. Rows are returned whole as a DataFrame; streaming rows is not supported.

You can test your wiring without a model, a sidecar or a database. Use FakeVerifier from haltsql.testing, and stand-ins for Vanna's arguments (args.sql and context.user.metadata): import asyncio from types import SimpleNamespace import pytest from haltsql import QueryDenied from haltsql.testing import FakeVerifier, make_verdict_dict from haltsql_vanna import HaltSQLSqlRunner def deny(sql, ctx, _policy): return make_verdict_dict(sql, allowed=False, codes=["E_TENANT_MISSING"]) async def no_db(): raise AssertionError("connected after a denial") def test_denial_never_connects(): runner = HaltSQLSqlRunner(FakeVerifier(deny), connect=no_db) user = SimpleNamespace(metadata={"haltsql_context": {"tenant_id": "acme"}}) with pytest.raises(QueryDenied, match="E_TENANT_MISSING"): asyncio.run(runner.run_sql(SimpleNamespace(sql="SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10"), SimpleNamespace(user=user))) The package's own tests use these stand-ins, Vanna's real SqlRunner, RunSqlToolArgs and User classes when Vanna is installed, and the lab Postgres for execution: make -C lab up pip install -e clients/python -e 'integrations/vanna[vanna,test]' pytest -q integrations/vanna FULL=1 clients/python/run-all-tests.sh runs them with the other Python suites.

Symptom Cause Fix PermissionError: no HaltSQL context for this user The resolved user has no metadata["haltsql_context"] mapping. Set it in your UserResolver, or pass context_from_user. Every query on a tenant table is denied with E_CONTEXT_MISSING The context is empty or misses a key the policy needs. Check the context your resolver or callable returns. ContextUnavailable The context callable or context_from_user returned None. Return the context for the current request. ValueError: pass exactly one of dsn= or connect= Both or neither were given. Pass one. ValueError: RunSqlToolArgs.sql must be a string The tool arguments had no SQL string. Check how the runner is called. GuardError: an async verifier was passed to a sync execute() The legacy run_sql got AsyncHaltSQLClient or AsyncLocalVerifier. Use HaltSQLClient or LocalVerifier with install_legacy_run_sql. HaltSQLUnavailable The sidecar or CLI failed, timed out, or returned a verdict for a different string. Check HALTSQL_URL and HALTSQL_TOKEN, or the haltsql binary. ImportError for pandas pandas is not installed. Install the vanna extra. ImportError: no pq wrapper available psycopg cannot find libpq. pip install 'psycopg[binary]', or install libpq.

Read-only only. Queries always run in a READ ONLY transaction. One statement per call. Rows are returned whole, up to max_rows; there is no streaming or pagination, and the DataFrame does not say whether rows were cut. The default row cap is 1000, higher than the other integrations' 200. HaltSQLSqlRunner subclasses Vanna's SqlRunner only when vanna.capabilities.sql_runner can be imported (Vanna 2.x). Otherwise it is a plain class. HaltSQL verifies the PostgreSQL dialect only.

The HaltSQL operator manages haltsql-server on Kubernetes with two custom resources: Resource What it is HaltSQLPolicy One policy: an inline policy document, or a signed bundle that the server fetches from an OCI registry, S3 or HTTPS. The operator validates it with the real haltsql validate and reports Valid and Synced conditions. HaltSQLServer A haltsql-server Deployment that loads a set of HaltSQLPolicy objects. The operator renders the config into a ConfigMap and creates the Deployment, Service and (optionally) a PodDisruptionBudget and a NetworkPolicy. When the configuration changes, it rolls the pods. Use the operator when policies have their own lifecycle and owners, such as a platform team running shared servers while application teams own their policies, or when you want policy validity and rollout state in kubectl get. For a single static deployment, the Helm chart (deploy/helm/haltsql, see deployment.md) is simpler. The operator lives in deploy/operator (Go, controller-runtime, kubebuilder layout). Its API group is haltsql.dev/v1alpha1. It may change incompatibly before v1.

The operator image has the controller and the haltsql CLI, which it uses for validation. Build it from the haltsql image that your servers run, so that validation and serving use the same loader: docker build -t haltsql:dev . # repository root docker build -t haltsql-operator:dev \ --build-arg HALTSQL_IMAGE=haltsql:dev deploy/operator Install the CRDs, RBAC and the operator in haltsql-system with kustomize: cd deploy/operator make install-manifests IMG=registry.example/haltsql-operator:0.0.1 | kubectl apply --server-side -f - kubectl -n haltsql-system rollout status deploy/haltsql-operator-controller-manager make install-manifests renders config/default (kubectl kustomize) and replaces the default image. In your own overlay, use kustomize edit set image controller=... instead. The operator runs one replica with leader election, as uid 65532, with a read-only root file system and all capabilities dropped. Its namespace enforces the restricted Pod Security level. Manager flags: Flag Default Meaning --haltsql-binary /usr/local/bin/haltsql The CLI used to validate policies. The operator exits at startup if it is missing. --watch-namespaces all Comma-separated namespaces to watch. --leader-elect false (true in the manifests) Needed with more than one replica. --metrics-bind-address :8080 Prometheus metrics (0 disables). --health-probe-bind-address :8081 /healthz and /readyz.

kubectl create namespace agents TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" # give this to the agent kubectl -n agents create secret generic haltsql-tokens \ --from-literal=orders-agent.sha256="$(printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1)" apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1alpha1 kind: HaltSQLPolicy metadata: name: orders namespace: agents spec: policy: | apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: name: orders-agent dialect: postgres search_path: [app] statements: allow: [select] require_limit: max: 100 tables: app.orders: columns: [id, status, total_cents] --- apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1alpha1 kind: HaltSQLServer metadata: name: haltsql namespace: agents spec: replicas: 2 image: ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 policies: - name: orders auth: tokens: - name: orders-agent policy: orders-agent # metadata.name inside the policy document sha256SecretRef: { name: haltsql-tokens, key: orders-agent.sha256 } podDisruptionBudget: enabled: true networkPolicy: enabled: true ingressFrom: - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-agent } } kubectl -n agents get haltsqlpolicies,haltsqlservers # NAME POLICY VALID SYNCED AGE # haltsqlpolicy.haltsql.dev/orders orders-agent True True 40s # NAME REPLICAS READY STATUS AGE # haltsqlserver.haltsql.dev/haltsql 2 2 Ready 40s kubectl -n agents port-forward svc/haltsql 8080:8080 & curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/verify -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"sql":"SELECT id, status FROM orders LIMIT 10"}' Agents in the namespace call http://haltsql.agents.svc:8080. More examples are in deploy/operator/config/samples.

Field Type Meaning spec.policy string A complete policy document (kind: Policy, see policy-reference.md) as YAML or JSON. At most 256 KiB. spec.bundleSource object Instead of policy: a signed bundle fetched by the server (below). Exactly one of the two is required (the API server enforces this). Servers, tokens, OIDC providers and defaultPolicy refer to the policy by the document's metadata.name, which is shown in status.policyName, not by the name of the Kubernetes object. An inline policy cannot reference a catalog file (catalog: ./schema.json), because neither the operator nor the pods have that file. Write the catalog snapshot inline instead. Such a policy is reported as Valid=False with reason InvalidSpec.

spec: bundleSource: oci: ref: ghcr.io/corp/haltsql-policies:prod # or registry/repo@sha256:<digest> auth: { type: basic, secretName: registry-credentials } publicKeys: - | -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- ... -----END PUBLIC KEY----- namePrefix: prod. pollIntervalSeconds: 60 Field Meaning oci.ref, oci.plainHTTP, oci.auth An OCI artifact. plainHTTP is accepted by haltsql only for loopback registries. https.url, https.auth An HTTPS URL. s3.bucket, s3.key, s3.region, s3.endpoint, s3.credentials An S3 object. credentials.source is env (set AWS_* with HaltSQLServer.spec.env), static (keys from secretName; key names default to access_key_id, secret_access_key, and an optional sessionTokenKey), web_identity or instance. auth {type: token, secretName, tokenKey: token} or {type: basic, secretName, usernameKey: username, passwordKey: password}. publicKeys Required, non-empty: trusted ed25519 keys as inline PEM or the base64 of the 32 raw bytes. Signature verification is always on. namePrefix Prepended to the bundle's policy names. With a prefix on every bundle, token and default-policy references are checked against it. pollIntervalSeconds 10 to 86400, default 60. Each form maps to the bundle_source config entry described in config-reference.md. The server keeps the last verified bundle in an emptyDir at /var/cache/haltsql/bundles/<name>. GCS bundle sources are not supported, because haltsql has no gcs bundle source.

The operator writes the policy (or, for a bundle source, a minimal kind: Config document holding it) to a private temporary directory and runs haltsql validate from its own image. That is the same loader haltsql-server uses, so unknown keys, out-of-range values and malformed references are caught with their file, line and key path. The validator runs with an empty environment and never sees a Secret. Bundle credentials are replaced with fixed placeholder values for the check. The bundle itself is fetched and its signature verified by the server, not by the operator. We chose this over calling a running haltsql-server because it needs no network, no credentials, and no server that already runs a good configuration. It also works before any server exists.

Condition Reasons Meaning Valid Validated, ValidationFailed, InvalidSpec, ValidatorError Whether the current generation passed validation. ValidationFailed carries the located errors in the message. ValidatorError (status Unknown) means the check itself could not run; it is retried with backoff. Synced Synced, RollingOut, NotReferenced, NotValid True when every HaltSQLServer that references the policy has finished rolling out its current content. status.contentHash is the SHA-256 of the validated content. status.observedGeneration tells you which generation Valid refers to.

Field Default Meaning replicas 2 Pods. The resource has a scale subresource, so kubectl scale and HPAs work on it. image, imagePullPolicy, imagePullSecrets required The haltsql image. Pin a digest in production. policies required Names of HaltSQLPolicy objects in the same namespace (1 to 256). config.defaultPolicy none default_policy. config.allowUnauthenticated false Development only. config.logLevel, config.logFormat haltsql defaults logging. config.maxRequestBytes haltsql default limits.max_request_bytes. config.telemetry, config.opa, config.admin, config.secrets none Rendered as is into telemetry, opa, server.admin and secrets (see config-reference.md). auth.tokens[] none {name, policy, sha256SecretRef: {name, key}}. The Secret key holds the lower-case hex SHA-256 of the token. A trailing newline is ignored. auth.oidc[] none server.auth.oidc entries, rendered as is. auth.mtls.identities[] none server.auth.mtls.identities entries. These need tls with clientAuth: optional or required. tls.secretName, tls.clientAuth, tls.minVersion none Built-in TLS from a kubernetes.io/tls Secret (tls.crt, tls.key, and ca.crt for client certificates). Probes then use a plain-HTTP health port (8081) that serves only /healthz and /readyz. audit.sinks[] [{type: stdout}] audit.sinks entries, rendered as is (stdout, file, s3, gcs, elasticsearch, kafka; see audit-sinks.md). audit.logRawSQL false audit.log_raw_sql. env none Extra container environment, for example AWS_* from a Secret, used by ${env:...} placeholders. resources 100m CPU and 64Mi requested, 256Mi limit Container resources. serviceAccountName, automountServiceAccountToken namespace default, false Set automountServiceAccountToken: true for Vault Kubernetes auth or IRSA. podAnnotations, podLabels, nodeSelector, tolerations, affinity, topologySpreadConstraints none Pod scheduling and metadata. service.type, service.port, service.annotations ClusterIP, 8080 The Service. podDisruptionBudget off {enabled, minAvailable | maxUnavailable}. minAvailable defaults to 1. networkPolicy off {enabled, ingressFrom[]}. Only the listed peers reach port 8080 (no peers means any pod in the namespace).

The operator never reads Secrets, and its ClusterRole has no access to them. Secret keys are mounted into the server pods through one projected volume at /var/run/haltsql/secrets/<secret>/<key>, and the config refers to them with ${file:...} placeholders. haltsql resolves those placeholders when it loads the config. Raw sections (auth.oidc, auth.mtls.identities, audit.sinks and the config.* sections) can use a Secret anywhere a string is expected. An object of exactly this form is replaced by the placeholder for that key, and the key is mounted: audit: sinks: - type: elasticsearch url: https://es.logging.svc:9200 data_stream: logs-haltsql-prod auth: api_key: { secretKeyRef: { name: es-credentials, key: api-key } } - type: kafka brokers: [kafka.logging.svc:9093] topic: haltsql.audit tls: { ca_file: { secretKeyRef: { name: kafka-tls, key: ca.crt } } } sasl: mechanism: scram-sha-512 username: haltsql password: { secretKeyRef: { name: kafka-credentials, key: password } } The checksum covers which Secret keys are mounted, but not their values, because the operator cannot read them. After you rotate a token hash or a credential, restart the pods with kubectl rollout restart deploy/<server>. Anyone who can create or edit a HaltSQLServer can make its pods send a Secret from the namespace to an endpoint of their choice, for example as an audit sink credential. Grant write access to HaltSQLServer only to people who may already read Secrets in that namespace. The aggregated haltsql-editor-role follows the built-in edit and admin roles, which can read Secrets.

For a server named hs, the operator creates: the ConfigMap hs-haltsql-config, holding config.yaml and one policy-<HaltSQLPolicy name>.yaml file per inline policy; the Deployment hs; the Service hs; the PodDisruptionBudget hs and the NetworkPolicy hs, when enabled. Every owned object carries an owner reference to the server, so deleting the server garbage-collects all of them. The operator only caches and touches objects labelled app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: haltsql-operator and controlled by the server. If an object with one of these names already exists and belongs to someone else, the server reports ConfigRendered=False with reason NameConflict and leaves that object alone. The rendered configuration's checksum is set on the pod template (haltsql.dev/config-checksum). Any change to a referenced policy, the server spec or the set of mounted Secret keys therefore starts a rolling update. The Deployment uses maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1, so a ready pod is never removed before its replacement is ready. reload.watch is off in the rendered config: rollouts, not file watching, deliver changes, so all replicas switch together and a pod never runs a half-updated ConfigMap. The operator fails closed at two points: Invalid policy. While a referenced policy is not Valid for its current generation, the server is not re-rendered. The ConfigMap and Deployment keep the last good configuration, and the server reports PoliciesReady=False (PolicyNotValid, PolicyNotFound or PolicyPendingValidation). The same applies when the server spec cannot be rendered (ConfigRendered=False, InvalidConfig). Examples are a token pinned to a policy that no referenced HaltSQLPolicy defines, and two policies with the same name. Configuration that does not start. Some errors can only be found with the Secret values, such as a malformed token hash or a bad OIDC entry. With those, the new pods exit with code 2 and never become ready. The rollout stops, the old pods keep serving, and after 180 seconds the server reports Progressing=False with reason RolloutFailed. The pod logs show the haltsql load error. The operator only re-applies an owned object when the desired spec changes. It records a hash of that spec in the haltsql.dev/spec-hash annotation. Manual edits to an owned object are therefore not reverted until the server or its policies change. A deleted owned object is re-created immediately.

Field Meaning observedGeneration The server generation the status refers to. replicas, readyReplicas, updatedReplicas From the Deployment. configChecksum Checksum of the last rendered configuration. appliedPolicies[] {name, contentHash} of the configuration that has fully rolled out (every replica updated and available). This drives the policies' Synced condition. Condition Reasons PoliciesReady PoliciesReady, PolicyNotFound, PolicyNotValid, PolicyPendingValidation ConfigRendered Rendered, InvalidConfig, NameConflict, NotRendered Available Ready, Unavailable, ScaledToZero, DeploymentMissing Progressing RollingOut, RolloutComplete, RolloutFailed, DeploymentMissing Ready Ready, or the reason of the first condition that is not satisfied kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready haltsqlserver/haltsql -n agents --timeout=5m

The operator's ClusterRole is generated from the controllers by controller-gen (config/rbac/role.yaml): Resources Verbs haltsqlpolicies, haltsqlservers get, list, watch haltsqlpolicies/status, haltsqlservers/status update haltsqlservers/finalizers update (to set blockOwnerDeletion on owner references) configmaps, services, deployments, poddisruptionbudgets, networkpolicies get, list, watch, create, update, delete It has no access to Secrets, Pods or anything cluster-scoped. A namespaced Role in haltsql-system covers leader-election Leases and Events. To confine the operator to some namespaces, run it with --watch-namespaces and replace the ClusterRoleBinding with RoleBindings in those namespaces. haltsql-editor-role and haltsql-viewer-role aggregate into the built-in admin/edit and view roles.

GCS bundle sources are not supported (haltsql has no gcs bundle source). Inline policies cannot reference catalog files. Write the snapshot inline, or ship it in a signed bundle. The rendered ConfigMap must stay below about 900 KiB. Use a bundle source for large policy sets. There is no admission webhook. Problems the CRD schema cannot express are reported in status, not rejected at kubectl apply time. Persistent spool_dir storage for S3/GCS audit sinks is not provisioned. Without it, each pod starts a new audit hash chain (see audit-sinks.md). Secret rotation needs a manual kubectl rollout restart (see Secrets).

cd deploy/operator make manifests generate # CRDs, RBAC, deepcopy (controller-gen) make test # unit tests + envtest reconcile tests make e2e # kind end-to-end test Unit tests cover rendering (config, Deployment, checksum, secret substitution) and the validator. The rendered config, together with mounted Secret files laid out as in a pod, is loaded by the real haltsql validate. Reconcile tests run both controllers against a real kube-apiserver and etcd from envtest (setup-envtest downloads them into bin/k8s), with the real haltsql CLI as the validator. They do not use a fake client. envtest has no controller manager, so the tests write Deployment status themselves and check owner references instead of garbage collection. HALTSQL_BIN points at the CLI (default: _build/default/bin/haltsql/main.exe in the repository). The end-to-end test (test/e2e, build tag e2e) does the following: builds the haltsql image from the repository Dockerfile (unless HALTSQL_IMAGE names an existing one) and the operator image; creates the kind cluster haltsql-operator and loads both images; installs config/default and checks that the operator's ServiceAccount cannot read Secrets; creates a token Secret, a HaltSQLPolicy and a two-replica HaltSQLServer, then waits for Ready and Synced; calls /v1/verify through kubectl port-forward: an allow, a column deny, a statement deny, and 401 for a missing or wrong token; updates the policy and waits for the new checksum, a new ReplicaSet and Synced again, then checks the query the update allows; applies an invalid policy and checks that the pods keep the last valid version; deletes the server, waits for garbage collection of the Deployment, pods, ConfigMap, Service, PDB and NetworkPolicy, and deletes the cluster. Set HALTSQL_E2E_KEEP_CLUSTER=1 to keep the cluster for debugging.

If you connected Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code or your own agent to PostgreSQL by following the MCP quickstarts, you are probably running @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres. That server sends whatever SQL the model writes straight to your database. It checks no columns, no tenants and no functions. It sets no row cap and no timeout. haltsql-mcp (in clients/mcp) is a replacement you can swap in directly. It exposes the same query tool with the same sql argument, and it takes the connection string the same way, as the last argument. The difference is what happens before a query runs: HaltSQL parses the SQL with the real PostgreSQL parser and checks it against your policy. Only after that check passes does the exact verified string run, with server-bound parameters, in a read-only transaction that has a statement_timeout and a row cap. { "mcpServers": { - "postgres": { - "command": "npx", - "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://localhost/mydb"] - } + "postgres": { + "command": "haltsql-mcp", + "args": ["--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost/mydb"], + "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } + } } } Or use Docker with nothing else installed: mount a folder that holds policy.yaml and pass the same connection string. Run it in Docker. Switch in five minutes · What changes for the agent · Reference

documents.t: It is archived and unmaintained. On 2025-05-28 the MCP project moved it to modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived. Every version on npm is marked deprecated with the notice "Archived and unmaintained; no security guarantees". It still had about 146,000 npm downloads in the first week of November 2026 (npm API). Its read-only guard can be escaped, and the published package was never patched. The server runs BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY, then passes the model's string to client.query(), which accepts several statements separated by semicolons. Datadog Security Labs showed that COMMIT; DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; ends the read-only transaction and runs the DROP. A SET placed after the COMMIT stays on the pooled connection and affects later callers. A fix was committed to git when the server was archived (PR #1889), but npm latest is still 0.6.2 (published 2024-12-04), and that build has the vulnerable code. Even when the guard works, read-only is not a policy. A READ ONLY transaction blocks writes and nothing else. Any model with the tool can still: read every column of every table the database role can see, including email, ssn and password_hash; read every tenant's rows, because nothing scopes a query to the user the agent is acting for; call any function the role can execute. That includes pg_sleep (the server sets no timeout) and, when the role is privileged, pg_read_file, pg_ls_dir and lo_export. The PostgreSQL docs warn that these bypass all in-database privilege checks; return as many rows as a query produces, because there is no row cap. Prompt injection makes each of these an attack, not just a mistake. A support ticket, a web page or a row in the database can tell the model to run one of these queries.

@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres 0.6.2 haltsql-mcp Maintenance Archived 2025-05-28; deprecated on npm Maintained in this repository; MIT Tool query(sql) query(sql), plus explain_denial, list_tables, describe_policy Connection string Positional argument Positional argument, --database-url or HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL SQL parsing None; the raw string goes to the driver The PostgreSQL parser (libpg_query) Several statements in one call Runs them all (COMMIT; DROP ... escapes read-only) Denied (E_MULTI_STATEMENT) before anything runs Statement types Anything; relies on READ ONLY Allowlist (statements.allow, usually select), and the query still runs in READ ONLY Tables and columns All that the role can see Explicit allowlist per table (E_TABLE_DENIED, E_COLUMN_DENIED) Tenant isolation None Proven tenant predicate on every tenant table, in every subquery, CTE and UNION branch (E_TENANT_MISSING). The tenant comes from the server, never from the model Functions All that the role can execute Allowlist with presets (E_FUNCTION_DENIED). Built-in functions that run a SQL string (query_to_xml, dblink, ts_rewrite, ...) are always denied Row cap None --row-cap (default 200), plus require_limit in the policy Timeout None statement_timeout per query (default 5 s) Connection state Pooled; SET persists between calls New connection per query; settings are transaction-local Row-level security None HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG sets the tenant for RLS in each transaction Denials Database errors Reason codes and hints the model uses to fix its SQL Multi-user stdio only, one database URL stdio, or streamable HTTP with a bearer token per tenant Audit None Hash-chained audit through the sidecar (audit sinks)

Here are queries a misled model might send. The haltsql-mcp column shows real output from haltsql verify against examples/policies/saas.yaml with the context {"tenant_id": "acme"}. The model sends server-postgres haltsql-mcp SELECT 1; COMMIT; DROP SCHEMA app CASCADE Drops the schema E_MULTI_STATEMENT: expected exactly one statement, found 3 SELECT name, email FROM customers LIMIT 10 Returns every tenant's email addresses E_COLUMN_DENIED (email) and E_TENANT_MISSING SELECT id, name FROM customers LIMIT 10 Returns every tenant's customers E_TENANT_MISSING: no provable tenant predicate on customers.tenant_id SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = 'globex' LIMIT 10 Returns another tenant's rows E_TENANT_MISMATCH: the policy binds the tenant; the model cannot choose it SELECT pg_sleep(60) LIMIT 1 Holds a connection for 60 s, with no timeout E_FUNCTION_DENIED SELECT pg_read_file('/etc/passwd') LIMIT 1 Runs if the role has the privilege E_FUNCTION_DENIED SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fails: it binds no parameters Allowed. The server binds $1 to acme and returns at most 200 rows A denial is a normal tool result, not an error. It carries the reason codes and hints, so the model can fix its query and try again. Nothing runs until the query passes.

Docker (nothing else to install). The ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp image includes haltsql-mcp and the haltsql CLI, so it verifies queries itself. You don't need a central server, Python or anything else. See Run it in Docker. docker pull ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp alias haltsql='docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w --entrypoint haltsql ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp' With the alias, a database on your machine is host.docker.internal rather than localhost (see Reaching your database). pip: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL && cd HaltSQL pip install ./clients/python './clients/mcp[yaml]' # Python 3.10+; installs haltsql-mcp With pip, install the haltsql CLI too. You need it to draft the policy and to verify queries without a central server. It comes as a release binary or through opam (quickstart).

You don't have to write the policy by hand. Snapshot the schema, then draft a policy from the snapshot: PGPASSWORD=... haltsql schema pull --dsn postgres://ro@localhost:5432/mydb \ --schema public -o catalog.json haltsql policy draft --catalog catalog.json --tenant-column tenant_id \ --schema public -o policy.yaml haltsql lint-policy policy.yaml The draft lists every table with an explicit column list. Columns whose names look like PII (email, phone, ssn, password, token and similar) are left out, each with a comment saying why. The draft also sets the tenant column wherever it exists and requires a LIMIT. Review it before you use it, especially the tenant columns. See schema-and-pii.md to import PII labels from dbt, DataHub and other catalogs, and the policy reference for every key. --tenant-column is required. If your database is not multi-tenant, pass a column name that none of your tables have. Every table is then global (the draft prints a warning saying so), and you can leave out HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT.
documents.s: 2. Draft a policy from your database

documents.t: Connect as a login role that is not a superuser and does not own the tables, never as your superuser or owner role. haltsql rls generate can give that role exactly the policy's column grants and tenant row-level security. Create the login role first, because the script only creates the role when it does not exist, and creates it as NOLOGIN: psql "$ADMIN_DSN" -c "CREATE ROLE agent_ro LOGIN PASSWORD '...'" haltsql rls generate -p policy.yaml --catalog catalog.json --role agent_ro -o rls.sql psql "$ADMIN_DSN" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f rls.sql Give the role the same search_path as the policy. HaltSQL resolves unqualified table names with the policy's search_path, and Postgres must resolve them the same way: ALTER ROLE agent_ro SET search_path = public; -- the policy's search_path Then set HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG='{"haltsql.tenant_id": "tenant_id"}' so that each query's transaction sets the tenant the RLS policies read. See rls-generation.md and Defense in depth.

With Docker. Put policy.yaml in a folder and mount it at /config. This works in Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json) and Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json or .cursor/mcp.json): { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "docker", "args": [ "run", "-i", "--rm", "--read-only", "-v", "/path/to/haltsql:/config:ro", "-e", "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT", "ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp", "postgresql://agent_ro@host.docker.internal:5432/mydb" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } With pip. Claude Desktop and Cursor use the same shape: { "mcpServers": { "postgres": { "command": "haltsql-mcp", "args": [ "--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json): { "servers": { "postgres": { "command": "haltsql-mcp", "args": ["--local-policy", "/path/to/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb"], "env": { "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}" } } } } Claude Code: claude mcp add postgres -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' -- \ haltsql-mcp --local-policy /path/to/policy.yaml postgresql://agent_ro@localhost:5432/mydb If haltsql-mcp or haltsql is not on the PATH your client starts servers with, use absolute paths: point command at the binary (for example .venv/bin/haltsql-mcp) and set HALTSQL_BIN in env. --local-policy verifies queries with the local haltsql CLI, so you don't need anything else running. In production, run the haltsql-server sidecar for central policies, hot reload and audit. Then replace --local-policy with HALTSQL_URL, HALTSQL_TOKEN and --policy-file (see Configuration). A single config file can replace the arguments and environment variables above. See Config file.
documents.s: 4. Swap the server in your client

documents.t: Restart the client and ask something like "how many orders did we get last week?" A well-behaved model calls describe_policy or list_tables first, then writes a scoped query. To check the guardrails, ask it to show you customer emails, or every tenant's orders. You should see a denial with reason codes, and no rows.

The ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp image is all a solo developer needs. It includes haltsql-mcp and the static haltsql CLI, runs as a non-root user, and works with a read-only root filesystem. MCP clients start it with docker run -i and talk to it over stdio. The same image can also call a central haltsql-server, or serve many clients over HTTP.

~/haltsql/ policy.yaml # from `haltsql policy draft`, or written by hand docker run -i --rm --read-only -v ~/haltsql:/config:ro \ -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp postgresql://agent_ro@host.docker.internal:5432/mydb When /config/policy.yaml exists and nothing else is configured, the image verifies every query against it with the bundled CLI. No other process is involved. Leave out HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT if your policy has no tenant tables.
documents.s: Solo: a folder and a connection string

documents.t: Add haltsql-mcp.yaml next to the policy. Then the client config is just docker run -i --rm --read-only -v ~/haltsql:/config:ro ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp: # ~/haltsql/haltsql-mcp.yaml database_url: postgresql://agent_ro:secret@host.docker.internal:5432/mydb policy: policy.yaml # relative to this file context: { tenant_id: acme } row_cap: 200 statement_timeout_ms: 5000

To verify through a central haltsql-server instead, use a server block in place of policy: # ~/haltsql/haltsql-mcp.yaml server: url: https://haltsql.internal:8443 token_file: token # file holding the sidecar bearer token policy: analytics-agent # optional; a token is usually pinned to one policy ca_file: ca.pem # optional: private CA for https database_url: postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal:5432/app policy_file: policy.yaml # optional: lets list_tables and describe_policy show the rules context: { tenant_id: acme } You can do the same with environment variables alone: -e HALTSQL_URL=https://haltsql.internal:8443 -e HALTSQL_TOKEN=.... A HALTSQL_URL, a config file or a --haltsql-url flag turns off the automatic /config/policy.yaml local mode. If the server can't be reached or rejects the token, the query is not executed.
documents.s: Central server: policies, audit and hot reload in one place

documents.t: docker run -d --name haltsql-mcp -p 127.0.0.1:8765:8765 --read-only \ -v /etc/haltsql-mcp:/config:ro ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp \ --transport http --tokens-file /config/tokens.json Clients connect to http://HOST:8765/mcp with a bearer token from the tokens file, and each token maps to its own tenant context. The image listens on all interfaces inside the container (HALTSQL_MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0). Without a tokens file, HTTP is refused off loopback. TLS is not built in, so put a TLS proxy in front.

In /config And not set Effect haltsql-mcp.yaml (or .yml, .json) HALTSQL_MCP_CONFIG, --config Loaded as the config file policy.yaml (or .yml, .json) a config file, HALTSQL_URL, HALTSQL_MCP_LOCAL_POLICY, --local-policy, --haltsql-url Verify locally with this policy Anything set explicitly wins. Flags override environment variables, which override the config file.

documents.t: Docker Desktop (macOS, Windows): use host.docker.internal as the host in the connection string. Linux: add --network host and use localhost, or use the database's address on a Docker network. Database in Compose: use its service name and attach the same network (--network NAME).
