documents.t: docker build -t haltsql-local:dev . # the haltsql CLI image docker build -f clients/mcp/Dockerfile --build-arg HALTSQL_IMAGE=haltsql-local:dev -t haltsql-mcp:dev . scripts/mcp-docker-smoke.sh # solo, config file, central, fail-closed Release images are signed with cosign and carry SLSA provenance and an SBOM, like the main image. Pin a version tag or digest in production.

The query tool is the same. It still takes one sql string. Results are structured ({allowed, executed, columns, rows, row_count, truncated, ...}) instead of a JSON text dump of the rows. Schema discovery is a tool, not a resource. server-postgres exposes a postgres://<host>/<table>/schema resource for each table in public. haltsql-mcp offers list_tables and describe_policy, which list only what the policy allows. Tables and columns the agent cannot read are not advertised. Queries need a LIMIT when the policy sets require_limit (drafts do). Tenant tables need a tenant predicate. In bound mode the model writes alias.tenant_id = $1 and the server binds the value. The model never sees or chooses the tenant ID. The server instructions and list_tables tell the model this. One statement per call. Send separate query calls instead.
If verification fails for any reason (the sidecar is down, a TLS error, a malformed verdict, or a verdict for a different string), nothing runs.

Tool Arguments What it does query sql Verify, then run read-only with statement_timeout and a row cap. Returns {allowed, executed, columns, rows, row_count, truncated, row_cap, shadow_reasons}, or {allowed: false, executed: false, reasons} when denied. explain_denial sql Verify only. Returns every reason (code, message, hint, loc), the tables and columns touched, and the policy name and version. Never executes. list_tables none Tables and columns the policy allows, which are tenant-scoped, and guidance on writing tenant predicates. Needs a policy file. describe_policy none /v1/policies (name, version, mode) plus the policy's rules from the policy file: statements, LIMIT rule, tenancy mode and key names, tables, functions. All tools are annotated read-only. Infrastructure failures (sidecar down, TLS errors, malformed verdicts, database errors) are MCP tool errors and nothing runs; their messages never include the sidecar token or internal exception details. Denials are normal results so the agent can fix its SQL.

The tenant context is never a tool argument. Extra arguments a model sends (for example tenant_id) are ignored. stdio: one context per process, from HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT or --context-file, set by whoever launches the server for a user. streamable HTTP: clients authenticate with a bearer token, and each token maps to its own context in the tokens file. Without a tokens file the server refuses to start (except --insecure-static-context on a loopback address, for development). Tokens file (JSON; only SHA-256 hashes are stored): { "tokens": [ { "name": "agent-acme", "token_sha256": "<sha256 hex>", "context": { "tenant_id": "acme" } }, { "name": "agent-globex", "token_sha256": "<sha256 hex>", "context": { "tenant_id": "globex" } } ] } printf %s "$TOKEN" | shasum -a 256 # value for token_sha256 Tokens are compared in constant time against every entry, and the raw token is never stored or logged.

A query that a mode: shadow policy would deny is not executed unless the server runs with HALTSQL_ALLOW_SHADOW=1; without it the tool returns the shadow reasons as a denial. Flags override environment variables, and environment variables override the config file. Variable Flag Default Meaning HALTSQL_MCP_CONFIG --config none (Docker: /config/haltsql-mcp.yaml if present) Config file, overridden by environment variables and flags. HALTSQL_URL --haltsql-url http://127.0.0.1:8080 Sidecar URL. HALTSQL_TOKEN none Sidecar bearer token (pinned to one policy there). HALTSQL_POLICY --policy none Policy name to send to the sidecar. HALTSQL_TIMEOUT 2 Sidecar timeout per attempt, seconds (3 attempts, bounded backoff). HALTSQL_CA_FILE system CAs CA bundle for an https sidecar with a private CA. HALTSQL_CLIENT_CERT none Client certificate (PEM; may also hold the key) for mutual TLS to the sidecar. HALTSQL_CLIENT_KEY none Private key for HALTSQL_CLIENT_CERT when it is a separate file. HALTSQL_MCP_LOCAL_POLICY --local-policy none Verify with the local haltsql CLI and this policy instead of a sidecar. HALTSQL_BIN haltsql on PATH CLI used in local mode (and to read YAML policies without PyYAML). HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL (or DATABASE_URL) --database-url, or the last positional argument none libpq DSN. Without it, query is disabled. HALTSQL_MCP_ROW_CAP --row-cap 200 Maximum rows returned (1-10000). HALTSQL_MCP_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS --statement-timeout-ms 5000 statement_timeout per query. HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG {} JSON {"app.tenant_id": "tenant_id"}: transaction-local custom settings taken from context keys, for row-level security. HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE --policy-file the local policy Policy document for list_tables / describe_policy. HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT --context-file {} stdio context (JSON object). HALTSQL_MCP_TOKENS_FILE --tokens-file none HTTP tokens file. HALTSQL_MCP_TRANSPORT --transport stdio stdio or http. HALTSQL_MCP_HOST / HALTSQL_MCP_PORT --host / --port 127.0.0.1 / 8765 HTTP listener; the endpoint is /mcp. HALTSQL_MCP_PUBLIC_URL --public-url http://HOST:PORT External URL (OAuth protected-resource metadata). Invalid configuration exits with status 2 and a message on stderr.

--config FILE or HALTSQL_MCP_CONFIG loads one YAML or JSON file. In Docker, /config/haltsql-mcp.yaml is loaded automatically. Relative paths are resolved against the file's own directory, so the same file works both natively and in a container. Unknown keys are an error, so a typo can't silently drop a guardrail. Key Same as database_url HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL policy HALTSQL_MCP_LOCAL_POLICY (verify locally; not with server) policy_file HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE context HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT (a mapping) tokens_file HALTSQL_MCP_TOKENS_FILE row_cap, statement_timeout_ms HALTSQL_MCP_ROW_CAP, HALTSQL_MCP_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS set_config HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG (a mapping) transport, host, port, public_url HALTSQL_MCP_TRANSPORT, _HOST, _PORT, _PUBLIC_URL haltsql_bin HALTSQL_BIN server.url HALTSQL_URL server.token_file HALTSQL_TOKEN (the file's contents). An inline server.token is rejected, to keep secrets out of config files server.policy, server.timeout HALTSQL_POLICY, HALTSQL_TIMEOUT server.ca_file, server.client_cert, server.client_key HALTSQL_CA_FILE, HALTSQL_CLIENT_CERT, HALTSQL_CLIENT_KEY

With the sidecar, from any stdio client: { "mcpServers": { "haltsql": { "command": "haltsql-mcp", "env": { "HALTSQL_URL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080", "HALTSQL_TOKEN": "…", "HALTSQL_MCP_DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal/app", "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}", "HALTSQL_MCP_POLICY_FILE": "/etc/haltsql/policy.yaml" } } } } Shared HTTP server: haltsql-mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765 \ --tokens-file /etc/haltsql-mcp/tokens.json \ --database-url postgresql://agent_ro@db.internal/app \ --policy-file /etc/haltsql/policy.yaml No sidecar (local CLI), with the DSN as the last argument as in server-postgres: HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' haltsql-mcp \ --local-policy policy.yaml postgresql://agent_ro@localhost/app

HaltSQL is the policy check; still connect as a restricted role with row-level security (see defense-in-depth.md). HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG sets the tenant for RLS policies inside each query's transaction. TLS is not built in; keep the HTTP listener on loopback or behind a TLS proxy.

cd clients/mcp python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e ../python -e '.[test,yaml]' .venv/bin/pytest -q The suite uses an in-process fake sidecar, the MCP in-process and streamable HTTP clients, and a stdio subprocess. Tests marked integration need the lab Postgres (make -C lab up) and skip without it.

haltsql-server gives you three kinds of signal: Signal Where Configured by Prometheus metrics GET /metrics telemetry.metrics.prometheus OpenTelemetry traces and metrics pushed over OTLP/HTTP (JSON) telemetry.otlp Structured logs stderr (JSON or text) logging The audit log is separate. It is a hash-chained compliance record, not telemetry; see audit-sinks.md.

telemetry: otlp: endpoint: https://otel-collector.observability:4318 headers: authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/otel#token}" service_name: haltsql-support-bot traces: true metrics: true export_interval_seconds: 15 timeout_seconds: 5 The exporter (library haltsql-server.telemetry, module Exporter) speaks OTLP/HTTP with the JSON encoding. Any OpenTelemetry Collector with the otlp receiver and its http protocol enabled accepts it, and so do most vendor endpoints that take OTLP/HTTP. Data is posted to: <endpoint>/v1/traces: an ExportTraceServiceRequest (resourceSpans, then scopeSpans, then spans); <endpoint>/v1/metrics: an ExportMetricsServiceRequest (resourceMetrics, then scopeMetrics, then metrics). Encoding follows the OTLP JSON mapping: trace and span ids are lower-case hex; 64-bit integers (timestamps, asInt, count, bucketCounts) are decimal strings; enums are integers. Resource attributes are service.name, service.version, telemetry.sdk.name=haltsql, telemetry.sdk.language=ocaml and host.name.

Each POST /v1/verify produces one SERVER span named haltsql.verify: Attribute Example haltsql.policy support-bot haltsql.policy_version 2024-06-01 haltsql.allowed false haltsql.shadow false (true when shadow-mode denials were recorded) haltsql.reason_codes ["E_TABLE_DENIED"] (enforced codes, then shadow codes) db.system postgresql db.statement.sha256 SHA-256 of the exact SQL string haltsql.elapsed_us 183 The SQL text is never exported, not even with audit.log_raw_sql: true. To correlate a span with an audit record, join on db.statement.sha256 = sql_sha256. A span's status is OK when the request was verified, including when the SQL was denied: a denial is a correct answer, not an error. The status is ERROR only when the request itself failed. Context propagation. An incoming W3C traceparent header is honoured: the verify span joins that trace, and its parent is the caller's span. The span is exported only when the caller's sampled flag is set. A missing or malformed header starts a new, sampled trace. The parser follows the spec strictly: hex must be lower-case; all-zero ids and version ff are rejected; future versions may carry extra fields.

OTLP metrics have the same names as the Prometheus metrics on /metrics, so dashboards work with either. They are cumulative: monotonic sums for counters and explicit-bucket histograms. Metric Type Attributes haltsql_verify_total sum policy, result (allowed, denied, shadow_denied) haltsql_reasons_total sum code haltsql_verify_duration_seconds histogram, buckets 0.1 ms to 1 s none haltsql_policy_reload_total sum result (success, error) haltsql_audit_errors_total sum none haltsql_http_requests_total sum route, status haltsql_policies_loaded gauge none haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total sum none The cloud audit sinks add haltsql_audit_sink_* metrics to /metrics; see audit-sinks.md.

Telemetry must never slow down or break verification, so: Finished spans go into a bounded queue (2048 by default). Recording a span is a constant-time, non-blocking operation. When the queue is full, new spans are dropped and counted in haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total. Export runs in the background. It runs every export_interval_seconds, and immediately once a batch of 512 spans is waiting. Every POST has a deadline of timeout_seconds. Failed exports are retried with exponential backoff (0.5 s, doubling, capped at 30 s, up to 5 retries). Retries happen on network errors, timeouts, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504. A Retry-After header (delta-seconds or HTTP-date) takes precedence over the backoff and is capped at 30 s. Any other status drops the batch without retrying. A batch that still fails after all retries is dropped and counted. Header values are never logged. Treat them as secrets; they usually hold collector credentials. Export failures are logged with the path, status and cause only. gzip compression (Content-Encoding: gzip) is supported by the library (Exporter.create ~gzip:true).

Condition Meaning rate(haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 The collector is unreachable or too slow. Verification is unaffected. This counter is exported over OTLP, not on /metrics, so alert on it in the backend that receives the OTLP metrics. rate(haltsql_audit_errors_total[5m]) > 0 An audit sink is failing. With fail_closed, requests are being refused. haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0 A cloud audit sink is refusing writes. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.05 Verification is slower than expected.

let exporter = match Haltsql_telemetry.Exporter.of_config ~service_version:"0.2.0" cfg.otlp with | Ok e -> e | Error msg -> failwith msg in Haltsql_telemetry.Exporter.start exporter; (* inside Lwt_main.run *) let span = Exporter.start_verify exporter ?traceparent:(header "traceparent") () in let verdict = Haltsql.verify policy ctx sql in Exporter.end_verify exporter span verdict; Exporter.observe_verify exporter ~policy ~result ~codes ~seconds; (* on shutdown *) Exporter.shutdown exporter Exporter.noop is a disabled exporter, so callers do not need to branch.

HaltSQL and Open Policy Agent (OPA) work together in both directions: HaltSQL asks OPA. After HaltSQL has allowed a query, haltsql-server can ask OPA for a second opinion based on organisation-wide rules written in Rego ("finance tables only for SSO users", "no writes from static tokens"). OPA can only further deny. OPA asks HaltSQL. When OPA is already your central decision point (an API gateway, Envoy ext_authz, an agent runtime), a Rego policy can call haltsql-server's POST /v1/verify with http.send and use the verdict. Both example policies are in examples/opa/, with Rego unit tests (opa test examples/opa).

opa: url: http://127.0.0.1:8181 # an OPA sidecar; https for anything else decision_path: haltsql/decision # POST <url>/v1/data/haltsql/decision timeout_ms: 500 on_error: deny # or allow_haltsql_verdict headers: Authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/opa#token}" # tls: { ca_file: ./certs/opa-ca.pem } # https only The keys are described in config-reference.md.

A query HaltSQL denies is denied without asking OPA. Nothing OPA answers can turn a HaltSQL denial into an allow. A query HaltSQL allows is sent to OPA. It stays allowed only if OPA's decision is an allow. An OPA denial adds one reason per OPA reason (or one generic reason) with the code E_EXTERNAL_POLICY and the rule opa.decision, so it can be told apart from HaltSQL's own reasons. In a policy in shadow mode, an OPA denial is reported in shadow_reasons and the query stays allowed, like HaltSQL's own shadow denials.

POST {url}/v1/data/{decision_path} with Content-Type: application/json, the configured headers, and this body: { "input": { "caller": { "name": "analytics-agent", "type": "token" }, "policy": "saas-analytics", "policy_version": "sha256:4f1c...", "statement_kind": "select", "tables": ["app.orders"], "columns": ["app.orders.id", "app.orders.total_cents"], "reasons": [], "shadow_reasons": [], "allowed": true, "sql_sha256": "9a0364b9...", "fingerprint": "5c2d...", "context_keys": ["tenant_id"] } } Field Meaning caller.name The caller as in audit records: a token name, oidc:<provider>, mtls:<subject> or anonymous. caller.type token, oidc, mtls or anonymous. policy, policy_version The HaltSQL policy the query was verified against. statement_kind select, insert, update, delete, ... or null when the SQL did not parse. tables, columns Qualified relations and schema.table.column names read or written, sorted. reasons, shadow_reasons HaltSQL reason codes (empty in enforce mode, since only allowed queries are sent). allowed HaltSQL's verdict (always true here). sql_sha256, fingerprint Hash of the exact SQL string and the normalized-query fingerprint. context_keys The names of the request context fields, sorted. What is never sent: the SQL text, context values (tenant ids, user ids), tokens, and the OIDC subject. Rules that need more should run in HaltSQL's own policy, which sees the full query and context.

The response must be 200 with a JSON object whose result is either: a boolean: true allows, false denies; or an object {"allow": <boolean>, "reasons": [<string>, ...]}. reasons is optional and only used for a denial. No other keys are accepted. At most 16 reasons are kept; each is cut to 200 bytes and stripped of control characters. Everything else is an error, handled by on_error: no result (an undefined decision, usually a wrong decision_path or a policy that is not loaded), a null, string or number result, an object with other keys or a non-boolean allow, a non-200 status, invalid JSON, a response over 1 MiB, a connection failure, a TLS failure, or no answer within timeout_ms. on_error Effect of an error deny (default) The query is denied with E_EXTERNAL_POLICY and a message saying the external check failed. allow_haltsql_verdict HaltSQL's verdict is kept. Use it only when OPA's rules are advisory. Error messages contain the OPA host, never header values or the response body.

examples/opa/haltsql.rego exposes both decision forms: haltsql/allow (a boolean) and haltsql/decision ({allow, reasons}): package haltsql import rego.v1 finance_tables := {"app.invoices"} static_caller if input.caller.type in {"token", "anonymous"} default allow := false allow if { input.allowed count(deny_reasons) == 0 } deny_reasons contains msg if { some t in input.tables t in finance_tables static_caller msg := sprintf("table %s needs an mTLS or SSO caller, not %s", [t, input.caller.type]) } decision := {"allow": allow, "reasons": sort(deny_reasons)} A query on app.invoices from a static token is then denied with: {"code": "E_EXTERNAL_POLICY", "rule": "opa.decision", "message": "denied by the external policy haltsql/decision (OPA): table app.invoices needs an mTLS or SSO caller, not token"} Run its tests with: docker run --rm -v "$PWD/examples/opa:/policies:ro" openpolicyagent/opa:1.10.1 test -v /policies

Run OPA as a sidecar on 127.0.0.1 (plain http is accepted only for loopback addresses) and keep timeout_ms small: every allowed query waits for the decision. OPA's own API can require a bearer token (opa run --authentication=token --authorization=basic with a system.authz policy); put it in headers with a secret placeholder. config show redacts header values. For a remote OPA use https, with tls.ca_file for a private CA.

examples/opa/verify_gate.rego lets OPA decide on a SQL statement by calling haltsql-server: package haltsql.gate import rego.v1 default server := "http://127.0.0.1:8080" server := data.haltsql_gate.server response := http.send({ "method": "POST", "url": concat("", [server, "/v1/verify"]), "headers": { "authorization": concat(" ", ["Bearer", opa.runtime().env.HALTSQL_TOKEN]), "content-type": "application/json", }, "body": {"sql": input.sql, "context": object.get(input, "context", {})}, "timeout": "2s", "raise_error": false, "cache": false, }) verdict := response.body if response.status_code == 200 default allow := false allow if verdict.allowed == true Query it with POST /v1/data/haltsql/gate/decision and {"input": {"sql": "SELECT ...", "context": {"tenant_id": "acme"}}}; the result is {"allow": true|false, "reasons": ["E_TABLE_DENIED", ...]}. The bearer token is a server.auth.tokens entry pinned to one policy; pass it to OPA as the HALTSQL_TOKEN environment variable, never in data. A transport error, a non-200 answer (401, 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, ...) or a missing verdict denies. Responses are not cached (cache: false), so a policy hot reload takes effect immediately. HaltSQL still writes its audit record for every call.

test/opa runs against the real openpolicyagent/opa image: allow and deny in both decision forms, the exact input document (no SQL, no context values), undefined and malformed decisions, a decision slower than timeout_ms, bearer-token headers against OPA's own authentication, https with a private CA, the reverse direction against a real haltsql-server, and opa test on examples/opa. The tests skip when Docker is unavailable.

This page is for teams running haltsql-server or haltsql-proxy where an outage stops agents from querying. It explains what state each process holds, how to run replicas behind probes and a load balancer, how to size them from the published benchmarks, and what clients see when the verifier is down.

Verification is a pure function of the policy, the context and the SQL string. haltsql-server never connects to the database, and replicas do not talk to each other. You can run as many as you need. Each process does hold some local state: audit chains, spool and cache directories, an in-memory report window. Give each replica its own. Clients fail closed. When no verifier answers, queries are not run. Plan capacity and probes so that this is rare, and keep it that way: HaltSQL has no fail-open switch.

State Where Shared between replicas? What to do Loaded policies, tokens, OIDC and mTLS settings Memory, rebuilt from the config on start and reload No. Each replica loads the same config independently. Deliver the same config to every replica (ConfigMap, bundle source). Policy bundles from a bundle_source Memory, plus the last accepted bundle in cache_dir No. Each replica polls on its own (poll_interval_s ± 10%). Give each server its own cache_dir; do not let two processes poll one source into the same directory. Replicas can briefly run different bundle versions between polls. Audit hash chain, file sink The file. Appending continues the chain from its last record. Must not be. Two writers on one file fork the chain. One file per process. A file whose last line is not a sealed record stops the process from starting; rotate it first. Audit hash chain, stdout sink Memory No Each process start begins a new chain at genesis (chain_restart warning in haltsql audit verify). Audit hash chain, s3/gcs sink Memory, plus spool_dir when set Must not be. One spool directory per sink. Object names carry the host and a per-process run id, so replicas never collide in the bucket. Without spool_dir, each restart starts a new chain. Audit hash chain, elasticsearch/kafka sink Memory only (no spool) No Each process starts a new chain; records still queued when the process dies are lost. Pair with a spooled object sink if that matters. OIDC signing keys Memory cache (jwks_cache_seconds) No Each replica fetches keys from the IdP. Shadow report window (GET /v1/admin/report) Memory No Behind a load balancer each call sees only one replica's verdicts, and the window is lost on restart. Use haltsql report over the audit records for a fleet-wide view. Metrics counters Memory No Aggregate across replicas in Prometheus. Counters reset on restart. Details: audit-sinks.md, policy-bundles.md, shadow-reports.md. haltsql-proxy adds per-connection session state: each client session keeps the configuration snapshot it was accepted under, its prepared statements and their verdicts, and a mapping from the proxy-issued cancel key to the upstream backend. That mapping lives in the process that owns the session.

haltsql-server: Endpoint Returns Use for GET /healthz (also HEAD) 200 {"status":"ok"} while the process runs. Liveness. GET /readyz (also HEAD) 200 {"status":"ready","policies":N} when at least one policy is loaded and every audit sink accepts writes. 503 with "policies":0 when nothing is loaded, with unhealthy_audit_sinks when an S3/GCS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or Kafka sink refuses writes, and with "draining": true during shutdown. Readiness and load-balancer health checks. A failed hot reload does not make the server unready: the last good policies stay active. A file or stdout sink that fails in fail_closed mode does not turn /readyz to 503. Each request retries the write and gets 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE while it fails. Watch haltsql_audit_errors_total. With server.tls.client_auth: required, serve probes on a separate plain port with --health-listen HOST:PORT. It has its own connection budget (64), so probes keep working while the main listener is saturated. The image has no HEALTHCHECK (no shell or curl). Use orchestrator probes. haltsql-proxy has no HTTP health or metrics endpoint. Use a TCP check on the listen port, and its logs. See proxy.md. Reference: http-api.md, deployment.md.

Sidecar (one server per agent pod, on 127.0.0.1) Shared service (replicas behind a load balancer) Failure domain One agent pod. A crash affects only that pod's queries. Every agent that uses it. Needs replicas, a PDB and spread across zones. Network Loopback. No TLS needed inside the pod (tokens still required). Crosses the network. Needs TLS (server.tls or a mesh) and an internal load balancer. Scaling Scales with the agent's replicas automatically. Scale replicas (or an HPA) to total traffic. Policy rollout Every agent pod must be rolled or reloaded. Fewer processes to update. Audit One chain per agent pod. One chain per server replica. Overhead One process per agent pod. Shared. deployment.md recommends the sidecar for most cases and the shared service when many agents need central policy management. haltsql-proxy is a third option when the agent's driver cannot be changed (proxy.md).

The Helm chart (deploy/helm/haltsql) already sets most of this up: Concern What the chart does Value Replicas 2 by default replicaCount Spread Soft zone spread and soft node anti-affinity topologySpread, podAntiAffinityPreset Disruptions PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable: 1) when at least 2 replicas run podDisruptionBudget.* Rolling update maxUnavailable: 0, so a ready pod is not removed before its replacement is ready built in Autoscaling Optional HPA on CPU (target 70%) autoscaling.* Probes startup and liveness on /healthz, readiness on /readyz startupProbe, livenessProbe, readinessProbe Shutdown terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 20; optional preStop sleep terminationGracePeriodSeconds, preStopSleepSeconds Priority Unset priorityClassName. The chart README recommends a high class, because callers fail closed while HaltSQL is unavailable. CPU limit None by default, to avoid throttling on the verify path resources The Kubernetes operator creates a Deployment with maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1, and an optional PodDisruptionBudget. It turns reload.watch off and delivers every change as a rollout, so all replicas switch together. Reference: Helm chart README.
documents.s: Running replicas of a shared server

documents.t: POST /v1/verify requests are independent. Any replica can answer any request, so no session affinity is needed. Clients use HTTP/1.1 keep-alive. A long-lived connection stays on one replica, so new replicas only receive traffic as clients open new connections. On shutdown the server sends connection: close, which moves clients off a draining replica. Health-check the load balancer target on /readyz. For haltsql-proxy, use a TCP load balancer. A PostgreSQL cancel request only works if it reaches the proxy process that owns the session, because the cancel-key mapping is per process. Rely on statement_timeout in the database rather than client-side cancel through a load balancer.

Every number below comes from performance.md: one run on one Apple M1 Max that was not idle. Treat it as a data point and run scripts/bench.sh on your own hardware before you plan capacity. Measured Value haltsql-server throughput, one instance levels off at about 4.5k requests/s; one event loop, one core haltsql-server p50 on one connection 278 µs (file audit sink) haltsql-server p50 at 32 connections 6,847 µs (queueing: the instance is saturated) Cost of the file audit sink about 10% of throughput at 32 connections haltsql-proxy throughput, one instance about 6k statements/s on one core haltsql-proxy added latency about 0.25–0.3 ms per statement at p50, plus about 5 µs per result row Library verify (in process) 48 µs (point lookup) to 247 µs (multi-CTE report) at p50 What this means for sizing: Scale out, not up. One server instance verifies on one event loop, so in the benchmark more connections only added queueing latency once it reached about 4.5k requests/s. Add replicas rather than cores per instance. performance.md suggests one core per ~4k verifies/s of similar traffic. Stay well below saturation if p99 matters. At saturation, latency grows with queue depth (Little's law: 32 connections / 4.2k/s ≈ 7.6 ms). Query complexity, not policy size, drives cost. Heavier agent queries (joins, CTEs, window functions) lower the per-instance ceiling. Benchmark with queries like yours. Plan for losing a replica. For example, if your measured per-instance ceiling were 4.5k/s and peak traffic 9k/s, two replicas would both run at saturation; you would want more, plus one to cover a failure or a rollout. Replace these numbers with your own measurements. Memory is not measured. The deployment examples use requests of 32–64 MiB and limits of 128–256 MiB, but no published benchmark measures memory. Watch container memory under your own load.

haltsql-server on SIGTERM or SIGINT: The listeners close. /readyz answers 503 with "draining": true on connections that are still open, and every response carries connection: close. Idle keep-alive connections are closed. In-flight requests get --shutdown-timeout seconds (default 15) to finish. After that, remaining connections are closed (logged as shutdown timeout reached; closing remaining connections). Batching audit sinks (S3/GCS, Elasticsearch, Kafka) and the OTLP exporter are flushed. The process exits 0. Because the listener closes at once, a load balancer that has not yet removed the replica will see refused connections for a moment. In Kubernetes, give endpoints time to update before the signal with a preStop sleep (Helm: preStopSleepSeconds, which must be lower than terminationGracePeriodSeconds), and keep the grace period longer than --shutdown-timeout. Clients retry connection errors (see below), so a short gap is normally absorbed by the retry. haltsql-proxy on SIGTERM or SIGINT stops accepting, lets sessions run for shutdown_grace_seconds (default 10), closes the rest, flushes its audit sinks and exits 0. Clients see their connection closed and must reconnect.

Reloading does not drop connections on either component. haltsql-server haltsql-proxy Triggers SIGHUP; file watch (reload.watch, polled every 2 s); a new bundle from a bundle source SIGHUP; reload.watch (reload.poll_interval_seconds, default 2) Atomicity All policies, tokens, OIDC, mTLS, OPA, admin settings and TLS material are swapped together, or nothing changes. New connections get the new config; existing sessions keep their snapshot until they close. On error reload failed; keeping the last good configuration, haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"} config reload failed; keeping the current configuration Needs a restart listen address, health listener, turning TLS on or off, audit sinks, the list of bundle_source entries, limits, logging, telemetry.metrics.prometheus listen address, audit sinks Notes: The server watches the config file, policy and bundle files and TLS files. It does not watch files referenced only through ${file:...}, such as a token hash file. Send SIGHUP after changing those. In Kubernetes, ConfigMap files mounted with subPath are not updated in running pods. Mount the whole ConfigMap as a directory if you rely on reload.watch, or roll the deployment. During a file-watch rollout, replicas pick up a change at slightly different times. For changes that must apply everywhere at once, roll the deployment instead (the operator always does). Reference: config-reference.md, proxy.md.

HaltSQL is designed so that an outage denies queries instead of letting them through. What the server returns. These are HTTP errors, not verdicts. Clients must treat them as denials: Response Cause connection refused, reset or timeout The process is down, restarting, or saturated past --max-connections (new connections wait in the listen backlog). 503 NOT_READY No policy is loaded. 503 POLICY_UNAVAILABLE The caller's pinned policy is not loaded. 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE A fail_closed audit sink cannot be written. 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE (with Retry-After) The OIDC provider's keys cannot be fetched and no usable cached keys remain. What the official SDKs do. They retry, then fail closed: Python TypeScript Go Java Timeout per attempt 2 s 5 s 5 s 5 s Retries after the first attempt 2 2 2 2 Retried on connection errors, timeouts, 502/503/504 network errors, timeouts, 503 connection errors, timeouts, 503 connection errors, timeouts, 503 Backoff is exponential with jitter and capped (also capping Retry-After). After the last attempt the SDK raises an error and the query is not run. With default settings, a call against a verifier that never answers takes roughly three timeouts plus backoff before the agent sees the error. See integrations.md and the SDK pages for the exact options. What the proxy does. A statement that cannot be audited under fail_closed is refused with SQLSTATE 58030 (PROXY_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE); the connection stays usable. When the proxy process is down, clients cannot connect at all. What the agent sees. An error instead of rows. Make sure your agent framework reports it as an infrastructure failure, not as a policy denial the model should try to work around, and caps its retries. For the response procedure, see runbooks.md.

Dependency Effect when it fails Mitigation Bundle source (OCI, S3, HTTPS) Running servers keep the last good bundle. A restarting server starts from cache_dir; with no cache it fails to start. Persistent cache_dir; alert on haltsql_bundle_source_healthy == 0. OIDC provider Cached keys stay usable for at most min(jwks_cache_seconds, 3600) seconds past expiry; then 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE for that provider. Alert on haltsql_auth_total{result="unavailable"}. Audit sink destination fail_closed: requests refused once the sink is unhealthy. buffer: requests continue until the bound, then refused. See runbooks.md. OPA (optional) on_error: deny denies every query HaltSQL allowed; allow_haltsql_verdict keeps HaltSQL's verdict. Run OPA as a sidecar on 127.0.0.1 with a small timeout_ms. Secret providers (Vault, AWS, GCP) A placeholder that cannot be resolved fails startup, or rejects the reload (the last good config stays). Restart only when the provider is reachable. OTLP collector None on verification: spans are dropped and counted. haltsql_otlp_spans_dropped_total.
Production checklist Runbooks Troubleshooting Deployment Performance Audit sinks

This page is for platform and SRE teams taking haltsql-server or haltsql-proxy to production. Work through it before go-live and again after each upgrade. Every item says why it matters, how to check it, and which page covers it in detail. Note: HaltSQL is pre-1.0. The 0.0.1 release notes in CHANGELOG.md say it is not yet recommended as the only control in front of production data. Several features on this page (built-in TLS, OIDC, mTLS, cloud and SIEM audit sinks, signed bundles and bundle sources, haltsql-proxy, the operator) are listed under Unreleased in the changelog at the time of writing. Check the release notes of the exact version you deploy.
Each section is a table. The Check column is something you can run or look at, not a promise. Items marked Required close a gap that HaltSQL cannot close for you; the others are strongly recommended.

Item Why Check Reference Required. Pin the image by digest, not by tag. Tags such as 0.0 move. A digest is what you tested. The pod spec or Helm image.digest holds sha256:.... deployment.md, Helm chart README Verify release signatures and provenance before promoting a version. Release artifacts are signed keylessly by the release workflow. A signature that does not verify means the artifact did not come from it. cosign verify-blob ..., cosign verify ... and gh attestation verify ... as shown in the reference. deployment.md Run the same HaltSQL version in policy CI and on the servers. The CLI that validates and tests policies in CI should load documents exactly as the server will. haltsql version in CI and haltsql_build_info{version} on /metrics match. upgrades.md

Item Why Check Reference Required. Unauthenticated access is off. With it on, any caller can use default_policy or name a policy. haltsql config show --config FILE shows allow_unauthenticated: false; HALTSQL_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED is unset; no --allow-unauthenticated flag. config-reference.md, authentication.md Required. Every caller is pinned to one policy. A compromised agent cannot pick a looser policy. Each server.auth.tokens entry has policy; each OIDC provider has exactly one of policy, policy_claim + allowed_policies, or policy_from_groups; each mTLS identity has policy. The config loader enforces this. authentication.md Tenant and user context comes from an authenticated identity where possible. With static tokens the request body supplies the whole context, so the calling service must be trusted to send the right tenant. With OIDC context_claims or mTLS identity context, the body cannot override it (403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED). Review which callers use static tokens. authentication.md Token hashes are never written inline. Config files end up in ConfigMaps, repositories and support tickets. token_sha256 uses ${env:...}, ${file:...} or a secret provider placeholder. config-reference.md TLS on every listener that is not loopback inside the agent's pod. Bearer tokens and SQL cross the network. server.tls is set (consider min_version: "1.3"), or a mesh or proxy terminates TLS in front and the server binds to 127.0.0.1. authentication.md, deployment.md With client_auth: required, probes use --health-listen. Kubelet probes cannot present a client certificate. The health listener serves only /healthz and /readyz. The Helm chart does this when tls.enabled is true (tls.healthPort, default 8081). cli.md, Helm chart README /metrics is reachable only by your monitoring. /healthz, /readyz and /metrics need no token. NetworkPolicy (networkPolicy.metricsFrom in the chart) or firewall rules. http-api.md The admin API is off, or limited to named callers. /v1/admin/status and /v1/admin/report reveal policies, sinks and query patterns. server.admin.enabled is false, or server.admin.callers lists only operator identities. config-reference.md Proxy: TLS required, least-privilege upstream user. The proxy holds the database credentials. tls.required: true (the default), upstream.tls.mode: verify-full, and the upstream role has only what the policy needs. proxy.md, proxy.md

Item Why Check Reference Required. Production policies run in mode: enforce. A shadow policy enforces nothing. GET /v1/policies shows "mode": "enforce"; haltsql lint-policy FILE warns about shadow mode. policy-reference.md, cli.md Tenancy uses bound mode. The tenant value is bound by your code from bind_params, never written by the model. tenancy.mode: bound. tenancy.md require_limit and limits are set deliberately. They bound result size and analysis cost. haltsql lint-policy reports a missing require_limit. policy-reference.md Required. Policies are validated and tested in CI. A broken policy is refused at load or reload; you want to find out before that. haltsql validate and haltsql test run on every change (GitHub Action, GitLab template or pre-commit). policy-ci.md, testing.md Policies are delivered as signed bundles. The server verifies the Ed25519 signature before it parses anything, so the delivery channel need not be trusted. policies entries use bundle or bundle_source with public_keys. policy-bundles.md The signing private key lives only in a CI secret store. Anyone with the key can publish policies your servers accept. The key is a protected CI secret (for example a GitHub environment with required reviewers); only .pub files are distributed. policy-bundles.md, policy-ci.md Polled bundles have a monotonic metadata.version. Bundle sources refuse a version that is not strictly greater than the current one (bundle_source_rollback). The GitHub Action's default bundle-version is a commit SHA, which has no order. bundle-version is set explicitly, for example 1.0.${{ github.run_number }}. policy-ci.md Bundle sources have a cache_dir on storage that survives restarts. With no cache and an unreachable source, startup fails closed. cache_dir is set (the Helm chart sets <cache.mountPath>/bundles; use a PVC to survive rescheduling). policy-bundles.md Policy rollouts go through shadow mode first. A stricter policy can deny legitimate agent queries. See Shadow before enforce. shadow-reports.md

Item Why Check Reference Required. Every non-200 response, timeout or connection error is a denial. A client that runs the query when the verifier is unreachable turns an outage into a bypass. Use the official SDKs, which fail closed. In custom clients, review the error path. http-api.md, integrations.md Required. The client runs exactly the verified string and binds bind_params. HaltSQL verified that string, not a reformatted one. The SDK guarded-execute helpers do this and check sql_sha256. verdict.md Required. Context comes from the authenticated session, never from the model. Attacks that control the context are out of scope for HaltSQL. Code review of every integration. threat-model.md, SECURITY.md Client timeouts and retries are known. They decide how long an agent waits during an outage. The SDK defaults are 2 s (Python) or 5 s per attempt, 2 retries. integrations.md Unknown reason codes are treated as denials. New codes may be added in minor releases. Clients branch on allowed, never on a list of known codes. reason-codes.md

Item Why Check Reference Required. Agent queries run as a dedicated read-only role, NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS, with column grants that match the policy. If HaltSQL has a bug or a caller skips it, the database still holds. defense-in-depth.md defense-in-depth.md Required. RLS is enabled and forced on every tenant-scoped table, keyed on a per-transaction setting. Same reason. haltsql rls check reports drift between the database and the policy (exit 1 on drift). rls-generation.md The role's search_path equals the policy's search_path. Otherwise a name can resolve to a different table in HaltSQL than in PostgreSQL. Compare the role setting with the policy. policy-reference.md statement_timeout, lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout are set on the role. A query within every policy limit can still be expensive. SHOW statement_timeout as the role. threat-model.md
documents.s: Database role and RLS (defense in depth)

documents.t: Item Why Check Reference At least one durable sink runs with on_error: fail_closed. fail_closed (the default) guarantees that no request is served without its audit record. haltsql config show lists each sink's on_error. audit-sinks.md drop is used only next to another fail_closed sink. drop serves requests without an audit trail in that sink. Review audit.sinks. config-reference.md S3/GCS sinks have a spool_dir on persistent storage, one per sink. Without it, records accepted but not yet uploaded are lost on a crash, and each restart starts a new chain, so deleting an earlier run's objects is not detected. spool_dir is set and backed by a persistent volume. The operator does not provision one. audit-sinks.md, kubernetes-operator.md Archive storage is write-once. A hash chain alone cannot detect someone rewriting the whole log. S3 object_lock, a GCS retention policy, an Elasticsearch key with only create_doc, Kafka cleanup.policy=delete (never compaction). audit-verify.md Chains are verified on a schedule, anchored on the previous head. Missing records at the end are only visible against a head recorded elsewhere. A scheduled haltsql audit verify --json --expect-head "$(cat last-head)" ... exits 0. audit-verify.md No two processes write the same audit file or spool directory. Each process seals its own chain; two writers on one file fork it. One file sink path per replica (no shared volume path). high-availability.md log_raw_sql is a deliberate decision. Raw SQL can contain sensitive literals; without it, shadow reports cannot name the denied objects. audit.log_raw_sql is false unless your data allows it. shadow-reports.md

Scrape /metrics (telemetry.metrics.prometheus, on by default) or export over OTLP (telemetry.otlp). These alerts use metrics that haltsql-server exposes today: Alert on Meaning any increase of haltsql_reasons_total{code="E_INTERNAL"} An analyzer bug. The query was denied. File a bug. rate(haltsql_audit_errors_total[5m]) > 0 An audit sink is failing. With fail_closed, requests are being refused. haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0 or haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy == 0 A cloud or streaming audit sink refuses writes; /readyz is 503. rate(haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total[5m]) > 0 Records were dropped (mapping error, too large, or on_error: drop). any increase of haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"} A reload was rejected; the last good configuration is still active. haltsql_bundle_source_healthy == 0 The last poll of a bundle source failed; the last good bundle is still active. any increase of haltsql_tls_reload_total{result="error"} New certificate material was refused; the previous material is still in use. any increase of haltsql_auth_total{result="unavailable"} OIDC signing keys could not be fetched; callers get 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE. any increase of haltsql_opa_decisions_total{outcome="error_denied"} OPA could not answer and on_error: deny denied the query. haltsql_policies_loaded lower than expected A policy is missing; its callers get 503 POLICY_UNAVAILABLE. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.05 Verification is slower than expected (threshold from observability.md). haltsql-proxy has no metrics endpoint. Alert on its stderr log lines (audit sink write failed; refusing the statement, config reload failed; keeping the current configuration) and on SQLSTATE 58030 errors seen by clients. See proxy.md.

Item Default Reference Request body cap: limits.max_request_bytes or --max-request-bytes 1 MiB config-reference.md Open connections: --max-connections 1024 (health listener: its own 64) cli.md Request head and body: --request-timeout 30 s cli.md Idle keep-alive and stalled writes: --idle-timeout 60 s cli.md In-flight requests on SIGTERM: --shutdown-timeout 15 s cli.md SQL size and parse-tree limits per policy: limits.max_bytes, max_depth, max_nodes, max_joins 16384, 64, 20000, 8 policy-reference.md OPA decision timeout: opa.timeout_ms 500 ms opa.md Proxy: limits.max_connections, max_message_bytes, idle_timeout_seconds, auth_timeout_seconds, upstream.connect_timeout_seconds, shutdown_grace_seconds 100, 1 MiB, off, 30 s, 10 s, 10 s proxy.md Also check: The orchestrator's grace period is longer than --shutdown-timeout (or the proxy's shutdown_grace_seconds), so in-flight requests can finish. The Helm chart's default terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 20. Container memory and CPU are set from your own load test. The documented benchmarks measure latency and throughput, not memory. See high-availability.md.

Item Check Reference No secret is written literally in a Config document. Every credential uses ${env:...}, ${file:...}, ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} or ${gcp-sm:...}. secrets.md haltsql config show output is clean. Run it after every change; secrets show as "<redacted>". config-reference.md Secret files are readable only by the service. The image runs as uid 65532; the systemd example uses an env file with mode 0640. deployment.md You know which secret changes need a restart. Rotated provider and file secrets are read on the next reload, but audit sinks, the bundle-source list and ${env:...} values are fixed for the life of the process. runbooks.md

Item Check Reference New or stricter policies start in mode: shadow. haltsql_verify_total{result="shadow_denied"} and shadow_reasons in the audit log show what would be denied. deployment.md Shadow results are reviewed before switching. haltsql report ... --suggest or GET /v1/admin/report. shadow-reports.md Shadow is never the only control. Database role and RLS are in place (see above). policy-reference.md

What Where it should live Notes Policy source files and test suites Version control The source of truth. policy.version in every verdict ties a decision to exact content. Signed bundles and signatures Your OCI registry, bucket or artifact store, kept by digest or version Keep old versions: rolling back a bundle source means republishing old content under a higher version. Public signing keys Version control and server images or ConfigMaps Safe to commit. Signing private key Your secret store, with its own backup and access controls Losing it means rotating to a new key on every server. Audit records A durable, write-once sink Retention is set on the destination (Object Lock retain_days, bucket retention, ILM, topic retention), not in HaltSQL. Chain heads Somewhere separate from the audit store Used with --expect-head to detect truncation. Spool directories, bundle cache_dir Persistent volumes These are working state, not backups. Do not restore an old spool into a running chain.

Item Reference At least two replicas of a shared server, with a PodDisruptionBudget. high-availability.md Readiness on /readyz, liveness on /healthz. http-api.md A runbook for "verifier down" exists and has been rehearsed. runbooks.md

This page is for maintainers. It describes how a release is cut, how to rehearse one without publishing anything, and what has to be configured in GitHub, PyPI and npm before the first real tag. Users who want to check a release should read supply-chain.md.

Workflow Builds Publishes (real mode) .github/workflows/release.yml Static Linux tarballs (amd64, arm64), macOS arm64 tarball, haltsql and haltsql-mcp images (amd64, arm64), Helm chart, CycloneDX SBOM, SHA256SUMS, cosign bundles, build-provenance attestations ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version>, ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp:<version>, oci://ghcr.io/haltsql/charts/haltsql, GitHub release .github/workflows/native-packages.yml Platform wheels, sdists (haltsql, haltsql-mcp), npm platform packages, @haltsql/client PyPI (haltsql, haltsql-mcp), npm (@haltsql/client, @haltsql/native-*) Both start on a v* tag push. release.yml ends with a verify job that runs scripts/verify-release.sh against the files it just published, so the verification commands in the docs are exercised on every run.

Trigger Mode Push vX.Y.Z Real Push vX.Y.Z-rc.N Dry run Run release.yml by hand, dry_run ticked (the default) Dry run; the tag input is only a label and needs no git tag. Without a matching tag there is no draft release (the workflow token cannot create a tag on a commit that changes workflows); the assets are in the run's release-assets artifact Run release.yml by hand, dry_run unticked Real rebuild of an existing tag Run native-packages.yml by hand, dry_run ticked (the default) Builds and tests, then the publish dry run A dry run does everything a real release does except the final publication: Step Real Dry run Images ghcr.io/haltsql/<name>:<version> and :<major>.<minor> ghcr.io/haltsql/dryrun/<name>:dryrun-<run id> Helm chart oci://ghcr.io/haltsql/charts/haltsql, version X.Y.Z oci://ghcr.io/haltsql/dryrun/charts/haltsql, version X.Y.Z-rc.N Cosign signatures, SBOMs, provenance Yes Yes, the same steps (entries in the public Sigstore transparency log are made either way) GitHub release Published (pre-release for v0.*) Draft, titled DRY RUN PyPI haltsql, haltsql-mcp twine check --strict; TestPyPI upload only if TESTPYPI_PUBLISH is set (below) npm npm publish --provenance npm publish --dry-run After a dry run, delete the draft release and the rc tag (if you pushed one). The dryrun/ packages can be deleted from the organisation's package settings.

# Version strings agree, and match the tag you are about to push scripts/check-versions.sh --tag v0.0.1 # Dry run from a branch, no tag needed gh workflow run release.yml --ref my-branch -f tag=v0.0.1-rc.1 -f dry_run=true gh workflow run native-packages.yml --ref my-branch -f dry_run=true # Or as a release candidate, which also signs with the tag identity users verify git tag -s v0.0.1-rc.1 && git push origin v0.0.1-rc.1 # Verify the draft locally (needs write access to see a draft; private dryrun/ # packages need `docker login ghcr.io` with read:packages) scripts/verify-release.sh v0.0.1-rc.1 A manual run signs with the branch's workflow identity, so verify it with --identity https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/<branch>.

Everything versions in lockstep. scripts/check-versions.sh (run by ci.yml on every change and by both release workflows) fails when any of these differ: dune-project, the three *.opam files, lib/haltsql/haltsql.ml, clients/python (pyproject.toml, _version.py), clients/mcp (pyproject.toml, __init__.py), clients/typescript (package.json, its lock file, the @haltsql/native-* pins, src/client.ts), clients/go/haltsql/client.go, clients/java (pom.xml, HaltSQLClient.java) and deploy/helm/haltsql/Chart.yaml (version, appVersion and the Artifact Hub image). A release candidate vX.Y.Z-rc.N is checked against X.Y.Z. The Go SDK is a module in a subdirectory, so Go needs its own tag, clients/go/haltsql/vX.Y.Z, on the same commit for go get ...@vX.Y.Z to resolve.

These are not configured yet. Each is a setting only a maintainer can create. What Where Settings PyPI trusted publisher for haltsql pypi.org, "Publishing" (pending publisher, the project does not exist yet) Owner HaltSQL, repository HaltSQL, workflow native-packages.yml, environment pypi PyPI trusted publisher for haltsql-mcp pypi.org, same Same, but environment pypi-mcp. PyPI refuses two pending publishers with the same repository, workflow and environment, so each project has its own environment and publish job npm org haltsql npmjs.com Free plan; owns the @haltsql scope NPM_TOKEN, first publish only npm environment secret Granular token, read and write on @haltsql, 2FA bypass, shortest expiry. Needed once: npm trusted publishers can only be added to packages that already exist npm trusted publishers, after the first publish npmjs.com, each package's settings, for @haltsql/client and the three @haltsql/native-* Owner HaltSQL, repository HaltSQL, workflow native-packages.yml, environment npm; then delete NPM_TOKEN and the npm token itself pypi, pypi-mcp and npm environments Repository settings, Environments Add required reviewers so a tag alone cannot publish GHCR package visibility Organisation packages, after the first real run Make haltsql, haltsql-mcp and charts/haltsql public; new packages are created private Optional: TestPyPI test.pypi.org trusted publishers for haltsql (workflow native-packages.yml, environment testpypi) and haltsql-mcp (environment testpypi-mcp), then repository variable TESTPYPI_PUBLISH=true TestPyPI accepts each version once; rc runs re-uploading X.Y.Z are skipped Not published by any workflow: the Java SDK (Maven Central needs a Sonatype account, a verified com.haltsql namespace and a GPG signing key) and the Kubernetes operator image.

Move the [Unreleased] notes in CHANGELOG.md under ## [X.Y.Z] - <date>; the release notes are taken from that section. Run a dry run on the release commit and check verify is green. Push the signed tags vX.Y.Z and clients/go/haltsql/vX.Y.Z. Approve the pypi, pypi-mcp and npm environment deployments. Make new GHCR packages public, then run scripts/verify-release.sh vX.Y.Z from a clean machine.

This page is for on-call engineers responding to HaltSQL incidents. Each playbook says how the incident shows up, how to confirm it, how to restore service without weakening the controls, and what to check afterwards. Use troubleshooting.md for symptom-level detail. All commands assume a server on 127.0.0.1:8080; adjust for your environment. Log lines are JSON on stderr with a msg field, so jq filters such as select(.msg == "...") work on them.

HaltSQL fails closed by design. When it cannot verify or audit a query, the query does not run. There is no fail-open switch in the server, the proxy or the official SDKs. Do not add one during an incident. Do not turn on allow_unauthenticated, switch policies to mode: shadow, or widen a policy to restore service. Each of these removes a control. If the business decides to accept that risk, record the decision. Preserve audit data first when an incident might be a security event. Copy it before anything rotates it.

Trigger. Agents report errors instead of query results; SDK errors such as HaltSQLUnavailable (Python) or transport/HTTP errors in the other SDKs; alerts on /readyz, pod restarts, or a drop in haltsql_verify_total. Through haltsql-proxy: clients cannot connect. Impact. Agents cannot run queries. No unverified query runs.

Is the process up? curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=haltsql # adjust the selector Pick the branch: What you see Branch /healthz fails; pods in CrashLoopBackOff; exit code 2 Startup failure. Read the last log lines: failed to load configuration and the error field name the cause. See troubleshooting.md. /readyz 503 with "policies":0 No policy loaded. Check bundle sources (bundle source poll failed; keeping the last good bundle) and the config. /readyz 503 with unhealthy_audit_sinks Go to Audit sink outage. /readyz 200, but callers get 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE The OIDC provider's keys are unreachable. Check egress to the IdP; oidc signing keys unavailable in the logs. /readyz 200, but callers get 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE A file or stdout sink is failing (these do not flip /readyz). Go to Audit sink outage. /readyz 200, slow responses or timeouts Saturation. Check CPU, haltsql_http_open_connections, and connection limit reached; new connections wait in the listen backlog. Everything healthy on the pod, failures at the client Network path: Service, load balancer, NetworkPolicy, TLS. Test from the agent's pod with curl. What changed? Check the last deploy, config change, bundle version (GET /v1/admin/status → bundle_sources[].current), certificate expiry and IdP changes.

Cause Action A bad config or image Roll back to the last good revision (helm rollback, revert the manifest or HaltSQLServer). With maxUnavailable: 0, old pods may still be serving; do not delete them. A bundle source is down and pods cannot start Running pods keep their last good bundle. Stop restarting pods until the source is back, or restore a cache_dir volume. Saturation Add replicas (kubectl scale, HPA). One instance verifies on one event loop, so more cores per pod do not help (high-availability.md). IdP outage Nothing on the HaltSQL side; cached keys are used for a bounded time, then requests fail closed. Static tokens or mTLS identities are unaffected. Node or zone loss Check the PodDisruptionBudget and spread; reschedule.

/readyz is 200 on every replica, haltsql_verify_total is back to its usual rate, and agents succeed. If audit sinks restarted their chains, verify them (Audit chain verification). Review alerts, replica count and probes against the production checklist.

Trigger. rate(haltsql_audit_errors_total[5m]) > 0; haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0 or haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy == 0; /readyz lists unhealthy_audit_sinks; callers get 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE; proxy clients get SQLSTATE 58030. Impact. With on_error: fail_closed (the default), requests are refused until the sink can be written. This is intended: no request is served without its audit record.

Identify the sink: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics | grep -E 'haltsql_audit_(sink|stream_sink)_' kubectl logs deploy/haltsql | jq -c 'select(.msg == "audit sink write failed; failing request closed") | {ts, sink, error}' With the admin API: GET /v1/admin/status → audit_sinks[] with healthy. Find the cause on the destination side: S3/GCS permissions or Object Lock configuration, Elasticsearch cluster health and mappings, Kafka topic and leaders, disk space for file sinks. The error types are listed in troubleshooting.md.

Fix the destination. Recovery is automatic: S3/GCS: the background loop retries held objects every batch.max_seconds; the first success makes the sink healthy. Elasticsearch/Kafka: a background loop retries the held batch after a growing, jittered delay. file/stdout: every request retries the write. Proxy stdout/file: every statement retries the write; s3/gcs recover when a background upload succeeds. Do not restart pods to "clear" the error unless you have to. Records accepted into an S3/GCS batch but not uploaded are kept in memory, or in spool_dir if configured; streaming sinks have no spool, so a restart loses their queued records. Changing on_error is a compliance decision, not a quick fix. Switching a sink to buffer (or drop for streaming sinks and the proxy) needs a restart, and drop serves requests without an audit trail in that sink. Only do it with the approval of whoever owns the audit requirement, and only when another sink still fails closed.

Confirm haltsql_audit_sink_pending_objects or haltsql_audit_stream_sink_buffered_records drain to 0 and /readyz is 200. Verify the chain across the outage: # object sinks, against the live spool (one host) aws s3 cp --recursive s3://BUCKET/PREFIX/ ./audit/ haltsql audit verify --spool /path/to/spool --host HOST ./audit/ # file sinks haltsql audit verify /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl For Elasticsearch and Kafka, use test/siem/verify_chain.py (see audit-sinks.md). Account for gaps: haltsql_audit_stream_sink_records_dropped_total{reason} shows dropped records; a process that died with records queued in a streaming sink lost them. Record the outage window and the requests refused (haltsql_audit_sink_rejected_writes_total, haltsql_audit_stream_sink_rejected_writes_total).

Trigger. After a policy change: a spike in denials (haltsql_verify_total{policy,result="denied"}), one reason code jumping in haltsql_reasons_total, agents failing on queries that used to work. Or the opposite: a policy that allows more than intended. Impact. Too strict: agents cannot do their work. Too permissive: a security issue; the database role and RLS are the remaining controls.

Confirm which version is live: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $HALTSQL_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/policies kubectl logs deploy/haltsql | jq -c 'select(.msg == "policies reloaded") | {ts, policies}' Every verdict and audit record carries policy_version, so you can find the first decision made under the new version. See what the new version denies: haltsql report AUDIT_FILES --since 1h --policy NAME --format markdown (by reason code, table, column, caller, and top denied queries). With the admin API, GET /v1/admin/report?since=1h&policy=NAME gives the same view for one replica.

Use the path that matches how the policy is delivered: Delivery Rollback Policy files or ConfigMap, reload.watch on Revert the change in version control and redeploy the files; the server reloads within about 2 seconds. Check for policies reloaded. Policy files, no watch Revert and kill -HUP <pid> / systemctl reload haltsql, or roll the deployment. ConfigMap mounted with subPath, Helm or operator Revert and roll out (helm upgrade/helm rollback, revert the HaltSQLPolicy). Local bundle: file Put the previous .haltsqlbundle and its .sig back (atomic write, then rename) and reload. bundle_source Rebuild the previous policies as a bundle with a higher metadata.version than the bad one, sign it, and push it. Servers refuse older or equal versions (bundle_source_rollback), and the config file cannot turn that off. Servers pick it up on the next poll (poll_interval_s, default 60). haltsql-proxy Revert the policy files and reload. New connections get the old policy, and sessions bound to the changed policy are ended at their next transaction boundary (FATAL 57P01, at most limits.termination_grace_seconds later) so their clients reconnect under it. With reload.terminate_changed_sessions: false, existing sessions keep the bad one until they close: restart the proxy.

GET /v1/policies (or the policies reloaded log line) shows the previous policy.version, or for bundle sources GET /v1/admin/status shows the new rollback version as current. Denial rates return to their earlier level. For a too-permissive policy, list what was allowed under the bad version: jq -c 'select(.policy_version == "sha256:BAD..." and .allowed == true) | {ts, request_id, caller, fingerprint, sql_sha256}' audit.jsonl
Add the queries that broke (or that should have been denied) as cases in the policy's test suite, so CI catches it next time. Roll stricter changes out in mode: shadow first (deployment.md).

Bundles are verified against the Ed25519 public keys in each bundle or bundle_source entry's public_keys. Any listed key may verify. The steps come from policy-bundles.md. Note: For a local bundle: entry, a reload applies a new public_keys list. For a bundle_source entry, changing public_keys changes the entry, and changes to the list of bundle sources need a restart.

Generate the new key and store the private key in your CI secret store: haltsql bundle keygen -o policy-signing-2.key # prints the key id Add policy-signing-2.key.pub to every server's public_keys next to the old key, and roll it out (reload or restart as noted above). Optionally dual-sign while both keys are trusted: haltsql bundle sign B --key old.key haltsql bundle sign B --key new.key --append Switch CI to the new key. Confirm with haltsql bundle verify B --public-key policy-signing-2.key.pub and, on the servers, GET /v1/admin/status → bundle_sources[].current.signed_by. Once no bundle signed only by the old key is in circulation, remove the old public key from the servers.

Generate a new key pair. Rebuild the current, known-good policies from version control, sign them with the new key only, and publish with a higher metadata.version than anything the compromised key could have signed into circulation. Remove the compromised key from public_keys and add the new one, then reload (local bundles) or restart (bundle sources). Bundles signed only by the removed key stop loading. A cached bundle in cache_dir is verified again with the current keys at start, so a bundle signed only by the removed key is not used from the cache either. Make sure step 2 is done before step 3 for bundle sources: a server that restarts with no bundle it can verify (neither cached nor at the source) fails to start. Find decisions made under policies from suspect bundles: compare the policy_version values in the audit records with the versions your known-good bundles produce (haltsql bundle inspect lists each policy's version). Review who had access to the key and your registry's push history.

HaltSQL does not detect prompt injection: it judges the SQL, not the prompt (threat-model.md). What it gives you is a tamper-evident record of every SQL string an agent tried and what happened to it. An injected prompt usually shows up as an agent suddenly producing queries outside its normal pattern. Trigger. A spike in denials for one caller or policy, or codes that a well-behaved agent rarely produces: Code What the agent tried E_TABLE_DENIED Tables outside the policy, including system catalogs (pg_catalog, information_schema). E_FUNCTION_DENIED Functions such as pg_sleep, set_config, file access or dblink. E_MULTI_STATEMENT A second, stacked statement. E_STATEMENT_KIND, E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE, E_WRITE_DENIED, E_SELECT_INTO, E_LOCKING_CLAUSE Writes, DDL or locks from a read-only agent. E_TENANT_MISMATCH, E_TENANT_MISSING Another tenant's data, or no tenant filter. E_CAST_DENIED Casts to a type outside the policy's casts allowlist, and reg* casts that look up catalog objects. E_COLUMN_DENIED Columns the policy hides. Also watch 403 responses on /v1/verify (haltsql_http_requests_total{route="/v1/verify",status="403"}): CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED means a caller tried to set a context field, such as the tenant, that its identity does not allow. Refused requests (401, 403) are not verdicts, so they have no audit record.

Copy the audit records for the window (file, objects, or an export). Verify the chain before you analyse it, and record the head: haltsql audit verify --json audit.jsonl | jq '{ok, heads: [.inputs[].heads[]]}'

An audit record has ts, request_id, caller (token name, oidc:<provider> or mtls:<subject>), caller_type, subject (OIDC sub, SPIFFE ID or CN), policy, policy_version, allowed, shadow, codes, sql_sha256, fingerprint and, only with audit.log_raw_sql, sql. Summarise: haltsql report audit/ --since 24h --format markdown By caller, By reason code, Over time and Top denied queries (by fingerprint) point to the session and the query shapes. List the suspect caller's denials: jq -c 'select(.caller == "oidc:corp-okta" and .allowed == false) | {ts, request_id, subject, codes, fingerprint, sql_sha256}' audit.jsonl Check what was allowed for the same caller in the same window. These queries passed the policy and ran: jq -c 'select(.caller == "oidc:corp-okta" and .allowed == true) | {ts, request_id, subject, codes, shadow, fingerprint}' audit.jsonl A record with "allowed": true and "shadow": true was allowed only because its policy is in shadow mode: its codes are what enforcement would have denied. Treat those as unprotected. Get the SQL text. Audit records hold it only with audit.log_raw_sql. Otherwise join on identifiers your application logs: request_id (send your own X-Request-Id), or sql_sha256 (the SHA-256 of the exact SQL string) against the agent's own logs; OpenTelemetry spans carry the same hash as db.statement.sha256. Then find the prompt or document that led to it in your agent's conversation logs. For haltsql-proxy, records carry user, reasons, shadow_reasons, tables, and local denials as event parse, bind or function_call.

Stop the session or user in your application. HaltSQL has no per-user block list. If a credential may be misused, revoke it: remove the static token entry and reload, disable the identity in your IdP, or remove the mTLS identity and reload (Token and credential rotation). If the attempts found a gap (an allowed query that should have been denied), tighten the policy through the normal rollout, and report a possible bypass privately per SECURITY.md.
Confirm the database role and RLS held for every allowed query in the window (defense-in-depth.md). Add the attack queries to the policy's test suite.

What applies without a restart, and what does not: Credential Where it lives Apply the change with Static token hashes (server.auth.tokens) Config, usually through ${env:...} or ${file:...} Reload, if the hash comes from the config file or a ${file:...} file (send SIGHUP: ${file:...} targets are not watched). A hash from ${env:...} needs a restart, because the process environment does not change. OIDC provider settings Config Reload. Key caches of unchanged providers are kept. IdP signing keys The IdP's JWKS Nothing: an unknown kid triggers a refresh (at most every 30 s per provider). Server TLS certificate, key, client CA Files in server.tls Reload or file watch; haltsql_tls_reload_total{result="success"}. A broken key keeps the previous material. mTLS identities Config Reload. OPA and OTLP headers Config with secret placeholders Reload (opa and telemetry.otlp are applied on reload; a reload resolves placeholders again). Audit sink credentials (static S3 keys, Elasticsearch API key, Kafka SASL password) Config with secret placeholders Restart: audit sinks are opened once. Temporary credentials (web_identity, instance, GCS metadata) refresh by themselves. Bundle source auth Config with secret placeholders Restart: the running pollers keep their settings. Proxy users (scram_verifier) and identities Proxy config Reload. New connections use the new credentials, and sessions of a user whose verifier changed or who was removed are ended at their next transaction boundary (FATAL 57P01), unless reload.terminate_changed_sessions is false. Proxy upstream password Proxy config Reload; applies to new connections. Kubernetes Secrets under the operator Projected Secret volume kubectl rollout restart deploy/<server>: the operator cannot read Secret values, so it does not roll on value changes. Kubernetes Secrets under Helm Secret injected as env The chart rolls pods when tokens change; with existingTokenSecret it does not, so restart the pods.

Token names and hashes must be unique, and the audit caller field is the token name, so give the new token a new name. Generate the token and its hash: token="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" printf '%s' "$token" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1 Add a second entry pinned to the same policy: server: auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent-2025a # old token_sha256: ${file:/etc/haltsql/secrets/analytics-agent-2025a.sha256} policy: analytics-agent - name: analytics-agent-2025b # new token_sha256: ${file:/etc/haltsql/secrets/analytics-agent-2025b.sha256} policy: analytics-agent Apply it (see the table above) and confirm policies reloaded in the logs. Switch the client to the new token. A client that reads the token only when it is constructed (for example from HALTSQL_TOKEN at startup) must be restarted. Confirm the old token is unused: no new audit records with "caller": "analytics-agent-2025a". Remove the old entry and apply again. For a compromised token, skip to step 6 immediately: remove the entry and reload. Requests with that token get 401 UNAUTHORIZED from then on.

Remove its spiffe_id or subject_cn identity and reload. Its certificate still completes the TLS handshake if it chains to client_ca, but it no longer matches an identity; without a bearer token, the request is refused with 401. The proxy does not check CRLs or OCSP for client certificates; remove the identity there too.

PostgreSQL keeps one password per role, so there is a short window between changing it in the database and reloading the proxy in which new proxy connections fail with 08006. Existing sessions are not affected. Do both steps back to back, or switch the proxy to a second login role with the same grants and retire the old one.
