This page is for operators and on-call engineers. It is organised by symptom: for each one it says what the symptom means, how to confirm the cause with a command, endpoint, log line or metric that HaltSQL actually produces, and how to fix it.

Most diagnosis uses four tools. The examples assume a server on 127.0.0.1:8080 and a token in $HALTSQL_TOKEN. Tool Command Readiness and loaded policies curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz and curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $HALTSQL_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/policies Metrics curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics | grep '^haltsql_' Logs JSON lines on stderr, with ts, level and msg fields. For example kubectl logs deploy/haltsql | jq -c 'select(.msg == "reload failed; keeping the last good configuration")' Reproduce a verdict offline haltsql explain --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' --sql '...' with the same policy file and context the server uses If server.admin is enabled, GET /v1/admin/status (as an admin caller) shows the loaded policies with their versions and origins, bundle sources with last_error, audit sink health and audit_restart_pending. See http-api.md. Every response carries X-Request-Id. Send your own to find a request in the server logs and audit records (request_id). A denial is not an error. A denied query returns 200 with "allowed": false and reason codes. Any non-200 status means the check did not happen. Start by telling these apart.

Symptom Section Every query is denied Every query is denied E_TENANT_MISSING on a query that has a tenant filter E_TENANT_MISSING on queries that look scoped 401, 403 from /v1/verify 401 and 403 from the server 503 from /v1/verify, or /readyz not ready 503 responses and not ready A policy change did not take effect Policy reload failed or did not happen The server or proxy exits at startup The process will not start A bundle is refused Bundle signature or bundle source failures Audit errors, AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, SQLSTATE 58030 Audit sink errors haltsql audit verify reports problems Audit chain verification fails OIDC tokens rejected, groups_overage OIDC rejections and groups overage Clients cannot connect to haltsql-proxy Proxy connection errors Slow verifies High latency

What it means. The server is answering (200), but every verdict has "allowed": false. The cause is almost always the same for every query: missing context, a name that does not resolve, or a policy rule the agent never satisfies. How to confirm. Look at the codes: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/metrics | grep haltsql_reasons_total. One code dominating points to the cause. Take one denied query and run haltsql explain with the same policy file and context. Check that the server runs the policy you think it does: compare policy.version in a verdict (or GET /v1/policies) with the policy.version from haltsql verify --json on your local file. For a bundle with a name_prefix, the version reflects the prefixed name; use haltsql bundle inspect BUNDLE to see the versions inside it. Dominant code Usual cause Fix E_CONTEXT_MISSING The request does not carry the context field the policy's tenancy needs. The field name is the one after ctx. in tenancy.keys, for example tenant_id in "${ctx.tenant_id}". For OIDC callers, the context comes from context_claims; for mTLS callers, from the identity's context. Send the field from the authenticated session, or fix context_claims. See reason-codes.md. E_TABLE_DENIED Unqualified table names resolve through the policy's search_path; if it does not match the agent's schema, every table is "not in the allowlist". Fix search_path, or have the agent qualify names. See policy-reference.md. E_LIMIT_REQUIRED, E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH require_limit is set and the agent omits LIMIT or uses a parameter. Teach the agent (tool description) to add a constant LIMIT n within max. E_PARAM_UNBOUND The agent uses $n for values other than the tenant, or reuses the tenant placeholder outside its predicate. Also returned by haltsql-proxy for bound tenancy over the simple query protocol. Literals for non-tenant values; prepared statements through the proxy. See reason-codes.md. E_TENANT_MISSING See the next section. E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED Unqualified or ambiguous columns in joins. Qualify every column with its alias. E_EXTERNAL_POLICY OPA denies, or OPA is unreachable and opa.on_error is deny. Check haltsql_opa_decisions_total{outcome} (error_denied means OPA failed) and the opa check failed log line. See opa.md. E_INTERNAL An analyzer bug. File a bug with the SQL, policy and version. If it looks like a bypass attempt, report it privately (SECURITY.md). If the verdicts are "allowed": true but carry shadow_reasons, the policy is in shadow mode and nothing is being enforced.

What it means. HaltSQL needs to prove, for every occurrence of every tenant-scoped table in every scope, that a tenant predicate filters it. The proof only accepts simple, auditable shapes, so some safe-looking queries are denied on purpose. How to confirm. haltsql explain prints each reason with its position in the SQL and a caret under the table occurrence that lacks a predicate, plus a hint naming the alias. Then compare the query with this table: Query shape Why it is denied Fix WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR status = 'open' Only top-level AND conjuncts count. OR, NOT, CASE, COALESCE and function arguments prove nothing. Make the tenant predicate a top-level AND. Filter only in the outer query of a subquery or CTE Each scope must prove its own occurrences. Add the predicate inside the subquery or CTE body. A UNION with a filter in one branch Each branch is a scope. Filter every branch. EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.tenant_id = o.tenant_id) with WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 outside Equality is propagated only within one SELECT, not into a subquery. Add AND c.tenant_id = $1 inside the subquery. Filter in the ON of a LEFT JOIN for the preserved side The preserved side's rows are not filtered by ON. Move it to WHERE. Filter in HAVING Rows are already grouped. Only WHERE and ON count. Move it to WHERE. A composite tenancy (org_id and workspace_id) with one predicate Every tenant column needs its own predicate. Row-value comparisons such as (a, b) = ($1, $2) are not recognized. One conjunct per tenant column. tenant_id <> $1, IS DISTINCT FROM, LIKE Only = (and = ANY / IN for sets) count. Use =. A view or table listed with a tenant column but queried without a predicate Views are opaque relations; they need predicates like tables. Add the predicate, or review the policy entry. Reference: tenancy.md, tenancy.md, tenancy.md, reason-codes.md. E_TENANT_MISMATCH is different: in literal mode the literal differs from the context value, or in bound mode a literal was used instead of $1.
documents.s: E_TENANT_MISSING on queries that look scoped

documents.t: What it means. The request was refused before verification. The body says why: {"error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}}. How to confirm. haltsql_auth_total{method,result} shows which authentication method is failing (method is token, oidc, mtls, anonymous or none; result is ok, rejected or unavailable). OIDC rejections are logged at info as oidc token rejected with a reason field. Response Message or log Cause Fix 401 UNAUTHORIZED missing bearer token No Authorization: Bearer header, and no matching client certificate. Configure the client's token. 401 UNAUTHORIZED invalid bearer token No token_sha256 matches. A common cause is hashing the token with a trailing newline (echo instead of printf '%s'). Recompute: printf '%s' "$token" | sha256sum | cut -d' ' -f1, update the hash and reload. See config-reference.md. 401 UNAUTHORIZED client certificate does not match any configured identity The certificate verified against client_ca but matches no spiffe_id or subject_cn, and there is no bearer token to fall back to. Fix the identity entry. A CN in a TeletexString or with control characters never matches. 401 UNAUTHORIZED OIDC reason: expired, not_yet_valid, issued_in_future, wrong_audience, wrong_issuer, bad_signature, unknown_kid, missing_kid, alg_not_allowed, malformed, claim_mismatch, policy_not_allowed, missing_claim, bad_claim, no_group_policy, groups_overage The JWT failed its provider's checks. See OIDC rejections. 403 FORBIDDEN The request names a policy other than the caller's pinned one. On /v1/admin/*: the caller is not in server.admin.callers. Omit policy in the request, or fix the pinning. 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED An OIDC or mTLS caller sent a context field that is not in its request_context_fields. Repeating an identity-provided field with the same value is accepted. Stop sending the field, or add it to request_context_fields if the caller may set it. 404 POLICY_NOT_FOUND The request names an unknown policy, or names none and there is no default. Check GET /v1/policies. Reference: http-api.md, authentication.md.

Response Meaning How to confirm Fix 503 NOT_READY; /readyz {"status":"not_ready","policies":0} No policy is loaded. haltsql_policies_loaded is 0. Check the startup logs; see The process will not start. 503 POLICY_UNAVAILABLE The caller's pinned policy is not currently loaded. GET /v1/policies and, with the admin API, GET /v1/admin/status. Restore the policy (or its bundle) and reload. 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE; /readyz lists unhealthy_audit_sinks A fail_closed audit sink cannot be written. See Audit sink errors. 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE with Retry-After The OIDC provider's keys cannot be fetched and the cache has run out. Log oidc signing keys unavailable (with request_id); haltsql_auth_total{method="oidc",result="unavailable"}. Restore egress to the IdP (in Kubernetes, check the NetworkPolicy egress rules; the Helm chart opens TCP 443 only when oidc is set). /readyz "draining": true The process received SIGTERM and is shutting down. Log shutting down, draining connections. Expected during rollouts. 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE The body is larger than limits.max_request_bytes (default 1 MiB). Raise the limit or send smaller requests. The SQL itself is limited separately by the policy's limits.max_bytes (E_LIMIT).

What it means. Either the server tried to reload and rejected the new configuration (the last good one stays active), or it never saw a change. How to confirm. A failed reload logs reload failed; keeping the last good configuration with an errors list, and increments haltsql_policy_reload_total{result="error"}. A successful reload logs policies reloaded with every policy as name@version, and increments {result="success"}. Neither line means no reload happened. Cause Fix The new policy or config does not load (unknown key, bad YAML, invalid value). Run haltsql validate FILE and haltsql config show --config FILE with the same files. Errors carry file, line, column and key path. A token, OIDC provider, mTLS identity or default_policy references a policy that is no longer loaded. Restore the policy or fix the reference. The whole reload is refused, not just the reference. A secret placeholder cannot be resolved. The error is located (file:line:col: ${vault:...}: ...). Fix access to the provider. The change turns server.tls on or off. Restart; this cannot be done by reload. New TLS material is broken or the key does not match. haltsql_tls_reload_total{result="error"}; the previous material stays. Fix the files. No reload happened: the ConfigMap is mounted with subPath. Such mounts are not updated in running pods. Mount the directory, or roll the deployment. No reload happened: reload.watch is off. Send SIGHUP (systemctl reload haltsql) or roll. The operator turns watching off on purpose and rolls instead. No reload happened: the change was in a file referenced only through ${file:...} (a token hash, for example). Those files are not watched. Send SIGHUP. The reload succeeded but audit sinks did not change. Audit sinks need a restart. The reload logs audit sink changes need a restart; keeping the current audit sinks and GET /v1/admin/status shows audit_restart_pending: true. A bundle source entry was added, removed or changed but nothing happened. The list of bundle sources needs a restart. After a failed reload, the server does not retry the same broken files on every poll; it tries again when they change. For haltsql-proxy, the log line is config reload failed; keeping the current configuration, and a reload applies only to new connections. Reference: config-reference.md, proxy.md.
documents.s: Policy reload failed or did not happen

documents.t: What it means. haltsql-server exits with code 2 when the configuration cannot be loaded or the listener cannot start. Load errors are logged as failed to load configuration with an error field; other startup problems are logged at error level with the reason as the message (or as startup failed for operating-system errors). Cause How to confirm Fix Config or policy does not load. haltsql config show --config FILE; haltsql validate FILE. Fix the reported location. An unknown --default-policy (or default_policy). Startup error. Name a loaded policy. A secret placeholder cannot be resolved. Located load error naming the placeholder (never its value). Fix the provider, the env var or the file. A bundle signature does not verify, or the bundle is malformed. haltsql bundle verify BUNDLE --public-key KEY exits 1. See Bundle failures. A bundle source is unreachable and cache_dir holds no usable bundle. Startup fails closed. Restore access to the source, or provide a cache directory that survived. The audit file's last line is not a sealed record (a crash during a write). An error log line at startup; the file sink refuses to continue a chain from a line it cannot read as an audit record. Move the file aside (rotate it) and start; keep the old file for verification. The listen address is in use or invalid. An error log line at startup. Fix server.listen / --listen / HALTSQL_LISTEN. An invalid HALTSQL_* environment value. Load error naming the variable. Fix or unset it. In Kubernetes, a pod in this state never becomes ready. With maxUnavailable: 0 the old pods keep serving. The operator reports Progressing=False with reason RolloutFailed after 180 seconds. haltsql-proxy validate -c FILE checks a proxy config (exit 0 valid, 1 invalid, 2 unreadable). Its command-line errors exit 2.

What it means. A bundle failed one of the verification steps (size, signature, canonical form, digest, structure, policies), or a bundle source could not fetch or accept a new version. The last good bundle stays active. How to confirm. Local file: haltsql bundle verify BUNDLE --public-key KEY (exit 1 on failure; add --json for details). haltsql bundle inspect BUNDLE lists the signer key ids; without --public-key it says UNVERIFIED. Bundle source: the log line bundle source poll failed; keeping the last good bundle carries source, code and error; haltsql_bundle_source_healthy{source} is 0; GET /v1/admin/status shows last_error and the current bundle (version, signed_by). code Usual cause Fix bundle_source_signature Signed with a key that is not in public_keys, or a malformed .sig. Add the new public key to public_keys (and reload), or re-sign. During key rotation, dual-sign with haltsql bundle sign --append. bundle_source_rollback The new bundle's metadata.version is not strictly greater than the current one, or it has another metadata.name. Commit SHAs as versions trigger this. Publish with a monotonic version, for example 1.0.<run number>. bundle_source_rejected The server refused the verified bundle, for example because a token references a policy the bundle no longer has. Restore the policy in the bundle, or change the reference first. bundle_source_invalid Too large, not canonical, wrong digest, or a policy or catalog that does not load. Rebuild with haltsql bundle build; check with haltsql bundle verify. bundle_source_integrity A manifest or blob does not match its digest or size. Re-push; check for a proxy or mirror rewriting content. bundle_source_denied HTTP 401/403 or rejected credentials. Fix the auth credentials. Changing a bundle source entry needs a restart. bundle_source_not_found No such tag, digest, object or URL. Fix the reference. bundle_source_unavailable Connection failure, timeout, TLS failure, 429 or 5xx. Restore network access; the poller retries at the next interval. bundle_source_protocol Another unexpected response. Check the registry or server. bundle_source_cache cache_dir cannot be read or written. Never fatal. Fix permissions or the volume. If the bundle was refused at startup but a cached last good bundle exists, the server starts from it and logs bundle refused at startup; starting from the cached last good bundle. Reference: policy-bundles.md, policy-bundles.md.
documents.s: Bundle signature or bundle source failures

documents.t: What it means. A sink could not write a record. What happens next depends on the sink's on_error: on_error haltsql-server haltsql-proxy fail_closed (default) /v1/verify returns 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE. For S3/GCS, Elasticsearch and Kafka the sink turns unhealthy after a batch fails all its attempts, and /readyz is 503 until a retry succeeds. For file/stdout, each request retries the write. The statement is refused: ERROR, SQLSTATE 58030, detail HaltSQL reasons: PROXY_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE. The connection stays usable. buffer Records wait in memory and requests continue, up to a bound; then requests are refused as above. Records wait in memory up to max_buffer_records; then 58030. drop (streaming sinks, and the proxy) Records are dropped, counted and logged; requests continue. Records are dropped and logged (audit sink write failed; record dropped (on_error: drop)). How to confirm. Signal Where audit sink write failed; failing request closed (with sink, error, request_id) server log audit sink write failed; record buffered server log, buffer mode audit sink write failed; refusing the statement proxy log haltsql_audit_errors_total server metrics haltsql_audit_sink_healthy{sink}, _pending_objects, _upload_failures_total, _rejected_writes_total server metrics, S3/GCS haltsql_audit_stream_sink_healthy, _delivering, _delivery_failures_total, _records_dropped_total{reason} server metrics, Elasticsearch/Kafka unhealthy_audit_sinks in /readyz; audit_sinks[].healthy in /v1/admin/status server endpoints Cause Fix S3 AccessDenied, expired credentials Check the identity has s3:PutObject (and s3:PutObjectRetention with Object Lock). Temporary credentials are refreshed automatically. S3 refuses Object Lock headers The bucket must have Object Lock enabled. Kafka UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION Topics are never created automatically. Create it. Kafka broker name with _, or PLAIN to a non-loopback leader without TLS Refused on purpose. Use valid DNS names and TLS. Elasticsearch mapping drops A field changed type. Fix the index template; see records_dropped_total{reason="mapping"}. Disk full or unwritable path for a file sink Free space or fix permissions; the next write recovers. Changing on_error or any sink setting needs a restart. A streaming sink drops records only in drop mode or when the destination rejects a record for good (mapping, too_large); both are counted and logged, and a dropped record that was already sealed shows as a gap in chain verification. Records still queued in memory are lost if the process dies. Reference: audit-sinks.md, proxy.md.

Run haltsql audit verify on the sink's output. Exit 0 means every chain verifies, 1 a chain is broken, 2 a usage error or unreadable input. Problem kind Usual benign cause When to worry chain_restart (warning) A stdout sink after a process restart, or several replicas in one log. Never on its own; an error with --strict. mid_chain_start You verified a time range or one day of objects. Pass --any-start or --initial-prev HASH for partial exports. duplicate_record Kafka at-least-once re-delivery. Pass --allow-redelivery for Kafka exports; otherwise investigate. truncated The process died during a write. Expected only at the end of a file after a crash. broken_link, bad_hash, seq_gap, body_mismatch, fork, head_mismatch, spool_head_mismatch None. Records were edited, deleted, inserted or reordered. Treat as a security incident. For Elasticsearch and Kafka exports, use test/siem/verify_chain.py as shown in audit-sinks.md. Full list of problem kinds: audit-verify.md.

How to confirm. jq -c 'select(.msg == "oidc token rejected")' over the server log; the reason field is a stable code. The 401 body's message also says why. reason Cause Fix groups_overage Entra ID (Azure AD) left the groups claim out because the user is in too many groups (_claim_names / _claim_sources, or hasgroups). HaltSQL never calls Microsoft Graph, so it rejects the token. Set groupMembershipClaims to ApplicationGroup and assign only the relevant groups to the enterprise application, or map app roles with claim: roles. missing_claim The groups (or another required) claim is absent. Keycloak omits the groups claim for a user in no group. Add the claim mapper, or give policy_from_groups a default. bad_claim The groups claim is not a string or an array of strings. Fix the mapper. no_group_policy No group in the token is in map and there is no default. Add the mapping or a default. Groups are compared exactly and are case-sensitive; Keycloak's Full group path adds a leading /. wrong_audience aud contains none of audiences. Request the token for the right audience. expired, not_yet_valid, issued_in_future Clock skew beyond leeway_seconds (default 60), or a stale token. Fix time sync; refresh tokens. unknown_kid The IdP rotated keys. The server refreshes once per unknown kid, at most every 30 seconds per provider. Usually resolves itself; if not, check jwks_uri reachability. claim_mismatch A required_claims entry did not match. Fix the token's claims or the requirement. policy_not_allowed policy_claim names a policy outside allowed_policies. Fix the claim or the allowlist. Reference: authentication.md, authentication.md.

haltsql-proxy reports problems as PostgreSQL errors, so drivers show the SQLSTATE. Session and audit events go to its stderr log. SQLSTATE and message Cause Fix 28000 haltsql-proxy requires an SSL/TLS connection tls.required is true (the default) and the client did not upgrade. Use sslmode=require or stricter. 28000 a TLS client certificate is required / certificate identity is not authorized auth.method: cert and the certificate is missing or matches no identity. Fix the client certificate or auth.identities. 28P01 password authentication failed for user "..." Wrong password, unknown user, or a bad scram_verifier. Unknown users get the same message on purpose. Regenerate with haltsql-proxy scram-verifier. 3D000 database "..." does not exist The client asked for a database other than upstream.database. Use exactly that database name. 28000 replication connections are not allowed through haltsql-proxy A replication connection. Not supported through the proxy. 53300 sorry, too many clients already (haltsql-proxy limits.max_connections) limits.max_connections (default 100) reached. Raise it, pool connections, or add replicas. 08006 haltsql-proxy could not connect to the upstream database / did not respond / the upstream database rejected the session Upstream down, unreachable, TLS or credential failure (log: upstream rejected the session). Check upstream.*, credentials and upstream.tls. With verify-full, the host must be in a DNS SubjectAltName of the server certificate. 08006 authentication timed out Startup and authentication took longer than limits.auth_timeout_seconds (default 30). Check the client and network. 08P01 message exceeds the haltsql-proxy size limit A message larger than limits.max_message_bytes (default 1 MiB). Raise the limit or send smaller statements. 08P01 COPY sub-protocol is not allowed through haltsql-proxy COPY. Not available through the proxy. 57P05 terminating connection due to idle timeout ... limits.idle_timeout_seconds is set and the session was idle. Raise it, or let the pool reconnect. 42501 haltsql: query denied by policy "<name>": ... A policy denial (deny_sqlstate). The detail lists the reason codes. Fix the query; see Every query is denied. 58030 haltsql: the audit log could not be written; statement refused A fail_closed audit sink failed. See Audit sink errors. The client may retry. 42P05, 26000 A named prepared statement already exists, or is unknown. Driver statement handling; see proxy.md. Reference: proxy.md.

What it means. Verify calls take longer than expected. Separate the time spent verifying from the time spent waiting. How to confirm. haltsql_verify_duration_seconds measures verification only. histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(haltsql_verify_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) above 0.05 is the alert threshold in observability.md. elapsed_us in each verdict and audit record is the same per request. If verification is fast but clients see slow responses, the server is queueing. Check haltsql_http_open_connections, CPU on the instance, and the log line connection limit reached; new connections wait in the listen backlog. Cause Fix The instance is saturated. One server instance verifies on one event loop; in the published benchmark throughput levels off at about 4.5k requests/s and latency then grows with queue depth. Add replicas. See high-availability.md. CPU throttling from a container CPU limit. The Helm chart sets no CPU limit by default for this reason. Heavy queries. Cost grows with query complexity (joins, CTEs, window functions); pathological inputs take low milliseconds and are denied by the policy limits. Tighten limits (max_bytes, max_depth, max_nodes, max_joins). OPA is slow. Every allowed query waits for the decision. haltsql_opa_duration_seconds; run OPA on 127.0.0.1 and keep timeout_ms small. OIDC key refreshes. An unknown kid triggers at most one refresh per 30 s per provider. Client-side retries. The SDKs retry timeouts and 503s with backoff; a slow first attempt can triple the latency the agent sees. Per-invocation CLI use. One haltsql verify --sql ... process costs about 10 ms to start. Use --batch, the server, or the in-process library. Through the proxy: large result sets. The proxy relays each row message (about 5 µs per row in the benchmark). Reference: performance.md.

This page is for operators who upgrade HaltSQL and need to know what can change between releases. It covers what the project promises to keep stable, what it does not promise, how to upgrade each component, how to check a release before rolling it out, and how to roll back.

HaltSQL follows Semantic Versioning and records every notable change in CHANGELOG.md. The stable contracts and their rules: Contract Promise Source Verdict JSON (haltsql.dev/v1) Within v1, fields are only added, never renamed, removed or changed in meaning. Clients must ignore unknown fields. A v2 format, if ever needed, would be served side by side with v1. ADR-0004, verdict.md Reason codes Never renamed or reused, even before 1.0. New codes may be added in minor releases; clients must treat unknown codes as denials. message, rule and hint text may change at any time. ADR-0004, reason-codes.md, CHANGELOG.md HTTP API under /v1 Fields are only added, never renamed or removed. http-api.md Prometheus metric names Stable within /v1. http-api.md Determinism For the same SQL, policy and context: allowed, the reason codes, tables, columns and bind_params are identical across runs and platforms. ADR-0004 Document apiVersion Documents must say haltsql.dev/v1. "Every released schema version will keep loading, or fail with a clear migration error." policy-reference.md haltsql audit verify problem kinds The kind values in --json output are stable. audit-verify.md Change process Changes to a stable contract (policy schema, verdict JSON, reason codes, HTTP API, CLI exit codes) need an Architecture Decision Record merged first. GOVERNANCE.md

Read these before you plan an upgrade cadence: Before 1.0, minor releases may contain breaking changes. They are called out under Changed or Removed in the changelog (CHANGELOG.md). Read those sections for every version you skip over. Verdicts can change between releases. Determinism holds for one version. A release that fixes a bypass denies queries an older release allowed. For example, the unreleased changes deny a tenant placeholder reused outside its tenant predicate (E_PARAM_UNBOUND, rule params.tenant_reuse) and SQL-executing functions even when allowlisted (E_FUNCTION_DENIED, rule functions.dynamic_sql). Plan to test agent traffic against every new version. Only the latest release receives security fixes. Per SECURITY.md, 0.1.x (latest) is supported and anything older is not. After 1.0, the latest minor release and the current LTS line (if any) will be supported. There is no published support window, end-of-life schedule or SLA beyond the response targets for vulnerability reports in SECURITY.md. haltsql explain output is for people and may change between releases. Use haltsql verify --json in scripts. The operator API (haltsql.dev/v1alpha1) may change incompatibly before v1 (kubernetes-operator.md). No formal deprecation period is documented. Watch the changelog. The docs do not state whether policy.version (the SHA-256 over the normalized policy) stays identical for the same policy file across HaltSQL releases. Do not treat a version change seen only during a binary upgrade as proof that a policy changed; compare the policy files themselves. Note: At the time of writing, no release has been tagged yet; the first will be 0.0.1, and many features documented on this site are listed under Unreleased in the changelog. Check the release notes of the exact version you deploy.

Where How to read it Release tags vX.Y.Z. The release workflow marks v0.* tags and tags with a - as pre-releases on GitHub. Container image ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version> (e.g. 0.0.1) and :<major.minor> (e.g. 0.0). Pin by digest in production. Release archives haltsql-<tag>-linux-{amd64,arm64}.tar.gz, haltsql-<tag>-darwin-arm64.tar.gz; each holds haltsql, haltsql-server and haltsql-proxy. Running CLI haltsql version (or --json): HaltSQL, PostgreSQL grammar and OCaml versions. Running server haltsql_build_info{version,pg} on /metrics; version in GET /v1/admin/status. Helm chart Chart version and appVersion (the default image tag) in deploy/helm/haltsql/Chart.yaml. The chart versions in lockstep with HaltSQL and requires Kubernetes 1.27+.

Do this before a version enters any environment. Each GitHub release has SHA256SUMS, a keyless cosign bundle (*.sigstore.json) per archive, a GitHub build-provenance attestation and a CycloneDX SBOM (haltsql-<tag>.cdx.json). The image is signed with cosign and has a provenance attestation and an SBOM. sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing cosign verify-blob \ --bundle haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \ haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz gh attestation verify haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL cosign verify ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql@sha256:<digest> \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com These commands come from deployment.md; the signing steps are in .github/workflows/release.yml. Warning: The repository moved to github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL. Use this repository's workflow identity in cosign verify. Images published under the old ghcr.io/ardada2468/... path are not republished (CHANGELOG.md).

Read the changelog for every version between yours and the target, especially Changed, Removed and Security. Run your policy tests with the new CLI. haltsql validate and haltsql test on every policy and suite. A changed verdict shows up as a failing case. Diff verdicts on real queries. If you keep a corpus of agent SQL (for example from audit records written with audit.log_raw_sql: true), run it through both versions and compare: # queries.jsonl: {"id": ..., "sql": ..., "context": {...}} per line old/haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --batch < queries.jsonl > old.jsonl new/haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --batch < queries.jsonl > new.jsonl jq -c '{id, allowed, codes: [.reasons[]?.code]}' old.jsonl > old.cmp jq -c '{id, allowed, codes: [.reasons[]?.code]}' new.jsonl > new.cmp diff old.cmp new.cmp Each output line carries the input id, in input order. Lines that could not be read have an error field instead of a verdict. Check config compatibility both ways. Unknown keys are errors in every HaltSQL document. A config, policy or bundle that uses a key added in the new release will not load on the old one, which matters if you need to roll back. Adopt new keys only after the upgrade is complete everywhere. Validate the config with the new binary: haltsql config show --config FILE and haltsql validate FILE.

Install the new release archive or image, or bump the pinned version input of the GitHub Action (HaltSQL/HaltSQL@<tag> with version: <tag>; pin it, the default is latest). Upgrade CI after or together with the servers, not before, so CI never accepts a document the servers cannot load. See policy-ci.md.

Roll replicas one at a time; the server holds no state that replicas share. Deployment How Helm Set image.digest (wins over image.tag) and helm upgrade. The chart uses maxUnavailable: 0. Operator Set image in the HaltSQLServer spec (pin a digest); the operator rolls the Deployment with maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1. Sidecar Update the sidecar image in the agent's pod template; the agent rolls with it. systemd Replace /usr/local/bin/haltsql-server and systemctl restart haltsql. A reload (SIGHUP) does not replace the binary. Terraform Update the module's image input. See terraform.md. A new server that cannot load its config exits with code 2 and never becomes ready. With maxUnavailable: 0, the old pods keep serving. Audit chains across the restart: A file sink continues its chain from the file's last record. stdout, elasticsearch and kafka sinks start a new chain at genesis. s3 and gcs sinks continue the chain only with spool_dir. So expect chain_restart warnings from haltsql audit verify around an upgrade for sinks without continuity. See audit-sinks.md.

Restart each proxy instance. On SIGTERM it drains sessions for shutdown_grace_seconds (default 10), then closes them; clients must reconnect. Validate the config with the new binary first: haltsql-proxy validate -c FILE. A file audit sink whose last line is not a sealed record stops the proxy from starting. See proxy.md.

The operator validates policies with the haltsql CLI inside its own image, and its docs recommend building that image from the haltsql image your servers run, so validation and serving use the same loader. Upgrade the operator and the servers' image together. There is no published operator image in the release workflow; you build it (see kubernetes-operator.md). Because the API is v1alpha1, read the changelog for CRD changes before applying new manifests.

Upgrade them like any dependency: the Python package haltsql, the npm package @haltsql/client, the Go module github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/clients/go/haltsql, and the Java client in clients/java (com.haltsql:haltsql-client). Clients and servers talk /v1, which only gains fields, and the clients ignore unknown fields. No client/server version matrix is published; test the pair you run. The Python wheel and npm native packages bundle their own engine for local verification, so a local verifier runs the SDK's engine version, not your server's.

Shadow mode is a policy feature: it records would-be denials without enforcing them. You can use the same idea for a binary upgrade by running the new version next to the old one and comparing outcomes before it takes all traffic. Add one replica with the new version (a canary) behind the same load balancer, or upgrade one agent pod's sidecar. Compare, per pod, haltsql_verify_total{policy,result} and haltsql_reasons_total{code} between old and new replicas over the same window. A new reason code, or a shift from allowed to denied, needs an explanation from the changelog before you continue. Run haltsql report over each replica's audit records with --since to see which queries the new version denied, by reason, caller and fingerprint (shadow-reports.md). Roll the rest of the replicas, then upgrade CI. This compares traffic samples, not identical requests: each request goes to only one replica. For an exact comparison, use the batch diff in Before you upgrade. If a new release makes previously allowed agent queries fail, you can also take the cautious path for policies: keep the policy in mode: shadow on the new version for a while, read shadow_reasons, then switch back to enforce. Shadow mode enforces nothing, so do this only where the database role and RLS hold on their own (defense-in-depth.md).
documents.s: Rolling upgrades with a shadow comparison

documents.t: Every document's apiVersion must be haltsql.dev/v1; any other value is refused with unsupported apiVersion. Bundles are checked strictly: unknown members are errors at every level. Build bundles with a CLI no newer than your oldest server. A bundle source only accepts a bundle with the same metadata.name and a strictly greater metadata.version. This is unrelated to the HaltSQL version, but it decides how you roll back policies (below).

What How Watch out for Server or proxy binary Redeploy the previous image digest (helm rollback, revert the manifest, or reinstall the old binary). A config that uses keys only the new version knows will not load on the old one (exit 2). Revert the config first. Policy delivered as files or ConfigMap Revert in version control and redeploy, or reload. subPath mounts are not updated in place; roll the pods. Local bundle: file Put the previous .haltsqlbundle and .sig back and reload. Write both files atomically (write, then rename). bundle_source Republish the old policies under a new, higher metadata.version. Servers refuse older or equal versions (bundle_source_rollback). The config file cannot disable this check. Operator Revert the HaltSQLPolicy or HaltSQLServer object; the operator rolls the Deployment. While a policy is not Valid, the operator keeps the last good configuration. Step-by-step procedures are in runbooks.md.
CHANGELOG.md SECURITY.md GOVERNANCE.md ADR-0004: verdict schema and reason codes Production checklist Runbooks

Every number on this page was measured by the benchmark harness in bench/, in one run on one machine. The raw output is committed next to the harness: bench/results/m1max-2026-11-08.json (machine-readable) and bench/results/m1max-2026-11-08.md (the full tables). Read the numbers as one data point with the conditions listed below, not as a guarantee. Run the harness on your own hardware before you plan capacity.

Path Typical latency (p50) Throughput Library, Haltsql.verify in process 48 µs for a point lookup, 247 µs for a multi-CTE report query 3.5k–18k verifies/s on one core CLI, haltsql verify --batch 160 µs per query at --jobs 1 6.3k/s at --jobs 1, 22.5k/s at --jobs 8 haltsql-server, POST /v1/verify 278 µs on one connection about 4.5k requests/s (one core) haltsql-proxy, added to a query +246 µs on a point select 6.1k queries/s at 32 connections (one core) The main conclusions: Verification is cheap next to the query it guards. The full verdict (parse with the real PostgreSQL 17 parser, then analyse it against the policy) is 50–250 µs for realistic agent queries. That is well below the round trip to a database, and orders of magnitude below an LLM call. Cost grows with query complexity, not with policy size. The time goes up steadily from point lookups (t1) to six-way-join reports (t5). The pathological inputs (10,000-element IN lists, 500 levels of nesting, 50-way joins) stay in the low milliseconds and are denied by the policy's limits. haltsql-server and haltsql-proxy each verify on one core. Their throughput levels off at about 4.5k requests/s and 6k queries/s on this machine. Beyond that, adding connections only adds queueing latency. Scale them out by running more replicas: one sidecar per agent pod, or more instances behind the load balancer.

Machine Apple M1 Max (8 performance + 2 efficiency cores, 10 logical CPUs), 64 GiB RAM OS macOS 26.5.1 (Darwin 25.5.0), arm64 Toolchain OCaml 5.3.0, dune release profile (scripts/bench.sh) HaltSQL 0.1.0, branch feat/enterprise-adoption, 2026-11-08 PostgreSQL 17 (haltlab-pg17-1, postgres:17-alpine) in Docker Desktop, published on 127.0.0.1:5417 Run 2026-11-08T03:07Z, all suites, default sizes The machine was not idle. Other development work was running at the same time, including Docker containers and other builds. The 1/5/15-minute load averages were 67.89 171.08 167.20 at the start of the run and 63.22 122.71 147.30 at the end. An earlier run under much heavier load (a 1-minute load average above 150) measured p50 latencies up to 2x higher and tail latencies up to 10x higher. Expect better and more stable numbers, above all at p99 and p99.9, on a dedicated host. The harness records the load average in its JSON output so that you can tell runs apart. PostgreSQL runs inside Docker Desktop's Linux VM, and the benchmark client and haltsql-proxy run natively on macOS. Every database round trip therefore crosses Docker Desktop's port forwarding. This inflates the absolute PostgreSQL latencies, for both the direct path and the proxied path, compared with a database on the same host or network.

These are in-process calls, one at a time on one domain, cycling through each workload's queries. Each workload gets 20,000 timed calls after a warm-up; the pathological workload gets 1,000. The policy is test/fixtures/policies/saas.yaml (bound tenancy, catalog, function presets). All latencies are in microseconds. Workload Queries What it is p50 p90 p99 p99.9 verifies/s t1_point 4 point lookups by id, ~80–100 bytes 47.9 73.9 114 356 17,926 t2_filter_aggregate 4 filters, GROUP BY, aggregates, HAVING 78.0 109 170 600 11,435 t3_joins 4 2–3 joins, each table tenant-scoped 112 152 239 437 8,492 t4_cte_window 4 CTEs, window functions, correlated EXISTS 130 189 365 1,069 6,835 t5_report 4 3 CTEs + 5 joins + FILTER + CASE; 5-way UNION ALL; cohort retention 247 433 703 1,620 3,508 corpus_benign 170 test/corpus/benign_analytics.suite.yaml (all allowed) 64.1 108 211 523 13,516 corpus_attack 1,038 every other test/corpus suite against its own policy (mostly denials) 43.2 82.0 248 1,085 18,171 pathological 10 10k-element IN, 500-deep nesting, 50 joins, 15 KB query, 100-way UNION 869 5,524 6,294 7,969 507 The tiers t1–t5 (bench/corpus/complexity.jsonl) are queries of the kind an analytics agent writes against the haltlab-style SaaS schema. Before timing anything, the harness checks that each one is allowed, so that a fast denial cannot pass for a fast verify. Denials (corpus_attack) are a little cheaper than allowed queries, because the analysis stops at the first violation.

The CLI runs end to end as a separate process: it loads the policy, reads 24,000 JSONL lines on stdin (the t1–t5 queries round-robin), and writes 24,000 verdicts. Each figure is the median of 3 runs. Every verdict is checked to be "allowed":true. --jobs Wall time (median) Verdicts/s Per query 1 3.83 s 6,268 160 µs 2 1.91 s 12,557 79.6 µs 4 1.14 s 21,072 47.5 µs 8 1.07 s 22,514 44.4 µs --jobs scales almost linearly up to 4 domains. At 8 domains the run is bound by I/O and by the sequential read and write of each 4096×jobs-line block. One haltsql verify --sql ... invocation (process start, policy and catalog load, one verify) takes 9.8 ms at the median and 11.0 ms at p99, over 30 runs. For more than a handful of queries, use --batch.

The load generator is closed-loop and built into the harness. It opens C persistent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, spread over up to 4 forked client processes, and each connection sends its next request as soon as the previous response arrives. Every response must be 200 with "allowed":true; there were 0 errors. The server runs with --policy saas.yaml --allow-unauthenticated, the default info logging to a file, and a file audit sink (hash-chained, one record per request) unless noted. Each run lasts 10 s after a 2 s warm-up. Latencies are in microseconds and measured by the client. Connections Audit sink p50 p90 p99 p99.9 requests/s 1 file 278 460 752 2,159 3,192 8 file 1,735 2,184 3,320 8,601 4,466 32 file 6,847 10,288 18,741 38,148 4,187 128 file 26,908 37,301 58,559 79,690 4,488 32 none 6,410 8,599 16,378 34,690 4,655 The server verifies on a single Lwt event loop, so throughput saturates at about 4.5k requests/s on this machine. From there, latency rises in proportion to the queue depth (Little's law: 32 connections / 4.2k/s ≈ 7.6 ms). On one connection, the HTTP, JSON, logging and audit work adds roughly 150 µs to the bare verify. The file audit sink costs about 10% of throughput at 32 connections. To size a deployment, plan for one core per ~4k verifies/s of t1–t5-like traffic, keep each instance well below saturation if you care about p99, and scale out horizontally.

Both paths use the same client: the harness's simple-query client, which reuses the proxy's own Upstream module and authenticates with SCRAM-SHA-256. The direct path connects to PostgreSQL. The proxied path connects to haltsql-proxy, which verifies the statement against bench/fixtures/proxy-policy.yaml (literal tenancy), writes one audit record to a file, and relays the query over its own upstream connection. The table is app.orders, with 20,000 rows over two tenants and an index on (tenant_id, created_at). For each query, 10 rounds of 500 direct and 500 proxied executions are interleaved on one connection each, so that drift on the machine hits both paths equally. Before timing, the harness checks that the proxy denies a cross-tenant query with SQLSTATE 42501. Latencies are in microseconds. Query Rows Direct p50 Proxied p50 Added p50 Direct p99 Proxied p99 point select by primary key 1 441 687 +246 1,961 3,556 GROUP BY status aggregate 2 2,448 2,748 +300 7,974 8,701 range scan, ORDER BY ... LIMIT 100 100 525 1,280 +755 3,037 3,331 The proxy adds about 0.25–0.3 ms per statement at the median. That time goes to the extra loopback hop, the verify, and the audit write. Large result sets add more, because the proxy relays each row message: about 5 µs per row for the 100-row query. At the tail, the difference between paths is smaller than the run-to-run noise on this machine. Throughput with 32 concurrent connections running the point select, closed loop for 8 s: Path p50 p99 queries/s direct 1,149 5,022 23,394 via haltsql-proxy 4,564 12,545 6,070 Like the server, the proxy runs on a single event loop. It saturates at about 6k statements/s on one core, while PostgreSQL itself serves 23k/s for this query. If a workload needs more than that through one proxy, run several proxy replicas.

documents.t: make -C lab up # Postgres 17 on localhost:5417 (proxy suite only) scripts/bench.sh # release build + all suites (~4 min) # results: _build/bench-results/bench.json and bench.md scripts/bench.sh builds bench/bench.exe and the three binaries with --profile release and runs the harness. It passes any extra arguments through to the harness: Option Meaning --suite library,cli,http,proxy Suites to run (default: all). The proxy suite is skipped with a message if Postgres is unreachable. --small The short CI-sized run (~1 min). --iters N, --lines N Library calls per workload (default 20,000), CLI batch size (default 24,000). --pg-host, --pg-port, --pg-user Postgres for the proxy suite (default 127.0.0.1:5417, postgres; password from HALTSQL_PGPASSWORD, default haltlab). --json FILE, --markdown FILE Output files (scripts/bench.sh sets both under $OUT_DIR). --baseline FILE, --max-regress X The regression gate, described below. The proxy suite creates a scratch database, release_bench_<pid>, and always drops it. The HTTP and proxy suites start their own server and proxy on free loopback ports and stop them afterwards. make bench (or dune build @bench) runs only the small library suite.

The JSON output ("schema": "haltsql-bench/1") records the host (OS, arch, CPU, logical CPUs, memory, OCaml version, load average at the end), the configuration (suites, sizes, load average at the start), and one object per workload. Each object has suite, name, unit, samples, p50, p90, p99, p99_9, max, mean, throughput_per_s, errors, gate and workload-specific fields (queries, concurrency, audit, jobs, calibration_ms, ...). Percentiles use the nearest-rank method. Timing uses Unix.gettimeofday, whose resolution is 1 µs. A run exits 1 if any request failed or any verdict was wrong.

The bench job of .github/workflows/build-images.yml runs on pull requests that touch bin/, lib/, vendor/, bench/ or the build files: scripts/bench.sh --small --suite library,cli,http \ --baseline bench/baseline/ci-small.json --max-regress 1.5 The job compares the gated workloads with the committed baseline bench/baseline/ci-small.json: the library tiers t1–t5; corpus_benign; cli/batch_jobs_1; http/verify_c1_audit_file. It compares p50, the most stable statistic on a shared runner. The baseline was recorded on the machine above, but CI runs on a GitHub-hosted x86-64 Linux runner, so absolute numbers are not comparable. Each p50 is therefore divided by a calibration time first: a fixed CPU workload that does not touch HaltSQL (SHA-256 over 64 KiB, sorting pseudo-random integers, hashing short strings). The calibration runs interleaved with each library workload, and before and after the CLI and HTTP suites, so that a busy or throttled machine slows both sides of the ratio: ratio = (p50_now / calibration_now) / (p50_baseline / calibration_baseline) The job fails when any gated ratio exceeds 2.5 (--max-regress 1.5), that is, when a workload got more than 2.5x slower relative to the machine's speed. p50 values below 5 µs are raised to 5 µs on both sides to absorb timer noise. This threshold is deliberately loose, for three reasons: On a quiet machine, two consecutive runs against the baseline gave ratios of 0.94–1.07. The same small run in a Linux container on the same Mac shifted the normalized library numbers by up to about 1.3x compared with macOS. Under heavy machine load (a load average above 150), ratios spread from 0.1 to over 2. So the gate catches algorithmic regressions (an accidental quadratic pass, a cache that stops working, recompiling the policy on every call) without failing on noise. Smaller regressions need a look at the uploaded bench-results artifact, or a local before/after run of scripts/bench.sh. To update the baseline after an intended change, run this on a quiet machine and commit the result: OUT_DIR=/tmp/b scripts/bench.sh --small --suite library,cli,http cp /tmp/b/bench.json bench/baseline/ci-small.json

A policy bundle packages validated policies (and, optionally, catalog snapshots) into one file that a HaltSQL server can trust without trusting the file system or the delivery channel it came through. CI builds and signs the bundle once. Every server verifies the signature before it reads a single policy.

# once: create a signing key pair (keep the private key in a secret store) haltsql bundle keygen -o policy-signing.key # writes policy-signing.key (0600) + .pub # in CI: build, sign, verify haltsql bundle build policies/*.yaml --catalog catalog/saas.snapshot.json \ --name prod-policies --bundle-version 1.4.0 \ --source-url https://github.com/acme/policies --source-commit "$GITHUB_SHA" \ -o dist/prod.haltsqlbundle haltsql bundle sign dist/prod.haltsqlbundle --key policy-signing.key haltsql bundle verify dist/prod.haltsqlbundle --public-key policy-signing.key.pub # anywhere: look inside (add --public-key to also check the signature) haltsql bundle inspect dist/prod.haltsqlbundle The server loads the bundle from its config: policies: - bundle: /etc/haltsql/bundles/prod.haltsqlbundle # signature: prod.haltsqlbundle.sig public_keys: - /etc/haltsql/keys/policy-signing.pub name_prefix: prod. # optional See config-reference.md for the config keys.

Command What it does Exit codes haltsql bundle keygen -o FILE [--force] Writes an Ed25519 private key to FILE (PKCS#8 PEM, mode 0600, never overwritten without --force) and the public key to FILE.pub. Prints the key id. 0, 2 haltsql bundle build POLICY... --name N --bundle-version V -o OUT [--catalog [NAME=]FILE]... [--created-by T] [--source-url U] [--source-commit SHA] Loads and validates every policy and catalog, then writes the canonical bundle. 0, 2 haltsql bundle sign BUNDLE (--key FILE | --key-env VAR) [--signature FILE] [--append] Validates the bundle (it refuses to sign one that does not load), then writes BUNDLE.sig. With --append the new signature is added next to the existing ones. 0, 1, 2 haltsql bundle verify BUNDLE --public-key KEY... [--signature FILE] [--name-prefix P] Full verification, the same checks the server runs. 0, 1, 2 haltsql bundle inspect BUNDLE [--public-key KEY...] Shows metadata, digest, policies (name, version, mode, tables), catalogs and signer key ids. Without keys it does not check the signature and says UNVERIFIED. 0, 1, 2 haltsql bundle push --oci REF BUNDLE / haltsql bundle pull --oci REF -o FILE --public-key KEY... Publish a signed bundle to an OCI registry, or fetch and verify one. See Bundle sources. 0, 1, 2, 3 The exit codes follow the CLI conventions. 0 means success. 1 means a bundle or signature failed verification or validation (verify fails with 1 on any such problem, including a missing bundle). 2 means a usage error or an input that cannot be loaded, such as a missing policy file or an unreadable or group-readable private key. Every command accepts --json. --public-key takes a PEM file or the base64 of the 32 raw key bytes. --key refuses a private key file that group or others can read (chmod 600). --key-env VAR reads the PEM key from an environment variable, which suits CI secrets. Keys made with openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 work too.

A bundle is one JSON document in canonical form. Object members are sorted by key in byte order. There is no insignificant whitespace, and the document ends with exactly one newline. Floats, out-of-range integers, duplicate keys and alternative string escapes are not allowed. Any other encoding of the same JSON is rejected, so a given bundle has exactly one valid byte sequence. {"apiVersion":"haltsql.dev/v1", "catalogs":{"saas":{"tables":{...}}}, "digest":"sha256:50f7bf7a...", "kind":"PolicyBundle", "metadata":{"created_by":"haltsql/0.2.0","name":"prod-policies", "source":{"commit":"4f0c2a91...","url":"https://github.com/acme/policies"}, "version":"1.4.0"}, "policies":[{"document":{...normalized policy...},"name":"saas-analytics"}]} (The example is wrapped for reading. The real file is a single line.) Member Meaning apiVersion haltsql.dev/v1 kind PolicyBundle metadata.name 1–128 characters: letters, digits, _ - ., starting with a letter or digit. metadata.version 1–64 printable characters, no spaces (for example a semver, a date or a CI run number). metadata.created_by Optional; the default is haltsql/<version>. metadata.source.url, .commit Optional provenance: an http(s) URL and a 7–64 character lower-case hex commit. policies[] 1–1000 entries {name, document}. document is the normalized policy JSON (the form Policy.version hashes, with presets expanded and the catalog inline). document.metadata.name must equal name. A catalog given as a path is rejected: bundles are self-contained. catalogs Catalog snapshots by name (may be {}). digest sha256: + hex SHA-256 of the canonical serialization of the document without digest. Builds are deterministic: the same policies, catalogs and metadata always give byte-identical bundles. There are no timestamps. A policy written in YAML or in JSON produces the same bundle. Rebuild in CI and compare digests to check that a deployed bundle matches its source commit.

A signature file is also canonical JSON. With one signature it looks like this: {"algorithm":"ed25519","keyid":"sha256:c380011f...","signature":"8pyF25qk...=="} With several signatures (sign --append, used while rotating keys) it looks like this: {"signatures":[{"algorithm":"ed25519","keyid":"sha256:...","signature":"..."},{"algorithm":"ed25519","keyid":"sha256:...","signature":"..."}]} keyid is sha256: + the hex SHA-256 of the 32 raw public-key bytes. It is only a lookup hint. It never replaces verification. signature is the base64 of the 64-byte Ed25519 signature (RFC 8032). It is computed over the ASCII domain separator haltsql.dev/v1 PolicyBundle signature\n followed by the exact bundle bytes. A file holds 1–16 signatures and is at most 64 KiB. Because the message is plain bytes, you can check a signature with standard tools: jq -r .signature prod.haltsqlbundle.sig | base64 -d > sig.bin { printf 'haltsql.dev/v1 PolicyBundle signature\n'; cat prod.haltsqlbundle; } > msg.bin openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey policy-signing.key.pub -rawin -in msg.bin -sigfile sig.bin

haltsql bundle verify and the server's loader (Haltsql_bundle.load_verified) run the same steps, in this order, and stop at the first failure: Size. The bundle must be a regular file of at most 16 MiB (configurable in the library), and the signature file at most 64 KiB. Reads are bounded, so a file that grows while it is read is still rejected. Signature. At least one signature must verify against one of the trusted keys. Signatures whose keyid matches no trusted key are skipped. Nothing in the bundle is parsed before this step succeeds. Canonical form. The bytes must be the canonical serialization of the parsed JSON. Digest. The recorded digest must equal the recomputed one. Structure. apiVersion and kind must be correct, and unknown members are errors at every level. Names, versions, provenance and limits are all checked. Policies and catalogs. Each one is compiled with the normal loaders (unknown policy keys are errors). The name_prefix is applied before compiling, so Policy.version reflects the final name. The tests in test/bundle/ cover each step. They include a flipped payload byte, a flipped signature bit, a wrong key, a forged key id, truncated bundle and signature files, unknown members (in the top level, metadata, policy entries and policy documents), a non-canonical encoding, a digest mismatch, duplicate keys, oversized files and catalog path references.

Generate keys with haltsql bundle keygen or openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519. Store the private key as a CI secret, such as HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY in a protected GitHub environment or a masked, protected GitLab variable. Never commit it. Distribute only the .pub file. It is safe to commit (for example keys/policy-signing.pub) and to bake into server images or ConfigMaps. Rotation: Generate the new key and add its public key to every server's public_keys list next to the old one. Any listed key may verify. Optionally, while both keys are in use, dual-sign: haltsql bundle sign B --key old.key and then haltsql bundle sign B --key new.key --append. Switch CI to the new key. Once no bundle signed only by the old key is in circulation, remove the old public key from the servers. Compromise: remove the key from public_keys and reload. Bundles signed only by that key stop loading at once. The server keeps the last good policy set if a reload fails.

A server does not need the bundle on its file system. A bundle_source policy entry makes it fetch the bundle from an OCI registry, an S3 bucket (or an S3-compatible store such as MinIO) or an HTTPS URL, and poll for new versions: policies: - bundle_source: oci: ghcr.io/acme/haltsql-policies:prod public_keys: [/etc/haltsql/keys/policy-signing.pub] # mandatory name_prefix: prod. poll_interval_s: 60 cache_dir: /var/cache/haltsql/bundles See config-reference.md for every key. The transport is never trusted. The Ed25519 signature is checked with the configured public_keys before anything in the bundle is parsed, exactly as for a local bundle, and a source without public_keys is a config error.

Start. If cache_dir holds a bundle from an earlier run, it is verified again with the current keys and used straight away. A key you removed from public_keys therefore also invalidates the cache. Then the source is polled once. Startup succeeds when either step produced a bundle, so a restart works while the source is down. With no cache and no reachable source, startup fails closed. Conditional fetch. For OCI, a HEAD of the tag returns the manifest digest, and nothing is downloaded when it is unchanged. A reference pinned to a digest is fetched once and never again. For S3 and HTTPS the bundle request carries If-None-Match with the ETag of the current bundle, and the signature (<key>.sig or <url>.sig) is only fetched when the bundle has changed. Verification. OCI manifests and blobs are hashed and must match their digests and sizes. Then come the signature and the usual verification steps. No rollback. Once a bundle is current, a new one is accepted only when it has the same metadata.name and a strictly greater metadata.version. An equal version with different content is refused too, and the bundle restored from the cache counts as current. Versions are compared in natural order: runs of digits compare as numbers and other runs compare bytewise. So 1.9.0 < 1.10.0, 2026.11.07 < 2026.11.08 and build-99 < build-100, and a - or ~ suffix marks a pre-release (1.4.0-rc.1 < 1.4.0). Git commit SHAs are not ordered, so give polled bundles a monotonic version (see policy-ci.md). To roll back, publish the old policies under a new, higher version. An embedding application can turn the check off (allow_downgrade), but the signature is still required. The config file does not expose this. Hand-over. The verified policies go to the server. If the server refuses them (for example because a token references a policy the new bundle no longer has), the current bundle stays. Only accepted bundles are cached. At startup a freshly fetched bundle is cached only after the server's startup checks accepted it. If they refuse it, the server starts from the bundle restored from cache_dir (the last accepted one) when that passes, logs bundle refused at startup; starting from the cached last good bundle, and reports the refusal as bundle_source_rejected; without a usable cached bundle, startup fails. Bundle-driven reloads are serialized, so two sources that update at the same time both take effect. Failure. Any failure (unreachable source, denied, bad digest, bad or untrusted signature, rollback, refusal) keeps the last good bundle. It is reported with a stable code and retried at the next poll. Code Meaning bundle_source_unavailable Connection failure, timeout, TLS failure, HTTP 429 or 5xx. bundle_source_denied HTTP 401/403, or rejected credentials. bundle_source_not_found No such tag, digest, object or URL. bundle_source_integrity A manifest or blob does not match its digest or size, an unexpected media type, a malformed manifest, or an oversized layer. bundle_source_protocol Any other unexpected response. bundle_source_signature Malformed signature file, or no signature verifies with a trusted key. bundle_source_invalid The bundle is too large, not canonical, has a wrong digest, or a policy or catalog does not load. bundle_source_rollback An older or same version, or another bundle name. bundle_source_rejected The server refused the verified bundle. bundle_source_cache The cache could not be read or written. This is never fatal.

cache_dir holds one subdirectory per source (mode 0700), named after a hash of the source. It contains the last accepted bundle and signature, named after the bundle's SHA-256, and a state.json with the source and its manifest digest or ETag. Each file is written to a temporary file, fsynced and renamed. state.json is written last, so a crash leaves either the old entry or the new one. The cache is not trusted: what it holds is verified again on every start, and a file whose content does not match its name is refused. Give each server its own cache_dir, or at least do not let two processes poll the same source into the same directory.

A bundle is published as one OCI artifact: an OCI image manifest (OCI image spec v1.1 artifact guidance) with two layers. This is what oras push --artifact-type produces, so either tool can publish and either can pull. Part Value manifest mediaType application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json artifactType application/vnd.haltsql.bundle.v1 config The empty descriptor application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json ({}, sha256:44136fa3...). bundle layer application/vnd.haltsql.bundle.v1+json, titled (org.opencontainers.image.title) with the bundle's file name. signature layer application/vnd.haltsql.bundle.signature.v1+json, titled <bundle file>.sig. manifest annotations dev.haltsql.bundle.name, dev.haltsql.bundle.version, dev.haltsql.bundle.digest. When reading, HaltSQL also accepts the artifact type as the config media type (the layout of oras 1.0). It requires exactly one bundle layer and one signature layer. It refuses any other layer, image indexes, Docker manifests, a bundle layer over 16 MiB and a signature layer over 64 KiB, and it checks the sizes before downloading. haltsql bundle push adds no timestamp, so the same bundle and signature always give the same manifest digest.

# publish (CI): validates the bundle, checks the signature against the key, uploads, tags haltsql bundle push --oci ghcr.io/acme/haltsql-policies:1.4.0 dist/prod.haltsqlbundle \ --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub \ --username "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-env REGISTRY_PASSWORD # -> pinned ghcr.io/acme/haltsql-policies@sha256:<manifest digest> # fetch and verify (e.g. an init container): nothing is written unless every check passes haltsql bundle pull --oci ghcr.io/acme/haltsql-policies@sha256:<digest> \ -o /etc/haltsql/bundles/prod.haltsqlbundle --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub Command What it does Exit codes haltsql bundle push --oci REF BUNDLE [--signature FILE] [--public-key KEY]... Refuses a bundle that does not load or a malformed signature file, and with --public-key a signature that does not verify. Then it uploads the config, bundle and signature blobs (skipping blobs the registry already has) and the manifest under the tag. Prints the digest-pinned reference. 0, 1, 2, 3 haltsql bundle pull --oci REF -o FILE --public-key KEY... [--name-prefix P] Verifies the manifest and both blobs against their digests, then the signature and every policy. Only then does it write FILE.sig and FILE (each atomically, signature first). 0, 1, 2, 3 Both commands accept --plain-http (loopback registries only), --username U --password-env VAR or --token-env VAR, --ca-file FILE, --timeout SECONDS and --json. With --json, a refused push, a failed verification or an unreachable registry also prints {"ok": false, "exit": N, "error": "..."} on stdout (exit code N), the shape bundle verify --json uses. Passwords and tokens come from environment variables, never from the command line. Exit code 3 means the registry could not be reached or refused the request. A digest or size mismatch is a verification failure (exit 1).
documents.s: Publishing and pulling with the CLI

documents.t: HTTPS only. plain_http: true (config) or --plain-http (CLI) is accepted only for localhost, 127.x and [::1]. A request first goes out with the credentials already established for it. On 401 the registry's WWW-Authenticate challenge decides what happens next: Bearer realm=…,service=…: a token is requested from realm for repository:<repo>:pull (or pull,push for push). The request is anonymous, or uses basic auth with the configured {username, password}. The realm must be https (or loopback http), so credentials never travel in clear text. Tokens are cached until shortly before expires_in. Basic: the configured credentials are sent. Without credentials this is a bundle_source_denied error. auth: {token} is a registry token you already have, sent as Authorization: Bearer to the registry. Blob redirects (registries backed by object storage) are followed, at most 3, only to https (or loopback http) targets. Credentials are dropped when the origin changes. Every manifest and blob is hashed (sha256 or sha512) and compared with the requested digest and the registry's Docker-Content-Digest. The unverified HEAD digest is used only to decide that nothing changed. Tested against registry:2 with anonymous access, htpasswd basic auth and token auth through cesanta/docker_auth, and with oras 1.2 pushing and pulling.

S3: SigV4-signed GETs of key and key.sig. The request is path-style (endpoint/bucket/key) when endpoint is set (MinIO and other S3-compatible stores) and virtual-hosted on AWS. Credentials come from s3.credentials, as for the S3 audit sink (env by default). Tested against MinIO. HTTPS: GET url and GET url.sig, with auth sent as Authorization: Basic or Bearer. Redirects are followed under the same rules as above. Tested against nginx with a private CA. Publishing order. Upload the new .sig first and the bundle second. Because the bundle request is conditional, a poll that sees the new bundle then always finds the new signature. In the other order, a poll in between reports bundle_source_signature once and succeeds at the next poll. An ETag that changes without a content change costs a download but no update: a bundle identical to the current one is ignored. There is no GCS source yet. Mirror bundles to S3 or serve them over HTTPS.

You can also sign the OCI artifact with cosign, for example keyless in GitHub Actions. Registry admission policies (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) can then require it: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/haltsql-policies@sha256:<digest> That signature protects the registry path. The HaltSQL Ed25519 signature is the one the server enforces, whatever the transport. HaltSQL does not run cosign.
documents.s: Optional: cosign on the OCI artifact

documents.t: (* haltsql.bundle *) let keys = List.map (fun f -> Result.get_ok (Haltsql_bundle.Key.public_of_file f)) key_files in match Haltsql_bundle.load_verified ~name_prefix:"prod." "/etc/haltsql/prod.haltsqlbundle" keys with | Ok policies -> (* Policy.t list, ready for Haltsql.verify *) | Error e -> prerr_endline (Haltsql_bundle.error_to_string e) (* refuse to start *) Haltsql_bundle.load_config_ref does the same for a Config.bundle_ref from the runtime config. It decodes the entry's public_keys and applies its name_prefix. See lib/bundle/haltsql_bundle.mli. Remote sources are in haltsql.bundle_source (lib/bundle_source/haltsql_bundle_source.mli): let* src = Haltsql_bundle_source.create cfg_bundle_source in (* Config.bundle_source *) Haltsql_bundle_source.start src ~on_update:(fun u -> (* u.policies: verified, prefixed; Error refuses the bundle *) install u) ~on_error:(fun e -> log (Haltsql_bundle_source.error_code e) (Haltsql_bundle_source.error_to_string e)) (* resolves after the cache restore and the first poll; polling continues until [stop] *)

Treat HaltSQL policies like code. Every change is validated, linted and tested against policy test suites before it merges. The main branch then produces a signed bundle that servers load. HaltSQL ships three integrations: Integration File For GitHub Action action.yml GitHub Actions workflows GitLab CI templates ci/gitlab/haltsql.gitlab-ci.yml GitLab pipelines (include: + extends:) pre-commit hooks .pre-commit-hooks.yaml Local checks before each commit All three run the same CLI commands: haltsql validate, haltsql lint-policy, haltsql test --json and, optionally, haltsql bundle build/sign. A pipeline always agrees with what you see locally. Ready-made examples are in examples/ci/.

# .github/workflows/policy-ci.yml on: [pull_request] permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write # only for comment-summary jobs: policies: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: HaltSQL/HaltSQL@v0.2.0 with: version: v0.2.0 policies: policies/**/*.yaml suites: tests fail-on-warnings: "true" comment-summary: "true"

Installs haltsql. It downloads the release archive for the runner (linux-amd64, linux-arm64 or darwin-arm64) and verifies it against the release's SHA256SUMS. The archive must be listed exactly once and its checksum must match. A mismatch fails the job and never falls back to another source. With verify-signature: true (and cosign on PATH), it also verifies SHA256SUMS with cosign keyless signatures. On other platforms, or if the download itself fails, it falls back to the container image ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version>, which needs Docker. The tag is resolved to a digest once, and the image is always run by that digest. With verify-signature: true, a failed download is fatal (there is no container fallback), and a container image (install-method: docker or an unsupported platform) is used only after cosign verify of its digest passes with the same identity constraints as the release. Validates every policy and suite file (haltsql validate --json). Lints every policy (haltsql lint-policy --json). Tests the suites (haltsql test --json). Writes a job summary ($GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY) with these sections: a check overview; per-suite pass/fail counts; failed cases with their reason codes; a collapsible table of denied cases per suite, showing whether the denial was expected, the reason codes and the first reason message; validation errors and lint warnings. With comment-summary: true on pull requests, the same Markdown is posted as one PR comment that is updated in place. With a read-only token (for example on fork PRs) this only produces a warning. Optionally builds a bundle (bundle: true). It runs only after all the checks pass. The bundle is signed when signing-key is set, verified against public-keys when given, and uploaded as the haltsql-policy-bundle artifact. All case names and messages are HTML-escaped in the summary, so a crafted test name in a pull request cannot inject Markdown or HTML. Inputs reach the scripts only as environment variables, never interpolated into shell code.

Input Default Meaning version latest Release to install (latest, v0.2.0 or 0.2.0). Pin it. policies policies Policy files, directories or globs, whitespace or newline separated. ** matches any depth, including none. Directories are searched for *.yaml, *.yml and *.json. suites (none) Test-suite files, directories or globs. Directories are searched for *.suite.yaml, *.suite.yml and *.suite.json. fail-on-warnings false Fail when lint-policy reports warnings. comment-summary false Post or update a PR comment with the summary. max-denied 50 Denied cases listed per suite in the summary. working-directory . Base directory for the globs. install-method auto auto, release (never use the container) or docker. verify-signature false Also verify the release (or the container image) with cosign. Disables the container fallback after a download failure. haltsql-path (none) Use an existing binary and skip the install. bundle false Build a bundle from policies after the checks pass. bundle-name repository name Bundle metadata.name. bundle-version first 12 characters of the commit SHA Bundle metadata.version. catalogs (none) Catalog snapshots to ship ([NAME=]FILE, whitespace separated). signing-key (none) PEM Ed25519 private key; pass ${{ secrets.HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY }}. public-keys (none) Public keys the signed bundle must verify against. upload-bundle true Upload the bundle and signature as a workflow artifact. github-token ${{ github.token }} Used for the PR comment and for resolving latest.
result (pass or fail), passed, failed, warnings, summary-file, haltsql-path, bundle-path, signature-path.

Put HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY in a protected environment that requires reviewers, and run the bundle job only on the default branch (see examples/ci/github-policy-ci.yml). The key reaches haltsql through an environment variable (--key-env), is never written to disk, and is never printed.

# .gitlab-ci.yml include: - remote: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/v0.2.0/ci/gitlab/haltsql.gitlab-ci.yml variables: HALTSQL_VERSION: v0.2.0 HALTSQL_POLICIES: policies HALTSQL_SUITES: tests policy-check: extends: .haltsql-check policy-bundle: extends: .haltsql-bundle needs: [policy-check] rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH The template only defines hidden jobs, so including it adds no jobs until you extend them. .haltsql-base: an alpine image that installs the static Linux release binary after checking it against SHA256SUMS, with the same fail-closed rules as the action. HALTSQL_RELEASE_BASE_URL points it at an https mirror. .haltsql-check: runs validate, lint (with HALTSQL_FAIL_ON_WARNINGS) and test. It writes haltsql-ci/test.json and a JUnit report (haltsql-ci/junit.xml), so merge requests show per-case results. Denied cases list their reason codes in the JUnit system-out. .haltsql-bundle: builds the bundle with the project URL and commit as its source. It signs the bundle when the masked, protected variable HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY is set and verifies it against HALTSQL_PUBLIC_KEYS. The bundle is kept as a job artifact. Pin the include: to a release tag, never a branch.

Servers with a bundle_source poll a registry for new bundles, so the last CI step is haltsql bundle push. Push only after the bundle is built, signed and verified, and only from the default branch. Use a version that increases. Servers refuse a bundle whose metadata.version is not strictly greater than the one they run (rollback protection). The action's default bundle-version is the commit SHA, which has no order, so set it explicitly when servers poll the registry. Good choices are 1.0.${{ github.run_number }}, a date with the run number such as 2026.11.07.42, or your release tag.

# .github/workflows/policy-publish.yml on: push: branches: [main] permissions: contents: read packages: write # push to ghcr.io jobs: publish: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 environment: policy-signing # holds HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY, requires reviewers steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - id: haltsql uses: HaltSQL/HaltSQL@v0.2.0 with: version: v0.2.0 policies: policies/**/*.yaml suites: tests bundle: "true" bundle-name: prod-policies bundle-version: 1.0.${{ github.run_number }} signing-key: ${{ secrets.HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY }} public-keys: keys/policy-signing.pub - name: Push the bundle env: HALTSQL: ${{ steps.haltsql.outputs.haltsql-path }} BUNDLE: ${{ steps.haltsql.outputs.bundle-path }} REGISTRY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} REF: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/haltsql-policies:prod run: | "$HALTSQL" bundle push --oci "$REF" "$BUNDLE" \ --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub \ --username "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --password-env REGISTRY_PASSWORD --json \ | tee push.json echo "Pinned: $(jq -r .pinned push.json)" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" The repository name in a reference must be lower case. If your owner name has capitals, lower-case it first.
