policy-bundle: extends: .haltsql-bundle needs: [policy-check] variables: HALTSQL_BUNDLE_NAME: prod-policies HALTSQL_BUNDLE_VERSION: "1.0.$CI_PIPELINE_IID" rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH policy-push: extends: .haltsql-base stage: deploy needs: [policy-bundle] # brings haltsql-ci/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle{,.sig} rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH script: - > haltsql bundle push --oci "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/haltsql-policies:prod" haltsql-ci/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub --username "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" --password-env CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD .haltsql-bundle writes haltsql-ci/<HALTSQL_BUNDLE_NAME>.haltsqlbundle and its .sig, and keeps them as job artifacts. The push job picks them up through needs:.

It refuses a bundle that does not load or a malformed signature file. With --public-key, it also refuses a signature that does not verify, so CI never publishes something servers would reject. Passwords and tokens are read from environment variables (--password-env, --token-env) and never appear in arguments or output. It prints the digest-pinned reference (pinned in --json). Deploy that when you want an immutable rollout, and use the tag when servers should follow new versions. The artifact is the layout oras push --artifact-type application/vnd.haltsql.bundle.v1 produces (see OCI artifact layout), so existing oras-based pipelines keep working and either tool can read the other's artifacts. For S3 or HTTPS sources, upload prod.haltsqlbundle.sig before prod.haltsqlbundle, for example with aws s3 cp in that order.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml repos: - repo: https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL rev: v0.2.0 hooks: - id: haltsql-validate - id: haltsql-lint-policy - id: haltsql-test args: [tests] The hooks use the haltsql binary on PATH (language: system): Hook Runs Files haltsql-validate haltsql validate FILE... YAML/JSON under policies/, policy/, haltsql/, tests/, suites/, catalog(s)/ haltsql-lint-policy haltsql lint-policy per changed policy YAML/JSON under policies/ or policy/, excluding suites haltsql-test haltsql test tests (once, not per file) runs when any of those files change If your layout differs, override files: or args:.

The action's shell steps and the GitLab job scripts are tested locally against a locally built binary. The tests make no network calls. dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe test/bundle/action/test_action.sh _build/default/bin/haltsql/main.exe PYTHON=python3 test/bundle/action/test_gitlab.sh _build/default/bin/haltsql/main.exe # needs PyYAML shellcheck -x .github/actions/policy-ci/*.sh test/bundle/action/*.sh These tests cover glob expansion (including **), checksum verification (match, mismatch, unlisted, duplicated), install argument validation, the summary Markdown (exact rows, escaping, denied-case details, truncation), exit codes, fail-on-warnings, the GitHub outputs, bundle build/sign/verify with provenance, that no key is ever logged, and JUnit well-formedness and escaping. The OCI, S3 and HTTPS bundle sources and haltsql bundle push/pull are tested against real servers in Docker (registry:2 with anonymous, htpasswd and token auth via cesanta/docker_auth, MinIO, nginx over HTTPS, and the oras CLI). The tests skip with a message when Docker is unavailable: dune test test/bundle_source # HALTSQL_SKIP_DOCKER=1 runs only the unit tests

A policy says which SQL a caller may run. It is a YAML or JSON document with kind: Policy. Both formats mean exactly the same thing and are validated against the same JSON Schema (haltsql schema export writes it as policy.schema.json). Policies are deny by default: anything not allowed here is denied.

apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: name: analytics-agent owner: data-platform description: Read-only analytics over orders and customers. dialect: postgres search_path: [app] catalog: ./schema.snapshot.json limits: { max_bytes: 16384, max_depth: 64, max_nodes: 20000, max_joins: 8 } statements: allow: [select] require_limit: max: 1000 tenancy: mode: bound keys: tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name, created_at] # email/phone intentionally absent tenant_column: tenant_id app.currencies: columns: "*" # global reference table functions: presets: [aggregates, datetime] allow: [coalesce, lower, upper] allow_explain: false mode: enforce The same policy in JSON: { "apiVersion": "haltsql.dev/v1", "kind": "Policy", "metadata": { "name": "analytics-agent", "owner": "data-platform" }, "search_path": ["app"], "statements": { "allow": ["select"] }, "require_limit": { "max": 1000 }, "tenancy": { "mode": "bound", "keys": { "tenant": "${ctx.tenant_id}" } }, "tables": { "app.orders": { "columns": ["id", "tenant_id", "customer_id", "status", "total_cents", "created_at"], "tenant_column": "tenant_id" }, "app.currencies": { "columns": "*" } }, "functions": { "presets": ["aggregates", "datetime"], "allow": ["coalesce"] }, "mode": "enforce" }

These apply to every HaltSQL document, not only policies. Format comes from the file extension: .yaml/.yml or .json. YAML 1.2 core schema. no, on, yes, and off stay strings, and 012 is not octal. Quote values when in doubt. Unknown keys are errors. A typo such as tenant_colum fails to load instead of silently loosening the policy. Duplicate keys are errors. Custom YAML tags are rejected, and alias expansion and document size are capped. All errors are reported at once, with file, line, column, and key path, for example policy.yaml:14:5: tables."app.orders".tenant_column: unknown column. Placeholders: the only placeholder allowed in a policy is ${ctx.NAME}, filled from the request context at verify time. ${env:...} and ${file:...} are not allowed in policies, so a policy gives the same result on every machine. Version hash. Each loaded policy has a policy_version of the form sha256:<hex>, computed over the normalized policy. The same policy written in YAML or JSON gets the same version.

Names in a policy follow Postgres rules: Unquoted names are folded to lower case: App.Orders means app.orders. To match a name that needs case or special characters, write it with double quotes inside the key, for example 'app."Orders"' in YAML. Unqualified table names are qualified with the first search_path entry.

Key Type Required Default apiVersion string yes none kind string yes none metadata object yes none dialect string no postgres search_path list of strings no [public] catalog string (path) or inline snapshot no none (empty) limits object no see below statements object no { allow: [select] } require_limit object no not required tenancy object no no tenancy keys tables map no {} (nothing readable) functions object no no functions allowed operators object no built-in default list casts object no built-in scalar types deny_casts list, or object no built-in default list allow_explain boolean no false mode string no enforce
Must be haltsql.dev/v1. Documents with a different version are rejected. Every released schema version will keep loading, or fail with a clear migration error.
Must be Policy.

Key Type Required Meaning name string yes Policy name. Tokens in the server config pin to this name; it appears in every verdict. owner string no Team or person responsible. Informational. description string no Free text. Informational.

postgres or a major-specific form such as postgres-17. Only PostgreSQL is supported. HaltSQL parses with the Postgres 17 grammar of its vendored libpg_query; run haltsql version to see the exact version.

The schemas used to resolve unqualified table names, in order, just as Postgres's search_path would. Unqualified names in tables are qualified with the first entry. Set this explicitly. HaltSQL does not read the database's search_path, and the database role that runs the queries should have the same search_path (see defense-in-depth.md). If the two differ, a name could resolve to a different table in HaltSQL than in Postgres. System schemas (pg_catalog, information_schema, pg_toast, and similar) are never readable, even if listed.

Optional schema snapshot: either a path to a snapshot file (relative to the policy file), or the snapshot written inline as an object. The catalog lists the complete set of columns of each table, with types, so that: SELECT * and t.* expand to the real column list (and are denied if that includes a column the policy does not allow); unknown or ambiguous columns can be detected precisely; tenant literals can be type-checked in literal mode. Snapshot format: { "tables": { "app.orders": { "columns": [ { "name": "id", "type": "int8" }, { "name": "tenant_id", "type": "text" }, "status" ] } } } Column entries may be objects with name and optional type, or plain strings. Generate a snapshot from a live database (information_schema) so it includes types; the analyzer only trusts entries that carry column types, because an entry must be the complete column list of the real table. A snapshot whose metadata.authoritative is false is refused, whether it is referenced as a file or written inline. haltsql schema fetch --snapshot-out writes such snapshots from a data catalog's view of the tables, which can lag behind the database; use haltsql schema pull for the policy's catalog (see schema-and-pii.md). Without a catalog, the catalog is empty. HaltSQL never builds one from the column lists in tables, since the real table may have columns the policy leaves out. Consequences without a snapshot: SELECT *, t.* and whole-row references are allowed only on tables with columns: "*"; on any other table they are denied (E_COLUMN_DENIED), with a hint to list the columns; unqualified columns in multi-table queries may be E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED; the hint says to qualify them. The catalog contents are included in policy_version.

Resource limits checked before and during analysis. Exceeding one gives E_LIMIT (or E_JOIN_BUDGET for joins). Key Type Default Meaning max_bytes integer 16384 Maximum SQL length in bytes, checked before parsing. max_depth integer 64 Maximum nesting depth of the parse tree. max_nodes integer 20000 Maximum number of parse-tree nodes. max_joins integer 8 Maximum number of joins in one statement. Omitted keys take their defaults.

statements: allow: [select] # any of: select, insert, update, delete The statement kinds a caller may run. Everything else (DDL, DO, CALL, COPY, SET, LOCK, VACUUM, transaction control, and so on) is always denied with E_STATEMENT_KIND. Write kinds also need per-table writes. Only one statement per request is ever allowed. Write support is limited in 0.0.1; read-only policies are the main target.

require_limit: max: 1000 When set, every SELECT (including each set-operation result) must end with a constant LIMIT n (or FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY) where n <= max. No LIMIT, or LIMIT ALL: E_LIMIT_REQUIRED. n greater than max, or not an integer constant (for example LIMIT $2 or LIMIT (SELECT ...)): E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH.

Declares which context values identify the tenant, and how tenant predicates must be written. The full semantics are in tenancy.md. tenancy: mode: bound # bound | literal keys: tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" # key name -> context field Key Type Default Meaning mode bound or literal bound How the tenant value appears in SQL. keys map of key name to ${ctx.FIELD} none Named tenancy keys and the context field each one reads. Key names use letters, digits, and _. Must not be empty if present. value ${ctx.FIELD} none Shorthand for a single key named tenant: value: ${ctx.tenant_id} equals keys: { tenant: ${ctx.tenant_id} }. Use value or keys, not both. mode: bound (recommended). Tenant predicates compare the tenant column with a parameter placeholder, tenant_id = $1. HaltSQL returns bind_params: [{param: 1, value: <context value>}] and the caller must bind exactly that value when running the query. The model never sees or emits the tenant ID. mode: literal. Tenant predicates compare with a literal, tenant_id = 'acme'. The literal must equal the context value exactly (no trimming or case folding); otherwise the verdict is E_TENANT_MISMATCH. Keys. Each key names one dimension of tenancy and maps to a context field. Most policies have one key. Composite tenancy (for example organization plus workspace) uses several: tenancy: mode: bound keys: org: "${ctx.org_id}" workspace: "${ctx.workspace_id}" If the context value for a key is a list (for example a parent organization and its children), the predicate may match any value in the set; see tenancy.md. A key whose context field is missing at verify time causes E_CONTEXT_MISSING for any query that touches a table using that key.

A map from table name to its rules. Only tables listed here can be read (or written). Views are listed the same way and are treated as opaque relations; HaltSQL does not look inside view definitions. tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, status] tenant_column: tenant_id writes: insert: false update: [status] delete: false Key Type Default Meaning columns list of strings, or "*" required Readable columns. "*" means every column. tenant_column string none Tenant column, for a policy with exactly one tenancy key. tenant_columns map of column to key name none Tenant columns for composite tenancy. writes object no writes Write permissions (see below). columns​ The columns a query may reference anywhere: select list, WHERE, JOIN ... ON, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, function arguments, and * expansion. A reference to any other column is E_COLUMN_DENIED. Whole-row references (t, t.*, row_to_json(t)) are treated as references to every column of the table. "*" allows every column. Use it only for tables with no sensitive data. The tenant column must be in the column list (it is referenced by the tenant predicate). tenant_column / tenant_columns​ A table with a tenant column is tenant-scoped: every occurrence of it in a query must carry a tenant predicate (see tenancy.md). A table with neither key is global and needs no tenant predicate. tenant_column: tenant_id is shorthand for a policy with exactly one tenancy key: the column is bound to that key. tenant_columns maps each tenant column to a key name, for composite tenancy. Every listed column needs its own predicate. tables: app.documents: columns: [id, org_id, workspace_id, title] tenant_columns: org_id: org workspace_id: workspace Use one or the other, not both. Every key name must exist in tenancy.keys. writes​ Write permissions for the table. Enabling a write whose statement kind is not in statements.allow is a load error. Key Type Default Meaning insert boolean false INSERT ... VALUES allowed, with an explicit column list. Every inserted column must be in the table's columns list, so a hidden column (e.g. password_hash) cannot be written either. INSERT ... SELECT and ON CONFLICT are not supported. update list of columns, or "*" not allowed Columns an UPDATE may assign. false means not allowed; true is an error (be explicit). delete boolean false DELETE allowed. A tenant column may not appear in update (load error). Tenant rules for writes: an INSERT must set every tenant column to the tenant value in every row; an UPDATE may never assign a tenant column and needs a tenant predicate; a DELETE needs a tenant predicate. Violations give E_TENANT_WRITE or E_TENANT_MISSING; writes to tables or columns not allowed here give E_WRITE_DENIED.

functions: presets: [aggregates, datetime] allow: [coalesce, lower, upper, app.safe_fn] Key Type Default Meaning allow list of strings [] Function names that may be called, unqualified (lower) or schema-qualified (app.safe_fn). Names must not be quoted. presets list of strings [] Named, built-in groups of functions to include. Every function call, including aggregates, window functions, and set-returning functions in FROM, must be allowed; anything else is E_FUNCTION_DENIED. Names are case-insensitive unless quoted. An unqualified entry such as lower also matches pg_catalog.lower. Built-in functions that run a SQL string (or dump a whole table, schema or database) passed as an argument are always E_FUNCTION_DENIED, even when they are listed in allow: ts_rewrite, ts_stat, query_to_xml*, cursor_to_xml*, table_to_xml*, schema_to_xml*, database_to_xml* and the dblink family. HaltSQL only sees a string literal there, so table, column and tenancy rules could not apply to the SQL they run. Built-in presets. The authoritative lists are in Policy_load.function_presets (lib/load/policy_impl.ml); they may grow in minor releases, but never to include functions with side effects. An unknown preset name is a load error. Preset Contents (0.0.1) aggregates count, sum, avg, min, max, bool_and, bool_or, every, string_agg, array_agg, stddev, stddev_pop, stddev_samp, variance, var_pop, var_samp, percentile_cont, percentile_disc, mode math abs, ceil, ceiling, floor, round, trunc, sign, sqrt, cbrt, power, mod, div, ln, log, log10, exp, pi, degrees, radians string lower, upper, length, char_length, character_length, octet_length, substring, substr, trim, btrim, ltrim, rtrim, replace, concat, concat_ws, left, right, position, strpos, split_part, starts_with, initcap, lpad, rpad, reverse, translate regex regexp_replace, regexp_match, regexp_like, regexp_count, regexp_instr, regexp_substr, regexp_split_to_array. Separate because user-supplied patterns can be slow; enable it knowingly. datetime now, date_trunc, date_part, extract, date_bin, age, make_date, make_time, make_timestamp, make_timestamptz, make_interval, to_char, to_date, to_timestamp, justify_days, justify_hours, justify_interval, isfinite json jsonb_extract_path, jsonb_extract_path_text, json_extract_path, json_extract_path_text, jsonb_array_length, json_array_length, jsonb_typeof, json_typeof, jsonb_build_object, json_build_object, jsonb_build_array, json_build_array, jsonb_agg, json_agg, jsonb_object_agg, json_object_agg, to_jsonb, to_json conditional num_nulls, num_nonnulls window row_number, rank, dense_rank, percent_rank, cume_dist, ntile, lag, lead, first_value, last_value, nth_value row_to_json is intentionally in no preset, because it serializes whole rows. Be careful with to_json/to_jsonb on whole-row arguments; the column rules still apply to them. Never allow functions with side effects or access to the server, for example set_config, nextval, setval, pg_sleep, pg_read_file, lo_import, lo_export, dblink, pg_terminate_backend, query_to_xml, or any function that runs dynamic SQL.

operators: allow: ["=", "<>", "<", "<=", ">", ">=", "+", "-", "*", "/", "||", "~~", "~~*"] # replaces the default list extend: ["<->"] # added to allow (or to the default) The operator symbols a query may use. Any other operator is E_OPERATOR_DENIED. Key Type Meaning allow list of strings Replaces the default list. extend list of strings Added to allow, or to the default list when allow is omitted. The default list (Policy_load.default_operators) in 0.0.1 is: comparison: =, <>, !=, <, >, <=, >= arithmetic (also date and interval arithmetic): +, -, *, /, % string concatenation: || LIKE/ILIKE and POSIX regular expressions: ~~, !~~, ~~*, !~~*, ~, ~*, !~, !~*. LIKE, ILIKE and SIMILAR TO are checked as the operators ~~, ~~* and ~ (and their ! negations), so removing them from operators disables that syntax too. JSON/JSONB: ->, ->>, #>, #>>, @>, <@, ?, ?|, ?& arrays: && (and @>, <@ above) To disallow regular expressions (slow patterns), set allow to the list above without the ~ operators. AND, OR, NOT, IS NULL, IN, BETWEEN, and CASE are syntax, not operators, and are always available.

casts: extend: [inet, app.order_status] # the defaults plus your additions Cast targets are denied by default: x::type, CAST(x AS type) and typed literals (interval '7 days') are allowed only for listed types. A cast runs the target type's input or conversion function, so an unlisted type is an unlisted function call. Anything else gives E_CAST_DENIED. Omitted: the built-in list (Policy_load.default_casts): text, varchar, bpchar, int2, int4, int8, numeric, float4, float8, bool, date, time, timetz, timestamp, timestamptz, interval, uuid, json, jsonb, bytea. allow: replaces the built-in list. extend: adds to it (or to allow). Use the names PostgreSQL's parser produces: INTEGER is int4, BIGINT is int8, BOOLEAN is bool, CHAR is bpchar, DOUBLE PRECISION is float8, DECIMAL is numeric. A bare name matches the type unqualified or pg_catalog.-qualified. A type in any other schema must be listed as schema.type; public.int8 does not match int8. Array casts (::int4[]) are checked by their element type.

deny_casts: extend: [inet] # recommended form: the defaults plus your additions Cast target types that are denied even when casts lists them ('x'::regclass, CAST(... AS regproc)), lower case and unqualified. It is a second guard: extending casts by mistake cannot open the reg* types. A denied cast gives E_CAST_DENIED. Omitted: the built-in default list (Policy_load.default_deny_casts): regclass, regproc, regprocedure, regoper, regoperator, regtype, regconfig, regdictionary, regnamespace, regrole, regcollation, txid_snapshot. The reg* object-identifier types can look up catalog objects by name. { extend: [...] }: the default list plus the given types. A plain list: replaces the default list. Keep the reg* types in it.

false by default. When true, plain EXPLAIN <statement> is allowed if the inner statement would itself be allowed. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and is always denied, as are other EXPLAIN options that execute the query.

Value Behavior enforce (default) Denials set allowed: false and are listed in reasons. shadow allowed is always true; would-be denials are listed in shadow_reasons. Use shadow mode to roll out a new or stricter policy: log the verdicts, review shadow_reasons, then switch to enforce. A shadow policy enforces nothing, so never use it as the only control.

haltsql validate policy.yaml # check one or more documents haltsql convert policy.yaml --to json # YAML -> JSON (lossless) haltsql schema export --out schemas/ # JSON Schemas for editors To get editor autocomplete in VS Code with the YAML extension, add a modeline: # yaml-language-server: $schema=./schemas/policy.schema.json apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy

haltsql-proxy is a PostgreSQL wire-protocol (v3) firewall. Clients (an LLM agent, a BI tool, any libpq/JDBC/psycopg/pgx driver) connect to the proxy as if it were Postgres. The proxy authenticates them, connects to the real database with its own service credentials, and runs every statement through Haltsql.verify under the policy and context bound to the client's identity before forwarding it. Denied statements never reach the database. The library and the HTTP sidecar ask "is this SQL allowed?" and trust the caller to act on the answer. The proxy enforces the answer itself: a client cannot skip verification, choose a looser policy, or pick its tenant.

# 1. A verifier for each proxy user (the password never appears in the config) printf '%s\n' "$AGENT_PASSWORD" | haltsql-proxy scram-verifier # SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:...$...:... # 2. A config (see below), then validate and run it haltsql-proxy validate --config proxy.yaml UPSTREAM_PASSWORD=... haltsql-proxy run --config proxy.yaml # 3. Connect with any driver psql "host=127.0.0.1 port=6432 dbname=app user=analytics-agent sslmode=require"

apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: ProxyConfig listen: 0.0.0.0:6432 tls: # client side TLS (optional) cert: /etc/haltsql/tls.crt key: ${file:/run/secrets/tls.key} # a path or inline PEM both work client_ca: /etc/haltsql/clients-ca.pem client_auth: optional # none | optional | require required: true # refuse plaintext clients (default true) upstream: host: db.internal port: 5432 database: app user: haltsql_service # a read-only role is strongly recommended password: ${env:UPSTREAM_PASSWORD} tls: { mode: verify-full, ca: /etc/haltsql/db-ca.pem } policies: - path: ./policies/analytics-agent.yaml auth: method: scram users: - name: analytics-agent scram_verifier: "SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:...$...:..." policy: analytics-agent # metadata.name of a loaded policy context: { tenant_id: acme } limits: max_connections: 200 max_unauthenticated_per_ip: 20 # per source address, before authentication max_message_bytes: 1048576 idle_timeout_seconds: 300 max_session_lifetime_seconds: 3600 # then FATAL 57P01 at a transaction boundary deny_sqlstate: "42501" audit: sinks: - { type: file, path: /var/log/haltsql/proxy-audit.jsonl } # on_error: fail_closed reload: { watch: true } # also reload on file changes (SIGHUP always works) logging: { level: info }

kind: ProxyConfig, apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1. Loaded with the same rules as every HaltSQL document (YAML 1.2 core schema or JSON, duplicate keys and unknown keys are errors). Strings may use ${env:NAME} and ${file:/path} (relative paths resolve against the config's directory; one trailing newline is trimmed; $${ is a literal ${). Placeholders are not allowed inside inline policies. tls.cert and tls.key accept either a file path or inline PEM: a value that contains -----BEGIN is parsed as PEM, so ${file:...} and ${env:...} placeholders work. Load errors for certificates and keys never echo the configured value, so key material does not end up in logs. Key Default Meaning listen 127.0.0.1:6432 host:port to accept clients on. --listen overrides it. tls.cert, tls.key none PEM server certificate chain and key. Enables SSLRequest upgrades. tls.client_ca none PEM CA bundle for client certificates. Required when client_auth is not none. tls.client_auth none none, optional (verify if presented) or require. tls.required true Refuse clients that do not upgrade to TLS (FATAL 28000). upstream.host, upstream.port -, 5432 The real server. Every resolved address is tried in order. upstream.database, upstream.user required Service credentials. Clients must ask for exactly this database name. upstream.password none For SCRAM-SHA-256, MD5 or cleartext (both only over TLS; see allow_insecure_auth). Omit for trust. upstream.tls.mode disable disable (plaintext), require (encrypted, any certificate accepted) or verify-full (encrypted, certificate chain and host verified). Only verify-full authenticates the database; see Upstream transport security. With verify-full, the host name is checked against DNS SubjectAltName entries only (a certificate that carries the name only in its CN is rejected), and upstream.host must be an IP address or a valid DNS host name (no _); a host the certificate check cannot use is a config error. There is no verify-ca mode. upstream.tls.ca none PEM CA bundle; required for verify-full. upstream.allow_insecure_auth false Allow MD5 password authentication over an unencrypted upstream connection. Off by default: the proxy refuses to answer an MD5 request without TLS. Cleartext passwords are never sent without TLS, whatever this says. upstream.connect_timeout_seconds 10 TCP connect timeout (authentication gets three times this). policies required List of {path: file} or {inline: {...policy...}}. Each is referenced by its metadata.name. auth.method required scram or cert. auth.users[] scram: name, scram_verifier (PostgreSQL's stored format), policy, context. auth.identities[] cert: exactly one of subject_cn or spiffe_id (URI SAN), plus policy, context. limits.max_connections 100 Extra clients get FATAL 53300. Counts every open connection, authenticated or not. limits.max_unauthenticated_per_ip 20 Connections one source address may have open that have not finished authentication. Further ones from that address get FATAL 53300 until one authenticates or closes. 0 disables the per-address limit. See Connection limits. limits.max_message_bytes 1048576 Largest client message; larger is FATAL 08P01. limits.idle_timeout_seconds 0 (off) Close sessions idle this long with nothing in flight (FATAL 57P05). limits.auth_timeout_seconds 30 Startup + authentication must finish within this (FATAL 08006). limits.max_session_lifetime_seconds 3600 A session is ended this long after it authenticated: at its next transaction boundary the client gets FATAL 57P01 and reconnects. 0 disables the limit. See Session lifetime. limits.termination_grace_seconds 30 How long a session that has to end (lifetime, reload) may take to finish its transaction before it is closed anyway (0 to 3600). limits.worker_threads CPUs, 2 to 8 Threads (1 to 64) that run policy verification and audit writes to stdout/file off the event loop, so a slow statement or a slow disk in one session does not stall the others. deny_sqlstate 42501 SQLSTATE of policy denials. allow_transaction_control true Let plain BEGIN/START TRANSACTION [modes], COMMIT, END, ROLLBACK, ABORT through without a policy check, so drivers work outside autocommit. Matching is exact, token by token: comments, quotes, savepoints, AND CHAIN and PREPARE TRANSACTION are not matched and go to the policy. audit.type stdout Single-sink form: stdout, file (with path) or none. audit.on_error, audit.max_buffer_records fail_closed Failure policy of the single sink (see Audit). audit.sinks[] Several sinks (instead of type): stdout, file, s3 and gcs entries with exactly the keys of the server's audit.sinks (audit-sinks.md), plus on_error (fail_closed, buffer or drop) and max_buffer_records (with buffer; default 10000 for stdout/file, 100000 for s3/gcs). elasticsearch and kafka are not supported by the proxy. audit.log_raw_sql false Include the SQL text in audit records (otherwise only its SHA-256). reload.watch false Poll the config file and every file it pulled in (policies, TLS material, ${file:...}) and reload on change. reload.poll_interval_seconds 2 Watch interval (0.1 to 3600). reload.terminate_changed_sessions true After a reload, end the sessions whose credentials, policy, context or upstream it changed (see Hot reload). false: they keep running under the configuration they started with. logging.level info debug, info, warn, error. Logs are JSON lines on stderr. shutdown_grace_seconds 10 On SIGTERM/SIGINT, how long to let sessions finish before closing them. Validation also checks that every user's/identity's context provides every value its policy's tenancy needs, that TLS files parse, that cert auth has tls.client_auth: require, and that names are unique.

SCRAM-SHA-256 (auth.method: scram). The proxy implements the server side of RFC 5802/7677 exactly as PostgreSQL does (mechanism SCRAM-SHA-256, no channel binding). Verifiers use PostgreSQL's stored format, so you can also copy one from pg_authid.rolpassword. Unknown users go through a full fake exchange with a deterministic per-process salt, so user names cannot be probed. Failures are always FATAL 28P01 password authentication failed for user "...". Passwords should be ASCII (SASLprep is the identity for ASCII). Client certificates (auth.method: cert). The TLS handshake verifies the chain against tls.client_ca; the proxy then matches the leaf's subject CN or a spiffe:// URI SAN against auth.identities. The startup user name is not used for authorization. Certificate revocation lists are not checked. The CN is decoded from UTF8String, PrintableString, BMPString or UniversalString; a CN that is a TeletexString, malformed, empty or contains control characters never matches a subject_cn identity (fail closed). Upstream. The proxy authenticates to PostgreSQL with trust, cleartext (only over TLS), MD5 (only over TLS unless upstream.allow_insecure_auth) or SCRAM-SHA-256, and verifies the server's SCRAM signature (mutual authentication). It refuses a server that asks for fewer than 4096 or more than 600000 SCRAM iterations (PostgreSQL's default is 4096). It always sends client_encoding=UTF8, and terminates the session if the server ever reports a different client_encoding or standard_conforming_strings other than on, because the verified bytes must mean the same thing to the server as to the parser. search_path is pinned. The verifier resolves unqualified names against the policy's search_path, so the upstream session has to resolve them the same way. The proxy does not trust the role's or database's default: The upstream startup packet sets search_path to the search_path of the policy the client is bound to, each schema double-quoted, followed by pg_temp (unless the policy places pg_temp itself). A startup-packet setting overrides ALTER ROLE ... SET and ALTER DATABASE ... SET. pg_temp is listed last because PostgreSQL otherwise searches temporary tables first, ahead of every schema the policy names. pg_catalog, when the policy does not list it, is searched first by both PostgreSQL and the verifier. For search_path: [app] the proxy sends "app", "pg_temp". Once the upstream session is ready the proxy runs SHOW search_path and compares the answer, parsed the way PostgreSQL parses it, with what it asked for. Only then does the client see ReadyForQuery; no client statement is forwarded before the check. On a mismatch (a pooler that drops the parameter, a login trigger that changes it) the session is refused with FATAL 08006 and the log line upstream search_path does not match the policy carries both values. PostgreSQL 18 and later report search_path changes as ParameterStatus. A reported value that differs from the pinned one ends the session. A session is bound to one policy for its whole life, so the pinned path always belongs to the policy that verifies its statements. On PostgreSQL 17 and earlier a later change inside the session is not reported to the proxy. A policy cannot allow SET (only select, insert, update and delete exist), which leaves functions: do not put set_config in a policy's functions list. A connection pooler between the proxy and PostgreSQL must run in session mode and pass the search_path startup parameter through; PgBouncer rejects it unless it is tracked or listed in ignore_startup_parameters, and ignoring it makes the check fail, which is the intended outcome.

A connection takes one of the limits.max_connections slots from the moment it is accepted, and may hold it for limits.auth_timeout_seconds without ever sending a byte. Without a second limit, one client opening max_connections sockets would lock everybody else out for as long as it keeps reopening them. limits.max_unauthenticated_per_ip caps how many such not yet authenticated connections a single source address may hold (TLS handshake, startup packet, SCRAM exchange and cancel requests all count). The connection over the cap is answered with FATAL 53300 sorry, too many unauthenticated connections from your address and closed at once; the first, 10th, 100th, ... refusal is logged with the address. A connection stops counting when it authenticates, so the limit does not bound how many sessions an address may have, only how many it may have in the handshake at the same time. The default of 20 is well above what a connection pool opens concurrently (the handshake takes milliseconds), and a fifth of the default max_connections. Choose the value with the network path in mind: clients behind one NAT gateway, or behind a TCP load balancer that does not preserve source addresses, share one address and one budget. What this limit cannot do is stop a flood from many addresses; for that, restrict who can reach the listener (network policy, security groups) and consider a lower auth_timeout_seconds.

The connection from the proxy to PostgreSQL carries every statement, every result row and the service role's login. upstream.tls.mode decides what protects it: Mode Encrypted Server authenticated Protects against disable (default) no no nothing on the network. Acceptable only on a loopback address or a network you fully control. require yes no: any certificate is accepted, self-signed or an attacker's passive eavesdropping. Someone who can redirect or intercept the connection (DNS, ARP, a compromised hop) can still pose as the database, read every statement and result, and answer with data of their choosing. verify-full yes yes: chain to upstream.tls.ca, and the certificate must be for upstream.host eavesdropping and impersonation. Use this for any database that is not on the same host. require here means what sslmode=require means in libpq: encryption without identity. It does not mean "TLS is verified". The mode libpq calls verify-ca (chain checked, host name not) does not exist in the proxy, because a certificate for any other host under the same CA would pass it; use verify-full. The default stays disable so that existing configurations keep working, but the proxy does not stay quiet about it: At start, on reload and in haltsql-proxy validate, disable towards a host that is not localhost, 127.0.0.0/8 or ::1 logs a warning, INSECURE UPSTREAM TRANSPORT, with the host and the setting to change. require towards such a host logs an info line saying the certificate is not verified. Host names other than localhost are not resolved for this check: a name that points at the local machine still gets the warning. MD5 authentication is refused without TLS. An MD5 response can be replayed against the server by anyone who also learns the stored hash, and a captured exchange can be brute-forced offline. If the server asks for MD5 on a plaintext connection the proxy does not answer; sessions fail with FATAL 08006 and the log says upstream requested MD5 password authentication over an unencrypted connection; refusing to send it. Fix it by enabling upstream.tls, or by moving the role to SCRAM (password_encryption = scram-sha-256, then set the password again), or, if you accept the risk (a loopback sidecar, for example), with upstream.allow_insecure_auth: true, which itself logs a warning. A cleartext password is never sent without TLS. SCRAM-SHA-256 is safe to run over plaintext as far as the password goes (the proxy also verifies the server's proof), but it does not protect the statements and results that follow.

Message Behaviour SSLRequest S + TLS handshake when tls is configured, else N. Bytes pipelined after the request are a protocol violation (CVE-2021-23214). GSSENCRequest Always refused with N. StartupMessage Protocol 3.x only; a newer minor version or _pq_.* options get NegotiateProtocolVersion (3.0). Needs user; database must equal upstream.database; any replication parameter is refused; only application_name is forwarded. options and every other parameter are ignored, so clients cannot set GUCs such as search_path (the proxy sets it itself, from the policy). CancelRequest Proxy-issued (pid, key) pairs are random and map to the upstream backend; the key is compared in constant time; the request is forwarded over a fresh upstream connection (TLS if configured). Query (simple) Verified as a whole. Denied if the verdict denies, or if it needs bound tenancy parameters (they cannot be bound in the simple protocol: use prepared statements). Parse Verified; the verdict is remembered per statement name. A named statement that already exists is refused (42P05). Bind The statement's verdict is looked up. Every $n in verdict.bind_params is replaced with the session's context value (text format), whatever the client sent; binary format for those parameters is refused. Unknown statements are refused (26000). Execute Audited (one execute record per message, see Audit), then relayed. If the record cannot be written under fail_closed, the Execute is refused (58030) and does not reach the database. Describe, Close, Flush, Sync, Terminate Validated and relayed. FunctionCall Refused in-band (deny_sqlstate, PROXY_FUNCTION_CALL). CopyData/CopyDone/CopyFail, unknown types, malformed or oversized messages FATAL 08P01 and the connection is closed. COPY statements are already denied by the policy (E_STATEMENT_KIND); a server that enters COPY mode anyway ends the session. The SQL forwarded upstream is always byte-for-byte the SQL that was verified; only Bind parameter values are rewritten.

A denial looks exactly like a PostgreSQL error, so every driver surfaces it normally, and the connection stays usable: Field Value S, V ERROR C deny_sqlstate (default 42501, insufficient_privilege) M haltsql: query denied by policy "<name>": <first reason> D HaltSQL reasons: E_COLUMN_DENIED, ... (reason codes, see reason-codes.md) H the first reason's hint, when it has one Denials raised by the proxy itself use these pseudo-codes in D: E_PARAM_UNBOUND (bound tenancy over the simple protocol, binary or missing tenancy parameter), PROXY_STATEMENT_EXISTS (42P05), PROXY_STATEMENT_UNKNOWN (26000), PROXY_FUNCTION_CALL. Inside a transaction a denial aborts the transaction, exactly like a real permission error. In the extended protocol, messages after a denied one are discarded until Sync, as PostgreSQL does. How ordering is preserved. Clients pipeline. Instead of writing the error directly (which could overtake responses to earlier messages), the proxy replaces the denied message with a statement that cannot parse (haltsql_deny_<random>), so the server's own error handling produces an error at exactly the right position and skips to Sync. The proxy swaps that error for the denial. The random token is per denial and never reaches the client. Statement bookkeeping. A Parse takes effect only when the server answers ParseComplete; after an error the server ignores later messages until Sync. The proxy therefore commits a statement's verdict only on ParseComplete, drops pending ones on ErrorResponse, and makes a Bind that depends on an unresolved Parse from an earlier Sync segment wait for it. A missing entry always denies, so bookkeeping can only err towards denial; a client cannot make the proxy apply one statement's tenancy positions to another statement.

One JSON object per verified statement and per execution, per sink, hash-chained exactly like the server's audit log (same Audit_chain code, same sink implementations): {"ts":"2026-11-07T22:45:17.297Z","event":"statement","session":"49fd05aacd53", "user":"agent","policy":"proxy-test","policy_version":"sha256:...", "protocol":"extended","allowed":false,"reasons":["E_COLUMN_DENIED"], "shadow_reasons":[],"sql_sha256":"...","fingerprint":"...", "tables":["app.users"],"bind_params":[1],"statement":"", "prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ L), where L is the compact JSON of the record without hash; the first record of a chain has prev_hash = 64 zeros. bind_params lists parameter numbers only, never values. Proxy-level denials (bind, parse, function_call events) carry reasons and message. Verify any of these outputs with haltsql audit verify. What is recorded when. Event Written Meaning statement, protocol: simple per Query The verdict, and (when allowed) the one execution of that statement. statement, protocol: extended per Parse The verdict of a prepared statement. Preparing is not executing. execute per Execute the proxy forwards One execution of a prepared statement. A statement prepared once and run 1000 times leaves one statement record and 1000 execute records. bind, parse, function_call per proxy-level denial See above. {"ts":"2026-11-07T22:45:17.301Z","event":"execute","session":"49fd05aacd53", "user":"agent","policy":"proxy-test","policy_version":"sha256:...", "protocol":"extended","portal":"","statement":"s1","sql_sha256":"...", "fingerprint":"...","max_rows":0,"prev_hash":"<64 hex>","hash":"<64 hex>"} statement, sql_sha256 and fingerprint are those of the statement record of the same session that prepared it (join on session and sql_sha256). portal is the portal name ("" for the unnamed portal) and max_rows the row limit of the Execute message (0: all rows). Parameter values are never recorded, and there is no option to record them. statement, sql_sha256 and fingerprint are null for a portal the proxy did not see being bound, which is a cursor opened with SQL DECLARE. An execute record means the Execute was forwarded: like a statement record, it does not say whether the database then raised an error. Messages the proxy discards after a denial (up to Sync) leave no execute record.

audit: sinks: - type: file path: /var/log/haltsql/proxy-audit.jsonl on_error: fail_closed - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 prefix: haltsql/proxy/ spool_dir: /var/lib/haltsql/proxy-spool object_lock: { mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: 365 } on_error: buffer log_raw_sql: false Sink Chain stdout Starts at genesis in every process. Operational logs go to stderr, so stdout carries only audit records (verify a combined log with --mixed). file Appends (created 0640). The chain continues from the file's last record across restarts; a last line that is not a sealed record stops the proxy from starting (rotate the file). s3, gcs The server's object sinks: batches, ordered create-only uploads, optional spool, one chain across objects (and across restarts with spool_dir). Same keys, credentials and object names as in audit-sinks.md. The single-sink form (audit: {type: file, path: ..., on_error: ...}) is still accepted; type: none disables auditing. Two sinks may not share a file or a spool directory. Sinks are process-wide: every config generation writes into the same chains.

Mode While a sink cannot be written Recovery fail_closed (default) The statement is refused: ERROR, SQLSTATE 58030 (io_error), message haltsql: the audit log could not be written; statement refused, detail HaltSQL reasons: PROXY_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE. No statement reaches the database without its audit record. Denials are refused the same way. stdout/file: every statement retries the write, so the proxy recovers with the sink. s3/gcs: writes are refused until a background upload retry succeeds. buffer Records are queued in memory (in order; sealed when written, so the chain stays intact) and statements keep flowing, up to max_buffer_records. At the bound, statements are refused with 58030. Buffered records are written before the next record and every second, in order. drop The record is discarded, counted and logged at warn level (audit sink write failed; record dropped). Statements keep flowing. Dropped records are never sealed, so the chain has no gap marker: use drop only where availability matters more than completeness. Records written after recovery continue the chain. The refusal is in-band like a policy denial: the connection stays usable and, inside a transaction, the transaction is aborted. 58030 was chosen because it is PostgreSQL's code for an I/O failure outside the statement itself; it is distinct from deny_sqlstate, so clients can retry it. Every write error is logged to stderr (audit sink write failed; ..., with the sink name and the OS error); a write that fails after part of a line reached a file makes the next record start on a new line, so the fragment shows up as one invalid line in haltsql audit verify rather than corrupting the next record.

The proxy is a single event loop. Verification and writes to stdout/file sinks run on a small thread pool (limits.worker_threads) so that neither a large statement nor a slow disk, a full pipe or a stalled network mount stops other sessions. This does not weaken the failure policy: a session still waits for its record to be written (or refused) before the statement is forwarded, and within a session messages are still handled strictly one after the other. Audit writes are serialized process-wide and served in arrival order, and the timestamp is taken when a record's turn comes, so in every sink the chain order, the timestamp order and the order in which statements were accepted agree. While a write is blocked, statements wait for it (none is forwarded unaudited); at shutdown a write that is still blocked after 5 seconds is abandoned with an error log instead of hanging the exit.

Operational logs (stderr, JSON lines) record connections, authentication results, denials, audit failures, reloads and errors. Neither logs nor audit records ever contain passwords, verifiers, SCRAM messages, keys, S3 secrets or bind values, and SQL text only with log_raw_sql: true. On shutdown the stopped log line carries per-sink audit counters (records_written, write_failures, dropped, buffered, uploads) and the reload counters.

SIGHUP reloads the config file and everything it pulls in (policies, TLS certificates and keys, ${env:...}/${file:...} placeholders), with the same --listen/--log-level overrides. With reload.watch: true the proxy also polls those files every reload.poll_interval_seconds and reloads when one changes (write files atomically, e.g. write then rename). New connections use the new configuration (policies, users, identities, contexts, upstream, limits, deny_sqlstate, TLS certificates, log_raw_sql, log level). Sessions the reload changed are ended, the others keep running. A session is never switched to another policy while it is open (its upstream search_path was pinned for the policy it started with); it is told to reconnect instead. A session is ended when the new configuration no longer has its user or certificate identity, has another SCRAM verifier for its user (a rotated or revoked password), or, for certificate sessions, another tls.client_ca bundle, binds it to another policy, or the policy's content changed (its policy_version differs), or its context changed, points at another upstream (host, port, database, user, password, TLS mode or CA), or changes allow_transaction_control. An idle session gets FATAL 57P01 (admin_shutdown) at once. A session inside a transaction or with statements in flight keeps its old policy until the transaction ends, then gets the error after the last ReadyForQuery; after limits.termination_grace_seconds it is closed regardless (the upstream rolls the open transaction back). Until then its statements are still verified, under the old policy, and audited with the old policy_version. 57P01 is what PostgreSQL sends on pg_terminate_backend: drivers and pools drop the connection and open a new one. Set reload.terminate_changed_sessions: false to keep the earlier behaviour (sessions run under their snapshot until they close or reach limits.max_session_lifetime_seconds). Other changes (limits, deny_sqlstate, log_raw_sql, TLS server certificate) apply to new connections only. Any error keeps the last good configuration: a parse or validation error, an unreadable policy or certificate, unusable TLS material. The error is logged (config reload failed; keeping the current configuration) and the proxy keeps serving. A watched file that stays broken is reported once, and retried when it changes again. The listen address and the audit sinks need a restart: a reload that changes them is applied without that part, with a warning. Each reload logs trigger (sighup or watch), generation (1 at start, +1 per successful reload), reloads, reload_failures, and how many authenticated sessions there were and how many are sessions_ending. Session logs carry config_generation. Cancel requests reach the upstream their session runs on, across reloads. kill -HUP "$(pidof haltsql-proxy)" # {"level":"info","msg":"config reloaded","trigger":"sighup","policies":["analytics-agent"], # "sessions":3,"sessions_ending":3,"generation":2,"reloads":1,"reload_failures":0}

Not everything a session depends on is in the configuration (a role's privileges, the upstream's own state), and a reload may be missed. Every session is therefore ended limits.max_session_lifetime_seconds after it authenticated, the same way as after a reload: FATAL 57P01 at the next transaction boundary, or after limits.termination_grace_seconds. The default of one hour is in the range connection pools already use for their own maximum connection age (HikariCP 30 minutes, PgBouncer server_lifetime one hour), so a pool in front of the proxy sees nothing unusual; 0 turns the limit off. limits.idle_timeout_seconds is separate and off by default.

haltsql-proxy run -c FILE [--listen HOST:PORT] [--log-level L] haltsql-proxy validate -c FILE [--json] prints the effective config with secrets redacted. Exit 0 valid, 1 invalid, 2 unreadable. haltsql-proxy scram-verifier [--iterations N] reads a password from stdin. SIGTERM/SIGINT: stop accepting, drain for shutdown_grace_seconds, close the rest, flush the audit sinks (final S3/GCS uploads), exit 0. SIGHUP: reload (see Hot reload). haltsql audit verify FILE|DIR|s3://... checks the audit chains (audit-verify.md). Give the upstream user the least privilege that works (for a read-only agent: SELECT on the policy's tables only, default_transaction_read_only), and keep row-level security on as a second layer (see defense-in-depth.md).

No SCRAM channel binding (SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS), no GSSAPI, no CRL/OCSP for client certificates. COPY, the fastpath function-call protocol, replication connections, LISTEN-style asynchronous workflows that need non-SELECT statements, and savepoints (unless the policy allows them, which v1 policies cannot) are not available through the proxy. No metrics endpoint yet: audit and reload counters are in the logs, and the audit stream itself. The upstream search_path is confirmed once, at session start. PostgreSQL 17 and earlier do not report later changes, so a policy must not allow set_config (a policy cannot allow SET itself). limits.max_unauthenticated_per_ip sees the address of the TCP peer. The PROXY protocol is not supported, so behind a load balancer that hides client addresses every client shares one budget. Client options/GUC startup parameters are ignored, not forwarded.

make -C lab up # Postgres 17 on localhost:5417 dune test test/proxy test/proxy/test_pgwire_unit.ml covers the codecs, SCRAM (RFC 7677 vector), config validation, enforcement decisions and statement bookkeeping. test/proxy/test_proxy_session.ml runs the engine in-process against a fake PostgreSQL backend (fake_pg.ml) and needs nothing else: search_path pinning and the refusal on a mismatch, the worker pool, pipelined message order, execute audit records, the lifetime limit, which sessions a reload ends and when, the MD5-without-TLS refusal and the per-address limit on unauthenticated connections. test/proxy/test_proxy_integration.ml starts the real binary four times (SCRAM + optional TLS, client-cert auth, tight limits, unavailable upstream TLS) against database haltsql_proxy_test and drives it with psycopg 3 from lab/.venv and a raw protocol client: allowed and denied queries, tenancy overwrite (the client asks for another tenant and gets only its own rows), pipelining, transactions, cancel (plain and TLS), COPY, auth failures, protocol violations, limits, audit content, log hygiene and graceful shutdown. It skips when Postgres or the venv is unavailable. test/proxy/test_proxy_audit.ml runs the binary against database haltsql_audit_proxy: chained file records (also across a restart), stdout records in a combined log verified with haltsql audit verify --mixed, a failing file sink (a FIFO whose reader goes away, so writes get EPIPE) with fail_closed (statements refused with 58030, then recovery), buffer (refusal at the bound, in-order drain) and drop, SIGHUP and reload.watch (new sessions get the new policy, existing ones keep theirs with reload.terminate_changed_sessions: false, a broken config is kept out), and an S3 sink writing to a real MinIO container (host port 16002) whose objects then verify. test/proxy/test_proxy_audit_unit.ml covers the audit/reload config sections and the file sink's chain. lab/proxy runs a haltlab scenario through the proxy and checks parity with the CLI, row-for-row equality with directly bound execution (while the client always sends another tenant's id), and honeytokens: cd lab && .venv/bin/python -m proxy run proxy/scenarios/proxy-smoke.yaml
This walks through installing the CLI, writing a small policy, and checking a few queries an LLM might produce.
documents.s: Quickstart: your first deny in five minutes

documents.t: Pick one: # Release binary (Linux amd64 shown; also linux-arm64 and darwin-arm64) curl -LO https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/releases/download/v0.0.1/haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz tar -xzf haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH="$PWD/haltsql-v0.0.1-linux-amd64:$PATH" # Or from source with opam (OCaml 5.1+) opam pin add haltsql https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL.git # Or Docker (the CLI is in the image too) alias haltsql='docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w --entrypoint haltsql ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1' Check it works: haltsql version

Save this as policy.yaml. It lets an analytics agent read two tables of a multi-tenant app, hides customer email and phone, and requires a tenant filter and a LIMIT. apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: name: analytics-agent search_path: [app] statements: { allow: [select] } require_limit: { max: 1000 } tenancy: mode: bound keys: tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id functions: presets: [aggregates] allow: [date_trunc] Validate it: haltsql validate policy.yaml validate exits 0 and prints nothing alarming if the policy is well formed. Typos are errors, not warnings: try changing tenant_column to tenant_colum and run it again.

In bound mode the model writes $1 where the tenant ID goes, and your application binds the real value. The model never sees it. haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ --sql 'SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 GROUP BY status LIMIT 100' echo "exit: $?" The exit code is 0. Add --json to see the full verdict, including what to bind: "bind_params": [ { "param": 1, "value": "acme" } ] Your application now runs that exact SQL string with $1 = 'acme'.

Drop the tenant filter, the kind of query a prompt-injected model might write: haltsql verify --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' --json \ --sql 'SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders LIMIT 100' echo "exit: $?" The exit code is 1 and the verdict contains: { "allowed": false, "reasons": [ { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "message": "...", "rule": "...", "hint": "..." } ] } A few more to try, each denied for a different reason: SQL Expected code SELECT email FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 E_COLUMN_DENIED SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 E_LIMIT_REQUIRED SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR true LIMIT 10 E_TENANT_MISSING SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10; DROP TABLE orders E_MULTI_STATEMENT SELECT pg_sleep(10) E_FUNCTION_DENIED SELECT * FROM pg_catalog.pg_user LIMIT 1 E_TABLE_DENIED DELETE FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 E_STATEMENT_KIND

explain prints the same verdict for people: the statement kind, the tables and columns it found, each reason, and a hint. haltsql explain --policy policy.yaml --context '{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ --sql 'SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10' Here customers has no tenant predicate of its own. The fix is to add AND c.tenant_id = $1. See tenancy.md for why the filter on orders does not cover customers.

Write test cases next to the policy so a policy change cannot silently loosen it. Save as policy.test.yaml: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: TestSuite metadata: { name: analytics-agent } policy: ./policy.yaml defaults: context: { tenant_id: acme } cases: - name: filtered aggregate is allowed sql: SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 GROUP BY status LIMIT 100 expect: allow bind: [{ param: 1, value: acme }] - name: missing tenant filter is denied sql: SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 100 expect: deny codes: [E_TENANT_MISSING] haltsql test policy.test.yaml

Wire HaltSQL into your agent with the HTTP sidecar and the integration snippets. Read the policy reference and the reason codes. Set up the database-side controls. HaltSQL is one layer, not the only one.

Every denial carries one or more reasons, each with a stable code. Codes are part of HaltSQL's public API: they are never renamed or reused, and new codes may be added in minor releases. Clients should match on code and treat any code they do not recognize as a denial. The examples below assume this policy unless noted otherwise: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: { name: example } search_path: [app] statements: { allow: [select] } require_limit: { max: 1000 } limits: { max_joins: 4 } tenancy: { mode: bound, keys: { tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" } } tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name] tenant_column: tenant_id app.currencies: columns: [code, name] functions: { presets: [aggregates] } and the context {"tenant_id": "acme"}. The "Fix" column is written for the agent that produced the SQL. The hint field of each reason carries a query-specific version of the same advice.

Code Meaning E_PARSE SQL did not parse E_EMPTY No statement E_LIMIT Byte, depth, or node-count limit exceeded E_MULTI_STATEMENT More than one statement E_STATEMENT_KIND Statement kind not allowed E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE Write inside a CTE E_TABLE_DENIED Relation not in the allowlist E_COLUMN_DENIED Column not allowed E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED Ambiguous or unknown column E_FUNCTION_DENIED Function not in the allowlist E_OPERATOR_DENIED Operator not in the allowlist E_CAST_DENIED Cast to a type that is not allowed E_TENANT_MISSING Tenant-scoped relation without a provable tenant predicate E_TENANT_MISMATCH Tenant literal differs from the context value E_TENANT_WRITE Write sets or changes a tenant column incorrectly E_CONTEXT_MISSING A context value the policy needs was not supplied E_PARAM_UNBOUND A $n parameter HaltSQL cannot bind E_LIMIT_REQUIRED LIMIT missing E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH LIMIT too large or not a constant E_LOCKING_CLAUSE FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE E_SELECT_INTO SELECT ... INTO E_JOIN_BUDGET More joins than limits.max_joins E_WRITE_DENIED Write to a table or column the policy does not allow E_UNSUPPORTED Syntax HaltSQL does not analyze E_INTERNAL Analyzer bug; fails closed E_EXTERNAL_POLICY Denied by the external policy engine (OPA)

The SQL is not valid PostgreSQL. loc points at the parser's error position when it is known. Input containing a NUL byte is also rejected with this code. SELEC id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: correct the syntax. Send only SQL, with no Markdown fences or prose around it.
The input contains no statement (empty, whitespace, or only comments). -- just a comment Fix: send exactly one SQL statement.

The SQL exceeds limits.max_bytes, limits.max_depth, or limits.max_nodes. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id IN (1, 2, 3, /* ...20,000 more... */) LIMIT 10 Fix: make the query smaller: fewer literals in IN lists, less nesting, fewer subqueries.

More than one statement was sent. HaltSQL verifies exactly one statement per request. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10; DROP TABLE orders Fix: send a single statement, with no semicolon-separated extras.

The statement kind is not in statements.allow. DDL, DO, CALL, COPY, SET, LOCK, VACUUM, LISTEN, transaction control, and similar statements are always denied. Also used for EXPLAIN when allow_explain is false, and for EXPLAIN ANALYZE. DELETE FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 Fix: use only the allowed statement kinds (usually a single SELECT).

A WITH clause contains INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, which would modify data even though the outer statement is a SELECT. WITH d AS (DELETE FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM d LIMIT 10 Fix: remove the data-modifying CTE. Read-only CTEs (WITH x AS (SELECT ...)) are fine.
The query uses FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, or FOR KEY SHARE, which take row locks. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE Fix: remove the locking clause.
SELECT ... INTO new_table creates a table. SELECT id INTO copy_of_orders FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: remove INTO; return the rows instead.

The statement has more joins than limits.max_joins. Every join counts, including comma-separated FROM lists and CROSS JOIN. SELECT o.id FROM orders o, customers c WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND c.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: join with an explicit condition (JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id) and use fewer joins.

A relation is not listed in tables. System schemas (pg_catalog, information_schema, and so on) are always denied. Catalog-qualified names (db.schema.table) are denied too. SELECT usename FROM pg_catalog.pg_user LIMIT 10 Fix: query only the tables listed in the policy. Do not query system catalogs.

A column that the policy does not allow is referenced anywhere in the query, or * / a whole-row reference expands to include one. SELECT email FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 SELECT * FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 -- if the table has columns beyond id, tenant_id, name Fix: reference only allowed columns, and list them explicitly instead of using *.

A column reference is ambiguous (it exists in more than one relation in scope) or does not exist in any relation in scope. HaltSQL denies rather than guess. SELECT id FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND c.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: qualify every column with its table alias (o.id), and check the column name against the schema.

A function is not in functions.allow or an enabled preset. This includes aggregates, window functions, and set-returning functions in FROM. Functions that run a SQL string themselves (ts_rewrite, ts_stat, query_to_xml, dblink, ...) are denied even when allowlisted (rule functions.dynamic_sql). SELECT pg_sleep(10) SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', 'globex', false) Fix: use only allowed functions. Do not call functions that change settings, sleep, read files, or access other databases.

An operator is not in the policy's operator list. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (id # 1) = 0 LIMIT 10 -- # (bitwise XOR) is not in the default list Fix: use an allowed operator, or rewrite the condition with comparison and arithmetic operators.

A cast targets a type that is not in the policy's casts allowlist (casts are denied by default), or a type in deny_casts, such as the reg* object-identifier types that look up catalog objects by name. SELECT 'app.orders'::regclass Fix: remove the cast. There is no need to reference database objects by OID.

A tenant-scoped relation occurs in a scope that does not prove it is filtered to the caller's tenant. See tenancy.md for the exact rules. Common causes: no filter; the filter is inside an OR, NOT, or CASE; the filter is only in an outer query; a UNION branch has no filter; the filter is in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN for the preserved side. SELECT id FROM orders LIMIT 10 SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR status = 'open' LIMIT 10 SELECT id FROM (SELECT id, tenant_id FROM orders) o WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: add alias.tenant_column = $1 as a top-level AND condition in the WHERE clause of the same query level as the table (or in the ON clause of an inner join that attaches it), for every occurrence of every tenant-scoped table, including inside CTEs, subqueries, and each UNION branch.

In literal mode, the tenant literal does not equal the context value. Also used in bound mode when a tenant predicate uses a literal instead of a parameter. Context {"tenant_id": "acme"}, literal mode: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'globex' LIMIT 10 Fix: in literal mode, use exactly the tenant value you were given. In bound mode, use the placeholder $1 instead of a literal.

A write would set or change a tenant column incorrectly: an INSERT that does not set the tenant column to the tenant value in every row, or an UPDATE that assigns a tenant column. (INSERT ... SELECT is denied outright as E_UNSUPPORTED.) Only possible when writes are enabled. UPDATE orders SET tenant_id = 'globex' WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = 7 Fix: never assign a tenant column in UPDATE; in INSERT, set it to $1 (bound mode) or the context value (literal mode) in every row.

The policy needs a context value (for example tenant_id) that the request did not supply. This is a caller integration error, not a problem with the SQL. Context {}: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix (application): always pass the context fields named in the policy's tenancy.keys, taken from the authenticated session. An agent cannot fix this.

The query uses a $n placeholder that HaltSQL cannot bind: a parameter that is not a tenant predicate value, a tenant parameter that is also used outside its tenant predicate (for example cast with $1::float8, which would change how PostgreSQL types the bound tenant value), a parameter used for two different tenancy keys, or any parameter in literal mode. HaltSQL only allows placeholders whose value it supplies in bind_params, so the caller never has to bind something the model chose. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = $2 LIMIT 10 Fix: use $n only for tenant values; write other values as literals (status = 'open').
require_limit is set and the query has no LIMIT (or uses LIMIT ALL). SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 Fix: add LIMIT n with n no larger than the policy maximum.

The LIMIT is larger than require_limit.max, or is not an integer constant. SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 100000 Fix: use a constant LIMIT no larger than the maximum. Paginate with OFFSET or keyset conditions if you need more rows.

A write targets a table without the matching writes permission, an UPDATE assigns a column not in writes.update, an INSERT has no explicit column list, or an INSERT names a column that is not in the table's columns list. Only possible when the statement kind is allowed. UPDATE orders SET total_cents = 0 WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = 7 -- writes.update: [status] Fix: write only to tables and columns the policy allows.

The query uses syntax that HaltSQL does not analyze, for example TABLESAMPLE, XMLTABLE, JSON_TABLE, ROWS FROM, or another construct the converter does not map. HaltSQL denies anything it cannot fully analyze. WITH RECURSIVE is always E_UNSUPPORTED: a recursive CTE can produce unbounded rows, and an outer LIMIT does not bound the work done by an aggregate, ORDER BY or DISTINCT over it. SELECT id FROM orders TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (10) WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 Fix: rewrite the query with common SQL constructs. If you believe the construct is safe and should be supported, open a feature request.

The analyzer hit an unexpected condition (a bug). The query is denied. Operators should alert on any occurrence of this code. Fix (agent): try a simpler query. Fix (operator): file a bug with the SQL, policy, and HaltSQL version. If the input looks like a bypass attempt, report it privately per SECURITY.md.

Only haltsql-server emits this code, and only when the optional opa check is configured. HaltSQL allowed the query, then Open Policy Agent denied it, or OPA could not be asked (timeout, error, undefined decision) and opa.on_error is deny. The rule is always opa.decision; the message carries OPA's reasons (sanitized) or says the external check failed. In a shadow-mode policy the reason appears in shadow_reasons and the query stays allowed. OPA can never turn a HaltSQL denial into an allow, so this code never appears next to an allow. Fix (agent): the query is outside what the organization's OPA policy allows for this caller; do not retry it unchanged. Fix (operator): read the OPA decision log and the haltsql_opa_decisions_total metric; see opa.md.

haltsql rls generate turns a HaltSQL policy into PostgreSQL DDL that enforces the same rules inside the database: a dedicated role, column-level grants, and row-level security (RLS) policies keyed on transaction-local settings. haltsql rls check connects to a live database and reports where it has drifted from the policy. These are layers 1 and 2 of defense in depth. If HaltSQL has a bug, or the application forgets to call it, the database still enforces the policy's tables, columns and tenant isolation.
documents.s: Generating row-level security from a policy

documents.t: haltsql rls generate -p policy.yaml --catalog catalog.json -o rls.sql psql "$ADMIN_DSN" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f rls.sql # run as an admin or the table owner PGPASSWORD=... haltsql rls check -p policy.yaml --catalog catalog.json \ --dsn "postgres://admin@db:5432/app?sslmode=verify-full"

The output runs in one transaction (BEGIN ... COMMIT) and works on PostgreSQL 13 to 17. It is idempotent: running it again brings the database back to the same state. It is deterministic: the same policy and options always produce the same bytes, so you can commit it and review diffs. The header records the policy name and its sha256: version. Policy Generated SQL (always) A DO block creates <role> with NOLOGIN NOBYPASSRLS if it does not exist. If the role exists and is SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS, the script raises an error and stops, because RLS would not apply to it. every schema in tables: REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES and ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA s, REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA s, then GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA s. columns: [a, b] GRANT SELECT (a, b) ON TABLE ... columns: "*" GRANT SELECT ON TABLE ... writes.insert: true GRANT INSERT (<readable columns>) (or table-level for "*"), plus USAGE on the table's owned (serial) sequences. writes.update: [c, ...] / "*" GRANT UPDATE (c, ...) / GRANT UPDATE ON TABLE writes.delete: true GRANT DELETE ON TABLE ... tenant-scoped table ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (and FORCE with --force-rls). Then one haltsql_tenant_<cmd> policy per allowed command. Writes are granted only when the policy's statements.allow also includes that statement kind. SELECT is always granted on the readable columns, because UPDATE ... WHERE, DELETE ... WHERE and RETURNING need it. The per-command policies are: Policy Clause haltsql_tenant_select FOR SELECT ... USING (pred) haltsql_tenant_insert FOR INSERT ... WITH CHECK (pred) haltsql_tenant_update FOR UPDATE ... USING (pred) WITH CHECK (pred) haltsql_tenant_delete FOR DELETE ... USING (pred) All four names are dropped with DROP POLICY IF EXISTS before the allowed ones are created, so a command the policy no longer allows loses its policy. With --drop-existing, every policy on each managed tenant table is dropped first. Use it when other permissive policies exist: PostgreSQL ORs permissive policies together, so another policy that applies to the role widens what it can see. Global tables (no tenant_column(s)) get grants only, with no RLS.

Each tenant column is compared with a custom setting named <prefix>.<context_field>. The prefix comes from --setting-prefix (default haltsql). The context field comes from the policy's tenancy keys, so tenant: ${ctx.tenant_id} uses haltsql.tenant_id: tenant_id = NULLIF(pg_catalog.current_setting('haltsql.tenant_id', true), '') When a table has several tenant columns (a composite key), the comparisons are joined with AND. A missing setting matches no rows. current_setting(name, true) returns NULL when the setting was never set, and col = NULL is never true. Once a session has used the setting, PostgreSQL returns '' (not NULL) after the transaction that set it ends. NULLIF(..., '') turns that '' back into NULL, so a later transaction that forgets to set it still sees nothing. The integration test checks both cases. Set-valued context. For a context field that carries several tenants (for example a parent org and its children, { "tenant_ids": ["acme", "acme-eu"] }), pass --set-field tenant_ids. The setting then holds the values joined with commas, and the predicate becomes: tenant_id = ANY (pg_catalog.array_remove( pg_catalog.string_to_array(NULLIF(pg_catalog.current_setting('haltsql.tenant_ids', true), ''), ','), '')) Empty elements are ignored, and an empty list matches nothing. Tenant values must not contain a comma. A set field is never guessed. Without --set-field, a comma-joined value is compared as one string and matches nothing, which fails closed. The generator warns when a field name ends in _ids and has no --set-field. Column types. The setting is text. When the catalog says a tenant column is not text (--catalog, or the policy's own catalog:), the setting is cast to that type, for example ...::int8 or ...::int8[] for sets. A value that does not parse raises an error (22P02), which also fails closed. Without type information the setting is compared as text and the generator prints a warning. If the column is actually bigint, CREATE POLICY fails with "operator does not exist", so the mistake is loud. Array-typed tenant columns and type names with quotes are rejected.

Every identifier is quoted exactly as PostgreSQL's quote_ident() would quote it. A name stays bare only if it is lower-case ASCII letters, digits and underscores, and is not a reserved, column-name or type/function-name keyword of the PostgreSQL 17 grammar. So app."Customers", "TenantId", "user", "order" and "select" are quoted, while name and action are not. Embedded double quotes are doubled. String literals double single quotes, and use E'...' when the value contains a backslash. DO bodies use a dollar-quote tag that does not occur in the body.

The generated header documents this. In the same transaction as the SQL that HaltSQL allowed, the application sets each setting from the same context values it passed to HaltSQL. These come from its authenticated session, never from the model or the prompt. Then it switches to the role: BEGIN; SELECT pg_catalog.set_config('haltsql.tenant_id', $1, true); -- $1 = ctx.tenant_id SET LOCAL ROLE haltsql_agent; <the exact SQL HaltSQL allowed, binding verdict.bind_params> COMMIT; set_config(name, value, true) is transaction-local, like SET LOCAL. Pass the value as a bind parameter. SET LOCAL haltsql.tenant_id = 'acme' works too, but the value must then be written as a correctly quoted SQL literal. For set fields: set_config('haltsql.tenant_ids', array_to_string($1::text[], ','), true). Do not use session-level SET or set_config(..., false). A pooled connection would carry the tenant into the next request. HaltSQL denies SET, set_config() and RESET in agent SQL, so the model cannot change these settings. The login role the application uses must be able to SET ROLE to the agent role (GRANT haltsql_agent TO app_login;). The generated role is NOLOGIN.

Option Default Meaning -p, --policy FILE (required) Policy file. --catalog FILE policy's catalog: Snapshot used for tenant column types. --role ROLE haltsql_agent Role the grants and policies are for. public, none, current_user and similar, and names starting with pg_, are refused. --setting-prefix P haltsql Setting namespace. Use dot-separated names of letters, digits and underscores. --set-field FIELD none Context field holding a set (repeatable). Must be a tenancy context field of the policy. --owner-role ROLE none Run the table DDL under SET LOCAL ROLE ROLE, the role that owns the tables. Only owners may enable RLS and create policies. Role creation still runs as the invoking user. --force-rls off FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY: the table owner is subject to RLS too. With no policy for the owner, the owner then sees no rows. --drop-existing off Drop every existing policy on managed tenant tables first. -o, --output FILE stdout Write the SQL to a file. --json off Print the plan as JSON (tables, grants, predicates, settings, warnings) with the SQL, or with output when -o is given. Exit codes: 0 success, 2 usage error, unloadable policy or catalog, or invalid option. Warnings go to stderr.
