PGPASSWORD=... haltsql rls check -p policy.yaml --dsn postgres://admin@db/app [--role ...] [--json] Pass the same --role, --setting-prefix, --set-field, --catalog and --force-rls that you used to generate. The check runs in a READ ONLY transaction that is rolled back, and it only reads the system catalogs and the has_*_privilege functions. Privileges are the role's effective privileges, so grants to PUBLIC and to roles it is a member of count too. Kind Severity Meaning role_missing critical The role does not exist. role_bypasses_rls critical The role is SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS. role_can_login warning The role can log in directly. schema_missing / table_missing / column_missing warning Something the policy names does not exist. missing_grant warning The database grants less than the policy (fails closed). over_broad_grant critical Schema CREATE; table-level SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE where the policy lists columns; extra columns; DELETE/TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER not allowed; any privilege on a table outside the policy. rls_disabled critical A tenant-scoped table has RLS off. rls_not_forced warning --force-rls was requested, but the table is not FORCEd. role_owns_table critical The role owns a tenant table, so RLS does not apply to it. policy_missing / policy_mismatch critical A haltsql_tenant_* policy is absent, or has the wrong command, roles, or permissive flag, or a different USING/WITH CHECK expression. unexpected_policy warning A haltsql_tenant_* policy exists for a command the policy does not allow. foreign_policy critical Another permissive policy applies to the role (directly, through membership, or to PUBLIC) and widens what it can see. The expression comparison is a heuristic over pg_get_expr output. Each tenant column and its setting literal must appear, with exactly one current_setting per column. Nothing that could widen a conjunction may appear (OR, NOT, IS, CASE, or an extra true). Exit codes: 0 no drift, 1 drift, 2 usage, load or connection error.

--dsn (or HALTSQL_DSN) takes postgres://user[:password]@host[:port]/db?sslmode=...&connect_timeout=N. Prefer PGPASSWORD over a password in the URL, because command lines are visible to other users. Defaults follow libpq: localhost, port 5432, user $PGUSER or $USER, database equal to the user name, and sslmode=prefer. HaltSQL ships its own small client instead of pgx, because pgx cannot do SCRAM-SHA-256, the default since PostgreSQL 14. The client supports: SCRAM-SHA-256. The server's signature is verified in constant time, and a server that skips the final SCRAM step is rejected. MD5. Cleartext passwords, only over TLS. sslmode=disable|prefer|require|verify-full. verify-ca is treated as verify-full, which uses the system trust store and checks the host name. Passwords never appear in output or error messages. The DSN is always shown redacted.

Policy names are fixed per table (haltsql_tenant_<cmd>). Generating for a second role over the same tables replaces the first role's policies. Use one agent role per database, or one role per policy over disjoint tables. RLS is enforced on tables and partitioned tables. Views run with their owner's privileges unless created with security_invoker (PostgreSQL 15+), so do not list views as tenant-scoped tables. REVOKE and GRANT only touch the role named. Grants to PUBLIC (for example functions and the public schema on PostgreSQL 14 and older) are not changed. rls check reports table privileges that reach the role through PUBLIC. Function privileges, statement_timeout and other role settings are out of scope. See defense in depth.

test/rlsgen/golden/*.sql: golden output for test/fixtures/policies/ saas, composite, hierarchical (with --set-field tenant_ids), writes and mixed_case, plus options.sql, which uses every option with a quoted role name. Every golden file must parse with the bundled PostgreSQL 17 parser. To accept an intended change: dune build @test/rlsgen/runtest --auto-promote. test/rlsgen/t_integration.ml: runs against make -C lab up, or HALTSQL_TEST_PG_DSN. It creates haltsql_rls_test, loads lab/schemas/saas_shared.sql and applies the generated SQL twice. Then, as the role, it checks the following: each tenant sees only its own rows; a missing or reset setting sees nothing; set fields work; denied columns and tables raise 42501; inserts for another tenant and moving a row to another tenant fail; other tenants' rows cannot be updated or deleted. rls check must report no drift, and then exactly the drift the test injects. The test drops its database and roles afterwards, and it is skipped with a message when Postgres is not reachable.

Three commands take you from a live database to a reviewable policy: # 1. Snapshot the schema (typed, complete column lists). PGPASSWORD=... haltsql schema pull --dsn postgres://ro@db.internal:5432/app \ --schema app -o policies/catalog.json # 2. Import PII classifications from your data catalog (one or more tools). haltsql schema import --from dbt target/manifest.json -o policies/pii.dbt.json haltsql schema import --from datahub datahub_export.json -o policies/pii.datahub.json # 3. Draft a starter policy, then review and lint it. haltsql policy draft --catalog policies/catalog.json \ --pii policies/pii.dbt.json --pii policies/pii.datahub.json \ --tenant-column tenant_id --schema app -o policies/agent.yaml haltsql lint-policy policies/agent.yaml haltsql schema fetch reads the labels of step 2 from a live data catalog API instead of an export file; see below. All three exit 0 on success, 1 when the result fails validation, and 2 on usage errors, unreadable input or connection failures. --json prints a machine-readable summary when -o is given. Every command has --help with examples.
documents.s: Catalog snapshots, PII metadata and starter policies

documents.t: Connects to PostgreSQL and writes a catalog snapshot (kind: Catalog, see policy-reference.md). Option Meaning --dsn DSN Connection string, URL or keyword form. Also read from HALTSQL_DSN. --schema S Only this schema; repeatable. Default: every schema except pg_catalog, information_schema, pg_toast* and pg_temp_*. -o FILE Write the snapshot to FILE (atomically). Default: stdout. --timeout SECONDS Connection timeout (default 10). The query itself runs with statement_timeout = 120s. What is captured. Every relation a query can name in FROM: tables, partitioned tables, partitions, views, materialized views, foreign tables and sequences. Each has its complete column list in position order, with the type as lower(format_type(atttypid, atttypmod)) (bigint, character(2), numeric(10,2), timestamp with time zone, text[]). Dropped columns are left out. Relations are sorted by schema and name (byte order), so repeated pulls of an unchanged database produce identical files that diff cleanly. metadata.relations records each relation's kind; the policy drafter uses it. Names are stored exactly as Postgres stores them. A name that is not a plain lower-case identifier is double-quoted in the table key, for example "app.\"Mixed Case\"", so it loads back unchanged. Why pg_catalog, not information_schema.columns. information_schema.columns only shows columns the connecting role has a privilege on. A snapshot made by a restricted role would then list fewer columns than the real table, and the analyzer trusts typed snapshot entries as complete (that is how SELECT * is expanded). pg_attribute always lists every column, so the snapshot is complete whatever the role's grants are. Sequences and partitions are included for the same reason: the analyzer's search_path shadowing check assumes it knows every relation in a schema. Safety. The session starts with default_transaction_read_only=on, and the introspection runs in a REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction that is always rolled back. Use a role with no write privileges anyway. The password is never printed, written to the snapshot, or included in error messages (they show postgres://user@host:port/db?sslmode=...). Prefer PGPASSWORD or HALTSQL_DSN over a password on the command line, where it is visible in the process list. The output is loaded with the catalog loader before it is written. A pull that finds no relations exits 1. Connection strings. URL form postgres://user:pass@host:port/db?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ca.pem (percent-encoding decoded, IPv6 hosts in brackets) or keyword form host=db port=5432 user=ro dbname=app sslmode=require. Missing fields come from PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGDATABASE, PGPASSWORD, PGSSLMODE and PGSSLROOTCERT. Supported parameters: host, hostaddr, port, user, password, dbname, sslmode, sslrootcert, connect_timeout, application_name. Any other parameter is an error, so a typo such as sslmod= cannot silently turn TLS off. A host starting with / is a Unix-socket directory. sslmode Behaviour disable Plaintext. prefer (allow) TLS if the server offers it, else plaintext. The default for loopback hosts and Unix sockets. require TLS required, certificate not checked (libpq semantics). The default for every other host. verify-ca TLS required; the chain must verify against sslrootcert, or the system CAs. verify-full As verify-ca, and the certificate must match the host name (or IP). Use this across networks. Note that HaltSQL's default for remote hosts (require) is stricter than libpq's (prefer). Authentication. SCRAM-SHA-256 (the server's signature is verified, and a server that skips that step is refused), MD5, and trust. Cleartext password authentication is refused unless the connection uses TLS or goes to a loopback host. Kerberos, GSSAPI, SSPI and SCRAM channel binding (-PLUS) are not supported. The client is a small built-in implementation of the PostgreSQL v3 protocol (Haltsql_catalog_tools.Pg_wire), because pgx supports neither SCRAM nor TLS.

HaltSQL verifies SQL against the schema the policy describes. It never looks at the database, so a policy that has fallen behind the schema gives verdicts about a database that no longer exists. schema check compares the two: PGPASSWORD=... haltsql schema check -p policy.yaml --dsn postgres://ro@db:5432/app haltsql schema check -p policy.yaml --snapshot catalog.json --strict --json Code Severity Meaning E_DRIFT_CATALOG_STALE error The policy's catalog: entry lists other columns than the table has. SELECT * is expanded against that entry, so a column added since the snapshot would be read unchecked. Re-run schema pull. E_DRIFT_TABLE_MISSING error A policy table does not exist. E_DRIFT_COLUMN_MISSING error An allowed, tenant or writable column does not exist. E_DRIFT_SHADOWED error A relation with the same name exists in a schema that comes earlier in search_path; the unqualified name reaches it, not the policy table. W_DRIFT_VIEW warning A policy table is a view, materialized view or foreign table. HaltSQL does not see its definition; tenant and column rules apply to its output only. W_DRIFT_NO_CATALOG warning The policy has no catalog: entry for the table. W_DRIFT_SCHEMA_NOT_PULLED warning The snapshot does not cover a policy schema, so its tables were not checked. Exit status is 1 when there are errors (with --strict, also on warnings). Run it in CI after every migration and before every policy release; it is the check that keeps "the policy says" and "the database is" the same thing.

Normalizes the PII classifications of a data catalog export into a PII manifest: { "metadata": { "source": "dbt", "file": "manifest.json", "generated_by": "haltsql schema import" }, "tables": { "app.customers": { "columns": { "email": { "classifications": ["pii"], "source": "dbt" }, "ssn": { "classifications": ["classification=confidential", "gdpr"], "source": "dbt" } } } } } Option Meaning --from TOOL dbt, datahub, unity, atlan or collibra. FILE The export (JSON). -o FILE Write the manifest to FILE. Default: stdout. --pii-tag TERM A tag/classification term that marks PII; repeatable. Replaces the defaults. --pii-term TERM A business-glossary term that marks PII; repeatable. Replaces the defaults. Default terms for both lists: pii, sensitive, confidential, restricted, gdpr, phi, pci, personal, email, phone, ssn, secret. Matching. Labels and terms are split into lower-case words on every non-alphanumeric character and on camelCase boundaries. A term matches when its words appear consecutively in the label: pii matches contains_pii, urn:li:tag:PII and pii_email, but not piiset; credit card matches is_credit_card_number. A single-word term of three or more letters also matches the acronym of a multi-word label (Personally Identifiable Information matches pii). Key/value metadata becomes key (for true values) or key=value labels; false, null, no, 0 and empty values do not count. The manifest records the matching labels as the tool shows them, without URN prefixes. Matching errs towards flagging: a false positive only removes a column from the draft, which you can add back after review. A file in which the importer finds no column metadata at all exits 1 (it is probably the wrong --from).

Tool Accepted input Labels used dbt target/manifest.json (models, seeds, snapshots, sources; tests are ignored) column tags, meta, config.tags, config.meta, policy_tags; nested meta such as {governance: {sensitivity: restricted}}. The table is schema plus alias, identifier or name. dbt target/catalog.json column comment, matched word by word, recorded as comment:<term>. DataHub file-sink exports (MCE snapshots, MCPs with aspect.json or a JSON-string aspect.value) and GraphQL dataset responses urn:li:tag:* tags and urn:li:glossaryTerm:* terms (plus their name/properties.name) on schemaMetadata and editableSchemaMetadata fields. The table is the last two dot-separated parts of the dataset URN name; v2 field paths are reduced to the last name. Unity Catalog information_schema.column_tags rows (JSON array, {"column_tags": [...]}, or a SQL Statement Execution API result), or REST table JSON (one table, a list, or {"tables": [...]}) tag_name and tag_name=tag_value; REST column tags as a map or a list of {key, value}. The catalog name is ignored. Atlan asset search results ({"entities": [...]}, a list, or {"entity": ...}) of Column assets classifications/atlanTags (typeName, displayName, tagName), classificationNames, glossary meanings (displayText) and meaningNames. The table is tableName/viewName/materialisedViewName with schemaName, else the end of qualifiedName. Collibra asset exports (a list, {"results": [...]} or {"assets": [...]}) of Column assets attributes whose type name mentions classification, sensitivity, privacy, confidentiality, personal/PII, security (as a list of {type: {name}, value} or a map); tags; classificationMatches/dataClassifications that are not REJECTED; relations to Business Terms. The column is identified by fullName (db>schema>table>column, or dotted). Atlan classification typeNames are often opaque hashes; export with display names (displayName) so they can be matched. Sample exports for every tool, based on the lab/schemas/saas_shared.sql schema, are in examples/metadata/.

Reads the same PII labels as schema import straight from a data catalog's API over HTTPS, so the manifest does not depend on someone exporting a file: export OPENMETADATA_TOKEN=... # never on the command line haltsql schema pull --dsn "$DATABASE_URL" --schema app -o policies/catalog.json haltsql schema fetch --from openmetadata --url https://om.example.com/api \ --service prod_pg --database app --schema app -o policies/pii.om.json haltsql policy draft --catalog policies/catalog.json --pii policies/pii.om.json \ --tenant-column tenant_id --schema app -o policies/agent.yaml The manifest is the same format as schema import's, with metadata: {source: PROVIDER, url: URL, generated_by: "haltsql schema fetch"} (the URL never carries credentials). Exit codes are those of schema import: 0 on success, 1 when the catalog returns no column metadata, 2 on usage errors and network or HTTP failures.

A data catalog is a good source of labels (tags, classifications, glossary terms). A stale or missing label can only make HaltSQL exclude too little, which the column-name heuristics and review mitigate, and matching errs towards flagging. A data catalog is never trusted for structure. HaltSQL's analyzer treats a typed catalog snapshot as the complete column list of every table (to expand SELECT *) and as the complete list of relations in each schema (to rule out search_path shadowing). A catalog crawler that has not yet seen ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN ssn text would turn that trust into a leak. So there are two ways to use schema fetch: Authoritative mode (recommended). Structure from haltsql schema pull against Postgres, labels from haltsql schema fetch, as in the example above. The draft references the pulled snapshot with catalog:, and SELECT * is expanded against the real columns (and denied when it would read an excluded one). Catalog-only mode (no database access). --snapshot-out FILE also writes the tables and columns the catalog knows as a non-authoritative snapshot: every column untyped, metadata.authoritative: false, metadata.source: "haltsql schema fetch". haltsql policy draft --catalog accepts it to choose the column lists, but the draft has no catalog: key and a header comment saying why. SELECT *, t.* and whole-row references therefore stay denied (E_COLUMN_DENIED), and queries must name the allowed columns. The policy loader (catalog: as a file or inline, haltsql validate, the server, bundles) refuses a non-authoritative snapshot, with an error telling you to use haltsql schema pull. Switch to authoritative mode later by pulling a snapshot and redrafting.
documents.s: Security model: labels are trusted, structure never is

documents.t: Option Meaning --from PROVIDER The data catalog (see the status table below). --url URL Base URL of the catalog API. https only (http is accepted for loopback hosts); a path prefix such as https://datahub.example.com/gms is kept; no credentials, query or fragment. --token-env VAR Environment variable that holds the API token. Default: the provider's (for example OPENMETADATA_TOKEN). If the default variable is unset and there is no --token-file, requests are unauthenticated (with a warning). A --token-env you name explicitly must be set. --token-file FILE Read the token from FILE (surrounding whitespace removed). Warns if the file is readable by other users. --ca-file PEM Trust only the CA certificates in this PEM file (private CA). Default: the system trust store. --service NAME Provider-specific scope: OpenMetadata database service, DataHub platform instance, Unity Catalog catalog. --database NAME Database name as the catalog records it. --schema S Only this schema; repeatable. Default: all. -o FILE Write the manifest to FILE (atomically). Default: stdout. --snapshot-out FILE Also write the non-authoritative snapshot (catalog-only mode). --pii-tag TERM, --pii-term TERM As for schema import. --timeout SECONDS Timeout of each HTTP request (default 30). --max-pages N Fail after N pages of one listing (default 1000), so a misbehaving server cannot page forever. A repeated page cursor is also an error. --json Machine-readable summary (with -o): output, source, url, scanned and PII column counts, tables, requests, snapshot, warnings. Token handling. There is deliberately no option that takes the token itself: it would be visible in shell history and in the process list. The token is sent only as an Authorization: Bearer header, only to the --url origin (redirects are not followed), and is never printed, written to the manifest, or included in an error message. Error messages name the method, path and HTTP status (GET /api/v1/tables: HTTP 401) but never include response bodies. Responses are capped at 32 MiB.

Provider --from Default token variable Status providers are added by their own PRs Coming soon (not yet validated against a live instance): Atlan, Collibra, dbt Cloud, Unity Catalog. The offline schema import --from atlan|collibra file importers (and --from dbt for manifest.json) remain available. Unity Catalog live sync is on hold because the open-source Unity Catalog server (v0.7.0, the newest image) has no column-tag API. Its ColumnInfo has no tags field, column tags are silently dropped on create, PATCH /tables returns 405, and the tag endpoints return 404. A live provider therefore cannot be validated against a runnable instance. Databricks-hosted Unity Catalog column tags are still supported offline through schema import --from unity, using information_schema.column_tags rows or table JSON with column tags.

Generates a starter policy from a snapshot and any number of PII manifests (merged). Option Meaning --catalog FILE Snapshot from schema pull (required), or a non-authoritative snapshot from schema fetch --snapshot-out (the draft then has no catalog:; see catalog-only mode). --pii FILE PII manifest; repeatable. --tenant-column COL Tenant column (required). Every table that has it is tenant-scoped. --tenancy-key KEY Tenancy key name (default tenant). --context-field FIELD Context field read by ${ctx.FIELD} (default tenant_id). --schema S Only this schema; repeatable. Also becomes search_path. Default: all schemas in the snapshot. -o FILE Output file. Default: stdout. --name NAME metadata.name (default: the output file name without extension). --require-limit N require_limit.max (default 1000). --no-name-heuristics Do not exclude columns by name. --name-pattern WORD Column-name words that mark PII; repeatable, replaces the defaults (email, phone, mobile, ssn, password, passwd, secret, token, api_key, apikey, iban, card, dob, birth, address, ip). --include-partitions Also list partitions (default: only their parents). --catalog-ref PATH Value of catalog: (default: the snapshot path relative to the output file). The draft: lists every table, partitioned table, view, materialized view and foreign table in scope with an explicit column list that leaves out every column flagged by a manifest or by the name heuristics. A comment above each table says what was left out and why, for example # excluded ssn (dbt+unity: gdpr, pii; name matches "ssn"); sets tenant_column on tables that have the tenant column and marks the others # GLOBAL: no tenant_id column. The tenant column itself is never excluded (tenant predicates must reference it); a comment says so if it was flagged; skips partitions, sequences, and tables whose every column is excluded, listed under # Not drafted:; uses statements: {allow: [select]}, bound tenancy, require_limit: {max: 1000}, the aggregates, math, string and datetime presets, mode: enforce and a catalog: reference to the snapshot, so SELECT * is expanded against the real columns and denied when it would read an excluded one. From a non-authoritative snapshot (schema fetch --snapshot-out) there is no catalog: reference, and SELECT * is always denied. The draft is loaded with the policy loader (including the check that every table and column exists in the referenced catalog) before it is written; if it does not load, nothing is written and the command exits 1. Names from the catalog and manifests are quoted as needed, and control characters in comments are replaced, so a hostile column name cannot inject YAML. Review before use. A draft is a starting point, not a policy: remove the tables and columns the agent does not need; check every GLOBAL table: if it holds tenant data under another column name, add the right tenant_column (or tenant_columns) by hand; data that is sensitive but untagged in your catalog is only caught if its name matches a heuristic; re-pull the snapshot and re-run haltsql lint-policy when the schema changes.

The commands are thin wrappers over the haltsql.catalog_tools library: Pg_dsn (connection strings), Pg_wire (protocol client), Scram, Schema_pull, Snapshot, Pii (manifest and matcher), Pii_import and Policy_draft. schema fetch uses the separate haltsql.catalog_fetch library (it adds the HTTPS client): Fetch_client (endpoint checks, bearer auth, bounded pagination), Provider (the signature each data catalog implements) and Catalog_fetch (provider registry, import, non-authoritative snapshots).
github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/clients/go/haltsql is a client for the HTTP sidecar that uses only the standard library (net/http, database/sql). Go 1.21 or newer. Source: clients/go/haltsql.
go get github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/clients/go/haltsql

hc, err := haltsql.New("http://127.0.0.1:8080", haltsql.WithToken(os.Getenv("HALTSQL_TOKEN")), // pinned to one policy on the server haltsql.WithTimeout(2*time.Second)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } verdict, err := hc.Verify(ctx, "SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50", haltsql.Context{"tenant_id": session.TenantID}) // from the session, never the prompt if err != nil { return err // fail closed: do not run the query } if !verdict.Allowed { return deny(verdict.Reasons) // Code, Message, Hint for the agent } Run SQL only when err == nil && verdict.Allowed.

GuardedQueryTx / GuardedExecTx verify the SQL and, only if it is allowed, run exactly that string in a transaction that uses the policy's search path, binding the verdict's bind params as $1..$n. They take a *sql.DB or a *sql.Conn (anything with BeginTx): import ( "github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/clients/go/haltsql" _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib" ) db, _ := sql.Open("pgx", os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")) var ids []int64 verdict, err := haltsql.GuardedQueryTx(ctx, hc, db, sqlFromModel, haltsql.Context{"tenant_id": session.TenantID}, func(rows *sql.Rows) error { // called inside the transaction for rows.Next() { var id int64 if err := rows.Scan(&id); err != nil { return err } ids = append(ids, id) } return nil }, haltsql.OnVerdict(func(v *haltsql.Verdict) { audit(v.Policy.Version, v.Fingerprint, v.Allowed) })) var denied *haltsql.DeniedError switch { case errors.As(err, &denied): return deny(denied.Verdict.Reasons) // nothing was sent to Postgres case err != nil: return err // sidecar error or database error; the transaction was rolled back } res, verdict, err := haltsql.GuardedExecTx(ctx, hc, db, writeFromModel, vctx) // a write policy On one connection they send: BeginTx, read-only when verdict.StatementKind is select; SELECT set_config(name, value, true) for each entry of haltsql.TxSettings(map[string]string{...}), in name order (for example "app.tenant_id" for row-level security, or "statement_timeout"); SELECT set_config('search_path', ..., true) with verdict.Policy.SearchPath, each schema quoted as an identifier. This is the pin: the verified orders is the policy's orders whatever the role's or the database's default search path is. It is applied last, so a search_path in TxSettings does not override it, and it is transaction-local, so the session's own search path is back afterwards; the verified string, unchanged; Commit, or Rollback on any error. A denial, a shadow would-deny or a HaltSQL error returns before a transaction is opened. A verdict without Policy.SearchPath (an engine older than the field) still runs, without step 3. GuardedQueryTx hands the rows to a function instead of returning them: a *sql.Rows cannot be read after its transaction has ended, and the guard must end the transaction it opened. Read the rows inside the function; an error it returns rolls the transaction back and is returned to you unchanged.

GuardedQuery and GuardedExec are the low-level forms. They verify and then make one QueryContext / ExecContext call on any database/sql handle (*sql.DB, *sql.Tx, *sql.Conn); GuardedQuery returns the *sql.Rows. They do not pin the search path and open no transaction. Use them only when one of these holds: the session already uses the policy's search path: you set it on the connection (search_path=app in the pgx connection string), the role or the database; or the SQL names every table with its schema (app.orders). Otherwise a default such as ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path = public, app can make a verified orders read public.orders. They are also the forms to use inside a *sql.Tx you manage yourself; pin the search path there with SELECT set_config('search_path', $1, true) and verdict.SearchPathSetting(). Passing TxSettings to them is a usage error. With pgx's database/sql driver: a scalar bind param is a Go string; pgx encodes it into the parameter's inferred type, so a tenant id binds into text, bigint or uuid columns (tested against Postgres 17 with a bigint tenant column); a set-valued bind param (hierarchical tenants, org_id = ANY($1)) is a []string, sent as a Postgres array. For drivers that cannot encode []string (for example lib/pq), pass haltsql.ArrayLiteralArgs() to bind sets as {"a","b"} literals. To bind manually: verdict.Args() returns []any in $1..$n order (or verdict.ArgsArrayLiteral()); both return an error unless the verdict is an allow with contiguous, unique placeholders. haltsql.PGArrayLiteral encodes a []string.
documents.s: GuardedQuery / GuardedExec: one statement, no pin

documents.t: Verify returns a verdict only for a strictly validated HTTP 200 body. Every other outcome is an *haltsql.Error with a Kind: Kind When KindHTTP Non-200 status. Status and Code (UNAUTHORIZED, FORBIDDEN, AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, ... or HTTP_<status>). Redirects are never followed. KindTimeout An attempt exceeded the timeout (after retries). KindTransport Connection or TLS error, or the caller's context was canceled. KindProtocol Body is not JSON, a required field is missing or mistyped, allowed is true while reasons is not empty, the body is too large, or sql_sha256 does not equal the SHA-256 of the SQL that was sent. KindUsage Bad options or arguments (float/bool context values, invalid UTF-8 SQL, a token or request id with control characters). The Guarded* functions additionally return *haltsql.DeniedError for a policy denial. Helpers: haltsql.IsDenied(err), haltsql.IsKind(err, k). Every error type's Allowed() returns false. Unknown verdict fields are ignored (compatibility rules); unknown reason codes are kept as strings. The Guarded* functions return a *DeniedError for SQL that a mode: shadow policy would deny, unless you pass haltsql.AllowShadow() (for a shadow rollout). Search path. The verdict holds only under the policy's search path (verdict.Policy.SearchPath). GuardedQueryTx and GuardedExecTx set it for the transaction that runs the SQL, as the Python guard, the MCP server and haltsql-proxy do. GuardedQuery and GuardedExec run one statement on your connection and do not change session settings: with them, configure the connection or role with that search_path, or have the model write schema-qualified names (when that is acceptable).

Option Default Meaning WithToken(t) none Bearer token for /v1/*. Never included in errors. WithTimeout(d) 5s Per-attempt timeout. WithRetries(n, base, max) 2, 100ms, 2s Retries on 503, connection errors and timeouts; exponential backoff with full jitter; max also caps Retry-After. WithHTTPClient(c) new client (http.DefaultTransport) Custom transport, proxy or TLS. Copied; redirects are disabled on the copy. WithTLSConfig(cfg) system roots TLS for an https sidecar: RootCAs for a private CA, Certificates for mutual TLS. Cloned onto a copy of http.DefaultTransport; refuses InsecureSkipVerify. Apply after WithHTTPClient if you use both. WithMaxResponseBytes(n) 8 MiB Response size cap. WithoutSQLHashCheck() check on Disable the sql_sha256 check. Per call: WithPolicy(name), WithRequestID(id) (at most 200 printable ASCII characters, else a KindUsage error before anything is sent). Cancel with the ctx argument; a canceled context is not retried. Every request has a deadline (the per-attempt timeout, or the caller's ctx if it is sooner) and carries User-Agent: haltsql-client-go/<Version>. The worst case for one Verify is about (retries + 1) * timeout plus the backoff delays. Only 503, connection errors and timeouts are retried (Ready never is); POST /v1/verify has no side effects, so retrying it is safe.

Certificate verification uses the system roots by default. For a private CA and a client certificate: caPEM, _ := os.ReadFile("/etc/haltsql/ca.crt") roots := x509.NewCertPool() roots.AppendCertsFromPEM(caPEM) clientCert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("/etc/haltsql/client.crt", "/etc/haltsql/client.key") if err != nil { ... } hc, err := haltsql.New("https://haltsql.internal:8443", haltsql.WithToken(os.Getenv("HALTSQL_TOKEN")), haltsql.WithTLSConfig(&tls.Config{ RootCAs: roots, Certificates: []tls.Certificate{clientCert}, // mTLS MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12, })) An untrusted certificate or a host-name mismatch is a KindTransport error.

A *Client is safe for concurrent use. Create one per sidecar and share it: the underlying http.Transport keeps connections alive, and the SDK always drains and closes response bodies so they can be reused. The token is only placed in the Authorization header. It is not in any Error message (transport errors include the URL, which cannot carry credentials: New rejects a URL with user info). Other endpoints: Health(ctx), Ready(ctx) (a 503 returns Ready: false and is not retried), Policies(ctx).

cd clients/go/haltsql go vet ./... && go test -race ./... Tests use httptest and replay real haltsql-server responses from testdata/vectors.json, plus a recording database/sql driver for the guard. pgx integration tests live in a separate module so the SDK stays dependency-free. They need Postgres (make -C lab up; HALTSQL_PG* variables override the defaults), create and drop the database haltsql_polyglot_go, and skip cleanly when Postgres is unreachable. With HALTSQL_REQUIRE_POSTGRES=1 (set in CI) unreachable is a failure instead: cd clients/go/pgxtest go test ./...

com.haltsql:haltsql-client is a client for the HTTP sidecar for Java 17+. It uses java.net.http and Jackson (jackson-databind), and its JDBC helper needs only java.sql at compile time, with PgJDBC at runtime. Source: clients/java.
<dependency> <groupId>com.haltsql</groupId> <artifactId>haltsql-client</artifactId> <version>0.0.1</version> </dependency>

HaltSQLClient haltsql = HaltSQLClient.builder("http://127.0.0.1:8080") .token(System.getenv("HALTSQL_TOKEN")) // pinned to one policy on the server .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); Verdict v = haltsql.verify( "SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50", Map.of("tenant_id", session.tenantId())); // from the session, never the prompt if (!v.allowed()) { return deny(v.reasons()); // code(), message(), hint() for the agent } verify returns only for a strictly validated HTTP 200 body and otherwise throws the checked HaltSQLException, so a failure can never be read as an allow.

HaltSQL verifies SQL with PostgreSQL's own $1, $2, ... placeholders, but JDBC uses ?. PgJDBC does not understand $n in a PreparedStatement: it would send the statement with zero parameters and the server rejects it. And preferQueryMode does not change placeholder parsing. JdbcGuard solves this without changing what runs: It replaces each $n that is real code (not inside a string, quoted identifier, dollar-quoted string, or comment) with ?. PgJDBC rewrites each ? back to $1, $2, ... in order before sending the query. So when the verified SQL uses its placeholders in textual order ($1 then $2, each once), the server receives the verified string byte for byte. The test suite proves this against Postgres with current_query(). If placeholders repeat or appear out of order (for example JOIN c ON c.tenant_id = $2 WHERE o.tenant_id = $1), each occurrence gets its own ? bound to the right value. The server receives the verified statement with renumbered placeholders and identical values in identical positions. Call requireByteIdenticalSql() to refuse these instead. Values are bound with setObject(i, value, Types.OTHER): PgJDBC sends them with an unspecified type and the server infers it from the column, so a tenant id binds into text, bigint or uuid columns. A set (hierarchical tenants, org_id = ANY($1)) is bound as a Postgres array literal. The translation fails closed (HaltSQLException, kind USAGE) on SQL it cannot handle with certainty: any ?, { or } character (PgJDBC treats them as placeholders or JDBC escapes, even the ? jsonb operators), unterminated quotes or comments, and placeholders glued to identifier characters. It also refuses any driver other than PgJDBC, and checks that the SQL uses exactly the placeholders the verdict binds. JdbcGuard guard = new JdbcGuard(haltsql) .onVerdict(v -> audit.log(v.policy().version(), v.fingerprint(), v.allowed())); try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) { List<Long> ids = guard.queryInTransaction(conn, sqlFromModel, Map.of("tenant_id", session.tenantId()), rs -> { // called inside the transaction List<Long> out = new ArrayList<>(); while (rs.next()) out.add(rs.getLong(1)); return out; }); } catch (HaltSQLDeniedException e) { return deny(e.verdict().reasons()); // nothing reached the database } queryInTransaction (and updateInTransaction for writes allowed by a write policy) runs the verified SQL in a transaction on the connection you pass, pinned to the policy's search path: autocommit is turned off if it was on (PgJDBC then sends BEGIN); SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY when the verdict's statement kind is select; SELECT set_config(name, value, true) for each entry of guard.transactionSettings(Map.of("app.tenant_id", tenantId)) (row-level security, statement_timeout, ...); SELECT set_config('search_path', ..., true) with verdict.policy().searchPath(), each schema quoted as an identifier. This is the pin: the verified orders is the policy's orders whatever the role's or the database's default search path is. It is applied last, so a search_path in the settings does not override it, and it is transaction-local, so the session's own search path is back afterwards; the verified statement; your handler reads the ResultSet; commit(), or rollback() on any error, including one your handler throws; autocommit is turned back on if it was on. A denial, a shadow would-deny or a HaltSQL error is thrown before any of this. A verdict without a search path (an engine older than the field) still runs, without step 4. The connection must have no transaction in progress: with autocommit off, the guard's transaction is the connection's next one, it is committed or rolled back as above, and autocommit stays off. A connection that PgJDBC reports as inside a transaction is refused (USAGE), because the guard's commit would also commit your earlier statements.

guard.prepare(conn, sql, context) returns the verified, bound PreparedStatement (you execute and close it); guard.query(conn, sql, context, handler) and guard.update(conn, sql, context, opts) execute it as one statement on the connection as it is. These low-level forms do not pin the search path and do not touch the transaction. Use them only when one of these holds: the session already uses the policy's search path: you set it on the connection (currentSchema=app in the JDBC URL), the role or the database; or the SQL names every table with its schema (app.orders). Otherwise a default such as ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path = public, app can make a verified orders read public.orders. They are also the forms to use inside a transaction you manage yourself; pin the search path there with SELECT set_config('search_path', ?, true) and JdbcGuard.searchPathSetting(verdict). Keep PgJDBC's default extended query protocol. With preferQueryMode=simple, PgJDBC substitutes parameters into the SQL text on the client (correctly escaped, but no longer server-side binding). To bind manually with another API, BindParams.positional(verdict) returns the values in $1..$n order (a String, or a List<String> for a set) and throws unless the verdict is an allow with contiguous, unique placeholders. BindParams.pgArrayLiteral(list) encodes a set as {"a","b"}.
documents.s: prepare, query, update: one statement, no pin

documents.t: Every failure is a HaltSQLException whose kind() is one of: Kind When HTTP (HaltSQLHttpException) Non-200 status: status() and code() (UNAUTHORIZED, FORBIDDEN, AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, ... or HTTP_<status>). Redirects are never followed. TIMEOUT An attempt exceeded the timeout (after retries). TRANSPORT Connection or TLS error, or the thread was interrupted. PROTOCOL Body is not JSON, has duplicate keys or trailing data, a required field is missing or mistyped, allowed is true while reasons is not empty, the body is too large, or sql_sha256 does not equal the SHA-256 of the SQL that was sent. USAGE Bad options or arguments, or SQL the JDBC path cannot run safely. DENIED (HaltSQLDeniedException) JdbcGuard only: the policy denied the SQL. allowed() on every exception returns false. Unknown verdict fields are ignored (compatibility rules); unknown reason codes are kept as strings. JdbcGuard throws HaltSQLDeniedException for SQL that a mode: shadow policy would deny, unless you use new JdbcGuard(client).allowShadow() (for a shadow rollout). Search path. The verdict holds only under the policy's search path (verdict.policy().searchPath()). queryInTransaction and updateInTransaction set it for the transaction that runs the SQL, as the Python guard, the MCP server and haltsql-proxy do. prepare, query and update run one statement on your connection and do not change session settings: with them, configure the connection or role with that search_path, or have the model write schema-qualified names (when that is acceptable).

Builder method Default Meaning token(t) none Bearer token for /v1/*; never in exception messages or toString(). timeout(d) 5s Connect and per-attempt request timeout. retries(n, base, max) 2, 100ms, 2s Retries on 503, connection errors and timeouts; exponential backoff with full jitter; max also caps Retry-After. maxResponseBytes(n) 8 MiB Response size cap. sslContext(ctx) JVM default trust store TLS for an https sidecar: a trust store with a private CA, a key manager with a client certificate for mutual TLS. sslParameters(p) JVM defaults TLS protocols and cipher suites. httpClient(c) built-in Custom HttpClient (proxy, executor, TLS); must use Redirect.NEVER. Cannot be combined with sslContext / sslParameters: configure TLS on it instead. withoutSqlHashCheck() check on Disable the sql_sha256 check. Per call: verify(sql, context, VerifyOptions.policy("name").withRequestId(id)). The request id is sent as X-Request-Id (1-200 printable ASCII characters, else a USAGE error before anything is sent). Context values may be String, Integer, Long, Short, Byte, BigInteger (within ±2^53), or collections of those. Other endpoints: health(), ready() (a 503 returns ready() == false and is not retried), policies(). Every request has a timeout (it covers the connect, the headers and the response body) and carries User-Agent: haltsql-client-java/<VERSION>. The worst case for one verify is about (retries + 1) * timeout plus the backoff delays. Only 503, connection errors and timeouts are retried; POST /v1/verify has no side effects, so retrying it is safe. An interrupted thread stops at once (kind TRANSPORT, interrupt flag restored).

KeyStore trust = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12"); trust.load(null, null); trust.setCertificateEntry("haltsql-ca", CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509") .generateCertificate(Files.newInputStream(Path.of("/etc/haltsql/ca.crt")))); TrustManagerFactory tmf = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm()); tmf.init(trust); KeyStore identity = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12"); // client cert + key, for mTLS identity.load(Files.newInputStream(Path.of("/etc/haltsql/client.p12")), password); KeyManagerFactory kmf = KeyManagerFactory.getInstance(KeyManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm()); kmf.init(identity, password); SSLContext tls = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS"); tls.init(kmf.getKeyManagers(), tmf.getTrustManagers(), null); HaltSQLClient haltsql = HaltSQLClient.builder("https://haltsql.internal:8443") .token(System.getenv("HALTSQL_TOKEN")) .sslContext(tls) .build(); Certificate and host-name verification stay on. An untrusted certificate is a TRANSPORT error.

HaltSQLClient is immutable and thread-safe. Create one per sidecar and share it; the underlying HttpClient pools keep-alive connections. The token is only placed in the Authorization header. It is not in any exception message or in toString().

cd clients/java mvn test Tests use a com.sun.net.httpserver fake that replays real haltsql-server responses from src/test/resources/vectors.json. The PgJDBC tests need Postgres (make -C lab up; HALTSQL_PG* variables override the defaults), create and drop the databases haltsql_polyglot_java and haltsql_polyglot_java_tx, and are skipped (JUnit assumptions) when Postgres is unreachable. With HALTSQL_REQUIRE_POSTGRES=1 (set in CI) unreachable is a failure instead.

The haltsql package (in clients/python) is the official Python client for haltsql-server. It needs Python 3.9 or newer and depends only on httpx; guarded execution uses psycopg 3 or asyncpg if you install them. pip install 'haltsql[psycopg]' # or [asyncpg], or plain haltsql On Linux (manylinux_2_28, x86_64 and aarch64) and macOS arm64, pip install haltsql also installs the compiled verification engine, so you can verify in-process with no sidecar: see In-process verification.

Fail closed. A verdict is returned only when the sidecar answered 200 with a well-formed verdict for exactly the SQL that was sent (its sql_sha256 is checked). Timeouts, connection errors, 4xx/5xx responses, and malformed bodies raise. No code path turns an error into "allowed". Context from your session. Every API takes the context from you; nothing reads it from the model. Run the verified string. The guarded executors send the same str they verified to the driver with verdict.bind_args() as $n parameters.
documents.s: The rules it enforces for you

documents.t: from haltsql import HaltSQLClient, AsyncHaltSQLClient, RetryPolicy hs = HaltSQLClient( "http://127.0.0.1:8080", token=os.environ["HALTSQL_TOKEN"], timeout=2.0, # seconds, per attempt retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, backoff_base=0.05, backoff_max=1.0), ) verdict = hs.verify(sql, {"tenant_id": tenant}) # allowed or denied verdict verdict = hs.check(sql, {"tenant_id": tenant}) # raises QueryDenied if denied hs.policies() # [PolicyInfo(name, version, mode)] hs.healthz(); hs.readyz(); hs.is_ready() HaltSQLClient.from_env() reads HALTSQL_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:8080), HALTSQL_TOKEN, HALTSQL_TIMEOUT (seconds), HALTSQL_POLICY, and for TLS HALTSQL_CA_FILE, HALTSQL_CLIENT_CERT and HALTSQL_CLIENT_KEY (see below). Keyword arguments to from_env(...) override the environment. AsyncHaltSQLClient has the same methods as coroutines (async with AsyncHaltSQLClient.from_env() as hs: ...). Optional arguments: policy= (default policy name to send), request_id= on verify/check (sent as X-Request-Id, at most 200 printable characters; the response's id is in verdict.request_id), transport= / http_client= (custom httpx setup), verify_sql_hash= (default True; leave it on).

Argument Default Notes timeout 2.0 s Per attempt (connect, read, write and pool each). An httpx.Timeout is accepted. The worst case for one call is about max_attempts * timeout plus the backoff delays. retry RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, backoff_base=0.05, backoff_max=1.0, jitter=True) max_attempts=1 disables retries. verify True (system CAs) A CA bundle path for a private CA, or an ssl.SSLContext. False turns certificate checks off: local testing only. cert none Client certificate for mutual TLS: one PEM file with certificate and key, or (cert_file, key_file). max_response_bytes 8 MiB A larger response raises HaltSQLUnavailable. hs = HaltSQLClient( "https://haltsql.internal:8443", token=os.environ["HALTSQL_TOKEN"], verify="/etc/haltsql/ca.crt", # private CA cert=("/etc/haltsql/client.crt", "/etc/haltsql/client.key"), # mTLS ) Secrets. The token is never included in repr(), in exception messages, or in exception chains (httpx errors, which carry the request headers, are not chained; only their type name is reported). Redirects are never followed; a 3xx is an error. Proxies. httpx honours HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY from the environment. For anything else (custom proxies, HTTP/2, pool limits), build your own httpx.Client and pass http_client=; then configure TLS on it, since verify= / cert= cannot be combined with http_client=. Sharing. A HaltSQLClient holds a pool of keep-alive connections and is safe to share between threads; create one at startup and close() it at shutdown (or use it as a context manager). Use one AsyncHaltSQLClient per event loop.

Exception When Retried QueryDenied The policy denied the query (check, guard.*). e.verdict has the reasons. no HaltSQLUnavailable Connection error, TLS failure, timeout, HTTP 3xx/5xx, oversized, malformed or mismatched response. status, code, request_id when known. connection errors, timeouts, 502/503/504 HaltSQLRequestError HTTP 4xx: UNAUTHORIZED, FORBIDDEN, POLICY_NOT_FOUND, BAD_REQUEST, PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE. no GuardError The guarded executor refused (unsupported connection, connection already in a transaction). no All derive from HaltSQLError; catching it and carrying on means treating the query as denied. Retries back off exponentially with jitter and honour Retry-After up to backoff_max. Verification is idempotent (it has no side effects on the server), so a retried POST /v1/verify is safe. /healthz and /readyz are never retried, so a probe reports the current state.

Verdict, Reason, BindParam, and PolicyRef mirror verdict.md as frozen dataclasses (reasons, tables, ... are tuples). Unknown fields are ignored and kept in verdict.raw. verdict.allowed # bool verdict.codes # ["E_TENANT_MISSING", ...] verdict.reasons[0].hint # text an agent can follow verdict.bind_args() # ["acme"] or [["acme", "acme-eu"]] for tenant sets verdict.matches_sql(sql) # SHA-256 check bind_args() returns the values for $1..$n in order and keeps tenant sets as Python lists (bound as Postgres arrays by psycopg and asyncpg). It raises QueryDenied on a denied verdict and ValueError if the placeholders are not exactly $1..$n.

Shadow mode. A verdict from a mode: shadow policy is allowed even when the policy would deny the query (shadow_reasons is then non-empty). The guard raises QueryDenied for such a verdict unless you opt in with haltsql.guard.set_allow_shadow(True) or HALTSQL_ALLOW_SHADOW=1. See rolling out a policy. from haltsql import guard result = guard.execute(conn, sql, {"tenant_id": tenant}, verifier=hs, statement_timeout_ms=5000, max_rows=500, settings={"app.tenant_id": tenant}) result.columns, result.rows, result.rowcount, result.truncated, result.verdict Function Connection guard.execute(conn, sql, ctx, ...) psycopg.Connection (psycopg 3.2+) await guard.execute_async(conn, sql, ctx, ...) asyncpg.Connection or psycopg.AsyncConnection guard.execute_on_engine(engine, sql, ctx, ...) SQLAlchemy engine with postgresql+psycopg:// Steps: verify (or take a verdict= from guard.authorize), check it allows this exact string, open a transaction, SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY (default for select verdicts; pass read_only=False for write policies), apply statement_timeout_ms and settings with set_config(name, value, true), then send the SQL unchanged (psycopg RawCursor, asyncpg prepared statement) with verdict.bind_args(). Denied or unverifiable queries raise before the connection is touched. guard.authorize(sql, ctx, verifier=...) verifies without a connection, so you can verify before taking one from a pool and pass verdict= later. The connection must be idle (not inside a transaction) when read_only, statement_timeout_ms, or settings apply; otherwise GuardError. With psycopg's default (autocommit off), call conn.rollback() or conn.commit() after your own statements. verifier= defaults to a client built from the environment. Guard(verifier, **defaults) binds a verifier and defaults once. max_rows limits what is returned, not what the server computes; keep require_limit in the policy. psycopg2 cannot send $n SQL unchanged and is refused.

from haltsql import LocalVerifier, AsyncLocalVerifier lv = LocalVerifier("policy.yaml", binary="/usr/local/bin/haltsql", timeout=30) lv.verify(sql, ctx) # one verdict lv.verify_many([(sql1, ctx), (sql2, ctx)]) # one process for many Each call runs haltsql verify --policy FILE --batch and exchanges JSONL over stdin/stdout (the SQL never appears on a command line). The binary defaults to $HALTSQL_BIN, then the CLI bundled in a platform wheel, then haltsql on PATH. A missing binary, timeout, non-zero exit, or malformed line raises HaltSQLUnavailable. Local verifiers work anywhere a verifier is accepted (guard.*, integrations, haltsql-mcp).

Platform wheels ship the engine itself: haltsql/_native/libhaltsql.so (the OCaml analyzer and the PostgreSQL parser in one self-contained shared library) and the haltsql CLI, which pip also puts on PATH. Wheels exist for manylinux_2_28 x86_64 / aarch64 and macOS arm64; anywhere else pip falls back to the pure-Python wheel (HTTP client and LocalVerifier only). from haltsql import NativeVerifier, AsyncNativeVerifier hs = NativeVerifier("policy.yaml") # or NativeVerifier(policy=doc, policy_format="json") hs.backend # "library" (in-process) or "process" verdict = hs.verify(sql, {"tenant_id": tenant}) verdict = hs.check(sql, {"tenant_id": tenant}) # raises QueryDenied hs.verify_many([(sql1, ctx), (sql2, ctx)]) hs.policy_info() # {"name": ..., "version": "sha256:...", "mode": "enforce" | "shadow"} hs.close() # or: with NativeVerifier(...) as hs: ... guard.execute(conn, sql, ctx, verifier=hs) # works anywhere a verifier is accepted AsyncNativeVerifier takes the same arguments and has the same methods as coroutines (calls run in a worker thread; async with closes it). Backend How Cost per call "library" libhaltsql loaded with ctypes, in-process. ctypes releases the GIL; the library serializes calls, so one verifier can be shared by all threads. ~0.05-0.15 ms "process" One long-lived haltsql verify --batch child, one request at a time over pipes. ~0.15 ms LocalVerifier (for comparison) A new CLI process per call. ~20 ms backend="auto" (default) uses the library if it loads, else the process backend, else raises HaltSQLUnavailable saying what to install; hs.fallback_reason says why the library was not used. Other arguments: base_dir= (resolves a relative catalog: in an in-memory policy; default the current directory), binary=, timeout= (per request, process backend; default 30 s), verify_sql_hash= (leave it on). Variable Effect HALTSQL_LIB Use this libhaltsql instead of the bundled one (no silent fallback to the bundled copy if it fails to load). HALTSQL_BIN Use this CLI for the process backend and LocalVerifier. HALTSQL_NATIVE With backend="auto" only: 0 forces the process backend, library forces the library. Fail closed. A NULL result, unparseable output, a malformed verdict or one whose sql_sha256 does not match, an ABI mismatch, or a crashed, hung (past timeout) or garbled child raises HaltSQLUnavailable; a request the engine rejects raises HaltSQLRequestError (BAD_REQUEST); a policy that cannot be loaded raises ValueError with the engine's message. After close(), every method raises HaltSQLUnavailable. SQL is passed with its length, so a NUL byte is denied (E_PARSE) rather than truncating the string. The process backend kills a misbehaving child; the next call starts a new one (a child found dead between calls is replaced transparently). fork(). The OCaml runtime inside the library does not survive fork(). Create verifiers after forking (gunicorn: in post_fork; multiprocessing: in the worker, or use the spawn start method). If a process uses the library and then forks, the child gets HaltSQLUnavailable (never a crash) when it calls it, and backend="auto" in the child picks the process backend. Build a platform wheel yourself with clients/python/scripts/build_wheel.sh (see --help).

haltsql.testing has FakeSidecar (an in-process HTTP server with scripted responses: push(503), delays, raw bodies), FakeVerifier, make_verdict, and temporary_database() (a throwaway database on the lab Postgres). Use them in tests only.
MCP server: mcp.md LangChain: integrations/langchain LlamaIndex: integrations/llamaindex Vanna: integrations/vanna

cd clients/python python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[psycopg,asyncpg,test]' .venv/bin/pytest -q Integration tests (marked integration) use the binaries in _build/default/bin (or HALTSQL_BIN / HALTSQL_SERVER_BIN), the shared test vectors, and the lab Postgres on port 5417. They skip when those are unavailable. The native tests use _build/default/native/libhaltsql.so (or HALTSQL_LIB); HALTSQL_REQUIRE_NATIVE=1 makes a missing engine fail instead of skip, and HALTSQL_WHEEL=dist/haltsql-*.whl installs that wheel into a fresh venv and checks it.

@haltsql/client is a small client for the HTTP sidecar. It has no runtime dependencies, ships ESM and CommonJS builds with type declarations, and needs Node.js 18 or newer (it uses the global fetch). Source: clients/typescript.
npm install @haltsql/client On Linux x64/arm64 (glibc) and macOS arm64 this also installs the compiled engine, so LocalVerifier can verify SQL locally with no sidecar.

import { HaltSQLClient } from "@haltsql/client"; const haltsql = new HaltSQLClient({ baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:8080", token: process.env.HALTSQL_TOKEN, // pinned to one policy on the server }); const verdict = await haltsql.verify( "SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50", { tenant_id: session.tenantId }, // from the authenticated session, never from the prompt ); if (!verdict.allowed) { // Give the reasons back to the agent so it can fix its query. return verdict.reasons.map((r) => ({ code: r.code, message: r.message, hint: r.hint })); } CommonJS works the same way: const { HaltSQLClient } = require("@haltsql/client").

guardedTransaction verifies the SQL and, only if it is allowed, runs exactly that string with pg in a transaction that uses the policy's search path, binding verdict.bind_params as $1..$n: import pg from "pg"; import { HaltSQLClient, HaltSQLDeniedError, guardedTransaction } from "@haltsql/client"; const pool = new pg.Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL }); try { const { result, verdict } = await guardedTransaction( haltsql, pool, // a pg.Pool sqlFromModel, { tenant_id: session.tenantId }, { onVerdict: (v) => audit.log({ policy: v.policy.version, fp: v.fingerprint, allowed: v.allowed }) }, ); return result.rows; } catch (e) { if (e instanceof HaltSQLDeniedError) return { denied: e.codes, reasons: e.verdict.reasons }; throw e; // sidecar unreachable, timeout, ... : nothing ran } On a client it checks out of the pool, guardedTransaction sends: BEGIN READ ONLY when verdict.statement_kind is select, otherwise BEGIN; SELECT set_config(name, value, true) for each entry of the settings option (for example { "app.tenant_id": tenantId } for row-level security, or { statement_timeout: "5000" }); SELECT set_config('search_path', ..., true) with verdict.policy.search_path, each schema quoted as an identifier. This is the pin: the verified orders is the policy's orders whatever the role's or the database's default search path is. It is applied last, so a search_path in settings does not override it, and it is transaction-local, so the session's own search path is back afterwards; the verified string, unchanged; COMMIT, or ROLLBACK on any error (the error is rethrown and the client goes back to the pool). A denied verdict, a shadow would-deny or a HaltSQL error rejects before a client is checked out. A verdict without policy.search_path (an engine older than the field) still runs, without step 3. Which handle to pass: You have Call a pg.Pool guardedTransaction(haltsql, pool, sql, ctx, opts). It needs connect(): a transaction must stay on one session, and pool.query may use a different one for each statement. a connected pg.Client, or a PoolClient you checked out guardedTransactionOnClient(haltsql, client, sql, ctx, opts). The client must be idle (not inside a transaction): the function sends its own BEGIN and COMMIT. A pool is refused here.

guardedQuery(haltsql, db, sql, ctx, opts) is the low-level form. It verifies and then makes one db.query(sql, values) call on a pg.Pool, pg.Client or PoolClient. It does not pin the search path and opens no transaction. Use it only when one of these holds: the session already uses the policy's search path: you set it on the connection (options: "-c search_path=app"), the role or the database; or the SQL names every table with its schema (app.orders). Otherwise a default such as ALTER ROLE ... SET search_path = public, app can make a verified orders read public.orders. It is also the form to use inside a transaction you manage yourself; pin the search path there with SELECT set_config('search_path', $1, true) and searchPathSetting(verdict). pg is not a dependency of the SDK: the helpers accept anything with the methods they call (connect() resolving to a client with query and release; or query(text, values)). A set-valued bind param (hierarchical tenants, org_id = ANY($1)) is passed as a JS string[], which node-postgres sends as a Postgres array. To bind manually, use bindParamsToPositional(verdict); it returns the values in $1..$n order and throws unless the verdict is an allow with contiguous, unique placeholders. toPgArrayLiteral(values) encodes a string[] as {"a","b"} for drivers that need a literal.

LocalVerifier verifies SQL on the same machine with the compiled haltsql engine, so a Node.js service or agent needs no sidecar at all: import { LocalVerifier } from "@haltsql/client"; const haltsql = await LocalVerifier.create({ policyFile: "policies/saas.yaml" }); const verdict = await haltsql.verify(sqlFromModel, { tenant_id: session.tenantId }); if (verdict.allowed) { /* run exactly sqlFromModel, binding verdict.bind_params */ } await haltsql.check(sql, ctx); // throws HaltSQLDeniedError unless allowed const verdicts = await haltsql.verifyMany([a, b], ctx); // pipelined, input order await guardedTransaction(haltsql, pool, sql, ctx); // same helper as with HaltSQLClient await haltsql.close(); // or: await using haltsql = await LocalVerifier.create(...) Zero setup on supported platforms. The engine ships in per-platform npm packages that @haltsql/client lists as optionalDependencies (the same scheme esbuild uses); npm installs only the one matching the machine: Platform Package Linux x64, glibc @haltsql/native-linux-x64 Linux arm64, glibc @haltsql/native-linux-arm64 macOS arm64 (Apple silicon) @haltsql/native-darwin-arm64 Each package holds bin/haltsql (the CLI the client runs), lib/libhaltsql (the same engine as a C shared library, include/haltsql.h; reserved for a future in-process binding) and the licenses. On other platforms (musl/Alpine, macOS x64, Windows), with npm install --omit=optional, or with Yarn PnP setups that drop optional packages, build or download haltsql yourself and point HALTSQL_BIN at it. Finding the engine, in order (the first that applies wins; an explicit choice that is not an executable file is an error, never a silent fallback): the binary option; the HALTSQL_BIN environment variable; the installed platform package @haltsql/native-<platform>-<arch>; haltsql in an absolute PATH directory. If none is found the constructor throws a HaltSQLUsageError that names the expected platform package. verifier.binary and verifier.binarySource (option, env, package or path) say which one was used; resolveLocalBinary() runs the same lookup without starting anything. Options: new LocalVerifier({ policyFile: "policy.yaml", // or policy: "<YAML or JSON text>" (exactly one of the two) policyFormat: "yaml", // for `policy` only; default: json if it starts with "{" binary: "/opt/haltsql/bin/haltsql", timeoutMs: 30000, // per request, from the call to the answer verifySqlHash: true, // check verdict.sql_sha256 against the SQL sent }); An in-memory policy is written to a private temporary file (directory 0700, file 0600) that close() removes (and, as a fallback, process exit). Relative paths inside it, such as catalog: ../catalogs/app.json, would resolve against that temporary directory, so use absolute paths there or use policyFile. new LocalVerifier(...) validates options and finds the binary but starts nothing; the engine starts on the first call. LocalVerifier.create(...) (or await verifier.start()) starts it immediately and waits for a probe answer, so a policy that does not load fails at startup with the engine's message (HaltSQLUsageError: haltsql engine failed to start (policy or usage error): haltsql: cannot load policy: ...). How it works. The engine runs as one long-lived child process, haltsql verify --policy=FILE --batch, which reads one JSON request per line on stdin and writes one verdict per line, in order, flushing each. Only the policy path is on the command line; SQL and context only ever travel over the pipe. Concurrent verify() calls are pipelined with increasing ids, and every answer must carry the id of the oldest request in flight. An idle verifier holds no reference on the event loop, so a script that never calls close() still exits (the engine sees end-of-file and exits too). Latency. After the first call (process start and policy load, tens of milliseconds) a sequential verify() costs roughly 0.1-0.5 ms on a laptop: the engine's own analysis (elapsed_us, typically 30-100 us) plus a pipe round trip. Pipelined calls (verifyMany, or many concurrent verify()s) amortize the round trip. One process verifies on one core; for heavy multi-core throughput run haltsql-server and use HaltSQLClient. Fail closed. verify() resolves only with a strictly validated verdict whose sql_sha256 equals the SHA-256 of the UTF-8 SQL that was sent. Situation Result Bad options or context, SQL that is not a string or contains a lone UTF-16 surrogate, no engine found, closed verifier HaltSQLUsageError before anything is sent Policy cannot be loaded (engine exits with code 2 before answering) HaltSQLUsageError with the engine's stderr A request takes longer than timeoutMs that request: HaltSQLTimeoutError; the engine is killed and everything else in flight rejects with HaltSQLTransportError The engine crashes, is killed or cannot be started every request in flight: HaltSQLTransportError (with the exit status and stderr tail) A line that is not JSON, an invalid verdict, an answer out of order, or a sql_sha256 mismatch every request in flight: HaltSQLProtocolError; the engine is killed The engine rejects one request ({"id":..,"error":..}) that request: HaltSQLProtocolError; the engine keeps running close() while requests are in flight they reject with HaltSQLTransportError After any failure that kills the engine, the next call starts a fresh one. NUL bytes, newlines and any Unicode in SQL are safe: requests are JSON-encoded and the engine denies a NUL byte with E_PARSE; SQL over the engine's size limit is denied with E_LIMIT.

verify() resolves only with a strictly validated verdict from an HTTP 200 response. Everything else rejects with a subclass of HaltSQLError, whose allowed property is always false: Error When HaltSQLHttpError Non-200 status. status and code (UNAUTHORIZED, FORBIDDEN, POLICY_NOT_FOUND, AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE, ... or HTTP_<status>). Redirects are never followed. HaltSQLTimeoutError An attempt exceeded timeoutMs (after retries). HaltSQLTransportError Connection refused/reset, DNS or TLS failure, or the caller aborted. HaltSQLProtocolError Body is not JSON, a required field is missing or mistyped, allowed is true while reasons is not empty, the body is too large, or sql_sha256 does not equal the SHA-256 of the SQL that was sent. HaltSQLUsageError Bad options or arguments (a non-integer context value, a token or header with control characters, an invalid requestId, a denied verdict passed to bindParamsToPositional). HaltSQLDeniedError guardedTransaction, guardedTransactionOnClient, guardedQuery and LocalVerifier.check: the policy denied the SQL. verdict and codes are available. Unknown fields in a verdict are ignored, as the compatibility rules require. Unknown reason codes are kept as strings; only allowed === true permits running a query. The guarded helpers reject with HaltSQLDeniedError for SQL that a mode: shadow policy would deny, unless you pass { allowShadow: true } (for a shadow rollout). Search path. The verdict holds only under the policy's search path (verdict.policy.search_path). guardedTransaction and guardedTransactionOnClient set it for the transaction that runs the SQL, as the Python guard, the MCP server and haltsql-proxy do. guardedQuery runs one statement on your connection and does not change session settings: with it, configure the connection or role with that search_path, or have the model write schema-qualified names (when that is acceptable).

new HaltSQLClient({ baseUrl: "http://127.0.0.1:8080", // http or https; no credentials in the URL token: "...", // sent only to /v1/*; never included in errors timeoutMs: 5000, // per attempt maxRetries: 2, // on 503, network errors and timeouts retryBaseDelayMs: 100, // exponential backoff with full jitter retryMaxDelayMs: 2000, // also caps Retry-After maxResponseBytes: 8 << 20, checkSqlHash: true, headers: { "x-tenant-shard": "eu" }, // cannot set Authorization; CR/LF rejected dispatcher: agent, // undici Dispatcher: private CA, mTLS, proxy, pool tuning fetch: customFetch, // a fetch implementation; defaults to the global one }); Per call: verify(sql, context, { policy, requestId, signal }). requestId is sent as X-Request-Id (1-200 printable ASCII characters, else a HaltSQLUsageError before anything is sent); an aborted signal stops immediately without retrying. Every request carries User-Agent: haltsql-client-js/<VERSION> and an AbortSignal that fires after timeoutMs, so no call can hang. The worst case for one verify() is about (maxRetries + 1) * timeoutMs plus the backoff delays. Only 503, network errors and timeouts are retried (/readyz never is); POST /v1/verify has no side effects, so retrying it is safe.

Certificate verification is on by default (Node's bundled CA store, plus anything in NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS). For a private CA or a client certificate, pass an undici Agent as dispatcher; it is forwarded to every fetch call. Install undici yourself (the SDK has no dependencies): import { readFileSync } from "node:fs"; import { Agent } from "undici"; const haltsql = new HaltSQLClient({ baseUrl: "https://haltsql.internal:8443", token: process.env.HALTSQL_TOKEN, dispatcher: new Agent({ connect: { ca: readFileSync("/etc/haltsql/ca.crt"), cert: readFileSync("/etc/haltsql/client.crt"), // mTLS key: readFileSync("/etc/haltsql/client.key"), }, }), }); A TLS failure (untrusted certificate, wrong host name) rejects with HaltSQLTransportError like any other connection error.
documents.s: TLS, private CAs and mutual TLS

documents.t: The token is kept in a private field: it is not visible through JSON.stringify, util.inspect, or any error message. Errors keep the underlying fetch error as cause (which never contains request headers). One HaltSQLClient is safe to share across concurrent requests; create it once at startup. Connection reuse is handled by fetch (or your dispatcher). Other endpoints: health() (GET /healthz), ready() (GET /readyz; a 503 resolves { ready: false } and is not retried), and policies() (GET /v1/policies).

cd clients/typescript npm ci npm test # builds ESM + CJS with tsc, then runs node:test The tests replay real haltsql-server responses from testdata/vectors.json against a local fake server, and run integration tests that skip cleanly when their dependency is missing: node-postgres against Postgres 17 (make -C lab up; override with HALTSQL_PGHOST, HALTSQL_PGPORT, HALTSQL_PGUSER, HALTSQL_PGPASSWORD). The tests create and drop their own databases (haltsql_polyglot_ts, haltsql_polyglot_ts_tx). With HALTSQL_REQUIRE_POSTGRES=1 (set in CI) an unreachable Postgres fails the run instead of skipping these tests. the real sidecar binary (_build/default/bin/server/main.exe, or HALTSQL_SERVER_BIN). the real haltsql CLI for LocalVerifier (_build/default/bin/haltsql/main.exe, or HALTSQL_BIN): every case in clients/testvectors/cases, concurrency, crash and timeout handling (also against fake engines), the event loop not being held, and warm latency. They skip when the binary is missing unless HALTSQL_REQUIRE_NATIVE=1. Platform packages are built from the compiled engine and checked end to end (pack, offline install into a fresh project, ESM and CommonJS consumers with no binary option and no HALTSQL_BIN): opam exec -- dune build ./bin/haltsql/main.exe ./native/libhaltsql.so cd clients/typescript node scripts/build-native-package.mjs --platform linux-x64 \ --binary ../../_build/default/bin/haltsql/main.exe \ --lib ../../_build/default/native/libhaltsql.so --out ../../dist-native/linux-x64 npm run smoke:native # builds and tests the package for this machine build-native-package.mjs checks the binary and library against the target (ELF/Mach-O, CPU) and refuses dynamic dependencies a stock system may not have (for example Homebrew's libgmp); --allow-nonsystem-deps downgrades that to a warning for local testing only. Publish the three platform packages before @haltsql/client, all at the same version: the client pins them exactly in optionalDependencies. Regenerate the shared vectors after a server change (writes the TypeScript, Go and Java copies): eval $(opam env); dune build ./bin/server/main.exe node clients/typescript/scripts/gen-testvectors.mjs

Configuration values never need to contain secrets. Any string in a Config document, outside inline policies, may use placeholders: Placeholder Source ${env:NAME} environment variable ${file:/path} file contents, minus one trailing newline ${vault:<path>#<field>} HashiCorp Vault KV v2 ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]} AWS Secrets Manager ${gcp-sm:<name>[#<json-key>]} Google Secret Manager $${ a literal ${ The three provider schemes are configured in the secrets section. That section may itself use only ${env:..} and ${file:..}. secrets: vault: address: https://vault.corp.example:8200 namespace: platform # Vault Enterprise, optional ca_file: /etc/haltsql/vault-ca.pem auth: { method: kubernetes, role: haltsql } aws: region: eu-west-1 gcp: project: corp-prod telemetry: otlp: endpoint: https://otel.corp.example:4318 headers: authorization: "Bearer ${vault:secret/data/haltsql/otel#token}" audit: sinks: - type: s3 bucket: corp-haltsql-audit region: eu-west-1 credentials: source: static access_key_id: "${aws-sm:prod/haltsql/s3#access_key_id}" secret_access_key: "${aws-sm:prod/haltsql/s3#secret_access_key}"

The library is haltsql.cloud, module Secrets. The CLI and the server load a config in two passes: Config.secrets_of_file decodes only the secrets section. A resolver is built from it. The resolver finds every provider placeholder in the file text and fetches them concurrently. Each distinct reference is fetched once per load; Vault logs in at most once per load. Config.of_file ~resolve decodes the whole document, taking each placeholder's value from the resolver. A failure is a located load error, for example: haltsql.yaml:12:22: ${vault:secret/haltsql/otel#token}: vault: read secret/haltsql/otel failed: HTTP 403: permission denied The CLI exits with code 2 and the server refuses to start or reload. Error messages and logs never contain secret values, tokens or key material. A reload (SIGHUP or file watch) builds a fresh resolver, so rotated secrets are picked up on the next reload.

Reads. ${vault:<mount>/<path>#<field>} reads GET /v1/<mount>/data/<path> (KV v2) and returns data.data.<field>. If the path already contains data as its second segment, as in secret/data/haltsql/otel, it is used as written. Write mounts that have several segments in that explicit form, for example team/kv/data/app#token. Numbers and booleans are returned in their JSON spelling. Objects and arrays are errors. auth.method Login token X-Vault-Token: <token> (use ${env:VAULT_TOKEN} or ${file:..}). kubernetes POST /v1/auth/<mount>/login with {role, jwt}. The JWT is read from jwt_path (default: the pod's service-account token). approle POST /v1/auth/<mount>/login with {role_id, secret_id}. Tokens. The login token is reused until 30 s before its lease ends. A 403 on a read triggers one re-login. Headers and TLS. namespace is sent as X-Vault-Namespace. ca_file replaces the system trust store; a missing or invalid file fails the load. Plain http is accepted only for loopback addresses, such as a local Vault agent.

Call. ${aws-sm:<secret-id>[#<json-key>]} calls GetSecretValue (JSON 1.1 protocol, SigV4 service secretsmanager). The endpoint is https://secretsmanager.<region>.amazonaws.com, or secrets.aws.endpoint. Value. The result is SecretString, or the decoded SecretBinary. With #key, the value is parsed as a JSON object and that key's scalar is returned. Credentials. These come from the standard chain: environment variables, then web identity (IRSA), then container credentials (the ECS task role or EKS Pod Identity), then the EC2 instance profile (IMDSv2). See audit-sinks.md for details. On an expired-credential error the credentials are refreshed and the call is retried once. Required IAM permission: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret ARNs (plus kms:Decrypt for customer-managed keys).

Names. <name> is one of: projects/P/secrets/S/versions/V; projects/P/secrets/S (the latest version); a short S or S/versions/V, in secrets.gcp.project. Call and value. The resolver calls GET /v1/<name>:access on https://secretmanager.googleapis.com, or secrets.gcp.endpoint. It base64-decodes payload.data and verifies payload.dataCrc32c (CRC-32C). With #key, the value is parsed as JSON and that key's scalar is returned. Credentials. The service-account key in GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS when that variable is set; otherwise the metadata server (Workload Identity). A 401 refreshes the token once. Required role: roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on the secrets.

(* CLI: outside any Lwt loop *) match Haltsql_cloud.Secrets.load_config_blocking path with | Ok cfg -> run cfg | Error errs -> report errs; exit 2 (* Server: inside Lwt (startup or reload) *) Haltsql_cloud.Secrets.load_config path >>= function | Ok cfg -> swap cfg | Error errs -> keep_old_config errs Lower-level API. Secrets.create takes Config.secrets. Secrets.prefetch fetches placeholders concurrently. Secrets.cached_resolver returns a Config.resolver that serves only values already fetched, so it is safe inside Lwt. Secrets.blocking_resolver fetches missing values with Lwt_main.run. Use it only outside Lwt.

This page maps HaltSQL features to controls in common security and privacy frameworks, and lists the evidence each feature can produce. It is for compliance, GRC and audit teams who need to explain where HaltSQL fits in an organization's control set. Note: HaltSQL is open-source, self-hosted software. It is not certified or attested under SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, HIPAA or any other framework, and this page does not claim that it is. It maps HaltSQL features to controls that you operate. Whether a control is met depends on how you configure, run and monitor HaltSQL together with your other controls, and that responsibility stays with you and your auditor.

HaltSQL is a preventive and detective technical control for one specific access path: SQL that an LLM agent generates for PostgreSQL.
