It: restricts access: a query can read only the relations, columns and functions the policy lists, and, for tenant-scoped tables, only the caller's tenant (tenancy.md); binds callers to policies: every authenticated identity is pinned to one policy (authentication.md); records decisions: one hash-chained audit record per verdict (audit-sinks.md); controls policy change: policies can be tested in CI, signed, and verified by every server before use (policy-bundles.md). It does not cover identity lifecycle, the database's own access controls, encryption at rest, backups, the data returned by allowed queries, or the prompt. Pair it with the database controls in defense-in-depth.md.

These artifacts appear in the tables below. Evidence How to produce it E1. Audit chain verification haltsql audit verify --json --expect-head <head> <file, directory or s3://...>; keep the output and the head hash (audit-verify.md) E2. Audit records The sink itself (file, S3 with Object Lock, GCS with retention, Elasticsearch, Kafka). Each record has caller, subject, policy version, verdict, reason codes and SQL hash. E3. Policy CI results haltsql validate --json, haltsql lint-policy --json, haltsql test --json, and the JUnit report from the GitHub Action or GitLab template (policy-ci.md) E4. Signed policy bundles The .haltsqlbundle and .sig files, haltsql bundle verify --json output, and the bundle's metadata.source.commit (policy-bundles.md) E5. Running configuration haltsql config show (secrets redacted) and GET /v1/admin/status: loaded policies, versions, origin, bundle signer key ids, audit sink health, OPA settings (http-api.md) E6. Policy version in each decision policy_version in every verdict and audit record: a content hash of the normalized policy (verdict.md) E7. Metrics haltsql_verify_total, haltsql_reasons_total, haltsql_auth_total, haltsql_audit_errors_total, haltsql_policy_reload_total (http-api.md) E8. Shadow reports haltsql report over audit records, or GET /v1/admin/report (shadow-reports.md) E9. Database drift check haltsql rls check --json against the live database (rls-generation.md) E10. Release verification cosign verify, cosign verify-blob and gh attestation verify output for the artifacts you deploy (supply-chain.md)

Criterion HaltSQL feature Evidence CC6.1 Logical access security over protected information assets Policy allowlists of tables, columns, functions and statement kinds; tenant predicate proof; bound tenancy mode E3, E4, E5 CC6.1 (authentication of system users) mTLS identities, OIDC/JWT verification, hashed static tokens; proxy SCRAM-SHA-256 or client certificates E5, E7 (haltsql_auth_total) CC6.2, CC6.3 Authorization and modification of access Each identity pinned to one policy; OIDC allowed_policies or policy_from_groups ties access to IdP groups; changes go through policy CI and signing E3, E4, E5 CC6.6 Protection against threats from outside system boundaries Denies SQL outside the policy before it reaches the database (statement smuggling, catalog access, side-effecting functions) E2, E7 (haltsql_reasons_total) CC6.7 Restriction of transmission of information Built-in TLS 1.2/1.3 and mTLS on the server; TLS on both sides of the proxy E5 CC6.8 Prevention of unauthorized or malicious software Signed releases and provenance for HaltSQL itself; signed policy bundles E4, E10 CC7.2 Monitoring of system components for anomalies Audit records per decision; metrics and OTLP traces; alerts on internal errors and audit failures E2, E7, E8 CC7.3 Evaluation of security events Reason codes identify why a query was denied; shadow reports group denials by query and reason E2, E8 CC8.1 Change management Policies in version control, tested in CI, built into deterministic signed bundles with source commit; servers refuse unsigned or rolled-back bundles from bundle sources; shadow mode for staged rollout E3, E4, E6

Control HaltSQL feature Evidence 5.15 Access control Allowlist policies; deny by default for tables, columns and functions E3, E5 5.18 Access rights Policy pinning per identity; group-to-policy mapping from the IdP E5 5.33 Protection of records Hash-chained audit records; S3 Object Lock or GCS retention for WORM storage E1, E2 8.2 Privileged access rights Admin API off by default and limited to listed callers; allow_unauthenticated off by default E5 8.3 Information access restriction Column allowlists, tenant scoping, require_limit row bounds E3, E5 8.5 Secure authentication OIDC with algorithm allowlist (no none or HMAC), mTLS, constant-time token comparison E5, E7 8.9 Configuration management Unknown and duplicate config keys are load errors; config show; atomic reload that keeps the last good configuration E5 8.11 Data masking Sensitive columns can be left out of a policy (HaltSQL denies them; it does not mask values) E3 8.12 Data leakage prevention Denies queries touching columns, tables or tenants outside the policy E2, E8 8.15 Logging One audit record per decision, fail-closed by default; raw SQL off by default E1, E2 8.16 Monitoring activities Metrics, traces, shadow reports E7, E8 8.20 Networks security TLS and mTLS; NetworkPolicy in the Helm chart with egress denied by default E5 8.24 Use of cryptography TLS 1.2/1.3 with AEAD ciphers; Ed25519 bundle signatures; SHA-256 audit chain E4, E5 8.25, 8.29 Secure development and security testing Policy test suites in CI; HaltSQL's own attack corpus, fuzzing and lab (how-it-works/assurance.md) E3 8.32 Change management Signed, versioned policy bundles with source commit; no rollback from bundle sources E4, E6

HaltSQL processes whatever personal data appears in SQL text and context values, in your environment. It sends nothing to the HaltSQL project. Principle or article HaltSQL feature Evidence Art. 5(1)(c) Data minimisation Column allowlists let an agent read only the columns its task needs; require_limit bounds rows; PII-flagging helps find sensitive columns (schema-and-pii.md) E3 Art. 5(1)(f) Integrity and confidentiality Tenant isolation proof; TLS; hash-chained audit records E1, E5 Art. 25 Data protection by design and by default Deny by default; raw SQL not logged by default; context values not written to audit records; OPA receives no SQL and no context values E5 Art. 32 Security of processing Access restriction, encryption in transit, audit, fail-closed behaviour E1, E2, E5 Art. 5(2) Accountability Audit records tie every decision to a caller, subject and policy version E2, E6 Things to consider in your own records of processing: Audit records contain the caller's identity (caller, and subject for OIDC and mTLS callers), which may be personal data. sql_sha256 and fingerprint are not anonymisation. With audit.log_raw_sql: true the SQL text, including literals, is stored. HaltSQL has no built-in retention or deletion of audit records. Retention is set where records are stored (bucket lifecycle, Object Lock period, index lifecycle, topic retention). WORM retention conflicts with erasure requests, so choose it with your DPO.

Safeguard HaltSQL feature Evidence Not covered by HaltSQL (a)(1) Access control Policy allowlists, tenant scoping, policy pinning E3, E5 Access to ePHI through any path other than the agent (a)(2)(i) Unique user identification Audit subject from the OIDC sub or certificate identity E2 Static tokens and proxy users identify a service, not a person. Use OIDC tokens that carry the end user if you need per-user records. (a)(2)(ii) Emergency access procedure None Your procedure (a)(2)(iii) Automatic logoff Proxy idle_timeout_seconds; OIDC token expiry E5 Application sessions (a)(2)(iv) Encryption and decryption None at rest Encrypt audit storage, spool and cache volumes, and the database (b) Audit controls One audit record per decision; fail-closed by default; chain verification E1, E2 Database audit logs, review process (c)(1) Integrity Write statements denied unless the policy allows them; side-effecting functions and data-modifying CTEs denied E3 Database integrity controls and backups (c)(2) Mechanism to authenticate ePHI None for data. Audit records are hash-chained; policy bundles are signed. E1, E4 Integrity of ePHI itself (d) Person or entity authentication mTLS, OIDC, static tokens; SCRAM or certificates on the proxy E5, E7 (e)(1), (e)(2)(i), (e)(2)(ii) Transmission security TLS 1.2/1.3 on the server and on both sides of the proxy E5 TLS for paths HaltSQL is not on Also relevant: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D), information system activity review, is supported by E2, E7 and E8.

documents.t: HaltSQL 0.0.1 has not had an external security audit or penetration test (threat-model.md). Audit records do not include the context values (for example the tenant id) of a request, or the caller's network address. Join with your application logs if you need them. The audit chain is a hash chain, not a signature. It needs WORM storage or an independently kept head hash to detect whole-log rewrites. HaltSQL does not encrypt anything at rest. There is no switch that forbids unsigned policy files; enforce "signed bundles only" in change control (see hardening.md). The sidecar and the library trust the calling code to enforce the verdict. Only the proxy enforces it itself.

This page is a secure configuration baseline for production deployments of HaltSQL. It is for platform and security engineers who deploy haltsql-server or haltsql-proxy and want one list of settings to review. Each row gives the setting, the recommended value, the reason and the page with the details. Most defaults are already the safe choice. The rows marked (not default) need an explicit change.

HaltSQL is one layer of three. A bug in HaltSQL, a policy mistake, or a caller that skips the check is contained only by the database's own controls (defense-in-depth.md). Setting Recommended value Why Details Database role for agent queries A dedicated role: NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION NOBYPASSRLS, SELECT granted only on the policy's tables and columns The database still enforces the basics if HaltSQL is bypassed or wrong Layer 1 Role session defaults default_transaction_read_only = on, statement_timeout (for example 5s), lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout HaltSQL does not bound how long an allowed query runs Layer 1 Role search_path Identical to the policy's search_path Otherwise an unqualified name can resolve to a different table than the one HaltSQL checked defense-in-depth.md Row-level security ENABLE and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on every tenant table, keyed on a setting your application sets per transaction Tenant isolation holds even if a query escapes HaltSQL Layer 2 RLS coverage check Run haltsql rls check against the live database in CI or after migrations Reports where the role, grants and RLS policies in the database have drifted from the HaltSQL policy rls-generation.md Dangerous functions Revoke EXECUTE from PUBLIC on functions you do not need (for example pg_sleep) Defense in depth for functions a policy might allow by mistake defense-in-depth.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details mode enforce (the default). Use shadow only during a rollout. A policy in shadow mode reports violations but allows the query policy-reference.md tenancy.mode bound (the default) The tenant value is a bound parameter supplied from the context, never written by the model tenancy.md statements.allow [select] (the default) unless writes are required Read-only agents should not be able to write, whatever the SQL says policy-reference.md require_limit.max Set it (not default), for example 1000 Bounds rows per query; every SELECT must end in a constant LIMIT n with n <= max policy-reference.md limits Keep the defaults (max_bytes 16384, max_depth 64, max_nodes 20000, max_joins 8) or lower Bounds parsing and analysis cost and query shape policy-reference.md tables.*.columns Explicit column lists; avoid "*" on tables with sensitive columns "*" allows every current and future column schema-and-pii.md allow_explain false (the default) Plans expose planner estimates (row counts) that the agent does not need; EXPLAIN ANALYZE is always denied policy-reference.md Policy tests Run haltsql validate, haltsql lint-policy and haltsql test in CI on every policy change Catches policies that allow more than intended before they ship policy-ci.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details Policy source Load policies only from signed bundles: policies[].bundle or policies[].bundle_source (not default) The server verifies the Ed25519 signature before it reads a policy, so a compromised file system or delivery channel cannot change them policy-bundles.md public_keys Only the current signing key, plus the next one during a rotation Any listed key may sign Key management Signing key Generated with haltsql bundle keygen, stored as a protected CI secret, never committed Whoever holds it can authorize any policy policy-ci.md bundle_source.oci A digest-pinned reference (repo@sha256:...) for immutable deployments, or a tag with monotonic metadata.version The poller refuses rollbacks; a digest pins the exact artifact config-reference.md cache_dir Set, on a writable volume The server can restart from the last verified bundle while the source is down; the cache is re-verified on every start policy-bundles.md Note: there is no setting that forbids plain path: or inline: policies. To enforce "signed bundles only", review the config in change control, and check that every policy in GET /v1/admin/status has origin: bundle_source (or bundle_or_file for local bundles).

Setting Recommended value Why Details server.tls Enabled (not default) whenever traffic leaves the pod or host; min_version: "1.3" if all clients support it Without it, tokens and SQL cross the network in clear text Built-in TLS server.listen 127.0.0.1:8080 (the default) when TLS is terminated elsewhere or the agent is in the same pod Keeps the plaintext listener off the network. The container image sets HALTSQL_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080, which overrides the config file. config-reference.md server.tls.client_auth required with server.auth.mtls identities, for service-to-service callers Strong workload identity; the context comes from config, not the request mTLS identities Caller authentication OIDC or mTLS rather than static tokens when the tenant or user must come from an authenticated identity With static tokens the request body supplies the whole context authentication.md server.auth.oidc[].context_claims Map the tenant (and user) fields to claims The tenant comes from the signed token; the body cannot override it (403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED) OIDC request_context_fields [] (the default), or the smallest list that works Every listed field is supplied by the caller, not the identity authentication.md server.auth.oidc[].required_claims A scope or audience-specific claim, for example scope: sql.verify Rejects tokens the IdP issued for other purposes OIDC policy_from_groups Most privileged groups first; default: null; on Entra ID prefer app roles (claim: roles) The first match wins; no default means unknown callers are rejected; app roles never overflow Policies from IdP groups Static tokens One token per agent, at least 32 random bytes (openssl rand -hex 32), only token_sha256 in config HaltSQL stores an unsalted SHA-256, which is safe only for high-entropy tokens config-reference.md server.auth.allow_unauthenticated false (the default); leave HALTSQL_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED unset Unauthenticated callers can name any loaded policy or use default_policy config-reference.md default_policy Unset (the default) Only used for unauthenticated requests and requests that name no policy config-reference.md server.admin Disabled (the default), or callers limited to mTLS or OIDC identities of operators The admin report reveals query patterns, and with log_raw_sql some SQL config-reference.md /metrics, /healthz, /readyz Restrict with a NetworkPolicy, or serve probes on --health-listen and disable Prometheus (telemetry.metrics.prometheus: false) if unused These endpoints need no authentication; metrics are labelled with policy names and reason codes http-api.md limits.max_request_bytes 1048576 (the default) or lower Bounds request size config-reference.md secrets and placeholders Every credential through ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...}, ${file:...} or ${env:...}; never inline Config files and ConfigMaps hold no secrets secrets.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details on_error fail_closed (the default) on at least one sink No verdict is served without its audit record Failure policy buffer / drop buffer only where availability matters more than synchronous auditing; drop only next to another fail_closed sink drop discards records with no gap marker in the chain config-reference.md audit.log_raw_sql false (the default) SQL can contain sensitive literals; records always carry sql_sha256 and the fingerprint config-reference.md Durable sink s3 with object_lock: {mode: COMPLIANCE, retain_days: N} and a spool_dir on persistent storage (not default), or gcs with a bucket retention policy WORM storage stops whole-log rewrites; the spool keeps the chain continuous across restarts Restarts and chain continuity Chain verification Run haltsql audit verify --expect-head <recorded head> on a schedule and alert on failure A chain proves nothing unless someone checks it audit-verify.md Kafka sink tls enabled, sasl with scram-sha-512, acks: all (the default) Without tls the sink is plaintext config-reference.md File sink volume Mount a writable volume at /var/log/haltsql only if you use the file sink The rest of the root filesystem stays read-only deployment.md Alerts On haltsql_audit_errors_total, haltsql_audit_sink_healthy == 0 and haltsql_reasons_total{code="E_INTERNAL"} Detects audit loss and internal errors early http-api.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details opa.on_error deny (the default) An unreachable or misconfigured OPA must not allow queries opa.md opa.url A loopback sidecar, or https with tls.ca_file Plain http is accepted only for loopback config-reference.md opa.headers A bearer token from a secret placeholder, with OPA's own authentication enabled Stops other workloads from changing OPA's answers opa.md OPA can only add denials: a query HaltSQL denies is never sent to OPA, and no OPA answer turns a denial into an allow. There is nothing to configure for this.

Setting Recommended value Why Details tls Configured (not default); required: true (the default once tls is set) Without a tls section the proxy accepts plaintext clients proxy.md auth.method cert with tls.client_auth: require, or scram with long random passwords The identity selects the policy and the context proxy.md upstream.tls.mode verify-full with upstream.tls.ca (not default; the default is disable) require encrypts without verifying the server proxy.md upstream.user A least-privilege, read-only role, as in Database The proxy's credentials are the only ones clients use proxy.md upstream.password A ${env:...} or ${file:...} placeholder Never in the file proxy.md limits Set max_connections, max_message_bytes, idle_timeout_seconds for your load Bounds what one client can consume proxy.md audit A sink with on_error: fail_closed (the default) No statement reaches the database without its audit record proxy.md Network Only the proxy can reach the database (security groups, NetworkPolicy, pg_hba.conf) A client that reaches PostgreSQL directly bypasses the proxy deploy-aws.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details Image ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql pinned by digest, signature verified with cosign verify Ensures you run the artifact the release workflow built supply-chain.md Base image The default distroless/static-debian12:nonroot runtime stage No shell, no libc, no package manager deployment.md User Non-root, uid/gid 65532 (the image default) Limits the impact of a process compromise Dockerfile Root filesystem readOnlyRootFilesystem: true / docker run --read-only Nothing in the image writes to the root filesystem Dockerfile Container security context allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: [ALL], seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, runAsNonRoot: true Set by the Helm chart's defaults values.yaml Service account token automountServiceAccountToken: false (the chart default) unless Vault Kubernetes auth needs it HaltSQL does not call the Kubernetes API values.yaml NetworkPolicy networkPolicy.enabled: true (the chart default) with ingressFrom set to the agent pods (an empty list allows any pod in the namespace); egress limited with extraRules to the endpoints you configured Egress is denied by default because verification needs no network access values.yaml Sidecar topology One haltsql-server per agent pod, reached on 127.0.0.1 Verification traffic never leaves the pod deployment.md systemd The shipped unit (DynamicUser, ProtectSystem=strict, NoNewPrivileges, empty CapabilityBoundingSet, and more) Same isolation outside containers; check with systemd-analyze security deployment.md

Setting Recommended value Why Details Execution path Only the SDK's guarded-execute helper It checks sql_sha256, binds bind_params, and treats any error as a denial deployment-modes.md statement_timeout_ms, max_rows (Python SDK) Set both HaltSQL does not limit run time sdk-python.md haltsql-mcp row cap and timeout Keep --row-cap (default 200) and --statement-timeout-ms (default 5000) Bounds what one tool call can return and how long it runs mcp.md haltsql-mcp HTTP transport A tokens file, and a TLS proxy in front The MCP server has no built-in TLS mcp.md

haltsql config show --config FILE prints the effective configuration (flags, HALTSQL_* environment and file merged) with secrets redacted. GET /v1/admin/status shows loaded policies, their origin and mode, bundle signer key ids, audit sink health and the OPA settings. haltsql-proxy validate -c FILE --json prints the proxy's effective config with secrets redacted.

This page is the starting point for a security review of HaltSQL. It is for security engineers, architects and auditors who need to know what HaltSQL does, what data it touches, what it sends where, and which guarantees hold. Each section links to the reference page that has the details.

HaltSQL is a policy firewall for SQL that a large language model (LLM) generates for PostgreSQL. It receives three inputs: a SQL string, a policy and a context (tenant id, user id and so on, taken from your application's authenticated session). It parses the SQL with libpg_query, which is extracted from the PostgreSQL source, and returns a verdict: allowed or denied, with reason codes. See threat-model.md for the assets, adversary and guarantees. HaltSQL is self-hosted software, licensed MIT. It is not a hosted service: nothing it processes is sent to the HaltSQL project.

It does not rewrite SQL. A verdict is about the exact input string. The verdict carries sql_sha256, the SHA-256 of that string, so a caller can check that it runs what was verified. The wire proxy forwards the verified SQL byte for byte; the only thing it changes is the value of tenancy parameters in Bind messages, which it overwrites with the session's context values (proxy.md). The verifier does not connect to the database. The library, haltsql verify and haltsql-server have no database connection; the server does not link the PostgreSQL client code. The components that do connect are listed in Data flows. It does not detect prompt injection. It judges the SQL, not the prompt. It does not replace database permissions or row-level security (RLS). It is one of three layers (defense-in-depth.md). It does not decide whether showing allowed data is appropriate. It limits which relations, columns, functions and rows a query may touch.

Component Binary or package Talks to PostgreSQL? Library OCaml library haltsql; the native libhaltsql used by the Python and TypeScript packages No CLI haltsql Only haltsql schema pull and haltsql rls check, which you run with a DSN you supply (schema-and-pii.md, rls-generation.md) HTTP sidecar haltsql-server No Wire proxy haltsql-proxy Yes: it is the client's connection to the database, using its own service credentials SDK guarded-execute helpers clients/python, clients/typescript, clients/go, clients/java Yes, through the connection your application passes in MCP server haltsql-mcp Yes: it runs verified queries in a read-only transaction (mcp.md) Kubernetes operator deploy/operator No; it manages ConfigMaps and haltsql-server Deployments (kubernetes-operator.md)
Everything stays in your process. The library writes no audit records and makes no network calls. Your code is responsible for running only allowed SQL and for any logging.
The server answers; the caller enforces. Outbound calls happen only for features you configure (dotted lines).

The proxy enforces the verdict itself. The client never sees the database credentials and cannot choose its policy or tenant: both are bound to the proxy user or certificate identity in the proxy config.

Data Library / CLI haltsql-server haltsql-proxy SQL text Sees it Sees it; not stored or logged unless audit.log_raw_sql: true Sees it; not logged unless audit.log_raw_sql: true Context values (tenant id, user id) Sees them Sees them; not written to audit records Holds them in its config; not written to audit records Bind parameter values Not involved Returned to the caller in bind_params; not audited Writes them into Bind; audit records list parameter numbers only, never values Query results Never Never Relayed from PostgreSQL to the client; not stored or logged Credentials None Stores SHA-256 hashes of static tokens, never the tokens; OIDC tokens are verified and never logged or stored Stores SCRAM verifiers, never passwords; holds the upstream password in memory
documents.s: What each component sees, stores, logs and sends

documents.t: haltsql-server writes one record per verify request that reaches a verdict, to every configured sink (bin/server/lib/audit.ml, Audit.record_fields): Field Content ts Timestamp request_id Request id caller Token name, oidc:<provider>, mtls:<subject> or anonymous caller_type token, oidc, mtls or anonymous subject OIDC sub, SPIFFE ID or certificate CN; null for static tokens policy, policy_version Policy name and content hash allowed, shadow Verdict, and whether shadow-mode reasons were present codes Reason codes sql_sha256 SHA-256 of the exact SQL string fingerprint libpg_query fingerprint (equal for queries that differ only in literals) elapsed_us Verification time sql Only with audit.log_raw_sql: true prev_hash, hash Hash chain Not recorded: context values, bind values, bearer tokens, the request body, the caller's IP address. haltsql-proxy writes one record per verified statement (lib/pgwire/session.ml): ts, event, session (a session id), user (the proxy user), policy, policy_version, protocol, allowed, reasons, shadow_reasons, sql_sha256, fingerprint, tables, bind_params (parameter numbers only), the prepared statement name when there is one, sql only with log_raw_sql: true, and the hash chain. Proxy-level denials carry reasons and message. See proxy.md. Note: sql_sha256 is not anonymisation. A hash of a short query with guessable literals can be recovered by trying candidates. Treat audit records as potentially sensitive even with log_raw_sql off.

Logs are JSON (or text) lines on stderr. Secret values, tokens and key material are never logged (secrets.md). OIDC rejections are logged with a reason code and the peer address (authentication.md). Proxy logs record connections, authentication results, denials, audit failures and reloads, and never contain passwords, verifiers, SCRAM messages, keys or bind values (proxy.md). OTLP spans carry the SQL hash (db.statement.sha256), never the SQL, even with log_raw_sql on. GET /metrics exposes counters labelled by policy name, reason code, route and status. It contains no SQL or context values. HaltSQL does not send usage telemetry anywhere. Outbound connections go only to endpoints you configure.

When opa is configured, haltsql-server sends OPA the caller name and type, policy name and version, statement kind, tables, columns, reason codes, sql_sha256, fingerprint and the names of the context fields. It never sends the SQL text, context values, tokens or the OIDC subject (opa.md).

With server.admin.enabled, the server keeps a rolling in-memory window of recent verdicts for GET /v1/admin/report, bounded by report_window (default 24h) and max_tracked_queries. It keeps raw SQL for one record per query fingerprint only when audit.log_raw_sql is on. Nothing is kept while the admin API is disabled (shadow-reports.md).

Listener Default Notes haltsql-server API 127.0.0.1:8080 (the container image sets 0.0.0.0:8080) /v1/* requires authentication. /healthz, /readyz and /metrics do not. haltsql-server --health-listen off Plain HTTP, serves only /healthz and /readyz haltsql-proxy 127.0.0.1:6432 PostgreSQL wire protocol haltsql-mcp HTTP transport 8765 in the documented examples Bearer tokens from a tokens file; no built-in TLS; refuses HTTP off loopback without a tokens file (mcp.md) The container image exposes 8080 and 6432. Server connection limits (--max-connections 1024, --request-timeout 30 s, --idle-timeout 60 s, a 64 KiB cap on request heads, a 1 MiB body limit by default) and proxy limits (max_connections, max_message_bytes, auth_timeout_seconds) bound what a client can consume (deployment.md, proxy.md). Outbound connections, all opt-in: Feature Destination OIDC Discovery document and JWKS of each configured issuer (HTTPS) Secret placeholders Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager Audit sinks S3, GCS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Kafka Bundle sources OCI registry, S3, HTTPS OPA The configured OPA URL OTLP The configured collector Proxy The upstream PostgreSQL server

haltsql-server authenticates every /v1/* request, in this order (authentication.md): mTLS identity: a client certificate verified against server.tls.client_ca whose SPIFFE ID or subject CN matches a configured identity. OIDC/JWT: signature checked against the issuer's JWKS (RS256, RS384, RS512, PS256, ES256, ES384, EdDSA; none and HMAC are always rejected), plus iss, aud, exp, nbf, iat and required_claims. Static bearer tokens: the token's SHA-256 compared in constant time with every configured hash. Authorization is by policy pinning. Every identity is pinned to exactly one policy (OIDC can select from an allowlist, or map IdP groups to policies). A request that names another policy gets 403. For OIDC and mTLS callers the context comes from the verified identity; the request body may add only the fields listed in request_context_fields, and anything else is refused with 403 CONTEXT_NOT_ALLOWED. Static-token callers supply the whole context in the body, so the calling service is trusted to fill it from its session. server.auth.allow_unauthenticated (default false) accepts requests without credentials. It is for local development only. The admin API (/v1/admin/status, /v1/admin/report) is off by default. When enabled, only callers listed in server.admin.callers may use it, and unauthenticated callers never can. haltsql-proxy authenticates clients with SCRAM-SHA-256 (no channel binding) or a TLS client certificate. Unknown users go through a full fake exchange so user names cannot be probed. Client certificate revocation (CRL, OCSP) is not checked (proxy.md).

Use Algorithm Source haltsql-server TLS TLS 1.2 and 1.3 (min_version: "1.3" for 1.3 only). TLS 1.2 limited to ECDHE with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305; TLS 1.3 to AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Renegotiation disabled. bin/server/lib/tls_setup.ml haltsql-proxy TLS (client side and upstream) The defaults of the ocaml-tls library: TLS 1.2 and 1.3, AEAD cipher suites, no renegotiation. The version range is not configurable. lib/pgwire/server.ml, lib/pgwire/upstream.ml Client certificate validation RFC 5280 path validation against the configured CA authentication.md Outbound HTTPS host checks Host name matched against DNS SubjectAltName entries only authentication.md Policy bundle signatures Ed25519 (RFC 8032) over a domain separator plus the exact bundle bytes policy-bundles.md Bundle and object digests SHA-256 (OCI blobs: SHA-256 or SHA-512) policy-bundles.md Audit chain hash = sha256_hex(prev_hash ^ record). This is a hash chain, not a signature or MAC. audit-sinks.md Static token storage SHA-256 of the token config-reference.md Proxy client passwords SCRAM-SHA-256 verifiers in PostgreSQL's stored format (haltsql-proxy scram-verifier refuses fewer than 4096 iterations) proxy.md AWS requests SigV4 lib/cloud/sigv4.ml The TLS and cryptography implementations are OCaml libraries (tls, x509, mirage-crypto, digestif, kdf), statically linked into the release binaries; the release builds do not link OpenSSL. HaltSQL makes no FIPS 140 claim. Note: the audit hash chain detects edits, deletions, insertions and reordering relative to other records. Someone who can rewrite the whole log can rebuild a valid chain. Keep the head hash elsewhere, ship to a second sink, or use WORM storage (audit-verify.md).

Config files never need to contain secrets. Placeholders resolve values from environment variables, files, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager and Google Secret Manager at load time (secrets.md). An unresolvable placeholder is a load error; HaltSQL never substitutes an empty string. Placeholders are rejected inside policies. haltsql config show and haltsql-proxy validate print the effective config with secrets redacted. Static tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes; proxy passwords as SCRAM verifiers. Bundle signing private keys are written with mode 0600, and haltsql bundle sign --key refuses a key file that group or others can read. Error messages and logs never contain secret values, tokens or key material. A reload builds a fresh resolver, so rotated secrets are picked up on the next SIGHUP or file-watch reload.

Situation Result Parse error, unsupported syntax, limit breach, internal error allowed: false. verify never raises. Audit sink cannot be written (on_error: fail_closed, the default) Server: 503 AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE instead of a verdict, and /readyz returns 503. Proxy: the statement is refused with SQLSTATE 58030. OIDC keys unavailable past the stale window 503 AUTH_UNAVAILABLE OPA unreachable or malformed answer (on_error: deny, the default) Query denied with E_EXTERNAL_POLICY Bundle signature, digest or structure invalid Bundle not loaded; at startup with no cached good bundle, the server does not start Config or policy fails to load Startup exits with code 2; a failed reload keeps the last good configuration Any non-200, timeout or connection error from the sidecar SDKs and haltsql-mcp treat it as a denial; nothing runs These defaults can be relaxed on purpose: audit.on_error: buffer (and drop on streaming sinks and the proxy), opa.on_error: allow_haltsql_verdict, allow_unauthenticated, and policies in mode: shadow, which report violations but allow the query. See hardening.md for the recommended values.

If HaltSQL returns allowed: true for a tenancy-scoped policy, every occurrence of a tenant-scoped relation is filtered to the caller's tenant in its own scope, as a top-level AND conjunct of WHERE or ON. In bound mode the tenant value is a $n parameter that the caller binds from bind_params, so the model never sees or chooses it (tenancy.md). The guarantee rests on assumptions: The context is trusted. If the context comes from the prompt, the model or the SQL, the proof is about the wrong tenant (threat-model.md). The caller runs exactly the verified string and binds exactly bind_params. With the library and the sidecar, application code is trusted to do this; with the proxy, the proxy does it. Views and functions are opaque. A view or function the policy allows may read other tenants' data internally. Inference and timing channels on the database side are not addressed. One process, many policies. A single haltsql-server can serve many callers and policies. They are separated by policy pinning, not by process isolation. Run separate instances if you need separate failure or blast-radius domains. Keep database-side controls (a least-privilege role and RLS) as the second and third layers (defense-in-depth.md).

HaltSQL is pre-1.0. Version 0.0.1 has not had an external security audit (threat-model.md). Testing includes an attack corpus, property tests, a mutation fuzzer and a lab that runs every allowed query against real PostgreSQL under independent oracles (how-it-works/assurance.md). Vulnerabilities are reported privately (SECURITY.md).

This page answers questions that commonly appear in vendor security questionnaires (SIG, CAIQ and in-house forms). It is for the people filling those forms in about HaltSQL, and for reviewers who receive them. Answers are short and link to the page with the details. Many service-oriented questions do not apply: HaltSQL is self-hosted software that you run in your own environment, not a service operated by the HaltSQL project.

Question Answer What is HaltSQL? A policy firewall that checks LLM-generated PostgreSQL queries against an allowlist policy and a trusted context before they run. See overview.md. Is it SaaS, hosted or self-hosted? Self-hosted. You run the library, CLI, haltsql-server, haltsql-proxy or haltsql-mcp in your own infrastructure. Licence MIT (LICENSE). The vendored libpg_query has its own licence, shipped as LICENSE.libpg_query. Maturity Pre-1.0 (0.1.x). Only the latest release receives security fixes (SECURITY.md). Who maintains it? The maintainers listed in GOVERNANCE.md. A change needs approval from one maintainer. Is there a commercial support agreement or SLA? None is described in this repository.

Question Answer What customer data does the vendor access? None. HaltSQL does not send data to the HaltSQL project and has no usage telemetry. What data does HaltSQL process? SQL text, the context (for example tenant and user ids), policies and caller credentials. The wire proxy and haltsql-mcp also relay query results. See overview.md. Does it store query results? No. Does it log SQL text? Not by default. Audit records carry the SHA-256 and fingerprint of the SQL; the text is added only with audit.log_raw_sql: true. Does it log bind values or context values? No. The proxy's audit records list bind parameter numbers only. Does it log credentials or tokens? No. Tokens, passwords, SCRAM messages, keys and secret values are never logged (secrets.md, proxy.md). Data residency Wherever you deploy it. Data goes only to endpoints you configure (audit sinks, OIDC provider, secret stores, OPA, OTLP collector, bundle sources, the database). Subprocessors Not applicable: there is no hosted service. Data retention HaltSQL has no retention period of its own. Audit records are kept as long as the sink you choose keeps them (bucket lifecycle or Object Lock period, index lifecycle, topic retention). The admin report window is in memory and bounded by report_window (default 24h). Data deletion Delete records in the sink. HaltSQL has no deletion API. With WORM storage (S3 Object Lock, GCS retention), records cannot be deleted before the retention period ends. Backups Not applicable to HaltSQL itself; it is stateless apart from audit spools and bundle caches. Back up your audit storage and policy repository.

Question Answer Encryption in transit haltsql-server: built-in TLS 1.2/1.3 with ECDHE and AEAD ciphers only, optional mTLS. haltsql-proxy: TLS to clients and to PostgreSQL. Outbound HTTPS checks the certificate chain and the host name against DNS SubjectAltNames. See authentication.md and proxy.md. Is TLS on by default? No. The server listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 in plain HTTP unless server.tls is set; the proxy accepts plaintext unless tls is configured, and connects upstream without TLS unless upstream.tls.mode is set. See hardening.md. Encryption at rest HaltSQL does not encrypt data at rest. Audit files, spool directories and bundle caches are written in plain text; use encrypted volumes and buckets. Cryptographic libraries OCaml tls, x509, mirage-crypto and digestif, statically linked. The release builds do not link OpenSSL. FIPS 140 validation No. Key management You manage all keys: TLS certificates (hot-reloaded on SIGHUP or file change), bundle signing keys (Ed25519), static token hashes. See policy-bundles.md.

Question Answer How do callers authenticate? mTLS client certificates, OIDC/JWT bearer tokens, or static bearer tokens stored as SHA-256 hashes. The proxy uses SCRAM-SHA-256 or client certificates. See authentication.md. SSO / IdP integration OIDC: any issuer with a discovery document and JWKS. Policies can be selected from IdP groups or roles. MFA Not applicable: callers are services or tokens issued by your IdP. MFA is enforced by your IdP when it issues tokens. Authorization model Each identity is pinned to exactly one policy. The policy is an allowlist of statements, tables, columns and functions, with tenant scoping. Can a caller choose its tenant? Not with OIDC or mTLS: the tenant comes from the token or certificate configuration, and body fields outside request_context_fields are refused. With static tokens the calling service supplies the context. With the proxy, the context is bound to the proxy user. Admin access The admin API is off by default. When enabled, only callers listed in server.admin.callers may use it (config-reference.md). There is no web console and no default account or password. Unauthenticated endpoints /healthz, /readyz and /metrics. Restrict them at the network level, or use --health-listen (http-api.md).

Question Answer Does it produce audit logs? Yes. One record per decision, hash-chained, to stdout, file, S3, GCS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or Kafka (audit-sinks.md). What is in an audit record? Timestamp, request id, caller, caller type, subject, policy and policy version, verdict, reason codes, SQL hash, fingerprint, timing, and the chain hashes (overview.md). Are logs tamper-evident? The chain detects edited, deleted, inserted and reordered records. It is a hash chain, not a signature; use WORM storage or an independently stored head hash to detect a full rewrite (audit-verify.md). What happens if logging fails? By default the request is refused (503 from the server, SQLSTATE 58030 from the proxy). buffer and drop modes are opt-in. SIEM integration Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Kafka sinks; stdout for any log shipper. Monitoring Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry (OTLP) traces and metrics (observability.md).

Question Answer Where are secrets stored? In your secret store. Config files reference them with ${env:...}, ${file:...}, ${vault:...}, ${aws-sm:...} or ${gcp-sm:...} placeholders (secrets.md). Are secrets ever shown? No. haltsql config show and haltsql-proxy validate redact them; error messages never include them. Hard-coded credentials None. There are no default passwords or tokens.

Question Answer Listening ports haltsql-server 8080 (default 127.0.0.1), an optional health port; haltsql-proxy 6432 (default 127.0.0.1). See overview.md. Outbound connections Only to endpoints you configure. None are required for verification. Does it need internet access? No.

Question Answer Secure SDLC Changes go through pull requests with maintainer approval; security-sensitive changes need allowed and denied tests; every fixed bypass adds an attack-corpus case (GOVERNANCE.md, SECURITY.md). Testing About 3,300 OCaml test cases, an attack corpus, property tests, a mutation fuzzer, integration tests, and a lab that runs every allowed query against real PostgreSQL under independent oracles (how-it-works/assurance.md, testing.md). Static analysis (SAST) No SAST tool runs on the OCaml code; CodeQL does not support OCaml. Trivy scans configuration and secrets weekly. Penetration testing / external audit None. HaltSQL 0.0.1 has not had an external security audit (threat-model.md). Bug bounty No bug bounty programme is described. SECURITY.md offers safe harbor for good-faith research.

Question Answer How are vulnerabilities reported? Privately through GitHub Security Advisories (SECURITY.md). Response targets Acknowledgement within 3 business days, assessment within 10 business days, fixes for confirmed high or critical issues normally within 30 days (SECURITY.md). Disclosure policy 90-day coordinated disclosure. Confirmed vulnerabilities get a GitHub Security Advisory and, where appropriate, a CVE. How are customers notified? Through GitHub Security Advisories and the changelog. There is no private customer notification list. Dependency scanning Weekly Trivy image scans (HIGH/CRITICAL), dependency review on pull requests, Dependabot for Actions, base images and SDK dependencies. OCaml dependencies are pinned by opam-repository commit and updated by hand (supply-chain.md). Incident response for the service Not applicable: there is no hosted service. Your incident response covers your deployment.

Question Answer Major dependencies libpg_query (vendored, PostgreSQL's parser), OCaml libraries for TLS, X.509, crypto, HTTP and YAML/JSON. The exact opam package list is in /usr/share/doc/haltsql/opam-packages.txt in the image. SBOM Yes: a CycloneDX SBOM per release and an SPDX SBOM attestation on the image. Neither is guaranteed to list every statically linked OCaml library (supply-chain.md). Signed releases Yes: keyless cosign signatures on tarballs, checksums, SBOM and images; GitHub build-provenance attestations; npm provenance (supply-chain.md). Container base image gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot, pinned by digest; runs as uid 65532 with a read-only root filesystem.

Question Answer SLA / uptime Not applicable: you operate it. High availability haltsql-server is stateless; run several replicas behind a Service (the Helm chart includes a PodDisruptionBudget and HPA), or one sidecar per agent pod (deployment.md). Behaviour on failure Fail closed: errors produce denials, and an unavailable audit sink, IdP or OPA leads to refusals rather than unaudited or unchecked queries (overview.md). Policy updates without downtime Atomic hot reload on SIGHUP, file change or a new signed bundle; a failed reload keeps the last good configuration.

Question Answer Certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS) None. HaltSQL is open-source software, not a certified service. compliance.md maps its features to controls you operate. Will you sign a BAA or DPA? Not applicable: the HaltSQL project does not process your data.
overview.md hardening.md compliance.md supply-chain.md threat-model.md SECURITY.md

This page describes how HaltSQL releases are built and published, and how to verify an artifact before you run it. It is for security reviewers and platform teams who need to check signatures, provenance and SBOMs, or answer supply-chain questions about HaltSQL. Everything here is taken from the workflows in .github/workflows/, the Dockerfile and .github/dependabot.yml.

A release is triggered by pushing a vX.Y.Z tag (or by running the release workflow by hand for an existing tag). Release-candidate tags (vX.Y.Z-rc.N) and manual runs with dry_run are rehearsals: they run every build, signing and provenance step but publish only a draft release and packages under ghcr.io/haltsql/dryrun/; see releasing.md. .github/workflows/release.yml produces: Artifact Where Built by haltsql-<tag>-linux-amd64.tar.gz, haltsql-<tag>-linux-arm64.tar.gz GitHub release The dist stage of the Dockerfile: static musl binaries haltsql, haltsql-server, haltsql-proxy, plus licences haltsql-<tag>-darwin-arm64.tar.gz GitHub release A macos-15 runner with ocaml/setup-ocaml; links only system libraries haltsql-<tag>.cdx.json GitHub release CycloneDX SBOM (see SBOMs) haltsql-<version>.tgz GitHub release The Helm chart archive (helm package deploy/helm/haltsql) haltsql-<tag>.oci.txt GitHub release The digests of the three images and the chart as pushed to GHCR SHA256SUMS GitHub release SHA-256 of every tarball, the chart archive, the SBOM and haltsql-<tag>.oci.txt *.sigstore.json GitHub release Keyless cosign signature bundle for every file above and SHA256SUMS ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:<version> GHCR The runtime stage of the Dockerfile, linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp:<version> GHCR clients/mcp/Dockerfile, on top of the haltsql image by digest ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-console:<version> GHCR The console stage of the Dockerfile, linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 oci://ghcr.io/haltsql/charts/haltsql, version <version> GHCR The same chart archive, pushed with helm push .github/workflows/native-packages.yml publishes, on v* tags: Artifact Where Notes haltsql wheels and sdist, haltsql-mcp wheel and sdist PyPI Trusted publishing (OIDC, no long-lived PyPI token), through the pypi and pypi-mcp environments @haltsql/client and @haltsql/native-<platform> npm Published with npm publish --provenance, through the npm environment, by npm trusted publishing (OIDC); the first publish only uses a short-lived NPM_TOKEN Not published by these workflows: the Kubernetes operator image (you build it from deploy/operator, see kubernetes-operator.md), the Java SDK and the Go SDK (Go modules are fetched from the repository).

Control What exists Source Pinned GitHub Actions Every third-party action in every workflow is pinned to a full commit SHA, with the version in a comment .github/workflows/*.yml Pinned base images Builder (ocaml/opam:alpine-3.22-ocaml-5.3) and runtime (gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot) pinned by digest; the Dockerfile syntax image too Dockerfile Pinned OCaml dependencies The Linux release build resolves opam packages against a fixed opam-repository commit (OPAM_REPOSITORY_COMMIT), so tarballs and image ship the same dependency versions. The resolved list is written to /usr/share/doc/haltsql/opam-packages.txt in the image. Dockerfile Vendored parser libpg_query is vendored in vendor/libpg_query and compiled from source Dockerfile, vendor/ Static linking check The build fails unless every binary is statically linked, runs, and runs on an empty (scratch) filesystem Dockerfile, release.yml Smoke test before push Each architecture's image is built on a native runner (amd64 and arm64, no emulation), run against PostgreSQL 17 by scripts/docker-smoke.sh (including the proxy), and only then pushed by digest and merged into the multi-arch index release.yml Least-privilege workflow tokens Workflows default to permissions: contents: read; jobs that publish add only packages: write, id-token: write, attestations: write or contents: write as needed .github/workflows/*.yml No persisted checkout credentials actions/checkout runs with persist-credentials: false .github/workflows/*.yml Workflow linting actionlint, from a digest-pinned image, on every PR security.yml Known gaps: The macOS release tarball, the macOS wheel and npm package, and the Linux libhaltsql.so in the wheels and npm packages are built with opam install --deps-only against the current opam-repository, not the pinned commit. Their OCaml dependency versions can differ from the Linux tarballs and the image. The manylinux_2_28 build container used for libhaltsql.so is referenced by tag, not digest. Builds are not documented or tested as bit-for-bit reproducible. The macOS binaries are not signed with an Apple Developer ID or notarized. (The libhaltsql dylib in the macOS wheel has an ad-hoc signature only.)

Artifact Signature Provenance Release tarballs Keyless cosign (cosign sign-blob --bundle) GitHub build-provenance attestation (actions/attest-build-provenance) Helm chart archive Keyless cosign (cosign sign-blob --bundle) GitHub build-provenance attestation SHA256SUMS, SBOM, haltsql-<tag>.oci.txt Keyless cosign None Helm chart in GHCR Keyless cosign on the chart's OCI digest, verified in the same job GitHub build-provenance attestation pushed to the registry haltsql, haltsql-mcp and haltsql-console images Keyless cosign on the image digest, verified in the same job BuildKit SLSA provenance (provenance: mode=max) attached to the image index, plus a GitHub build-provenance attestation pushed to the registry PyPI files Trusted publishing through pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish See the PyPI file page npm packages npm registry signatures npm provenance (--provenance) Keyless signatures are issued by Sigstore to the identity of the GitHub Actions workflow that ran, so there is no long-lived signing key to protect or leak. The certificate identity is the workflow file and ref, for example https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v0.0.1, and the OIDC issuer is https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Note: a release rebuilt by hand (workflow_dispatch) runs from the branch the workflow was dispatched on, so its certificate identity ends in @refs/heads/<branch> instead of @refs/tags/<tag>. The commands below accept only tag identities. If one fails for this reason, check with the maintainers before relaxing the identity.

SBOM Format Produced by Covers haltsql-<tag>.cdx.json (release asset) CycloneDX JSON anchore/sbom-action (Syft), run on the source tree (path: .) The dependency manifests Syft finds in the repository Image SBOM attestation SPDX (BuildKit default) docker/build-push-action with sbom: true The contents of the built image Warning: the release binaries are static OCaml executables. Neither SBOM is guaranteed to list every OCaml library linked into them, and the source-tree SBOM also includes manifests from parts of the repository that are not in the binaries (SDKs, the docs site, the lab). For the exact OCaml packages in the image and Linux tarballs, use /usr/share/doc/haltsql/opam-packages.txt from the image. That file is not included in the tarballs. There are no VEX documents.

Control What runs When Container image scan Trivy (digest-pinned) on the built image, HIGH and CRITICAL, unfixed ignored; fails the job on findings; SARIF uploaded to GitHub code scanning Weekly (Mondays) and on demand; not on pull requests Configuration and secret scan Trivy fs --scanners misconfig,secret on the repository, MEDIUM and above, SARIF uploaded Weekly and on demand Dependency review actions/dependency-review-action, fails on high severity; denies AGPL and SSPL licences Every pull request (public repository only) Static analysis of OCaml code None. CodeQL does not support OCaml. Dependabot Weekly, with a 7-day cooldown on new releases: GitHub Actions, the root Dockerfile base images, npm (clients/typescript, website), pip (clients/python, clients/mcp, lab), Go modules (clients/go/...), Maven (clients/java) .github/dependabot.yml Dependabot does not support opam. OCaml dependencies move only when the OPAM_REPOSITORY_COMMIT in the Dockerfile is bumped by hand. Dependabot is not configured for deploy/operator (Go) or for clients/mcp/Dockerfile and deploy/operator/Dockerfile base images. Vulnerability reports go through GitHub Security Advisories (SECURITY.md). Only the latest release receives security fixes while HaltSQL is pre-1.0.

You need cosign v2.4 or later (v3 works too), the GitHub CLI 2.49 or later, and jq. Replace v0.0.1 with the release you are checking. scripts/verify-release.sh v0.0.1 runs every command below (and checks that every asset is present, listed in SHA256SUMS and signed) against a downloaded release; the release workflow runs it on every release before anyone else can. The steps by hand:

TAG=v0.0.1 gh release download "$TAG" --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL --dir "haltsql-$TAG" cd "haltsql-$TAG" ID='^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' ISSUER=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com # 1. The checksum file was signed by the release workflow cosign verify-blob --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \ --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \ SHA256SUMS # 2. Every downloaded file matches it sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # macOS: shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS # 3. A tarball's own signature cosign verify-blob --bundle "haltsql-$TAG-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sigstore.json" \ --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \ "haltsql-$TAG-linux-amd64.tar.gz" # 4. Build provenance: built by this repository's workflow from this commit gh attestation verify "haltsql-$TAG-linux-amd64.tar.gz" --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL

IMAGE=ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql:0.0.1 ID='^https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' # Signature cosign verify "$IMAGE" \ --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com # GitHub build-provenance attestation gh attestation verify "oci://$IMAGE" --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL # BuildKit SBOM and SLSA provenance attached to the image index docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE" --format '{{ json .SBOM }}' docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE" --format '{{ json .Provenance }}' Deploy by digest (ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql@sha256:...), not by tag; the release notes print the digest, and haltsql-<tag>.oci.txt (covered by the signed SHA256SUMS) lists the digest of each image and the chart. The same commands work for ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp. To enforce signatures at admission time, use Sigstore policy-controller or Kyverno with the identity and issuer above.

CHART=ghcr.io/haltsql/charts/haltsql DIGEST=$(awk '$1 == "helm-chart" {sub(/.*@/, "", $2); print $2}' haltsql-$TAG.oci.txt) cosign verify "$CHART@$DIGEST" \ --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com gh attestation verify "oci://$CHART@$DIGEST" --repo HaltSQL/HaltSQL helm install haltsql "oci://$CHART" --version "${TAG#v}" # or pull the verified release asset The chart's content layer in the registry is byte-for-byte the haltsql-<version>.tgz release asset, so the asset's signature and attestation cover the registry copy too.

Note: the Python and npm packages are not published to PyPI or npm yet. These checks apply once the release workflow publishes them; until then, install from a verified source tarball or the repository. npm install @haltsql/client npm audit signatures # checks registry signatures and provenance attestations

The wheels and sdist are uploaded by trusted publishing from .github/workflows/native-packages.yml. Check the file's provenance on its PyPI page, and pin hashes in production (pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt).

The signatures above cover HaltSQL itself. Your policies have their own supply chain: signed with your Ed25519 key in your CI, and verified by every server before any policy is read. See policy-bundles.md and policy-ci.md.

A new or stricter policy usually starts in shadow mode: queries are still allowed, and the would-be denials go to the audit log as shadow reasons. haltsql report reads those audit logs and tells you what the policy would have blocked, and why. It then suggests small, conservative changes, each with the exact YAML to add. It can also write a patched policy for you to review. The same report is served live by haltsql-server at GET /v1/admin/report. haltsql report /var/log/haltsql/audit.jsonl --since 7d haltsql report audit/ --suggest --policy-file policy.yaml --pii pii.json haltsql report audit.jsonl --apply-to policy.yaml -o policy.next.yaml

The report reads the JSON-lines audit records of both producers. Records of both kinds can be mixed in one run. Producer Where the records are What a record carries haltsql-server audit.sinks: stdout, file, and the s3/gcs objects (download them; the report searches directories recursively) caller, policy, policy_version, allowed, shadow, codes, fingerprint, sql_sha256, [sql] haltsql-proxy its audit sink user, policy, allowed, reasons, shadow_reasons, tables, fingerprint, [sql], and local denials (event: parse, bind, function_call) The record formats are described in audit-sinks.md and proxy.md. INPUT is a file, a directory (searched recursively for *.jsonl, *.ndjson, *.json and *.log, in name order), or - for stdin. Lines that are not audit records, such as log lines or other JSON, are skipped and counted. For each file, the report states whether its hash chain verifies (hash chain ok (N records), HASH CHAIN BROKEN at line N, or not hash-chained). Run haltsql audit verify for a strict check from genesis.

An audit record has reason codes only. A record says E_COLUMN_DENIED, but not which column was denied. To name the column, function, table or LIMIT, the report needs one of these: Raw SQL in the records plus the policy. Set audit.log_raw_sql: true (server) or audit.log_raw_sql (proxy), and pass --policy-file. The report re-verifies each denied record's SQL against that policy. It keeps only the reasons whose codes the record itself carries: the record decides what happened, and the re-verification only names the objects. The server endpoint. It sees the full verdict of every request, so it can name the objects even without raw SQL. Without detail, the summary still works, but suggestions can't be made for those records. The report counts them as missing_detail. Raw SQL can contain sensitive literals. The report prints SQL only from records that already contain it.

Section What it shows Totals Records, and how many were allowed, denied (enforce mode) or shadow-denied (allowed, but the shadow policy would have denied them). By reason code Records carrying each code. By table / By column Relations and schema.table.column the records touched or were denied on. By caller / By policy Server caller (token name, oidc:<provider>, mtls:<subject> or anonymous; the OIDC subject is in the audit record's subject, not grouped here) or proxy user, and the policy name. Over time Counts per time bucket. The bucket is 5 minutes for spans up to 6 h, 1 h up to 3 days, otherwise 1 day. Override it with --bucket 15m. Top denied queries Groups by query fingerprint, worst first, with their codes and callers. Each group shows an example SQL only when a record contains one.

Add --suggest to get suggestions. Each suggestion has: a stable id, used by --accept; an evidence count of records, split into denied and shadow-denied, plus distinct queries and callers; a one-line summary; the exact YAML to merge; review notes, if any. For example: [shop/column/app.orders.region] 23 shadow-denied queries by caller analytics read app.orders.region (E_COLUMN_DENIED); add region to tables.app.orders.columns tables: app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, status, total_cents, created_at, region] Only four kinds of change are ever suggested: Code Suggestion Conditions E_COLUMN_DENIED Add the column to the table's columns. The table is already in the policy. The column is not sensitive (see PII). E_FUNCTION_DENIED Add the function to functions.allow. The function is not on the deny list: no side effects, no dynamic SQL, no server state (pg_*, lo_*, dblink*, set_config, current_setting, nextval, query_to_xml, ts_stat, ts_rewrite, setseed, brin_summarize_*, gin_clean_pending_list, row_to_json, ...). It is not schema-qualified: user-defined functions need a human to read their definition. Identity functions such as CURRENT_USER are never allowed. E_LIMIT_TOO_HIGH Raise require_limit.max to the largest constant LIMIT seen. At most 10 times the current maximum, and at most 100000. Anything larger is listed for review ("make the queries page instead"). LIMIT $n and non-constant limits need a query fix. E_TABLE_DENIED Add the table, with the columns the queries actually read. Never a system schema. When the policy has tenancy, the new table is always tenant-scoped, on the tenant column(s) that every existing tenant-scoped table uses. If that is ambiguous (composite or mixed tenant columns), or the catalog shows the table without that column, the suggestion is listed for review instead. --min-count N sets an evidence threshold: a change must be seen in at least N records to be suggested. The default is 1. To find a new table's columns, the report re-verifies the queries with the table temporarily added. This needs records with raw SQL. Without SQL, the table suggestion is still shown, but as not applicable automatically, with an empty column list for you to fill in. Columns are always listed explicitly, never "*".

These are never turned into a policy change. Each one is listed with its record count and advice: Category Codes Advice Never relaxed: tenancy E_TENANT_MISSING, E_TENANT_MISMATCH, E_TENANT_WRITE, E_CONTEXT_MISSING Fix the query's tenant predicate, or have the caller send its context. Tenant isolation is never weakened. Never relaxed: writes E_WRITE_DENIED, E_STATEMENT_KIND, E_DATA_MODIFYING_CTE, E_SELECT_INTO, E_LOCKING_CLAUSE Grant writes deliberately, by hand. Never relaxed: external policy E_EXTERNAL_POLICY Denied by OPA; change the OPA policy, not the HaltSQL policy. Needs a query fix E_PARAM_UNBOUND, E_UNSUPPORTED, E_PARSE, E_EMPTY, E_MULTI_STATEMENT, E_LIMIT, E_LIMIT_REQUIRED, E_COLUMN_UNRESOLVED, E_OPERATOR_DENIED, E_CAST_DENIED, E_JOIN_BUDGET, E_INTERNAL The query must change, not the policy. A record can carry both a fixable code and a tenancy code, for example a denied column in a query that has no tenant predicate. In that case the column may be suggested, but the record stays denied for tenancy, and --apply-to checks that it does (see below). Individual objects that are not suggested are also listed, with a category: unsafe: a function or system catalog on the deny lists; query_fix: SELECT *, or a table that is already listed but did not resolve through search_path; already_allowed: older records, from before the policy changed; needs_review: a LIMIT far above the current maximum, or undecidable tenancy.

A column flagged as sensitive is reported under Sensitive columns (flagged, never suggested). It is never added to a policy, and it is left out of new tables. A column is flagged when either of these marks it: A PII manifest passed with --pii FILE (repeatable). This is the output of haltsql schema import. To read a raw dbt, DataHub, Unity Catalog, Atlan or Collibra export directly, add --pii-source dbt (or datahub, unity, atlan, collibra). The column-name heuristic, the same as haltsql policy draft. A name whose words include email, phone, ssn, pii, secret, personal, sensitive, and the other default terms is flagged. Turn the heuristic off with --no-pii-heuristics.

haltsql report audit/ --pii pii.json --apply-to policy.yaml -o policy.next.yaml haltsql report audit/ --apply-to policy.yaml --accept shop/function/md5 -o next.json --apply-to FILE implies --suggest and loads FILE as a policy. It applies every applicable suggestion for that policy, or only the ones you name with --accept ID. It then writes the result to -o OUT. It never edits FILE in place. The edits are structural, made on the policy document: append to tables.<t>.columns; append to functions.allow; set require_limit.max; add a tables entry with columns and tenant_column (or tenant_columns). Everything else stays as written: presets, the catalog reference, tenancy, writes and mode. A relative catalog: path is rewritten so that it still points at the same file from OUT's directory. The output format follows OUT's extension. The result is validated with the policy loader before anything is written. If it does not validate, nothing is written and the exit code is 1. YAML comments are not preserved. The document is re-serialized. The output starts with a comment that lists the applied suggestion ids and says that comments were dropped. Review the diff, or copy the per-suggestion YAML snippets into your file by hand to keep its comments. After writing, the report re-verifies the denied records that have raw SQL against the patched policy, and reports two counts: how many no longer hit any of their recorded codes; how many tenancy denials are still denied. If any tenancy denial were to become an allow, the command exits 1. That can't happen by construction: the test suite checks it with a property test over random queries, using the real verifier.

Option Meaning --format text|json|markdown text (default) for terminals. markdown for pull requests and wikis: tables, plus fenced YAML for the suggestions. json for tools: the same data, see the shape below. --since TIME, --until TIME An RFC 3339 timestamp, YYYY-MM-DD, or a duration before now (24h, 7d). Records without a timestamp are excluded when either is given. --policy NAME Only records of this policy. --policy-file FILE A policy the records were verified against (repeatable), used for detail and exact snippets. --top N, --rows N Top denied queries (default 20), and rows per breakdown table in text and markdown (default 15). Text and Markdown output strip control characters from every value taken from audit records. Markdown output also escapes table cells. Exit codes: 0 on success; 1 when the patched policy fails validation (or a tenancy denial would become an allow); 2 on usage or load errors. JSON shape (abridged): { "generated_at": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z", "since": null, "until": null, "inputs": [{"input": "audit.jsonl", "status": "120 record(s), 0 skipped line(s), hash chain ok (120 records)"}], "summary": { "records": 120, "totals": {"total": 120, "allowed": 90, "denied": 2, "shadow_denied": 28}, "by_code": [{"code": "E_COLUMN_DENIED", "total": 23, "allowed": 0, "denied": 0, "shadow_denied": 23}], "by_table": [], "by_column": [], "by_caller": [], "by_policy": [], "by_source": [], "bucket_seconds": 3600, "buckets": [{"start": "2026-11-07T09:00:00Z", "total": 120}], "top_denied": [{"fingerprint": "...", "count": {"total": 23}, "codes": [], "callers": [], "example_sql": null}] }, "suggest": { "suggestions": [{"id": "shop/column/app.orders.region", "policy": "shop", "code": "E_COLUMN_DENIED", "change": {"kind": "add_column", "table": "app.orders", "column": "region"}, "summary": "...", "yaml": "tables:\n app.orders:\n ...", "notes": [], "applicable": true, "evidence": {"records": 23, "denied": 0, "shadow_denied": 23, "distinct_queries": 2, "callers": [{"caller": "analytics", "count": 23}]}}], "pii_flagged": [], "not_suggested": [], "codes": [{"code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "category": "never_weaken", "records": 4, "advice": "..."}], "missing_detail": 0 }, "notes": [] }

When server.admin is enabled, haltsql-server keeps a rolling window of its own recent verdicts. It serves the same report as JSON (the shape above) to the configured admin callers. Unauthenticated callers can never use it. The window is bounded in three ways: By age: records older than report_window (default 24h) are dropped. By distinct queries: at most max_tracked_queries fingerprints (default 10000) are tracked. When a new one arrives at the limit, the least recently seen fingerprint and its records are evicted. Per query: at most 32 recent records of one fingerprint are kept. Older ones are counted in sampled_out, so counts for very frequent queries are lower bounds. Only one record per query keeps its raw SQL, and only when audit.log_raw_sql is on. Its re-derived details are shared with the query's other records. Nothing is kept while the admin API is disabled. Disabling it on reload drops the window. Query parameter Default Meaning since start of the window RFC 3339, YYYY-MM-DD, or a duration (1h). It is clamped to the window. policy all Only this policy. suggest true Include suggestions. The server flags sensitive columns with the column-name heuristic. It has no PII manifest, so run the CLI with --pii for manifest-based flagging. top 20 Top denied queries, 1 to 100. An unknown or repeated parameter gives 400 BAD_REQUEST. A disabled admin API gives 404 NOT_FOUND. The body adds window_seconds, max_tracked_queries, tracked_queries, tracked_records, evicted_queries, records_per_query and sampled_out to the report fields.

Deploy the new policy with mode: shadow, with audit.log_raw_sql: true if your data allows it. After real traffic, run haltsql report audit/ --suggest --policy-file policy.yaml --pii pii.json --format markdown and review it with the policy owner. Apply what you agree with: --apply-to policy.yaml --accept ID ... -o policy.yaml.next. Review the diff, run haltsql test, and commit. Fix the agents' queries for everything listed under Needs a query fix. When the shadow-denied rate is acceptable, switch to mode: enforce.

This page defines exactly what HaltSQL must prove before it allows a query that touches a tenant-scoped table. It is the most security-critical part of the analyzer. The design decision behind it is ADR-0003. The short version: every occurrence of a tenant-scoped table must be filtered to the caller's tenant by a top-level AND condition in its own query level.

Tenancy key: a named dimension of tenancy declared in tenancy.keys, mapped to a context field. Example: tenant: ${ctx.tenant_id}. Tenant-scoped table: a table with tenant_column or tenant_columns in the policy. A table without them is global. Tenant value: the context value for a key, from the caller's authenticated session. It is either one value ("acme") or a set of values (["acme", "acme-eu"]). Occurrence: each place a table appears in a FROM clause or join tree. FROM orders a JOIN orders b has two occurrences of orders. Scope: one query level (one SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ...). Every CTE body, subquery in FROM, LATERAL subquery, scalar subquery, EXISTS or IN subquery, and each branch of UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT is its own scope. Top-level conjunct: one of the terms of the AND chain that makes up a WHERE or ON expression. In WHERE a AND (b OR c) AND d, the top-level conjuncts are a, (b OR c), and d.

For every occurrence of a tenant-scoped table R, with alias a (the table name if there is no alias), in any scope, and for every tenant column col of R, HaltSQL must find a tenant predicate for a.col in a place that filters that occurrence (see where the predicate may appear). If any occurrence lacks one, the query is denied with E_TENANT_MISSING. A tenant predicate is a top-level conjunct of one of these forms: Mode Single tenant value Set of tenant values bound a.col = $n a.col = ANY($n) literal a.col = <literal> a.col = <literal> or a.col IN (<literal>, ...) The column reference must resolve to that occurrence (a.col, or an unqualified col that is unambiguous in the scope). The tenant-value side must be a parameter or literal as shown. Other shapes, such as an expression, function call, subquery, or a column of another table, are not tenant predicates. A query whose only filter has one of those shapes is denied, even if it happens to be safe. This is deliberate: the proof rules are simple enough to audit.

Only the AND chain counts. A tenant comparison under any of these is not a top-level conjunct and proves nothing: OR: WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR status = 'open' NOT: WHERE NOT (tenant_id <> $1) CASE: WHERE CASE WHEN x THEN tenant_id = $1 ELSE true END function arguments, COALESCE, or comparison of expressions: WHERE coalesce(tenant_id, $1) = $1 IS DISTINCT FROM, <>, LIKE, and other operators: only = (and = ANY / IN for sets) count. HAVING: rows are filtered after grouping, so aggregates may already mix tenants. Only WHERE and ON count.

The model writes a parameter placeholder: SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 50 HaltSQL returns bind_params: [{"param": 1, "value": "acme"}]. The caller runs the exact SQL with $1 bound to acme. The model never sees the tenant ID, so it cannot leak it, and prompt injection cannot change it. Rules: The same $n may be used for every occurrence that uses the same tenancy key: WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND c.tenant_id = $1. It is bound once. One parameter may serve two different keys only if both keys resolve to the same context value. If the values differ, the query is denied (E_TENANT_MISMATCH). Mixing = $1 and = ANY($1) for the same parameter is also E_TENANT_MISMATCH. Every parameter in the query must be a tenant parameter, because HaltSQL must supply every bound value itself. Any other $n is E_PARAM_UNBOUND. A tenant parameter may appear only as the value of a tenant predicate. Using it anywhere else ($1::float8 IS NOT NULL, status = $1, SELECT $1, $1 = 'acme' under an OR) is E_PARAM_UNBOUND (rule params.tenant_reuse). Such a use could change the type PostgreSQL infers for the parameter, and with it how the tenant value is compared. For example, float8 rounds a large bigint tenant ID, so a neighbouring tenant's rows could match. A literal where a tenant parameter is expected is not accepted (E_TENANT_MISMATCH, or E_TENANT_WRITE in INSERT ... VALUES), so a model that learned a tenant ID cannot use it.

The model writes the tenant value as a literal: SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = 'acme' LIMIT 50 The literal must equal the context value exactly: no trimming, no case folding. 'acme ' and 'ACME' do not match acme. A mismatch is E_TENANT_MISMATCH. String literals compare by their exact text. Integer literals compare by their decimal text (42 matches context "42" or 42). When the catalog knows the column's type, the literal must be compatible with it; a string literal compared with an integer column, or the reverse, is denied rather than relying on Postgres's implicit casts. Parameters ($n) are not allowed in literal mode (E_PARAM_UNBOUND). Literal mode means the model must know the tenant ID, which is exactly the value an attacker would like to change. Prefer bound mode.

A table can be scoped by several keys, for example an organization and a workspace: tenancy: mode: bound keys: org: "${ctx.org_id}" workspace: "${ctx.workspace_id}" tables: app.documents: columns: [id, org_id, workspace_id, title] tenant_columns: { org_id: org, workspace_id: workspace } Every tenant column needs its own predicate, in the same scope: -- allowed: bind_params = [{param 1: org}, {param 2: workspace}] SELECT id, title FROM documents WHERE org_id = $1 AND workspace_id = $2 LIMIT 20 -- denied: E_TENANT_MISSING (no workspace predicate) SELECT id, title FROM documents WHERE org_id = $1 LIMIT 20 A row-value comparison such as (org_id, workspace_id) = ($1, $2) is not recognized; write separate conjuncts.

The context value for a key can be a list, for example a parent organization that may see its child organizations: { "tenant_id": ["acme", "acme-eu", "acme-us"] } Then: Bound mode: write a.col = ANY($n). HaltSQL returns the whole list as the value to bind ("value": ["acme", "acme-eu", "acme-us"]); bind it as a Postgres array. With a set-valued context, a.col = $n and a.col IN ($n) are not proofs (E_TENANT_MISSING; the hint says to use = ANY($n)). Literal mode: a.col = 'acme-eu' is allowed if the literal is in the set; a.col IN ('acme', 'acme-eu') is allowed if every listed literal is in the set. Any literal outside the set is E_TENANT_MISMATCH. An empty list allows nothing: every tenant-scoped query is denied with E_CONTEXT_MISSING.

The predicate must filter the occurrence in its own scope: Location Which occurrences it can prove WHERE of the scope Every occurrence in that scope's FROM clause and join tree ON of an INNER JOIN Occurrences in either operand of that join ON of a LEFT JOIN Only occurrences on the right (nullable) side ON of a RIGHT JOIN Only occurrences on the left (nullable) side ON of a FULL JOIN None USING (...) / NATURAL None HAVING, select list, ORDER BY None Any other scope (outer query, sibling subquery, other UNION branch) None

A filter in an outer query runs after the inner query has already read the table. The inner query can aggregate, join, or reshape rows from every tenant before the outer filter sees them: -- Denied: the filter is outside the subquery that reads orders. SELECT * FROM ( SELECT count(*) AS n, max(tenant_id) AS tenant_id FROM orders ) x WHERE x.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 1 Here x.tenant_id is just the largest tenant ID in the table, and n counts every tenant's orders.
