Build, sign and verify version 1.0.1: mkdir -p dist haltsql bundle build policies/saas.yaml --name prod-policies --bundle-version 1.0.1 \ --source-commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle haltsql bundle sign dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle --key ~/.haltsql-keys/policy-signing.key haltsql bundle verify dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub haltsql bundle inspect dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle --public-key keys/policy-signing.pub sign writes dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle.sig. verify prints a line starting with OK and exits 0. inspect shows the bundle's name and version, its digest, each policy with its sha256: version and mode, and status verified. Builds are deterministic: the same policies always give a byte-identical bundle. Add dist/ to .gitignore. In CI, the bundle job from step 4 does the same on every push to main. Store the private key's PEM as the secret HALTSQL_SIGNING_KEY in a GitHub environment named policy-release that requires reviewers, and the job uploads the signed bundle as the haltsql-policy-bundle artifact. See Signing in CI safely.

Point the server at a bundle instead of a policy file. Copy the public key to the server, and replace server/haltsql.yaml with: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Config server: listen: 127.0.0.1:8080 auth: tokens: - name: analytics-agent token_sha256: ${env:HALTSQL_ANALYTICS_TOKEN_HASH} policy: saas-analytics policies: - bundle: ./bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle # signature: same name + .sig public_keys: [./policy-signing.pub] reload: { watch: true } audit: sinks: - type: file path: ./audit/audit.jsonl log_raw_sql: false In the first shell, install the bundle (signature first) and start the server: cd ../server cp ../policy-repo/keys/policy-signing.pub . cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle.sig bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle.sig cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle haltsql-server --config haltsql.yaml The server verifies the signature, then the digest, structure and every policy, before it loads anything. Check which policy version is live, from the second shell: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $HALTSQL_TOKEN" localhost:8080/v1/policies The version is the same sha256:... that bundle inspect printed for saas-analytics. Every verdict and audit record carries it too, so you can always tell which policy made a decision. Now promote a second version. Suppose the team decides to hide customers.country. In policies/saas.yaml, change the customers columns to [id, tenant_id, name, created_at]. Then, from the second shell: cd ../policy-repo haltsql test tests/ git commit -am "saas-analytics: hide customers.country" haltsql bundle build policies/saas.yaml --name prod-policies --bundle-version 1.0.2 \ --source-commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o dist/prod-policies-1.0.2.haltsqlbundle haltsql bundle sign dist/prod-policies-1.0.2.haltsqlbundle --key ~/.haltsql-keys/policy-signing.key cd ../server cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.2.haltsqlbundle.sig bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle.sig cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.2.haltsqlbundle bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle With reload.watch the server notices within about two seconds. Without it, send SIGHUP (pkill -HUP haltsql-server). The server log shows policies reloaded with the new version, and /v1/policies returns it. A reload is atomic: the policy that was live keeps serving until the new set has fully loaded. A bundle that fails any check never goes live. If the file is signed with a key the server doesn't trust, the server logs reload failed; keeping the last good configuration with signature verification failed: signed by sha256:..., which is not a trusted key, and keeps serving the previous version. While the .sig and the bundle are being replaced one after the other, the server may log one such failed reload and then succeed on the next one. For a fleet, push the signed bundle to an OCI registry (haltsql bundle push --oci ...) and have each server poll it with a bundle_source. See Bundle sources.

Suppose a dashboard turns out to need customers.country, and 1.0.2 now denies its queries with E_COLUMN_DENIED. How you roll back depends on how the server gets bundles. Local bundle files (this tutorial). Copy the previous signed bundle back. It still verifies, because its signature has not changed: cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle.sig bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle.sig cp ../policy-repo/dist/prod-policies-1.0.1.haltsqlbundle bundles/prod-policies.haltsqlbundle The server reloads, and /v1/policies shows the 1.0.1 policy version again. Keep every released bundle and its .sig, for example as CI artifacts, so this is always possible. Bundle sources (OCI, S3, HTTPS). A polling server refuses a bundle whose metadata.version is not strictly greater than the one it runs. This is rollback protection: an attacker who can write to the registry cannot replay an old, looser bundle. To roll back, revert the policy change in git and publish the old content under a new, higher version: cd ../policy-repo git revert --no-edit HEAD haltsql bundle build policies/saas.yaml --name prod-policies --bundle-version 1.0.3 \ --source-commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o dist/prod-policies-1.0.3.haltsqlbundle haltsql bundle sign dist/prod-policies-1.0.3.haltsqlbundle --key ~/.haltsql-keys/policy-signing.key In CI that is a revert merged to main. The bundle job builds and signs it with a higher run number, and the servers pick it up at their next poll. Because builds are deterministic, the rolled-back policy has exactly the sha256: policy version it had before.

Generate database grants and row-level security from the same policy, so the database enforces it too: RLS generation. Watch shadow reports live from the server instead of the CLI: GET /v1/admin/report. Publish bundles to a registry and rotate signing keys: Signed policy bundles. Import PII labels from your data catalog so the report flags more sensitive columns: Schema and PII. Read how each stage protects you: The policy lifecycle.

In this tutorial you give Claude Desktop (or any MCP client) access to a PostgreSQL database through haltsql-mcp, and you watch HaltSQL deny the queries your policy does not allow. What you'll build: a local Postgres with two tenants (acme and globex), a least-privilege database role with row-level security, a HaltSQL policy, and an MCP server that runs only the queries the policy allows, for the acme tenant only. Time: about 20 minutes. Prerequisites: Docker, to run Postgres. Python 3.10 or newer, and git. The haltsql CLI, installed as in Quickstart: Install. Check it with haltsql version. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or another MCP client. Steps 1 to 8 don't need one.
documents.s: Tutorial: secure an MCP agent's access to Postgres

documents.t: Create a working directory for the files in this tutorial, and run every command from it: mkdir haltsql-mcp-tutorial && cd haltsql-mcp-tutorial Run PostgreSQL 17 in Docker, listening only on your machine: docker run -d --name haltsql-tutorial \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=tutorial-admin -e POSTGRES_DB=shop \ -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 postgres:17 The commands below run psql inside the container, so you don't need a local psql. If port 5432 is already in use, change the first 5432 in -p and use that port in every connection string below.

Save this as schema.sql. Every row carries a tenant_id, and customers.email is the kind of column an agent should never read: CREATE SCHEMA app; CREATE TABLE app.customers ( id bigint PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id text NOT NULL, name text NOT NULL, email text NOT NULL, country char(2) NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE app.orders ( id bigint PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id text NOT NULL, customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES app.customers (id), status text NOT NULL, total_cents bigint NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); INSERT INTO app.customers (id, tenant_id, name, email, country) VALUES (1, 'acme', 'Ada Lovelace', 'ada@acme.example', 'GB'), (2, 'acme', 'Grace Hopper', 'grace@acme.example', 'US'), (3, 'globex', 'Hank Scorpio', 'hank@globex.example', 'US'); INSERT INTO app.orders (id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at) VALUES (101, 'acme', 1, 'paid', 4200, now() - interval '3 days'), (102, 'acme', 2, 'open', 1999, now() - interval '1 day'), (103, 'acme', 1, 'refunded', 500, now() - interval '9 days'), (201, 'globex', 3, 'paid', 99900, now() - interval '2 days'); Load it: docker exec -i haltsql-tutorial psql -U postgres -d shop -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 < schema.sql

Save this as policy.yaml: apiVersion: haltsql.dev/v1 kind: Policy metadata: name: shop-agent search_path: [app] statements: { allow: [select] } require_limit: { max: 500 } tenancy: mode: bound keys: tenant: "${ctx.tenant_id}" tables: app.customers: columns: [id, tenant_id, name, country, created_at] # email is left out tenant_column: tenant_id app.orders: columns: [id, tenant_id, customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at] tenant_column: tenant_id functions: presets: [aggregates, datetime] What each part does: statements allows only SELECT. require_limit makes every query carry a LIMIT of at most 500. tenancy.mode: bound means the model writes tenant_id = $1 and the server binds the real tenant. The model never sees or chooses it. See Bound mode. tables lists the only readable tables and columns. email is not listed, so it cannot be read. functions allows aggregates (count, sum, ...) and date functions (date_trunc, ...). Everything else, including pg_sleep, is denied. Check it: haltsql validate policy.yaml haltsql lint-policy policy.yaml validate prints policy.yaml: ok (Policy: shop-agent sha256:...), and lint-policy ends with 0 warning(s). For a real database you can draft this file from the schema with haltsql schema pull and haltsql policy draft instead of writing it by hand (see Draft a policy).

The MCP server should connect as a role that can read only what the policy allows, even if HaltSQL were bypassed. Create the login role first: docker exec -i haltsql-tutorial psql -U postgres -d shop -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 <<'SQL' CREATE ROLE agent_ro LOGIN PASSWORD 'agent-tutorial-pw' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 10; ALTER ROLE agent_ro SET search_path = app; -- same as the policy's search_path ALTER ROLE agent_ro SET default_transaction_read_only = on; ALTER ROLE agent_ro SET statement_timeout = '5s'; SQL Then generate the grants and row-level security (RLS) that mirror the policy, and apply them: haltsql rls generate -p policy.yaml --role agent_ro -o rls.sql docker exec -i haltsql-tutorial psql -U postgres -d shop -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 < rls.sql rls generate warns that the tenant column type is unknown and is compared as text. That is correct here, because tenant_id is text. Pass --catalog from haltsql schema pull when your tenant column is another type. Open rls.sql to see what it did. It grants SELECT on exactly the policy's columns and creates a haltsql_tenant_select policy on each table: CREATE POLICY haltsql_tenant_select ON app.orders AS PERMISSIVE FOR SELECT TO agent_ro USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(pg_catalog.current_setting('haltsql.tenant_id', true), '')); Check the database layer on its own. Without the setting, agent_ro sees no rows. With it, it sees only that tenant's rows. email is refused: docker exec -i haltsql-tutorial psql -U agent_ro -d shop <<'SQL' SELECT count(*) FROM orders; -- 0: no tenant set BEGIN; SELECT pg_catalog.set_config('haltsql.tenant_id', 'acme', true); SELECT count(*) FROM orders; -- 3: acme's orders only COMMIT; SELECT email FROM customers LIMIT 1; -- ERROR: permission denied SQL See RLS generation for every option, and haltsql rls check to detect drift later.
documents.s: 4. Create a least-privilege role with row-level security

documents.t: The packages are not on PyPI yet, so install them from a clone of the repository into a virtual environment in your working directory: git clone https://github.com/HaltSQL/HaltSQL python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install ./HaltSQL/clients/python './HaltSQL/clients/mcp[yaml]' .venv/bin/haltsql-mcp --help Note the absolute paths of the two binaries. Your MCP client needs them in step 8: echo "$PWD/.venv/bin/haltsql-mcp" command -v haltsql Note: If you would rather not install Python packages, the ghcr.io/haltsql/haltsql-mcp image includes haltsql-mcp and the haltsql CLI. See Run it in Docker. From inside a container, the database host is host.docker.internal, not localhost.

haltsql-mcp needs four things, all set by you, never by the model: Setting Value in this tutorial Why --local-policy /abs/path/haltsql-mcp-tutorial/policy.yaml Verify each query with the local haltsql CLI. No sidecar needed. Connection string (last argument) postgresql://agent_ro:agent-tutorial-pw@localhost:5432/shop The least-privilege role from step 4. HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT {"tenant_id": "acme"} The tenant this server acts for. It is never a tool argument. HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG {"haltsql.tenant_id": "tenant_id"} Sets the RLS setting from the same context in each query's transaction. HALTSQL_BIN tells haltsql-mcp where the CLI is when the client starts servers with a short PATH. Every option is listed in haltsql-mcp configuration.

Before you involve an MCP client, call the server's tools from a short script. The mcp package it uses was installed with haltsql-mcp. Save this as smoke.py in your working directory: import asyncio, os, shutil, sys from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client server = StdioServerParameters( command=sys.argv[1], # path to haltsql-mcp args=["--local-policy", "policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro:agent-tutorial-pw@localhost:5432/shop"], env=dict(os.environ, HALTSQL_BIN=shutil.which("haltsql") or "haltsql", HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id": "acme"}', HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG='{"haltsql.tenant_id": "tenant_id"}'), ) async def main(): async with stdio_client(server) as (read, write): async with ClientSession(read, write) as session: await session.initialize() for sql in sys.argv[2:]: result = await session.call_tool("query", {"sql": sql}) print(sql) for item in result.content: print(item.text) asyncio.run(main()) Ask for customer emails without a tenant filter, the kind of query a prompt-injected model might send: .venv/bin/python smoke.py .venv/bin/haltsql-mcp \ 'SELECT name, email FROM customers LIMIT 10' The tool returns a normal result, not an error, with allowed: false and two reasons. Nothing ran in the database: { "allowed": false, "executed": false, "reasons": [ { "code": "E_COLUMN_DENIED", "message": "column email of app.customers is not readable under this policy", "rule": "columns.denied", "loc": 13, "hint": "Remove email from the query; readable columns of app.customers are: id, tenant_id, name, country, created_at." }, { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "message": "app.customers (as customers) has no provable tenant predicate on customers.tenant_id in the same SELECT", "rule": "tenancy.predicate", "loc": 24, "hint": "Add `WHERE customers.tenant_id = $1` as a top-level AND condition inside the same SELECT that reads app.customers (not in an outer query, not under OR/NOT, not in the ON of the preserved side of an outer join)." } ], "message": "HaltSQL denied the query. Fix it using the reasons and hints, then retry." } The hint is written for the model: it says how to fix the query. A few more to try, each denied before it reaches Postgres: SQL Reason codes SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE tenant_id = 'globex' LIMIT 10 E_TENANT_MISMATCH: in bound mode the model cannot write a tenant SELECT 1; COMMIT; DROP SCHEMA app CASCADE E_MULTI_STATEMENT SELECT pg_sleep(60) LIMIT 1 E_FUNCTION_DENIED SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 E_LIMIT_REQUIRED SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 OR status = 'open' LIMIT 10 E_TENANT_MISSING, E_PARAM_UNBOUND SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 LIMIT 10 E_TENANT_MISSING: customers needs its own predicate Now send a query the policy allows: .venv/bin/python smoke.py .venv/bin/haltsql-mcp \ 'SELECT status, count(*) AS orders FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 GROUP BY status LIMIT 50' This time haltsql-mcp binds $1 to acme, runs the exact string in a READ ONLY transaction with a 5-second statement_timeout, and returns allowed: true, executed: true, the columns, and one row per status of acme's three orders (paid, open, refunded). Globex's order is not counted: HaltSQL bound acme, and RLS would have filtered it out even if it hadn't. Note: If the allowed query fails with a tool error such as database connection failed, check that the container is running (docker ps) and that the connection string's port matches step 1. A verification failure never runs the query; it is a tool error, not a denial.

Add the server to your client's config. Replace each /abs/path/... with the absolute paths you noted in step 5, because MCP clients do not start servers in your working directory. For Claude Desktop, edit claude_desktop_config.json (on macOS it is in ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/): { "mcpServers": { "shop": { "command": "/abs/path/haltsql-mcp-tutorial/.venv/bin/haltsql-mcp", "args": [ "--local-policy", "/abs/path/haltsql-mcp-tutorial/policy.yaml", "postgresql://agent_ro:agent-tutorial-pw@localhost:5432/shop" ], "env": { "HALTSQL_BIN": "/abs/path/to/haltsql", "HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT": "{\"tenant_id\": \"acme\"}", "HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG": "{\"haltsql.tenant_id\": \"tenant_id\"}" } } } } Cursor uses the same shape in ~/.cursor/mcp.json. For Claude Code: claude mcp add shop \ -e HALTSQL_BIN=/abs/path/to/haltsql \ -e HALTSQL_MCP_CONTEXT='{"tenant_id":"acme"}' \ -e HALTSQL_MCP_SET_CONFIG='{"haltsql.tenant_id":"tenant_id"}' -- \ /abs/path/haltsql-mcp-tutorial/.venv/bin/haltsql-mcp --local-policy /abs/path/haltsql-mcp-tutorial/policy.yaml \ postgresql://agent_ro:agent-tutorial-pw@localhost:5432/shop VS Code and other clients are in Swap the server in your client. Restart the client. It should list four tools: query, explain_denial, list_tables and describe_policy.

Ask the model something that tempts it to break the rules: Show me the email addresses of all our customers. A typical sequence: The model calls list_tables or describe_policy. They list only the policy's tables and columns. email is not advertised. If the model still asks for email, or forgets the tenant filter, query returns allowed: false with E_COLUMN_DENIED or E_TENANT_MISSING and the hints from step 7. The model can call explain_denial with the same SQL for the full verdict. The model tells you it cannot read email addresses, or rewrites the query without them. Then ask a question the policy allows: How many orders do we have in each status, and who are our top customers by spend? The model writes queries such as: SELECT c.name, sum(o.total_cents) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id AND c.tenant_id = $1 WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY spent DESC LIMIT 10 They run, and the answer covers Ada Lovelace and Grace Hopper only. Hank Scorpio belongs to globex, and there is no way for the model to ask for that tenant: the context is fixed in the server's environment, and extra tool arguments such as tenant_id are ignored.
documents.s: 9. Watch a denial, then an allowed query

documents.t: docker rm -f haltsql-tutorial Remove the shop entry from your MCP client's config.

Two layers in the database: a role that can read only the policy's columns, and RLS keyed on a transaction-local setting. One layer in front of it: HaltSQL checks each statement's tables, columns, functions, tenant predicates, LIMIT and statement count before it runs. The tenant comes from configuration you control, never from the model.

Serve several users from one haltsql-mcp over streamable HTTP, with a bearer token per tenant: Tenant context. Move verification to a central haltsql-server for audit, hot reload and one place to manage policies: Configuration and HTTP API. Roll out policy changes with tests, shadow mode and signed bundles: Roll out a policy safely. Build your own agent instead of using an MCP client: Multi-tenant analytics agent. Read why each layer matters: Defense in depth and the Threat model.

Every check returns a verdict. The library returns a Haltsql.Verdict.t record; the CLI (--json) and the HTTP API return the same thing as JSON. The JSON shape is part of HaltSQL's public API: fields are only added, never renamed or removed, within haltsql.dev/v1.

{ "allowed": false, "reasons": [ { "code": "E_TENANT_MISSING", "message": "app.customers (alias c) has no tenant predicate in its scope", "rule": "tenancy.predicate", "loc": 43, "hint": "Add c.tenant_id = $1 to the WHERE clause or to the inner JOIN ... ON clause that attaches c." } ], "shadow_reasons": [], "policy": { "name": "analytics-agent", "version": "sha256:4f1c9a..." }, "statement_kind": "select", "tables": ["app.customers", "app.orders"], "columns": ["app.customers.id", "app.customers.name", "app.orders.customer_id", "app.orders.id", "app.orders.tenant_id"], "bind_params": [], "fingerprint": "6c1e0b7f3a2d9e41", "sql_sha256": "c0ffee...", "elapsed_us": 187 }

{ "allowed": true, "reasons": [], "shadow_reasons": [], "policy": { "name": "analytics-agent", "version": "sha256:4f1c9a..." }, "statement_kind": "select", "tables": ["app.orders"], "columns": ["app.orders.status", "app.orders.tenant_id"], "bind_params": [ { "param": 1, "value": "acme" } ], "fingerprint": "0a9d55c2e1f04b7c", "sql_sha256": "5e8f...", "elapsed_us": 94 } Messages, hints, and hash values above are illustrative.

Field Type Meaning allowed boolean true if the caller may run this exact SQL string. In enforce mode, true exactly when reasons is empty. In shadow mode, always true. reasons array of Reason Why the query was denied. Empty when allowed. shadow_reasons array of Reason Shadow mode only: the reasons the query would have been denied. Always empty in enforce mode. policy.name string metadata.name of the policy used. policy.search_path list of strings The policy's search_path: the schemas unqualified names were resolved against. The verdict holds only if the session that runs the SQL uses this search path. The Python guard, the MCP server, the proxy and the transaction-owning guards of the other SDKs (TypeScript guardedTransaction, Go GuardedQueryTx / GuardedExecTx, Java JdbcGuard.queryInTransaction / updateInTransaction) pin it. The single-statement guards (guardedQuery, GuardedQuery / GuardedExec, JdbcGuard.prepare / query / update) do not. If you execute yourself, run SELECT set_config('search_path', <quoted schemas>, true) in the same transaction before the statement (each SDK has a helper that builds the value), or have the model write schema-qualified names. policy.version string sha256:<hex> hash of the normalized policy (identical for YAML and JSON forms). Log it to know exactly which policy made a decision. statement_kind string or null select, insert, update, or delete when the statement parsed and is one of those kinds; otherwise null. tables array of strings Qualified relations the statement reads or writes (schema.table), sorted and unique. May be partial when the query was denied early. columns array of strings Columns read, as schema.table.column, sorted and unique. May be partial when denied. bind_params array of {param, value} Bound tenancy mode: for each $n, the value the caller must bind. value is a string, or an array of strings when the context value is a set. Always empty when denied. fingerprint string or null libpg_query fingerprint: equal for queries that differ only in literal values. Useful for grouping in logs and dashboards. null if the SQL did not parse. sql_sha256 string Lower-case hex SHA-256 of the exact input string. Lets audit logs refer to the query without storing it. elapsed_us integer Time spent verifying, in microseconds. Informational; not deterministic.

Field Type Meaning code string Stable reason code, for example E_TENANT_MISSING. See reason-codes.md. Match on this, never on message. message string Human-readable explanation. May change between releases. rule string Identifier of the rule that produced the reason, for example tenancy.predicate. Useful for debugging; may change between releases. loc integer (optional) Byte offset (0-based) into the SQL string where the problem is. Absent when unknown. hint string (optional) A short instruction an LLM agent can follow to fix its query. May change between releases.

If allowed is false, do not run the query. Return the reasons (codes, messages, and hints) to the agent so it can try again. If allowed is true, run exactly the SQL string you verified. Do not reformat, append to, or template it. Bind every entry in bind_params as the value of its $n placeholder. If your driver needs other parameters too, the query would have been denied with E_PARAM_UNBOUND, so there are none. Log policy.version, fingerprint, sql_sha256, allowed, and the reason codes for audit.

Within haltsql.dev/v1: Existing fields keep their name, type, and meaning. New fields may be added. Clients must ignore fields they do not recognize. Reason code values are never renamed or reused. New codes may be added in minor releases, so clients must handle unknown codes (treat them as a deny). message, hint, and rule text may change at any time. For the same SQL, policy, and context, allowed, reasons[].code, tables, columns, and bind_params are deterministic. See ADR-0004 for the reasoning.
